The cabin stays put when its owner travels.

entries.card: notes:'He afterwards built a new residence and a small trading pos…
entries.text: 'He afterwards built a new residence and a small trading post' — Andreas, scan p. 185. THE USE AND THE SIZE-WORD ARE DOCUMENTED AND NOTHING ELSE IS. 'Small' is the only dimension any source gives any building of this group and it is a word, not a figure; the footprint below takes it as an instruction to draw the smallest thing in the group. WHAT A TRADING POST HELD HERE IS NOT STATED and this record does not choose: the goods the town's trade carried are recorded on the business layer, not on this building.

levels.8-10: Andreas wrote that Beaubien later built a new home and a small trading post. That tells what it was for and that it was small, and nothing more. Small is a word, not a size. So we build the smallest building in the group. No record says what was traded here, so we do not choose.

entries.card: notes:'In 1831 John Miller built a log house near his brother's ta…
entries.text: 'In 1831 John Miller built a log house near his brother's tavern that he used as a tannery.'

levels.8-10: A book says that in 1831, John Miller built a log house near his brother's inn and used it to tan hides.

entries.card: notes:'In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the bl…
entries.text: 'In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell' — Andreas names the use and the occupant in the same clause. Wau-Bun calls the whole group 'the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government'.

levels.8-10: A book says there were small log houses near it. The blacksmith, Mr. McKee, lived in one, and Billy Caldwell in one. It names the use and who lived there in one line. Wau-Bun says they were the homes of the men who worked for the government.

entries.card: notes:'In the rear was the large stable and the yard into which th…
entries.text: 'In the rear was the large stable and the yard into which the trains were driven. There were entrances to the yard from both streets, and this was one of the most important parts of the hostlery, for the teams were as numerous as were the guests.' The function is as well attested as anything in this dataset — the source says outright that it was one of the most important parts of the house — while the building itself is undescribed. That gap between a documented use and an undescribed fabric is the ordinary condition of every outbuilding in this project.

levels.8-10: The record says that in the back was the large stable and the yard where the wagon trains were driven. There were gates to the yard from both streets. It was one of the most important parts of the inn, for the teams were as many as the guests. Its use is as well known as anything here. The record says it was one of the most important parts. But the building itself is not told of. A known use with an unknown building is the usual state of every back building here.

entries.card: notes:'It was a two-story frame structure, the upper story for sch…
entries.text: 'It was a two-story frame structure, the upper story for school, the lower for religious purposes, and cost about nine hundred dollars.' One of the very few storey counts in this dataset that is stated outright in a transcribed period text rather than inferred from a description or asserted by a modern summary.

levels.8-10: A book says it was a wood frame building with two floors. The top floor was for school. The lower floor was for church. It cost about nine hundred dollars. Not many old papers tell us the number of floors. This one does.

entries.card: notes:'NEWBERRY & DOLE, Forwarding & Commission MERCHANTS' — the f…
entries.text: 'NEWBERRY & DOLE, Forwarding & Commission MERCHANTS' — the firm's own paid advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, the first contemporary document in this dataset and about as good as evidence of a trade gets, since the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. Andreas's summary of the paper's advertising columns lists the same firm in the same words (scan p. 755). Forwarding and commission is the lake trade: taking goods off vessels, holding them, and sending them on inland, on commission. The firm's wharf received the schooner Illinois, the first vessel through the new harbour cut, on 12 July 1834 (Andreas scan p. 503).

levels.8-10: Newberry and Dole, shipping and trading merchants. That is the firm's own paid ad in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833. It is the first paper of its time we have, and about as good as proof of a trade gets. He paid for it, and his buyers had to find him. A book lists the same firm in the same words. Shipping and trading was the lake trade. They took goods off ships, kept them, and sent them on inland, for a share. The firm's dock got the schooner Illinois, the first ship through the new harbor cut, on 12 July 1834.

entries.card: notes:'TWO BUILDINGS TO LET' - John Wright's own advertisement in…
entries.text: 'TWO BUILDINGS TO LET' - John Wright's own advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, offering them until 1 June 1834. Two buildings existed, they were his, and they were rental stock. This is one of the two. The advertisement's own term of 1 June 1834 is not the building's life: a building does not cease at the end of a tenancy, and the range runs to the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs.

levels.8-10: Two buildings to let. That is John Wright's own ad in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, offering them until 1 June 1834. Two buildings stood, they were his, and he rented them out. This is one of the two. The ad's end date of 1 June 1834 is not the building's end. A building does not stop when a rental ends. The dates run to the end of 1835.

entries.card: notes:'The abutments were built of heavy logs in the shallow water…
entries.text: 'The abutments were built of heavy logs in the shallow water near the banks.' Specific, and independently signed twice: Cleaver said it in the Tribune in 1893 and the same sentence stands in the 1883 statement he had signed with Caton, Bates and Noble ten years earlier — so it is one man's memory corroborated by three, not two witnesses. The ends were carried on log cribs standing OUT IN THE WATER rather than on dry-land bearings. It was called 'the one structural statement anybody made about these bridges' here until 2026-08-10, when the rest of the statement it comes from was found.

levels.8-10: Cleaver said the ends were built of heavy logs in the shallow water near the banks. He said it in the Tribune in 1893. The same line is in a paper of 1883 that he signed with Caton, Bates and Noble. So it is one man's memory, backed by three more. The ends stood on boxes of logs out in the water, not on dry land. We used to call it the only thing anyone said about how these bridges were built. Then, on 10 August 2026, the rest of that paper was found.

entries.card: notes:'The abutments were built of logs in the shallow water near…
entries.text: 'The abutments were built of logs in the shallow water near the banks. The bents were of four heavy logs... Stringers of heavy logs stretched from the abutments to the bents.' Round or hewn timber throughout rather than framed carpentry, which is what this archetype's 'log' value means.

levels.8-10: The old settlers' paper says the ends were built of logs in the shallow water near the banks. The bents were four heavy logs. Long heavy logs ran from the ends to the bents. All round or squared logs, not a carpenter's frame. That is what logs means here.

entries.card: notes:'The bents were of four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, i…
entries.text: 'The bents were of four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water.' The archetype builds four heavy logs under a cap at each support, which is the count and the heaviness the sentence gives. 'Resting on the bottom' is the other half of it and is invisible here: this project models neither the riverbed nor anything more than half a metre below the waterline, so a bent stood on the bed and a bent driven into it are the same picture above water. The distinction lives in this note, exactly as it does on the North Branch record.

levels.8-10: The old settlers' paper says the bents were four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water. We build four heavy logs under a cap at each support, as the line says. Resting on the bottom cannot be seen here. We do not build the river bed, or anything more than half a meter under the water. So a support standing on the bottom and one pounded into it look the same above water. That part lives in this note, as it does for the North Branch bridge.

entries.card: notes:'This lighthouse stood forty feet high and employed four, fo…
entries.text: 'This lighthouse stood forty feet high and employed four, fourteen-inch reflectors in its bird-cage lantern room.' Andreas, more cautiously, says it 'boasted of a fourteen-inch reflector', singular. THE REFLECTORS ARE NOT MODELLED - a bird-cage lantern is glazed and this archetype builds a glazed drum, not an optic - so what the mesh claims is that a lantern stood on the tower, which both sources support.

levels.8-10: One record says the lighthouse was forty feet high, with four mirrors to send out the light, in a lantern room like a bird cage. Andreas, more careful, says it had one mirror. We do not build the mirrors. We build a glass room at the top, which both records agree on.

entries.card: notes:'a log house ... that he used as a tannery, Chicago's first…
entries.text: 'a log house ... that he used as a tannery, Chicago's first recorded factory' (DRLOIH); 'run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern' (Andreas). The function is the best-attested thing about this building and the model cannot show it: what stands is a log house, because a log house is what was built and because the yard that made it a tannery is not modelled. WHETHER IT WAS STILL TANNING ON 1835-07-01 IS UNATTESTED — Andreas's tanner partner arrives in 1832 and the trade then disappears from the record — so this value states what the building was for, not what it was doing on the scene date.

levels.8-10: A book says a log house used to tan hides, Chicago's first known factory. Another says he ran a tannery just north of Miller's inn. Its use is the best known thing about it, but the model cannot show it. What stands is a log house, because that is what was built, and the yard that made it a tannery is not built. If it was still tanning on 1 July 1835 is not known. The partner came in 1832, and then the trade drops out of the record. So this tells what the building was for, not what it was doing that day.

entries.card: notes:'a log house' - the one thing about this building's fabric t…
entries.text: 'a log house' - the one thing about this building's fabric that any source states. Hewn log with notched corners is what this archetype builds for that value; whether the logs were hewn or round, and how the house was chinked, roofed or floored, is unattested.

levels.8-10: A log house. That is the one thing any record says about its walls. We build it of cut logs with notched corners. Whether the logs were cut or round, and how the gaps, roof and floor were done, are not known.

entries.card: notes:'a slaughter-house erected on the South Branch of the river,…
entries.text: 'a slaughter-house erected on the South Branch of the river, where some three hundred head of cattle and fourteen hundred hogs were packed during the year' (scan p. 1151). The building and its first season's throughput are the whole of what is recorded. Note that July is between packing seasons — the trade is winter work — so the honest reading of the scene date is a standing plant not in operation.

levels.8-10: A book says a meat plant was built on the South Branch, where about three hundred cattle and fourteen hundred hogs were packed that year. The building and its first season are all that is known. July is between packing seasons, which are in winter. So on the day we show, the plant is standing, but not working.

entries.card: notes:'a two-story frame building' (DRLOIH), and chicagology's wit…
entries.text: 'a two-story frame building' (DRLOIH), and chicagology's witnesses use the second floor throughout — 'a stairway in this hall led to the second floor'.

levels.8-10: A book calls it a frame building of two floors. People who stayed there talk about the second floor again and again. One said a stairway in the hall went up to the second floor.

entries.card: notes:'added a TWO-STORY house to the cabin, fronting the river',…
entries.text: 'added a TWO-STORY house to the cabin, fronting the river', with the 1833 view's 'a two-story building and adjoining log cabin' saying the same thing from the south bank. This is the storey count the sources actually give, and until 2026-08-10 it was recorded on `stories`, where the archetype spent it on the log core instead; see the note there.

levels.8-10: A book says they added a house of two floors to the cabin, facing the river. The 1833 picture shows a building of two floors next to a log cabin, from the south bank. That is the number of floors the records give. It used to sit in the wrong place in our record, and went to the log part by mistake.

entries.card: notes:'built a log house near his brother's tavern that he used as…
entries.text: 'built a log house near his brother's tavern that he used as a tannery' (DRLOIH). Andreas calls it a tannery and does not describe the fabric, so the log statement rests on the one source; it is consistent with everything else standing at the forks in 1831.

levels.8-10: A book says he built a log house near his brother's inn and used it to tan hides. Another book calls it a tannery but does not say what it was made of. So the logs rest on one record. They fit everything else at the forks in 1831.

entries.card: notes:'cost about nine hundred dollars'. Not a build instruction,…
entries.text: 'cost about nine hundred dollars'. Not a build instruction, but the ONLY quantitative fact this record has about the building's size, and the footprint above is derived from it against the two churches' attested cost-per-square-foot. If the footprint is ever corrected from a real dimension, this figure is what will have been wrong about the derivation, not the other way round.

levels.8-10: It cost about nine hundred dollars. That is not a thing to build, but it is the only number we have about its size. The shape above comes from it, using what the two churches cost for their size. If a real size is ever found, this number is what was wrong about the math, not the other way round.

entries.card: notes:'soap and candle manufactory, by Daniel Elston & Co.' — Andr…
entries.text: 'soap and candle manufactory, by Daniel Elston & Co.' — Andreas's summary of the Chicago Democrat's early advertising columns (scan p. 755), and the advertisement itself in the issue of 26 November 1833, which offers cash for tallow and for house ashes. THE TALLOW IS THE INTERESTING PART: it is the by-product of the slaughtering trade this parcel also models, so Clybourne's plant on the North Branch and Newberry & Dole's on the South Branch are this manufactory's suppliers, and a town that kills 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs in a season has the raw material for a candle works whether or not these particular firms dealt with each other. That connection is the reason this record was judged placeable at all, and it is a connection between TRADES, not a documented business relationship.

levels.8-10: A book lists a soap and candle works run by Daniel Elston and partners. The ad itself, from 26 November 1833, offers cash for tallow and for ashes. The tallow is the interesting part. Tallow is fat left over from killing animals, and we build those butcher houses too. A town that killed 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs in a season had the fat for a candle works. That is why we felt we could place this record at all. It links two trades, not two known businesses.

entries.card: notes:'the original log slaughter-house, built by Archibald Clybou…
entries.text: 'the original log slaughter-house, built by Archibald Clybourne in 1827' (scan p. 1149) and 'his log slaughter-house on the east side of the North Branch' (scan p. 1151). Two independent sentences in the same chapter, and the word is the same in both. This is the single best-attested attribute of the building.

levels.8-10: A book calls it Clybourne's first log butcher house, built in 1827. A few pages later it calls it his log butcher house on the east side of the North Branch. Two lines, the same word. This is the best-known fact about the building.

entries.card: notes:'the stopping place for all the farmers town from the west',…
entries.text: 'the stopping place for all the farmers town from the west', accommodating 'farmers and teamsters, who constituted the traveling public' — the west-side wagon-trade house, distinct in clientele from the Green Tree a block north and from the Sauganash across the river. chicagology also calls it one of the best hotels in the town.

levels.8-10: A website says it was the stopping place for all the farmers coming to town from the west. It took in farmers and wagon drivers, who were the travelers then. It was the west side's inn for the wagon trade. Its guests were not like those of the Green Tree a block north, or the Sauganash across the river. The website also calls it one of the best hotels in town.

entries.card: notes:1.35 m clear - wide enough to barrow bark through, narrower…
entries.text: 1.35 m clear - wide enough to barrow bark through, narrower than a wagon door, and it stands on a 2.44 m wall which carries it with a jamb either side. Invented.

levels.8-10: Our guess. 1.35 meters wide, wide enough to push a barrow of bark through, and narrower than a wagon door. It fits in the 2.44 meter wall with a post on each side.

entries.card: notes:12 TENTS, AND NOT A COUNT OF ANYBODY. The register's 77 unse…
entries.text: 12 TENTS, AND NOT A COUNT OF ANYBODY. The register's 77 unseated visitors at the sale would fill this many wall tents about one and a half times over at four men to a tent; most of them slept where the transient model already sleeps the crowd, in rooms and on floors, and twelve is the share drawn as having come with canvas. Invented. L355.

levels.8-10: Our guess. 12 tents, and not a count of anyone. 77 visitors at the land sale had no bed. At four men to a tent, they would fill this many tents and more. Most slept in rooms and on floors. Twelve tents is our share for those who came with tents.

entries.card: notes:A CORRECTION TO A CLAIM IN CIRCULATION. The Green Tree is so…
entries.text: A CORRECTION TO A CLAIM IN CIRCULATION. The Green Tree is sometimes described as whitewashed, including in this project's own research summary, but the attested whitewash is INTERIOR: Edwin Gale writes that 'The walls, ceilings, and board partitions had evidently received a coat of whitewash when the house was built'. Nothing describes the exterior finish. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the reading adopted, and it is positively supported by the Sauganash's white paint being remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — if the Green Tree had been painted white two years later, the contrast the sources draw would be weaker. Not attested either way; the c. 1859 photograph would settle it.

levels.8-10: A fix to a mistake people repeat. Some say the Green Tree was whitewashed, even our own notes. But the whitewash was inside. Edwin Gale wrote that the walls and ceilings inside had been whitewashed when it was built. Nothing tells of the outside. We use bare gray boards. In 1831, people wrote of the white paint on the Sauganash as something special. That fits. A photo from about 1859 would settle it.

entries.card: notes:A COUNT OF ZERO IS A CLAIM, NOT AN ABSENCE, and the archetyp…
entries.text: A COUNT OF ZERO IS A CLAIM, NOT AN ABSENCE, and the archetypes treat it as one. Nothing is attested about heating here; zero is recorded because a store house for barrels and hides is the one building type in this parcel with no reason to have a hearth, and because the slaughtering that would have needed fire is attested as happening in a YARD rather than indoors. If the building doubled as an office it had a stove and this is wrong by one.

levels.8-10: No chimney. Zero is a claim too. Nothing is known about heat here. A store house for barrels and hides is the one kind of building here with no reason for a fire. The killing that needed fire was done in a yard, not inside. If the building was also an office, it had a stove, and this is wrong by one.

entries.card: notes:A COUNT OF ZERO IS A CLAIM, NOT AN ABSENCE. A provision stor…
entries.text: A COUNT OF ZERO IS A CLAIM, NOT AN ABSENCE. A provision store is the one building in a fort you do not want a fire in, and nothing describes a stack on this one. The record says none and the model builds none.

levels.8-10: No chimney is a claim, not a gap. A food store is the one building in a fort where you do not want a fire. Nothing tells of a chimney on it. So we say none, and build none.

entries.card: notes:A COUNT OF ZERO IS A CLAIM. An artillery shed is unheated; there is no stack.
entries.text: A COUNT OF ZERO IS A CLAIM. An artillery shed is unheated; there is no stack.

levels.8-10: No chimney. Zero is a claim too. A gun shed had no heat, so it has no chimney.

entries.card: notes:A FREIGHT SHED HOLDS GOODS, NOT PEOPLE, and whose goods they…
entries.text: A FREIGHT SHED HOLDS GOODS, NOT PEOPLE, and whose goods they were is not on the record. The building and its use come from the owner's brief of 2026-08-18, whose plate draws low warehouses on the banks of the reach below the Dearborn drawbridge, and from the place itself: this reach is where the river traffic and the town's one crossing of the main stem met in July 1835. No source names a forwarding house, a merchant or a keeper for any one of these sheds. A forwarding firm written onto it here would be an invented business, and a household seated in it would be an invented person sleeping in a store shed. So the roof states its use and the gap, and nobody is seated. A source naming the warehouses on this reach is what would replace this statement with a keeper.

levels.8-10: A freight shed held goods, not people, and whose goods they were is not known. The building and its use come from a picture the owner gave us on 18 August 2026. It draws low store houses on the banks below the Dearborn bridge. This stretch is where the river traffic and the town's one bridge over the main river met in July 1835. No record names a shipper or keeper for any of these sheds. A firm written in here would be made up. A family placed in it would be made up people sleeping in a shed. So the roof says its use and what is missing, and no one is placed in it. A record naming the store houses here would give it a keeper.

entries.card: notes:A GARDEN'S RANGE IS ITS GARRISON'S. It is drawn and labelled…
entries.text: A GARDEN'S RANGE IS ITS GARRISON'S. It is drawn and labelled on the 1830 plan and described full of fruit by someone who walked past it in 1831, so it is standing either side of the scene date. It is closed at the final evacuation of 29 December 1836 rather than at the demolition of the buildings, because a company garden is kept by companies and there were none after that date; nothing reached records what happened to the plot.

levels.8-10: A garden's dates are its fort's. It is drawn and named on the 1830 plan, and in 1831 someone walking by saw it full of fruit. So it was there on both sides of 1835. We end it when the soldiers left on 29 December 1836, not when the buildings were torn down. Soldiers kept the garden, and after that date there were none. Nothing tells what happened to it.

entries.card: notes:A NEGATIVE FINDING, RECORDED SO IT CANNOT BE UNDONE BY INFER…
entries.text: A NEGATIVE FINDING, RECORDED SO IT CANNOT BE UNDONE BY INFERENCE. The church had no tower. This is the same trap St Mary's carries in a sharper form - see that record, where a low open tower is attested at an undated 'some time afterwards' and would age the building forward if it were built - and it is recorded here because a visitor's expectation of what a church looks like is the strongest force acting on this model.

levels.8-10: A no, written down so no one adds one by guessing. The church had no tower. St. Mary's has the same trap: it got a low tower some time later, and building it would make that church look newer than 1835. We say so here because people expect a church to have a tower.

entries.card: notes:A PARTY OF FOUR WAGONS, invented: families came overland to…
entries.text: A PARTY OF FOUR WAGONS, invented: families came overland to Chicago from Indiana and Ohio in 1835 as well as by lake, and a party travelled together. L355.

levels.8-10: Four wagons in a group, our guess. In 1835, some families came to Chicago by land, from Indiana and Ohio. Others came by lake. A group went on the road together.

entries.card: notes:A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE.…
entries.text: A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE. The Cook County Court of County Commissioners, sitting at Chicago on 13 April 1831, 'Ordered that the following rates be allowed to tavern keepers', among them 'For each horse fed 25' and 'Keeping horse one night 50' (Andreas, scan p. 249). That order set what a licensed Chicago house might charge to keep a traveller's horse; it is read here as standing for every public house the lodging model sizes, which is an inference, because no licence for this house in particular has been read. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: a dedicated building. A horse can be kept at a picket line, in a fenced lot or at a livery up the street; this record draws the building because a house of this size on a Lake Street lot with an alley behind it is the ordinary case, and says so.

levels.8-10: A price proves a service. The building is our guess. On 13 April 1831 the county set the prices tavern keepers could charge. Feeding a horse was 25 cents, and keeping a horse one night was 50 cents. We take that to cover every inn here. That is a guess, since we have not read this hotel's own license. It does not prove a stable. A horse can be tied to a rope, kept in a fenced lot, or kept up the street. We build a stable because a hotel this size, on a lot with an alley, usually had one.

entries.card: notes:A SQUARE OF ABOUT 53 m (174 ft), AND EVERY PART OF THAT SENT…
entries.text: A SQUARE OF ABOUT 53 m (174 ft), AND EVERY PART OF THAT SENTENCE HAS A DIFFERENT WARRANT. That it was SQUARE is Andreas in terms: 'The fort, as rebuilt, consisted of a square stockade inclosing barracks, quarters for the officers, magazine and provision-store' - and the 1830 plan agrees, drawing the two wall-to-wall distances within 3 percent of each other (161 and 157 pixels). THE SIZE IS DERIVED, NOT STATED. No source reached gives a dimension of this stockade; Quaife, who wrote the standing monograph on the fort and had the War Department files, prints Captain Whistler's measured 1808 draught of the FIRST fort and states no dimension of the second one anywhere. So 53 m is the 1830 plan measured at the scale that record's position note derives, and it carries +/-20 percent - the fort is somewhere between about 140 and 210 ft on a side. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the polygon is a rectangle because the plan draws a quadrangle, and nothing attests the corners were true or the sides equal to the foot.

levels.8-10: A square about 53 meters on a side. That it was square comes from a book on the rebuilt fort, and the 1830 plan agrees. The size is worked out, not written. No record gives its size. So 53 meters is measured from the 1830 plan, and it could be off by a fifth. The fort was somewhere from 140 to 210 feet on a side. We build a box because the plan draws one. Nothing says its corners were square or its sides exactly equal.

entries.card: notes:A blacksmith shop from October 1833, doing the ironwork the…
entries.text: A blacksmith shop from October 1833, doing the ironwork the town and the road trade needed: Andreas records the order from John T. Temple & Co. for 'doing the ironing for the first stage line between Chicago and St. Louis' in January 1834, and the manufacture of the old-fashioned 'Bull' plough with a wooden mould-board from the spring of 1834 (scan p. 1161). THAT PLOUGH IS THE REASON THIS BUILDING MATTERS BEYOND ITS OWN CORNER: it is the wet-prairie tool, and a smith on the west side making them is the town's agricultural hinterland arriving in the town. Whether he was making them on 1835-07-01 specifically is not attested.

levels.8-10: A blacksmith shop from October 1833, doing the iron work the town and the road trade needed. A book says Temple and Co. asked him to do the iron work for the first coach line between Chicago and St Louis in January 1834. From the spring of 1834 he made the old Bull plow, with a wood blade. That plow is why this building matters beyond its corner. It was the tool for wet prairie. A blacksmith on the west side making plows is the farm land around the town coming into the town. If he was making them on 1 July 1835 is not known.

entries.card: notes:A bounded July 1835 worksite, not a reconstruction of the co…
entries.text: A bounded July 1835 worksite, not a reconstruction of the completed hotel. The 10 June Chicago Democrat notice establishes a house building in Kinzie's Addition, understood to be named Lake House. No source measures the July progress. Within the existing 24 × 15 m plan and 4 m maximum, 0.46 m thick brick walls now step down from the higher north working front to the lower rear lift. Seven selected work bays have real unglazed openings and only the first three have their brickwork bridged above reconstructed timber lintels; a broad rear break admits material. Two short timber working stages stand inside the shell. Bay count, wall thickness, lift heights, apertures, staging stock and placement are reconstructed working choices, not features traced from the later print. The existing external brick, timber and footing-stone piles remain separately declared in the yard layer. No excavation or below-grade interior is represented. L-lake-house-worksite-2379.

levels.8-10: A building site in July 1835, not the finished hotel. A notice in the Chicago Democrat of 10 June says a house was being built in Kinzie's Addition. It is thought to be the Lake House. No record measures how far the work was in July. Thick brick walls step down from a higher front to a lower back. Some openings for windows are cut, and only a few have wood across the top. A wide gap at the back lets in supplies. Two short wood platforms stand inside for the builders. All of these are our guesses for a working site, not taken from the later picture. Piles of brick, wood and stone stand in the yard. No digging or basement is shown.

entries.card: notes:A brickmaker's cottage beside Blodgett's yard, which this da…
entries.text: A brickmaker's cottage beside Blodgett's yard, which this dataset already models.

levels.8-10: A small home for a man who made bricks. It is next to Blodgett's yard, where bricks were made. We build that too.

entries.card: notes:A carpenter's own house on the north side - built, one assum…
entries.text: A carpenter's own house on the north side - built, one assumes, rather better than the ones he was raising for other people, though nothing attests that and the record claims only the schedule's ordinary D4 cottage.

levels.8-10: A carpenter's own house on the north side. Maybe he built it better than the ones he built for others. But nothing says so. We claim only a plain cottage.

entries.card: notes:A consequence of the open side rather than a finding: an ele…
entries.text: A consequence of the open side rather than a finding: an elevation you can walk a barrow straight through does not need a doorway, and cutting one would assert a wall that this record does not model.

levels.8-10: This follows from the open side. You can push a cart straight in, so no door is needed. Cutting one would mean a wall that we do not build.

entries.card: notes:A finite 3.35 m eave choice exposes 0.91 m of core above the…
entries.text: A finite 3.35 m eave choice exposes 0.91 m of core above the existing reconstructed 2.44 m palisade, as both retrospective pictures show a substantial log block above the enclosure. This replaces the previous archetype-default 2.66 m choice, which hid almost all wall fabric. Neither plate measures metres; exact height and July continuity are reconstruction. No footprint, site coordinate, street control, storey count or separate later cell is added.

levels.8-10: The wall is 3.35 meters to the roof edge. That shows about 0.9 meters of log wall above the fence of posts, as both later pictures show a big log block above the fence. Our old height hid almost all the wall. Neither picture gives a measure. The exact height, and that it was so in July 1835, are our guesses.

entries.card: notes:A freight shed is a building goods go into and out of by car…
entries.text: A freight shed is a building goods go into and out of by cart, so the opening is the archetype's `wagon` door rather than a man door - which is also what the crosswalk's F1 entry means by 'wide doors; low openings'. It stands on the yard between the two sheds, which is sized for a wagon to stand in at either door and is entered off the east end of South Water Street's travelled way. Invented, like the building.

levels.8-10: Our guess, like the building. Goods go in and out of a freight shed by cart. So it gets a wagon door, not a door for people. Our list says wide doors for this kind too. entries.card: notes:AN ADVERTISEMENT PROVES A TRADE, NOT A BUILDING, AND CERTAIN…
entries.text: AN ADVERTISEMENT PROVES A TRADE, NOT A BUILDING, AND CERTAINLY NOT A BUILDING NINETEEN MONTHS LATER. That sentence is the source record's own warning about the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 and it is the whole difficulty with this record. What is documented is that Daniel Elston & Co. were carrying on a soap and candle manufactory in Chicago in November 1833, paying cash for tallow and house ashes; Andreas's summary of the paper's early advertising columns lists the same firm and trade (scan p. 755), which corroborates the advertisement and adds nothing to it. The range opens in November 1833 because that is the date of the copy, NOT because the works were built then — a manufactory that is advertising for raw material is already running. THE SURVIVAL TO 1835-07-01 IS AN ASSUMPTION AND THE CONFIDENCE SAYS SO: nothing reached follows this business past that advertisement, the scene date is nineteen months later in the fastest-changing period of the town's history, and the man himself is next seen in the sources decades on — an alderman in 1851, president of St George's Society in 1847, running the largest of Chicago's five brickyards by 1854 (Andreas scan pp. 389, 1073, 1169). A long career in the town is a reason to think he did not fail in 1834, and it is not evidence about a building. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

levels.8-10: An ad proves a trade, not a building. Our own record warns of that, about the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833. We know Daniel Elston and partners made soap and candles in Chicago that November. They paid cash for tallow, which is animal fat, and for ashes from people's homes. A book lists the same business. We start in November 1833 because that is the ad's date. The works were already running then. That it lasted to July 1835 is a guess, and our confidence says so. Nothing follows the business after that ad. Elston shows up again years later, as a town leader and running the biggest brickyard by 1854. A long life in town hints he did not fail in 1834. That is not proof about a building. The record ends at the end of 1835.

Both dimensions built here are his. The date is the weakness - 'had been a sun-dial' is a man describing a relic in 1850, and nothing puts it on the parade in 1835 except that a post with a garrison has more use for a sun-dial than an abandoned one. WHERE IT STANDS IS OURS: Fergus puts his on a knoll near the southern end of a parade four hundred feet long, which is ground this record does not model, so the archetype stands it in the southern part of the court instead.

entries.card: notes:Andreas dates the warehouse and slaughter yard to 1832 and g…
entries.text: Andreas dates the warehouse and slaughter yard to 1832 and gives no month, so the range opens at the start of that year. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS INFERENCE AND THERE IS A SPECIFIC REASON TO DOUBT IT: in 1834 Newberry and Dole built a slaughter-house on the South Branch, which is where a slaughtering business goes when it outgrows a yard behind a warehouse two blocks from the river. So at least half of what Andreas describes here had probably moved by the scene date. The warehouse itself is a different question and nothing reached follows it either way; it stands in this scene on the ordinary continuity argument. A LOCATION GUARD THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THIS RECORD: Newberry and Dole's forwarding warehouse — the one at whose wharf the schooner Illinois was cheered on 12 July 1834 — was on the NORTH side of the river, immediately east of where Rush Street bridge later stood. This record is the separate SOUTH-side 1832 warehouse and slaughter yard. Do not merge them and do not move this one to the river.

A butcher trade moves there when it outgrows a yard behind a store. So the yard had likely moved by 1835. The warehouse is another matter. Nothing follows it, so we keep it. Note: their other warehouse, where a ship was cheered in July 1834, was on the north side of the river. This is a different one, on the south side. Do not mix them up.

entries.card: notes:Andreas says 'frame' and no more, and the word does not dist…
entries.text: Andreas says 'frame' and no more, and the word does not distinguish the two methods available. Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method within a few years; this building's date is not fixed and may precede that, so braced frame is the safer reading, exactly as the Sauganash record argues for 1831. levels.8-10: Andreas says it was wooden, and that is all. We build it with a sawn wood frame, not logs. A frame holds up one big open room, and logs do not. New stores in town in 1833 and 1834 were going up in frame. The records never say which kind of frame.

entries.card: notes:Andreas states the paper, its founder, its establishment dat…
entries.text: Andreas states the paper, its founder, its establishment date, its format and the location of its office. What is documented is that the office was there; that the office was a building of its own is not, and is argued on the footprint.

levels.8-10: Andreas tells the paper's name, who started it, when, how big it was, and where its office was. We know the office was there. That it had a building of its own is not known.

entries.card: notes:Andreas's clause is the whole of it: 'In its vicinity were s…
entries.text: Andreas's clause is the whole of it: 'In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell, an Indian chief, who was also interpreter for the agency.' The use is attested; which of the two men had which building is not, and this record does not claim it.

levels.8-10: Andreas wrote one line. He says small log houses near the agency were lived in by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and by Billy Caldwell. Caldwell was a chief and a speaker of languages for the agency. We know the two men lived here. We do not know which man had which house.

entries.card: notes:Andreas, 'Chicago from 1833 to 1837', vol. 1 p. 128, describ…
entries.text: Andreas, 'Chicago from 1833 to 1837', vol. 1 p. 128, describing the town a visitor would have seen: 'It did not show a single steeple nor a chimney four feet above any roof. A flagstaff at the fort, some fifty feet high, flaunted, in pleasant weather and on holidays - a weather-beaten flag, as an emblem of civilization, patriotic pride, national domain, or anything else that might stir hearts of the denizens of the town.' The same paragraph sees it from the southern approach: 'a line of almost indefinable structures, and the flag over the fort, if perchance it was flying.' THIS IS THE SECOND FORT. It is not the 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812' passage, it is not Whistler's 1808 index, and it is not a plate; it is Andreas's own narrative of the years the scene date sits in.

levels.8-10: A book tells of the town a visitor saw in the 1830s. It says there was not one church tower, nor a chimney four feet above a roof. A flagpole at the fort, about fifty feet high, flew a worn flag in fair weather and on holidays. Coming from the south, the same book says, you saw a line of hard-to-make-out buildings, and the flag over the fort, if it was flying. This is the second fort. It is the book's own story of the years around 1835.

entries.card: notes:Andreas, of the rebuilt fort: 'was defended by bastions at t…
entries.text: Andreas, of the rebuilt fort: 'was defended by bastions at the northwest and southeast angles. The block-house was in the southwest corner.' Kinzie, independently: 'bastions at the alternate angles'. Hubbard in 1827: 'the block-house was located at the southwest and the bastion at the northwest corners'. The 1830 plan draws a work at exactly three angles and leaves the north-east plain. GUARD: the widely repeated 'two blockhouses, one on the south-east corner, the other at the north-west' belongs to the FIRST fort - the passage it comes from ends 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812' - and applying it here is the commonest error about this building.

levels.8-10: A book says the rebuilt fort had strong corners at the north-west and south-east, and the blockhouse in the south-west. Kinzie says strong corners at every other corner. Hubbard says in 1827 the blockhouse was at the south-west and a strong corner at the north-west. The 1830 plan draws one at three corners and leaves the north-east plain. Many say there were two blockhouses, at the south-east and north-west. That was the first fort, before 1812, not this one. It is the most common mistake about it.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: 'Another tower, forty feet high, was begun and comp…
entries.text: Andreas: 'Another tower, forty feet high, was begun and completed by Mr. Jackson in 1832.'

levels.8-10: A book says Mr. Jackson built one more tower, forty feet high, in 1832.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: 'In 1834, Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole had a…
entries.text: Andreas: 'In 1834, Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole had a slaughter-house erected on the South Branch'.

levels.8-10: A book tells of it. In 1834, Oliver Newberry and George Dole had a plant built on the South Branch. It was a place to kill and pack meat.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: 'It was formed of stringers.' Cleaver: 'The abutmen…
entries.text: Andreas: 'It was formed of stringers.' Cleaver: 'The abutments were built of heavy logs.' Two independent accounts, both describing round or hewn timber rather than framed carpentry, which is what this archetype's 'log' value means.

levels.8-10: A book says it was made of long logs laid across. Cleaver says the ends were built of heavy logs. Two records, both telling of round or squared logs, not a carpenter's frame. That is what logs means here.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: 'The Mansion House was built in 1831 by Dexter Grav…
entries.text: Andreas: 'The Mansion House was built in 1831 by Dexter Graves'; the frame front this scene shows was added two years later.

levels.8-10: A book says the Mansion House was built in 1831 by Dexter Graves. The frame front in this scene was added two years later.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: 'a two roomed log house'. No source describes the c…
entries.text: Andreas: 'a two roomed log house'. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking, or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at Chicago in 1831 and what the source names.

levels.8-10: Andreas calls it a log house of two rooms. No record tells how the corners or gaps were done, or if it had boards on it. We build squared logs, the most common kind in Chicago in 1831, and what the record says.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: 'the original log slaughter-house, built by Archiba…
entries.text: Andreas: 'the original log slaughter-house, built by Archibald Clybourne in 1827'.

levels.8-10: A book calls it the first log butcher house, built by the owner in 1827.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: Asahel Pierce 'commenced the erection of a blacksmi…
entries.text: Andreas: Asahel Pierce 'commenced the erection of a blacksmith shop' on 8 October 1833.

levels.8-10: A book tells us when it began. Asahel Pierce began to build a blacksmith shop on 8 October 1833.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: Carpenter 'erected a small store' in the summer of 1833.
entries.text: Andreas: Carpenter 'erected a small store' in the summer of 1833.

levels.8-10: A book says Carpenter built a small store in the summer of 1833.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: Carpenter 'purchased a lot on South Water Street, b…
entries.text: Andreas: Carpenter 'purchased a lot on South Water Street, between LaSalle and Wells streets' and 'erected a small store' in the summer of 1833. The range opens at 1 August, the middle of that summer, because no month is given and a mid-season date claims less than either end of it. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY ARGUMENT, and it is stronger here than on most records in this parcel: this is the building Carpenter MOVED INTO, two years old on the scene date, on the street he had just bought a lot on, and nothing suggests a man does that and then leaves. Carpenter's own advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 — drugs, medicines, oils, paints, dye-stuffs, and also dry groceries, glass and nails — shows him trading three months after building it, though it gives no address and so cannot say which of his two premises it was placed from. THE END IS A HOUSEKEEPING BOUND at the scene year, not a demolition date.

levels.8-10: A book says Carpenter bought a lot on South Water Street and built a small store in the summer of 1833. No month is given, so we start it on 1 August, the middle of summer. He moved into this store, so it likely still stood in 1835. His ad in a paper in November 1833 sold drugs, paints, food, glass and nails. That shows him at work three months later. The ad has no address, so it could be from his other shop. The end date is just where our record stops.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: Mark Beaubien 'completed another house on the north…
entries.text: Andreas: Mark Beaubien 'completed another house on the northwest corner' of Wells and Lake in 1834.

levels.8-10: A book says Mark built one more house on the corner of Wells and Lake in 1834.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: a log building. No source describes the corner trea…
entries.text: Andreas: a log building. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at the forks in 1832 and what the source names.

levels.8-10: A book says a log building. No record tells how the corners or gaps were done, or if it had boards on it. We build squared logs, the most common kind at the forks in 1832, and what the record says.

entries.card: notes:Andreas: a two-story frame store. The unfinished loft over t…
entries.text: Andreas: a two-story frame store. The unfinished loft over those two storeys is stated separately as `loft` and is not counted here — the storey count is the finished, floored accommodation, which is what the archetype extrudes wall height from.

levels.8-10: A book says it was a wood frame store of two floors. The unfinished loft above them is counted on its own, not here. The number of floors counts only the finished floors.

entries.card: notes:Anonymous count-unit toward the July 1835 665-roof programme…
entries.text: Anonymous count-unit toward the July 1835 665-roof programme. No evidence establishes that this particular building existed, and no source names an occupant of this lot.

levels.8-10: One of the 665 made-up roofs that fill the town for July 1835. Nothing proves this building stood, and no record names anyone on this lot.

entries.card: notes:Anonymous count-unit toward the July 1835 programme. No evid…
entries.text: Anonymous count-unit toward the July 1835 programme. No evidence establishes that this particular building existed.

levels.8-10: One of the made-up roofs that fill the town for July 1835. Nothing proves this building stood.

entries.card: notes:Attested standing in 1831 by Juliette Kinzie and by nobody e…
entries.text: Attested standing in 1831 by Juliette Kinzie and by nobody else at any date. The range opens with the fort and closes at the final evacuation, because a root house is kept by a garrison; nothing reached follows it further.

levels.8-10: Juliette Kinzie saw it in 1831, and no one else ever did. It starts with the fort. It ends when the soldiers left for good, since soldiers kept a root house. Nothing follows it after that.

entries.card: notes:Attested twice in Andreas, in two chapters, with dates eithe…
entries.text: Attested twice in Andreas, in two chapters, with dates either side of the scene date: 'In August of 1834, Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this new hotel, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House. They remained there until 1836, when they removed to the old Sauganash, the name of which they changed to United States Hotel'; and, in the life of Mark Beaubien, the house was 'first kept by Mr. and Mrs. John Murphy'. So 1835-07-01 falls inside their tenancy with eleven months either side, which makes this the best-attested occupancy in the parcel. A CONFLICT WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN RESOLVING: this project's dossiers have Abram A. Markle 'associated from 1835-36' with the house, and the American's advertisement of August 1836 does call it 'Markle's Exchange Coffee House'. Andreas has Markle taking the MANSION HOUSE in 1835 and keeping it two years. Either Markle held both houses, or one of the two datings is loose; the Murphy tenancy is the one with dates on both sides of the scene date and it is what this record carries.

levels.8-10: A book says so twice, with dates on both sides of July 1835. It says the Murphys took over the new hotel in August 1834 and stayed until 1836. Then they moved to the old Sauganash. So July 1835 falls in their time, with eleven months on each side. That makes this the best-known stay in this part of town. One record does not agree. Our notes link Abram A. Markle to the house in 1835 and 1836, and an 1836 ad calls it Markle's Exchange Coffee House. But the book says Markle ran a different hotel in 1835. Either he ran both, or one date is loose. We keep the Murphys, since their dates are on both sides.

entries.card: notes:BUILT IN THE SPRING OF 1835, WHICH IS INSIDE THE SCENE YEAR…
entries.text: BUILT IN THE SPRING OF 1835, WHICH IS INSIDE THE SCENE YEAR AND BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Andreas: 'In the spring of 1835, he built a house on what he supposed was his lot, only to find that he was on Monroe Street, not Adams, whither he proceeded to remove it on rollers.' The house, its season, its owner and the fact that it was moved a block are all documented. The range opens on 1835-03-01 as the earliest reading of 'the spring'.

levels.8-10: Built in the spring of 1835, before the day we show. A book says he built a house on what he thought was his lot. Then he found he was on Monroe Street, not Adams. So he moved it there on rollers. The house, the season, its owner, and that it was moved a block are all known. The dates start on 1 March 1835, the earliest spring could be.

entries.card: notes:Bare brick. Nothing says this building was rendered, painted…
entries.text: Bare brick. Nothing says this building was rendered, painted or whitewashed; the whitewash in the sources belongs to the board fence of the 1850s compound and to John H. Kinzie's boyhood memory of the FIRST fort's blockhouses.

levels.8-10: Bare brick. Nothing says it was painted or whitewashed. The whitewash in the old records is on a board fence of the 1850s. It is also in one man's memory of the first fort.

entries.card: notes:Beaubien is documented as the man who used the cabin as a ba…
entries.text: Beaubien is documented as the man who used the cabin as a barn and as the resident of the homestead group from 1817 to about 1840. A barn has no occupants in the sense this field usually carries; the value records whose farm building it was.

levels.8-10: Records show that Beaubien used the cabin as a barn. He lived at this home from 1817 to about 1840. No one lived in a barn, so this tells whose farm building it was.

entries.card: notes:Book1902 p51 places John Beach in a house partly inside the…
entries.text: Book1902 p51 places John Beach in a house partly inside the jail enclosure facing Randolph during the retrospective1835-framed walk. The actual illustration says1836. Bounds are continuity conventions, not construction/demolition dates, and do not prove every pictured detail existed by1July1835.

levels.8-10: A book of 1902 puts John Beach in a house partly inside the jail yard, facing Randolph Street, in a walk set in 1835. But its picture says 1836. The dates are our usual limits, not when it was built or torn down. They do not prove every part of the picture was there by 1 July 1835.

entries.card: notes:Both halves are attested and they are attested separately. T…
entries.text: Both halves are attested and they are attested separately. The store: Peck was a licensed merchant advertising dry goods, hardware and groceries through 1834-35. The dwelling: Andreas has Peck living at the store, and this project's exclusion of his 1837 brick house rests on exactly that reading. The loft over the two storeys was let for lodging at least once, to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter in May 1833.

levels.8-10: Both of its uses are known, each on its own. The store: Peck had a license to sell, and put ads in the paper for cloth, tools and food in 1834 and 1835. The home: a book says Peck lived at the store. The loft above the two floors was let to a guest at least once, to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter in May 1833.

entries.card: notes:Both men are named for the yard's establishment in the sprin…
entries.text: Both men are named for the yard's establishment in the spring of 1833 (scan p. 1161). Whether either was still working this ground on 1835-07-01 is not attested; Andreas later has Daniel Elston running the largest of the city's five brickyards by 1854 (scan p. 1169), which is two decades past the scene and says nothing about 1835.

levels.8-10: Both men are named for starting the yard in the spring of 1833. No record says if either still worked here on 1 July 1835. Andreas says Daniel Elston ran the biggest of the city's five brickyards by 1854. That is twenty years later and tells us nothing about 1835.

entries.card: notes:Both pictures show the keeper house under a gable; its depic…
entries.text: Both pictures show the keeper house under a gable; its depicted orientation differs between the independent drawings.

levels.8-10: Both pictures show the keeper's house with a roof of two slopes. Which way it faces is not the same in the two drawings.

entries.card: notes:Both printings are signed JOHN HOLBROOK and dated at Chicago…
entries.text: Both printings are signed JOHN HOLBROOK and dated at Chicago, the Democrat's 10 June 1835 and the American's 13 June 1835. That he traded, what he traded in, and the street and cross street he traded on are all documented; his building, its size, its height and the metres between his door and the corner are inference or invention.

levels.8-10: Both ads are signed John Holbrook, at Chicago, on 10 and 13 June 1835. That he traded, what he sold, and his street and corner are all known. His building, its size and height, and how far his door was from the corner are our guesses.

entries.card: notes:Both sources call it a log building, and the congregation's…
entries.text: Both sources call it a log building, and the congregation's own account of the 1838 move — floating the cabin across the river and rolling it on logs — only makes sense for a log structure light and rigid enough to move whole.

levels.8-10: Both records say it was made of logs. In 1838 the church group moved it. They floated the cabin across the river and rolled it on logs. That only works for a log house that is light and strong enough to move in one piece.

entries.card: notes:Both sources have Stow building and operating the house; the…
entries.text: Both sources have Stow building and operating the house; the hotel chronology says outright that it was 'built and operated by W.H. Stow'. He came to Chicago about 1833, so he is present at the scene date on either build date.

levels.8-10: Both records say Stow built the house and ran it. The list of hotels says it plainly: built and run by W. H. Stow. He came to Chicago about 1833, so he was here on the day we show, whichever year it was built.

entries.card: notes:Both sources name Davis as the keeper in 1835, and Andreas's…
entries.text: Both sources name Davis as the keeper in 1835, and Andreas's list of the Chicago American's advertising patrons carries 'John Davis, Steamboat Hotel' in the paper's first year. THE GRAIN IS THE YEAR, NOT THE DAY: DRLOIH has J. Dorsey and J. Force taking over the management on 9 November 1835, so Davis's tenure covers the scene date if the house was open at all. Note the coincidence this project should not resolve by assumption: a 'Mr. Davis' also took over the Sauganash Hotel in 1835, and whether that is the same John Davis is unattested.

levels.8-10: Both records name Davis as the keeper in 1835. A book's list of people who put ads in the Chicago American in its first year has John Davis, Steamboat Hotel. But that is the year, not the day. A website says J. Dorsey and J. Force took over running it on 9 November 1835. So Davis ran it on the day we show, if it was open at all. A Mr. Davis also took over the Sauganash in 1835. If that was the same John Davis is not known, and we do not guess.

entries.card: notes:Both witnesses give it the same double use and disagree only…
entries.text: Both witnesses give it the same double use and disagree only on which came first: chicagology says Walker erected it 'for a place of worship, and for a school house'; Wau-Bun says it was 'originally designed for a school-house, but occasionally used as a place of worship whenever any itinerant minister presented himself'. Either way, on 1835-07-01 it is the settlement's only building put up for worship or teaching. Jesse Walker himself died in 1835.

levels.8-10: Both records say it had two uses. They do not agree on which came first. A website says Walker built it for a place to pray, and for a school house. Wau-Bun says it was first meant for a school house, but used now and then for church, when a traveling minister came by. Either way, on 1 July 1835 it is the only building here put up for church or school. Jesse Walker himself died in 1835.

entries.card: notes:Braunhold's engraving draws the annex's two front sash bare,…
entries.text: Braunhold's engraving draws the annex's two front sash bare, with log wall alongside their casings rather than open shutter leaves. The main hotel's shutters in the later Trowbridge copy are a different building's treatment and do not license shutters on this cabin. This governs the front only; no claim is made about the unseen rear face.

levels.8-10: Braunhold's print draws the two front windows bare, with log wall next to their frames, and no open shutters. The main hotel's shutters in a later copy belong to a different building, and do not mean this cabin had them. This is for the front only. Nothing is claimed about the back.

entries.card: notes:Braunhold's public-domain Andreas 1884 Sauganash engraving s…
entries.text: Braunhold's public-domain Andreas 1884 Sauganash engraving shows this attached log cabin with one doorway between two tall sash, their heads approximately on the doorway's head line. The identity is the existing the Illinois History Journal's Beaubien caption caption ruling in this record, not a new independent witness. These centres preserve the archetype's former symmetric stations on the attested 6.096 m frontage (centre 3.048 m, flanks at centre plus or minus 28 percent of the frontage), rounded to millimetres. They are reconstructed rather than measured from a solved camera. Stating the set-out lets the existing archetype align the tall sash heads with the retained 1.95 m door head; no historical door or window station is claimed.

levels.8-10: Braunhold made an old print of the Sauganash for a book of 1884. It shows this log cabin joined to it. The cabin has one door between two tall windows. The tops of the windows are about level with the top of the door. Which cabin it is comes from a caption we already use, not a new record. The windows are set evenly along the front, as before. That is our guess, not measured from the picture.

entries.card: notes:Braunhold's public-domain Andreas 1884 engraving draws one c…
entries.text: Braunhold's public-domain Andreas 1884 engraving draws one chimney on this attached log cabin, which the existing the Illinois History Journal's Beaubien caption caption ruling identifies as Carpenter's former shop. This replaces the earlier count inferred only from a winter-heating need. The roof-piercing placement is pictured; its exact station/shaft/head dimensions are reconstructed in the three ridge-stack attributes. The engraving's masonry detail and Petford's red rendition still differ from the archetype's hardcoded stick-and-clay material; that unresolved material is not claimed as a match.

levels.8-10: Braunhold's print of 1884 draws one chimney on this log cabin. A caption we already use says the cabin was Carpenter's old shop. We used to guess one chimney only because it needed heat in winter. Now the picture shows it. That it comes up through the roof is from the picture. Its exact place and size are our guess. The print's brick and another artist's red do not match our chimney's stick and clay, and we do not claim they do.

entries.card: notes:Built 'for the killing of such cattle as were required by th…
entries.text: Built 'for the killing of such cattle as were required by the garrison at Fort Dearborn' (scan p. 1149) and working as a commercial packing house from 1833, when Clybourne 'packed some two hundred and fifty head of cattle and about two thousand hogs' and George W. Dole packed a further 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs at the same place; Andreas gives the prices, $2.80 a head average for the cattle and $3 per hundred pounds net for the hogs (scan p. 1151). THIS IS THE FIRST SLAUGHTER-HOUSE IN CHICAGO and the head of the trade that the city was later built on. Andreas elsewhere calls Archibald Clybourne 'the Government butcher for the Pottawatomies' (scan p. 253), a treaty-provision post — recorded here because it is what the man was, and flagged for review with the rest of this record's Indigenous content rather than paraphrased away.

levels.8-10: It was built to kill cattle for the soldiers at the fort. From 1833 it packed meat to sell. That year the owner packed about 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs. A man named Dole packed 250 cattle and 1,000 hogs here too. The book gives the prices. This was the first butcher house in Chicago. The city later grew big on this trade. The book also calls the owner the government's butcher for the Potawatomi. A treaty set up that job. That is what the man was, so we keep it. We mark it to be checked, like the rest of this record's Native history.

entries.card: notes:Built 1833 by James Kinzie — 'the first structure ever erect…
entries.text: Built 1833 by James Kinzie — 'the first structure ever erected in the place for hotel purposes' — and standing at the north-east corner of Lake and Canal until it was moved in 1880 to 35 and 37 Milwaukee Avenue to clear the site for the Jones & Laughlin works. Both ends are attested, which is why a forty-seven-year span is tagged documented rather than being a research gap in disguise. IT IS STILL TOO LONG TO BE ONE FORM-STATE, and that is a known limitation: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, recalls 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left', so the building demonstrably grew, and nothing dates those additions. The phase should be split the moment they can be dated. A second, smaller conflict: chicagology's Green Tree page dates the move to 1880, while its Town of Chicago page, written in 1883, says the building was 'removed two years ago', i.e. 1881. Immaterial to the 1835 scene. The carpenter is disputed too — chicagology names 'Philo Cobb', DRLOIH names Silas B. Cobb, who is the historically real person and is almost certainly correct.

levels.8-10: Built in 1833 by James Kinzie, the first building in town made to be an inn. It stood at the corner of Lake and Canal until 1880. Then it was moved to Milwaukee Avenue, to make room for a big iron works. Both dates are known. But the building grew in that time. John Gray ran it from 1838 to 1841. He remembered a low one-floor room added on the right, the same as on the left. No one dates those rooms. Two pages of one website give 1880 and 1881 for the move. That does not matter for 1835. Who built it is mixed up too. One page says Philo Cobb. A book says Silas Cobb, a real man, and is almost for sure right.

entries.card: notes:Built in 1834: its builder, Nelson R. Norton, began it in Ma…
entries.text: Built in 1834: its builder, Nelson R. Norton, began it in March 1834 and Andreas dates its acceptance to that summer.

levels.8-10: Built in 1834. Nelson R. Norton began it in March 1834, and a book says the town took it that summer.

entries.card: notes:CATON'S ATTIC IS THE POINT. It is the only account in this c…
entries.text: CATON'S ATTIC IS THE POINT. It is the only account in this corpus of what an educated newcomer actually did for money and where he slept in the town's first summer, and it makes this building a lodging as well as an office - which is exactly the mixed use the reconstruction schedule's C-family roofs are for.

levels.8-10: Caton's attic is the point. It is the only record here of what a newcomer with schooling did for money, and where he slept, in the town's first summer. It makes this building a place to sleep as well as an office. That is the mixed use our plans have for this kind of building.

entries.card: notes:CORRECTED 2026-08-10 FROM 'crib', WITH ITS RE-BAKE. This rec…
entries.text: CORRECTED 2026-08-10 FROM 'crib', WITH ITS RE-BAKE. This record picked a disagreement and picked it wrong, and the source that settles it was signed by the eyewitness the losing argument leaned on. The 1883 old-settlers statement printed at Andreas pp. 631-632 — Caton, Bates, CLEAVER and Noble — says 'both bridges were built on abutments and two "bents"', and describes them: 'The bents were of four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water.' So 'Bent' in the Kinzie Street page's chronology table is not a modern type-word applied down a column, as the superseded reasoning assumed; it is very probably that table reading this footnote, and it is the settlers' own word. WHAT THE MESH CAN AND CANNOT SHOW OF IT: the archetype now builds four heavy logs under a cap at each support, which is the count and the heaviness the sentence gives. 'Resting on the bottom' is the other half of it and is invisible here — this project models neither the riverbed nor anything more than half a metre below the waterline, so a bent stood on the bed and a bent driven into it are the same picture above water. The distinction lives in this note. THE SUPERSEDED REASONING, kept because it is what an honest reading of the thinner evidence looked like: A DISAGREEMENT PICKED WITH REASONING RATHER THAN SILENTLY. Cleaver describes heavy logs standing in shallow water, which is a crib — a log box, sunk and filled. The Kinzie Street page's chronology table instead types the bridge 'Wood, Fixed, Bent', and a bent is framed and usually pile-borne. Crib is adopted because Cleaver is an eyewitness describing what he saw and the table is a modern editorial classification applied uniformly down a column covering six bridges and a century. THE INFERENCE IS THE STEP FROM ABUTMENTS TO PIERS, not the choice between the two words: Cleaver describes the ends, nobody describes the middle, and this record assumes the intermediate supports were built the way the ends were. That last sentence is the one the footnote overturned: somebody did describe the middle.

levels.8-10: Fixed on 10 August 2026. We had picked wrong between two readings. The record that settles it was signed by the man the losing side leaned on. The old settlers' paper of 1883, signed by Caton, Bates, Cleaver and Noble, says both bridges stood on ends and two bents. It says the bents were four heavy logs, resting on the bottom, in deeper water. So bent is the settlers' own word. We now build four heavy logs under a cap at each support. Resting on the bottom cannot be seen here, since we do not build the river bed. So that part lives in this note. Our old reason was that Cleaver told of logs in shallow water, like a box of logs. A modern table called it a bent, and we trusted the man who saw it over the table. We also guessed the middle supports were built like the ends. That is what the 1883 paper overturned: someone did tell of the middle.

levels.8-10: Cameron shows a dark, open door with a person in it. We build a dark, open door. Nothing is known about the inside, the door itself, who the person was, or if the door was open in July 1835. It follows the picture of 1833, made years later.

Its local +x assignment, 0.7 by 0.8 m size and 3.35 m centre are reconstructed within the existing roof, not a compass bearing or metric dimension from the painting. levels.8-10: Records show that Chappel lived here in 1833 and 1834, and left before 1835. No record names anyone here in 1835. So we give his stay its end date, and do not carry him into 1835. That is on purpose.

entries.card: notes:Chicago's first brickyard, established spring 1833 by Tyler…
entries.text: Chicago's first brickyard, established spring 1833 by Tyler K. Blodgett with Henry S. Lampman of Ann Arbor as workman and, in Andreas's words, 'undoubtedly the first brick-maker' (scan p. 1161). Andreas adds that the yard supplied the brick for the first building in Chicago constructed of the material — Blodgett's own dwelling house, one and a half storeys and twenty feet square, which stood ACROSS THE RIVER opposite this yard. That dwelling is a separate structure and is not modelled by this record or by any other in this dataset yet; it is a strong candidate for the south-side parcel.

levels.8-10: This was Chicago's first brickyard. Tyler K. Blodgett started it in the spring of 1833, with Henry S. Lampman as his worker. Andreas calls Lampman the first brick-maker here. He says the yard made the bricks for the first brick building in Chicago. That was Blodgett's own house, across the river from the yard. It was 20 feet square, with one and a half floors. That house is not built in the model yet.

entries.card: notes:DOCUMENTED IN FABRIC, USE, KEEPER AND POSITION, and absent f…
entries.text: DOCUMENTED IN FABRIC, USE, KEEPER AND POSITION, and absent from this dataset until now. Andreas describes a log house kept as a first-class boarding house by Mrs Rufus Brown, 'the first building in the rear of this store' - Peck's store at South Water and LaSalle. The range opens at the start of 1833, which is not a build date: what is documented is that the house was standing and keeping boarders in the town of 1833-34, and nothing follows it past 1835.

levels.8-10: We know what it was made of, what it was for, who ran it and where it stood. Andreas tells of a log house run as a fine boarding house by Mrs. Rufus Brown. It was the first building behind Peck's store, at South Water and LaSalle. We start it at the beginning of 1833. That is not when it was built. It is when we know it stood and took in boarders. No record follows it past 1835.

entries.card: notes:DOCUMENTED, WHICH IS RARE HERE: 'The outside of the building…
entries.text: DOCUMENTED, WHICH IS RARE HERE: 'The outside of the building was not painted and it had neither steeple nor tower.' This is the only exterior finish directly attested on any building in this parcel, and it is worth noting that it CORROBORATES the reading the Green Tree and the Presbyterian church records adopt by inference - unpainted weathered boarding was the norm and the Sauganash's white paint was the exception worth recording. The quoted no-tower state is the original 1833 construction state, not a dated 1835 absence; the present belfry is a separate reconstructed choice.

levels.8-10: Known, which is rare here. A book says the outside of the building was not painted, and it had no steeple or tower. It is the only outside finish told of on any building on this land. It backs our guess for the Green Tree and the Presbyterian church: bare gray boards were the usual. The Sauganash's white paint was the one worth writing about. The line about no tower is from when it was built in 1833, not 1835. The bell tower we build is our guess.

entries.text: Documented and not a build instruction: no interior is modelled in this project, and the division leaves no external trace this archetype builds - not a separate outside stair, not a differently fenestrated upper storey. levels.8-10: Known, but not a thing to build. We do not build insides. Splitting the floors left no sign outside that we build, no outside stair and no different windows above. It is recorded because it is the whole point of the building, and it is what ties Sproat's school to this place.

entries.card: notes:Documented and not built. The benches are the single most vi…
entries.text: Documented and not built. The benches are the single most vivid documented fact about the inside of this building and they fix its capacity, which is the only independent check on the 40 x 25 ft footprint: 1,000 sq ft for 200 people is 5 sq ft each, tight but exactly what bench seating gives. No interior is modelled in this project, so nothing of them is shown.

levels.8-10: Known, but not built. The benches are the clearest fact about the inside. They also check the size: 1,000 square feet for 200 people is 5 square feet each. That is tight, but it is what bench seats give. We do not build insides, so they can't be seen.

entries.card: notes:Documented and not built. The pairing is worth keeping toget…
entries.text: Documented and not built. The pairing is worth keeping together because it is a statement about money: the walls were finished and the floor was not, which is what a $600 subscription church looks like from the inside. It also separates this building from St Mary's, which was not plastered at all. No interior is modelled, so neither surface is shown.

levels.8-10: Known, but not built. These two go together because they tell about money. The walls were finished but the floor was not. That is what a $600 church paid for by its members looks like inside. St. Mary's had no plaster at all. We do not build insides, so neither can be seen.
