levels.8-10: Known, but not built. It is the most lively known fact about the inside of the building. We do not build insides, so none of it is shown.

entries.card: notes:Documented and not built. This is the only thing any source…
entries.text: Documented and not built. This is the only thing any source says about the building's arrangement, and it is what distinguishes it from an ordinary cabin - the schoolroom and the teacher's own quarters under one roof. No interior is modelled in this project, so the partition is invisible; it is the reason the footprint is a two-room size rather than a single pen, so it does reach the mesh indirectly, through a number a human chose.

levels.8-10: Known, but not built. This is the only thing any record says about the inside. The schoolroom and the teacher's rooms were under one roof. We do not build the insides of buildings, so the wall between them can't be seen. But it is why the house is sized for two rooms, not one.

entries.card: notes:Documented twice and once contemporaneously: the advertiseme…
entries.text: Documented twice and once contemporaneously: the advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is headed 'Grocery & Provision Store', and Andreas records the same trade with forwarding and commission added by 1834. The trade is the best-evidenced thing about this record.

levels.8-10: Known twice, once from its own time. The ad in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 says it was a food store. A book says the same, with a shipping trade added by 1834. The trade is the best known thing about it.

entries.card: notes:Explicit anchor on the separately modelled roof spar, not th…
entries.text: Explicit anchor on the separately modelled roof spar, not the hotel bounding box. Coordinates are footprint metres[east,north,up] mapped to glTF[east,up,south] before the existing placement matrix. Head/foot agree with the reconstructed32degree/7.8m envelope and4.25m spar; all are reconstructed. Source picks stafftop(1034,192),base(1034,279); approximate flag outline x1000..1034,y197..224 gives projected fly/staff~0.39 and hoist/staff~0.31. Perspective/folds do not yield metres: working fly1.85m/hoist1.30m sit within broad0.35..0.50/0.25..0.40 staff-height ratios. Both dimensions,0.035m square-spar half-width, pattern, date use and orientation/pose are reconstructed; opposite wind/image fit remain open. Phase/date mismatch or invalid/stale/out-of-bounds anchor refuses cloth and reports why. This interval prevents carrying the24-star reconstruction into later patterns without review.

levels.8-10: The flag hangs on its own pole on the roof. The pole is 4.25 meters tall, our guess. From the picture, the flag is about 1.85 meters long and 1.3 meters tall. Those sizes are our guess too, since a picture with depth and folds cannot give meters. If the date or the pole does not match, the flag is not shown. That keeps the 24 star flag from showing in later years without a check.

entries.card: notes:FLOWN AT THE OWNER'S DIRECTION (2026-10-05), AS A RECONSTRUC…
entries.text: FLOWN AT THE OWNER'S DIRECTION (2026-10-05), AS A RECONSTRUCTION. Andreas says the flag flew 'in pleasant weather and on holidays'; the scene date, Wednesday 1 July 1835, is not a holiday and no source reached records its weather. The scene is drawn in fair summer weather, so the flag is up under the source's own condition, and it is graded reconstructed: it is a claim about the forenoon that no source makes. The wind that holds it out (a south-westerly breeze) is reconstructed with it (L390).

levels.8-10: Flown because the owner asked, as our guess. The book says the flag flew in fair weather and on holidays. Wednesday 1 July 1835 was not a holiday, and no record tells the weather. The scene is drawn on a fair summer day, so the flag is up, as the book's rule allows. No record says so. The breeze that holds it out is our guess too.

entries.card: notes:FOUR IS THE ARCHETYPE'S NUMBER; WHAT THE SOURCE GIVES IS THE…
entries.text: FOUR IS THE ARCHETYPE'S NUMBER; WHAT THE SOURCE GIVES IS THE LOAD. The 1883 statement calls both branch bridges WAGON bridges with stringers of heavy logs running abutment to bent and bent to bent, and the 18 August 1835 procession crossed this one. A deck carrying teams over three spans of 18.7 m needs more than the two stringers of a footway, so four under a full-width deck is the load-carrying reading — but the number itself is nobody's, and a source that said three or five would replace it without disturbing anything else on this record. The North Branch record reaches the same value by a harder route, because that crossing is described as a footway in 1833 and has to be argued forward to 1835; this one is described as a wagon bridge from the start.

levels.8-10: Four is our number. What the record gives is the load. The 1883 paper calls both river bridges wagon bridges, with long heavy logs from end to bent and bent to bent. The parade of 18 August 1835 crossed this one. A deck carrying wagons over three spans of 18.7 meters needs more than the two logs of a footbridge. So four under a full deck is the strong reading. But the number is no one's. A record that said three or five would take its place, and change nothing else here. This one was called a wagon bridge from the start.

entries.card: notes:FOUR ROOMS AND A KITCHEN ARE ATTESTED; NO DIMENSION IS. Read…
entries.text: FOUR ROOMS AND A KITCHEN ARE ATTESTED; NO DIMENSION IS. Read as the commonest way four rooms were got under one roof in a frame house of 1834: a 24 x 18 ft story-and-a-half front range, two rooms on the ground floor and two chambers in the half-storey, with the kitchen as a 12 x 14 ft rear ell. 'With a kitchen ... attached to it' is read as an ell rather than a detached cook-house because the advertisement lists the barn and the garden in the same breath and they were plainly separate; a detached kitchen is the other honest reading and would change the plan, not the count. The whole is 24 x 32 ft, inside the D6 band (20x26-24x34 ft). Every number is invented.

levels.8-10: Every number is our guess. Four rooms and a kitchen are known. No size is. We read it as the most common way to get four rooms under one roof in a wood house of 1834. A front part of 24 by 18 feet with a floor and a half: two rooms below, and two bedrooms under the roof. The kitchen is a 12 by 14 foot wing at the back. The ad says with a kitchen attached. We read it as a wing, not a cook house on its own. The ad names the barn and garden in the same line, and those were clearly apart. A kitchen on its own is the other fair reading. It would change the plan, not the count. The whole is 24 by 32 feet, inside our sizes.

entries.card: notes:FOUR ROOMS IS THE EVIDENCE: two below and two in the half-st…
entries.text: FOUR ROOMS IS THE EVIDENCE: two below and two in the half-storey is the reading that keeps the house inside the town's commonest dwelling form; a one-storey four-room plan (the D5 deep plan) is the alternative, and it would be a larger footprint for the same count.

levels.8-10: Four rooms is the proof. Two below and two under the roof keeps the house in the town's most common kind. One floor with four rooms is the other choice. That would be a bigger building for the same number of rooms.

entries.card: notes:FRAME IS DOCUMENTED AND THE FRAMING SYSTEM IS NOT, so the ta…
entries.text: FRAME IS DOCUMENTED AND THE FRAMING SYSTEM IS NOT, so the tag follows the weaker half. The source says 'a two-story frame structure' and no more. Braced rather than balloon frame follows the argument the Sauganash record makes: the sources never use a word that separates the two systems, and this building's date is unpinned across exactly the years when balloon framing was taking over in Chicago, so either is possible. If the date firms up at 1835 rather than 1833, balloon frame becomes the better reading.

levels.8-10: Frame is known, but the kind of frame is not. So the grade follows the weaker half. The record says a frame building of two floors, and no more. We pick the older kind of frame, as for the Sauganash. The records never use a word that tells the two kinds apart. This building's date falls in just the years when the light frame was taking over in Chicago. If the date turns out to be 1835, not 1833, the light frame is the better guess.

entries.card: notes:Fergus names 'the building where the artillery was housed' i…
entries.text: Fergus names 'the building where the artillery was housed' in 1850 and gives it no other name. GUARD ON THE GUNS THEMSELVES: 'The Fort was furnished with three pieces of light-artillery' belongs to the passage about the FIRST fort, which ends 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812'. Nothing reached says what ordnance stood at this fort in 1835, and no gun is modelled.

levels.8-10: Fergus, writing in 1850, names the building where the cannons were kept. He gives no other name. A warning: the line about three small cannon is about the first fort, before 1812. Nothing says what guns were at this fort in 1835. No gun is built.

entries.card: notes:Five sash and one end door reproduce the visible long-wall c…
entries.text: Five sash and one end door reproduce the visible long-wall count of the undated Moss engraving. Their transfer to the unaltered 1835 range is reconstructed, not an attested 1835 opening schedule. The existing sash size and glazing remain reconstructed; precise source perspective is not treated as a metric survey.

levels.8-10: Five windows and one door at the end, to match the long wall in Moss's old print, which has no date. Using them for 1835 is our guess, not a known list of openings in 1835. The window size and panes are our guess too. The picture is not treated as a measure.

entries.card: notes:Four separate capped stack silhouettes are visible: approxim…
entries.text: Four separate capped stack silhouettes are visible: approximately source pixels (904,292), (1019,278), (1114,293), (1202,309). Their metric station/height and which roof slope each penetrates remain reconstruction; using the undated retrospective form in 1835 is inferred.

levels.8-10: Four chimneys with caps can be seen in the picture. Their exact places and heights, and which side of the roof each one comes through, are our guess. Using this picture, which has no date and was made years later, for 1835 is our guess too.

entries.card: notes:Fourteen feet, and INVENTED — see the footprint note for the…
entries.text: Fourteen feet, and INVENTED — see the footprint note for the arithmetic. Eight feet of wagon way and six feet of plank footway beside it, because the owner asked for a crossing for the road and one for the sidewalk and this is the narrowest deck that carries both. It is deliberately NOT read as evidence that this crossing was grander than the town's main bridges: it is one wagon and one footway wide, which is what the ask describes.

levels.8-10: Fourteen feet, and our guess. See the note on its shape for the math. Eight feet for wagons and six feet of boards for people to walk, because the owner asked for a crossing for the road and for the sidewalk. This is the narrowest that carries both. It does not mean this crossing was finer than the town's main bridges. It is one wagon and one path wide, as asked.

entries.card: notes:Frame is attested; the framing METHOD is not. Balloon framin…
entries.text: Frame is attested; the framing METHOD is not. Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and had become the dominant local method by the time this building went up, which makes it the better reading for 1834 — the opposite conclusion from the Sauganash of 1831, where the same reasoning argues for a braced frame. The distinction changes stud rhythm behind the sheathing and is not visible at this level of detail; it is recorded so the dataset's two frame taverns do not silently carry the same value for different reasons.

levels.8-10: Frame is known. The kind of frame is not. The light kind was first used in Chicago in 1832 and 1833. By the time this building went up, it was the usual one here. So it is the better guess for 1834. That is the opposite of the Sauganash of 1831, where the same reason gives the older kind. It cannot be seen from outside. We record it so our two frame inns do not quietly get the same answer for different reasons.

entries.card: notes:Gable is inferred from the frame building's typology and the…
entries.text: Gable is inferred from the frame building's typology and the undated Moss engraving. The previous statement that the absence of a steeple was attested specifically for 1835 is superseded: the text dates that absence to construction in 1833, and the present belfry is a declared reconstruction within the unresolved addition interval. The original gabled type, footprint and wall height are retained; its pitch is a separate reconstructed picture-bounded choice.

levels.8-10: A roof of two slopes is our guess, from its kind and from Moss's old print, which has no date. We used to say it had no steeple in 1835. But the book says it had none when it was built in 1833. The bell tower we build now is our guess, since no one knows when it was added. The roof's shape, the building's size and its wall height stay the same.

entries.card: notes:Gale 1902 p 51 explicitly calls the first Tremont yellow in…
entries.text: Gale 1902 p 51 explicitly calls the first Tremont yellow in the retrospective 1835-framed walk. Retain the pictured three-storey, shuttered canonical form already represented; adopt only this compatible colour evidence as inferred. The monochrome Gifford drawing establishes no pigment. The renderer stock yellow and exact trim tones remain reconstructed. Gale’s smaller two-storey dimensional interpretation is an optional native version, not a dated earlier stage or enlargement chronology.

levels.8-10: A book of 1902 says the first Tremont was yellow, in a walk set in 1835. We keep the three floors and shutters from the picture, and take only the yellow color from the book. Gifford's black and white drawing shows no color. The exact yellow and trim colors are our guess. The book's smaller size with two floors is kept as another version, not as an earlier stage.

entries.card: notes:HIGH OUTER RAKERS, NUMERIC TRIAL. The Andreas 1884 p.631 pla…
entries.text: HIGH OUTER RAKERS, NUMERIC TRIAL. The Andreas 1884 p.631 plate shows prominent long outer braces attaching high on the gallows posts. The old helper attached them only 2.60 m above the deck. A 5.2 m attachment, below the unchanged 6.4 m frame head, tests that pictured relationship. The unchanged 2.85 m nominal run and all timber sections remain reconstructed; this number is not measured from the principal-point-bound provisional camera.

levels.8-10: Long outer braces, a test. The 1884 picture shows long braces on the outside, fixed high on the tall posts. Before, ours were fixed only 2.6 meters above the bridge floor. Now they are fixed at 5.2 meters, below the top of the frame. That tests what the picture shows. The other sizes are our guess, not measured.

entries.card: notes:HORIZONTAL-BOARD PARAPETS. The public-domain plate published…
entries.text: HORIZONTAL-BOARD PARAPETS. The public-domain plate published in Andreas in 1884, page 631, draws broad side parapets with horizontal joints along the approaches and closed draw. This is retrospective pictorial form, inferred for the 1835 bridge rather than a contemporary specification, coordinate, footprint dimension or surveyed height. Retain the existing 0.95 m overall parapet height and approximately 2.2 m post bays; five 162 mm courses, 40 mm thickness, 10 mm gaps, 40 mm lower clearance and 200 by 60 mm cap are reconstructed scantlings. Panels and caps stop at post bays, draw ends and the existing two-leaf meeting line. Post heads end at 0.89 m under the cap. The old pole-rail description records the prior default detail. The flat deck, original cribs and every existing height/placement control remain unchanged; the central rise, approaches, mechanism and camera remain unresolved. No accepted match is claimed.

levels.8-10: Side walls of boards laid flat. A picture printed in a book in 1884 shows wide side walls with flat boards along the bridge. That picture was drawn later, so using it for 1835 is a guess. The height of the side wall stays at 0.95 meters, with posts about 2.2 meters apart. The sizes of the boards and caps are our guess. Nothing else on the bridge changes. We do not claim a match.

entries.card: notes:HOW TALL THE GALLOWS STOOD IS THE MOST VISIBLE UNKNOWN IN TH…
entries.text: HOW TALL THE GALLOWS STOOD IS THE MOST VISIBLE UNKNOWN IN THIS DATASET. No source gives the height, the section, the bracing or the tackle of these frames; what survives is that they were tall enough to be frightening at night and strong enough to hold a sixty-foot draw suspended for forty-eight hours. 6.4 m above the deck — about twenty-one feet — is the archetype's own number, chosen so that a frame is unmistakably a gallows against the sky and not a gatepost, and it is not a finding. THE REASON IT IS BUILT AT ALL, rather than declared absent: the confidence view exists exactly for this. A dithered translucent frame says 'this shape is ours' in a way no footnote can, and leaving the frames out would tell a visitor the town's one piece of engineering was a plain causeway, which is a stronger false claim than a tagged guess. The alternative reading was on this record for a few hours on 2026-08-11 and is recorded here because it is a real argument: build nothing, declare it, and let the liberties document carry the frames in prose. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the February 1834 proposals Andreas mentions, the trustees' specification, the twenty-five-dollar premium drawing, or any period view of the river mouth looking west.

levels.8-10: How tall the tall frames over the bridge stood is the biggest thing we can see but do not know. No record gives their height, shape or ropes. We know they were tall enough to look scary at night, and strong enough to hold the sixty-foot bridge part up for two days. 6.4 meters, about 21 feet, is our usual number. It makes a frame look like a lifting frame, not a gate post. It is not a finding. We build them anyway, see-through in the confidence view, to say this shape is ours. Leaving them out would say the bridge was just a plain road over the water, and that would be more wrong. Plans from 1834, or any old picture of the river mouth, could settle it.

entries.card: notes:HUBBARD SAYS TWO STOREYS OF THE FACTOR HOUSE; THIS RECORD SA…
entries.text: HUBBARD SAYS TWO STOREYS OF THE FACTOR HOUSE; THIS RECORD SAYS THEY ARE BLOCK A'S, AND THAT SECOND STEP IS THE INFERENCE. The prose names one building — 'the "Factor House", a two-story, squared-log structure' — and the plate letters that name against three blocks, so which of the three carries the storeys is not on the sheet. A is taken to be it on two grounds stated rather than assumed: the label's first letter stands about 2 m clear of A's north-east end and touches no other block, and A at 20.4 x 7.9 m is the only one of the three a two-storey dwelling-and-store will fit (B is a 16.6 x 5.1 m bar set across it, C is 6.7 x 5.0 m). Neither ground is proof and the grade is `inferred` because of it. THE ALTERNATIVE THE TICKET ALLOWED — 'not determinable, so the storey count is inferred from the type' — would have put ONE storey here on no evidence at all while a witness was sitting on the shelf saying two; taking the witness and writing down exactly how far it had to be carried is the better of the two answers, and this note is that distance.

levels.8-10: Hubbard says the trading house had two floors. We say the two floors are block A's, and that is our guess. Hubbard names one building, a two-floor house of squared logs. The plan writes that name over three blocks. So which block it is, is not on the map. We pick A for two reasons. The label starts just past A's corner and touches no other block. And A is the only one big enough for a home and store with two floors. Neither reason is proof. The other way would have put one floor here on no proof at all, while a man who saw it said two. Taking his word, and saying how far we had to carry it, is the better answer.

entries.card: notes:HUBBARD'S ADJECTIVE IS THE WHOLE OF THE EVIDENCE AND IT IS N…
entries.text: HUBBARD'S ADJECTIVE IS THE WHOLE OF THE EVIDENCE AND IT IS NOT A MATERIAL. He calls them 'rude wash-houses', which says rough and says nothing about what they were rough in. Plank — sawn boards nailed up vertically with the gaps showing — is the archetype's reading of a rough working building put up quickly for a wet trade, and it is preferred to log here for one stated reason: a laundry wants air and light through its walls and a notched log pen gives neither. The reasoning is the inference; nobody wrote it down.

levels.8-10: Hubbard's one word is all we have, and it does not say what it was made of. He calls them rough wash houses. That says rough, but not rough in what. We build it of boards nailed up and down, with gaps between. That is our idea of a rough work building put up fast for wet work. We pick it over logs for one reason. A wash house wants air and light through its walls, and a log building gives neither. That is our reason. No one wrote it down.

entries.text: Hubbard calls it 'the military barn' and the 1830 plan draws the Big Barn with Cupola inside the fort's own fenced ground, beside the Cultivated Field belonging to The Fort. The post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836 (the stockade's own occupants block, after Andreas), so on 1 July 1835 its service buildings were the garrison's; the people are seated on the stockade and are not repeated here.

levels.8-10: Hubbard calls it the military barn. The 1830 plan draws the Big Barn with Cupola inside the fort's fence, by the fort's field. levels.8-10: Hubbard calls it the military barn, in those words. The plan calls it the Big Barn with Cupola and draws it inside the fort's fence, next to the field that belonged to the fort. entries.text: Hubbard names 'the sutler's store' in 1827 and the 1855 photograph key letters 'D is the Sutler's'. That building is at the other end of the fort from this one, so it is either a second building this project does not model or a confused memory; either way no quartermaster's quarters is built, because a source that cannot decide between two names is not evidence for either.

levels.8-10: Hubbard names the fort's store in 1827, and the 1855 list names it too. There is another answer, and it is not settled. In 1850 Robert Fergus told of a building just east of the blockhouse. He said it was the rooms of the quartermaster or the fort's store. That is at the other end of the fort. So it is a second building we do not build, or a mixed-up memory. We build no quartermaster's rooms. A record that cannot pick between two names is not proof of either.

entries.text: Hubbard: 'the magazine, of brick'. One of only two brick buildings in the fort. GUARD ON A TEMPTING PARALLEL: the 1803 War Department instruction for this class of post specified 'the magazines for powder to be of brick of a conic figure', which is quoted in the same literature - but that is the specification for the FIRST fort, and it is not evidence that this magazine was conical. It is built as a plain gabled block.

levels.8-10: Hubbard says the powder house was of brick. It is one of only two brick buildings in the fort. An order from 1803 said powder houses should be brick and shaped like a cone. But that was for the first fort. It does not prove this one was a cone. It is built as a plain block with a roof of two slopes.

Fergus puts the artillery house on the east of the parade with the barracks and the storehouse; the 1830 plan draws only one range on that side and this project reads that range as the barracks, because Hubbard's 1827 sentence fixes the barracks there and the sutler's north of it. So there is no drawn building for this record to sit on. It is placed inside the east curtain at the south end - the one part of that side the plan leaves empty - clear of the barracks by about a metre and of the south wall by about three. Every one of those numbers is ours.

levels.8-10: Made up, on a side we know. Fergus puts the gun house on the east side of the parade ground, with the barracks and the store house. The 1830 plan draws just one building on that side, and we read it as the barracks. So there is no drawn building for this one. We put it at the south end of the east wall, the one empty spot. Every number is ours.

This record draws a whole building on the strength of a premises, which is the single biggest liberty in it.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED, AND DELIBERATELY THE LARGEST RECTANGLE IN THIS PAR…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND DELIBERATELY THE LARGEST RECTANGLE IN THIS PARCEL. 15.24 x 9.144 m is 50 x 30 ft. No source gives this building a dimension, but the one thing the source does say about it is a statement about VOLUME: Hubbard packed a season's work of some five thousand hogs inside it in 1834, which is not a season a man gets through in a 40 x 25 ft shop. The rectangle is scaled up from the parcel's borrowed 40 x 25 ft on that reasoning alone. THAT REASONING IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS and the record should say so: a packing season is months long, hogs come in and barrels go out continuously, and the building needed to hold a day's work rather than a season's. The documented 55 ft cap on South Water Street lots is not evidence about Lake Street and is not applied.

levels.8-10: Our guess, and on purpose the biggest box on this land. 50 by 30 feet. No record gives its size. But the one thing the record does say is about how much it held. Hubbard packed about five thousand hogs in it in the season of 1834. A man does not do that in a 40 by 25 foot shop. So the box is made bigger for that reason alone. That reason is weaker than it looks, and we should say so. A packing season lasts months. Hogs come in and barrels go out all the time. The building needed to hold a day's work, not a season's. The 55 foot limit on South Water lots does not apply to Lake Street.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED, AND INVENTED AS A CABIN RATHER THAN AS A BARN, whi…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND INVENTED AS A CABIN RATHER THAN AS A BARN, which is the one thing about this footprint that is not free. Andreas gives no dimension. 6.1 x 4.88 m is 20 x 16 ft — a single-pen log cabin, the smallest unit of dwelling this settlement built — because what the source describes is a house that stopped being a house: Beaubien did not build a barn, he moved out and left one. Drawing this as a barn-sized building would assert a rebuilding nobody records. 20 ft is borrowed from Hogan's store, the one log footprint in this dataset with a documented dimension, and 16 ft is the shallower of the two common single-pen depths. Every number is invented and this polygon cites no sources.

levels.8-10: Made up, and made as a cabin, not a barn. Andreas gives no size. 20 by 16 feet is a one-room log cabin, the smallest home built here. The book tells of a house that became a barn. Beaubien did not build a barn. He moved out and left the cabin as one. So we keep it cabin-sized. 20 feet comes from Hogan's store, and 16 feet is a common depth. Every number is made up.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED, AND THE ARITHMETIC BEHIND IT IS STATED SO IT CAN B…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND THE ARITHMETIC BEHIND IT IS STATED SO IT CAN BE ARGUED WITH. No source reached gives this building a dimension. What IS documented is its cost, about $900, and its storey count, two - and this dataset now holds two contemporary buildings whose cost AND area are both attested: the First Presbyterian Church at $600 for 1,000 sq ft ($0.60/sq ft) and St Mary's at $400 for 875 sq ft ($0.46/sq ft). Two storeys at the midpoint of that range, about $0.55 per square foot, buys roughly 1,600 sq ft of floor, i.e. about 800 sq ft per storey. 30 x 25 ft is 750 sq ft, which at $0.55 gives $825 against the attested $900 - close, and on the conservative side. 9.144 x 7.62 m is 30 x 25 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated. THIS IS STILL AN INVENTION AND IT IS TAGGED AS ONE. The cost-per-square-foot of a two-storey building is not the cost-per-square-foot of a single-storey one (a second floor is cheap relative to a roof and a foundation, which would make the real building BIGGER than this), and both reference figures rest on the citation problem set out in the Presbyterian record's research note. The 25 ft depth is additionally borrowed - it is the depth of both churches and of the rectangle four other records in this dataset use - so the shape is a claim about the type and not about this building.

levels.8-10: Our guess, and the math behind it is given so it can be argued with. No record gives its size. What is known is its cost, about $900, and that it had two floors. We also know the cost and size of two other buildings of the time. The Presbyterian church cost $600 for 1,000 square feet. St Mary's cost $400 for 875 square feet. In between, about 55 cents a square foot, $900 buys about 1,600 square feet, or 800 a floor. 30 by 25 feet is 750 square feet, a little under. That is close, and on the safe side. It is still a guess, marked as one. A second floor costs less than a roof and base, so the real building may have been bigger. The 25 foot depth is borrowed too, from both churches.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED, AND THE ONE ATTRIBUTE HERE THAT A SOURCE COULD EAS…

Frame is taken because the works at this station were federal contract carpentry under Samuel Jackson and because a dwelling raised beside a masonry tower in 1832 on the Michigan shore is as likely to be sawn frame as it is to be logs — which is an argument about the decade and the paymaster, not about this house. Log would be the equally defensible reading, and that is what makes this reconstructed rather than inferred — the generator builds it at 1.0 confidence, which is the massing the eye should read as ours. L288 owns it.

levels.8-10: Made up, and a record could easily have told us. Nothing says what the house was built of. We chose sawn wood. The work here was done by hired carpenters under Samuel Jackson, for the government. A house next to a stone tower in 1832 could just as well be wood or logs. That is a guess about the time and who paid, not about this house. Logs would be just as fair a guess.

Measured under this deck the water is 0.17 m deep on the deck's own centre line and 0.38 m at its edges, so half a metre of air is the same reading here as there. Nothing passed under it; the branch bridges' documented six feet is a winter road under a river crossing and has no business on a drain.

levels.8-10: Our guess, taken from the other crossing, since both cross the same kind of water. Our notes put the bottom of these wet ditches 1.5 to 3 feet below the land around them. So a deck at street level sits about half a meter over the water. Under this deck the water is only 0.17 to 0.38 meters deep. Nothing passed under it. The six feet under the big river bridges was for a winter road, and does not fit a ditch.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED, and the same borrowed rectangle this parcel uses o…
entries.text: INVENTED, and the same borrowed rectangle this parcel uses on every South Water store whose size nobody recorded: 12.192 x 7.62 m is 40 x 25 ft, the frontage attested for the Green Tree Tavern and the Western Hotel's front, and the depth derived from the Green Tree's attested room module. Andreas gives this building no dimension; the 26 November 1833 issue gives none either. The one documented constraint is the street's: South Water lots were 55 ft wide (Andreas), so a single-lot building here cannot have fronted more than 55 ft, and 40 ft sits inside that. IT IS SIZED AS A WHOLE BUILDING, NOT AS AN OFFICE, and that is a decision the evidence supports rather than a default: Andreas says Calhoun 'secured an office IN a building', so the press occupied part of a larger structure, and the same first issue advertises 'the New Store on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' — see this record's occupants block. A building holding a store and a printing office is not a shed.

levels.8-10: Made up. It is 40 by 25 feet, the same size we use for every store on South Water whose size no one wrote down. That comes from a hotel nearby. Neither Andreas nor the paper gives a size. Lots here were 55 feet wide, so 40 fits. It is built as a whole building, not just an office. Andreas says Calhoun got an office in a building, so the press was in part of a bigger house. The same first paper has an ad for the new store on that same corner. A building with a store and a print shop is not a shed.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED, but invented inside a described plan rather than f…
entries.text: INVENTED, but invented inside a described plan rather than freely: Andreas says two rooms and says log, so the building is a double pen, and 9.144 x 5.486 m is 30 x 18 ft, two rooms of about 15 x 18 ft. THE NUMBER IS DELIBERATELY SMALLER THAN THE ONE COMPARABLE BUILDING THIS DATASET HAS EVIDENCE FOR. Hogan's store, the only log footprint here that is documented, is 45 x 20 ft and held a store and a post office side by side, and Andreas offers that size as an example of how LITTLE room the town needed. A house Andreas describes only as 'a two roomed log house' should not be modelled as large as that, so the frontage is cut by a third and the depth by two feet. The reasoning is about the type; nothing in it is about this building. The 55 ft South Water lot width is a documented cap and this sits well inside it.

levels.8-10: Our guess, but inside a known plan. Andreas says two rooms and says logs. So it is two log rooms side by side. 30 by 18 feet is two rooms of about 15 by 18 feet. It is smaller than the one like it that we know. Hogan's log store is 45 by 20 feet, and held a store and a post office. Andreas uses that size to show how little room the town needed. A house he calls only a log house of two rooms should not be as big. So the front is cut by a third and the depth by two feet. That is a reason about its kind, not this building. A lot on South Water was 55 feet wide, and this fits well inside.

levels.8-10: Every number is our guess. 8 by 14 feet fits our sizes for a small work shed. Hides are hung to dry out of the sun and rain. That wants a long, narrow shed with air through it, not a room. Nothing says this yard had a drying shed.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. 2.4384 x 4.2672 m is 8 x 14 ft, inside family A5's…
entries.text: INVENTED. 2.4384 x 4.2672 m is 8 x 14 ft, inside family A5's band (6-8 ft front, 12-16 ft deep) - the crosswalk's small mixed utility outbuilding. Soap is boiled with lye, lye is leached from wood ash, and ash is kept dry under its own roof or it is worthless. The works' own footprint note allows 'an ash leach' inside the main shed; this building is the store the leach draws on, which is the part that has to stand out of the rain. Nothing states that this works had one. Every number is invented.

levels.8-10: Made up. It is 8 by 14 feet, a small shed. Soap is boiled with lye, and lye comes from soaking wood ash. Ash must stay dry under a roof, or it is no good. So this is the shed that keeps the ash dry. Nothing says this soap works had one. Every number is made up.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. 2.4384 x 4.8768 m is 8 x 16 ft, inside family A4's…
entries.text: INVENTED. 2.4384 x 4.8768 m is 8 x 16 ft, inside family A4's band (6-8 ft front, 12-18 ft deep) - the crosswalk's woodshed and storage outbuilding, which is what a salt house is. The size is the family's, not a reading: nothing states that this plant had a salt house, let alone how big it was. What can be said for a small one is that salt came up the lake in barrels and was used by the barrel, so the building is a store between the landing and the packing floor rather than a warehouse. Every number is invented and the polygon cites no sources.

levels.8-10: Our guess. 8 by 16 feet fits our sizes for a wood shed or store shed, which is what a salt house is. The size is from our list. Nothing says this plant had a salt house, or how big. What we can say is that salt came up the lake in barrels and was used by the barrel. So this is a small store between the landing and the packing floor, not a big store house. Every number is our guess, and no record is given.

A bark shed is a store: hemlock or oak bark brought in, kept dry, and ground as it is wanted. The size is the family's and nothing states that this yard had a bark shed at all. Every number is invented.

levels.8-10: Every number is our guess. 8 by 16 feet fits our sizes for a wood shed or a store shed. A bark shed was a store. Bark from trees was brought in, kept dry, and ground up when it was needed. The size is from our list. Nothing says this yard had a bark shed at all.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. 5.4864 x 7.9248 m is 18 x 26 ft, the floor of fami…
entries.text: INVENTED. 5.4864 x 7.9248 m is 18 x 26 ft, the floor of family A1's band (18-26 ft front, 20-32 ft deep) - the crosswalk's lofted stable, the family whose visible signature is a stable door and ventilation. The floor of the band rather than the middle of it, because this is a holding shed for stock waiting to be killed and for the plant's own draught oxen, not a livery. The documented throughput constrains the order of magnitude and nothing finer: 300 cattle across a whole season is a few beasts standing at a time, not a herd. Every number is invented.

levels.8-10: Every number is our guess. 18 by 26 feet is the smallest of our sizes for a stable with a loft. Smallest, because this is a shed for animals waiting to be killed, and for the plant's own work oxen, not a stable for hire. 300 cattle in a whole season is a few animals at a time, not a herd.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING ANY DIMENSIO…
entries.text: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING ANY DIMENSION, a plan, or a room count. 14 x 9 m is about 46 x 30 ft, sized between the Green Tree's 40 x 25 ft - itself derived from a room module rather than measured - and the Western Hotel's attested 40 ft front, on the reasoning that this was Mark Beaubien's second and later house, built in the boom rather than at the forks in 1831, and that it was carrying a hotel and a public room. None of that is evidence about this building. The rectangle is a rectangle because no source describes a plan, and no sources are cited on this attribute because none supports it. TO RESOLVE: the Chicago Democrat and the Chicago American, in both of which this house was a standing address - Dr. Temple's stage line advertised that seats could be taken here - and where a hotel advertisement of the ordinary period kind would count its rooms.

levels.8-10: Made up. No record gives a size, a plan or how many rooms. It is about 46 by 30 feet. That is between two hotels nearby, one 40 by 25 feet and one with a 40-foot front. This was Beaubien's second, later house, built while the town was booming. It held a hotel and a public room. None of that is proof about this building. Old papers could settle it. The house was an address in both of the town's papers, and a hotel ad of the time would count its rooms.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. No source describes a window on this building. Fiv…
entries.text: INVENTED. No source describes a window on this building. Five openings across 40 ft is 8 ft per bay, which is an ordinary period rhythm and is what the archetype's own frontage rule would give at this width if it were allowed an odd number; the archetype derives four from the frontage, and four is refused with a centre-passage front because a centred door needs an odd count. So the number is a consequence of the archetype's grammar and of the choice of `plan` above, not a finding. A depiction or a description of the elevation would settle it.

levels.8-10: Made up. No record tells of a window. Five windows across 40 feet puts one every 8 feet, a usual spacing then. Our builder would give four, but a door in the middle needs an odd number. So five comes from how we build, not from a finding. A picture or a description could settle it.

entries.text: INVENTED. No source describes an opening on this building. Three - a centred door with one window either side, repeated above - is the plainest symmetrical front the archetype will build, and the archetype would otherwise derive three from the 30 ft frontage anyway, so the number is at least not inflated. It is still a guess about a facade nobody described.

levels.8-10: Our guess. No record tells of a door or window on this building. Three across, a door in the middle with a window on each side, and the same above, is the plainest even front we build. Our builder would pick three for a 30 foot front anyway, so the number is not made bigger. It is still a guess about a front no one told of.

entries.text: INVENTED. No source gives this building a dimension. 8.0 x 5.0 m is about 26 x 16 ft, which is a shed that will hold the three field pieces a post of this class carried and their carriages, and it is sized to fit the gap the plan leaves rather than from any evidence.

levels.8-10: Made up. No record gives a size. It is about 26 by 16 feet, a shed big enough for three small cannon and their carts. We sized it to fit the empty spot, not from proof.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. No source gives this building a dimension. It is t…
entries.text: INVENTED. No source gives this building a dimension. It is the parcel's borrowed rectangle turned end-on: 12.192 m of frontage along Dearborn and 7.62 m of depth back from it, which is 40 x 25 ft — the frontage attested for the Green Tree Tavern and the Western Hotel and the depth derived from the Green Tree's room module. THE ONE THING THE USE ARGUES FOR IS A CLEAR SPAN: an auction room is one room with a crowd standing in it, not a partitioned store, so a rectangle with no internal structure is at least the right kind of shape. That is an argument about the type and not about this building, and the polygon carries no evidence.

levels.8-10: Made up. No record gives a size. It is 40 by 25 feet, borrowed from two hotels in town. An auction room is one big room full of standing people, with no walls inside. So a plain box is at least the right kind of shape. That comes from what the room was for, not from a record of it.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. No source gives this building's size, and the 1830…
entries.text: INVENTED. No source gives this building's size, and the 1830 plan does not draw it. 4.57 x 3.66 m is fifteen by twelve feet, which is a powder magazine for a two-company post and nothing more than that. The reason there is a polygon at all is that the alternative is not modelling a brick building two sources describe; the reason it is graded conjectural is that a visitor looking at this outline is looking at our arithmetic.

levels.8-10: Our guess. No record gives its size, and the plan does not draw it. 15 by 12 feet is a powder house for a fort this size, and no more. We build it because two records tell of a brick building. But what you see of its shape is our math.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. No source places Harmon's cabin. What is known is…
entries.text: INVENTED. No source places Harmon's cabin. What is known is negative: he pre-empted a hundred and forty acres whose northern boundary was near Sixteenth Street, which is two kilometres south of the modelled ground and is a farm rather than a residence. This record sits in the South Division outer band where the reconstruction recipes put older log dwellings, at the first free position the placement rule found. It is a guess inside the right district.

levels.8-10: Our guess. No record says where Harmon's cabin was. What we know is where it was not. His land of 140 acres went up to about Sixteenth Street. That is two kilometers south of the town we build, and a farm, not a home. This cabin sits on the south side, where we put older log homes. It is a guess inside the right part of town.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. No source reached gives this tower a diameter, a p…
entries.text: INVENTED. No source reached gives this tower a diameter, a plan or a wall thickness. 5.6 m - about eighteen feet - is the base a forty-foot masonry tower of the period needs, and the square polygon is the archetype's convention for a round shaft: the generator refuses a tower whose footprint is not square and builds a twelve-sided tapering shaft inside it. What a visitor sees of this outline is entirely ours. CURRENT PICTURE-BOUNDED PROTOTYPE: replace the former invented 5.6 m square with a reconstructed 3.04 m physical diameter, in local bounds 1.28 to 4.32 m on both axes, keeping the same centre at (2.8, 2.8), surveyed origin and world placement. The Castelnau harbour print constrains visible proportions under a provisional camera; it does not measure a historical diameter or plan. This is the saved visible prototype, not an accepted match.

levels.8-10: Made up. No record gives the tower's width or shape. At first we made it 5.6 meters wide, what a 40-foot stone tower of the time would need. Now it is about 3 meters across, to fit an old print of the harbor. The middle stays in the same spot. The print helps with how it looks, but it gives no true size. This is our best try so far, not a match.

entries.card: notes:INVENTED. Nothing describes an opening. A trading post is a…
entries.text: INVENTED. Nothing describes an opening. A trading post is a room goods and people went in and out of on foot, and `man` is the archetype's door for one person and an armful of goods; a wider door would claim wagon trade at this building, which nothing records.

levels.8-10: Made up. Nothing tells of a door. People walked in and out of a trading post with goods in their arms. So it gets a door for one person. A wider door would claim wagons came here, and nothing says so.

A druggist's shop is the smallest kind of store on the street, which is the only reason the small rectangle rather than the 40 x 25 ft one is used. levels.8-10: The house was painted white, so it had boards on the outside. Long boards that lap over each other were the usual then. Not known for sure.

entries.card: notes:In operation as a public house throughout the scene window:…
entries.text: In operation as a public house throughout the scene window: bar-room serving as office and reception, dining room cleared for dancing, chambers above and lodging in the attic when full. Renamed the Chicago Hotel by 1844, which is after the scene date and is a change of sign, not of trade.

levels.8-10: It was an inn all through these years. The bar room was the office and front desk. The dining room was cleared for dancing. There were rooms above, and beds in the attic when it was full. By 1844 it was called the Chicago Hotel. That is after 1835, and only a new sign, not a new trade.

entries.card: notes:Ingersoll's tenancy is given as 1834-1837, which covers 1835…
entries.text: Ingersoll's tenancy is given as 1834-1837, which covers 1835-07-01, with Martin M. Ford associated. DRLOIH's list — 'initially by David Clark and then by Edward Parsons' — carries no dates and is compatible rather than contradictory: Clark (or Clock) is named elsewhere as the landlord who opened the house in 1833, before Ingersoll.

levels.8-10: Ingersoll ran it from 1834 to 1837, which covers 1 July 1835, with Martin Ford. A book lists David Clark and then Edward Parsons, with no dates. That fits too. Clark is named as the man who opened the inn in 1833, before Ingersoll.

levels.8-10: How tall the door is, used to size the window. The picture has no scale. So the door is about as tall as a person, our usual, not a measure.

entries.card: notes:Interpretive placement on a GENERATED lot, not a recovered p…

The lot geometry is the K7 plat module's — this project has never read Thompson's numbering off a sheet, and the side lot lines and the alley are conjectural even where the block face is not. The whole footprint — not its centre — is tested against the platted street corridors, against its own lot lines and against every other footprint in the dataset, so no invented building of this parcel stands in the roadway; clearing the roadway is not the same as standing on a recovered lot.

entries.text: Juliette Kinzie, inside it in 1831: 'The fort was inclosed by high pickets, with bastions at the alternate angles.' Andreas: 'a square stockade'. A picket line - upright posts set in the ground - is what both describe, and it is the one thing about this wall that two sources state rather than imply.

levels.8-10: Juliette Kinzie lived inside it in 1831. She wrote that the fort was fenced in by high posts, with strong corners at every other corner. A book calls it a square fence of posts. A line of tall posts set in the ground is what both tell of. It is the one thing about this wall that two records say.

levels.8-10: Kinzie wrote in 1831 about the soldiers' root houses on the bank west of the fort. So whose they were is in her words. This is the second one she tells of. Where it stood is not said. entries.card: notes:Log remains the existing inferred reading from settlement bu…
entries.text: Log remains the existing inferred reading from settlement building practice, not an attested material for this residence. Beaubien’s 1817 purchase concerned the separate Dean house; 1822 is an earliest allowed date rather than a known building year. Wentworth’s annotation beneath the keyed 1831 panorama places its Beaubien house near the same northeast corner used for this sale-located dwelling, making this the preferred working identification at inferred confidence. Both locators come from Wentworth, not independent witnesses. The building’s lineage and July 1835 appearance remain unresolved. No pictured material, Factory House description or numerical form is transferred here.

levels.8-10: Logs are still our guess from how people built here. They are not known for this house. Beaubien's 1817 buy was a different house, the Dean house. 1822 is the earliest it could be, not a known year it was built. Wentworth wrote a note under his 1831 picture of the town. It puts Beaubien's house near the same corner as this one. So this is our best guess for which house it is. Both clues come from Wentworth, not from two different people. Where the house came from and how it looked in July 1835 are still not known. Nothing from a picture or from the trading house is used here.

entries.card: notes:MARCH 1832, AND THE YEAR THIS RECORD CITED ANDREAS FOR IS NO…
entries.text: MARCH 1832, AND THE YEAR THIS RECORD CITED ANDREAS FOR IS NOT A YEAR ANDREAS GIVES. Until 2026-08-16 the range opened at 1833-03-01, under a note reading 'MARCH 1833 IS ATTESTED AS A MONTH AND CONTESTED AS A YEAR ... The dossier notes that some accounts give 1832 instead'. Andreas gives 1832 in both places he treats the pen, and 1833 in neither. The narrative: 'The result of this generosity on the part of the State was seen in March, 1832, when, through the architectural skill of Samuel Miller, contractor, there arose upon the southwest corner of the square, the so-called "estray-pen." Although sometimes designated and dignified as "the first public building ever erected in Chicago," the "pen" was a small wooden enclosure and quite roofless' (Andreas I scan p. 365). The chronological index: the entry 'First public building (the "Estray Pen") erected' stands under the heading 1832, between '1832 - (January) - First Methodist quarterly meeting' and '(April) - First street leading to the lake laid out' (scan p. 1315). The month was read off that index correctly and the year off the wrong heading. NOTHING IN THE SCENE MOVES. The pen stands on 1835-07-01 under either reading and is roofless under both - which is why it is worth saying that the correction is to the CITATION and not to the town: a note that cites a source for a value the source does not carry is wrong in the way this project cares most about, whether or not anything visible depends on it. THE RANGE IS NOW WIDE, AND HONESTLY SO: 1832-03-01 is the first day of the attested month in the attested year, and 1835-12-31 remains A HOUSEKEEPING BOUND, NOT A REMOVAL DATE. Nothing reached says when the pen came down. What IS attested is that its role as a place of confinement ended in the fall of 1833 when the log jail went up at the other corner of the same block - which is a change of use, not of fabric, and does not close the phase. ROADMAP T-I3.

levels.8-10: March 1832. Our record used to say 1833 and cite a book for it, but the book never gives 1833. It gives 1832 both times it tells of the pen. It says that in March 1832, Samuel Miller built the so-called stray pen on the corner of the square. People called it the first public building in Chicago. It was a small wooden fence with no roof. The book's list of dates puts it under 1832 too. We read the month right but the year from the wrong line. Nothing in the scene changes. The pen stands in July 1835, with no roof, either way. We fix it because citing a book for something it does not say is the kind of mistake this project cares about most. The end date is just where our record stops. The pen stopped holding prisoners in the fall of 1833, when the log jail went up nearby.

entries.card: notes:MEASURED, AND LARGER THAN A BLOCKHOUSE OUGHT TO BE. 14.52 x…
entries.text: MEASURED, AND LARGER THAN A BLOCKHOUSE OUGHT TO BE. 14.52 x 9.80 m is about 48 x 32 ft, read off the 1830 plan at the derived scale after correcting for the fort's rotation. A period blockhouse is usually 20 to 30 ft square, so this is either an unusually large one or - more likely - the plate drawing the blockhouse together with the return of the curtain round it as a single heavy block. The measurement is recorded rather than quietly shrunk to the expected size, because shrinking it would be substituting a typology for the only plan that exists. Carry +/-25 percent and read the note.

levels.8-10: Measured, and bigger than a blockhouse should be. It is about 48 by 32 feet, read from the 1830 plan. A blockhouse then was usually 20 to 30 feet square. So either this one was big, or, more likely, the plan drew the blockhouse and the wall around it as one heavy block. We keep the measure, not shrink it to the usual size. Shrinking it would put a rule of thumb ahead of the only plan we have. It could be off by a quarter.

entries.card: notes:NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE and both are the honest bou…
entries.text: NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE and both are the honest bounds of what is attested. THE START is McKee's own arrival: Andreas has him engaged as the agency blacksmith the 1821 treaty required and reaching Fort Dearborn in June 1823, finding 'but two houses on the north side of the river' and building the fourth himself. 1823 is the first year he can have kept a house here and it is the year the neighbouring shop record opens on for the same reason. THE END IS THE HONEST MINIMUM, and it is the weakest line on this record: Andreas's vicinity list describes the settlement about 1830 and Wau-Bun the ring in 1831, and after that nothing names this building. The argument for 1835 is the argument the shop record makes — a Government smith was still owed to the Potawatomi under the 1821 and 1833 treaties — and it is an argument about an obligation rather than about a house. Tagged inferred for that reason.

levels.8-10: No record dates either end. Both are the honest limits of what is known. The start is McKee's own arrival. A book says he was hired as the blacksmith the 1821 treaty called for. He reached Fort Dearborn in June 1823, and found only two houses on the north side of the river. He built the fourth himself. 1823 is the first year he could have kept a house here. The end is the weakest line in this record. A book tells of the place about 1830, and Wau-Bun in 1831. After that, nothing names this building. The case for 1835 is that the Potawatomi were still owed a blacksmith by the treaties of 1821 and 1833. That is about a promise, not a house. So it is marked as our guess.

entries.text: NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE. THE START is the light itself: Samuel Jackson completed the second tower in 1832, and the keepership Andreas records — Samuel Lasby, the first keeper, 'at $350 a year with quarters' — is an office that exists from the night the light was first kept. A station's quarters are not later than its light. THE END is the scene's own window and not a statement about the building: nothing reached says when these quarters were replaced, and the 1835-12-31 bound is the honest limit of what this project's corpus covers rather than a fate. Both ends are inferred for those reasons.

levels.8-10: No record dates either end. The start is the light itself. Samuel Jackson finished the second tower in 1832. Samuel Lasby was the first keeper, paid $350 a year, with a place to live. A keeper's house is not newer than its light. The end is just where our record stops, not when the house came down. Both ends are our guess.

entries.card: notes:NO SOURCE DATES THIS BUILDING AT EITHER END; both dates are…
entries.text: NO SOURCE DATES THIS BUILDING AT EITHER END; both dates are the honest bounds of what is attested. THE START: Andreas says only 'After the second Fort Dearborn was built, David McKee was appointed Government blacksmith, his shop being situated near the Agency House, at the foot of State Street' — the fort was rebuilt in 1816 — but the same book fixes McKee's arrival: he was engaged as the agency blacksmith the 1821 treaty required and, by his own recollection, reached Fort Dearborn in June 1823, finding 'but two houses on the north side of the river' and building the fourth himself. 1823 is therefore the first year the shop can have stood under him, and the range opens there rather than at 1816. THE END IS THE HONEST MINIMUM. The shop is attested standing around 1830 — 'In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell' — and in 1831 Wau-Bun still describes the ring of agency log residences with a blacksmith among them. After that nothing. McKee himself had other work by then; he was carrying the Government mail to Fort Wayne monthly from 1827-28 and later farmed on the Des Plaines. A GOVERNMENT SMITH WAS STILL OWED TO THE POTAWATOMI IN 1835 under the 1821 and 1833 treaties, which is the argument for the shop still standing on the scene date, and it is an argument about an obligation rather than about a building. Tagged inferred for that reason.

levels.8-10: No record dates this building at either end. Andreas says David McKee was the government's blacksmith, with a shop near the Agency House. McKee came here in June 1823, so that is the first year the shop could stand. Records show the shop around 1830 and 1831. After that, nothing. McKee had other work by then. He carried the mail from 1827, and later farmed. But by treaties of 1821 and 1833, the Potawatomi were still owed a government blacksmith in 1835. That is why we think the shop still stood. It is a guess about a promise, not about a building.

entries.card: notes:NOBODY DESCRIBED THE MIDDLE OF THIS BRIDGE AND ZERO IS THE A…
entries.text: NOBODY DESCRIBED THE MIDDLE OF THIS BRIDGE AND ZERO IS THE ANSWER THAT INVENTS LEAST. The archetype accepts 0 explicitly — 'a short crossing lands abutment to abutment with nothing in the water' — and without a stated count it would fall back to a spacing of 4.5 m and put a support in the middle of an 8 m span. An 8 m run of log stringers needs no intermediate bent; the branch bridges needed two each over 56 and 72 m. So the count is inference from the span, and it keeps a pier out of a stream nobody says had one.

levels.8-10: No one told of the middle of this bridge, and none is the answer that makes up least. Our builder allows it: a short crossing goes end to end with nothing in the water. Without a number, it would put a support in the middle of an 8 meter span. An 8 meter log needs no support in the middle. The river bridges needed two each over 56 and 72 meters. So the number comes from the span, and keeps a post out of a stream no one says had one.

The archetype places stacks against the ridge, and this structure has no ridge. Inferred from the construction state rather than from any statement.

levels.8-10: This is not how many chimneys the finished hotel had. No one records that. A building one floor up has no chimneys standing above it yet. It also has no roof top to put them on. A guess from how far it was built, not from a record.

entries.card: notes:NOT AN INN AT THE SCENE DATE, and that is the most important…
entries.text: NOT AN INN AT THE SCENE DATE, and that is the most important fact this record carries. Miller's tavern competed with the Wolf Point Tavern from 1830, but Wau-Bun, describing 1831, already calls the Miller house 'at this time vacant', Miller having removed to the place that was becoming Michigan City; DRLOIH has the business converted to a store run by P. F. W. Peck after 1832; and a third account has Miller retiring from the field in 1834. The three disagree in their chronology and agree in their direction. Modelled as present and in secondary store or residential use, not innkeeping. The specific claim that Peck was running it does not survive to the scene date either — this project's own exclusions record places Peck in 1835 at his two-storey frame store at South Water and LaSalle.

levels.8-10: Not an inn on the day we show. That is the most important fact here. Miller's inn competed with the Wolf Point inn from 1830. But Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, already calls the Miller house empty at this time. Miller had moved to what was becoming Michigan City. A book says it became a store, run by Peck, after 1832. Another says Miller left the trade in 1834. The three do not agree on dates, but all point the same way. So we show it standing, used as a store or home, not an inn. Peck running it does not last to 1835 either. Our own notes put Peck in 1835 at his store of two floors at South Water and LaSalle.

entries.card: notes:NOT AN OPERATING INDIAN AGENCY BUILDING AT THE SCENE DATE, m…
entries.text: NOT AN OPERATING INDIAN AGENCY BUILDING AT THE SCENE DATE, most likely, and that is the fact this record has least evidence for. Andreas has it 'left unoccupied by the death of Dr. Wolcott' in 1830, then in the autumn of 1832 describes 'the old Indian agency-house in which Colonel Hamilton then resided' — Colonel R. J. Hamilton, the county's clerk and commissioner of school lands, living in it as a private house while the agency's business ran down through the 1833 treaty. Nothing reached says who was in it in July 1835 or what it was being used for, so the value records a residence and this record carries no occupants block rather than guessing at one.

levels.8-10: Most likely it was not used as the agency's office in 1835. We have little proof. A book says it was left empty when Dr. Wolcott died in 1830. In the fall of 1832, the book calls it the old agency house where Colonel Hamilton then lived. Hamilton worked for the county. He lived in it as a home while the agency's work came to an end after the 1833 treaty. Nothing says who was in it in July 1835, or what it was used for. So we call it a home and place no one here.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY, and the archetype reads it, so leav…
entries.text: NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY, and the archetype reads it, so leaving it out would have chosen a finish silently. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the default reading for a frontier tavern's addition and it is weakly supported by the contrast Wau-Bun draws at Wolf Point in 1831, where a painted white building was 'the admiration of all the little circle' precisely because the buildings around it were not painted. Still a choice.

levels.8-10: Not known either way, but our builder needs a choice, so leaving it out would pick one without saying. Bare gray boards are our usual for a new part on an inn in a frontier town. A book backs it a little. At Wolf Point in 1831, one white painted building was the wonder of the town, because the buildings around it were not painted. Still, it is a choice.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY, and this attribute is read by the a…
entries.text: NOT ATTESTED EITHER WAY, and this attribute is read by the archetype, so leaving it out would have painted the building white by default - which is a claim. THERE IS ONE REASON TO WONDER, and it is not enough to act on: the man who built this house had built the white two-storey Sauganash with bright blue shutters that Wau-Bun calls 'the admiration of all the little circle at Wolf Point', so a painted front would be in character. Nothing says he painted this one, and unpainted is the cheaper reading for a speculative-boom house. Still a choice.

levels.8-10: Not known either way. We must choose a color, or it would be painted white by default, and that would be a claim too. One thing makes us wonder. The man who built it also built the Sauganash, a white house with bright blue shutters that people admired. So he might have painted this one. Nothing says he did. Bare wood is the cheaper choice for a house built fast in a boom. It is still a choice.

Unpainted is the cheaper reading for a 1835 speculative-boom house and it is still a choice.

levels.8-10: Not known either way. But our builder needs a choice, and leaving it out would paint the building white. That would be a claim. Wau-Bun's story of the Sauganash's white paint, the wonder of Wolf Point in 1831, shows it was worth pointing out then. Bare boards are the cheaper reading for a house built fast in the boom of 1835, and still a choice.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED FOR THIS BUILDING BY ANY SOURCE REACHED, and th…
entries.text: NOT ATTESTED FOR THIS BUILDING BY ANY SOURCE REACHED, and the number is inference from use rather than from description. Calhoun secured an OFFICE in the building while a store traded from the same corner, so the building held at least two tenancies; a two-storey block is how that is normally arranged on a corner lot on this street, and Peck's store one block west is documented two-storey frame. A single storey is possible and would make the building a third smaller in elevation. DO NOT READ THE WOODCUT IN THE 26 NOVEMBER 1833 ISSUE AS EVIDENCE: the 'Two Buildings to Let' advertisement carries an engraving of a three-storey building with regular fenestration, and it is a printer's generic stock cut, not a picture of a Chicago building. Nothing in this record derives from it.

levels.8-10: No record says, so this is a guess from how it was used. The paper had an office here, and a store sold goods from the same corner. So at least two businesses shared it. A building with two floors was the usual way to do that on a corner. Peck's store, a block away, had two floors. It might have had one floor, and then it would be shorter. A drawing in the paper shows a three-floor building, but that was a stock picture, not this house. We do not use it.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED FOR THIS CROSSING, AND DELIBERATELY NOT THE BRA…
entries.text: NOT ATTESTED FOR THIS CROSSING, AND DELIBERATELY NOT THE BRANCH BRIDGES' DOCUMENTED FIGURE. Charles Cleaver's 'these bridges were ten feet wide' (3.05 m) is evidence about the North and South Branch crossings and this project treats it as documented THERE; here it is only a yardstick. 3.0 m is a hair under it: what is inferred is that a bridge carrying a graded public street had to be about a wagon wide, and that nobody built a street crossing wider than the town's main river bridges. The number should be read as 'about a wagon's width', not as a measurement.

levels.8-10: Not known for this crossing, and on purpose not the river bridges' known size. Charles Cleaver said those bridges were ten feet wide. That is proof about the two river bridges, and we use it there. Here it is only a guide. 3 meters is a little under it. Our guess is that a bridge carrying a public street was about a wagon wide. No one built a street crossing wider than the town's main river bridges. Read the number as about a wagon's width, not a measure.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED, AND IT IS THE NUMBER THAT STANDS FOR 'SOME LIT…
entries.text: NOT ATTESTED, AND IT IS THE NUMBER THAT STANDS FOR 'SOME LITTLE DISTANCE BACK FROM THE STREET'. Andreas says the log tavern stood back and the frame addition reached the frontage; he does not say how far back, so the depth of the new block is the size of an unmeasured setback. 4 m is about 13 ft, which leaves 5 m of log core behind it inside the 9 m footprint - enough to still be a building, which the archetype checks. Anything from a two-metre porch-depth to a full second range is compatible with the sentence.

levels.8-10: Not known. This number stands for a little way back from the street. The book says the log inn stood back and the frame part reached the street. It does not say how far back. So the depth of the new part is the size of a gap no one measured. 4 meters is about 13 feet. That leaves 5 meters of log building behind it, enough to still be a building. Anything from a porch two meters deep to a whole second building fits the sentence.

entries.text: NOT ATTESTED, AND NOT INFERRED EITHER. The plan draws a filled rectangle and letters it; it says nothing about fabric, and no second source mentions these buildings at all. Log is this project's default for a secondary building at a frontier post whose principal ranges were of logs, and it is recorded as INVENTED rather than dressed up as an inference from the garrison's practice. The wash house next door carries `plank` on Hubbard's word `rude`; there is no equivalent word here.

levels.8-10: Not known, and not worked out either. The plan draws a filled box with a label. It says nothing about what it was made of, and no other record tells of these buildings. Logs are our usual choice for a small building at a fort whose main buildings were logs. It is marked as our guess.

entries.card: notes:NOT ATTESTED, AND THE ALTERNATIVE WAS LOG. Bonnell says noth…
entries.text: NOT ATTESTED, AND THE ALTERNATIVE WAS LOG. Bonnell says nothing about this building's fabric. Chicago in 1835 is three years into balloon framing - invented here in 1833 at St Mary's church, which this project already records - and the north bank east end is new ground being built on by men with money, so a frame house is the reconstruction and a braced frame or a log house are the refused alternatives. Recorded as reconstructed, not inferred: there is no evidence about THIS building to reason from.

levels.8-10: Not known. The other choice was logs. Bonnell says nothing about what it was made of. In 1835 Chicago had built with light wood frames for three years. The first was St Mary's church in 1833. The east end of the north bank was new land, built on by men with money. So a light frame house is our choice. It is marked as our guess, since there is nothing about this building to work from.

levels.8-10: Not known. 5.2 meters is about 17 feet, two floors of the usual height with the floors between. It is the same as the Miller house's part with two floors. It is as unsure as the number of floors, which is a guess too.

One storey is chosen because the building it was added to is modelled at one storey with a loft, and a two-storey front on a one-storey log tavern would be the more remarkable thing and would probably have been said. That is an argument from silence, so the tag is conjectural rather than inferred.

levels.8-10: Not known. The book gives the new part what it was made of, a side and a year, but no height. One floor is chosen because the log inn it was added to has one floor with a loft. A front of two floors on a log inn of one floor would be more special, and would likely have been said. That reason is from silence, so it is marked as a weaker guess.

entries.card: notes:NOTHING IN ANY SOURCE PLACES THIS WORKS. The advertisement n…
entries.text: NOTHING IN ANY SOURCE PLACES THIS WORKS. The advertisement names the firm and the trade and no street; Andreas's summary of the same columns names the firm and the trade and no street. So this coordinate is a proposal and is tagged conjectural, and it cites no sources because none supports it. THE REASONING, WHICH IS A PREFERENCE AND NOT EVIDENCE, IN TWO PARTS. First the DIVISION: Daniel Elston is a North Branch figure. Elston Avenue, the plank road that ran north-west along the branch, is named for him, and Andreas's street-naming chapter refers to 'the Elston road' as a fixed landmark (scan p. 409); his later brickyard, the largest in the city by 1854, worked clay on the same side of the town (scan p. 1169). None of that is 1833 and none of it is this building. Second the SITING: soap and candle making is rendering — boiling tallow with lye leached from wood ash — and it is one of the loudest-smelling trades there is. Nuisance trades sit at the edge of a town, downwind and on water, near the slaughtering that supplies the tallow; Archibald Clybourne's slaughter-house was on this same branch. That is an argument about how towns arrange themselves, and towns are not obliged to obey it. THE ALTERNATIVE READING IS AT LEAST AS GOOD: every other advertiser in that issue of the Democrat whose address is known was on or near South Water Street, and a manufactory that wanted the town's house ashes had a reason to be where the houses were. METHOD, such as it is: the works stand on the east bank of the North Branch about 190 m above the forks, 16 m back from the traced bank line, on modelled ground and clear of every other structure in the dataset. Facade bearing 270, due west onto the branch. TREAT THE WHOLE PLACEMENT AS A PROPOSAL, correctable by one line of an 1834 or 1835 advertisement.

levels.8-10: Nothing in any record says where these works stood. The ad and the book name the business, but no street. So this spot is our idea, and no record backs it. We had two reasons. First, Elston is tied to the North Branch. A road there is named for him, and his later brickyard was on that side. But that is not 1833. Second, making soap and candles means boiling fat, and it smells very bad. Smelly work sat at the edge of town, on water, near the butchers who sold the fat. But towns do not always follow that rule. Another guess is just as good: the ads all came from near South Water Street, and he wanted ashes from people's homes. So treat this spot as an idea. One line of an ad from 1834 or 1835 could fix it.

levels.8-10: No record tells of a door. Our stable door is wide enough to lead a horse or a cow through, 1.35 meters. It is the smallest door that fits the work. Cattle walked in, 250 of them in 1833 alone. A door for one person would say the killing was done outside, and nothing says that.

levels.8-10: No record tells of its front. Evenly spaced windows were the usual for a hotel of two floors this size. That much is safe. How many windows, and how far apart, is our guess.

entries.card: notes:No source gives a storey count. One storey with a loft under…
entries.text: No source gives a storey count. One storey with a loft under the roof is the standard form for a log tavern of this date and region, and it is what the attested loft implies: Caton's court sat 'in the unfinished loft', which is a roof space and not a second storey. It is also the conservative reading - the sources that do describe height in this town single out the Sauganash's two storeys and Miller's two-storey frame range as remarkable, which they would not be if every tavern had two. Not attested either way.

levels.8-10: Not known either way. No record gives the number of floors. One floor with a loft under the roof was the usual log inn of this time and place. It is what the known loft means. Caton's court sat in the unfinished loft, which is a roof space, not a second floor. It is also the safer reading. The records that tell of height in this town point out the Sauganash's two floors, and Miller's frame house of two floors, as special. They would not, if every inn had two.

One storey is inferred by the same argument as the storey count above: the sources that do describe height at Wolf Point single out the Sauganash's two storeys and Miller's two-storey frame addition as remarkable, which they would not be if the Wolf Point tavern's frame piece had also stood two storeys. Inference, not attestation.

levels.8-10: No record gives the frame part a height. One floor is our guess, for the same reason as the number of floors above. The records that tell of height at Wolf Point point out the Sauganash's two floors and Miller's frame part of two floors as special. They would not, if the Wolf Point inn's frame part had two floors too. A guess, not a record.

levels.8-10: No chimney is known. One is our usual, and the smallest claim for a heated house with two floors. A building this big might have had two. We do not guess more. Our guess.

levels.8-10: No one says this barn had a loft. It is usual for a barn: hay goes above the floor the wagon uses. It is a guess, and marked so. What you see of it is the hay door in the end wall.

entries.card: notes:Not a build instruction; a scale check and a comparison. $60…
entries.text: Not a build instruction; a scale check and a comparison. $600 for 1,000 sq ft of single-storey frame is $0.60 per square foot, against St Mary's $400 for 875 sq ft ($0.46) and the Temple Building's $900 for two storeys. The Temple Building's invented footprint is derived from exactly this ratio, which is why the figure is carried here rather than left in prose.

levels.8-10: Not something to build. It checks the size. $600 for 1,000 square feet is 60 cents a square foot. St. Mary's was $400 for 875 square feet. The Temple Building was $900 for two floors. We sized the Temple Building from this number, so we keep it here.

entries.card: notes:Not a build instruction; a scale check. 'The total cost of t…
entries.text: Not a build instruction; a scale check. 'The total cost of the edifice was about $400' for 875 sq ft is $0.46 per square foot, against the Presbyterian church's $0.60. The two figures together are what the Temple Building's invented footprint is derived from.

levels.8-10: Not a thing to build, but a check on size. A book says the whole building cost about $400. For 875 square feet, that is 46 cents a square foot. The Presbyterian church cost 60 cents. The two numbers together are what we use to size the Temple Building, whose shape is our guess.

entries.card: notes:Not attested directly, but Andreas's 'eaves to the street' p…
entries.text: Not attested directly, but Andreas's 'eaves to the street' presupposes a roof with eaves and a ridge, which for a frame building of this type, period and region means a gable. Typological derivation with a documented constraint on its orientation, not a measurement.

levels.8-10: Not known for sure. But a book says its roof edge faced the street. That means a roof with a peak, which for a wood building of this kind, time and place means two slopes. It is worked out from its kind, with a known clue to which way it faces, not a measure.
