entries.text: Not attested for 1835. The post was garrisoned on the scene date and Andreas gives two companies of infantry in 1833; no strength figure for mid-1835 was reached, so no number is recorded.

levels.8-10: Not known for 1835. There were soldiers here then, and a book says two groups of them in 1833. We found no count for mid-1835, so no number is given.

entries.card: notes:Not attested for this building. A forwarding warehouse store…
entries.text: Not attested for this building. A forwarding warehouse stores above the floor it loads on, and the archetype builds exactly one external trace of that — the door goods are hoisted through, high in a gable end — and nothing else: no dormer, no floor line, no second range of windows. Andreas's description of the firm's 1839 warehouse hoisting wheat to the upper storey is the practice this infers from, four years the wrong side of the scene date.

levels.8-10: Not known for this building. A shipping store house keeps goods above the floor it loads on. We build only one sign of that outside: a door high in the pointed end, where goods were lifted through. Nothing else: no roof window, no floor line, no second row of windows. The book tells of the firm's 1839 store house lifting wheat to the upper floor. That is how it was done, but four years after the day we show.

entries.card: notes:Not attested for this building. Frame is the reading for a s…
entries.text: Not attested for this building. Frame is the reading for a shop 'opened' in the village in the autumn of 1833: the town had sawn lumber and carpenters by then, and Silas B. Cobb - who is almost certainly the Cobb of this firm - is named by DRLOIH as the carpenter who built the Green Tree Tavern at this very corner earlier the same year. Braced rather than balloon is the conservative reading for 1833, when balloon framing in Chicago was one or two years old. The distinction changes stud rhythm behind the sheathing and is not visible at this level of detail.

levels.8-10: Not known for this building. A wood frame fits a shop opened in the village in the fall of 1833. By then the town had sawn wood and carpenters. Silas Cobb was a carpenter, and almost for sure the Cobb of this shop. A book says he built the Green Tree inn at this same corner that year. Which kind of frame it was cannot be seen from outside.

entries.card: notes:Not attested for this building. The attested finishes are IN…
entries.text: Not attested for this building. The attested finishes are INTERIOR - plastered walls and bare puncheon floors - and nothing describes the outside. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the reading adopted, on the same grounds the Green Tree record gives: white paint was remarkable enough at Chicago in 1831 to be worth recording of the Sauganash, and the one 1833 church whose exterior finish IS attested, St Mary's, was expressly 'not painted'. Not attested either way.

levels.8-10: Not known. The known finishes are inside: plastered walls and bare floors of split logs. Nothing tells of the outside. So it is bare wood boards, grayed by the weather. White paint was rare enough here in 1831 that people wrote about the white Sauganash. The one 1833 church whose outside is known, St. Mary's, was not painted.

entries.card: notes:Not attested for this crossing. Puncheon — split logs laid f…
entries.text: Not attested for this crossing. Puncheon — split logs laid flat side up — is what the 1883 old-settlers statement describes on both branch bridges ('on those stringers puncheons or split logs were laid for a floor'), and a smaller, cruder, unremarked street crossing of the same decade is not going to have carried better. Inference from local practice, not from this bridge.

levels.8-10: Not known for this crossing. Split logs laid flat side up are what the 1883 old settlers' paper tells of on both river bridges, laid on the long logs for a floor. A smaller, rougher street crossing of the same years would not have had a better deck. A guess from how the town built, not from this bridge.

entries.card: notes:Not attested for this crossing. `bent` is the old settlers'…
entries.text: Not attested for this crossing. `bent` is the old settlers' own word for what stood in the deeper water on the branch bridges — 'four heavy logs, resting on the bottom' — and it is the only one of the archetype's three kinds that a town would put in half a metre of slough water. A crib is a sunk and filled box and a pile is driven; neither is worth the trouble here.

levels.8-10: Not known for this crossing. Bent is the old settlers' own word for what stood in the deeper water under the river bridges: four heavy logs resting on the bottom. It is the only one of our three kinds a town would put in half a meter of ditch water. A box filled with stones, or a post pounded into the ground, is not worth the work here.

entries.text: Not attested for this fort. Whistler's 1808 index says the FIRST fort's barracks were 'two storeys high with shingled Roofs' (Quaife) and two companies do not fit on one floor of a 90 ft range with their stores. Both are arguments; neither is a statement about the 1816 fort.

levels.8-10: Not known for this fort. A list from 1808 says the first fort's barracks had two floors and shingle roofs. And two groups of soldiers and their goods do not fit on one floor of a 90-foot building. Both are reasons, but neither is a record of the 1816 fort.

entries.card: notes:Not attested for this structure. A single slope is the cheap…
entries.text: Not attested for this structure. A single slope is the cheapest roof there is and is the ordinary covering for a drying shed, whose whole job is to keep rain off stacked green brick while air moves through underneath. The archetype treats `shed` as a first-class form rather than a fallback for exactly this class of building.

levels.8-10: No record says. A roof with one slope is the cheapest roof. It is the usual roof for a drying shed. A drying shed keeps rain off new bricks while air moves under it. So we build it as a shed roof on purpose.

levels.8-10: No record says. It is a safe guess. A blacksmith shop is one tall room with a forge, and every building in this group was small and made of logs.

entries.card: notes:Not attested. 'Compact little building' and 'two large rooms…
entries.text: Not attested. 'Compact little building' and 'two large rooms' both read as a single storey, and a building that grew by adding wings at the sides and tails at the rear is a building that could not grow upward — which is the argument. The counter-example is in the same book: the FIRST agency house, built beside old Fort Dearborn in 1803-4 on the south side, was 'a two-story log building, covered with split oak siding'. That is a different building and it is why this value is inference rather than type.

levels.8-10: No record says. Compact little building and two large rooms both sound like one floor. A house that grew by adding wings and back parts is a house that could not grow up. The same book tells of the first agency house, from 1803, which had two floors. That is a different building. So this is a guess.

levels.8-10: Not known. A 90-foot barracks split into rooms needed a chimney for each group of rooms. Three is the least that would heat a building this long. The count is our guess.

levels.8-10: Not known. A building used for church and school through Chicago winters needed heat. One chimney is the least, and the usual, for a log building of one room. A guess, not proof.

entries.card: notes:ONE WITNESS, AND IT IS PRE-1835. The range opens 24 February…
entries.text: ONE WITNESS, AND IT IS PRE-1835. The range opens 24 February 1830, the date on the Harrison plan, because that plan is the only source this project holds that says anything at all about this building — Hubbard describes the fort's well and its wash-houses and says nothing about out buildings, so the second witness the wash house record carries does not exist here. IT CLOSES 29 DECEMBER 1836, the evacuation, and that is a floor rather than a demolition: nothing attests when the fort's outer buildings came down. WHAT CARRIES THE SCENE DATE OF 1 JULY 1835 is the middle of that range and not either end of it — the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836, so a service building the garrison's own engineer drew in 1830 is standing five years later unless something says it stopped, and nothing does. That is an argument, not an assumption, and it is the argument every Fort Dearborn record here rests on. IT IS A THINNER ARGUMENT THAN THE WASH HOUSE'S because it stands on one witness instead of two, and the grade says so.

levels.8-10: One record, and it is from before 1835. It starts on 24 February 1830, the date on the Harrison plan. That plan is the only record we have about this building. It ends on 29 December 1836, when the soldiers left. That is not when it came down. Nothing tells when the fort's outer buildings were torn down. What counts for July 1835 is the middle. Soldiers were here the whole time from June 1832 to the end of 1836. A building drawn in 1830 still stood five years later, unless something says it stopped. Nothing does. With only one record, this is a weaker case than for the wash house.

entries.text: PICTURE-BOUNDED 1835 RECONSTRUCTION. Andreas p.290 states that the church had no tower when built in 1833 and received a low open tower and bell some time afterwards, without an installation date. The undated Moss engraving on p.291 shows an open belfry, curved pointed cap and cross. This model chooses that recognizable form for 1835 as a reconstruction, not proof of its presence by July 1835 or a dated interpretation of the engraving. The four posts, low crossed rails, curved braces, boarded plinth, small bell, cap and cross use chosen dimensions recorded in the liberty. No later enlargement, relocation or phase is adopted. Tower presence is a chosen temporal reconstruction, not a dated witness.

entries.card: notes:PLACED 2026-08-09. NO SURVIVING INTERSECTION LOCATES THIS BU…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-09. NO SURVIVING INTERSECTION LOCATES THIS BUILDING — the streets platted across this ground in Kinzie's Addition were staked in 1833-35 and the point itself has since been rebuilt — so the coordinate is derived from the datum origin at the forks confluence and from bank geometry. What is attested is unusually consistent for this dataset: chicagology, 'The Miller House stood on the point of land between the North Branch and the Main Channel'; Wau-Bun, 'on the north side of the river ... near the forks'; DRLOIH, a store 'on the north bank of the river at the forks'; and the Miller-Clybourn ferry ran across the North Branch between this house and the Wolf Point Tavern, which requires it to be on the point. A FOURTH SOURCE DISAGREES AND IS TREATED AS AN ERROR: the hotel chronology places Miller on the 'south branch of Chicago River, opposite Wolf Point'. Four independent statements against one, and the ferry route settles it. Method: modern water polygons from OpenStreetMap put the nose of the point at about 39 m north of the datum origin, with the main-stem north bank running east from there and the North Branch east bank running north-west. The footprint's south face is set 14 m north of the main-stem bank and its west face about 22 m east of the North Branch bank, which puts the building on the point and off both waters. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for the modern banks not being the 1835 banks — this ground was filled and wharfed and is now built over, and unlike the west bank there is no street line here to check it against, so treat the along-bank position as the softer of the two axes. Facade bearing 180, due south onto the main stem, from 'a two-story house ... fronting the river'. On a point the river is on two sides: a bearing of about 215, fronting the confluence and Wolf Point across the water, is equally arguable and would rotate the building about 35 degrees. Local-origin normalization for the reconstructed adjacent compound translates the origin(-6,+5)m in the retained180-degree footprint frame, equivalent to UTM(+6,-5)m. This keeps the tall range's wall box and six front opening world positions unchanged while moving the low core beside it; it does not add a surveyed location. The old20 m placement uncertainty and facade bearing remain. Roof-joint vertices and fractional flue station are governed by the end-route limits, not a whole-mesh equality claim.

levels.8-10: No street corner left today shows where this building stood. The streets here were laid out in 1833 to 1835, and the point has been built over since. So its place is worked out from where the rivers meet and the shape of the banks. What is known agrees well. One page says the Miller House stood on the point of land between the North Branch and the main river. Wau-Bun says on the north side of the river, near the forks. A book says a store on the north bank at the forks. And the Miller ferry ran across the North Branch between this house and the Wolf Point inn, which puts it on the point. One record puts Miller on the south branch, across from Wolf Point. We treat that as a mistake. It is four against one, and the ferry settles it. We used today's river maps to find the point, and set the house back from both rivers. It could be off by about 20 meters, more along the bank, since the banks have been filled and built over. The front faces south onto the river, from a house facing the river. On a point, the river is on two sides, so it could face the forks instead.

entries.card: notes:PLACED 2026-08-09. The corner is documented — chicagology an…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-09. The corner is documented — chicagology and the Chicago Landmark record both put the Sauganash at the south-east corner of Lake and Market — but the COORDINATE is inferred, so the tag follows the weaker half. Method: Market Street is today's N Wacker Drive and Lake Street is unchanged, an equivalence the research dossier states and the georeference independently corroborates, since the 1834 plats warped onto the modern street centrelines at 17.5 m RMS. The modern intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap (EPSG:26916 E 447161.9, N 4637285.4) and the footprint origin offset 12.2 m east and 20.2 m south of it: half of an 80 ft platted street to reach the kerb, and the footprint's own 8 m depth so the building's north face sits on the Lake Street frontage of a south-east corner lot. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's, not an additional guess. Facade bearing 0 (north, onto Lake Street): the sources say it faced the forks to the north-west, so the true bearing is likely nearer 315, but the plat lot lines are orthogonal and a corner building fronting Lake is the defensible reading until better evidence appears.

levels.8-10: Placed on 9 August 2026. The corner is known. A website and the city's landmark record both put the Sauganash at the south-east corner of Lake and Market. But the exact spot is our guess, so the grade follows the weaker half. Market Street is today's Wacker Drive, and Lake Street is the same. The old maps fit today's streets well. We found the corner on today's maps, and set the building just inside the south-east corner lot, facing Lake Street. It could be off by about 20 meters. The front faces north, onto Lake Street. The records say it faced the forks to the north-west, so it may have turned more that way. But the lots are square to the streets, so a corner building facing Lake is the safer reading.

entries.card: notes:PLACED 2026-08-11, AND ONE BOOK CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT WHI…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND ONE BOOK CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT WHICH SIDE OF CLARK STREET IT WAS ON. The schools chapter says twice that the building stood 'on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street' and 'on the river bank just east of Clark Street'. The Methodist chapter says 'the Watkins school-house, which was located on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle' — which is WEST of Clark, about a block away. THE SCHOOLS CHAPTER IS ADOPTED because it is the more specific statement, it is made twice, and it is the chapter about this building; the church chapter is naming a meeting place in passing. IF THE CHURCH CHAPTER IS RIGHT, THIS BUILDING STANDS ABOUT 110 M WEST OF WHERE IT IS DRAWN. Method: Clark Street's modern centreline was read from OpenStreetMap through the Kinzie intersection (EPSG:26916 E 447646.20, N 4637668.88, local E +573.5, N +273.1) and carried south on the OSM bearing, giving an east kerb 12.2 m east of it, half an 80 ft platted street; the 1834 north bank and the North Water Street frontage were read off the Wright 1834 sheet through this project's fitted affine, which puts the drawn bank at local N +98 along this stretch and the block row's south line — the street's north kerb — at about N +128. The building is set with its west face 6 m east of the Clark kerb and its south face 12.5 m north of the bank, i.e. on the bank strip the street occupies, which is what 'on the river bank' says. Facade bearing 180, due south to the river, is inferred from that frontage and from nothing anybody wrote. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus the ~5 m of reading the sheet by eye, plus the block-scale disagreement above, which is far larger than either. There is no modelled terrain under this building — it stands about 280 m east of the terrain box.

levels.8-10: Placed on 11 August 2026. One book does not agree with itself about which side of Clark Street it was on. The school pages say twice that it stood on the river bank, just east of Clark Street. The church pages say it was on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle. That is west of Clark, about a block away. We follow the school pages. They are more exact, they say it twice, and they are about this building. The church pages name a meeting place in passing. If the church pages are right, it stood about 110 meters west of where we draw it. We found Clark Street on today's maps, and the 1834 river bank on an old map. The school sits just east of Clark, on the strip of bank by the river. It faces south to the river, our guess. It could be off by 20 meters or more, and the block question is far bigger than that.

entries.card: notes:PLACED BY A SENTENCE, NOT BY THE PLAN. The 1830 plan draws n…
entries.text: PLACED BY A SENTENCE, NOT BY THE PLAN. The 1830 plan draws no magazine; the only positional evidence is Hubbard in 1827: 'the magazine, of brick, was situated about half way between the west end of the guard and block-houses.' That reading is what put the guard house on the WEST side of the south gate rather than the east - it is the only assignment of the two flanking buildings that leaves a real gap for the magazine to stand in - and this position is the midpoint of that gap, just inside the curtain in the south-west quarter of the enclosure. UNCERTAINTY IS LARGER THAN THE REST OF THE COMPLEX: 'about half way' is the whole of it, and the sentence can be parsed two ways (midway between the two buildings' west ends, or midway between the guard house's west end and the block-house), which move the point about 4 m apart. The rotation is the fort's.

levels.8-10: Placed from one sentence, not from the plan. The 1830 plan draws no powder house. Hubbard wrote in 1827 that it was brick, about half way between the guard house and the blockhouse. That put the guard house on the west side of the south gate. It is the only way that leaves a gap for the powder house. We put it in the middle of that gap. About half way is all we have. The sentence can be read two ways, which moves it about 4 meters.

Andreas: 'The block-house was in the southwest corner.' Hubbard, 1827: 'the block-house was located at the southwest and the bastion at the northwest corners of the fort.' Three sources, one corner. The rotation is the fort's.

levels.8-10: Placed from the plan, and backed by two writers. The 1830 plan draws a heavy box at the south-west corner, sticking out past both walls. It is the only part of the fort drawn that way. A book says the blockhouse was in the south-west corner. Hubbard said the same in 1827. Three records, one corner.

entries.card: notes:PLACEHOLDER - NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, BUT THE SIZE IS BOUN…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER - NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, BUT THE SIZE IS BOUNDED TWICE AND THE TWO BOUNDS PULL AGAINST EACH OTHER. Bonnell calls it "a small yellow house" and then says Mrs. Kelsey "had all the boarders that she could accommodate" and turned him away. So: small enough to be called small, and full enough to refuse a lodger. 8.5 x 6.1 m is about 28 x 20 ft - a hall-and-parlour front range with chambers in the half storey, which is where boarders slept. Every number is invented; what is not invented is that this is the smallest of the two houses this parcel raises, because one source calls it small and the other calls its neighbour a residence.

levels.8-10: No size is known, but two clues pull against each other. Bonnell calls it a small yellow house. Then he says Mrs. Kelsey had all the boarders she could take, and turned him away. So it was small, but full. 8.5 by 6.1 meters is about 28 by 20 feet. It has two front rooms, and rooms under the roof where boarders slept. Every number is our guess. What is not a guess is that it is the smaller of the two houses here. One record calls it small, and calls the other a home.

BEWARE THE ONE DIMENSION THE SOURCE DOES GIVE, BECAUSE IT BELONGS TO A DIFFERENT BUILDING: Watkins's FIRST schoolroom, in the autumn of 1832, was Colonel Hamilton's horse stable — 'The building belonged to Colonel Hamilton, was erected for a horse stable and had been used as such. It was twelve feet square.' That is not this house, and a 12 ft square building is not what the second passage means by 'the first house built for a school in Chicago'.

levels.8-10: Every number is our guess. No size is known. 24 by 18 feet is a school of one room, big enough for the thirty children Watkins wrote his sign-up for. Every number is invented. NOTE ALSO WHAT IS NOT DRAWN: a tannery is its yard — bark mill, lime pits, tan vats, drying sheds, and a water supply — and none of that is in this polygon or in the model. The record models the log house the sources name and nothing else. To resolve: any account of Miller and Hall's tanyard, or the Chicago Democrat's advertisements.

levels.8-10: Every number is our guess. No size or plan is known. The records give only a kind: a log house used to tan hides. 7 by 5.5 meters is a usual one-room log house of the time. It looks like a house put to work, not a building made for the trade, as the records say. Note what is not built. A tannery is mostly its yard: a mill for bark, pits, big tubs, drying sheds and water. None of that is in the model. We build only the log house the records name. To settle it, look for any record of Miller and Hall's yard, or their ads in the Chicago Democrat.

entries.card: notes:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, but unlike most of t…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, but unlike most of the invented footprints in this dataset this one has a CAPACITY behind it and the size was chosen against that capacity rather than freely. Andreas records 250 head of cattle and about 2,000 hogs packed here by Clybourne in 1833, plus 250 head of cattle and 1,000 hogs packed at the same place by George W. Dole (scan p. 1151) — a season's throughput on that scale needs a killing floor several beasts wide, hanging room, and a working yard beside it. 12 x 9 m is about 39 x 30 ft, which is a large log building by the standards of this town and a small one by the standards of that throughput; the 12 m runs along the bank and the 9 m is the depth. Every number is invented and the polygon cites no sources. WHAT IS NOT MODELLED IS ARGUABLY THE BIGGER HALF: the killing pens, the stock yard that later gave the trade the Bull's Head name, and the packing gear are all outside this footprint and outside this archetype, which builds a building and not a works. To resolve: Andreas vol. 1 at page-image level around scan pp. 1149-1151, or any Cook County or Fort Dearborn contract paper describing the premises.

levels.8-10: This is a guess, but we chose it to fit how much work was done here. In 1833 about 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs were packed here by Clybourne, and more by George W. Dole. That much work needs a floor wide enough for several animals, a room to hang them and a yard. So it is about 39 by 30 feet, big for a log building here. The long side runs along the river bank. Every number is made up. We do not build the pens, the stock yard or the tools. We build only the building.

entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSIONS ARE ATTESTED. Only two adjectives are, and THEY CONFLICT: Wau-Bun calls it 'a small square log building', chicagology calls it 'an oblong building'. Square is adopted for the proportion because Wau-Bun is the earlier and nearer-primary witness and was describing what she saw, while chicagology's is a recollection transcribed at further remove — but a 7 x 7 m square is a guess at scale wearing an attested proportion, so the whole polygon is tagged conjectural and cites no sources. 7 m is about 23 ft, a single-pen log building large enough for ten founding members and a school. The disagreement over the shape is itself weak evidence for the two-buildings hypothesis in the position note: a square building and an oblong one may be two different buildings.

levels.8-10: No size is known. Only two words are, and they do not agree. Wau-Bun calls it a small square log building. A website calls it an oblong building. We use square, because Wau-Bun is earlier, and she told of what she saw. The website's is a memory written down further away. But a 7 by 7 meter square is a guess at size wearing a known shape. So the whole shape is marked as our guess, with no record given. 7 meters is about 23 feet, a log building of one room, big enough for ten church members and a school. The fight over its shape hints that there may have been two buildings, one square and one long.

entries.card: notes:PREVIOUS CRIB-ONLY RECONSTRUCTION, retained as history: NOBO…
entries.text: PREVIOUS CRIB-ONLY RECONSTRUCTION, retained as history: NOBODY SAID. The branch bridges' supports are documented as bents of four heavy logs resting on the bottom, because four men who used them wrote it down; nothing equivalent exists for this crossing, and the sentence that would have settled it is the one Andreas did not write. Crib is chosen over the archetype's other two readings — bent and pile — on the ground that it is the archetype's own default and that the harbour works at the mouth of the same river were at that moment being built of timber cribs by federal engineers, in a town whose one shipwright had just framed this bridge. That is a reason to prefer it and not evidence for it, so the tag is conjectural rather than inferred, and the count beside it carries the same chip for the same reason. CURRENT PICTURE-BOUNDED RECONSTRUCTION: the retrospective Andreas plate distinguishes broad draw-bearing foundations from the lighter trestle-like approach supports. Use the existing four-log bent for the remaining approach stations; that count, section and riverbed seating are reconstructed, not evidence that the Dearborn crossing used the branch bridges' documented construction. The two selected frame bearings override this general kind with separately dimensioned reconstructed crib platforms. No source coordinate, surveyed foundation footprint or accepted whole-picture match follows. CURRENT PLATFORM CORRECTION: the two selected bearings now use boarded pile-supported caps rather than the rejected V3 solid-crib trial; all numerical sections and counts remain reconstructed.

levels.8-10: No one wrote down what held the bridge up. The branch bridges stood on frames of four heavy logs, because four men who used them said so. Nothing like that exists for this bridge. We first chose boxes of logs filled with stone, our usual kind. The harbor works nearby were being built that way then. That is a reason, not a proof. Now an old picture from 1884 shows big wide bases under the lifting part, and lighter frames under the rest. So the rest stand on four-log frames, our guess. The two big bases are built on their own.

entries.card: notes:READ FROM A DRAWING CONVENTION, NOT FROM A CAPTION. The 1830…
entries.text: READ FROM A DRAWING CONVENTION, NOT FROM A CAPTION. The 1830 plate draws two sides of this plot as a continuous zigzag line and the other two as plain lines. A zigzag boundary on a period American survey is the standard convention for a worm - snake - rail fence, which is the fence a garrison with axes and no post-hole digger builds. The reading is inferred from the convention; the sheet does not say 'fence'.

levels.8-10: Read from how the map is drawn, not from a word on it. The 1830 plan draws two sides of the garden as a zigzag line, and two as plain lines. On old American maps, a zigzag means a rail fence that zigzags. Soldiers with axes and no tools for digging post holes built that kind. This is a guess from how maps were drawn. The map does not say fence.

entries.card: notes:Reconstructed open-shell choice for 1 July 1835. The 10 June…
entries.text: Reconstructed open-shell choice for 1 July 1835. The 10 June notice establishes work before the scene but dates no roof or lift. levels.8-10: Open with no roof is our choice for 1 July 1835. The 10 June notice says work had started, but not when the roof went on. The later facts do not prove there was no roof in July either. A later print shows a finished roof and a little tower, but it is from after 1836. It cannot tell us how far the work was in July.

entries.card: notes:Records the rejected reading so it stays visible. W. H. Stow…

Adopted as false for the reasons in the construction note; if it is true, the 1835 building is a weatherboarded log structure rather than a frame one, which changes the wall section but not the massing, the plan or the placement.

levels.8-10: We keep this note on a view we do not use, so it stays in sight. W. H. Stow said the Green Tree was first made of logs, and covered in boards years later. We take that as wrong, for the reasons in the note on how it was built. If he is right, it is logs under boards, not a wood frame. That changes the walls, but not the shape, plan or place.

entries.text: Retained 35-degree reconstruction, bounded by the steep front gable in the retrospective panorama and log-roof practice. The tiny engraving and illustrative camera do not supply a measured pitch.

levels.8-10: The roof slopes at 35 degrees, our guess. It fits the steep front roof in an old drawing, and how log roofs were built. The drawing is tiny and does not measure the slope.

levels.8-10: The tall part keeps its 38 degree roof, our guess. The low part has its own lower roof, a 25 degree guess. The chimney on the tall part sits under the same roof slope. The roof ends and the chimney's place moved a little where the two parts join. The real ends and places are not measured, and neither change is a new claim about history.

entries.card: notes:SAWN PLANK RATHER THAN RIVEN PUNCHEON, AND IT IS THE FIRST R…
entries.text: SAWN PLANK RATHER THAN RIVEN PUNCHEON, AND IT IS THE FIRST RECORD IN THIS DATASET TO CARRY THE VALUE. The branch bridges' floor is documented as 'puncheons or split logs', which is what a crew lays without a sawyer. This bridge was different in the one way that decides the question: Norton 'commenced cutting the lumber' in the winter of 1833-34 and spent three months building from it, to a design that had won a premium, on a structure with a moving leaf. Riven stock of uneven width is not what a ship-carpenter frames a hoisted draw and its approaches from. The mesh differs accordingly — narrower boards, laid regularly, with the ends in line instead of the ragged butts a split floor gives. THE INFERENCE IS FROM THE BUILDER AND THE MATERIAL WORD, not from any statement about the deck, and 'cutting the lumber' could in principle describe felling rather than sawing. It is graded inferred for that reason.

levels.8-10: Sawn boards, not split logs. This is the first record where we use that. The bridges on the branches had floors of split logs, what a crew lays without a saw. This bridge was different. Norton began cutting the lumber in the winter of 1833, and spent three months building it, with a part that lifted. A ship's carpenter does not build that from rough split wood. So the boards are narrow and even. But cutting the lumber could mean cutting trees, not sawing boards. So it is a guess.

entries.card: notes:SELF-REPORTED IN THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT, AND THE ADVERTISEMENT…
entries.text: SELF-REPORTED IN THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT, AND THE ADVERTISEMENT RAN FOR A YEAR. Mason & Co. advertise as blacksmiths in the issue of 26 November 1833, on 'Main-street, nearly opposite Graves' Tavern'. The '& Co.' says the shop employed more than one man. Eleven printings of that one notice are now read out of the Democrat, the last on 10 December 1834, all under the same copy date - so the firm is documented trading thirteen months and not one day, and the far end of the range is inferred from a shorter reach than it was: a working smithy in a town growing tenfold is far more likely to have continued than to have closed. THE NOTICE CHANGES ITS ANCHOR PART WAY THROUGH, and the position note is where that is set out.

levels.8-10: Mason and Co. put an ad in the Chicago Democrat, and the ad ran for a year. The ad of 26 November 1833 says they are blacksmiths on Main Street, nearly across from Graves' inn. The and Co. means more than one man worked there. Eleven printings of the ad are read, the last on 10 December 1834. So the shop is known to have run thirteen months. A working blacksmith in a town growing ten times over is far more likely to have kept going than to have shut. Partway through, the ad changes how it tells where the shop is. The note on its place tells about that.

entries.card: notes:SIX FEET, AND THE REASON IS BETTER THAN THE NUMBER. Andreas…
entries.text: SIX FEET, AND THE REASON IS BETTER THAN THE NUMBER. Andreas prints at the foot of pp. 631-632 a statement signed by J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble: 'These were both wagon bridges, and were about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice freely.' The clearance is not a builder's convenience, it is the winter road under the deck, stated by four men who used the crossing. It is also the sentence that does the most damage to the raft reading recorded in this record's research note: a floating deck has no clearance at all, and nothing passes under it on the ice.

levels.8-10: Six feet, and the reason is better than the number. A book prints a paper signed by Caton, Bates, Cleaver and Noble. It says both were wagon bridges, about six feet above the water, so teams passed under them on the ice. The space under it was not for the builders' ease. It was the winter road under the deck, told by four men who used the crossing. It also does the most harm to the idea that it was a raft. A floating deck has no space under it, and nothing passes under it on the ice.

entries.card: notes:SIX FEET, BORROWED FROM THE NEIGHBOURS AND LABELLED AS BORRO…
entries.text: SIX FEET, BORROWED FROM THE NEIGHBOURS AND LABELLED AS BORROWED. No source reached states how high this deck stood above the water. The only clearance figure this project holds for any Chicago river crossing of the decade is the 1883 old-settlers statement's 'about six feet above the water' for the two branch bridges, and it is adopted here as an inference from adjacent evidence rather than as evidence about this structure. TWO THINGS SUPPORT THE BORROWING AND ONE COMPLICATES IT. Supporting: the three crossings were built within two years of each other by or for the same corporation, and a bridge that needed a sixty-foot opening for the passage of craft cannot have been high — a high fixed deck is precisely the alternative to a draw, and this town chose the draw. Complicating: the main stem carried masted lake vessels where the branches carried scows and teams, so its bridge had more reason to be built up, and the branch bridges' six feet was set by a use this one did not have, the winter road passing underneath on the ice. The figure is kept because it is the only one there is and because both arguments point low rather than high, and the tag says it is a reading and not a measurement.

levels.8-10: Six feet, borrowed from the bridges nearby, and marked as borrowed. No record says how high this bridge stood over the water. The only number we have is from 1883, when old settlers said the two bridges on the branches stood about six feet up. Two things fit. The bridges were built within two years of each other, for the same town. And a bridge that opened sixty feet for boats could not be high, or it would not need to open. One thing does not fit. This river carried tall-masted ships, so its bridge had more reason to be high. We keep six feet because it is the only number we have.

entries.card: notes:Same reasoning as the officers' quarters: galleries fronting…
entries.text: Same reasoning as the officers' quarters: galleries fronting the parade are documented for the FIRST fort and for no building in this one, and a plain front is a claim the visitor sees.

levels.8-10: The same reason as the officers' rooms. Porches facing the parade ground are known for the first fort, but for no building in this one. A plain front is a claim the visitor sees.

entries.card: notes:Sawn boards nailed up vertically, the archetype's `plank`, t…
entries.text: Sawn boards nailed up vertically, the archetype's `plank`, the same fabric as the packing house at the other end of the band. Invented.

levels.8-10: Our guess. Sawn boards nailed up and down, the same as the packing house at the other end.

entries.card: notes:Sawn boards nailed up vertically, the archetype's `plank`. C…
entries.text: Sawn boards nailed up vertically, the archetype's `plank`. Chicago had sawn lumber on the branches by 1834 and the plant it serves is a purpose-built works rather than a settler's cabin, so boards rather than `log`. Invented - nothing states how any building on this reach was built.

levels.8-10: Sawn boards nailed up and down. Chicago had sawn wood by 1834, and this is a building made for the work, not a settler's cabin. So boards, not logs. Our guess. Nothing says how any building here was built.

entries.card: notes:Sawn boards nailed up vertically. Elston's was a manufactory…
entries.text: Sawn boards nailed up vertically. Elston's was a manufactory advertised in the town's own newspaper rather than a settler's outbuilding, so boards rather than logs - which is an argument about the concern and not a source. Invented.

levels.8-10: Sawn boards nailed up and down. Elston's works was a business that put ads in the town paper, not a settler's shed. So it has boards, not logs. That is a guess about the business, not from a record. Made up.

entries.card: notes:Shutter OCCURRENCE is visible around the Gifford picture's w…
entries.text: Shutter OCCURRENCE is visible around the Gifford picture's windows. Green is an explicit reconstructed stock-palette colour: the monochrome reproduction supplies no original paint colour. Plain 25 mm-thick open leaves at 42 percent of sash width, their stations and concealed hardware are reconstructed; no louvre pattern is asserted.

levels.8-10: Shutters can be seen around the windows in Gifford's picture. Green is our chosen color. The black and white picture gives no color. Their size, how far they open and their parts are our guess. No slats are claimed.

entries.card: notes:St. Cyr selected the lot in 1833 and, per the same page's ac…
entries.text: St. Cyr selected the lot in 1833 and, per the same page's account of the removal, was succeeded by Father O'Meara only after 1837, so he is the pastor across the whole scene window. Tagged inferred rather than documented because the page states his arrival and his succession and does not state who was in charge on any particular day in 1835.

levels.8-10: Father St. Cyr picked the lot in 1833. The same page says Father O'Meara took his place only after 1837. So he led the church through all these years. It is marked as our guess, because the page tells when he came and when he was replaced, not who was in charge on any one day in 1835.

entries.card: notes:Stow is documented as the builder and operator of the hotel;…
entries.text: Stow is documented as the builder and operator of the hotel; that the stable behind it was his follows from its being described as part of the house, and is not separately stated. No hostler is named.

levels.8-10: Stow is known as the man who built and ran the hotel. That the stable behind it was his follows from its being part of the house. It is not said on its own. No stable hand is named.

entries.card: notes:TEN FEET, AND UNUSUALLY FOR THIS DATASET IT IS SAID TWICE. T…
entries.text: TEN FEET, AND UNUSUALLY FOR THIS DATASET IT IS SAID TWICE. The 1883 old-settlers statement: 'These bridges were about ten feet wide and without railings, for the first few years.' Cleaver in the Tribune ten years later: 'These bridges were ten feet wide.' Both sentences are about BOTH branch bridges, which is what makes this crossing's width evidence rather than an analogy from its neighbour. Cleaver signed the first and gave the second, so the two are one man corroborated by three rather than two independent witnesses; the North Branch record makes the same reservation about the same sentence. Recorded as 3.048 m exactly, being the conversion and not a rounding. The same footnote adds, of the North Branch bridge alone, 'ten or twelve feet wide' — a spread this record does not inherit, because it is stated of the other crossing.

levels.8-10: Ten feet, and for once it is said twice. The old settlers' paper of 1883 says these bridges were about ten feet wide, with no railings for the first few years. Cleaver said in the Tribune ten years later that these bridges were ten feet wide. Both are about both river bridges. So this crossing's width is proof, not a guess from the bridge next to it. Cleaver signed the first and gave the second, so it is one man backed by three. We record it as exactly 3.048 meters, ten feet. The same paper says the North Branch bridge was ten or twelve feet wide. This one does not take that, since it was said of the other bridge.

entries.card: notes:TEN FEET, from Charles Cleaver, of both branch bridges. This…
entries.text: TEN FEET, from Charles Cleaver, of both branch bridges. This is the only dimension of any structure in this dataset that a source actually states, and it is worth saying why it is trusted at tier 2: Cleaver was recalling a bridge he had used and had driven a team across, and a width is the kind of number a user of a narrow bridge remembers. Recorded as 3.048 m exactly, being the conversion and not a rounding.

levels.8-10: Ten feet, from Charles Cleaver, for both bridges over the river's branches. It is the only size of any building here that a record really gives. Here is why we trust it. Cleaver used this bridge and drove a team across it. A width is the kind of number someone who used a narrow bridge remembers. We record it as exactly 3.048 meters, which is ten feet.

entries.card: notes:THE 1835 READING OF A BRIDGE THAT CHANGED. Andreas describes…
entries.text: THE 1835 READING OF A BRIDGE THAT CHANGED. Andreas describes the 1832 structure as 'formed of stringers and only fitted for foot passengers' and 'useless for teams' even in the summer of 1833; six and a half weeks after this scene's date a procession of hundreds crossed it, and Cleaver remembered driving over it. Something was rebuilt or widened between 1833 and 1835 and no source reached says what. Four stringers under a full-width deck is the later, load-carrying reading, chosen because the scene date is 1835-07-01 and the evidence for 1835 is a crowd on the deck. The alternative — the 1832 walkway, two stringers and a plank — is a defensible model of a different year and would be the right value in an 1833 scene.

levels.8-10: How this bridge looked in 1835, after it changed. A book says the 1832 bridge was made of long logs and fit only for people on foot. Even in the summer of 1833 it was useless for wagons. But six and a half weeks after the day we show, hundreds of people crossed it in a parade, and Cleaver remembered driving over it. So it was rebuilt or made wider between 1833 and 1835. No record says how. Four logs under a full deck is the later, stronger reading. We chose it because the day is 1 July 1835, and the proof for 1835 is a crowd on it. The 1832 walkway, two logs and a board, would be right for a scene of 1833.

entries.card: notes:THE 1835 USE IS ATTESTED, WHICH IS NOT WHAT THIS RECORD EXPE…
entries.text: THE 1835 USE IS ATTESTED, WHICH IS NOT WHAT THIS RECORD EXPECTED TO FIND. Andreas's schools narrative, having just placed George Davis in the Presbyterian church 'later, in 1835', continues: 'John Watkins was THEN teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building erected by Colonels Hamilton and Owen.' So the building was in use as a public school in the year of the scene. THE GRAIN IS THE YEAR AND NOT THE DAY, and Andreas adds the limit himself: 'Mr. Watkins taught as late as 1835, but the exact date of his retirement is not known.' A building may stand while its function lapses; here the function is attested for 1835 and cannot be tied to 1 July.

levels.8-10: Its use in 1835 is known, which we did not expect. A book puts George Davis teaching in the Presbyterian church in 1835. Then it says John Watkins was then teaching a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building put up by Colonels Hamilton and Owen. So it was a public school in the year we show. But that is the year, not the day. The book says Watkins taught as late as 1835, but no one knows when he stopped. So it cannot be tied to 1 July.

entries.card: notes:THE ATTESTED TRAFFIC IS THE ARGUMENT, AND IT IS ALSO WHY THI…
entries.text: THE ATTESTED TRAFFIC IS THE ARGUMENT, AND IT IS ALSO WHY THIS IS NOT A WAGON DOOR. The source drives wagons into the YARD — 'the yard into which the trains were driven' — and puts horses in the STABLE. So what has to get through this building's opening is a horse led in hand, which is what the archetype's 'stable' door is (1.35 m clear); a 2.90 m wagon door would silently move the source's wagon train indoors. NOTE THE ALTERNATIVE, because it is live: a wagon house at a teamsters' inn often had a cart bay at one end, and the outbuilding archetype's own golden case for a hotel stable uses a wagon door. Nothing rules it out and nothing states it, so the smaller opening is recorded.

levels.8-10: The known traffic is the reason, and also why this is not a wagon door. The record says wagons were driven into the yard, the yard into which the trains were driven, and horses went in the stable. So what goes through this building's door is a horse led by hand. That is a stable door, 1.35 meters wide. A wagon door 2.9 meters wide would quietly move the wagons indoors. There is another real answer. A wagon house at an inn for drivers often had a cart bay at one end. Nothing rules it out, and nothing says so. So the smaller door is recorded.

entries.card: notes:THE BEST-FOUNDED WALL HEIGHT IN THE DATASET, because a ceili…
entries.text: THE BEST-FOUNDED WALL HEIGHT IN THE DATASET, because a ceiling height is actually attested: 'Seven and one-half feet is rather low for a hotel ceiling.' Two storeys at 7 1/2 ft = 15 ft, plus floor structure between them and a sill course, gives about 16 1/2 ft = 5.0 m to the plate. The 7 1/2 ft is documented; the allowance for joists and sill is the inference.

levels.8-10: The best known wall height we have, because someone told how high a ceiling was. A guest wrote that seven and a half feet was rather low for an inn's ceiling. Two floors at 7 and a half feet is 15 feet. Add the floors between, and it is about 16 and a half feet, or 5 meters, to the roof. The 7 and a half feet is known. The rest is our guess.

entries.card: notes:THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED, 1834 AGAINST 1835, AND THE DISPU…
entries.text: THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED, 1834 AGAINST 1835, AND THE DISPUTE IS RESOLVED HERE RATHER THAN LEFT OPEN — but the reasoning matters, because the two dates mean different things for this scene. chicagology reports W. H. Stow, who 'came to Chicago about 1833', saying of his own hotel that 'it was built in 1834'. The hotel chronology says it 'opened in 1835'. 1834 is adopted because it is the BUILDER'S OWN STATEMENT about his own building, recorded with the same detail that gives the 40 ft front, the 60 ft wing and the yard, against an undated one-line entry in a chronology that also mis-sizes the building. THE PHASE MECHANISM WAS CONSIDERED AND DELIBERATELY NOT USED. If the 1835 date were right, the hotel might have been unfinished or brand new on 1835-07-01, and a construction phase would be the honest way to show that. But a construction phase would have to invent a start month, a duration and a state of completeness, none of which any source gives, and it would silently adopt the weaker date to do it. One completed phase on the better-attested date, with the alternative recorded here and in the dossier, claims less. If the 1835 date is ever confirmed, split this phase then. The end of the range is set at the end of 1840, past the last account reached that describes the house in operation; it is not a demolition date and no source reached gives one.

levels.8-10: The year it was built is argued, 1834 or 1835, and we settle it here. But the reason matters, because the two dates mean different things for this scene. A website tells of W. H. Stow, who came to Chicago about 1833. He said of his own hotel that it was built in 1834. A list of hotels says it opened in 1835. We use 1834, because it is the builder's own word about his own building. It comes with the same details that give its sizes and yard. The list gives one line, no date of its own, and gets the size wrong. If 1835 were right, the hotel might have been unfinished on 1 July 1835. But showing that would mean making up a month and how far it was built, which no record gives. One finished stage on the better date claims less. If 1835 is ever proved, we can split it then. The dates end in 1840, after the last record of it being run. That is not when it came down. No record gives that.

entries.card: notes:THE BUILD YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT, so the ra…
entries.text: THE BUILD YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT, so the range opens at the start of 1827: Andreas, in the packing-house chapter, 'The site of the original log slaughter-house, built by Archibald Clybourne in 1827, for the killing of such cattle as were required by the garrison at Fort Dearborn' (scan p. 1149). THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS UNUSUALLY WELL SUPPORTED for this dataset: the same building is working six years later — 'The following year [1833] Archibald Clybourne, the Government butcher for the Pottawatomies, engaged in the packing business, at his log slaughter-house on the east side of the North Branch, where he packed some two hundred and fifty head of cattle and about two thousand hogs' (scan p. 1151) — which puts it in full operation nineteen months before 1835-07-01. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim; Andreas writing in 1883 says the site was BY THEN occupied by a later frame slaughter-house of Clybourne's 'now falling into pieces from sheer old age', so the log building came down at some point between 1835 and 1883 and nothing reached dates that.

levels.8-10: We know the year it was built, but not the month, so we start at the beginning of 1827. A book says Archibald Clybourne built a log butcher house in 1827, to kill cattle for the soldiers at Fort Dearborn. We know it still worked in 1833. That year he packed about 250 cattle and 2,000 hogs here. So it was busy less than two years before July 1835. The record ends at the end of 1835. By 1883 a newer wood one stood here, falling apart from age. So the log one came down some time between 1835 and 1883.

entries.card: notes:THE DATES ARE THE BUSINESS'S AND NOT THE BUILDING'S. Andreas…
entries.text: THE DATES ARE THE BUSINESS'S AND NOT THE BUILDING'S. Andreas lists 'Jim Kinzie's store, P. F. W. Peck's store, Harmon's and Loomis's' as all being on South Water Street by 1833, and separately records J. H. Kinzie advertising as a forwarding and commission merchant in 1834. The range opens at the start of 1833 on the first of those and closes at the end of the scene year on the ordinary continuity cut. Nothing reached dates the BUILDING at either end. A NAME CAUTION THAT AFFECTS NOTHING GEOMETRIC BUT SHOULD TRAVEL WITH THE RECORD: Andreas's 'Jim Kinzie' is James Kinzie, who kept the Wolf Point Tavern and the Green Tree on the west bank, while the 1834 forwarding advertisements are John H. Kinzie's. Whether the South Water store belonged to one brother, the other, or both at different times is not settled by anything reached, and the id follows the initials Andreas uses in the advertisement rather than the nickname he uses in the list.

levels.8-10: The dates are the shop's, not the building's. A book lists Jim Kinzie's store, Peck's, Harmon's and Loomis's on South Water Street by 1833. It also says J. H. Kinzie put ads in the paper in 1834 as a shipper. The dates start in 1833 and end with the year. Nothing dates the building. A word of warning about the name. The book's Jim Kinzie is James Kinzie, who kept two inns on the west bank. The 1834 ads are John H. Kinzie's. Which brother owned the store, or both at different times, is not settled. Our name for it follows the book's ad.

entries.card: notes:THE DECK, AND NOT ONE OF ITS NUMBERS IS A RECORD'S. Its u ex…
entries.text: THE DECK, AND NOT ONE OF ITS NUMBERS IS A RECORD'S. Its u extent is the span, 12 m, and its v extent the width, 3 m. THE SPAN IS SIZED OFF THE STREAM, as both its siblings' are: 6.65 m of open water at this northing — 55 % of the span — with 2.60 m and 2.75 m of dry seat left at the two abutments. It is the La Salle crossing's span over a narrower channel, and it is not the Slough Log Bridge's 8 m because 8 m here would leave 0.7 m of seat at each end. THE WIDTH IS THE SMALLEST OF THE THREE AND THAT IS THE ARGUMENT FOR IT. Charles Cleaver's 'these bridges were ten feet wide' (3.05 m) is documented for the two BRANCH bridges and is only a yardstick here; 3.0 m is a hair under it, the same figure the Slough Log Bridge takes, and this crossing has less claim to width than either sibling. It carries North Water Street, whose own record calls its traffic `light` and gives it a 6.0 m track — against South Water Street's 10.5 m, which is what the La Salle crossing's 4.27 m deck answers to. A crossing wider than the road it carries needs is a claim, and nothing here supports one. THIS IS NOT A RIVER BRIDGE AND MUST NOT BE SIZED LIKE ONE: the two branch bridges span 72 m and 56 m; this is a street crossing of a six-metre backwater.

levels.8-10: The deck, and not one of its numbers comes from a record. It is 12 meters long and 3 meters wide. Its length is sized to the stream, like the other two crossings. There are 6.65 meters of open water, with dry ground left at both ends. It is the width that matters most. It is the smallest of the three, and that is the reason for it. Cleaver's ten feet is for the two river bridges, and is only a guide here. 3 meters is a little under it. This crossing carries North Water Street, a quiet street with a narrow track. South Water is much wider, so its crossing is wider. A crossing wider than its road needs would be a claim, and nothing backs one. This is not a river bridge. The two river bridges are 72 and 56 meters long. This crosses a six meter backwater.

entries.card: notes:THE END OF THIS RANGE IS AN UPPER BOUND, NOT A DATE. The pic…
entries.text: THE END OF THIS RANGE IS AN UPPER BOUND, NOT A DATE. The pickets are attested standing in 1831 by someone living inside them - Juliette Kinzie, 'The fort was inclosed by high pickets' - and drawn on the 1830 plan. Robert Fergus, describing the fort in 1850, says 'The whole Fort enclosure was surrounded by a rough-board fence, white-washed, about 6 feet high; the pickets having been removed at an earlier date'. NOTHING REACHED DATES THAT REMOVAL, so the range is closed at the last day before Fergus's view rather than at a real terminus, and the buildings inside carry a longer range than the wall round them for that reason. On 1835-07-01 the post is garrisoned and the pickets stand: the removal belongs to the years after the troops left in December 1836, and a stockade is not pulled down round an occupied garrison.

levels.8-10: The end of this range is a limit, not a date. Juliette Kinzie lived inside the fort in 1831. She wrote that it was fenced in by high posts. The 1830 plan draws them too. In 1850 Robert Fergus wrote that a rough board fence, whitewashed, about 6 feet high, ran round the fort, and the posts had been taken away. Nothing tells when they came down. On 1 July 1835 there were soldiers in the fort, and the posts stood. No one pulls down a fort's wall with soldiers inside it.

entries.card: notes:THE ENVELOPE IS ATTESTED AND THE PLAN IS NOT. Original units…
entries.text: THE ENVELOPE IS ATTESTED AND THE PLAN IS NOT. Original units: 'The front was about forty feet and the wing sixty feet. It was in an L.' 40 ft = 12.19 m and 60 ft = 18.29 m, which is the polygon's bounding box exactly. What the source does not give is the arms' WIDTH, so the 7.0 m depth of the front range and of the wing is invented — chosen as about 23 ft, enough for a room and a passage, which is the shallowest width that makes an L rather than a solid block. Areas follow from that and are not attested: about 164 m2 on the ground, 1,770 sq ft. The word 'about' in 'about forty feet' is the source's own. DISPUTED: the hotel chronology calls the Western 'a small structure', which contradicts a 40 by 60 ft two-storey L outright. chicagology's figures are preferred because they come with the builder's account and with the yard and stable description; the chronology gives no dimensions at all, so 'small' is an impression, not a measurement. The stables and yard are attested and are NOT in this polygon.

levels.8-10: Its outer size is known, but not its plan. The record says the front was about forty feet and the wing sixty feet, in an L shape. 40 feet is 12.19 meters and 60 feet is 18.29 meters. That is the box around our shape, exactly. The record does not say how wide each arm was. So 7 meters, about 23 feet, is our guess, enough for a room and a hall. It is the narrowest that makes an L, not a solid block. The record's own word is about. Not everyone agrees. The list of hotels calls the Western a small building. That does not fit a 40 by 60 foot L with two floors. We prefer the website's sizes. They come with the builder's story, and with the yard and stable. The list gives no sizes at all, so small is a feeling, not a measure. The stable and yard are known, but are not in this shape.

entries.card: notes:THE FLAG IS ATTESTED AND ITS PATTERN IS THE LAW'S. Andreas (…
entries.text: THE FLAG IS ATTESTED AND ITS PATTERN IS THE LAW'S. Andreas (vol. 1 p. 128) has this staff fly 'a weather-beaten flag'; a garrison staff of the United States flew the national flag. Its star count is not described anywhere reached and is read from the Flag Act of 4 April 1818, which adds a star on the 4th of July after a state's admission: Missouri's (admitted 10 August 1821) made 24 stars on 4 July 1822, and Arkansas's (admitted 15 June 1836) made 25 only on 4 July 1836. So the flag in law on 1 July 1835 has 24 stars and 13 stripes. The arrangement of the stars (four rows of six), the size of the cloth and its wear beyond Andreas's word are reconstructed (L390).

levels.8-10: The flag is known, and its pattern comes from the law. A book says this pole flew a worn flag. A fort flew the national flag. No record says how many stars. A law of 1818 adds a star on the 4th of July after a new state joins. Missouri made 24 stars on 4 July 1822. Arkansas made 25 only on 4 July 1836. So on 1 July 1835 the flag had 24 stars and 13 stripes. How the stars were laid out, four rows of six, the flag's size and its wear are our guess.

entries.card: notes:THE FLOOR IS THE ADVERTISEMENT, NOT THE BUILDING, AND TWO PA…
entries.text: THE FLOOR IS THE ADVERTISEMENT, NOT THE BUILDING, AND TWO PAPERS PRINT IT. The Chicago Democrat of 1835-06-10 carries the card over the copy line 'Chicago, June 10, 1835.—8tf' and the Chicago American of 1835-06-13 carries the same card over 'Chicago, June [13], 183[5]'; the Democrat's is the earlier printing and the floor is its date. Both say the subscriber IS NOW OPENING an assortment at these premises, so the trade opens in the second week of June 1835 and the range opens with it. THE BUILDING is necessarily older than the trade in it and no source dates it, so what this range really records is that a clothing and boot store was open at a describable door on South Water Street three weeks before the scene date. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR: the Democrat's file here runs to 1835-08-12 and the American's to 1835-08-29, and nothing reached says when Holbrook left, so 31 December 1835 is this dataset's standing convention and not a reading.

levels.8-10: The start date is the ad's, not the building's, and two papers print it. The Chicago Democrat ran it on 10 June 1835, and the Chicago American on 13 June. The Democrat's came first, so its date is the start. Both say he is now opening his goods here. So the shop opens in the second week of June 1835. The building must be older than the shop, but no record dates it. What we know is that a clothes and boot store was open on South Water Street three weeks before the day we show. The end is just the end of the year. The papers we have run to August 1835, and nothing says when Holbrook left.

entries.card: notes:THE FORT WAS OCCUPIED ON 1835-07-01 AND THIS PROJECT CHECKED…
entries.text: THE FORT WAS OCCUPIED ON 1835-07-01 AND THIS PROJECT CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED IT. Andreas gives the sequence: the garrison was withdrawn in 1823, the post was re-garrisoned in October 1828, the troops were removed to Green Bay in May 1831, and 'In June [1832] the fort was once more garrisoned. Major William Whistler being assigned to the command' - held continuously from then until 29 December 1836. For the scene date itself Andreas brackets the command rather than naming it: DeLafayette Wilcox 'commanded until December 18, 1833, and again from September 16, 1835', with 'Major John Bender, Major John Greene and Captain and Brevet-Major Joseph Plympton ... in command at various times' between. The drloihjournal chronology fills the bracket with Maj. John Greene, 5th Infantry, 18 December 1833 to 16 September 1835, which is unfootnoted but lands exactly inside Andreas's two dates. STRENGTH IS NOT ATTESTED for mid-1835; Andreas gives two companies of infantry in 1833 and nothing later, so no number is recorded here. The garrison is why the gates are built shut rather than open and why the fort is modelled maintained rather than decaying.

levels.8-10: There were soldiers here on 1 July 1835, and we checked it. A book gives the order. The soldiers left in 1823. They came back in October 1828. They left for Green Bay in May 1831. In June 1832 soldiers came again, and they stayed until 29 December 1836. Wilcox was in charge until December 1833 and again from September 1835. Others led in between. A list fills that gap with Major John Greene. How many soldiers there were in 1835 is not known. A book says two groups in 1833, and nothing later. So no number is given. The soldiers are why the gates are shut, and why the fort is kept up, not falling down.

entries.card: notes:THE FUNCTION IS THE NAME AND EVERY WITNESS USES IT. A United…
entries.text: THE FUNCTION IS THE NAME AND EVERY WITNESS USES IT. A United States factory was the government's own trading house — the post at which the Indian trade was carried on the government's account — and all three sources name it as such: the plate letters `U.S. Factor's House`, Hubbard has it occupied 'by a Mr. Jouett, United States factor', and Hurlbut has the American Fur Company buying 'the Factory House' from the United States. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED IS WHAT WENT ON INSIDE IT IN 1835. The factory system was abolished in 1822, which is the same year Hurlbut has the building sold out of government hands; by the scene date this is a private house that used to be a trading house, and nothing this project holds says whether any trade was still carried on in it.

levels.8-10: Its name tells what it was, and every record uses it. A United States factory was the country's own trading house. It is where trade with the Native people was done for the government. All three records name it so. The plan names it the U.S. Factor's House. Hubbard says a Mr. Jouett, the factor, lived in it. Hurlbut says the American Fur Company bought it from the United States. What went on inside in 1835 is not claimed. The trading houses were shut in 1822, the same year Hurlbut says it was sold. By 1835 this was a private house that used to be a trading house. Nothing we have says if any trade still went on in it.

entries.card: notes:THE HIGHEST-VALUE SINGLE BUILDING PHASE ONE FOUND, and the r…
entries.text: THE HIGHEST-VALUE SINGLE BUILDING PHASE ONE FOUND, and the reason is that boarding houses bridge the gap between 3,265 people and 398 dwellings. Andreas on the houses of 1834: they 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides', with emigrants living in their covered wagons outside. The building is log rather than frame on Andreas's own word, which also makes it one of the few log records in the commercial core.

levels.8-10: This is one of the most useful buildings we found. In 1835 there were 3,265 people and only 398 homes, and boarding houses held the rest. Andreas says the houses of 1834 were always full. Full sometimes meant three in a bed, with more people on the floor. New settlers lived in their covered wagons outside. Andreas says this house was made of logs. That makes it one of the few log buildings in the middle of town.

entries.card: notes:THE INITIAL DISAGREES BETWEEN THE TWO SOURCES AND THE RECORD…
entries.text: THE INITIAL DISAGREES BETWEEN THE TWO SOURCES AND THE RECORD DOES NOT PICK ONE. Andreas writes 'H. Jones'. The advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 reads 'B. JONES'. A contemporary advertisement is the man's own word about his own name and would normally win outright, but the reading comes off a scan of a damaged sheet, the letters B and H are among the easiest to confuse in a display face of this period, and this project has been warned that the transcription accompanying the scan is imperfect elsewhere in the same issue. So the surname is carried, the initial is not, and the record id keeps the H that this project's dossier assigned it because renaming a record is worse than annotating one. Both readings are recorded in aka.

levels.8-10: The two records give his first letter two ways, and we do not pick one. A book says H. Jones. The 1833 ad says B. Jones. An ad is the man's own word on his own name, and should win. But the old page is damaged, and B and H are easy to mix up in big print of that time. The typed copy of that paper has other mistakes too. So we keep Jones, but not the letter. Both are kept in the record.

entries.card: notes:THE LABEL IS THE FUNCTION AND THE LABEL IS A CATEGORY. `Out…
entries.text: THE LABEL IS THE FUNCTION AND THE LABEL IS A CATEGORY. `Out Buildings` names what a building is NOT — not the barn, not the shop, not the wash house, all three of which this plate letters separately a hundred metres north of here — and says nothing about what went on inside. A post's out buildings are privies, wood sheds, stores and pens; which of those this was is not on the sheet and is not guessed at here.

levels.8-10: The label tells what it was not. Out Buildings means not the barn, not the shop and not the wash house. The plan names those three on their own, to the north. It says nothing about what went on inside. A fort's out buildings were toilets, wood sheds, stores and pens. Which this was is not on the map, and we do not guess.

entries.text: THE MARGIN IS ONLY 2 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

levels.8-10: It is only 2 meters inside the edge of that land. That is closer than our map can be trusted, so the grade drops one step. The land is right only if our drawn survey line is right. entries.card: notes:THE NEAREST THING TO AN ATTESTED FABRIC ANY OUTBUILDING IN T…
entries.text: THE NEAREST THING TO AN ATTESTED FABRIC ANY OUTBUILDING IN THIS DATASET HAS, AND IT IS STILL AN INFERENCE. Andreas calls the building 'the old cabin', not 'the old log cabin', so the word 'log' is not on the page. What is on the page is that every building described at Chicago before 1820 was of logs: Andreas's own account of the 1816 rebuilding finds 'a few dilapidated log huts, covered with bark' on the ground, David McKee's recollection of the houses he found and built on the north bank in 1823 is 'All these houses were of logs', and this project's dossier records no brick of consequence on the south side before 1837 and no sawn-lumber supply at Chicago until the mills of 1832-33. A cabin standing at Chicago before 1817 is a log cabin. Recorded inferred rather than documented because the distinction between what a source says and what a source makes certain is the one this project is built on.

levels.8-10: Our closest thing to a known wall for any shed here, but still a guess. Andreas calls it the old cabin, without the word log. But every building written about here before 1820 was made of logs. Andreas found a few run-down log huts with bark roofs in 1816. McKee said all the houses he found in 1823 were logs. No sawn boards came to Chicago until the mills of 1832 and 1833. So a cabin here before 1817 was made of logs. We call it a guess, not a fact, because that line is what this project is built on.

entries.card: notes:THE ONE DESCRIBED THING ABOUT THIS BUILDING, and it is expli…
entries.text: THE ONE DESCRIBED THING ABOUT THIS BUILDING, and it is explicit: 'a two-story frame structure'. It is the reason the record exists at all — a two-storey store was worth remarking on when Lake Street was still mostly cabins and mud, and the sentence is offered precisely as a first-of-its-kind. SOURCE CAVEAT THAT TRAVELS WITH EVERY DOCUMENTED TAG ON THIS RECORD: the claim sits in an uncredited modern editorial addendum at the foot of a chicagology map gallery, graded tier 4 by this project's own source record, which says in terms that the addendum is the weakest text in that set and must never outrank Andreas. It is cited because it is explicit and because it is the only place this building has been found, not because it is strong.

levels.8-10: The one thing told about this building, and it is plain: a frame building of two floors. It is why this record exists at all. A store of two floors was worth noting when Lake Street was still mostly cabins and mud. The line calls it the first of its kind. A warning goes with every known fact here. The claim is in a note with no author, added at the foot of a page of maps on a website. Our own notes call it the weakest text in that set, never to rank above Andreas. We use it because it is plain, and the only place this building is found, not because it is strong.

entries.card: notes:THE OPENING IS DISPUTED BY TEN WEEKS AND THE DISPUTE IS BETW…
entries.text: THE OPENING IS DISPUTED BY TEN WEEKS AND THE DISPUTE IS BETWEEN THE BUILDER AND HIS COMPILER. Nelson R. Norton, the ship-carpenter who built it, in a letter Andreas prints: 'I came to Chicago November 16, 1833. Soon after I arrived, I commenced cutting the lumber for a drawbridge... In March, 1834, I commenced building it, and I think it was completed by the 1st of June.' Andreas corrects him on the spot: 'Mr. Norton is evidently in error as to the time of the completion of the bridge, since the Democrat states that it was formally accepted by the Trustees in August, the first proposals having been received in February.' The range opens on the LATER of the two, 1 August 1834, because the question a range answers is when the structure certainly stood as a working public crossing, and 'I think it was completed by' is the weaker of the two claims even before Andreas contradicts it. Nothing turns on the choice for this scene: the bridge is standing eleven months before 1835-07-01 either way. THE CLOSE IS THE BEST-ATTESTED DATE ON THIS RECORD: 'the Common Council ordered its removal in July, 1839', and 'a large crowd gathered upon the river before daylight, the next morning, and going to work with a will, in a very short time chopped the bridge to pieces.' A structure destroyed within a day of a dated order is a rarity in this dataset. THE INFERRED TAG IS FOR THE OPENING AND NOT THE CLOSE. The August acceptance rests on an 1834 issue of the Chicago Democrat that this project does not hold, quoted by Andreas fifty years later; the paper itself is the thing that would move this to documented.

levels.8-10: When it opened is in doubt by ten weeks. The man who built it and the man who wrote the book disagree. Nelson R. Norton, a ship's carpenter, wrote that he came in November 1833, began the drawbridge in March 1834, and thought it was done by 1 June. The book says he was wrong, since a paper says the town accepted it in August. We start on 1 August 1834, the later date, when it surely stood. Either way it stood long before July 1835. The end is well known: in July 1839 the town ordered it taken away. Before dawn the next morning a big crowd chopped it to pieces. Our August date comes from an 1834 paper we have not seen ourselves.

entries.card: notes:THE PRICED SERVICE IS THE ARGUMENT, as at the Wolf Point sta…
entries.text: THE PRICED SERVICE IS THE ARGUMENT, as at the Wolf Point stable: a horse kept overnight is a horse led in and out, and the archetype's 'stable' door (1.35 m clear) is the opening that allows it.

levels.8-10: The town set a price for keeping a horse, so horses were kept. A horse kept overnight is led in and out. So the stable gets our horse door, 1.35 meters wide.

entries.card: notes:THE PRICED SERVICE IS THE ARGUMENT. What the county's 1831 o…
entries.text: THE PRICED SERVICE IS THE ARGUMENT. What the county's 1831 order documents is that a horse could be fed and kept overnight at a licensed Chicago tavern for a stated price; a horse that is kept is a horse that is led in and out, and the archetype's 'stable' door is exactly the opening that allows (1.35 m clear). A man's door would make this a feed store, which would leave the documented service happening outdoors and the building unexplained.

levels.8-10: The priced service is the reason. The county's order of 1831 says a horse could be fed and kept overnight at a licensed Chicago inn, for a set price. A horse that is kept is led in and out. A stable door, 1.35 meters wide, allows that. A door for people would make this a feed store. Then the known service would happen outside, and the building would make no sense.

entries.card: notes:THE RANGE HAS ONE WITNESS, NOT TWO, AND THAT IS THE DIFFEREN…
entries.text: THE RANGE HAS ONE WITNESS, NOT TWO, AND THAT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS RECORD AND THE OTHER TWO PLACED BESIDE IT. Only the plan names a Shop here; Hubbard walks the same ground on the same two pages and does not mention it. IT OPENS 24 FEBRUARY 1830, the date on the Harrison plan, because that is the earliest date any source this project holds fixes to this building; Hubbard's narrative of the fort's surroundings is of the late 1820s and carries it earlier without dating it. IT CLOSES 29 DECEMBER 1836, the evacuation, and that is a floor rather than a demolition: nothing attests when the fort's outer buildings came down, and a range that ran on to 1856 with the fort's principal structures would claim a survival for a workshop that nobody wrote down. WHAT CARRIES THE SCENE DATE OF 1 JULY 1835 is the middle of that range and not either end of it — the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836, so a service building the garrison's own engineer drew in 1830 is standing five years later unless something says it stopped, and nothing does. That is an argument, not an assumption, and it is the argument every Fort Dearborn record here rests on.

What counts for July 1835 is the middle. Soldiers were here the whole time from June 1832 to the end of 1836. A building drawn in 1830 still stood five years later, unless something says it stopped. Nothing does.

entries.text: THE RANGE IS THE FORT'S, NOT THIS BUILDING'S. No source reached dates any individual building inside Fort Dearborn. It opens with the rebuild of 1816 (Andreas; Wentworth quoting the Adjutant-General, 'the post was reoccupied about June, 1816 ... Nothing is on file respecting the rebuilding of the Fort') and closes with the demolition of the fort's principal structures in the summer of 1856 (Andreas). What carries the scene date is the middle: this building is drawn standing on the 1830 plan and described standing in Hubbard's 1827 walk round the inside, and the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

levels.8-10: These dates are the fort's, not this building's. No record dates any one building inside Fort Dearborn. We start with the rebuilding in 1816, when soldiers came back about June. We end when the main buildings were torn down in the summer of 1856. What shows it in 1835: this building is on the 1830 plan, and a man named Hubbard saw it on his walk around inside in 1827. Soldiers were at the fort from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.
