entries.text: THE ROOF IS AN INVENTION AND THIS CANNOT OUTRANK IT. The footprint stands 0 m inside the tract's nearest boundary, which on a documented building would carry the middle tier, but this building was dealt to its lot by a recipe and is not there. The tract is real and the register's words about it are read; what is graded here is the claim that THIS roof stands on it, and that claim is the recipe's. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

entries.card: notes:THE SCENE DATE IS BRACKETED BY TWO ATTESTATIONS AND NAMED BY…
entries.text: THE SCENE DATE IS BRACKETED BY TWO ATTESTATIONS AND NAMED BY NEITHER. Before it: Andreas, on the Methodist society organised in 1834, 'For a time services were held in various places — in Billy Caldwell's log council-house, in Chester Ingersoll's tavern, or in Watkins's school-house' — a sentence set in 1834, before the congregation's own frame building was contracted on 30 June that year. After it: the Chicago Tribune's account of 18 August 1835, six and a half weeks past the scene date, has the assembly for the last war dance form 'at the "Council House" on the north side of the river'. A building in use in 1834 and in use in August 1835 was standing in between unless something took it down and put it back, which nothing says. THAT INFERENCE IS THE STRONGEST THING IN THIS RECORD AND IT CARRIES A JOIN: Andreas's 'Billy Caldwell's log council-house' and the Tribune's 'Council House' are treated as the same building, on the grounds that both are a council house on the north side in the same two years and neither source knows of a second one. Neither source makes the identification, and if they are two buildings then this record's construction comes from one and its position from the other. The range opens on 1 January 1834 as the earliest day the attested year allows — the treaty council of September 1833 on the same Tribune page mentions 'the council house' too, which may push the building earlier, and the page does not say it is this one — and closes at the end of 1835 as this record's claim horizon.

levels.8-10: Two records come before and after July 1835, and neither names that date. Before: a book says that in 1834 church was held in a few places. One was Billy Caldwell's log council house. After: a paper of 18 August 1835 says the crowd for the last war dance met at the Council House on the north side of the river. A building in use in 1834 and in August 1835 stood in between, unless something took it down. But we treat the two as one building. Neither record says so. If they are two, our shape comes from one and our place from the other. We start on 1 January 1834 and end at the end of 1835.

entries.card: notes:THE SEASON IS DOCUMENTED AND NO EXACT DATE IS. Andreas: 'In…
entries.text: THE SEASON IS DOCUMENTED AND NO EXACT DATE IS. Andreas: 'In the spring of 1833, Tyler K. Blodgett established a brick-yard, on the North Side, not far from the river bank, between Dearborn and Clark streets. He engaged Henry S. Lampman, then of Ann Arbor, as a workman. As Mr. Blodgett operated the first brick-yard in the city, so Mr. Lampman was undoubtedly the first brick-maker' (scan p. 1161). The range opens on 1 March 1833 as the conventional start of spring rather than as a stated date; brickmaking is a summer trade — clay is dug in autumn, weathered over winter, moulded and dried through the warm months — so the yard's first working season is 1833. SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS INFERENCE, and it is better supported than most in this dataset: the Lake House, begun on the north bank in 1835, is three storeys and a basement of BRICK, and Andreas's own sentence traces the town's first brick building to this yard, so somebody was making brick in Chicago through the boom. Whether it was still Blodgett on this ground on 1835-07-01 is not attested. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

levels.8-10: We know the season, but not the day. Andreas says that in the spring of 1833 Tyler K. Blodgett started a brickyard on the North Side. Henry S. Lampman worked for him, the first brick-maker in the city. We start it on 1 March 1833, the usual start of spring. Bricks were made in summer, so 1833 was the yard's first season. That it still ran in 1835 is a guess, but a good one. A brick hotel went up in 1835, so someone was still making bricks. The record ends at the end of 1835.

entries.card: notes:THE SOURCE GIVES AN ADJECTIVE AND THIS RECORD NEEDS A NUMBER…
entries.text: THE SOURCE GIVES AN ADJECTIVE AND THIS RECORD NEEDS A NUMBER. Kinzie says 'high pickets' and nobody else says anything at all. 3.7 m is twelve feet, the common height for a frontier stockade of this class, and it is a guess dressed in a plausible number. A visitor looking at the height of this wall is looking at our arithmetic, not at evidence.

levels.8-10: The record gives a word, and we need a number. Kinzie says high posts, and no one else says anything. 3.7 meters is twelve feet, the usual height for a fort's fence like this. It is a guess with a number on it. The height you see is our math, not proof.

entries.text: THE SOURCE OFFERS TWO YEARS AND THIS RANGE TAKES THE LATER ONE AS A FLOOR. Andreas: 'a wooden structure, erected in 1833 or 1834, by John Bates, for an auction-room.' The range opens at the start of 1834, the later of the two; if Andreas meant 1833 the building is a year older than this says, and if he meant late 1834 the range opens a few months early. Neither reading changes the 1835 scene, which is why the ambiguity is recorded rather than resolved. Bates is independently attested as the auctioneer for the school-section sale of October 1833 and as an active advertiser in 1834, and he was deputy postmaster from 1833, so the man is well placed in the town on either date. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR; no source reached follows the building past its erection.

levels.8-10: A book gives two years, and we take the later one. Andreas says John Bates put up a wooden building in 1833 or 1834, as a room for auctions. So we start it at the beginning of 1834. Either year is fine for 1835. Other records show Bates in town then. He sold land at an auction in 1833, and he helped run the post office. No record tells what became of the building, so we end it at 1835.

entries.card: notes:THE START DATE DEPENDS ON WHICH BUILDING THIS IS, WHICH IS T…
entries.text: THE START DATE DEPENDS ON WHICH BUILDING THIS IS, WHICH IS THE SAME DISPUTE AS THE POSITION. Wau-Bun describes the log school-house standing at Wolf Point in 1831, and the first Methodist society was organised on 14 June 1831 with ten members in a log cabin, so 1831 is the start under the reading adopted here. Under the competing reading the building standing in 1835 is a cabin the congregation BUILT IN 1834 on the other bank, in which case this range begins three years too early. The end is firmer: the congregation floated the cabin across the river in 1838 and rolled it on logs to Washington and Clark, which ends the phase wherever it began — and is itself the reason phases carry their own position in this schema. Tagged inferred rather than documented because the start rests on identifying the 1835 building with the 1831 one.

levels.8-10: The start date depends on which building this is. That is the same question as where it stood. Wau-Bun tells of the log school house at Wolf Point in 1831. The first Methodist group formed on 14 June 1831, with ten people, in a log cabin. So 1831 is the start, by our reading. By the other reading, the building of 1835 is a cabin the group built in 1834 on the other bank. Then these dates start three years too early. The end is firmer. In 1838 the group floated the cabin across the river, and rolled it on logs to Washington and Clark. That ends this stage wherever it began. It is marked as our guess, since the start rests on the 1835 building being the 1831 one.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS DOCUMENTED TO THE DAY AND IT IS THE NEWSPAPER'S…
entries.text: THE START IS DOCUMENTED TO THE DAY AND IT IS THE NEWSPAPER'S DATE, NOT THE BUILDING'S. The Chicago American was established by T. O. Davis on 8 June 1835 — a weekly, sheet 15.5 x 21.5 inches, six columns, published Saturday mornings — with its office on Water Street near the draw-bridge. So on 1835-07-01 the paper is TWENTY-THREE DAYS OLD, which is the fact this record exists to put in the scene: Chicago has two newspapers in July 1835 and one of them is three weeks old. The BUILDING is necessarily older than the paper and nothing reached dates it, so the range's start is a floor. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR. The American outlived 1835 comfortably — by 1839 the Daily Chicago American was printing from the third floor of the Harmon and Loomis building at Clark and South Water, which is a different address and is why this record does not follow it — but no source reached follows this building at all.

levels.8-10: The start is known to the day, but it is the newspaper's date, not the building's. T. O. Davis started the Chicago American on 8 June 1835. It came out on Saturday mornings. Its office was on Water Street, near the drawbridge. So on 1 July 1835 the paper was 23 days old. That is why this record exists: in July 1835 Chicago had two newspapers, and one was three weeks old. The building must be older than the paper, but no record dates it. The paper went on long after 1835, but from a different place by 1839. No record follows this building.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS DOCUMENTED TO THE DAY, WHICH IS RARE IN THIS DA…
entries.text: THE START IS DOCUMENTED TO THE DAY, WHICH IS RARE IN THIS DATASET. Andreas: 'It was upon the eighth day of October, 1833, that a young man named Asahel Pierce arrived in Chicago from Vermont, and commenced the erection of a blacksmith shop, on Lake Street, corner of Canal' (scan p. 1161). The range opens on that date, which is when building BEGAN rather than when the shop was working — nothing says how long it took, and a small board shop is a matter of weeks. The range is tagged inferred rather than documented for the far end only: nothing reached follows the building past 1834, and it closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim. THE SURVIVAL IS BETTER SUPPORTED THAN MOST HERE: Andreas has Pierce ironing the first Chicago-to-St-Louis stage line for John T. Temple & Co. in January 1834 and beginning the manufacture of the old-fashioned 'Bull' plough with a wooden mould-board in the spring of that year, which is a business growing rather than folding, and Pierce is still a Chicago figure decades later, an alderman in 1843 and 1844 with two streets named after him (scan pp. 387, 411).

levels.8-10: The start is known to the day, which is rare here. A book says that on 8 October 1833, a young man named Asahel Pierce came to Chicago from Vermont. He began to build a blacksmith shop on Lake Street, at the corner of Canal. The dates start then, when building began, not when the shop was working. Nothing says how long it took. A small board shop takes weeks. The end is our guess. Nothing follows the building after 1834, and the dates end with 1835. But that it lasted is better backed than most here. The book says Pierce did the iron work for the first coach line from Chicago to St Louis in January 1834. That spring he began making the old Bull plow, with a wood blade. A business growing does not close. Pierce was still known in Chicago years later, a city leader in 1843 and 1844, with two streets named after him.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS THE DATE OF THE DESCRIPTION, NOT OF THE BUILDIN…
entries.text: THE START IS THE DATE OF THE DESCRIPTION, NOT OF THE BUILDING, as for the rest of this ring: Andreas's vicinity list is of about 1830 and Wau-Bun's ring of 1831, and the 1830-31 agency staffing is where the office of striker is listed at all. THE END IS THE HONEST MINIMUM on the group's continuity argument. Nothing dates this building at either end.

levels.8-10: The start is the date someone wrote about the place, not the date it was built. Andreas's list is from about 1830, and the book Wau-Bun's from 1831. A list of agency workers from 1830 and 1831 names the job of striker, a blacksmith's helper. The end is the least we can claim. No record tells when this building went up or came down.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS THE DATE OF THE DESCRIPTION, NOT OF THE BUILDIN…
entries.text: THE START IS THE DATE OF THE DESCRIPTION, NOT OF THE BUILDING. Andreas's vicinity list describes the settlement about 1830 and Wau-Bun the same ring in 1831; nothing says when any of these buildings went up, so the range opens at the earlier of the two descriptions rather than inventing a construction year. THE END IS THE HONEST MINIMUM, on the same continuity argument the whole group carries: the agency still owed the Potawatomi a blacksmith in 1835 and its establishment was still staffed, so the ring round the agency house is inferred to be standing on the scene date. No source reached gives this building a fate.

levels.8-10: The start is the date someone wrote about the place, not the date it was built. Andreas wrote about the town around 1830, and the book Wau-Bun about 1831. Nothing says when these buildings went up, so we start at the first of the two. The end is the least we can claim. In 1835 the agency still owed the Potawatomi a blacksmith, and it still had workers. So we think the houses around it still stood. No record tells what became of this one.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT PUTS THE…
entries.text: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT PUTS THE BUSINESS IN CHICAGO. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries a display advertisement headed 'Grocery & Provision Store. B. JONES. CHICAGO-ILLINOIS.' — which is primary evidence that a Jones grocery was trading in the town on that day. Andreas independently records 'grocery and provision store and forwarding and commission store by H. Jones' among the 1834 advertisers. THAT IS EVIDENCE ABOUT A BUSINESS AND NOT ABOUT A BUILDING; nothing reached dates the premises at either end, and the range closes at the end of the scene year on the ordinary continuity cut.

levels.8-10: It starts on the first date a paper of the time puts the shop in Chicago. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 has an ad for B. Jones's food store. That proves a Jones shop was open in town that day. A book also lists a food store and shipping shop by H. Jones in 1834. That tells about a business, not a building. Nothing dates the building, and the dates end with the year.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT PUTS THI…
entries.text: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT PUTS THIS BUILDING IN EXISTENCE, AND IT IS THE BUILDING'S OWN TENANT SAYING SO. The Chicago Democrat's first issue, Tuesday 26 November 1833, carries an imprint that gives its own address: 'THE DEMOCRAT, Is published every Tuesday, in the village of Chicago, Cook co. Ill. in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets.' A newspaper stating where it is printed on the day it is printed is as good as evidence at this date gets. The building is OLDER than that: Andreas says the office was secured in November 1833 in a building 'which was unfinished at the time', so it was under construction earlier in that year and the range's start is a floor, not a build date. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR. The Democrat was published continuously through 1835 — Andreas quotes its columns for 1834 and 1835 repeatedly, including Hogan's mail notice of 19 September 1835 — but no source reached follows the BUILDING past its tenancy, and 1835-12-31 is a housekeeping bound rather than a demolition date.

levels.8-10: The start is the first date a record from the time shows this building. Its own renter says so. The first Chicago Democrat came out on 26 November 1833. It says it is printed in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets. A paper that says where it is printed, on that same day, is as good a record as we have. The house is older than that. A book says it was not done in November 1833, so it was going up that year. The paper came out all through 1835, but no record follows the house. The end date is just where our record stops.

entries.card: notes:THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THE FIRM IN BUSINE…
entries.text: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THE FIRM IN BUSINESS, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME AS PUTTING THE BUILDING IN EXISTENCE, and this range does not pretend otherwise. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries a display advertisement headed 'C. & I. HARMON', dated 18 November 1833, offering dry goods, crockery, hardware, wet and dry groceries and 'on commission, a large lot of Leather, Saddlery, &c.' — contemporary proof that a Harmon store was trading at Chicago three weeks before the town was a month into having a newspaper. Andreas independently lists 'Jim Kinzie's store, P. F. W. Peck's store, Harmon's and Loomis's' as all being on South Water Street by 1833. NEITHER STATEMENT DATES THE BUILDING. The corner attribution comes from a later Andreas passage describing the three-storey building at Clark and South Water that housed the Daily Chicago American on its third floor in 1839, and whether the 1835 building was that building, or its predecessor on the same lot, is unattested. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR, not a demolition date.

levels.8-10: It starts on the first date a record puts the shop in business. That is not when the building went up, and we do not say it is. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 has an ad for C. and I. Harmon, dated 18 November. It sells cloth, dishes, tools, food and drink, and leather and saddles for others. So a Harmon store was open in Chicago then, just weeks after the town got a paper. A book also lists Harmon's with other stores on South Water Street by 1833. Neither dates the building. A later page tells of a three-floor building at Clark and South Water, with a paper on its top floor in 1839. If that was the 1835 building, or one before it on the same lot, is not known. The dates end with the year, not because it was torn down.

entries.card: notes:THE STREET IS DOCUMENTED AND NOTHING ELSE IS. 'On Lake Stree…
entries.text: THE STREET IS DOCUMENTED AND NOTHING ELSE IS. 'On Lake Street' is the whole of the evidence: no cross street, no side, no block. This record sits on the Lake Street south frontage band the reconstruction recipes use, west of the Clark Street crossing, in the first free frontage the placement rule found. The position is an invention within a documented street and is graded accordingly.

levels.8-10: The street is known, and nothing else. On Lake Street is all the record says: no cross street, no side, no block. It sits on the south side of Lake Street, west of Clark, in the first free spot our rule found. The place is our guess on a known street, and is graded so.

entries.card: notes:THE USE IS DOCUMENTED, THE CAMP IS DRAWN. The American of 13…
entries.text: THE USE IS DOCUMENTED, THE CAMP IS DRAWN. The American of 13 June 1835: 'our wharves are covered with [men], women and children just landed from the vessels ... who [had else] remained under the open [sk]y upon the wharves. Some build tents upon the spot [t]hey [we]re landed from the b[oa]ts.' Inferred, not attested, because the paper does not say where on the riverfront, and this is one stretch of it.

levels.8-10: Its use is known, but the camp is our drawing. The American of 13 June 1835 says the docks were covered with men, women and children just off the boats. They would have stayed out under the sky on the docks. Some put up tents right where they landed. The paper does not say where on the river front, and this is one stretch of it. So it is our guess, not a record.

entries.card: notes:THE WORD ON THE PLATE IS 'Shop' AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED.…
entries.text: THE WORD ON THE PLATE IS 'Shop' AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. A post of this size kept a smith and usually a carpenter, and it would be easy to write either onto this record; neither is written, because the plate says shop and a trade would be this project inventing an occupant for a building it can barely size. What the record holds is a workshop on the fort's outer ground. Which shop is an open question and belongs to whoever finds a post return.

levels.8-10: The plan says Shop and nothing more. A fort this size had a blacksmith and often a carpenter. It would be easy to write either one here. We do not, because the plan says only shop. A trade would be us making up who worked in it. What we have is a workshop on the fort's outer ground. Which shop is still a question, for whoever finds the fort's papers.

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS ATTESTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT, so the range open…
entries.text: THE YEAR IS ATTESTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT, so the range opens on 1 January 1831 rather than claiming a build date. DRLOIH: 'In 1831 John Miller built a log house near his brother's tavern that he used as a tannery, Chicago's first recorded factory.' Andreas, independently and with a direction the other source lacks: 'John Miller, brother of Samuel, the landlord, came in 1831, and run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern.' THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE HONEST MINIMUM, NOT A FATE. Nothing reached follows this building past its founding: Andreas adds a partner, 'Benjamin Hall, tanner, a partner of John Miller, who came in 1832', and then the trade drops out of the record, while Samuel Miller — the brother whose tavern fixes this building's position — 'sold the tavern and moved away following the death of his wife in 1832'. So the anchor moved on three years before the scene date and the tannery's own survival rests on the ordinary continuity argument: a standing building stands until something says otherwise. Tagged inferred for that reason.

levels.8-10: The year is known, but not the month. So the dates start on 1 January 1831, not on a build day. A book says that in 1831, John Miller built a log house near his brother's inn and used it to tan hides. It was Chicago's first known factory. Another book says John Miller, brother of Samuel, came in 1831 and ran a tannery just north of Miller's inn. The end is the least we can say, not its fate. Nothing follows this building after it opened. The book adds a partner, Benjamin Hall, a tanner who came in 1832. Then the trade drops out of the record. Samuel Miller sold the inn and moved away after his wife died in 1832. So the tannery lasting to 1835 rests on our usual reason: a building stands until something says it did not. So it is marked as our guess.

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS ATTESTED, THE MONTH IS NOT, AND THE BUILDING ITS…
entries.text: THE YEAR IS ATTESTED, THE MONTH IS NOT, AND THE BUILDING ITSELF IS DISPUTED BY THE MAN WHO TAUGHT IN IT. Andreas: 'It is stated in Mr. Wells's report that these gentlemen [Colonels Hamilton and Owen] afterwards built a house on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street, in which Mr. Watkins continued his school, and that it was the first house built for a school in Chicago. BUT THIS DOES NOT RECUR TO MR. WATKINS'S RECOLLECTION.' Andreas prints the doubt and then, forty pages later, states the building as fact and dates it: 'John Watkins was then teaching what had become a public school on the North Side, on the river bank just east of Clark Street, in the building erected by Colonels Hamilton and Owen, as has already been stated, in 1833.' A THIRD PASSAGE CORROBORATES A SCHOOL BUILDING THERE, independently of Wells: Andreas's Methodist chapter has Jesse Walker's first quarterly meeting held 'in the Watkins school-house, which was located on North Water Street, between Clark and LaSalle'. So a Watkins school-house existed on North Water Street near Clark in 1834, whatever Watkins remembered about who built it. The range opens on 1 January 1833 as the earliest day the attested year allows and closes at the end of 1835 as this record's claim horizon; no source follows the building past Watkins, who 'taught as late as 1835, but the exact date of his retirement is not known'.

levels.8-10: The year is known, but not the month. And the man who taught there did not remember it the same way. A book says that, by Mr. Wells's report, two men built a house on the north bank, just east of Clark Street. Mr. Watkins kept his school in it. It was the first house built for a school in Chicago. But the book says Mr. Watkins did not remember it so. Forty pages on, the same book says it as fact, and gives 1833. A third page backs a school there too. Jesse Walker held his first church meeting in the Watkins school house, on North Water Street. So a Watkins school house stood near Clark in 1834, whoever built it. The dates start on 1 January 1833 and end with 1835. Watkins taught as late as 1835, but no one knows when he stopped.

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT. Andreas, in the…
entries.text: THE YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE MONTH IS NOT. Andreas, in the packing-house chapter: 'In 1834, Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole had a slaughter-house erected on the South Branch of the river, where some three hundred head of cattle and fourteen hundred hogs were packed during the year' (scan p. 1151). The range therefore opens at the start of 1834 for want of a month; packing is winter work, so the plant was probably up by the autumn of that year rather than in January, and the phrase 'during the year' means the 1834 season. THE SURVIVAL TO 1835-07-01 IS ORDINARY CONTINUITY AND IS NOT ATTESTED — nothing reached follows this building past its first season. What can be said for it is that a purpose-built plant which handled 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in its first year was not abandoned within eighteen months, and that the firm was still trading in Chicago through the decade. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

levels.8-10: The year is known, but not the month. A book says that in 1834, Oliver Newberry and George Dole had a meat plant built on the South Branch. About three hundred cattle and fourteen hundred hogs were packed there that year. So the dates start in 1834, since no month is given. Packing is winter work, so the plant was likely up by fall, not January. That it lasted to 1 July 1835 is our usual guess, not known. Nothing follows it past its first season. But a plant made for the work, that handled 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in its first year, was not left empty in eighteen months. The firm kept trading in Chicago for years. The dates end with 1835.

entries.card: notes:THE YEAR IS DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS AND THE MONTH IS NOT…
entries.text: THE YEAR IS DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS AND THE MONTH IS NOT. In his hotel chapter: 'Mr. Beaubien had meanwhile built a new house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets. In August of 1834, Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this new hotel, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House.' In his life of Mark Beaubien: 'In the latter year [1834] he completed another house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets, which was called the Exchange Coffee House, and first kept by Mr. and Mrs. John Murphy.' So the house was finished and trading by August 1834, eleven months before the scene date, and 1834-01-01 is the first day the attested year permits rather than a date anybody gives - which is why this range is inferred and not documented. THE SCENE DATE IS NOT AT RISK: whatever month in 1834 the building went up, it was open under the Murphys from August 1834 and they 'remained there until 1836'. THE END IS A BOUND WHERE THE EVIDENCE STOPS, NOT A DEMOLITION: the Murphys left for the old Sauganash in 1836 and this project has nothing dating the building's fate. Andreas's list of minor houses in 1845 includes 'the Illinois Exchange, corner Wells and Lake streets', which may be the same fabric under a later sign or may not; the phase is closed at the end of the attested tenancy rather than run on speculatively.

levels.8-10: A book gives the year twice, but not the month. It says Mr. Beaubien built a new house on the corner of Wells and Lake streets. In August 1834 Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took it over as a hotel and named it the Exchange Coffee House. So it was done and open by August 1834, eleven months before July 1835. We start on 1 January 1834, the first day that year allows. Whatever month it went up, it was open in 1835. The Murphys stayed until 1836. We end where the record stops, not when it came down. A list from 1845 names a hotel on the same corner. It may be the same house or may not.

entries.card: notes:THIS RANGE IS ANDREAS'S DESCRIPTIVE WINDOW, NOT THE STAFF'S…
entries.text: THIS RANGE IS ANDREAS'S DESCRIPTIVE WINDOW, NOT THE STAFF'S LIFE. His section 'Chicago from 1833 to 1837' opens at the close of 1833 with the town legally organized and describes what a visitor saw across those four years; the flagstaff sentence sits in that description. Nothing reached says when the staff was raised or when it came down, so the range is set to the window of the only text that puts it there and both ends are limits of the SOURCE rather than of the object. The scene date sits comfortably inside it. The obvious candidate for a real end - 29 December 1836, when the troops were permanently withdrawn under a printed order - is deliberately NOT used: it dates the garrison, not the spar, and the buildings stood into the 1850s.

levels.8-10: These dates come from the book's account, not the flagpole's life. Its chapter on Chicago from 1833 to 1837 tells what a visitor saw in those four years, and the flagpole line is in it. Nothing says when the pole went up or came down. So the dates are the book's limits, not the pole's. July 1835 sits well inside. We did not end it on 29 December 1836, when the soldiers left. That dates the soldiers, not the pole, and the buildings stood until the 1850s.

entries.card: notes:TO LET, AND THE TENANT IS NOT NAMED. The advertisement docum…
entries.text: TO LET, AND THE TENANT IS NOT NAMED. The advertisement documents rental housing stock and nobody in it. This building is deliberately left without an occupant household: the honest reading of 'to let' is a building whose tenant this project cannot name.

levels.8-10: To let, and the renter is not named. The ad shows houses for rent, and nobody in them. So no family is placed in this building, on purpose. To let honestly means a building whose renter we cannot name.

entries.card: notes:TRANSVERSE PLATFORM PROJECTION, RECONSTRUCTED. The full Andr…
entries.text: TRANSVERSE PLATFORM PROJECTION, RECONSTRUCTED. The full Andreas plate shows the broad cap projecting toward the foreground of the view, rather than growing only along the bridge toward a bank. Shift the selected platform 1.0 m toward local negative-v, the provisional source-camera side, while keeping both unchanged gallows post footprints supported. This signed offset and the platform plan dimensions are a finite visual trial; no geographic coordinate, shoreline, deck width or surveyed footprint is moved or inferred from a drawing. No claim that the bounded camera is a historic metric solve follows.

levels.8-10: The base sticks out sideways, our guess. The full 1884 picture shows the wide base sticking out toward the front of the view, not just along the bridge. So we moved it 1 meter that way, and kept both tall posts standing on it. This is a test of how it looks. No real place, shore or width is moved or measured from the drawing.

entries.card: notes:TWO READINGS THAT DO NOT AGREE, AND THIS RECORD TAKES THE ST…
entries.text: TWO READINGS THAT DO NOT AGREE, AND THIS RECORD TAKES THE STATED ONE. The 1855 key gives 'the Officers' Quarters, B (wood, about 30x60 ft,)' - 9.14 x 18.29 m, which is the polygon here. The 1830 plan draws the west range about 30 ft deep and about 80 ft long at the scale this project derives, so the two agree on the depth to within 3 percent and disagree on the length by nearly 40 percent. THE STATED FIGURE WINS, and the reasoning is worth writing down because it decides several records: the scale that would overrule it was itself calibrated on the other stated figure in the same caption, so using it to correct that caption's second number is close to circular. What that costs is legible - the modelled building is about 6 m shorter than the plan draws its range - and it is why this footprint is inferred while the commandant's is documented. If the 1830 plan is right the officers were housed in an 80 ft range; if the 1855 caption is right they were in a 60 ft one; nothing reached settles it.

levels.8-10: Two readings that do not agree, and we take the one in words. The 1855 list says the officers' rooms were wood, about 30 by 60 feet. That is the shape here. The 1830 plan draws this side about 30 feet deep and about 80 feet long. So the two agree on depth, but not on length. The words win. The scale that would overrule them was set from the same list, so using it would go in a circle. Our building is about 6 meters shorter than the plan draws it. If the plan is right, the room was 80 feet long. If the list is right, it was 60. Nothing settles it.

entries.card: notes:The 1830 plan letters a Shop on the fort's outer ground betw…
entries.text: The 1830 plan letters a Shop on the fort's outer ground between the stockade and the lake shore, south of the wash house; the plate does not say whose shop, and it is the post's because it stands on the post's ground among the post's own lettered buildings. Which trade worked in it is not claimed. The post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836 (the stockade's own occupants block, after Andreas), so on 1 July 1835 its service buildings were the garrison's; the people are seated on the stockade and are not repeated here.

levels.8-10: The 1830 plan names a Shop on the fort's outer ground, between the fort and the lake, south of the wash house. It does not say whose shop. It is the fort's because it stands on the fort's land, with the fort's other named buildings. Which trade worked in it is not claimed. Soldiers were here from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 the fort's work buildings were the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

entries.card: notes:The 1830 plan letters this pair Out Buildings and draws them…
entries.text: The 1830 plan letters this pair Out Buildings and draws them on the fort's own ground south of the stockade; the plate does not say whose they were, and they are the post's because they stand on the post's ground and the plate draws no other keeper there. What went on inside is not claimed. The post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836 (the stockade's own occupants block, after Andreas), so on 1 July 1835 its service buildings were the garrison's; the people are seated on the stockade and are not repeated here.

levels.8-10: The plan names it Out Buildings and draws it on the fort's ground, south of the fence. It does not say whose it was. It is the fort's because it stands on the fort's land. What went on inside is not claimed. Soldiers were here from June 1832 to the end of 1836. So on 1 July 1835 the fort's work buildings were the soldiers'. The people are placed in the fort, not again here.

entries.card: notes:The Beaubiens owned it until 1834; the hotel chronology give…
entries.text: The Beaubiens owned it until 1834; the hotel chronology gives 'Davis (1835)' as operator, possibly the John Davis running the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street. Mark Beaubien himself had moved on by the scene date — he built the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells in 1834. The 1835 proprietor is a lead, not a settled fact.

levels.8-10: The Beaubiens owned it until 1834. A list of hotels gives Davis in 1835 as the man running it. He may be the John Davis who ran the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street. Mark Beaubien had moved on by the day we show. He built the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells in 1834. Who ran it in 1835 is a lead, not a settled fact.

entries.card: notes:The Castelnau harbour print shows a rounded crown, finial, o…

levels.8-10: An old print of the harbor shows a round top, a point on top, an open lantern room and a railing. That print is from about 1838, and we use it for 1835. entries.card: notes:The Clybournes lived on this ground and butchered from it: A…
entries.text: The Clybournes lived on this ground and butchered from it: Andreas has Jonas Clybourne living several miles up the North Branch among the county's taxpayers (scan p. 215) and 'Jonas Clybourne and his son Archibald were the early butchers of Chicago. They furnished the garrison at Fort Dearborn' (scan p. 221). So the cabins are a farmstead at the head of a stock-raising and butchering business rather than town houses, and that is an inference from the family's trade rather than a description of the buildings. Who was living in them on 1835-07-01 is not attested and this record carries no occupants block: Archibald had a larger house of his own from 1829, and the household's composition eleven years after the cabins went up is not recorded anywhere reached.

levels.8-10: The Clybourne family lived here and killed animals for meat here. A book says Jonas lived a few miles up the North Branch. It says Jonas and his son were the town's first butchers. They sold meat to the fort. So the cabins were a farm that raised animals for meat, not town houses. That is a guess from the family's work. No record says who lived here on 1 July 1835. The son had his own bigger house from 1829. So no one is placed here.

For 1 July 1835, our flag of 24 stars and 13 stripes is right for that year, by the flag law of 1818. Its layout is our guess for this hotel. The black and white picture shows no color or stars. It stops on 3 July 1836, before the flag got its 25th star.

entries.card: notes:The closed vocabulary has no `stock shed`; `stable` is famil…
entries.text: The closed vocabulary has no `stock shed`; `stable` is family A1's own term and the nearest it carries. The specific use - holding beasts before the kill, and the plant's own draught oxen - is in the record's NAME and in this note. The use comes from the plant. A slaughter-house that took 300 head of cattle and 1,400 hogs in a season held stock somewhere before it killed them, and the plant's own record says the pens and the stock yard are outside its footprint and outside its archetype. This record models the roofed half of that; the pens themselves are a fence line and this archetype builds buildings. No occupant is claimed and no animal is drawn.

levels.8-10: Our list has no word for an animal shed. Stable is the closest. Its real use, holding animals before the kill and the plant's work oxen, is in its name and in this note. A meat plant that took 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs in a season kept them somewhere first. The plant's own record says the pens are outside its walls. This is the roofed part. The pens are a fence line, and we build buildings. No one is placed in it, and no animal is drawn.

levels.8-10: The color of packed ground. No record tells of it. We give it so it is not the color of wood.

NO SOURCE REACHED NAMES THE MINISTER IN CHARGE ON 1835-07-01, so the occupancy is stated as the congregation and not as a person.

levels.8-10: The church group began in June 1833 under the Rev. Jeremiah Porter. He came that May and slept in the unfinished loft of Peck's store. No record names the minister here on 1 July 1835. So we name the church group, not a person.

levels.8-10: The open ground where soldiers line up. It is built as ground worn bare and packed, raised 6 centimeters. That is all we claim about it.

One of the owner's pictures, and the town's own buildings, make logs usual on the north side in 1835. It also breaks up the row. Four sheds built the same would claim they were built together, and nothing backs that. Our guess either way. Nothing says how any building on this bank was built.

entries.card: notes:The detailed public-domain 1902 plate shows one upright barr…
entries.text: The detailed public-domain 1902 plate shows one upright barred-looking light in the log gable beside the keeper house. The light sits on the east end facing the keeper-house side: 0.48 x 0.85 m dark recess, three uprights, one horizontal crossbar, 55 mm frame, head 0.73 m above eave. These metric choices, count of uprights, material, compass and July continuity are not measured or attested. The opening does not assert a second storey or hay loft. Other outbuildings retain their default layout.

levels.8-10: The 1902 picture shows one tall window with what look like bars, in the log end next to the keeper's house. It is on the east end, toward the keeper's house. It is a dark opening with three bars up and one across. Its size, its bars, what it was made of, and that it was there in July 1835 are our guesses. entries.text: The detailed public-domain Gale/Trowbridge 1902 plate, captioned 1836, depicts a gabled log core behind the palisade. levels.8-10: A picture from 1902, labeled 1836, shows a log building with a roof of two slopes, behind a fence of posts. We use that roof now, not the flat one from an earlier note. A picture in Andreas's 1884 book shows a pointed roof that slopes on all sides. We keep that as a place where the two pictures do not agree. Using the 1902 picture for July 1835 is our choice. It does not claim the picture shows July.

entries.text: The door faces NORTH, onto the yard between this shed and e1, and that is why this record is rotated 0.000 where e1 is rotated 180.000: the archetype's front faces north at rotation 0, so `front` here is the north wall and the two sheds' doors face each other across the yard. The two platted corridors are at either end of the building, so those two sides were never candidates, and the south wall faces away from the only made approach this ground has. Invented, like the building.

levels.8-10: Our guess, like the building. The door faces north, onto the yard between this shed and the one next to it. So the two sheds' doors face each other across the yard. Streets run at both ends of the building, so the door could not go there. The south wall faces away from the only way in.

entries.card: notes:The door faces the river street, which is the side the traff…
entries.text: The door faces the river street, which is the side the traffic and the bridge are on. The archetype's front faces north at rotation 0 and this record is rotated to face the street, so `front` here is the river side. Invented.

levels.8-10: Our guess. The door faces the river street, the side with the traffic and the bridge. This building is turned to face the street, so its front is the river side.

entries.card: notes:The dossier groups this building with Newberry & Dole's as o…
entries.text: The dossier groups this building with Newberry & Dole's as one of the two river warehouses with docks, which puts it in the forwarding and commission trade by association rather than by statement — no source reached says what Kinzie & Hunter forwarded. Andreas has a firm of Kinzie, Hunter & Co. in the LUMBER trade in the middle 1830s, taking it up a couple of years after the first cargo of pine was landed on the south bank between LaSalle and Wells (scan p. 1139), so a lumber yard rather than a general warehouse is a live alternative reading of what this building was for. Recorded as inference with the alternative named.

levels.8-10: Our notes put this building with Newberry and Dole's, as one of two store houses on the river with docks. That makes it a shipping house by being next to one, not because a record says so. No record says what Kinzie and Hunter shipped. A book says a firm of Kinzie, Hunter and Co. sold wood in the middle 1830s. So a wood yard, not a store house, is another real answer. We record it as our guess, and name the other one.

entries.card: notes:The dossier's sentence says log cabins, and it is unattribut…
entries.text: The dossier's sentence says log cabins, and it is unattributed; the family's own slaughter-house on the same ground is twice called log in Andreas (scan pp. 1149, 1151), and every settler dwelling on the branches in the 1820s that any source describes is log. So the material is inference resting on the neighbourhood and on the same household's other building, not on a statement this project can point at. If the dossier's sentence is ever traced to its source this becomes documented without anything else in the record moving.

levels.8-10: Our notes say log cabins, but do not say where that came from. A book twice says the family's butcher house on the same land was made of logs. Every settler home on the river's branches in the 1820s that any record tells of was logs. So logs is a guess from the houses nearby and the family's other building. If we ever find where our note came from, this becomes a fact.

levels.8-10: An old note guessed long boards from the words partly sided. The board sizes and the sides no one sees are our guesses. A picture made years later does not settle how it looked in July 1835.

entries.card: notes:The firm names itself in its own advertisement, which is the…

levels.8-10: The business names itself in its own ad. That is the best kind of proof here. Who else was a partner, and whether anyone worked here on 1 July 1835, are not known.

levels.8-10: The first Catholic church in Chicago. It was in use from October 1833. The first mass was on 5 May 1833. It was said in a different place, a small log cabin twelve feet square. That cabin was Mark Beaubien's. It is not this building.

entries.card: notes:The identification of the partners is the dossier's and rest…
entries.text: The identification of the partners is the dossier's and rests on the surname pairing: John H. Kinzie and Lieutenant Hunter came to Chicago together in February 1833 to lay out lots through their property north of the river, and both are among the backers of the Lake House in 1835. Andreas's own 'Kinzie, Hunter & Co.' in the lumber trade (scan p. 1139) is the same pairing. No source reached expands the firm name for the warehouse itself, so the men behind it are inference and not attestation. THREE DIFFERENT KINZIES TRADE IN THIS TOWN AND THIS DATASET CARRIES PREMISES FOR ALL OF THEM — John H., James, and Robert A. — so the identification matters and is stated rather than assumed.

levels.8-10: Who the partners were comes from our notes, from the pair of last names. John H. Kinzie and Lieutenant Hunter came to Chicago together in February 1833. They laid out lots on their land north of the river. Both helped pay for the Lake House in 1835. A book's Kinzie, Hunter and Co., who sold wood, is the same pair. No record gives the firm's full name for the store house. So the men behind it are our guess. Three different Kinzies traded in this town, John, James and Robert. We have buildings for all of them. So who this is matters, and we say so.

The two may well be different events, an enlargement in 1827 and a conversion to innkeeping in 1830, in which case both are right. Either way the building had its 1835 form well before the scene date. THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE HONEST MINIMUM, NOT A FATE: no source reached says when the Miller house came down, so the range is closed at the end of 1835 — the last date this record needs to claim — rather than run on speculatively. Extend it when evidence appears; do not widen it to make something pass.

entries.card: notes:V3 SOLID-CRIB TRIAL, retained as history: TWO BROAD DRAW-BEA…
entries.text: V3 SOLID-CRIB TRIAL, retained as history: TWO BROAD DRAW-BEARING PLATFORMS. The retrospective Andreas plate shows broad foundations under the gallows rather than a forest of identical narrow box cribs. The two selected bearing cribs use a reconstructed 3.6 m nominal box length away from the draw and 4.4 m width across it. These are bounded visual-trial dimensions, not a survey, geographic footprint or historical specification; visible log joints project slightly beyond that box. Existing draw endpoints and the twelve support stations remain unchanged. The remaining approaches use separately reconstructed timber bents; whole source comparison stays differs. CURRENT PILED-CAP CORRECTION: direct inspection of the complete 1920 px plate shows a boarded cap over closely spaced vertical piles, not a solid horizontal-log crib. The selected 3.6 m along by 6.0 m across platform is centered on each existing frame bearing. Its 0.30 m diameter perimeter piles at at most 0.48 m spacing, two 0.20 m sleepers, 0.14 m boarded cap and below-water stopping depth are reconstructed visual choices, not dimensions or a foundation count attested by the retrospective drawing. No solid fill is built. Source-camera fitting remains provisional and whole-picture comparison stays differs until reviewed. CURRENT SIXTEEN-FOOT WIDTH ACCOMMODATION. Keep the reconstructed 3.6 m along-bearing plan and -1.0 m transverse offset. Across size grows from 6.0 m by the selected 1.8288 m deck-width increase to 7.8288 m, preserving the chosen foreground projection and supporting both gallows post footprints. The foundation dimensions and resulting 46 perimeter piles, formerly 38, remain reconstructed construction choices. Neither the 1895 width statement nor the retrospective drawing attests a foundation survey, count or specification. Native width resolution adds 0.2 mm; actual vertex bounds and post containment must be checked.

levels.8-10: Two wide bases under the lifting frames. The 1884 picture shows wide bases under the tall frames, not many small boxes. At first we built them as solid boxes of logs. Looking closer at the whole picture, it shows a board top over a row of upright posts driven down. So each base is now a platform about 3.6 by 6 meters, on posts set close together, with a board top. The sizes, the posts and how deep they go are our guess, not from the drawing. Nothing solid fills them. We do not claim a match yet.

entries.card: notes:WORKING APPEARANCE FIT, NOT A HISTORICAL MEASUREMENT. The so…
entries.text: WORKING APPEARANCE FIT, NOT A HISTORICAL MEASUREMENT. The source near-gable apex is approximately pixel (953,277). With the current reconstructed 15.24 x 9.14 x 7.8 m envelope and provisional six-wall-corner camera, the old 38-degree ridge projected near y260. About 31.5 degrees puts its apex near the source; 32 degrees is adopted as a rounded reconstruction. Camera, scale, paper perspective and roof thickness remain coupled; this does not provide a surveyed pitch.

levels.8-10: A fit to how it looks, not a measure. We matched the roof's peak to Gifford's picture. Our old 38 degree roof came out too high. About 31 and a half degrees fits, so we use 32. It is not a measured slope.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun calls the group 'a collection of log buildings'; And…
entries.text: Wau-Bun calls the group 'a collection of log buildings'; Andreas calls them 'small log buildings'; and McKee's own recollection of the houses he found and built on this bank in 1823 is 'All these houses were of logs'. The fabric is the one attribute of these buildings that three independent statements agree on.

levels.8-10: Three people wrote about these houses. Wau-Bun calls them a group of log buildings. Andreas calls them small log buildings. McKee, who built houses here in 1823, said they were all made of logs. Logs are the one thing all three agree on.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun calls them cabins 'occupied by' named people and lat…
entries.text: Wau-Bun calls them cabins 'occupied by' named people and later refers to the group as 'these residences'. They were homes.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun says named people lived in the cabins, and later calls the group these homes. They were homes.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun counts them loosely — 'two or three' — and the loose…
entries.text: Wau-Bun counts them loosely — 'two or three' — and the looseness is the evidence, so the value is kept as the source's words rather than resolved to a number. ONE CABIN IS BUILT. The archetype models a building, not a group, and choosing two or three would mean inventing the count the source declined to give, plus their spacing and their arrangement. So the model understates the place: a visitor sees one cabin where there were at least two, and the record says so here.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun counts them loosely, two or three, and that looseness is the record. So we keep the book's words, not a number. One cabin is built. We build a building, not a group. Picking two or three would make up the number the book would not give, and their spacing. So the model shows less than was there. You see one cabin where there were at least two, and this note says so.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun describes an odd-shaped roof. The reconstruction car…
entries.text: Wau-Bun describes an odd-shaped roof. The reconstruction carries five parallel gables: a dominant central roof, two recessed smaller wing roofs, and two narrow rear tail roofs. The keyed panorama supplies the dominant-front and visible-side-gable hierarchy; it cannot establish hidden valleys or rear roof forms. All exact junctions remain reconstructed.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun says it had an odd-shaped roof. We build five roofs side by side. There is a big middle roof, two smaller wing roofs and two narrow back roofs. An old drawing shows the big front roof and a smaller side roof. It can't show the back or where the roofs meet, so all of that is our guess.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun describes the buildings round the agency house as 'a…
entries.text: Wau-Bun describes the buildings round the agency house as 'a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government ... blacksmith, striker, and laborers'; Andreas records the 1830 north bank as having 'small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell' in the agency house's vicinity, and McKee's own account of the houses he found and built there — 'All these houses were of logs'. Note that the first two describe the blacksmith's RESIDENCE among the group; that the shop was of the same fabric is the reading, and it is the only fabric anybody reports on this ground in these years.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun says the buildings near the Agency House were log homes for the government's workers, the blacksmith among them. Andreas says the same of 1830, naming McKee. McKee himself said all the houses there were logs. But those writers tell of the blacksmith's home. That his shop was logs too is our guess. Logs are the only kind of wall anyone saw here then.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun names the OFFICE among the residences and not the bu…
entries.text: Wau-Bun names the OFFICE among the residences and not the building: 'Around the Agency House were grouped a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government ... blacksmith, striker, and laborers.' That the striker had one of the residences is what that sentence says; that it was a separate building rather than a room in the blacksmith's is the inference. Graded below the other two houses of this parcel for that reason.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun names the job, not the building. It says log houses around the Agency House were homes for the government's workers: the blacksmith, the striker and the laborers. So the striker had a home. That it was its own house, not a room in the blacksmith's, is our guess. So we trust it less than the other two houses here.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun states centre, two wings and two rear tails, with sy…
entries.text: Wau-Bun states centre, two wings and two rear tails, with symmetry from the front. The connected-room generator builds that composition; exact dimensions and roof arrangement are reconstructed from that text and the keyed panorama's dominant front gable and smaller visible side gable.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun says it had a middle part, two wings and two back parts, the same on both sides from the front. We build that shape. The sizes and roofs are our guess, from the book's words and an old drawing. The drawing shows a big front roof and a smaller side roof.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, says a house just finished by Mark Beaubien.

entries.text: Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'a house just completed by Mark Beaubien.' Destroyed by fire 4 March 1851. The 1838 rename to Chicago Hotel and the 1837 arrival of the Chicago Theatre Company in the dining room are changes of use, not of form, so they do not open a new phase.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun, telling of 1831, says a house just finished by Mark Beaubien. It burned down on 4 March 1851. It was renamed the Chicago Hotel in 1838. A theater company used the dining room in 1837. Those changed its use, not its shape, so they do not start a new stage.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building, with brigh…
entries.text: Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters.' Painted white siding was itself remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — the description exists because the building stood out.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun calls it a showy white building of two floors, with bright blue wood shutters. White paint was itself special at Wolf Point in 1831. The book tells of it because the building stood out.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building.'
entries.text: Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building.'

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun calls it a showy white building of two floors.

entries.card: notes:Wau-Bun: 'a substantial, compact little building of logs hew…
entries.text: Wau-Bun: 'a substantial, compact little building of logs hewed and squared'. Andreas, recording David McKee's account of the north side when he arrived in 1823: 'All these houses were of logs — the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up.' Hewn and squared log is exactly what this archetype builds. The clapboarding is recorded separately under `cladding`, with its unknown extent and date kept explicit there.

levels.8-10: Wau-Bun calls it a solid, compact little building of logs, cut and squared. McKee, who came in 1823, said all the houses there were logs. He said the agency house later got boards part way up its walls. Cut and squared logs is just what we build. The boards are kept in a separate note, since how far up they went, and when, are not known.

entries.text: Winter storage for the garrison's roots and vegetables, dug into the river bank.

levels.8-10: A place to keep the soldiers' roots and food for the winter. It is dug into the bank of the river.
