THE HEDGE IS THE SOURCE'S AND IS NOT SMOOTHED AWAY HERE: 'some fifty feet' is a round number in a retrospective description, so the metre figure is exact only in its conversion. It is the only dimension any source reached gives this object, and it is a dimension of the SECOND fort - which is more than the second fort's own stockade has (see the research notes on fort dearborn section 3).

levels.8-10: An old account says it was some fifty feet high. That is about 15 meters. The word some means it was a round guess, so the meters are not exact. It is the only size any paper gives for it.

entries.card: why:'the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up' —…
entries.text: 'the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up' — David McKee's recollection, printed by Andreas. This is an unusually specific finish for a building at this date and it is genuinely odd: siding taken part of the way up a log wall and no further, presumably to weather the lower courses. WHEN it was done is not stated beyond 'afterward', i.e. after 1823, so whether the boards were there on the scene date is not attested either. the lower-wall reconstruction now represents this occurrence through compound clapboard height (m); its chosen half-wall extent, neutral finish and corner clearances are liberties; the original date qualification remains.

levels.8-10: A man named David McKee remembered that the agency house later had boards nailed part way up its log walls. A history book printed this. It is an odd thing to do, maybe to keep the lower logs dry. No one says when it was done, so we can not be sure the boards were there in 1835. How far up they go is our guess.

entries.card: why:'the large stable and the yard into which the trains were dr…
entries.text: 'the large stable and the yard into which the trains were driven. There were entrances to the yard from both streets.' THE STABLE AND THE ENCLOSED WAGON YARD ARE THE POINT OF THIS BUILDING — it is the west-side teamsters' house and the yard is most of what a visitor would have seen from Randolph. Neither is dimensioned and neither is modelled by the frame tavern archetype, so the yard, the stable range and the two gateways are an attested absence in the geometry. Recorded in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: An old account tells of a large stable and a yard where the wagon teams were driven in. There were ways into the yard from both streets. The stable and yard were the main thing about this inn for teamsters. No one gives their size, and this building does not show them.

entries.card: why:'the yard into which the trains were driven. There were entr…
entries.text: 'the yard into which the trains were driven. There were entrances to the yard from both streets, and this was one of the most important parts of the hostlery, for the teams were as numerous as were the guests.' THE YARD IS BUILT AS OF 2026-08-18, AND NOT BY THIS RECORD. `geometry` here still reads `absent` and that is not an oversight: this field's declaration is about the OUTBUILDING ARCHETYPE'S MESH, which contains no yard and never will. What draws the yard is a second record of a new kind - the western hotel wagon yard data, which carries a PERIMETER rather than a footprint, no roof, and the two gateways this passage attests - drawn by the walkthrough's enclosures code at load, with no baked geometry. So the sentence this note used to carry, that a yard is an enclosure and there is no enclosure archetype in this project, is answered on the renderer side and still open on the generator side. The two gateways, on Randolph and on Canal, are drawn as gaps in the fence and no gate leaf is hung, because nothing describes one. Every dimension of that fence is invented and is claimed in the liberties register “The Western Hotel's wagon yard: an attested yard, and a fence nobody described”; the ground inside it is still drawn as prairie sward, which is the residual. See the research note, and the liberties register “Western Hotel: the stable and wagon yard are attested and not modelled” for what that entry now does and does not still admit. See the research note.

levels.8-10: An old account tells of a yard where the wagon teams were driven in, with ways in from both streets. There were as many teams as guests. Since August 2026 the yard is built, but by another record, not this one. Its fence has two gaps for the ways in, on Randolph and on Canal. No one describes a gate, so none is hung. Every size of the fence is our guess.

entries.card: why:(Sources that bear on the bank question — "Wolf's Point and…
entries.text:
(Sources that bear on the bank question — "Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology, Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West, OpenStreetMap contributors. Street centerline intersection nodes for downtown… — are discussed in the note below and in the dossier, but they are deliberately NOT listed in this field's `sources`. They attest that a log meeting house stood at the forks; not one of them attests THIS COORDINATE, and the validator is right that a conjectural value carrying citations is either mis-tagged or decorating itself with evidence for a different claim.)

POSITION DOWNGRADED TO CONJECTURAL BY THE ORCHESTRATOR, 2026-08-09. The dossier's own reconciliation is probably right and it undercuts this coordinate: the west-bank testimony (Wau-Bun, chicagology) describes 1831 and the north-bank claim is dated 1834, which is exactly the pattern you would see if these are TWO BUILDINGS — Walker's 1831 school-house-and-meeting place on the west bank, and a purpose-built 1834 congregation cabin on the north bank that was floated across the river in 1838. If that is what happened, this record may be modelling the wrong one, and the two stand about 150 m apart on opposite banks. A choice between two readings 150 m apart across a river is not a derivation from evidence, which is what 'inferred' claims; it is a coin flip with a reason, which is what 'conjectural' is for. The west-bank coordinate is retained because it is the only one any source places precisely enough to use — the north-bank claim names a division, not a position — but the confidence now says what it is.

PLACED 2026-08-09. THE BANK IS DISPUTED AND THIS COORDINATE ADOPTS ONE SIDE OF IT — read this before using the number. THE WEST-BANK READING, ADOPTED: chicagology, immediately after describing Wentworth's tavern, 'North of this tavern was an oblong building which had been erected by Father Walker, a missionary of the Methodist Episcopal Church, for a place of worship, and for a school house'; and Wau-Bun, describing 1831, placing it in the same west-side sequence as the tavern and the Robinson cabins — 'A little remote from these residences was a small square log building, originally designed for a school-house, but occasionally used as a place of worship whenever any itinerant minister presented himself.' THE NORTH-BANK READING, NOT ADOPTED: the successor congregation's own history says 'in 1834 the growing congregation built a log cabin north of the Chicago River'. WHY WEST WINS: two near-primary witnesses, one of them a witness remembering and contemporary with the building, both giving a RELATIVE POSITION that can be placed, against one modern unfootnoted institutional page giving a division rather than a location. The readings may also both be true of different buildings — an 1831 school-house on the west bank and a purpose-built 1834 cabin on the north bank — which is the most likely reconciliation and is the thing to test. IF THE NORTH-BANK READING IS RIGHT FOR 1835, THIS BUILDING IS ABOUT 150 m AWAY, ACROSS THE NORTH BRANCH. Note also that this project's own the exclusions record states in passing that the 1835 Methodist meeting house is on the north bank; that statement and this record disagree, deliberately, and the disagreement is flagged rather than either being edited to match the other. Method for the coordinate: derived from the datum origin and bank geometry, not from any intersection, since none survives here. The footprint's south face is set 35 m north of the Wolf Point Tavern's north face, which honours 'north of this tavern' and Wau-Bun's 'a little remote', and its east face sits between about 9 m and 14 m back from the modern west-bank line read from OpenStreetMap water polygons. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, about 40 m along the bank from the tavern's own inferred position which this one is stacked on, and a step change of about 150 m if the bank is wrong. Facade bearing 90, east onto the water, taken from the orientation of the river-front row rather than from any statement about this building; nothing attests which way it faced.

levels.8-10: Two old books say a log meeting house stood near Wolf Point. One puts it on the west bank of the river in 1831. A church history says a log cabin was built north of the river in 1834. They may be two different buildings. We chose the west bank, since two old witnesses put it there. We placed it a little north of the Wolf Point Tavern, near the water. If the north bank is right, it stood about 150 m away, across the river. So its place is only a guess.

entries.card: why:1 JULY 1835 FALLS SQUARELY INSIDE HIS TENURE, on two sources…
entries.text: 1 JULY 1835 FALLS SQUARELY INSIDE HIS TENURE, on two sources that do not disagree: chicagology's 1874 letter has him becoming proprietor in 1834, and Andreas has him running the house until 1836. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Ira Couch,” (f1839 v0087, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Couch' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins I. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Ira Couch” (33SQ-GYYJ-97P, printed page 211, line 3). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (“Sauganash Hotel: the pre-1830 position is not represented” matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Couch, Ira H. | Letter. | August 6, 1842. | Deceased.” (second presb 0537, printed page 183), admitted 1842-08-06 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Couch' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins I. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

levels.8-10: He kept this house on 1 July 1835. One letter says he took it over in 1834, and a history book says he ran it until 1836. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. We judged it is this same person. But 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are. A list of the members of the Second Presbyterian Church has a line with the same last name and first letter. That church list starts in 1842, so it is no proof about 1835.

entries.text: 16 BY 30 FEET, PRINTED. 9.144 x 4.8768 m is 30 x 16 ft exactly, and it is the whole reason this building is worth raising: it is a plan dimension from the paper rather than an archetype's deal, which is what every other house on these blocks stands on. WHICH DIMENSION RUNS ALONG LAKE IS NOT STATED, and this record does not pretend otherwise — the assumption is carried as form.gable orientation, graded there, and the polygon draws it: 30 ft of front on Lake Street, 16 ft of depth running north into the lot. THE FOUR HUNDRED AND EIGHTY SQUARE FEET IS THE ATTESTED PART; the orientation is the assumption laid over it, and rotating the rectangle 90 degrees is a one-line change to this polygon if a source ever settles it.

levels.8-10: A paper gives this building as 16 by 30 feet. That is a real size, not a guess like most houses on these blocks. But it does not say which side ran along Lake Street. We put the 30 foot side on Lake Street. That part is our guess.

entries.card: why:21.49 degrees is a reconstructed appearance choice from the…
entries.text: 21.49 degrees is a reconstructed appearance choice from the low annex in the Braunhold engraving published in Andreas (1884), not an attested historical pitch. It replaces the former generic 35-degree roof. Six approximate manually read annex wall corners, each with about 10 px uncertainty, gave the diagnostic camera on the retained 6.096 by 4.877 m documented-size footprint and existing inferred 2.5 m eave. Actual native before/after meshes lower the ridge by 0.8240216 m; the earlier 0.747 m estimate omitted the existing roof overhang. The finite native trial and direct visual review accepted the lower roof as closer to the depiction. The 0.472 m eye and off-centre principal point are diagnostic framing, not a historical visitor pose or metric survey. The retrospective plate does not establish unchanged appearance on 1 July 1835. Footprint, placement, eaves, openings and hotel remain unchanged; canonical native production, other pictures, application and final gates are separate acceptance steps.

levels.8-10: This low roof slope is our choice. We took it from an old picture of the low side wing, printed in a history book in 1884. It is lower than the roof we had before. The picture was made long after 1835, so it may not show the building as it was then.

entries.card: why:A BANK, NOT A POINT. Kinzie, of 1831: 'The bank of the river…
entries.text: A BANK, NOT A POINT. Kinzie, of 1831: 'The bank of the river which stretches to the west, now covered by the light-house buildings, and inclosed by docks, was then occupied by the root-houses of the garrison.' That names a stretch of riverbank and gives no position on it, and the 1830 plan - which labels the wash house, the well, the shop and the barn - does not draw them. This point is on that bank about 45 m north-west of the fort's centre and it is ours. THE PLURAL IS MODELLED SINCE other work: Kinzie says root-houses, this record is the first of them and Fort Dearborn — root house (b) is the second, 9.0 m due west on the same bank top. Two is the floor her plural states and no source gives a count beyond it, so two is what stands. MOVED 2026-08-11 FOR THE SAME REASON AS THE LIGHTHOUSE. The first point sat on the face of the river bank the newly extended heightfield draws, so the mound straddled a 0.85 m fall. It now stands at local E +1115, N +234, on the bank top west-north-west of the fort. Kinzie's 'bank of the river which stretches to the west' is satisfied either way; a cellar dug INTO the face of a bank is what she is describing and what this project cannot model, since the archetype banks earth over a level floor.

levels.8-10: A woman who lived at the fort wrote that the river bank to the west held the fort's root houses in 1831. Those are small cellars for food. She names a stretch of bank, not a spot. The old fort plan does not draw them. So the spot is ours. She says root houses, so we built two. We moved this one onto the top of the bank, so it does not sit on the slope.

entries.card: why:A BUILDER OF TAVERNS RATHER THAN A KEEPER OF THEM, which is…
entries.text: A BUILDER OF TAVERNS RATHER THAN A KEEPER OF THEM, which is why his structure links are thin. Andreas has him building the Green Tree and leasing it to David Clock; Charles Butler in August 1833 lodged at a tavern on the west side of the South Branch 'erected by James Kinzie, but kept by a Mr. Crook (?)' - the question mark is Andreas's or Butler's, not this project's. HALF BROTHER TO JOHN H. KINZIE, AND AN UNCITED CLAIM ABOUT ROBERT A. KINZIE — other work RULED ON BOTH. The John H. tie is carried by this card's `kin` row, graded and reciprocal, on Hurlbut's bracketed note of 1881 (bk afc 015). The Robert A. tie was a sentence in this note and nothing else, citing nothing, and it is NOT PROMOTED: no source this project holds states a relationship between James Kinzie and Robert Allen Kinzie, and the two sources that touch it do not chain into one — Hurlbut says HALF brother without saying which parent is shared, and on the reading where it is the mother, James and Robert have no parent in common at all. The sentence stands here as an inherited, uncited claim, marked as one. The reasoning, and what would reopen it, is in the kinzie kinship ruling data. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Kinzie, James” (poll 1833 017, line 38); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kinzie, James” (tax 1833 061, line 113); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Kinzie, James” (poll 1834 066, line 235). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kinzie' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). HALF BROTHER, NOT BROTHER, AND THE SOURCE IS AN EDITOR'S NOTE OF 1881. Hurlbut's bracketed note under the American Fur Company's 1821 consignment entry reads “[The late James Kinzie, formerly of Chicago, and half brother of the late John H. Kinzie.]” — the same father and different mothers, which is the form this dataset keeps, because flattening it to ‘brother’ is the move that lets the three Chicago Kinzies collapse into one another. The two men are James Kinzie in the James Kinzie household and John Harris Kinzie in the John H. Kinzie household, and this project models them as separate households. Read as bk afc 015 and cited to Henry H. Hurlbut, Chicago Antiquities: Comprising original items and relations…. entries.card: why:A CHIEF, A LICENSED TRADER AND A RECORDED VOTER OF THE SETTL…
entries.text: A CHIEF, A LICENSED TRADER AND A RECORDED VOTER OF THE SETTLEMENT. Andreas: born at Mackinaw about 1762, his father a Scots trader who had been an officer in the British army and his mother an Ottawa woman; he sheltered the Kinzie family after the 1812 massacre and carried Captain and Mrs Heald three hundred miles by bark canoe to Mackinaw. His personal property was assessed at $200 by the Peoria County assessor in 1825 and he is recorded as a voter in 1825, 1826 and 1830. He married Catherine Chevalier, daughter of the chief Francois Chevalier, on 28 September 1826, John Kinzie officiating as justice of the peace, and became chief of her father's band at his death. By the treaty of Prairie du Chien of July 1829 he was granted two sections on the Des Plaines; by Camp Tippecanoe in 1832 a life annuity of $200; and by the Chicago treaty of September 1833 a further $300 a year for life.

levels.8-10: He was a chief, a trader with a license, and a voter here. A history book says he was born at Mackinaw about 1762. His father was a Scots trader and his mother was Ottawa. After the fight of 1812 he hid the Kinzie family. He took Captain and Mrs. Heald three hundred miles by canoe to Mackinaw. He voted here in 1825, 1826 and 1830. In 1826 he married Catherine Chevalier, the daughter of a chief, and later he led her father's band. Treaties gave him land on the Des Plaines and money each year for life.

PRESENT AT CHICAGO ON 19 OCTOBER 1833, FROM THE CATALOGUE OF THE FOURTEEN BAPTISTS WHO ORGANISED THE FIRST BAPTIST SOCIETY. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 2 (1895), printed page 294 (claim bk mose2 010; the moses kirkland history of chicago v2 data): "At the date of the organization of the First Baptist society, October 19, 1833, there were twenty-five Baptists in the settlement, fourteen of whom were present and connected themselves with the new enterprise. The catalogue of those present is: Rev. Allen B. Freeman and Hannah C., his wife, S. T. Jackson, Martin D. Harmon, Peter Moore, Nathaniel Carpenter, John K. Sargent, Peter Warden, Willard Jones, Ebenezer and Betsey Crane, Susanna Rice, Samantha Harmon and Lucinda Jackson." THE CATALOGUE NAMES 'Nathaniel Carpenter', printed whole on both sides, AND IT IS NOT PHILO — the reading's own notes say `carpenter` 'here is Nathaniel and not Philo', and the crosswalk writes the Philo pairing down as an explicit refusal so it cannot be made again. A PRESENCE IS NOT AN ARRIVAL, AND IT BOUNDS ONE: a person standing in the settlement on 19 October 1833 had reached it by that day, so the bound is carried at 1833-10-19 with not later than precision — the same kind of statement the register made, moved earlier by a reading that saw the person sooner. THE CATALOGUE IS A ROLL AND NOT A CENSUS: the compiler says twenty-five Baptists were in the settlement and names the fourteen who were PRESENT that day, so the list is a floor. It can date the people it names and it can never be read to exclude anybody it leaves out. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois (1895) is a compiler sixty years after the fact, crediting Andreas and Hurlbut on the pages read here; every claim taken off it is transcription mediated and none is scan verified, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` however plainly it is printed (the rule set for the settlers table, kept here). AND IT ANSWERS A DIFFERENT QUESTION THAN PRESENCE ON THE SCENE DATE: being in the settlement in October 1833 says nothing about 1 July 1835, so present on scene date is untouched and goes on reading `uncertain`. THE REGISTER'S BOUND IS NOT LOST, IT IS SUBSUMED: a person present in October 1833 was necessarily in the town when the record below first named them. entries.card: why:A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER PRINTS THIS WOMAN BY NAME, IN T…
entries.text:
A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER PRINTS THIS WOMAN BY NAME, IN THE TOWN, KEEPING A HOUSE ON WATER STREET. The Chicago Democrat of 19 August 1835, page 3 column 2, over copy dated Chicago, 10 August 1835: "The Ladies and Gen[t]lemen of the town of Chicago are respec[t]fully in[v]ited to attend a sale of the \"Juvenile Society's\" work, [at] 3 o'clock P.[M.] next Saturday, the 22d inst., at the hous[e] of Mrs. C. Taylor, Water-st." THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER, rung G1b: an 1833-1835 newspaper naming the person in Chicago is `attested` on its own, and this printing names her, the town and her house at once.

WHY THE TOWN HAD NO CARD FOR HER, WHICH IS A FINDING ABOUT THE RULES AND NOT ABOUT HER. Her one appearance is not missing from the research tree — it is SPENT ON A MAN. the identity master data folds person taylor mrs c into id taylor charles and the grading proposal data lists it among that identity's evidence. R6 (#998) exists to stop exactly this — "a wife is not her husband and never merges onto him" — but it is EXACT-MATCH ONLY by design: it fires where the honorific strip leaves the husband's forename tokens letter for letter, as `Mrs. Rufus B. Brown` does against `Brown, Rufus B.` Here the printed forename is an INITIAL. Stripped of "Mrs." the reading is `Taylor, C.`, which is not identical to `Taylor, Charles`, so R6 never looks at it and M2 does — "an initial-only forename attaches to the ONE full forename of that surname carrying the initial" — and the one C-forename Taylor in the corpus is Charles. A female honorific carrying an initial is the shape R6 cannot see. The finding is recorded on other work, which already owns the two husband-name printings R6 cannot reach.

IS SHE THE WIFE OF A TAYLOR THE TOWN ALREADY HOLDS? ASKED, AND THE ANSWER IS NO ON THE EVIDENCE HELD. the households data carries five Taylor heads — Anson H., Augustine Deodat, Edmund D, William and William H — and not one of them has a forename beginning with C, so under the period's own usage ("Mrs. C. Taylor" is the wife of a man whose forename begins with C) she is the wife of NONE OF THE FIVE HEADS. The only C-forename Taylor this project holds is Charles H. Taylor, and he is not a head: he is Anson's brother inside the Anson Taylor household. Whether she was HIS wife is not decided by anything in this dataset. R6's own standard is that a source must print both readings, and no source prints `Taylor, Charles` and `Taylor, Mrs. C.` as two entries of one list — the Democrat prints them in different issues, six weeks apart, about different things. The one place a wife of a Charles Taylor is named at all is the record of Wolf Point Tavern, which has "Charles and Mary Taylor" keeping that house 1831-1833; the Anson Taylor household's own note REFUSES that identification outright, on the ground that the Taylor surname is carried by at least four distinct men in these sources. So no kin[] row is written here, and the absence is the finding: she stands as her own resident, which is what R6 would have done for her had it been able to see her.

ONE LATER RECORD THE CROSSWALK NOW REACHES, AND IT IS NOT AN 1835 FACT. Rebuilding the second presbyterian crosswalk data against this card matched it to a single roll line — second presb 0870, printed page 203, as read: "Taylor, Mrs. Charle's | Letter. | Januarys, 1843. | Dismissed." (the date token is the transcription's, unrepaired; the crosswalk reads the year as 1843). A woman entered on that roll under a man's forename, admitted by letter and afterwards dismissed. It says that the honorific shape read here is the shape this town's own paper used, and it is corroboration of nothing else: the roll is of 1842-1892, the ladder binds an 1843 appearance to CONTINUED RESIDENCE at best, and the town holds two men it could stand on — Charles H. Taylor the currier and the Charles Taylor Fergus 1843 prints as a merchant tailor on Clark Street. The match is left where the crosswalk put it, PROPOSED AND UNSPENT: no identity is asserted, the grade does not move, and this card cites the Democrat alone. 

WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the woman, her house's street and the source — no structure, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. No figure is drawn (“No people, anywhere”). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Taylor, Mrs. Charle's | Letter. | Januarys, 1843. | Dismissed.” (second presb 0895, printed page 203), admitted 1843 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Taylor' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins C. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a married womans entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. THE SAME ROLL LINE IS MET BY OTHER TOWNSPEOPLE OF THIS NAME: second presb 0895 is matched under this same rule to Charles H. Taylor (Charles H. Taylor), so it is met by two townspeople of this name, and it says which of them it was about no more than it says it was about this one — the test that decided it is a surname and a given initial agreeing, which cannot tell them apart. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

A list of the members of the Second Presbyterian Church has a line with the same last name and first letter. That church list starts in 1842, so it is no proof about 1835. That same church line also fits other people of this name in the town. The test is only a last name and a first letter, so it can not tell them apart. It does not change how sure we are. Other work asked for the camps of Native and Métis families in town to trade or awaiting the annuity payment; other work built the other camps and not these, because other work could put no count on them; and the owner answered other work on 2026-10-04: build one small camp at Wolf Point or the Agency as a declared reconstruction, review required and touches removal, no figures, bounded by a stated figure rather than a count. That is what this is. TRADE is the use because it is the one the owner named and the one Wolf Point's committed records support: a trader's store at the forks and Alexander Robinson's household beside it. No source says this family traded there, camped there or existed. “One trading family's camp at Wolf Point, a declared reconstruction the owner ruled built”.

levels.8-10: The owner of this project asked us to build one small camp of a Native or Métis family at Wolf Point. They came to town to trade, or to wait for treaty money. It is made up, and we say so. We chose trade, since the owner named it, and Wolf Point had a trader's store. No paper says this family traded there, camped there, or lived at all.

entries.text: A DISCREPANCY BETWEEN THE TWO SOURCES, RECORDED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED. Andreas names the concern 'Harmon's and Loomis's'. The advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is headed 'C. & I. HARMON' and names no Loomis. Those are compatible — a firm styled by the Harmon brothers in its own advertising and remembered fifty years later as Harmon and Loomis, or a partnership formed between 1833 and 1835 — but they are not the same statement and the record should not pretend they are. A SECOND POINT ABOUT THE SOURCE ITSELF: the transcription supplied with the scan reads 'C. & L. HARMON'; the scan reads 'C. & I. HARMON'. The scan is cited, not the transcription, and the same transcription's attribution of another advertisement in the issue is treated with the same caution in The Chicago Democrat Office.

levels.8-10: Two papers name this business in different ways. A history book calls it Harmon's and Loomis's. A paper of 1833 calls it C. and I. Harmon and does not name Loomis. Both could be true, but they do not say the same thing. A copy of the paper reads C. and L. Harmon. The old page itself reads C. and I. Harmon, so we go by the page.

entries.text: A DOCUMENTED ABSENCE, AND ONE OF THE FEW THINGS ANYBODY WROTE DOWN ABOUT THIS BUILDING. Ira Couch, who took the house in 1834, 'found the house a mere shell, WITHOUT ANY SIDEWALK AROUND IT, and poorly furnished' - Chicago Tribune, 2 February 1874, transcribed on "Tremont House." Chicagology. Compiling city-directory entries 1846-1870, an…. The same letter, under 'The Muddy Days': 'Around this corner, in early spring-time, it was impossible to drive the stage, and the passengers had to walk some two blocks; on account if the marshy state of the ground, the horses could not navigate' (the 'if' for 'of' is the page's). This project builds no plank walks anywhere, so the value is recorded rather than built: it is a negative finding about the ground around the building and never was a build instruction. It belongs in the record because the scene's ground treatment at this corner should be mud, not boards, and because the phrase 'a mere shell' is the closest thing to a description of the fabric that survives.

levels.8-10: Ira Couch took this house in 1834. A letter says he found it a mere shell, with no sidewalk around it, and poorly furnished. entries.text: A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT IN A CONTEMPORARY NEWSPAPER, which is worth more than any amount of Andreas. Two further things fix him in the town in this period: his house was the district polling place on 9 December 1833, and a travelling ventriloquist named Kenworthy advertised in the Democrat of 10 June 1834 the close of an engagement at 'the Travelers' Home, a hotel kept by Chester Ingersoll, on Wolf Point'. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 2 times, as “INGERSOLL CHESTER”, 1833-10-24 to 1835-06-26: 1 federal land entry — SW sec 28 T39N R13E and 1 parcel of the school section — BL37 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 163.79 acres stated in all, for $253.10 (ls0246, ls0849). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: INGERSOLL CHESTER matches Chester Ingersoll: the forename names Chester Ingersoll of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there.

entries.text: A DOCUMENTED WITNESS AS WELL AS A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT: Andreas prints an interview with him of 15 October 1883 describing the town of 1833 street by street, which this project uses elsewhere for the South Water Street row, the slough at the foot of State Street and the four-log footbridge. He is one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833. Andreas's 1835 town officers list has 'J. Bates and J. Haight, Measurers of Wood and Lumber' - an office he holds ON the scene date if the July election preceded it. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Bates, John, 275 State street, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Bates' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Bates, John, | 1832, May 20, | Fishkill, Duchess Co., N.Y. | 76 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “John Bates” (33S7-9YYJ-JM, printed page 224, line 20). This project has ruled the head a CANDIDATE and no more: the name agrees and is unique on both sides, but nothing independent of the name was found. A candidate is not an identity — nothing is asserted from it, no household of 1840 is carried back, and the ruling is recorded so that a reader can see it was made rather than missed. Under the rule that decided it (“Wolf Point: three buildings placed from bank geometry, not from a corner” candidate), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He knew the town and told about it. In 1883 he gave a long talk about the town of 1833, street by street. We use it for the South Water Street row, the slough, and a small log footbridge. He was one of twenty-eight voters in August 1833. In 1835 he was a measurer of wood, so he may have held that job on 1 July 1835. In 1882 a club in Chicago held a party for people who lived here before 1840, and this man was there. So he lived here some time before 1840. It gives no year he came. It does not change how sure we are. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. In 1879 a club in Chicago held a party for people who came before 1840. Its list has this man and the year he said he came. He gave that year forty or more years later, so it is his memory, not proof. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. The name was hard to read on the old sheet, so we call it only a maybe. Nothing is built on a maybe. And 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:A GARRISON OFFICER WHOSE TOUR BRACKETS THE SCENE DATE AT BOT…
entries.text: A GARRISON OFFICER WHOSE TOUR BRACKETS THE SCENE DATE AT BOTH ENDS - 3 February 1833 to 29 December 1836 - which makes him one of the few people in the dataset whose presence on 1 July 1835 is a matter of record rather than of inference. Born at Guilford, Windham Co., Vt., 3 April 1799; practised at Sackett's Harbor, N.Y., and sat in the New York legislature before his appointment. He was a witness to the Indian treaty of 26 September 1833.

levels.8-10: He was an army officer here from 3 February 1833 to 29 December 1836. So papers show he was here on 1 July 1835. He was born in Vermont in 1799. He worked in New York and sat in its law making body. He was a witness to the treaty with the Native nations in September 1833.

entries.card: why:A HOUSE THAT A SCHOOL WAS HELD IN, NOT A SCHOOL-HOUSE, and t…
entries.text: A HOUSE THAT A SCHOOL WAS HELD IN, NOT A SCHOOL-HOUSE, and the distinction is still the point: the building's own function is domestic and the teaching is an occupancy. WHAT CHANGED UNDER other work is that the domestic function now has a householder behind it rather than only a typology. Moses and Kirkland name Richard J. Hamilton as the man who built this house and say he lived in it for nineteen years, so on 1 July 1835 the ordinary reading is a dwelling in the occupation of its builder. The _former school use unattested half of the value is unchanged and still earns its keep: Watkins' school was the town's earliest and was set up by Cols. Hamilton and Owen, by 1834-35 the town had several schools in other buildings, and nothing reached says whether Watkins was still teaching here on the scene date. The value itself is not moved — it is the vocabulary the signage, yard-goods and building-material rules match on exactly, and the function did not change; its evidence did.

levels.8-10: School was held in this house, but it was a home, not a school house. A history book says Richard J. Hamilton built it and lived in it for nineteen years. So in 1835 it was most likely his home. Watkins' school, the town's first, was held here. By 1835 the town had other schools, and no one says if Watkins still taught here.

entries.card: why:A MANUFACTURER, WHICH THE 1835 TOWN HAS ALMOST NONE OF. Buyi…
entries.text: A MANUFACTURER, WHICH THE 1835 TOWN HAS ALMOST NONE OF. Buying tallow and house ashes is buying the by-products of the packing trade and of every household fire in the town, which makes this one business a measure of how many households there were. Andreas has a Daniel Elston running the largest of the city's five brickyards by 1854 - two decades past the scene and evidence of nothing about 1835 except that the man stayed. entries.card: why:A PLAIN FRONT DOUBLE GALLERY, ADOPTED FOR JULY 1835 AS A BOU…
entries.text: A PLAIN FRONT DOUBLE GALLERY, ADOPTED FOR JULY 1835 AS A BOUNDED CONTINUITY CHOICE. The actual public-domain 1881 contained cut after Alexander Hesler’s 1855 photograph, with its explicit printed p.93 key, securely identifies this brick range as Commandant’s Quarters A and shows two gallery levels along its parade front. That strongest named picture governs the broad form; it does NOT date the gallery’s construction or prove it was unchanged in 1835. The existing interpretation identifies this with the brick commanding-officer range Hubbard describes inside the north stockade in 1827 and Harrison draws in 1830, under the fort’s 1816 rebuilding range. A front piazza is compatible with that retained fabric and arrangement; Hubbard’s distinct 1818 officers’ quarters already had an upper piazza, so the form is possible at this post before the scene date. That analogy supports plausibility, not identity or independent attestation of this gallery. We fairly choose continuity of the pictured plain gallery into 1 July 1835 rather than invent an alteration date. The occurrence IN THIS SCENE, every dimension, plain posts, deck, rails and canopy remain reconstructed. Existing full front width 15.24m, reach 2.1m, upper walk at the unchanged 2.7m storey line, 0.14m posts/deck and 0.95m rail are the existing gallery kit’s bounded choices. Footprint, surveyed placement, bearing188degrees, walls, roof, stacks and openings stay as before. No wraparound corner connection, additional stairs, unidentified 1850 soldiers’ gallery, paint or elaborate joinery is copied backwards.

levels.8-10: We give this building a plain porch on two floors across its front, for 1835. A picture printed in 1881, from a photo of 1855, shows it on this brick building. That picture does not say when the porch was built. Older accounts and a fort plan of 1830 put this building here. Another fort building had a porch by 1818, so one here in 1835 was possible. We chose to keep the porch from the picture, not to guess a date it was added.

entries.card: why:A POINT CHOSEN IN A ROW, NOT A DERIVATION, so it is tagged c…
entries.text: A POINT CHOSEN IN A ROW, NOT A DERIVATION, so it is tagged conjectural and cites no sources. What Wau-Bun gives is an ORDER along the west bank and no distances: 'Facing down the river from the west was, first a small tavern kept by Mr. Wentworth... Near him were two or three log cabins occupied by Robinson... A little remote from these residences was a small square log building, originally designed for a school-house.' So the cabins lie between this project's Wolf Point Tavern (north face at local N -45) and its Walker Meeting House (south face at local N -10), and 'a little remote' says the meeting house stands clear of them. This coordinate splits that gap, about 20 m north of the tavern and 14 m south of the meeting house, and sets the cabin back from the water on the same frontage. THE UNCERTAINTY IS THE ROW'S, NOT A METRE FIGURE: both neighbours are themselves placed from bank geometry rather than from any surviving intersection — the Walker meeting house's own position is tagged conjectural and may be on the wrong bank entirely — so this record inherits two soft positions and adds a free choice between them. Treat it as good to about ±40 m along the bank and no better. Facade bearing 90, due east onto the river, follows Wau-Bun's 'facing down the river from the west' and the bearing this project gives the tavern and the meeting house in the same row.

levels.8-10: We chose this spot in a row. It is not taken from proof. An old book gives the order of buildings on the west bank, but no distances. First came Wentworth's tavern, then two or three log cabins of Robinson, then a small log school house a little way off. So we put this cabin between the tavern and the meeting house. Both of those are placed by guess too, so this spot is soft.

entries.card: why:A POINT CHOSEN ON A NAMED RIVER, NOT A DERIVATION. What Andr…
entries.text: A POINT CHOSEN ON A NAMED RIVER, NOT A DERIVATION. What Andreas gives is 'on the South Branch of the river' (scan p. 1151) and nothing else — no reach, no bank, no cross street, no distance from the town. The South Branch runs about 3 km south and south-west from the forks before the modelled ground gives out, so the attested statement locates this building to a corridor kilometres long. TWO CHOICES WERE MADE AND BOTH ARE INVENTIONS. First, the SIDE: the east bank, because it is the South Division side and because both partners' other premises in this dataset are in the South Division — George W. Dole's Warehouse at Lake and Dearborn, Newberry & Dole's Forwarding and Commission Warehouse on South Water Street — which is an argument about where the firm did business and not a statement about this building. Second, the REACH: local N -264 to -254, about 260 m south of the forks and 80 m south of the South Branch Bridge, which puts the plant below the town limits of November 1833 (Jackson Street on the south) and clear of the built-up ground, where a nuisance trade belongs and where the sources do put slaughtering generally. Both readings are plausible and neither is evidence. METHOD: the west face is set about 13 m back from the east bank line traced for this terrain epoch (the river data), which leaves room for the landing and the pens that are not modelled. Facade bearing 270, due west onto the branch, on the same reasoning as Archibald Clybourne's Log Slaughter-House — a killing floor works to the water — which is an argument from the trade, not a source. WORKING UNCERTAINTY IS THE COARSEST IN THIS PARCEL after the two displaced Clybourne records: hundreds of metres along the branch, and a coin-flip on the bank.

levels.8-10: A history book says only that this stood on the South Branch of the river. It gives no bank, no street and no distance. The river runs for miles. So we made two choices. We put it on the east bank, near the firm's other buildings. And we put it south of the town, away from homes, where a smelly trade belongs.

entries.card: why:A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE,…
entries.text: A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE, AND THIS RECORD IS GRADED AS ONE. Andreas, scan p. 249, on the special term of the Cook County Court of County Commissioners held at Chicago on 13 April 1831: 'The first two tavern licenses were granted by Cook County to Chicago landlords — Elijah Wentworth, for $7, and Samuel Miller, for $5', followed immediately by 'Ordered that the following rates be allowed to tavern keepers to wit:' and a schedule that includes 'For each breakfast and supper 25', 'For each dinner 37 1/2', 'For each horse fed 25', 'Keeping horse one night 50', and 'Lodging for each man per night 12 1/2'. Elijah Wentworth kept the Wolf Point Tavern from early 1830 until 1831-32 ("The Beginning of Wolf Point in Chicago, Illinois, including the history of the…), so this house is one of exactly two in the county holding a licence under that schedule. WHAT THAT PROVES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT: it proves that keeping a horse overnight was a priced service of this house, at twice the rate charged for a man's bed. It does not prove a dedicated building — a horse can be kept at a picket line, in a fenced lot, or in a lean-to against the tavern itself, and none of those is what this record draws. The function is therefore inferred rather than documented, and the whole building follows it.

levels.8-10: In April 1831 the county gave the first two inn licenses, to Elijah Wentworth and Samuel Miller. It set prices too, such as meals, a bed for a man, and keeping a horse for one night. Wentworth kept this tavern then. So this house was paid to keep horses overnight, at twice the price of a man's bed. That does not prove it had a stable. A horse could be kept in a fenced lot.

entries.card: why:A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE.…
entries.text: A PRICE DOCUMENTS A SERVICE; THE BUILDING IS THE INFERENCE. The Cook County Court of County Commissioners, sitting at Chicago on 13 April 1831, 'Ordered that the following rates be allowed to tavern keepers', among them 'For each horse fed 25' and 'Keeping horse one night 50' (Andreas, scan p. 249). That order set what a licensed Chicago house might charge to keep a traveller's horse; it is read here as standing for every public house the lodging model sizes, which is an inference, because no licence for this house in particular has been read. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: a dedicated building. A horse can be kept at a picket line, in a fenced lot or at a livery up the street; this record draws the building because a house of this size on a Lake Street lot with an alley behind it is the ordinary case, and says so. At the Tremont the case is stronger: it was a stage stop ("Tremont House." Chicagology. Compiling city-directory entries 1846-1870, an…).

levels.8-10: In April 1831 the county set what inns could charge, such as feeding a horse or keeping it for a night. We use that for every inn in our model. That is a guess, since we have not read a license for this house. It does not prove a stable. A horse could be kept in a fenced lot. We draw a stable since that was usual for an inn like this. At the Tremont the case is stronger, since stages stopped there.

entries.card: why:A RAILED DECK, AND THE ARCHETYPE'S DEFAULT SAYS NO. bridge t…
entries.text: A RAILED DECK, AND THE ARCHETYPE'S DEFAULT SAYS NO. bridge timber builds no railing unless a record asks for one, and the argument for that default is entirely about the two BRANCH bridges: the 1883 old-settlers statement has them 'about ten feet wide and without railings, for the first few years, after which guards, or railings, were added', and the only qualitative description of the North Branch crossing — 'formed of stringers', 'useless for teams' — describes something cruder than a piece of civil engineering. NONE OF THAT IS ABOUT THIS BRIDGE, and the same old-settlers paragraph is careful to say which two bridges it is describing. This one was framed by a ship-carpenter to a design that won a premium, cost the corporation $166.67 in repairs within weeks of acceptance, and carried the main street of the town across a navigable river six feet above the water. THE EVIDENCE IS THE PLATES: both engravings in the 2026-08-18 owner brief (README images 2 and 3) draw the deck railed. a modern reconstruction pictorial, so `inferred` and not `attested`. THE HEIGHT, THE POST SPACING AND THE POLE SECTION ARE THE ARCHETYPE'S — 0.95 m rails on posts at about 2.2 m — and no source gives any of the three; they are the same numbers the module has carried unused since 2026-08-10 and they are recorded in the liberties register “The Dearborn drawbridge, built to its engravings: the frames' bracing, the hoist chains, a two-leaf draw and a railed deck”. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the trustees' specification, the February 1834 proposals, or the repair accounts of September 1834 and 1835.

levels.8-10: This bridge has rails along its deck, though our rules give none unless asked. An old account says the two bridges over the river branches had no rails at first. But it is about those two bridges, not this one. This one was built by a ship's carpenter and carried the main street over the river. Two old pictures draw it with rails. They were made much later, so this is likely, not proven. The height and spacing of the rails are our guess.

The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data).

levels.8-10: He was a real man, named in a history book, but that he was here on 1 July 1835 is our guess. The book says he was one of the Couch brothers who bought this house. It says he took charge in 1836. He said the house was so full that people slept on every bit of floor. We think he lived here in 1835 because the brothers bought it together. In 1879 a club in Chicago held a party for people who came before 1840. Its list has this man and the year he said he came. He gave that year forty or more years later, so it is his memory, not proof. It does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:A SEPARATE MAN FROM 'ISAAC HARMON, TOWN CLERK', OR PERHAPS N…
entries.text: A SEPARATE MAN FROM 'ISAAC HARMON, TOWN CLERK', OR PERHAPS NOT, AND THE RECORD WILL NOT DECIDE. Andreas has an Isaac Harmon appointed clerk of the first board of trustees on 12 August 1833 and again as clerk and collector in 1834; he also prints an 1832 militia agreement signed by BOTH 'Isaac Harmon' AND 'Isaac D. Harmon', two lines apart, which is positive evidence that the town contained two men of that name. The town clerk is therefore NOT identified with this merchant and gets no person record here at all - writing him would risk creating a duplicate of a man already in this household. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Harmon, Isaac” (tax 1833 043, line 95). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Harmon' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Isaac D. Harmon,” (f1839 v0112, printed page 42, ward 1, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Harmon' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins I. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “HARMON ISAAC D”, 1833-10-22: 1 parcel of the school section — BL137 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 0.00 acres stated in all, for $130.00 (ls0229). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HARMON ISAAC D matches Isaac Dewey Harmon: the forename names Isaac Dewey Harmon of the 6 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He may or may not be the same man as Isaac Harmon, the town clerk. A history book says an Isaac Harmon was clerk in 1833 and 1834. It also prints a paper of 1832 signed by both Isaac Harmon and Isaac D. Harmon. So there were two men of that name. We do not join the clerk with this man, so we make no card for the clerk. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land once. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there.

entries.card: why:A SMALL FLAT-HOODED FRONTISPIECE ON THE MAIN BLOCK'S FRONT D…
entries.text: A SMALL FLAT-HOODED FRONTISPIECE ON THE MAIN BLOCK'S FRONT DOOR. Both street views of the 2026-08-18 owner brief draw it (the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18): the Petford 1831 watercolour puts 'a small flat-hooded entrance frontispiece/porch on the front door' (image 8), and the Braunhold engraving in Andreas draws 'the clapboard block's wide entrance surround' (image 9). This is a door SURROUND, not the veranda the gallery attribute records as absent — the same views that show the frontispiece show no gallery, so the two claims agree rather than conflict. a modern reconstruction retrospective views may drive form as inferred and never a dimension: the hood and pilaster sizes are the archetype's numbers, claimed at the liberties register “The Sauganash's fabric from the three views: wing door and hood, frontispiece, brick and moss, and the louvre pitch”. The brief's binaries are not yet committed, so the citation is the README until other work lands identifications.

levels.8-10: There is a small flat hood over the front door. Two old street pictures show it, a painting of 1831 and a print in a history book. It is a frame around the door, not a porch. The same pictures show no porch, so they agree. The pictures came later, so the sizes of the hood are our guess.

Nobody named him and nobody counted him: what is claimed is that the post was held on 1 July 1835 and that a held post of two companies had this many men in it at establishment. Frontier companies stood below establishment and this project has no return, so the number is a ceiling the ledger states rather than a strength anybody reported.

entries.card: why:A STATED SEQUENCE WITHOUT A DATE IN IT. The 1883 statement s…
entries.text:
A STATED SEQUENCE WITHOUT A DATE IN IT. The 1883 statement says the branch bridges were 'about ten feet wide and without railings, for the first few years, after which guards, or railings, were added'. The scene date is two years and four months after this bridge was built, so 'the first few years' covers it on the most natural reading and the value is false — but it is a reading of a sequence rather than a measurement, and it is the kind of phrase that cannot settle a particular July on its own. If a date for the guards is ever found and it falls before July 1835, this attribute flips. What hangs on it is not decoration: a railed deck reads to a visitor as considered infrastructure and an unrailed one reads as a causeway of logs, so the difference is a claim about how developed the town was.

AND THE TOWN PRINTED A SPECIFICATION FOR A TOWN BRIDGE'S RAILING FIFTEEN MONTHS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE — AND ONE CLAUSE OF IT IS THIS BRIDGE'S ALONE. The Board of Trustees' call for proposals, Chicago Democrat 4 February 1834, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-02-04, bills the materials for both town bridges: 'two complete sets of braces for each bridge, to be of oak timber 6 inches square, and oak railing 8 by 4 inches for both bridges; oak standards for railing 4 feet apart, 4 feet high; … and the railing to be well secured by spikes or pins' — and, before those, 'a new bent to the … south bridge of oak'. So the railing the town paid for was OAK, 8 by 4 inches in section, on oak standards four feet high at four-foot centres; and the south branch crossing specifically wanted a NEW OAK BENT, which is a statement that one of its supports had failed by February 1834. THE VALUE IS NOT CHANGED AND THE CONFIDENCE IS NOT MOVED. It is a call for proposals for a REPAIR seventeen months before the scene date — what the trustees asked to be supplied, not what was built and not what still stood in July 1835 — and the bent clause is cut at the column edge on both sides, so its count and position are unread. Reconciling the bill with the modelled railing and bents is work of its own.

levels.8-10: An old account of 1883 says the river bridges were about ten feet wide with no rails at first. Rails were added after a few years. This town is two years after this bridge was built, so we read it as having no rails. That is our reading, not a measure. If a date for the rails turns up before July 1835, this changes. A railed bridge looks well built, and one without rails looks like a road of logs.

entries.card: why:A STRUCTURE UNDER CONTINUOUS EXTENSION HAS NO STABLE PHASE,…
entries.text:
A STRUCTURE UNDER CONTINUOUS EXTENSION HAS NO STABLE PHASE, AND THIS RANGE IS TWO MONTHS WIDE FOR THE SAME REASON THE NORTH PIER'S IS. Andreas has the south pier 'extended 500 ft in 1835, total 700 ft', so this structure more than trebled during the season this scene sits in the middle of and no state of it lasted a fortnight. What the phase carries is a length INTERPOLATED FOR 1835-07-01, wrong by a growing margin either side of it, and the range is set to the two months around the target rather than to the pier's life. A scene at any other date finds no phase covering it and reports this structure as excluded, which is the correct answer: it stood, and this record does not say how long it was. Adding an 1834 phase and an 1836 phase is the fix and widening this one is not; both are writable from the same two sources and neither is written, because this project's first scene is 1835.

THE CONTRACTS ARE LET IN THE PLURAL, AND THAT IS WHERE THIS STRUCTURE'S 1834 SEASON IS DOCUMENTED. Five readings of the Chicago Democrat name the harbour works as a whole and therefore reach this pier as well as its neighbour: the Chicago Democrat of 1834-03-04 and the Chicago Democrat of 1834-03-18, the two printings of the call for oak timber 'for the Piers of the Chicago Harbor'; the Chicago Democrat of 1834-07-09, one thousand cords of prairie stone 'to be delivered into the Piers of the Harbour, or at such of the Piers as may be designated by the Superintendent of the works'; the Chicago Democrat of 1835-01-21, the engineer's return of the first full season with its one hundred and eighty arrivals; and the Chicago Democrat of 1835-03-25, the $32,800 appropriated by Congress towards completion. Together they say that at the scene date this pier stood inside a federal works that was under contract, unfinished, and newly funded. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: not one of the five distinguishes the south pier from the north. The plural and the phrase 'such of the Piers as may be designated' are the whole of the evidence that this structure was in those contracts, and no length, no rate of extension and no share of the thousand cords is apportioned to it here. The stone clause is in fact evidence against precision — the Superintendent chose which pier each load went into, and this corpus does not record his choice.

levels.8-10: This pier kept growing, so it has no one steady shape. A history book says it grew 500 feet in 1835, to 700 feet in all. So it changed a lot during the summer this town shows. We give its length as we think it was on 1 July 1835. That gets more wrong each day away from that date. So we show it only for two months around that day.

entries.card: why:A STRUCTURE UNDER CONTINUOUS EXTENSION HAS NO STABLE PHASE,…
entries.text:
A STRUCTURE UNDER CONTINUOUS EXTENSION HAS NO STABLE PHASE, AND THIS RANGE IS TWO MONTHS WIDE ON PURPOSE. Every other record in this dataset carries a range meaning 'the structure stood, unchanged in the respects this record models, between these dates'. That sentence cannot be written about this one: the north pier was 700 ft long at the end of 1834 and 1,260 ft at the end of 1835, so it grew by about half its own length during the season this scene sits in the middle of, and no state of it lasted a fortnight. What the phase actually carries is a length INTERPOLATED FOR 1835-07-01 and wrong by a growing margin on either side of it — about 3 ft of pier for every day away from the scene date, if the season's work were even. So the range is set to the two months around the target rather than to the pier's life, and a scene at any other date will find no phase covering it and report this structure as excluded, which is the correct answer: it stood, and this record does not say how long it was. ADDING PHASES IS THE FIX AND NOT WIDENING THIS ONE. An 1834 scene wants a 700 ft phase closing on 31 December 1834; an 1836 scene wants a 1,260 ft phase opening on 1 January 1836. Both are writable today from the same two sources; neither is written, because this project's first scene is 1835 and a phase nobody has checked against a scene is a claim nobody has read.

THE NEWSPAPERS DATE THIS PIER SEASON BY SEASON, AND THEY ARE THE ONLY SOURCE HERE THAT DOES. Eight readings of the Chicago Democrat carry the harbour works, and they are written on THIS block because what they document is WHEN the structure existed and how fast it was growing, not its form, which none of them gives. (1) The village ordinances of 7 November 1833, printed in the paper's first number, claim The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday…, walk the corporation's own boundary 'to the northern United States' Pier, thence westwardly along said pier to the termination thereof': on that day this pier existed, was walkable enough for a trustee to survey along, and had a definite landward end a man could point to. That is a harder statement of its existence than any retrospective plate this project holds. (2) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-01-21 prints the engineer's own report of the first season, and it says almost nothing had been built: no engineer officer could be spared, so the commanding officer at Fort Dearborn ran the work; materials and workmen could not be got; everything but timber and stone had to be drawn from Buffalo; the first proposals were rejected as exorbitant. (3) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-03-04 and the Chicago Democrat of 1834-03-18 are one advertisement for the timber OF THE PIERS, printed twice: 10,000 feet of hewn oak squared a full foot on the side in equal thirds of 30-, 25- and 20-foot logs, 350 round tie logs 24 feet long squaring about 11 inches, and 50 round white-oak piles 25 feet long squaring at least 12 inches at the small end. (4) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-07-09 advertises one thousand cords of prairie stone to be delivered INTO THE PIERS, at up to twenty-four cords a day from 10 August 1834. (5) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-08-13 has the North Pier 'gradually extending into the Lake' across the sand bar opposite the river's mouth, with about a hundred hands at work and more still wanted. (6) the Chicago Democrat of 1835-01-21 reports the first full season out of the federal Public Documents: one hundred and eighty arrivals discharged between the opening of navigation and 30 November 1834, and a recommendation 'that it be perfected as rapidly as circumstances will permit'. (7) the Chicago Democrat of 1835-03-25 has $32,800 appropriated by Congress towards completion, reported second-hand from a friend at Washington and printed as such. WHAT THEY DO NOT SUPPLY IS A LENGTH ON 1835-07-01, which is the one number this block would most like to have. The interpolated length above stands exactly as it did and no confidence moves. What the readings do supply is the reason the interpolation is legitimate rather than convenient: the work was continuous, contracted in advance, and still unfinished and still being paid for at the scene date.

levels.8-10: This pier kept growing, so it has no one steady shape. It was 700 feet long at the end of 1834 and 1,260 feet at the end of 1835. That is about 3 feet more each day. We give its length as we think it was on 1 July 1835. So we show it only for two months around that day. A town of 1834 or 1836 would need its own length.

entries.card: why:A tavern from 1829 and a hotel from 1831; the social centre…
entries.text:
A tavern from 1829 and a hotel from 1831; the social centre of the settlement in the target window. Chicago's first billiard table in a public house stood here.

THE HOUSE IS OPEN, AND FRESHLY DONE UP, THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Reviewing the town's public houses against Detroit's new American Hotel, the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-06-10, reports that 'The Sauganash has been re[paired,] fitted up and furnished with neatness and [taste,] and so far as it goes, will[, we have no doubt,] be found just the thing'. That is the only dated statement of this building's CONDITION the corpus holds, and it bears on how the scene should read it: on 1835-07-01 the Sauganash is a working, recently refitted public house and not the shabby survivor its 1829 log origins invite. 'so far as it goes' is the editor's qualification and it means small — his complaint in the same paragraph is that no establishment in Chicago is 'sufficiently extensive'. The refit is recorded here rather than in the form block below because nothing in it names a fabric, a storey or a colour, and inventing one from 'fitted up' is exactly the supply this project refuses.

levels.8-10: It was a tavern from 1829 and a hotel from 1831, and the heart of the town at this time. Chicago's first pool table in an inn stood here. A paper of 10 June 1835 says the Sauganash had been fixed up and furnished with taste. That is three weeks before the day this town shows. So on 1 July 1835 it was a working inn, freshly done up, not a worn out old log house. The editor adds that it was still small.
