entries.text: A two-storey house added to the log cabin, fronting the river. This is the element that faced the settlement across the water and the one a viewer standing at Wolf Point would have seen. THAT IT EXISTED IS DOCUMENTED AND ITS SIZE IS NOT, so the four attributes below state the side, the width, the depth and the storey count explicitly rather than leaving them to the archetype's defaults. Until 2026-08-10 they were left to the defaults, which is the failure the liberties register “Wolf Point Tavern: the frame bay's side, width and depth are invented” exists to stop one building over: a documented feature arriving at an invented size with nothing admitting it.

levels.8-10: A house two floors high was added to the log cabin, facing the river. It is the part people saw from across the water at Wolf Point. Papers show it was there, but not its size. So we say which side it is on, how wide and deep it is, and how many floors. Those are our guesses.

entries.card: why:ABOUT THREE HUNDRED FEET, AND THE RIVER AGREES WITH IT. Andr…
entries.text: ABOUT THREE HUNDRED FEET, AND THE RIVER AGREES WITH IT. Andreas, History of Chicago vol. 1 (read verbatim in the chicagology transcription; scan p. 415 per the research notes on structures south section 4): 'From various sources it is learned that it was about three hundred feet long, and the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' Andreas is hedging — 'from various sources it is learned' means he is reconciling second-hand reports, not reading a specification — which is why the value is recorded in its original unit as about 300 ft rather than as a figure to two decimal places, and 91.44 m is the exact conversion of a number that is itself approximate. THE MEASUREMENT, and it is this record's own contribution rather than another retelling. The distance between the two traced 1834 waterlines along the Dearborn Street alignment is 76.33 m, which is 250.4 ft of open water. That is independent of every text above: it comes from the Wright 1834 segmentation in the shoreline data through the same fitted affine that fixes the datum. A bridge about three hundred feet long crossing two hundred and fifty feet of river has about fifty feet of timber over land, twenty-five at either end — which is exactly the long low causeway with approaches that the research notes on structures south section 4 describes, and it is a convergence rather than a coincidence: two numbers from unrelated evidence that fit each other without adjustment. THE FIGURE THIS SUPERSEDES, recorded because the project believed it in one of its own dossiers and a reader deserves to know why it went. the research notes on structures north section 5 gives the bridge as '200 ft long, 60-ft draw at one end'; its citation is the chicagology page 'The First Bridge Across the Chicago River, 1834', transcribing a 1902 promotional history — 'Chicago Pictorial', Historical Chicago National Bank — whose sentence reads 'The bridge at Dearborn Street was 200 feet long, with a draw of sixty feet at one end.' Two hundred feet is fifty feet SHORTER than the water it would have to cross, so it cannot be a bank-to-bank length, and it is not cited here because this project holds no source record for that 1902 text: naming a source id that does not resolve would be inventing a citation. THE GEOMETRY DECLARATION says what the model does with all of this. It builds the 76.33 m between the traced waterlines and no approaches, so about a sixth of the length this attribute states is not in the mesh. That is the same missing approach the ground contact block declares, seen from the other side, and it is admitted in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: A history book says the bridge was about three hundred feet long, with a gap of about sixty feet for boats. The book says it learned this from different people, so the length is only a guess. We also measured the river on a map of 1834, along Dearborn Street. The water there was about 250 feet wide. So a bridge of about 300 feet fits.

A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. entries.card: why:AN ARGUMENT FROM SILENCE HAS BECOME AN ARGUMENT AGAINST A TI…
entries.text:
AN ARGUMENT FROM SILENCE HAS BECOME AN ARGUMENT AGAINST A TIMELINE, and the value survives it. The 1883 old-settlers statement at Andreas pp. 631-632 says the branch bridges were 'about ten feet wide and without railings, for the first few years, after which guards, or railings, were added'. For a scene dated 1835-07-01, three years after the build, 'the first few years' covers the scene date on the most natural reading and the value stays false — but it is now a reading of a stated sequence rather than an absence of evidence, and it is the kind of phrase that will not settle a particular July on its own. If a date for the guards is ever found and it falls before July 1835, this attribute flips. THE ORIGINAL REASONING, unchanged and still the argument for why the absence is stated rather than defaulted: No source reached mentions a railing on either branch bridge; the descriptions that exist run the other way, toward a causeway of logs rather than a piece of engineering. A railed deck reads to a visitor as considered infrastructure and an unrailed one reads as a plank over water, so adding one to look finished would change what the scene says about how developed the town was. The counter-argument is on the record in the bridge timber generator: a procession of hundreds crossing an unrailed deck nearly two metres above water is an alarming picture, and that is an argument about the 1835 rebuild rather than evidence about a railing.

AND THE TOWN PRINTED A SPECIFICATION FOR A TOWN BRIDGE'S RAILING FIFTEEN MONTHS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. The Board of Trustees' call for proposals, Chicago Democrat 4 February 1834, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-02-04, bills the materials for BOTH town bridges in the corporation's own words: 'two complete sets of braces for each bridge, to be of oak timber 6 inches square, and oak railing 8 by 4 inches for both bridges; oak standards for railing 4 feet apart, 4 feet high; … and the railing to be well secured by spikes or pins.' So the railing the town paid for was OAK, 8 by 4 inches in section, on oak standards four feet high at four-foot centres, spiked or pinned. That is a dimensioned bill from the body that owned the structure, and it is the first thing in this dataset against which the value above — reasoned from an 1883 reminiscence — can be read at all. THE VALUE IS NOT CHANGED AND THE CONFIDENCE IS NOT MOVED, for two reasons stated rather than glossed. It is a call for proposals for a REPAIR in February 1834, so it says what the trustees asked to be supplied, not what was built, and not what still stood in July 1835. And it does not distinguish the two bridges: the only clause that does is 'a new bent to the south bridge of oak', which is the other record's. Reconciling the bill with the modelled railing is work of its own.

levels.8-10: An old account of 1883 says the river bridges were about ten feet wide with no rails at first. Rails were added after a few years. This town is three years after the bridge was built. So we read it as having no rails yet. If a date for the rails turns up before July 1835, this changes. No other paper we have talks of rails on these bridges.

entries.text: AN UPPER PIAZZA, BUILT AS A RECONSTRUCTION ON HUBBARD'S EARLIER TEXT, NOT AS ATTESTATION. Hubbard, of the officers' quarters he saw in 1818: 'A piazza extended along the entire front on a line with the floor of the second story, and was reached by stairs on the outside' (Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard…, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358). It is rendered with the fort archetype's existing two-level gallery (gallery storeys 2): an open ground level of posts under an upper walk at the second floor, a rail along its front, and a canopy from the main eave. THE GRADE STAYS RECONSTRUCTED because the same unresolved questions the storey count carries apply here with more force: Hubbard puts that building OUTSIDE the pickets on p. 36 and the log officers' quarters WITHIN them on the west on p. 167, and nothing identifies the 1818 building with this 1835 range, so the piazza's continuity into the 1831-1835 garrison is conditional on both. THE PRIOR REFUSAL IS KEPT ON THE RECORD: until other work this attribute read false with the note that nothing said the 1816 fort's ranges had galleries, that Whistler's 1808 'Galliaries fronting the parade' belonged to the first fort, and that John H. Kinzie called the two forts 'differently constructed'. That was written without p. 36, and it is the alternative a visitor would have seen had the text not been read. EVERY DIMENSION IS RECONSTRUCTED: the 2.1 m reach, post sections and rhythm, deck, rail, pales and canopy fall are the helper's choices (the liberties register “the upper courtyard walks” and “The second fort's officers' quarters carry Hubbard's upper piazza, with the building it describes unresolved”); Hubbard gives none. THE OUTSIDE STAIRS ARE NOW MODELLED: the occurrence is Hubbard’s; the right-end side, straight run, width, risers and rails are reconstructed under gallery stair side. The prior refusal because their location was unrecorded is superseded by that explicit bounded choice. The 1855 photograph is diagnostic only and is not a matched July 1835 view.

levels.8-10: We built a porch on the second floor, but as a guess, not as proof. In 1818 Gurdon Hubbard wrote of the officers' rooms. He said a porch ran along the whole front at the height of the second floor, with stairs outside. We built it with posts below, a walk above, and a rail. But we can not tell if his building is this one of 1835. So it stays a guess.

entries.card: why:ANDREAS NAMES WHO USED THE LOG RING, and the household card…
entries.text: ANDREAS NAMES WHO USED THE LOG RING, and the household card refuses the seat. The source puts 'small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell, an Indian chief, who was also interpreter for the agency' in this vicinity, and that sentence is why this building stands. But the Caldwell household holds two candidate houses: this ring, and the frame house the Indian Department built for him near State Street and Chicago Avenue. Neither is dated to 1835, so his lives at is null and says why. Choosing this house because it is the one that got modelled would be the worst reason available. Which of the two men had which building is not attested either. So the roof states the refusal rather than seating anybody, and it carries no occupant until a source dates one of the two houses to 1835 or places him in either on the scene date.

levels.8-10: A history book says small log buildings here were used by the smith, Mr. McKee, and by Billy Caldwell. Caldwell was a chief who spoke for the agency. But Caldwell had two houses that could be his. One is here, and one was a frame house built for him near State Street. Neither is dated to 1835. So we do not put him in either one, and no one lives here until a paper says so.

entries.card: why:ANONYMOUS STOCK. This roof was raised by the inferred-househ…
entries.text: ANONYMOUS STOCK. This roof was raised by the inferred-household programme because an argued household needed somewhere to be; the owner retired that reconstructed resident population on 2026-09-02 and ruled the geometry kept - "keep as anonymous stock" - so the household this roof was raised for no longer exists and nobody is claimed to be here. It is unassigned until the later placement sweep, and it is counted as one of the anonymous count-units of the 665-roof programme. THE ROOF'S OWN EXISTENCE, POSITION AND FOOTPRINT REMAIN CONJECTURAL and are unchanged by the retirement: what was withdrawn is the occupant, not the building. The trade it was raised for is kept in `reconstruction.occupation` and in this record's own name, because that is what the placement sweep works from; the argument that raised it is kept as history in the 1835 inferred household programme data.

levels.8-10: This house is left empty on purpose. It was built for a made-up family. The owner of this project took away those made-up people on 2 September 2026, but kept the houses. So no one lives here now. The house itself is still our guess. We keep the kind of work it was built for, so a later step can fill it.

entries.card: why:APPOINTED THE TOWN'S FIRST STREET COMMISSIONER ON 7 NOVEMBER…
entries.text: APPOINTED THE TOWN'S FIRST STREET COMMISSIONER ON 7 NOVEMBER 1833 and resigned before his term expired: Andreas, 'It was during these days that Benjamin Jones was appointed Street Commissioner, but on account of ill-health resigned before his term expired, and was succeeded by O. Morrison and Silas W. Sherman.' His health is the only medical fact about any private resident in this parcel. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — A DATE OF DEATH, AND NOTHING ABOUT 1835. John Wentworth's roll of old settlers who had died since 1 January 1881, kept for the Calumet Club and printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 April 1882, carries “Benjamin Jones, Aug. 11, 1881.”. That corroborates a Chicago residence before 1840 and fixes the END of this life, which this record did not carry; it is not an arrival and it places nobody in the town on 1 July 1835. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Jones, Benjamin” (poll 1834 060, line 229). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Jones' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 5 times, as “JONES BENJAMIN”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-22: 1 lot in the platted town — lot 7 of block 35 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL35CHIOT, as printed) and 4 parcels of the school section — BL121 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 2 of block 117 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 23 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 80 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $7133.00 (ls0254, ls0255, ls0256, ls0257, ls1263). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $6000.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: JONES BENJAMIN matches Benjamin Jones: the forename names Benjamin Jones of the 6 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He became the town's first street boss on 7 November 1833. A history book says he left the job early because he was sick. That is the only fact about the health of anyone here. A notice in the paper of November 1833 is good proof he was here then. It is weaker proof that he was still here in July 1835. In 1882 a list was printed of old settlers who had died. It gives the day this person died. That backs up that they lived in Chicago before 1840. It says nothing about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 5 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:ARRIVED 19 JUNE 1833 - A DAY-PRECISE ARRIVAL, which only fou…
entries.text: ARRIVED 19 JUNE 1833 - A DAY-PRECISE ARRIVAL, which only four households in this parcel have. Andreas: 'The first lawyer in Chicago to make a living by his profession alone was Giles Spring; and separated from him by a few days was John Dean Caton, who arrived June 19, 1833.' Early in July the two of them kept office 'as was facetiously said, "On the head of a barrel at the corner of Lake and Wells"', and in December 1833 Caton rented from Dr Temple 'the back room and attic of his "building" on Lake Street, converting the attic into a bedroom, and extending to Spring the courtesy of desk-room in the room below, which thus became the first law-office in Chicago'. In August 1833 he defended six or seven free coloured men before the Court of County Commissioners and obtained certificates of freedom for them, his fee a dollar from each. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Caton, John Dean, 1900 Calumet avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Caton, John Dean” (tax 1833 015, line 67); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Caton, John Dean” (poll 1834 025, line 194). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Caton' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Caton, John Dean, | 1833, June, | Orange Co., N.Y. | 67 | Ottawa, Ill.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “John Dean Caton” (f1839 v0727, printed page 40, ward 3). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Caton' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He came on 19 June 1833. Only four homes here have a date that exact. A history book says he and Giles Spring were the first lawyers in Chicago to live by law alone. At first they worked on top of a barrel at Lake and Wells, as a joke went. In December 1833 he rented a back room on Lake Street. It became the first law office in Chicago. In August 1833 he helped six or seven free Black men get papers that proved they were free. In 1882 a club in Chicago held a party for people who lived here before 1840, and this man was there. So he lived here some time before 1840. It gives no year he came. It does not change how sure we are. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. In 1879 a club in Chicago held a party for people who came before 1840. Its list has this man and the year he said he came. He gave that year forty or more years later, so it is his memory, not proof. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are.

Andreas gives his later Chicago career - alderman in 1837, 1838, 1843, 1844 and 1845 and two streets named after him - which corroborates the man's long residence and says nothing at all about who was at the anvil in July 1835. Co., Vt. | 66 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Pierce' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins A. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He came from Vermont on 8 October 1833. No other home here has both a day and a place he came from. A history book says he later served on the city council many times, and two streets were named for him. That shows he stayed long. It says nothing about who worked at the forge in July 1835. He is here because the town of 1835 needs his kind of work. A history book's list is the only one we have that names such workers. So a real name takes the place of a made-up one. entries.text: ATTESTED IN THE WORD, and it is the rarest thing on this record. bk hub 063: 'a two-story, SQUARED-LOG structure'. Squared — hewn, not round — is what this archetype builds, so the fabric here is read and not invented, which is the difference between this building and the two out buildings 130 m north of it whose `log` is recorded at “A plural label, two drawn blocks, and everything above the ground invented” as pure default.

levels.8-10: An old book says this was a two story building of squared logs. Squared means cut flat, not round. That is just what we build. So its walls come from proof, not a guess.

entries.card: why:ATTESTED ONLY IN 1850 AND CARRIED BACKWARDS, WHICH IS THE WE…
entries.text: ATTESTED ONLY IN 1850 AND CARRIED BACKWARDS, WHICH IS THE WEAKEST DATE ARGUMENT IN THIS COMPLEX. Robert Fergus, describing the fort in 1850, puts 'the building where the artillery was housed, the soldier's barracks, and the storehouse' on the east of the parade. Nothing reached names an artillery house in 1827, in 1830 or at any date before 1850. The range opens with the fort because the post was abandoned as a military station on 29 December 1836 and nothing reached records anything being BUILT inside it afterwards, so a building standing in 1850 is most likely a building of the garrison years - the same continuity argument, run backwards, that the record of Hogan's Store runs forwards. It is an argument and not a citation, and if it is wrong this record belongs in the exclusions record rather than in the scene.

levels.8-10: We only know of this building from 1850, and we carry it back to 1835. That is the weakest date proof in the fort. In 1850 Robert Fergus wrote that the gun house, the soldiers' rooms and the store house were on the east side of the parade ground. Nothing names a gun house before that. The army left the fort in 1836, and nothing says new buildings went up after. So a building there in 1850 was most likely there in the army years. That is our reasoning, not proof.

NO SOURCE REACHED PLACES HIM IN THIS BUILDING ON THE SCENE DATE, and the record claims occupancy in 1835 as an inference from continuity rather than as a fact. Nothing further about the household is stated here; see review required and the research note.

levels.8-10: A history book says Madore Beaubien built this building. It says he was licensed to sell goods in 1831 and was chosen a town leader in 1833. No paper puts him in this building in 1835. We guess he was still there, but it is not proven.

entries.card: why:Andreas calls it 'a small store' without naming the trade; t…
entries.text: Andreas calls it 'a small store' without naming the trade; the trade is inferred from its owner, who was Chicago's first druggist and who advertised in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 — three months after building this store — offering drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs together with dry groceries, glass and nails. That advertisement carries no address, so it names the TRADE with certainty and the BUILDING not at all. A general store selling drugs among other things is the honest reading of what Carpenter was doing by 1833; 'drug store' is the label this dataset has for it. THE TRADE IS NO LONGER INFERRED FROM THE MAN: HE ADVERTISES IT, SIGNED, THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. "Drug[s], Medicines, Dye Woo[d]s, DYE STU[F]FS, &c. … a[n] [a]s[so]r[t]e[d] [a]ss[ort]me[nt of Drugs and] Medicines, Dye [St]u[ff]s, &c., &c.; among which are the [following]: A[l]o[e]s, Ipecac, Liquorice Ball … S[u]rgical In[st]rument[s], Trusses … Druggi[st]s, merchants and o[t]hers will find it for their advantage to call before they purchase elsewhere. PHILO CARPENTER." — The Chicago American, 1835-06-27, page 3 column 6, claim the Chicago American of 1835-06-27. That is a drug store selling WHOLESALE TO THE TRADE as well as over a counter, which is the strongest form of the reading this note already argued, and it dates it to the scene year rather than to 1833. SO THE GRADE MOVES FROM `inferred` TO `attested` AND THE VALUE DOES NOT: 'drug store' was already the right label and is now a documented one. THE ADDRESS IS STILL NOT ATTESTED — none of the American's Carpenter cards carries one, exactly as the 1833 Democrat advertisement carried none — so which of this project's two Carpenter records the advertisement was written from remains the continuity argument made on documented range and not a fact this claim supplies. THE READING IS TRANSCRIPTION-MEDIATED AND SAYS SO. Under the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 a claim read through this project's OCR-assisted transcriptions rather than off the page scan grades `attested` in this schema's vocabulary while carrying its own flag: reading = transcription mediated, with the transcription's own uncertainty brackets preserved inside the quotation rather than tidied away. Where a scan is later read, the scan is the authority and this claim upgrades under it — the standard The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday… set when a scan caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'.

levels.8-10: A history book calls it a small store and does not say what it sold. We know from its owner, Chicago's first druggist. In November 1833 his notice in the paper sold drugs, oils, paints and dyes, with groceries, glass and nails. It gives no address. Then three weeks before the day this town shows, he signed a notice for drugs and medicines. So now we know the trade from his own words.

entries.card: why:Andreas calls it a hotel in terms - 'Mr. and Mrs. Murphy too…
entries.text:
Andreas calls it a hotel in terms - 'Mr. and Mrs. Murphy took charge of this NEW HOTEL, which they christened the Exchange Coffee House' - and lists it in his index among the early hotels. A coffee house of this period is a public house that lodges and feeds people, not a modern cafe. THE STAGE OFFICE IS THE PART THIS PROJECT HAS BEEN GETTING SLIGHTLY WRONG, AND THE CORRECTION IS A YEAR. the exclusions record excludes a separate Frink & Walker stage office on the ground that 'in 1835-36 stage seats were taken at Markle's Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells', and the research notes on structures south line 144 says the same. The sentence behind it is Andreas on Dr John T. Temple's stage line: 'An advertisement that appeared in the American on AUGUST 6, 1836, specifies that John T. Temple & Co. are proprietors of a stage line from Chicago to Peoria... and that seats can be taken at Markle's Exchange Coffee House.' That is thirteen months AFTER the scene date. Temple's line itself is older - it carried the mail to Ottawa from 1 January 1834 - so seats were being sold somewhere in 1835; nothing reached says where. The exclusion of a separate stage-office BUILDING stands on its own feet, since no such building is attested before 1840. What does not stand is the claim that this house was the stage office in 1835, and this record does not make it.

THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS ATTESTS THE PUBLIC ROOM DIRECTLY, WHERE ANDREAS ONLY RECALLS THE HOUSE. 'a large and respectable Meeting of the Democratic friends of the National Administration of the town of Chicago, was hel[d] at the Ex[change] Coffee House in said town, on Tuesday Evening, April 13, 1835' — the Chicago Democrat of 20 May 1835, page 1 column 3, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-05-20, printing the proceedings with Col. T. J. V. Owen calling the meeting to order and Hiram Hugunin in the chair. The secretaries and the committee lists are not repeated here: the reading mints no one off them, and a name written into the town on a building's record is a name the inferred-household deal may no longer use. The same party met here again for the town-election caucus of 6 June 1835 and had moved to the Eagle Coffee House, Trowbridge's, by 24 June. So the house is in business either side of the scene date and its largest room is the town's political one in the spring of 1835, which is a use a tavern inn function covers and an innkeeping one does not say.
AND THE ADVERTISEMENT IN THE FOLLOWING WEEK'S PAPER NAMES THIS HOUSE AS A LANDMARK, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF WHAT IT DOES TO IT. Russell E. Heacock advertises an office '[in the 2d st]ory, opposite the Ex[cha]n[ge], [corne]r of Lake and Franklin-sts' (the Chicago Democrat of 1835-07-08). Read once as putting THIS house at Lake and Franklin, that looked like a conflict with Andreas's corner and was recorded as one on 2026-09-26. Other work ruled it the next day: the corner in the notice is Heacock's own address and the Exchange is the landmark opposite it, which is how the claim's own placement block and the business register had read it all along. The position does not move, and the reasoning — including what the ruling leaves unresolved about the word 'opposite' — is in position.note above.

AND THE TRUSTEES SAT HERE ON 3 NOVEMBER 1834. The ordinance 'for the further prevention of Fires' was adopted 'At a meeting of the President and Trustees of the Town of Chicago, held at “the Exchange,” in said town, on the 3d day of November A. D. 1834', and the Chicago Democrat printed it three times: claims the Chicago Democrat of 1834-11-05, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-11-12 and the Chicago Democrat of 1834-12-03 — the third of them the clearest. The first printing loses the house's name under a letter list woven through its column; the second and third carry it whole, and that is where the first's supply comes from. So this building held a sitting of the town's government on a named day eight months before the scene date, and it was a different house from the one the trustees had used three weeks earlier. WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED IS THE ORDINANCE — carrying fire from one house to another without care or caution, five dollars a breach, in force from 12 November 1834. That is town law and it places nothing. IT ALSO GIVES NO CORNER: all three printings say 'in said town' and no more, so the conflict this record already states between Andreas's north-west corner of Wells and Lake and Heacock's own Lake-and-Franklin advertisement is neither settled nor touched by them.

levels.8-10: A history book calls it a new hotel, kept by Mr. and Mrs. Murphy, named the Exchange Coffee House. A coffee house then was an inn with beds and meals, not a cafe. We once said stage seats were sold here in 1835. But the notice that says so is from August 1836, more than a year after this town. So we fixed that date.

entries.card: why:Andreas gives McKee a log building in this vicinity and give…
entries.text: Andreas gives McKee a log building in this vicinity and gives him no other house anywhere. That the building this record raises is THAT building is the inference, and it is the only candidate the corpus holds for him. His household card carried lives at: null with the note 'those buildings are not in the structures data, so there is nothing to link to'; this record is the thing to link to, and the seat is graded at the inference and not at Andreas's sentence.

levels.8-10: A history book gives McKee a log building near here and no other house. That this building is his is our guess. It is the only one that could be his. So the link is likely, not proven.

entries.card: why:Andreas names both uses in the same passage. The slaughter y…
entries.text: Andreas names both uses in the same passage. The slaughter yard's status at the scene date is doubtful for the reason given on documented range — Newberry and Dole built a South Branch slaughter-house in 1834 — and the yard is in any case not modelled.

levels.8-10: A history book names both uses at once. In 1834 Newberry and Dole built a new place to kill animals for meat. So the old yard may not have been used in 1835. We do not build the yard.

entries.card: why:Andreas says 'a frame building' and no more, and the word do…
entries.text: Andreas says 'a frame building' and no more, and the word does not distinguish the two methods available in Chicago in 1834. Balloon framing was developed here in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method within a few years, so a building raised in 1834 could be either; braced frame is the reading this project takes when a date sits on the cusp, the same argument P. F. W. Peck's Store and the Sauganash carry. The Western Hotel, raised the same year, is read the other way on a source that describes its framing — nothing describes this one's, which is why this is inferred and that one is not.

levels.8-10: A history book says only that it was a frame building. Chicago had two ways to frame a building in 1834. The new light way, the balloon frame, began here in 1832 or 1833. A building of 1834 could be either. So we use the older heavy frame, as we do for other buildings of that time. It is our guess.

entries.card: why:Andreas states the purpose in the same sentence as the const…
entries.text:
Andreas states the purpose in the same sentence as the construction: erected 'for an auction-room'. This is one of the few buildings in this parcel whose use is documented as the reason it was built rather than inferred from its occupant's trade.

THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS PUTS THE ROOM ON DEARBORN STREET AND SHOWS WHAT IT COULD HOLD. Two notices, one week apart, both in the Chicago Democrat. First, the land sale: 'WI]LL be sold at public auction, at [Bates'] Auction Room, Dearborn Street, Chic[ag]o, on the 12th and 13th of June, 50 of [the T]own Lots of Marseilles' — 10 June 1835, page 3 column 3, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-06-10, where the possessive is lost at the column edge. Second, the fair: the first annual Fair of the Ladies of the Protestant Episcopal Church 'to be held at Bates' new auction room, on Thursday, the 18th inst. at half past 7 o'clock P.M.' — 17 June 1835, page 2 column 4, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-06-17, which is what SUPPLIES the possessive the week before. THREE THINGS FOLLOW AND ALL THREE ARE THE PRESS'S, not Andreas's. The street is named, and it agrees with the position block below. The room is NEW in June 1835. And it is the only Chicago interior in this reading range described by two different uses — a two-day land auction and an evening bazaar thirteen days before the scene date — which is the evidence that it was a large clear-span public room and not a shop with a rostrum in it. The Episcopal ladies borrowing an auction room is also, negatively, weak evidence that their congregation had no building of its own; nothing here says it did, and none is placed.

levels.8-10: A history book says it was built to be an auction room. It is one of the few buildings here built for a use we know. Two notices in June 1835 put Bates' auction room on Dearborn Street. One sold fifty town lots there. The other was a church fair held in the new room in the evening. So it was big enough for a crowd.

entries.text: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'. It gives a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, and it is a retrospective of 1884: a YEAR off it is documented, a MONTH is not, and it says nothing whatever about 1835. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “E. H. Mulford,” (f1839 v0080, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Mulford' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins E. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: A history book of 1884 lists people in the town in the fall of 1833. It gives a name, a kind of work and often the year they came. A year from it counts as proof, but a month does not. It says nothing about 1835. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are.

Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $33010.00 to the money. entries.text: BONNELL'S ONE WORD, AND THE ONLY PAINT ANY SOURCE GIVES A DWELLING IN THIS TOWN. J. D. Bonnell, Chicago Times 15 March 1876, quoted by Andreas vol. 1, printed pp. 136-137: 'stood a small yellow house, occupied by Parnick Kelsey as a boarding-house'. The colour is attested; the shade is not, and nothing states one. The house builds in yellow paint (the materials generator): a straw yellow of the kind yellow ochre ground in oil with white lead gives, the cheapest yellow a house painter could buy in these years, held apart from the dealt `ochre` wash so the one stated colour cannot be mistaken for the programme's. The sighting is 26 August 1835, eight weeks after the scene date, so the paint is carried back with the house itself; that carry is the range's inference, not a second one.

levels.8-10: A man wrote in 1876 of a small yellow house where Parnick Kelsey kept a boarding house. It is the only paint color any paper gives a home in this town. The paper says yellow, but not what shade. We use a straw yellow, the cheapest kind a painter could buy then. He saw it in August 1835, eight weeks after this town, so we carry it back.

entries.card: why:BORN AT LYONS, FRANCE, 2 NOVEMBER 1803, AND EDUCATED THERE.…
entries.text: BORN AT LYONS, FRANCE, 2 NOVEMBER 1803, AND EDUCATED THERE. Andreas: 'He left France in June, 1831, reached St. Louis August 1, of the same year, and was there made a subdeacon. He was ordained at St. Mary's the Barrens by Bishop Rosatti in 1832, and on April 6, 1833, was by the same Bishop ordained priest.' He was sent to Chicago because 'Catholics were increasing in numbers in Chicago, and were becoming desirous' of a priest - a petition answered, not a migration chosen. He was succeeded by Father O'Meara only after 1837, so he is the pastor across the whole scene window.

levels.8-10: He was born at Lyons in France on 2 November 1803 and went to school there. A history book says he left France in 1831 and reached St Louis that August. He became a priest on 6 April 1833. He was sent to Chicago because more Catholics lived here and wanted a priest. No new priest came until after 1837. So he was the town's priest all through this time.

THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $66310.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He was born near Lake Killarney in Ireland on 28 September 1808. No one here has a home land we know better. A history book says Dr. William Egan came in the fall of 1833. He served on a health board in 1834 and gave a speech when work on the canal began in 1836. He bought the Tremont House block and built five houses on it, called Egan's Row. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 43 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:BOTH DIMENSIONS ARE ATTESTED AND THE SHAPE IS NOT. Verbatim:…
entries.text: BOTH DIMENSIONS ARE ATTESTED AND THE SHAPE IS NOT. Verbatim: 'they erected thereon a church building, twenty-five by thirty-five feet in size' ("St. Mary's Church." Chicagology. Transcribing A. T. Andreas, History of…, transcribing Andreas). 10.668 x 7.62 m is 35 x 25 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated here per the datum json's data units rule. WHAT IS INFERRED: that the plan was a plain rectangle - no vestibule, no chancel, nothing projecting, which is consistent with a $400 building that was not plastered and had a table for an altar, but is not stated; and WHICH DIMENSION IS THE FRONTAGE. The 35 ft is put on Lake Street here, and that is the weakest link in the record. A church of these proportions would ordinarily have turned its 25 ft gable end to the street with the 35 ft running back, which is the opposite of what is modelled. The frame dwelling archetype builds an eaves-front range only - the ridge always runs parallel to the facade - so a 25 ft frontage would produce a tall narrow roof over a deep range rather than the gable-front church that arrangement actually describes. The orientation is therefore the archetype's, and it is claimed in the liberties register rather than dressed up as a finding.

levels.8-10: A history book says the church was twenty-five by thirty-five feet. So both sizes are proven, but not its shape. We think it was a plain box, with nothing sticking out. That fits a cheap church of $400 with a table for an altar. We also do not know which side faced the street. We put the long side on Lake Street, and that is the weakest part. A church like this would more often face the street with its short end.

entries.card: why:BOTH ENDS ARE ATTESTED, WHICH IS RARE HERE. Andreas, printed…
entries.text: BOTH ENDS ARE ATTESTED, WHICH IS RARE HERE. Andreas, printed p. 635: 'In 1833, the first Tremont House, situated then on the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets, was built by Alanson Sweet.' The end is dated to the day, twice in the same volume: 'was managing it at the time it burned, October 27, 1839' (p. 635) and, in the year-by-year narrative, 'October 27, the most disastrous fire occurred that had ever visited Chicago. It commenced on Lake Street, near Dearborn. The Tremont House and seventeen other buildings were burned.' "Tremont House." Chicagology. Compiling city-directory entries 1846-1870, an…'s 1874 Tribune letter agrees on the year - 'In the fall of 1839, the Tremont House was first consumed by fire.' THE FROM DATE IS A BOUND, NOT A DATE: no source gives a month in 1833, so 1833-01-01 is the earliest day the attested year permits. The scene date sits nearly two years inside the range under any reading of that month, so nothing in this record turns on it - unlike the Steamboat Hotel, where the same kind of bound is the whole risk.

levels.8-10: We know when this building began and ended, and that is rare here. A history book says Alanson Sweet built the first Tremont House in 1833 at Lake and Dearborn. It burned on 27 October 1839, with seventeen other buildings. A letter of 1874 agrees it burned in the fall of 1839. No paper gives the month it was built. But 1835 is well inside these years either way.

entries.card: why:BOTH ENDS ARE READINGS AND NEITHER IS A DATE ANYBODY WROTE.…
entries.text:
BOTH ENDS ARE READINGS AND NEITHER IS A DATE ANYBODY WROTE. The opening: Charles Cleaver, in the Chicago Tribune of 29 October 1893, 'that the first bridge over the South Branch was built in the [winter] of 1832-33'. A winter is not a day, so the range opens on 1 March 1833 — the end of that winter, the earliest date on which the finished bridge certainly stood. The same caution the North Branch record applies to Cleaver applies here and more strongly: he did not reach Chicago until 23 October 1833, so a build date in the winter before his arrival is hearsay reported sixty years later, and it is the only date reached. THE 1883 STATEMENT'S SOUTH BRANCH DATES ARE DELIBERATELY NOT CITED: Statement on the first bridges over the branches of the Chicago River, agreed… records that the two archive.org scans of that footnote DISAGREE on them, and a number two readings cannot agree on is not evidence. The close: 18 August 1835, the last date on which any source reached puts this bridge in use — the procession that crossed it six and a half weeks after the scene date. THAT IS THE RANGE OF THE ATTESTATION AND NOT A CLAIM THAT THE BRIDGE FELL ON 19 AUGUST. Nothing reached says when it was replaced; the North Branch record could close in 1839 because a chronology table says so, and no equivalent table for this crossing was found. Closing on the last attestation rather than guessing forward is the conservative error: a later scene will exclude this bridge and report the exclusion, which is a visible question, where a widened range would be an invisible answer.

THE TOWN'S OWN ORDINANCES CARRY A BRIDGE ON THIS BRANCH FROM ITS FIRST FORTNIGHT TO THE MONTH AFTER THE SCENE DATE. Five readings of the Chicago Democrat, written on THIS block because what they document is that the crossing existed and was maintained, continuously, and not where it stood. (1) The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday…, the village ordinances of 7 November 1833: a fine on 'every person who shall remove from either of the bridges in said town, any plank or any piece of timber belonging thereto'. 'Either' is a two-term word, so the incorporated town had exactly TWO bridges in its first fortnight, and what it forbids men to carry off describes them — plank on timber. (2) the Chicago Democrat of 1833-12-10 records that on 4 December 1833 the Board appointed G. W. Dole, Medore B. Beaubien, Edmund S. Kimberly and John Miller a committee 'to make a contract with some person, for repairing the Bridges on the North and South branches of the Chicago River in said town' — bridges on BOTH branches, inside the town limits, in want of repair eighteen months before the scene date. (3) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-01-07 prints the same ordinance from a different forme, 'building the Bridges on the North and South [branches]'. (4) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-05-14, 14 May 1834: five dollars forfeit from 'any person who shall ride or drive over any bridge within the limits of said town, faster than a walk' — a decked crossing carrying ridden and driven traffic, legislated for by the corporation and attested by its clerk. (5) the Chicago Democrat of 1835-08-19, seven weeks after the scene date: 'No person shall ride or drive on the side walk of the bridges in said town, but shall walk', at five dollars, five times the penalty for riding along an ordinary sidewalk — so the town's bridges had a footway a horse was kept off. WHAT THEY DO NOT SUPPLY IS WHICH BRIDGE. Every one of the five says 'the bridges' or 'any bridge'; none names this crossing apart from the other. They are read onto both bridge records on the identification those records already make from other evidence, and this note adds no position, no span and no date to either.

levels.8-10: Neither date for this bridge was written down by anyone. A man wrote in 1893 that the first bridge over the South Branch was built in the winter of 1832 to 1833. He did not come to Chicago until October 1833, so he heard this from others. So we start it at the end of that winter. Two copies of another old account give different dates, so we do not use them. The last time any paper puts the bridge in use is 18 August 1835.

entries.card: why:BRICK STACKS, AND THE COLOUR RESTS ON ONE VIEW: the Petford…
entries.text: BRICK STACKS, AND THE COLOUR RESTS ON ONE VIEW: the Petford 1831 watercolour (image 8 of the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18) colours both chimneys brick-red over the white clapboard — the only coloured witness to this building — and the engraved views draw masonry stacks without being able to say of what. Brick is also the plausible reading on its own terms: a hotel raised in 1831 at the settlement's centre, when brick was reaching Chicago in trade, and no period text describes the stacks either way. A single a modern reconstruction view may drive a material as inferred; the brief's binaries are not yet committed, so the citation is the README until other work lands identifications.

levels.8-10: The chimneys are brick. Only one old picture shows this building in color, a painting of 1831. It colors both chimneys brick red over the white boards. Other prints show stone or brick chimneys but can not say which. Brick also makes sense for a hotel in the town center in 1831. No old writing says either way, so this is likely, not proven.

entries.card: why:Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and beca…
entries.text: Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method. This building predates that by a year, so balloon framing is the LESS likely reading: a braced frame built onto a log core is more probable for 1831. Flagged for correction — the value is retained only until the framing question is researched, and it should probably become braced frame. Do not treat this as settled.

levels.8-10: The light way of framing, the balloon frame, began in Chicago in 1832 or 1833. This building is a year older than that. So a heavy frame built onto a log core is more likely for 1831. We keep this value only until we look into it. It should probably change. Do not take it as settled.

entries.card: why:Beaubien is documented as the owner from 1817 and as the res…
entries.text: Beaubien is documented as the owner from 1817 and as the reservation's claimant in 1835. WHICH BUILDING OF THE HOMESTEAD GROUP HE ACTUALLY SLEPT IN ON THE SCENE DATE IS NOT ATTESTED — Andreas says he built a new residence. Other work stood it as a separate record with NO occupants; other work folded it into this one (§ 4 of the dossier), so this is the group's one dwelling, and the household stays here because it is the only house the scene draws for them — not because any source says which of Andreas's two houses they slept in. Nothing further about the household is stated here; see review required and the research note.

levels.8-10: Papers show Beaubien owned this land from 1817 and claimed it in 1835. But no one says which of the houses here he slept in on 1 July 1835. A history book says he built a new house. We show only one house for the family, so they stay in it. No paper says which of his two houses they used.

entries.card: why:Boards laid horizontally on a stick frame, the archetype's l…
entries.text: Boards laid horizontally on a stick frame, the archetype's light frame, which is the tightest wall this vocabulary can say. Salt that gets wet is salt that is lost, so the one thing a salt house wants is a wall that sheds rain - that is reasoning about the use, not a source, and the fabric itself is invented.

levels.8-10: Boards laid sideways on a wood frame make the tightest wall we can build. Salt that gets wet is lost, so a salt house needs a wall that keeps out rain. That is our reasoning about its use, not a paper. The walls are made up.

entries.card: why:Both halves are documented in the same sentence - 'the upper…
entries.text:
Both halves are documented in the same sentence - 'the upper story for school, the lower for religious purposes' - and both are corroborated from the other direction. Worship: 'With the exception of Rev. Jesse Walker's log house at the Point, this was the first house built for religious worship in Chicago', which also cross-checks this project's Walker Meeting House record. School: Andreas has Grenville T. Sproat opening his English and Classical School for Boys here on 17 December 1833 and it is operating in 1835 (the research notes on structures south sections 5 and 9). Sproat is NOT on the Baptist transcription, which is why both sources are cited and neither is stretched.

THE BAPTIST MEETING HOUSE IS NAMED IN THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS AND IS STILL A PUBLIC ROOM. School District No. 2's electors were called to meet 'at the Bapti[s]t Me[et]ing House' on Saturday 11 July 1835, to fill the offices of trustee, collector and clerk left vacant by their holders' removal from the district: the Chicago American of 4 July 1835, page 3 column 6, claim the Chicago American of 1835-07-04, signed Hans Crocker; and the Chicago Democrat of 8 July 1835, page 3 column 2, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-07-08 — the last dated use of the building this corpus reaches. THE AMERICAN'S PRINTING IS WHAT NAMES THE DENOMINATION. The Democrat of 27 June sets the same notice with it destroyed — 'at th[e … Meet]ing House' — and that reading declined to identify the building; the American's sets 'the Baptist Meeting House' whole, and the two together are what make this the Baptist house. TWO DISTRICTS, TWO MEETING HOUSES, ONE FORTNIGHT: District No. 2 meets here and District No. 4 meets in the Presbyterian church (see First Presbyterian Church). They are different buildings and different districts, which is a distinction a reconstruction can get wrong in exactly one way. Ten days after the scene date, it is also the reason the 1835-12-31 end of the documented range above is a housekeeping bound and not a fate.

A THIRD CONGREGATION WORSHIPPED HERE, ONCE, AND THE DATE IS PRINTED. Moses and Kirkland, vol. 2, printed page 348 (the text file's lines 40613-40622): 'The next Sunday (October 19, 1834), Rev. Isaac W. Hallam conducted services in the Episcopal form in the First Baptist church, the pastor of which had emulated the example of charity set by Mr. Porter' - Porter being the Presbyterian minister who had lent his own pulpit to an Episcopal clergyman the Sunday before. So the first Episcopal service Hallam held in Chicago was held in this room, on a Sunday nine months before the scene date. It is a USE and not a tenancy: the same page goes on to say that 'later' the Episcopalians met in a building at Kinzie and State fitted up at John H. Kinzie's expense, so nothing here makes the Episcopal congregation a keeper of this building on 1 July 1835, and the Keepers row does not name it.

levels.8-10: One old line gives both uses. The upper floor was for school and the lower for church. Other papers back up each one. Apart from Jesse Walker's log house, this was the first house built for church in Chicago. A history book says Grenville Sproat opened a school for boys here in December 1833. It still ran in 1835. A paper of 4 July 1835 called voters to meet at the Baptist Meeting House. So it was still a room for all.

entries.card: why:Both men are named for this yard's establishment. WHETHER EI…
entries.text: Both men are named for this yard's establishment. WHETHER EITHER WAS STILL ON THIS GROUND ON 1 JULY 1835 IS NOT ATTESTED and the building record says so; Andreas later has a Daniel Elston running the largest of the city's five brickyards by 1854, which is two decades past the scene. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR works at AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW the brickyard household#works at, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start

levels.8-10: Both men are named as starting this brickyard. No paper says either was still here on 1 July 1835. A history book says a Daniel Elston ran the biggest of the city's five brickyards by 1854. That is twenty years later. We copied this work link from the family's own record and changed nothing. It does not say when it began or ended.

entries.card: why:Both retrospective depictions show two. A tavern of this siz…
entries.text: Both retrospective depictions show two. A tavern of this size needed multiple fireplaces. Not attested by a period source; the number is inference. The stacks' material is carried by chimney material since other work.

levels.8-10: Two old pictures, both made later, show two chimneys. A tavern this size needed more than one fireplace. No paper of the time says so, so the number is our guess.

entries.card: why:Both sources have him building and operating the house, and…
entries.text: Both sources have him building and operating the house, and he came to Chicago about 1833, so he is present at the scene date on either build date this project holds for the Western. Andreas's later city rosters carry a William H. Stow as an alderman in 1839, which corroborates the man's continuing residence and says nothing about 1835. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — A DATE OF DEATH, AND NOTHING ABOUT 1835. John Wentworth's roll of old settlers who had died since 1 January 1881, kept for the Calumet Club and printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 April 1882, carries “William H. stow, Aug. 18, 1881.”. That corroborates a Chicago residence before 1840 and fixes the END of this life, which this record did not carry; it is not an arrival and it places nobody in the town on 1 July 1835. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “William 1 1. Stow” as alderman (f1839 r0015, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Stow' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins W. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Wm. H. Stow” (33S7-9YYJ-9HY, printed page 225, line 20). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (“Sauganash Hotel: the pre-1830 position is not represented” matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: Both papers say he built and ran this house, and he came to Chicago about 1833. So he was here in 1835, whichever build date is right. A history book lists a William H. Stow on the city council in 1839. That shows he stayed, but says nothing about 1835. In 1882 a list was printed of old settlers who had died. It gives the day this person died. That backs up that they lived in Chicago before 1840. It says nothing about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. We judged it is this same person. But 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:Both sources name the building by its function and neither d…
entries.text: Both sources name the building by its function and neither describes what happened inside it in a way this record repeats. WHAT THIS RECORD DOES NOT DO, and the reason it is flagged review required: the events the sources attach to this building — the treaty council of 1833 and the gathering of 18 August 1835 — are the removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago, which the project's rules places under a standing constraint. Nothing in this dataset depicts, stages or narrates them, and the scene date is six and a half weeks before the second. What is modelled is a log building on a bank.

levels.8-10: Both papers name this building by what it was for. Neither tells what happened inside it in a way we repeat here. The events tied to it are the treaty meeting of 1833 and the gathering of 18 August 1835. Those were the forced removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago. Our rules say we do not show, act out or tell those events in this town. So this card needs a careful look. What we build is only a log building on a river bank.

entries.card: why:Braunhold/Andreas 1884 draws horizontal wall courses on the…
entries.text: Braunhold/Andreas 1884 draws horizontal wall courses on the exposed annex gable rather than roof covering. The existing bearing and source-facing diagnostic view assign that end to local +x; the picture does not set a geographic coordinate. The unchanged existing Hogan production option replaces only the exposed roof-material cap triangle with horizontal neutral timber courses. Actual native three-control trial and direct visual review accepted the material-category correction; roof slopes, hidden end, footprint, eaves, openings, stack and hotel stay unchanged. The 0.20 m rhythm, 8 mm joints, 12 mm relief and neutral timber tone are reconstructed proxies, not measured joinery, authentic paint or a determination between logs and boards. The finish category is inferred; no new scene-date claim is made.

levels.8-10: An old print in a history book of 1884 shows boards laid sideways on the end wall of the side wing, not roof. So we changed that end from roof covering to wood boards. The size of each board, and the wood color, are our guesses. We do not say if they were logs or boards.

entries.card: why:Braunhold/Andreas 1884 shows one roof-piercing stack close t…
entries.text: Braunhold/Andreas 1884 shows one roof-piercing stack close to the exposed outer gable. The retained building bearing makes that free end local +x. Reconstructed station 0.94 replaces 0.80, shifting the stack 0.85344 m along the retained 6.096 m ridge toward the free end. Actual finite native trial and direct source comparison accepted this visible improvement; shaft width, head height, count and brick treatment stay unchanged. The approximate remaining 0.15 m cap-top/camera discrepancy is within other work tolerance and does not justify another detail fit. No historic stack measurement, coordinate or unchanged July 1835 state is claimed.

levels.8-10: An old print in a history book of 1884 shows one chimney near the open end of the roof. So we moved the chimney a little toward that end. We tried it and it looked closer to the print. We do not claim to know where the chimney really stood.

entries.card: why:Built for worship and in continuous use as the Presbyterian…
entries.text:
Built for worship and in continuous use as the Presbyterian meeting house across the scene window. It was also the town's largest single room, and the project's dossier reports Eliza Chappel's infant school moving into it during 1834 - see the Eliza Chappel's infant school record, where that move is what makes the school's own building's 1835 use unattested. The school claim is carried in the dossier from summaries with no source record in the sources data, so it is stated here as reported rather than cited.

THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS PUTS THE BUILDING IN CIVIC USE, three times in three weeks, and it is the only contemporary attestation of this church the project holds. School District No. 4 called its inhabitants to meet 'in the P[r]e[sby]t[erian] Church' at 6 o'clock on the evening of Tuesday 7 July 1835, to consider measures for building a school house and to elect a trustee. Three printings, one notice: the Chicago Democrat of 17 June 1835, page 3 column 3, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-06-17, signed by Byram King as the district's clerk; the Chicago American of 20 June 1835, page 3 column 6, claim the Chicago American of 1835-06-20; and the Democrat again on 1 July 1835, page 3 column 5, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-07-01, whose right-hand line ends are read out of the adjoining column. WHAT THE PRESS ADDS IS NOT THE CHURCH — Andreas has that — BUT THE USE: on 1835-07-01 this was the room a school district without a building of its own met in, which is what the town's largest single interior was for, and it is dated to the week. THE SCHOOL HOUSE IN THE SAME NOTICE IS A NEGATIVE AND IS NOT BUILT: the district is meeting to CONSIDER building one, so none stood on the scene date, and the three readings are refused on that half in the spend rulings data under the building is not standing at the scene date.

AND THE TOWN'S TRUSTEES SAT IN THIS CHURCH ON 20 SEPTEMBER 1834. The ordinance to prevent fires, printed in the Chicago Democrat of 1 October 1834 as claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-10-01, was passed '[At a meeting] of the President and [Trustees of the town] of Chicago, held at the Pre[sbyterian church in said] town, on the 20th day of [September]' 1834 — a documented use of this building by the corporation nine months before the scene date, and the earliest sitting of the town's government in a church that this corpus carries. WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED IS THE ORDINANCE'S GEOGRAPHY. The same ordinance divides the town into four wards by the centre lines of named streets and by the river; that is town geography the corpus carries and not a licence to cut a boundary, and the reconstruction's street, block and lot layers are derived from the plat and the survey control instead. The column is the worst on its page — the Vision reading lost the left edge of every line and the Tesseract fallback the first two or three characters — so the second ward's western boundary street is left unread in the claim rather than guessed. Nothing on this record is changed.
