entries.card: why:CARDED FROM THE BORDERLINE ROSTER'S R6 (stage `underdocument…
entries.text: CARDED FROM THE BORDERLINE ROSTER'S R6 (stage `underdocumented`, sub-stage church register). Named in St Mary's baptismal register at Chicago in 1833, with the priest's own word for an Indigenous woman written onto her name and onto no other name on the line. No 1835 corroboration and no card. The licence is R3's — a dated appearance inside the window, priced against the persistence model — and the husband and the children named on the same entries the town already carries. The register prints her as `Marianne (sauvage)`, in the mother's place of entry 14 of 1833, at `Chicago, Cook County, Illinois`, in the hand of J. M. I. Saint Cyr, dated 1833-10. NO SURNAME IS INVENTED: the book gives her a forename and the priest's parenthesis and nothing else, and her husband's surname is his. A baptism documents a person at a font on a day. It is not a residence, an address, an occupation or an arrival, and this card asserts none of them. What the dated appearance bounds is that she was at Chicago on that day; what it does not bound is where she slept, whose roof it was, or whether she was still here on 1 July 1835 — that last is what the persistence draw prices and says out loud. The research READ this row and left it `asserted`, handing the kinship on to other work; that ruling is not overturned, and this record is a reconstruction of what the town looks like if the name is admitted at the limit of its own evidence. The reading, the source and the ruling stand at church:the st marys bapt 1833 14 3 mother#0 data in the 1835 borderline roster data. REVIEW REQUIRED: this card is a record of a Native woman at Chicago in the three years of the removal. The flag retains that reason for care; the owner lifted its release block on 2026-10-16.

levels.8-10: St Mary's church book of 1833 names this woman. She was the mother at a baptism. The priest wrote his word for a Native woman next to her name, and to no other name there. No paper of 1835 backs her up. The book prints her as Marianne, with that word. Her husband and children on the same lines are already in this town. We make up no last name for her. The book gives only her first name and the priest's word. A baptism shows a person was at the church on one day. It is not where she lived, her work, or when she came. We can not say if she was still here on 1 July 1835. This card shows the town as it would be if we let her name in. This card is about a Native woman at Chicago in the three years when Native people were forced out. We take extra care with it. The owner of this project said on 16 October 2026 that it may be shown.

entries.card: why:CARRIED WITH ITS PARENT 2026-09-06 UNDER other work: the hom…
entries.text:
CARRIED WITH ITS PARENT 2026-09-06 UNDER other work: the homestead moved about 47 m north-east from the south-west corner of South Water and Michigan to the north-east, and this record's method is literally 'the homestead's easting, 16.3 m south of its origin', so it moves with it or the method stops being true. The offset, the direction and the bearing are unchanged; only the parent point is. Other work's argument is in Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Homestead's position.note and is not repeated here.

PLACED BY EYE INSIDE A GROUP, WHICH IS THE HONEST DESCRIPTION OF IT. NOTHING LOCATES THIS BUILDING. Andreas says only that it was 'the old cabin' Beaubien had lived in before he bought the Dean house, and the sentence immediately before it puts an earlier cabin 'on the south side of the river, not far from Beaubien's place' — a locator that names a river bank and nothing finer. METHOD: this coordinate shares the homestead record's easting and stands 16.3 m south of its origin, so the barn's north face is about 11 m behind the house's south wall, in the position a farmyard building takes behind a dwelling. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE BOTH INVENTED; south was chosen because the homestead record faces its building north toward the river, so the yard is behind it.

THE CONTRADICTION THIS RECORD USED TO INHERIT IS RESOLVED, AND IT RESOLVED THIS RECORD'S WAY. The 1839 sale passage (scan p. 339) puts 'Beaubien's house, out-buildings, and garden' together on Lots 6 to 10 of Block 5, on the EAST side of Michigan Avenue between South Water Street and the reserved lots, and this note used to observe that those lots sit on the opposite side of the avenue from the corner the parent had adopted off scan p. 185. Other work read both pages directly: p. 339 is John Wentworth's 1881 address reprinted and is expressly about finding this house, and p. 185's own second clause names the same 1839 sale — so the east side wins and the parent moved to it. The 45 m 'contested corner' term is therefore GONE from the uncertainty below rather than merely inherited.

THE CAVEAT THAT DOES TRAVEL WITH THE PARENT, UNCHANGED: neither street existed on the reservation in 1835 — it was unplatted and no street crossed it — so both books are locating an old building by a grid that arrived with the 1839 plat. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for placing an undescribed building beside a building located by a retrospective address, plus the parent's own unmeasured northward offset (Wentworth's lots 6-10 lie north of the corner lot, so the group's true position is at the corner or north of it). Facade bearing 0, north toward the house, inherited from the parent record and attested nowhere. MEASURED 2026-10-03 UNDER other work: this footprint stands 13.8 m from the fort road centreline, 7.8 m outside its 12 m corridor, and was left where it is. The piece of work's fault was the two records other work placed 17.9 m east of this pair, on the road itself; this one was already behind the house and off the road, and moving it would only swap one invented place for another.

levels.8-10: When we moved the Beaubien home 47 m in September 2026, this barn moved with it. It is set by the home's place, so it must follow. Nothing places this building. A history book says only that it was the old cabin Beaubien lived in before he bought the Dean house. So we put it by eye, 16 m south of the house, where a farm building would stand.

entries.card: why:CHAINS, FROM THE PLATES, AND THE THREE READINGS OF THE TEXTS…
entries.text: CHAINS, FROM THE PLATES, AND THE THREE READINGS OF THE TEXTS STILL ALL STAND. This attribute read `false` from 2026-08-11 to 2026-08-21 and the note it carried then was right about the texts and is kept in substance below, because nothing in them has changed. WHAT CHANGED IS THAT THIS PROJECT NOW HOLDS PICTURES. The owner's brief of 2026-08-18 supplies two engravings of this crossing (the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18, images 2 and 3) and both draw chains falling from the frames to the draw. ONE OF THE TWO IS NOW A SOURCE RECORD: other work identified image 3 on 2026-08-22 as the wood engraving 'Old Dearborn Street (Old Point) Bridge', signed BAKER-CO, and this row cites it as "Old Dearborn Street (Old Point) Bridge" — wood engraving, lettered in a panel…; the plate was retrieved and read, and the chains falling from the frame heads to the draw are on it. Image 2, the closer view, is a different plate and is still unidentified - see the identification table in the brief's README - so the phrase 'both engravings' above rests on one citation and one committed path. Those are a modern reconstruction PICTORIAL views — retrospective, drawn decades after 1835 — and the standing rule for one is that it may drive form as `inferred` and may never drive a coordinate. So the tag on this row is `inferred` and what it is inferred from is a picture, which is a weaker thing than the `attested` rows above it and a stronger thing than the silence it replaces. THE HONEST CAVEAT, STATED FIRST BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE A READER SHOULD CARRY: an engraver working in the 1880s had this project's problem and fewer scruples, and the chain he drew may be the 1834 bridge's or may be borrowed from a later one — the same contamination that put the words 'double-leaf' and 'chains' into every modern retelling from the 1890s bascule. That is why the mesh's chain is built and labelled rather than argued into the texts. THE TEXTS, UNCHANGED. Andreas gives 'gallows pattern', the frames 'one at either end', the draw 'hoisted', and the frames holding it 'suspended in mid-air'. Neither he nor the chicagology page transcribing him contains the word chain, rope, windlass or leaf about THIS bridge; on that page 'leaves' and 'double-leaf' belong only to the 1890s bascule and the 1907 and 1963 bridges. THREE READINGS STILL FIT EVERY WORD — one leaf hinged at one end and hoisted from both frames; two leaves, each hoisted by the frame at its own end; or the whole sixty-foot section lifted bodily between the two frames — and the texts do not choose. The plates do, and form.draw leaves is where that choice is recorded and tagged. WHAT IS BUILT: one chain each side of the deck at each frame, running from the underside of the head timber down to the free end of that frame's leaf at the centre of the opening, outboard of the deck edge so nothing crosses the footway. Straight rather than slack, drawn as a run rather than as links. The count, the section, the anchorage and the taut line are the archetype's and are recorded in the liberties register “The Dearborn drawbridge, built to its engravings: the frames' bracing, the hoist chains, a two-leaf draw and a railed deck”. THE DRAW IS STILL BUILT CLOSED. No leaf is raised, because that is the one thing neither text nor plate settles for a particular moment, and a raised leaf would put a guess in the most conspicuous position on the bridge. CURRENT EVIDENCE REPAIR — other work, 2026-10-29. The preceding Baker-Co citation describes the historical route by which the chain representation entered the project. Its source remains check required and is retained for textual history and comparison only. The active pictorial evidence for this selected model is now the independently verified public-domain Andreas 1884 volume 1, page 631 plate by L. Braunhold. That actually read plate also shows chains between the gallows heads and the closed draw. It independently supports the same qualitative inference; no existing timber, chain count, section, reconstructed mechanism or per-attribute confidence is promoted. New geometry and native comparisons use this cleared plate, with the sixteen-foot deck width separately inferred from Moses and Kirkland’s 1895 text. No new asset or camera is derived from the Baker-Co reproduction, and no claim that its publication, reproduction licence or copyright status has been resolved follows.

levels.8-10: The bridge has chains, from the old pictures. From 11 to 21 August 2026 we said it had none, since no old writing named them. Then the owner of this project gave us two old prints of this bridge. Both draw chains running from the frames down to the moving part. One print is now known: a wood print called Old Dearborn Street Bridge. We read it, and the chains are there. The other print is still not known.

entries.text: CONJECTURAL, AND ONLY THE STREET IS EVIDENCE. The point recorded here is at the west end of the Wells-to-LaSalle block, on the south side, and NOTHING SUPPORTS THAT CHOICE OF BLOCK — it is a lot on the right street with room on it, which is a rendering decision and not a finding. THE ALONG-STREET UNCERTAINTY IS THE WHOLE STREET, about 630 m from Market to State. THE SIDE OF THE STREET IS REASONED: the north side of South Water was the river bank, wharves and landings (the research notes on structures south § 12), so a store is on the south side. METHOD, for the cross-street position only: the modern West Upper Wacker Drive centreline was interpolated between the intersection centres at North Wells (EPSG:26916 E 447402.5, N 4637411.6) and North LaSalle (E 447525.2, N 4637408.1), read from OpenStreetMap 2026-08-11, and the south kerb taken 12.2 m south of it as half an 80 ft platted street. Working uncertainty about 20 m across the street from the georeference (the datum data, 17.5 m RMS) and the length of the street along it. Facade bearing 0, north onto South Water, inferred from the street rather than from any statement. RECONCILED WITH THE COMMITTED PLAT 2026-08-27, AND THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE — ONLY THE LINE IT WAS DERIVED AGAINST. The method above set this footprint's north face on the South Water frontage, and it found that frontage by taking the MODERN West Wacker Drive centreline out of OpenStreetMap and stepping 12.2 m south of it. That is not this project's own South Water Street: the committed centreline in the 1835 streets data, offset by half the committed 80 ft corridor, is what the plat lots generator builds every platted block edge from, and it is the line every derived layer in this scene reads. Measured against it, this record's north wall stood 8.17 m OUT PAST the block 19 frontage line, in the platted roadway — far enough into it that the frontage works generator refused the plank sidewalk along this stretch of South Water in writing and named this building in the refusal. THE REPAIR IS THIS RECORD'S OWN METHOD RUN AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S OWN LINE: the footprint is translated 9.67 m along the face's inward normal — dE +0.079 m, dN -9.671 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447420.0 N 4637391.3 becomes E 447420.079 N 4637381.629 — which leaves its north wall 1.50 m back from the committed frontage line, the same margin the block infill generator gives every reconstructed unit standing on this face, and the same repair the six reconciled under other work carry. WHY IT TOOK A SECOND RUN, AND WHOSE DECISION IT WAS. Other work measured this exact translation and REFUSED to apply it, for a reason that was real: reconciled onto the plat this building SEATS on lot 0 of block 19, and that lot is one the 665-roof schedule had already dealt to the anonymous South Water frontage run, which the block infill generator refused — one principal roof to a lot. Nothing overlapped; the worst overlap between any of the eleven South Water placements and any committed footprint in the town is zero. What refused this repair was a RULE about entitlement, not the ground. THE OWNER RULED ON 2026-08-27 that a platted business-front lot may carry a documented store at the street AND an anonymous dwelling behind it, on the reasoning that the geometry already permits it and the alternative pays eight roofs and two households for a rule the corrected data had itself called into question. levels.8-10: This spot is a guess on top of a guess. A history book says only that Thomas sold from two doors from the American office. And the American office's own spot is a guess, near the drawbridge on Water Street. So no paper backs this point. Here is the math, so it can be fixed. The book says South Water Street lots were 55 feet wide. So two doors is about 110 feet, or 33.5 m. We put it 33.5 m east of the American office. Two doors west would cross Dearborn Street, and two doors means the same block. So east is the only way that fits. But that rests on our guess of which side of Dearborn the office stood. Our first spot for this building was measured from a modern street, not from our own street of 1835. Against our own street, its front wall stood 6.25 m out in the road, so the plank walk could not pass it. So we moved it back. What we claim about it did not change, only the line we measured from. We moved this building 7.75 m so its north wall stands 1.50 m back from the street line. Our other made-up buildings on this street stand the same way. Nothing moved along the street. Fixing a point with better lines is not new proof, so how sure we are stays the same. At first we did not make this move. On our plan the store would sit on a lot already given to a made-up house, and our rule allowed one main roof to a lot. On 27 August 2026 the owner of this project ruled that a shop lot may hold a real store at the street and a made-up home behind it. So the move was made, and no house or family left the town. One small thing is still off. The front is turned a tiny bit from the line of the street, so one corner sits a little farther back. We leave it, since turning a real building would be a new claim.

entries.card: why:COUNTED INDIRECTLY AND NOT NAMED. Andreas: he removed in 183…
entries.text: COUNTED INDIRECTLY AND NOT NAMED. Andreas: he removed in 1834 'that his children might be nearer school', into a house on the east bank of the South Branch a little south of Randolph Street; in the spring of 1835 he built a house on what he supposed was his lot and 'Here his fifth son and youngest child was born'; and in the cholera of 1849 'he fled with his family to a farm he owned at Summit, where he himself, his wife, and two sons were attacked, and died in quick succession'. So the household on 1 July 1835 contains a wife and at least five sons. THE SOURCE COUNTS THEM AND NAMES NONE, so they are one placeholder entry and not seven invented people. Do not count this entry as a person.

levels.8-10: We count these people but can not name them. A history book says he moved in 1834 so his children could be nearer school. In spring 1835 he built a house, and his fifth son was born there. In 1849 he and his wife and two sons died of cholera. So in July 1835 his home held a wife and at least five sons. The book names none of them. So they are one stand-in, not seven made-up people. Do not count it as a person.

entries.card: why:CURRENT CLOSED-SHOULDER WORKING READING: Andreas's detailed…
entries.text:
CURRENT CLOSED-SHOULDER WORKING READING: Andreas's detailed retrospective engraving supplies a closed clapboard shoulder with a lower sash and small front-gable light, followed by a low connector and farther turned gabled range. The existing shoulder enclosed option is now true. Trowbridge/Gale's captioned1835 drawing instead shows an open post-and-roof wagon bay. That remains explicit counterevidence, not a demonstrated conversion year; the current choice is an evidence-bounded reconstruction of the July1835 scene. The independently drawn open shed/posts and its covered wagon are declined together by the yard source owner while this same canonical attribute is true, rather than drawn inside the closed shoulder.

 Every metric span, hidden depth, height, slope, opening station/section, local placement, plan turn, timber and colour choice remains exactly the existing reconstructed group. No new number, measured plan, surveyed coordinate, historical interior, occupant or extra lodging capacity is inferred. The main footprint and world placement are unchanged. The actual fixed-camera comparison now includes the closed wall, sash and dormer; left-cluster roof silhouette and relative proportions still differ. Original other work remains open/differs. The earlier open-bay model rationale is preserved verbatim in the research notes on green tree annex other work/the project's notes on previous open reading 20261103.

 SHOULDER DORMER CAP, 2026-11-04: front gable peak (m) is raised 4.50 to 4.85 m so the little front-gable light over the closed shoulder reads as the sharply pointed cap Andreas draws, rather than the blunt, nearly flat cap the 4.50 m value produced. Against the builder's existing 4.20 m dormer head and its 0.625 m roof half-span that turns the cap from about 25.6 to about 46.1 degrees. 4.85 m is a RECONSTRUCTED working control chosen for the drawn triangular shape; it is not a measurement off the retrospective plate, which carries no scale, dimension or camera, and it dates nothing. Nothing else moves: the peak stays below the unchanged 5.0 m main-wall head, and the dormer plan extent, the light, the lower sash, the connector, the turned range, the main block, the footprint and the world placement are untouched. The shoulder roof silhouette and the left group's relative proportions remain OPEN on other work.

 SHOULDER ROOF RISE TRIAL, 2026-11-09: the existing roof high (m) working control rises from 4.0 to 4.6 m at the main-block attachment, retaining the outer roof low (m) 3.2 m. Across the unchanged 3.6 m shoulder span this steepens the shed from about 12.5 to 21.3 degrees, following the stronger rise toward the main wall visible behind the little pointed light in Andreas. These are RECONSTRUCTED trial controls for relative form, not dimensions measured from the retrospective drawing, and establish no historical alteration or July-1835 stage. The accepted 4.85 m pointed cap, its light and lower sash, the 2.8 m shoulder wall, all three component spans/depths/occupied polygons and their turn, the main building and its surveyed placement remain unchanged. Existing source disagreement with Trowbridge’s open bay remains explicit. The actual new native mesh, unchanged-camera comparison and published compound review are still required; original other work remains open and the broader left-group proportions are not signed off by this one slope trial.

other work WHOLE LEFT GROUP, 2026-11-10: rereading the actual verified public-domain Andreas and Kurz pictures reveals two distinct far-left gable peaks: the low foreground range and a higher rear gable behind it. The former single constant-height range omitted that visible shape. A bounded rear raised roof section now sits inside the same range envelope, with reconstructed 1.6 m rear depth, 4.5 m wall and 37 degree roof; the front retains its existing 2.6 m wall and 37 degree roof. The existing range depth increases 3.0 to 3.7 m and its front set-out 1.0 to 1.7 m together, retaining the rear corner and 25 degree turn, bringing the low foreground gable forward. The low connector roof now falls away from the main block toward that foreground range, following the pictured link instead of the previous reversed wedge; its working upper edge is 3.0 m and lower edge remains 2.25 m. Existing stock clapboard continues over the shoulder and link upper infill, where the old proxy left a plain patch. Every new metric is RECONSTRUCTED, chosen for bounded relative form rather than measured from a retrospective picture; no historical alteration date, extra room or occupant, site move, new surveyed outline or grade is asserted. Andreas and Kurz may be dependent; Trowbridge’s competing open bay and upper/attic count, Gray’s later side entrance and bilateral additions, and the held c1859 catalogue lead remain explicit counterevidence. Final native/source pictures and actual app review are owed before acceptance; the old partial statements above are historical, not current blockers by themselves. The same original-piece of work whole-picture reading lowers the existing foreground range upper-light sill from3.1 to2.7m, retaining its0.65x0.70m section; this is a reconstructed placement within the low gable, not a measured sash height.

levels.8-10: An old print in a history book shows a closed side wing with boards and windows here. So we build it closed. A drawing labeled 1835 shows an open shed for wagons instead. We keep that as proof against our choice, but we do not know when it changed. So this is a guess. All its sizes stay as they were.

entries.card: why:DELIBERATELY EMPTY, AND NOT PRUYNE'S. P. Pruyne signs the no…
entries.text: DELIBERATELY EMPTY, AND NOT PRUYNE'S. P. Pruyne signs the notice as its VENDOR, so the address is the house he is selling and not the ground his own store stands on — that is other work's ruling, and it is recorded on business p pruyne co vendor placements in the gazetteer data. He is not carried here as occupant, resident or owner. The notice's own words are that possession could be had on the first of the month, i.e. that nobody was in it; who took possession, and who was in it fourteen months later on the scene date, is unattested, and this record leaves the house without a household rather than deal it one.

levels.8-10: This house is left empty on purpose, and it is not Pruyne's. P. Pruyne signs the notice as the man selling it. So it is the house he sold, not where his store stood. The notice says it would be empty from the first of the month. No paper says who moved in, or who lived there on 1 July 1835. So we leave it with no family.

entries.card: why:DERIVED FROM THE ATTESTED INTERIOR, not invented and not mea…
entries.text:
DERIVED FROM THE ATTESTED INTERIOR, not invented and not measured. This is the only footprint in the parcel with a textual basis. The arithmetic, in the original units: guest chambers 'about 12x12' feet, so a depth of two 12 ft ranks plus board partitions gives about 25 ft = 7.62 m; a hall 'divided the house' with the entrance 'about the middle of the long side', so the length is two end blocks either side of a hall of about 8 ft, and each end block must hold a 12 ft room plus partitions, giving about 40 ft = 12.19 m. The bar-room occupied one whole end, which is consistent. WHAT IS ATTESTED IS THE MODULE, NOT THE COUNT: no source gives the building's overall length or width, and a plan with three rooms rather than two on one side would make it about 52 ft. Treat the length as plus or minus about 20 per cent and the depth as firmer. The polygon is the two-storey core only — the 'low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left' that John Gray recalls is NOT included, because its size is unattested and its date is unknown. The c. 1859 photograph ("Green Tree Tavern, Chicago, 1859." Photograph of the Green Tree Tavern at the…) would settle the overall dimensions from the proportions of a known-height building; it has not been seen.

other work: this polygon remains the main block's dimension/coordinate reference. The separately reconstructed left connector and gabled range are described by form.enclosed left annex. Their exact resolved occupied polygons are carried separately to physical consumers; the open wagon bay is not silently filled by a bounding rectangle. This does not add an archival dimension or date to the core. This model-only preparation does not yet qualify additional occupied solids or navigation/ground consumers; the main-body footprint stays unchanged until the separate compound-consumer work is verified.

levels.8-10: This size comes from a written account of the inside, not a guess and not a measure. It is the only one here with words behind it. The guest rooms were about 12 by 12 feet. Two rows of them make the house about 25 feet deep. A hall split the house, with the door in the middle of the long side. So it was about 40 feet long. But no paper gives the whole size. With three rooms on a side it would be about 52 feet. So the length could be off by a fifth.

entries.card: why:DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED GROUND, not authored, and the sit…
entries.text: DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED GROUND, not authored, and the site is the one place on this watercourse where a town could put a log across it. THE CHANNEL: the attested north-side slough is carved into this terrain epoch as north side slough (the terrain spec data watercourses, from hydrology.geojson, Wright 1834). Measured on the committed heightfield at 0.05 m along east-west transects, it is a funnel where it meets the main stem — 68.5 m of open water at N +120, 32.4 m at N +130, 16.2 m at N +140 — and a steady channel above it: 5.0 m at N +157.5, 5.7 m at N +165, 7.7 m at N +190. Between the two, at N +147.5 to +150, sits a sill 2.5 to 4.1 m wide and only 0.18 m deep. SO THE DECK GOES ABOVE THE SILL AND BELOW NOTHING: at N +157.5 the channel is 6.65 m of water below the epoch's 0.00 m surface, running E +185.60 to +192.25, 0.265 m at its deepest, and the ground climbs to +1.10 m at E +178 and E +200. The deck is laid E +183.. +195, N +156.. +159 — twelve metres of span across six and a half of water, landing on ground standing +0.63 m at its west end and +0.73 m at its east, with 2.60 m and 2.75 m of dry abutment seat. That is the proportion its two siblings hold: the Slough Log Bridge spans 8 m over 3.30 m of water on 2.35 m seats, the La Salle Slough Crossing 12 m over 5.55 m on 3.10 m and 3.35 m. WHY IT IS NOT ON THE OLD STREET LINE, which is the only placement decision here. North Water Street's line is itself derived from the committed north bank (the derive north water tool) and stands half a platted street — 12.192 m — north of it. Where the bank swings north into the slough's funnel the street swings with it, so the corridor arrives at this reach at about N +158 and not at the N +130 a straight line down the river would give. A crossing on that straight line would have to span the funnel itself: 20 m of open water 1.54 m deep at N +137.5, and 68.5 m at N +120. That is a river bridge, and the town built two of those, both over branches of the Chicago River and both remembered by name. Nobody remembered one here. So the street goes round the head of the bay, as a bank road does, and crosses where the stream is six metres wide. WHAT IS INVENTED: that a crossing stood here at all, and the bearing. The deck is laid east-west at rotation 0, square across a channel that runs north-south through this reach (the traced centreline bears 010° between N +150 and N +165). WORKING UNCERTAINTY is the trace's own ±20 m, on top of the georeference's 20 m.

levels.8-10: We worked out this crossing from our map of the ground, not by guess. A slough, a wet ditch, ran north from the river. Near the river it was wide, then a shallow spot only a few steps wide, then a narrow channel. A town could only lay a log across it at one place. So the deck goes over the narrow channel, about twelve meters long.

entries.card: why:DERIVED FROM TWO COMMITTED LINES AND THE COMMITTED GROUND BE…
entries.text: DERIVED FROM TWO COMMITTED LINES AND THE COMMITTED GROUND BETWEEN THEM, not authored. The drain is lasalle slough lower in the terrain spec data, whose mouth is the south-shore re-entrant Wright 1834 draws at local E +462..+469; the street is south water in the 1835 streets data, whose committed centreline passes local N +8.11 at this longitude inside a 10.5 m travelled track (N +2.85..+13.35). The crossing is where those meet. WHY IT SITS IN THE TRACK'S SOUTHERN HALF, which is the one placement decision here and it was measured rather than chosen: the river's own traced re-entrant opens northward across this longitude, so on the committed heightfield the water under the corridor is 6.10 m wide at N +3 and 12.90 m wide at N +11. The travelled way a wagon could actually use is therefore the corridor's dry southern part, and a crossing laid on the platted centreline would have to span sixteen metres of a river mouth to reach it. The deck is set at local E +461.5..+473.5 and local N +3.0..+7.27 — twelve metres of span across six metres of water, landing on dry committed ground at every corner and holding 2.65 m of dry abutment seat at the thinnest. THE EAST OFFSET IS THE CHANNEL'S, not a preference: the drain's last reach was re-bent in the same piece of work to clear the platted block's north-west corner (see the terrain spec data and “Terrain: the La Salle slough's inland course and terminus rest on a 1933 reconstruction”), and the deck follows the water it crosses. This is the same argument the Slough Log Bridge's record makes for its own twenty-metre offset from the foot of State Street — the last crossing before a mouth lies a little upstream of it — reached here from a measurement instead of an assumption. WHAT IS INVENTED: the whole of it. No source places a crossing here. The bearing is 0, the deck laid east-west square across the drain, on the same reading as its sibling: the drain runs north into the river at its mouth and the street runs east-west over it. WORKING UNCERTAINTY is the street's and the trace's, about 20 m, on top of the georeference's 20 m; but unlike its sibling this record's uncertainty is not about where a documented thing stood, it is about whether it stood at all.

levels.8-10: We worked out this crossing from two lines we already had, not by guess. One is a slough that drains to the river, and one is South Water Street. The crossing is where they meet. Here the river's mouth opens toward the north, so the north part of the street was in water. Wagons could only use the dry south part. So the crossing sits in the south half of the street.

entries.card: why:DERIVED, AND THE REASON IS A CONTRADICTION IN THE SOURCES RA…
entries.text: DERIVED, AND THE REASON IS A CONTRADICTION IN THE SOURCES RATHER THAN A GAP. The same body of material that puts Walters in the house 1833-1836 also says the house stopped operating as a public house in 1834, and a landlord of a closed house is not a coherent claim. the record of Wolf Point Tavern records the occupancy as inferred for exactly this reason; this household inherits the doubt and does not paper over it.

levels.8-10: We worked this out because the papers do not agree. The same papers that put Walters in the house from 1833 to 1836 also say it stopped being an inn in 1834. A landlord of a closed inn does not make sense. So the tavern's record says his stay is only likely, and this family has the same doubt.

entries.card: why:DISPUTED FOR THE SCENE DATE. Three readings: William Walters…
entries.text: DISPUTED FOR THE SCENE DATE. Three readings: William Walters was landlord 1833-1836, which puts the house in ordinary innkeeping in July 1835 ("The Beginning of Wolf Point in Chicago, Illinois, including the history of the…); the hotel chronology says it 'ceased operations as a public house in 1834' ("A Chronology of Early Chicago Area Hotels." Digital Research Library of…); and a third account has the name changing successively to the Travelers' Home and the Western Stage House after 1834, which is a change of sign rather than of trade. Innkeeping is adopted because two of the three readings are compatible with it and because a stage house is still a public house, but the tag is inferred, not documented. Rates while it was a public house: 12 1/2 cents a night, 13 cents to stable a horse. In 1832 it served as Gen. Winfield Scott's headquarters during the Black Hawk War.

levels.8-10: Papers do not agree about 1835. One says William Walters ran it as an inn from 1833 to 1836. One says it stopped being an inn in 1834. A third says its name changed to the Travelers' Home and then the Western Stage House after 1834. That is a new sign, not a new trade. Two of the three fit an inn, so we use that, but it is a guess. A night there cost 12 1/2 cents, and 13 cents to keep a horse. In 1832 General Winfield Scott used it as his base in the Black Hawk War.

entries.text: DISPUTED, AND THE DISPUTE HAS A NAME ATTACHED TO IT. Two sources call the Green Tree a two-storey frame building outright. Against that, chicagology's Town of Chicago page reports that W. H. Stow — the man who built the Western Hotel two blocks south — 'did claim that the Green Tree was originally of logs and it was not until years afterward that it was covered with weatherboarding and given the appearance of a frame building.' Frame is adopted because it is the reading of both detailed accounts and because the interior the witnesses describe is a framed interior: board partitions, a stair hall, whitewashed plank walls, chambers laid out on a 12 ft module. The log-core claim is one man's recollection, recorded second-hand, about a rival's house, and it is carried in this record as log core so it is not lost. Braced versus balloon is separately unattested: balloon framing appeared in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date.

levels.8-10: Papers do not agree, and we know who says what. Two papers say the Green Tree was a two story frame building. But W. H. Stow, who built a rival hotel nearby, said it was first made of logs and covered with boards years later. We use frame, since both long accounts say so and describe a framed inside. Stow's claim is one man's memory, told by someone else, about a rival. We keep it so it is not lost.

entries.text: DRAWN NOW, ON THE WHARF LAYER, AND EVERY DIMENSION OF IT IS RECONSTRUCTED. What is stated remains the best-attested thing in this record: the dossier's sentence is 'Kinzie & Hunter and Dole & Newberry each had a warehouse WITH ITS DOCK ALONG THE RIVER FRONT' (the research notes on structures north section 3.10) — the dock is part of the one clause that attests this building's existence at all, which makes it stronger evidence than the warehouse's own bank. Nothing anywhere gives its length, width, height or construction. Until 2026-08-18 this attribute declared geometry: 'absent', so the strongest confidence chip in the dataset stood over nothing a visitor could see — exactly the failure the geometry declaration exists to make visible. Other work draws it: the river landings data, generated by the river wharves generator from the traced 1834 bank, this record's own footprint and the committed heightfield, and drawn at load by the walkthrough's wharves code. THE DECLARATION IS NOW 'simplified' AND THAT IS THE EXACT CLAIM: a reconstructed wharf of standard form stands in the place of this attribute, and the attribute's own value — true — is all of it that comes from evidence. Every metre of the outline is invented within stated bounds and claimed at the liberties register “Two river docks, stated in one clause and invented in every dimension”; the deck's HEIGHT is neither invented nor stated but sampled from the terrain at load. NOTE THAT THE BANK IS STILL A COIN FLIP: “Two river warehouses stand on banks that are disputed or unattested, and neither has its dock”'s open question is which side of the river this warehouse stood on, and the wharf inherits the answer this record gives rather than settling it.

Now we draw it along the river bank we traced from the map of 1834.

entries.card: why:Dole is documented as the builder and proprietor. His partne…
entries.text: Dole is documented as the builder and proprietor. His partnership under the style Newberry & Dole is documented separately, but the firm's forwarding house is the partnership's and this record does not attach a Newberry to this building. THE PARTNER'S NAME CORRECTED, other work (2026-09-12): this note read 'his partnership with Oliver Newberry'. Oliver Newberry of Detroit stands in the firm's own advertisement as its Detroit REFERENCE and not as its partner, and the Chicago Newberry of the style is inferred to be Walter L. — the argument is on Newberry & Dole's Forwarding and Commission Warehouse's own `occupants` note and the ruling is declared at the identity data § proprietor distinctions. Nothing about THIS building moves either way: it was Dole's alone before the firm and this record never attached the other partner to it. BY 1834 THIS IS THE FIRM'S STORE, INFERRED. The Chicago Democrat's advertisers place themselves off 'Newberry & Dole's store' on Dearborn Street with a neighbour on each side on that street — Tuttle & Brown 'one door south' (the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-04), Wm. H. Taylor 'a few rods north' (1835 05 20) — W. H. Brown 'one door from' it (1834 05 28), and D. Graves's bakery 'on South Water-street, a few doors north' of it (1834 03 25). That is a store on the Dearborn face south of South Water, which is this building's crossing on Andreas's word; no other committed building fits it. Dole was the Chicago partner of the style, so his 1832 house carrying the firm's store from late 1833 is the plain reading, and the firm's own card of 26 November 1833 says what it sold there: 'DRY GOODS, HARDWARE, CROCKERY, &c.'. The value above is left as Andreas gives it because Andreas is who names the building; the firm is carried here and on the signboard, graded inferred, because the paper names a store and not this house. The firm's forwarding and storage house is Newberry & Dole's Forwarding and Commission Warehouse on South Water, a different building that Peter Cohen places.

levels.8-10: Papers show Dole built and owned this. He was also part of a firm, Newberry and Dole. But the firm's shipping house is a different building. We once wrote that his partner was Oliver Newberry. That was wrong. Oliver was only named as someone to ask about the firm. The partner was most likely Walter Newberry. This building was Dole's alone, so that does not change it. By 1834 the papers call it Newberry and Dole's store. So we think the firm used it then.

entries.card: why:ELECTED A TRUSTEE OF THE TOWN AT THE SECOND ELECTION, 11 AUG…
entries.text: ELECTED A TRUSTEE OF THE TOWN AT THE SECOND ELECTION, 11 AUGUST 1834 - 'J. H. Kinzie, G. S. Hubbard, E. Goodrich, J. K. Boyer, and John S. C. Hogan were chosen Trustees' - so he is on the board through the municipal year that ends in the scene month. He is also the man whose 1881 correction of the Wau-Bun view of Fort Dearborn supplies four of the constraints this project's fort dossier rests on: that the enclosure ran 'nearly north and south, east and west', that the north picket line stood nowhere more than 80 ft from the water, that the ground at the fort was 'not over eight feet above the River at its lowest stage', and that the north and south gates were on one sight line. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Hubbard, Gurdon S.” (tax 1833 046, line 98); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Hubbard, G. S.” (poll 1834 055, line 224). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Hubbard' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Hubbard, Gurdon S. | 1818, Oct. 1, | Windsor, Vt. | 76 | 243 White St., Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 5 times, as “HUBBARD GURDON S”, “HUBBARD GORDON S”, 1830-09-27 to 1833-10-22: 4 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL19CHIOT, as printed); lot 2 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL19CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL19CHIOT, as printed); lot 8 of block 19 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L8BL19CHIOT, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — BL52 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 2.90 acres stated in all, for $293.00 (ls0239, ls1236, ls1237, ls1238, ls1239). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $133.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HUBBARD GURDON S matches Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard: the forename names Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard of the 5 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Gurdon S. Hubbard” (33S7-9YYJ-W6, printed page 232, line 17). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (“Sauganash Hotel: the pre-1830 position is not represented” matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He was chosen a town leader on 11 August 1834, so he served until the month of this town. In 1881 he also fixed an old picture of Fort Dearborn. His notes give four facts we use for the fort. Its walls ran north and south, east and west. The north wall was never more than 80 feet from the water. The ground was no more than eight feet above the river. And the north and south gates lined up. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. In 1879 a club in Chicago held a party for people who came before 1840. Its list has this man and the year he said he came. He gave that year forty or more years later, so it is his memory, not proof. It does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 5 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. We judged it is this same person. But 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:ELECTED ONE OF THE FIVE FIRST TRUSTEES OF THE TOWN on 10 Aug…
entries.text: ELECTED ONE OF THE FIVE FIRST TRUSTEES OF THE TOWN on 10 August 1833 with 20 of 28 votes, and Andreas notes that he 'being a candidate himself, refrained from voting' - so he is one of only two men in this parcel whose conduct at the poll is recorded. His brother Samuel Miller kept the tavern on the north bank at the forks and is not written as a household here, because Andreas's 1833 roster names him only in passing as 'Samuel, the landlord' and this project's Miller House record has the house 'past its innkeeping days' by the scene date. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. A YEAR off it is documented; a MONTH is not, and neither is anything about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Miller, John” (poll 1833 020, line 41); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Miller, John” (tax 1833 074, line 126); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Miller, John” (poll 1834 072, line 241). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Miller' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “John Miller” as fire warden (f1839 r0033, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Miller' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He was one of the town's first five leaders, chosen on 10 August 1833 with 20 of 28 votes. A history book says he ran for the job and did not vote himself. His brother Samuel Miller kept the tavern on the north bank. We give Samuel no home here, since the book only names him in passing, and his house was no longer an inn by 1835. A history book of 1884 lists people in the town in the fall of 1833. It gives a name, a kind of work and often the year they came. A year from it counts as proof, but a month does not. It says nothing about 1835. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 3 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are.

entries.text: ELECTED ONE OF THE FIVE FIRST TRUSTEES OF THE TOWN on 10 August 1833 with 23 of 28 votes - the third-highest poll. He is the son of Jean Baptiste Beaubien by his first wife Mah-naw-bun-no-quah, an Ottawa woman, which makes him the only person in this parcel who is both a documented office-holder of the incorporated town and a documented member of a Native family. THE RECORD STATES THAT AND STOPS THERE. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Beaubien, Madore” (poll 1834 010, line 179). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Beaubien' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data).

levels.8-10: He was one of the town's first five leaders. He was chosen on 10 August 1833 with 23 of 28 votes. His father was Jean Baptiste Beaubien. His mother, the first wife, was an Ottawa woman. So he is the only one here who held a town job and came from a Native family, by the papers. We say that and no more. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:ELEVEN YEARS, AND THE FIRST OF THEM IS THE SHAKIEST DATE IN…
entries.text: ELEVEN YEARS, AND THE FIRST OF THEM IS THE SHAKIEST DATE IN THIS PARCEL. the research notes on structures north section 3.6 states that Jonas Clybourn arrived with his sons Archibald and Hanley in August 1824 and that the family settled on the north branch, building two log cabins, and tags the whole of it [DOC] — but it names no source for the sentence, and that dossier's own list of sources reached does not include Andreas. A full-text search of Andreas vol. 1 for the phrasing returns nothing, which the source record for Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time warns is not proof of absence: its OCR index is demonstrably lossy and 'not found' is not 'not present'. WHAT ANDREAS DOES SUPPORT is the family's presence and its ground: 'Jonas Clybourne and John K. Clark lived several miles up the North Branch, where now are the North Chicago rolling-mills' (scan p. 215), in a passage listing the county's taxpayers of the 1820s; 'Jonas Clybourne and his son Archibald were the early butchers of Chicago. They furnished the garrison at Fort Dearborn' (scan p. 221); and Archibald's own slaughter-house on that bank from 1827 (scan pp. 1149, 1151), which needs the family to be living there. So the range opens in August 1824 on the dossier's unattributed date and would open within a year or two of it on Andreas's evidence alone. It closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim, not as a fate: Archibald had built himself a larger house by 1829 on what is now Elston Avenue, so at least one of the family had moved out of the cabins before the scene date, and what happened to the cabins themselves is unrecorded.

levels.8-10: This home stood here eleven years, and its first date is the shakiest one here. Our notes say Jonas Clybourn came with his sons in August 1824. They built two log cabins on the North Branch. But the notes name no paper for this. A history book does show the family up the North Branch in the 1820s. It says Jonas and his son were the town's first butchers and sold meat to the fort. So the date is about right. By 1829 his son had built a bigger house. So some of the family had moved out by 1835.

entries.card: why:END CHIMNEYS AT BOTH GABLES. Plate '11' of the owner's 2026-…
entries.text: END CHIMNEYS AT BOTH GABLES. Plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set (committed at the source files for prefire views kevin 2026 08, and its sibling Braunhold view written up as image 6 of the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18) draws one stack at each end of the ridge — a retrospective (a modern reconstruction) view driving massing as inferred. The plates are not yet held as source records, so the citation is a committed path. This replaces the archetype's frontage-fraction arrangement, which on this deeper-than-wide footprint had left both stacks standing OFF the ridge on the roof slopes — the before frame of other work shows it. The COUNT stays the chimneys attribute's own inference; the liberties register “Chimneys are counted in the records and fixed in the archetypes” (the town chimney arrangement) and “The Green Tree's fabric from the plates: bays, end stacks, and the rear ell” say what is invented here.

levels.8-10: There is a chimney at each end of the roof. An old print from the owner of this project shows one stack at each end. Before, our rules put both chimneys off the ridge, on the roof slopes. How many there are is still our guess.

entries.card: why:EVERY OCCUPANT ANY SOURCE NAMES BELONGS TO AN EARLIER YEAR.…
entries.text: EVERY OCCUPANT ANY SOURCE NAMES BELONGS TO AN EARLIER YEAR. Wau-Bun, describing 1831, calls the Miller house 'at this time vacant', Miller having removed towards Michigan City. DRLOIH has the business turned into a store run by P. F. W. Peck after 1832, and this project's own date guards place Peck in 1835 at his frame store at South Water and LaSalle instead. A third account has Miller leaving the field in 1834. The accounts agree that the house stood past its innkeeping days, in store or residential use. None places a person in it on 1 July 1835. the Miller household carries no address for the same reason. So the roof states its use and the gap rather than seating a guess.

levels.8-10: Every person any paper puts in this house is from an earlier year. An old book says it was empty in 1831, after Miller moved away. Another says it became a store run by P. F. W. Peck after 1832, but we put Peck in his own store in 1835. A third says Miller left in 1834. They agree it was no longer an inn. None puts anyone in it on 1 July 1835. So we say what it was used for and leave it empty.

entries.card: why:EVERYTHING ABOUT THIS COORDINATE IS INVENTED EXCEPT THAT THE…
entries.text: EVERYTHING ABOUT THIS COORDINATE IS INVENTED EXCEPT THAT THE BUILDING WAS ON THE RIVER. The dossier's sentence gives the warehouse a dock 'along the river front' and its section on gaps says the bank is unattested; the only argument for the north side is the one the dossier itself offers and tags [CONJ] — 'Given John H. Kinzie's north-side landholdings, a north-bank location is plausible' — and this record takes that reading while keeping the confidence honest. THE ALTERNATIVE IS ENTIRELY LIVE: the south bank was where the town's mercantile frontage was in 1835, this dataset already places seven South Water Street businesses along it, and Andreas puts a Kinzie forwarding and commission store on South Water Street (scan pp. 295, 755) — which this project models separately as J. H. Kinzie's Store and which may or may not be the same concern's town premises. So the bank is a coin flip with a reason. METHOD, such as it is: the building is set on the north bank at local E +103 to +115, about 14 m back from the traced bank line, so the strip between it and the water can carry the dock that is recorded and not built; that is about 90 m east of Miller House on the same bank and clear of it. The point within the north-bank frontage is free choice inside a bank that is itself a guess. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: not expressible as a radius. Treat the whole placement as a proposal. Facade bearing 180, due south onto the river and its dock, which follows the trade and not a source. WHAT WOULD RESOLVE IT: any Chicago Democrat advertisement carrying the firm's address — the paper's advertising columns are exactly where a forwarding house states where to find it — or Andreas at page-image level on the early river trade.

levels.8-10: All of this spot is made up except that the building was on the river. Our notes say the warehouse had a dock along the river front, but not on which bank. We put it on the north bank, since John H. Kinzie owned land there. But the south bank had the town's shops in 1835, and a history book puts a Kinzie store on South Water Street. So which bank is a coin toss. A notice in the paper with the firm's address would settle it.

entries.card: why:FIVE FEET ABOVE THE WATER, FROM A BAND WITH NO CITATION UNDE…
entries.text: FIVE FEET ABOVE THE WATER, FROM A BAND WITH NO CITATION UNDER IT. the research notes on terrain hydrology zone 24 gives '~+4 to +6' ft for the north pier's deck and cites nothing; zone 25 gives the south pier no height at all. So this value is doubly borrowed — the middle of an uncited band, stated of the other pier — and it is recorded inferred for exactly that reason. It is retained because the two piers were built in the same works, in the same seasons, by the same supervisors, to hold the same channel, and because the alternative is having no height for a structure whose whole visible form is a horizontal line above the lake. An error of a foot here is an error of a fifth in the only dimension the eye can check.

levels.8-10: We set the deck five feet above the water, but no paper backs that number. Our notes give four to six feet for the north pier and name no paper. They give the south pier no height. So we used the north pier's middle number. Both piers were built by the same men at the same time, so they were most likely alike. A foot off here changes a lot of how it looks.

entries.card: why:FIVE FEET ABOVE THE WATER, FROM A BAND WITH NO CITATION UNDE…
entries.text: FIVE FEET ABOVE THE WATER, FROM A BAND WITH NO CITATION UNDER IT. the research notes on terrain hydrology zone 24 gives the north pier's deck as '~+4 to +6' ft above the datum water surface, and the dossier cites nothing for it. The value is the middle of that band, and it is recorded inferred rather than documented for exactly that reason: this project could not trace the figure to a source, and the honest state in the meantime is the weaker tag. It is retained rather than replaced because it is the dossier's, because a crib pier's deck sits a course or two above the waterline by the nature of the thing, and because the alternative is having no height at all for a structure whose whole visible form is a horizontal line above the lake. WHAT HANGS ON IT: everything a visitor sees of this pier is the band between the waterline and this number, so an error of a foot is an error of a fifth in the only dimension the eye can check. A period view of the harbour mouth would settle it faster than any document.

levels.8-10: We set the deck five feet above the water, but no paper backs that number. Our notes give four to six feet and name no paper. We used the middle. A pier like this sits a little above the water by its nature. A foot off here changes a lot of how it looks. An old picture of the harbor would settle it.

entries.card: why:FOUR HUNDRED FEET, AN INTERPOLATION BETWEEN TWO YEAR-END FIG…
entries.text: FOUR HUNDRED FEET, AN INTERPOLATION BETWEEN TWO YEAR-END FIGURES, AND THE EARLIER OF THE TWO IS ITSELF DISPUTED. IT IS NOT DOCUMENTED. THE END OF THE ARITHMETIC THAT IS NOT IN DOUBT. Andreas: the south pier 'was extended 500 ft in 1835, total 700 ft' by the close of the season (Andreas I, scan pp. 487 and 489, per the research notes on structures south section 3). THE END THAT IS. Two figures are on the table for where 1835 started. Wikipedia's summary of the harbour works gives the south pier at about 200 ft at the end of 1834. Andreas himself, earlier in the same account, has 400 to 500 ft of the south pier built in the fall of 1833 under Major Bender before he resigned on 31 October 1833 (Andreas I, scan pp. 261 and 487). Those cannot both be true unless the pier lost a third to a half of its length between 1833 and 1835, which nothing reached reports. THE DISPUTE IS RECORDED AND NOT AVERAGED, and it is settled here by Andreas against Andreas rather than by preferring one author. His own 1835 sentence contains the arithmetic: extended 500 ft in 1835 to a total of 700 ft leaves 200 ft standing at the start of the season. That agrees exactly with Wikipedia's end-of-1834 figure, from a source that did not derive it from him. So two independent statements converge on 200 ft and one earlier statement in the same volume disagrees with both — the most likely reading being that the fall-1833 figure describes work attempted or contracted rather than pier standing, or that a first season's cribs did not survive the February 1834 storm that breached the bar. Neither of those is evidenced, and the point of recording the conflict is that it stays open. AVERAGING THE TWO WOULD HAVE BEEN THE WRONG MOVE: 200 and 450 average to 325, a number no source states and no reasoning supports, and it would have hidden a disagreement that is more informative than either figure. HOW 1 JULY WAS PLACED. From 200 ft at the end of 1834 to 700 ft at the end of 1835 is 500 ft in a season. Straight calendar interpolation puts 1 July at 450 ft; a season-weighted reading, because crib work runs roughly April to November, puts perhaps a third of the season's work in the water by then and gives about 365 ft. the research notes on structures south section 3 reaches 'roughly 300-500 ft' independently. Four hundred feet is the middle of that band and sits between the two arithmetics. THE ERROR BAR IS THE BAND: anything from 300 to 500 ft is equally consistent, which is plus or minus 30 m on a 122 m structure — a quarter of its own length, and the reason the footprint is graded on it. WHAT WOULD REPLACE ALL OF THIS: the Chief Engineer's annual report for 1835, or the House Document series.

levels.8-10: We set this pier at about four hundred feet, but that is our guess, not proof. A history book says the pier grew 500 feet in 1835, to 700 feet in all. So it was 200 feet at the start of 1835, and another paper agrees. The same book also says 400 to 500 feet were built in 1833. Both can not be true, and we do not know why. We do not average them. Work on the pier ran from spring to fall, so we guess about 400 feet by 1 July.

entries.card: why:FRAME IS DOCUMENTED THREE TIMES OVER; THE FRAMING SYSTEM IS…
entries.text: FRAME IS DOCUMENTED THREE TIMES OVER; THE FRAMING SYSTEM IS NOT. Andreas, of the first Tremont and its 1840 successor together: 'Both of these structures were of wood and far different in style and cost of construction from the costly edifice which to-day ranks among Chicago's leading hotels.' The 1874 Tribune letter calls it 'an unpretending frame structure'; Chicago Illustrated of January 1866 calls it 'a wooden structure'. What none of them says is whether it was braced or balloon framed. Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date - the same value and the same reasoning as the record of Green Tree Tavern, built the same year. The distinction changes stud rhythm behind the sheathing and is not visible at this level of detail.

levels.8-10: Three papers say this building was wood frame. A history book says both Tremont Houses were wood. A letter of 1874 calls it a plain frame building. None says if it had the heavy frame or the light balloon frame. The balloon frame began here in 1832 or 1833, so either is possible. We use the heavy frame, as for the Green Tree. You can not see the difference from outside.
