entries.card: why:Gale 1902 p51 places John Beach in a house beside the jail,…
entries.text: Gale 1902 p51 places John Beach in a house beside the jail, facing Randolph, and a house is a dwelling. INFERRED and not documented, deliberately: Trowbridge's plate and Gale's recollection are a modern reconstruction pictorial and retrospective sources, and the project's evidence ladder forbids a documented value resting on a modern reconstruction alone, so the use is read off a memoir rather than attested by a period record. Who the household was beyond Beach, when the house went up and came down, where exactly it stood and every dimension of it are reconstruction, recorded on the phase and in the liberties register under “the keeper dwelling and low compound gate”.

levels.8-10: A book of 1902 puts John Beach in a house beside the jail, facing Randolph Street. A house is a home. That rests on an old drawing and a man's memory, not a paper of the time. So it is likely, not proven. Who else lived there, when it was built, where it stood, and its size are our guess.

entries.card: why:Gifford shows three bays on the short gable and five on the…
entries.text: Gifford shows three bays on the short gable and five on the long eaves elevation, a centred ground entrance on each, and shutters. This opt-in scheme puts those counts on the existing 15.24 x 9.14 m rectangle without moving its position, bearing or footprint. Equal stations, 0.85 x 1.35 m sashes, 1.2 x 2.1 m doors, the 3.1/2.35/2.35 m floor divisions and mirrored unseen elevations/entrances are reconstructed. The picture does not identify compass faces; repeating the pictured pair on the unseen pair does not attest four historical entrances. Explicit opt-ins now draw raised landings, the opaque arched panel, plain entry outlines and the roof spar; the app flag layer attaches reconstructed cloth using the explicit phase/date-local flag anchor. Exact proportions, lettering and cloth pose remain open.

levels.8-10: Gifford's drawing shows three windows on the short end and five on the long side. Each has a door in the middle, and shutters. We put those on the building without moving it. The size of each window and door, the floor heights, and the sides we can not see are our guess. The drawing does not show which way is north. So four doors in all is not proven.

entries.card: why:HE CAME TO CHICAGO AND BOUGHT THE CABIN AND CULTIVATED FIELD…
entries.text: HE CAME TO CHICAGO AND BOUGHT THE CABIN AND CULTIVATED FIELD SOUTH OF THE OLD FORT IN 1812, and the house remained his residence until 1839. He was a trader at Milwaukee as early as 1800. He was one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833 and took six votes for trustee. HIS TWO MARRIAGES ARE DOCUMENTED AND THEY ARE WHY THIS HOUSEHOLD IS FLAGGED: he married first Mah-naw-bun-no-quah, an Ottawa woman, the mother of his sons Charles Henry and Madore; and in 1812 he married Josette LaFramboise, daughter of Francois LaFramboise, of an influential French trading family. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Beaubien, J. B.” (poll 1833 003, line 24); Poll list of 1835 — “Beaubien, Col. J. B.” (poll 1835 005, line 290). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Beaubien' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 13 times, as “BEAUBIEN J B”, 1830-09-27 to 1830-09-29: 4 federal land entries — NFR2NEVO sec 29 T39N R14E; NFRNE sec 29 T39N R14E; NWFRPTNW sec 29 T39N R14E; NWFRPTNWVO sec 29 T39N R14E and 9 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 17 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1B17CHIOT, as printed); lot 1 of block 18 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL18CHIOT, as printed); lot 2 of block 17 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2B17CHIOT, as printed); lot 3 of block 36 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL36CHIOT, as printed); lot 4 of block 36 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL36CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 35 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL35CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 16 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7B16CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 17 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL17CHIOT, as printed); lot 8 of block 17 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L8BL17CHIOT, as printed), 425.22 acres stated in all, for $2472.40 (ls0454, ls0455, ls0456, ls0457, ls0959, ls0960, ls0961, ls0962, ls0963, ls0964, ls0965, ls0966, ls0967). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS ILLINOIS, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $346.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: NAMED, NOT UPHELD — AND THE JUDGEMENT IS THE ONE other work MADE, NOT A NEW ONE. It stood as `upheld` while the mechanical forename rule reached Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien on its own and this file only had to confirm it. Other work minted the Catholic town St Mary's baptismal register names, and the layer's Beaubiens went from eight to eighteen; one of the new cards is a Joseph Beaubien, so the reading's J now stands for two of them and R3 — a reading is named onto exactly one or onto none — refuses the proposal the ruling used to adjudicate. A ruling on a refusal is a ruling on nothing, so the SAME finding is recorded in the direction that can carry it: `named`, under the guards this file states — the surname gathered rivals, the forename failed to choose among them, and the ruling names one of those rivals. NOTHING BELOW HAS CHANGED. UPHELD on the initials as the town itself prints them, and on a date only one Beaubien can reach. The town's record of this man does not hold a forename it has to have expanded for it: Andreas's 1833 roster prints 'J. B. Beaubien, merchant' and Fergus 1839 prints 'Beaubien, John B., Michigan ave., bet. Lake and So. Water sts' — J. B. is the form the town used, and the register's BEAUBIEN J B is that form. The layer holds ten Beaubiens and the sale is dated 29 September 1830: this card's arrival is attested at 1812 from Andreas — 'he came to Chicago and bought the cabin and cultivated field south of the old fort in 1812' — and it is the only Beaubien in the layer the record puts at Chicago that early. Four canal rows in section 29 of T39N R14E, two of them the register's own voided duplicates of the other two, carried at 212.61 acres and $1,063.20 net. TWO THINGS THIS DOES NOT DO: it does not touch the Fort Dearborn reservation claim, which this project holds no record of and makes no finding on, and it does not make the 1830 purchase evidence of residence — the Residence column reads ILLINOIS on the voided pair and UNKNOWN on the pair that stood, and neither names a town. AND WHY THE NEW RIVAL IS NOT THE MAN: the register prints BEAUBIEN J B, two initials, and Col. Jean Baptiste is the only candidate of the eighteen whose own middle initial is attested B — the town prints him 'J. B. Beaubien' in Andreas's 1833 roster and 'Beaubien, John B.' in Fergus 1839. Joseph Beaubien's card carries no middle initial at all: it is a person minted from a single baptismal entry, with no forename expansion, no middle name, no date before 1833 and nothing that reaches a tract entered on 29 September 1830. He is a rival the rule must count and not a candidate the record supports, and this ruling does not merge the two cards or say anything about him. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He came to Chicago in 1812 and bought the cabin and field south of the old fort. He lived there until 1839. He traded at Milwaukee by 1800. He was one of twenty-eight voters in August 1833 and got six votes to be a town leader. Papers show he married twice, and that is why this card needs care. His first wife was an Ottawa woman. She was the mother of his sons Charles Henry and Madore. In 1812 he married Josette LaFramboise. Her family were French traders. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 13 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are. The land book's J. B. Beaubien is this man. The town wrote his name J. Beaubien, and so does the land book. The sale was in September 1830. He is the only Beaubien here who was in Chicago that early. This says nothing about his claim to the fort's land. And the 1830 sale is not proof of where he lived. Another Beaubien, Joseph, is not the man. Only this man had the middle letter B. Joseph comes from one baptism and nothing before 1833. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:HE GUIDED THE MEN WHO BROUGHT EASTERN MONEY TO CHICAGO, and…
entries.text: HE GUIDED THE MEN WHO BROUGHT EASTERN MONEY TO CHICAGO, and he commanded its militia. Charles Butler's 1881 letter: preparing to travel from Detroit in the summer of 1833 they 'arranged with a young man, named Gholson Kercheval, who was familiar with the route, having been connected with the Indian agency at Chicago, to accompany us all the way from Detroit to Chicago'. The 1832 militia agreement Andreas prints begins 'we, the undersigned, agree to submit ourselves, for the time being, to Gholson Kercheval, Captain, and George W. Dole and John S. C. Hogan, First and Second Lieutenants, as commanders of the Militia of the town of Chicago, until all apprehension of danger from the Indians may have subsided' and carries about forty signatures. He is trustee for three of the payments in the 1833 treaty's schedule - $800 each for Alexander and Paschal Muller. He was one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833 and died in California. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Kercheval, Gholson” (poll 1833 019, line 40); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kercheval, Gholson” (tax 1833 055, line 107); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Kercheval, Gholson” (poll 1834 062, line 231). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kercheval' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data).

levels.8-10: He led the men who brought money from the east to Chicago, and he led the town guard. entries.card: why:HOW MUCH OF EACH POST IS THE SHARPENED HEAD, AND IT IS OURS…
entries.text: HOW MUCH OF EACH POST IS THE SHARPENED HEAD, AND IT IS OURS - NOTHING REACHED DESCRIBES THE HEAD OF A FORT DEARBORN PICKET. 0.312 m is 8.4 percent of the 3.7 m height and is CUT OUT OF that height rather than added to it, so the wall is not made taller by its own points. WHY THE NUMBER IS THIS NUMBER: one picket width and a bit (0.24 x 1.3), which is the proportion a splitting axe leaves on a post of this section, held under a ceiling of 18 percent of the height so a short picket cannot become a spike. That is a drawing argument and not a claim about 1816 - a flat-topped post reads as a fence rail and a pointed one reads as a stockade, and the sawtooth is what makes a visitor at the north wall see a fort rather than a paddock. THE PLATE SAID TO DRAW THEM POINTED DOES NOT: p4 0 rules the curtain's cap straight to 0.45 px rms over 138 resolved columns while resolving individual pickets at a 10 px pitch on a 43 px wall, so a head of this proportion would have serrated that line by 3.6 px, eight times the residual; p4 1 rules the same flat cap. That refutes 'the plate draws them pointed' without settling the head either way, so the head stays a reconstruction. THIS VALUE WAS A PYTHON EXPRESSION UNTIL other work. It lived in PalisadeParams.picket point (m), where the confidence model could not grade it and the popup could not show it; it is stated here at the grade it earns, at the identical number the expression produced, so no vertex moved when it was declared - the rebaked master is byte-for-byte the file that stood before. The archetype still derives the head for any palisade record that does not state one. the liberties register “The point on a Fort Dearborn picket is ours, and the plate that was said to draw it rules a flat top”.

levels.8-10: The sharp point on top of each post is our guess. Nothing we have describes the top of a Fort Dearborn post. We made the point a bit wider than a post, cut out of the post's height so the wall does not get taller. A flat top looks like a fence, and a pointed top looks like a fort. Someone said an old plan draws them pointed. We checked, and the plan shows a flat top line. That does not settle it either way, so the point stays our guess.

entries.card: why:HUBBARD SAYS TWO STOREYS OF THE FACTOR HOUSE; THIS RECORD SA…
entries.text: HUBBARD SAYS TWO STOREYS OF THE FACTOR HOUSE; THIS RECORD SAYS THEY ARE BLOCK A'S, AND THAT SECOND STEP IS THE INFERENCE. The prose names one building — 'the "Factor House", a two-story, squared-log structure' — and the plate letters that name against three blocks, so which of the three carries the storeys is not on the sheet. A is taken to be it on two grounds stated rather than assumed: the label's first letter stands about 2 m clear of A's north-east end and touches no other block, and A at 20.4 x 7.9 m is the only one of the three a two-storey dwelling-and-store will fit (B is a 16.6 x 5.1 m bar set across it, C is 6.7 x 5.0 m). Neither ground is proof and the grade is `inferred` because of it. THE ALTERNATIVE THE piece of work ALLOWED — 'not determinable, so the storey count is inferred from the type' — would have put ONE storey here on no evidence at all while a witness was sitting on the shelf saying two; taking the witness and writing down exactly how far it had to be carried is the better of the two answers, and this note is that distance.

levels.8-10: Gurdon Hubbard says the Factor House was two floors of squared logs. That it is block A of the three blocks here is our guess. The old plan writes the name across three blocks. Its first letter sits next to block A and no other. And only block A is big enough for a two story home and store. Neither reason is proof, so it is likely. Without Hubbard we would have had to guess one floor with no proof at all.

The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Hogan, John S. C.” (poll 1833 015, line 36); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Hogan, John S. C.” (tax 1833 045, line 97); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Hogan, John S. C.” (poll 1834 054, line 223). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. levels.8-10: He held a town job on the day this town shows, and quit another one the month before. He was one of twelve who voted to make the town in August 1833. The town wanted to borrow $2,000 to clean the streets, and he would not go along. A history book of 1884 lists people in the town in the fall of 1833. It gives a name, a kind of work and often the year they came. A year from it counts as proof, but a month does not. It says nothing about 1835. entries.text:
IN PUBLIC-HOUSE USE ACROSS THE WHOLE SCENE WINDOW AND ATTESTED CONTEMPORANEOUSLY. Andreas counts it among the town's four hotels in the fall of 1833 - 'an unpretentious log tavern kept by Dexter Graves' - and has Markle from 1835 'accommodated and entertained many of Chicago's early residents, and travelers coming this way to take an observation of the town lying in the mud'. THE CONTEMPORARY WITNESS IS THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE IN THIS RECORD and it is not from either source above: the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries 'Blacksmithing Business. MATTHIAS MASON & CO. Carries on the above business in all its various branches, on Main-street, nearly opposite GRAVES' TAVERN' - a paying advertiser using the house as the landmark his customers would find him by, in the town's own newspaper, in its own week. That is recorded here rather than cited on the attribute because the claim it supports is the tavern's existence and standing in November 1833, not its form. THE PROJECT'S DOSSIER ALSO HAS IT 'advertised in 1835 as Cook's Coffee House' (the research notes on structures south line 156, citing Andreas and "A Chronology of Early Chicago Area Hotels." Digital Research Library of…). THAT PHRASE IS NOT IN ANDREAS VOL. 1: a full-text search of the volume for 'Cook's Coffee House' returns nothing, and the Coffee House entries in its index are the Exchange, Lincoln's, the Eagle and the Lake Street. It may still be right and it may be drloih's alone; it is not asserted here.

THE TOWN GOVERNED ITSELF FROM THIS HOUSE, AND THE PAPERS RECORD FIVE SITTINGS IN IT. This record already identifies Dexter Graves's log tavern and Haddock's Mansion House as one building; these readings are written onto that identification and do not make it. (1) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-03-04 and (2) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-04-01 are two printings of one order: 'At a stated meeting of the Board of Trustees for the Town of Chicago, held at the house of Dexter Graves in said Town, on the 5th day of March 1834'. (3) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-18 and (4) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-07-02 are two printings of the next code: 'At a meeting of the Board of Trustees of the town of Chicago, held at the house of E. Haddock, on the 6th June, 1834'. (5) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-12-10 calls the citizens of School District No. 1 to meet 'at the Mansion [House]' on Tuesday 16 December 1834. So across 1834 this house was the seat of the town's government under two keepers' names and then a public meeting room under its own — a documented USE on three named days across five printings, which is what is asserted here. WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED IS THE BUSINESS TRANSACTED IN IT, and it is worth saying loudly: the March order is the South Water Street sidewalk order and the June one the assessment and street code. Both are town LAW, both place nothing, and both are carried as law and not drawn. No position, form or occupant on this record is changed, and the equation of Graves's house with Haddock's is this record's own — being cited five times does not strengthen it.

levels.8-10: This was an inn all through this time, and papers of the time show it. A history book counts it as one of the town's four hotels in 1833, a plain log tavern kept by Dexter Graves. From 1835 Markle kept it for travelers. The best proof is a notice of November 1833. A smith said his shop was nearly opposite Graves' Tavern. Our notes say it was called Cook's Coffee House in 1835, but we can not find that in the book. Papers also show the town leaders met in this house five times.

entries.text: INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATED RESIDENT. Originally documented in Chicago post-office evidence; independent resident research now corroborates the identity. FIRST READ AT THE POST OFFICE, AND THE CORPUS NAMES THEM AGAIN. The papers print 'Chas, Ul. Chapman' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 April 1834, column 1 — dated 1834-04-01. THE CORPUS NAMES THIS PERSON BESIDE THE RETURN: 3 ordinary readings of the papers, not lists of uncalled-for letters — the Democrat of 26 November 1833 (‘Chapman, C. H.’, The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday…); the American of 24 December 1833 (‘C. H. Chapman’, the Chicago American of 1835-06-08); the Democrat of 13 August 1834 (‘Charles H. Chapman’, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-08-13). That is why letter list only is no longer written on this record: the flag says ‘known only from the post office’ and this record says otherwise. The return below still stands, and is still the weakest thing said here. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (the liberties register “Three quarters of this town's people are a name on a post-office list and nothing else”), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (the letter list residents generator). No figure is drawn (“No people, anywhere”). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Chas. H. Chapman” (f1839 v0198, printed page 42, ward 2, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Chapman' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins C. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “CHAPMAN CHARLES H”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-28: 1 lot in the platted town — lot 1 of block 4 in the town the register codes CHI (L1BL4CHI, as printed) and 3 parcels of the school section — lot 3 of block 141 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 96 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 8 of block 93 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $3149.00 (ls0134, ls0135, ls0136, ls1028). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $2900.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: CHAPMAN CHARLES H matches Chas. H. Chapman: the forename names Chas. H. Chapman of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: We are fairly sure of this person. They were first found in post office lists. Now other research backs up who they were. The Democrat printed this name on 1 April 1834, in a list of letters no one had picked up at the post office. The paper also names this person 3 other times, not in a letter list. So they are no longer known only from the post office. The letter list is still the weakest proof here. All this tells us is that someone thought this person could get mail in Chicago then. It does not say they lived here, worked here, or were here on 1 July 1835. This is the weakest proof we take. If a paper puts them somewhere else, we take them out. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 4 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are. No figure is drawn for them.

entries.text: INTERPRETIVE PLACEMENT ON A COMMITTED BLOCK FACE, NOT A RECOVERED LOT. A meat market on the built streets, because a town of 3,265 does not walk three kilometres up the North Branch to Clybourne's for its dinner. This building does not stand where a centre in the programme put it: it stands on the north face of block 35, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in the thompson lots data — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is set 0.80 m back from that lot line, which is the one line every record on this face stands on, and its bearing is the face's own rather than the zero a hand-authored centre carried. What the programme still chooses is where along the face it stands — 68.936 m from the face's west end, the position it already occupied, so this repair moves no building along the street. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, and that it was this trade's. The dataset's 20 m working georeference uncertainty applies on top of an already invented position, and standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot.

entries.text: INTERPRETIVE PLACEMENT ON A COMMITTED BLOCK FACE, NOT A RECOVERED LOT. EIGHT DOCUMENTED DOCTORS AND NOT ONE OFFICE. A physician's office and apothecary's back room on the Lake Street frontage, where a doctor is found by people who need one. It is left unnamed on purpose: four of the eight are documented households in this dataset and attaching any of them to an invented building would turn a hypothesis into a false attribution. This building does not stand where a centre in the programme put it: it stands on the north face of block 34, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in the thompson lots data — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is set 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the one line every record on this face stands on, and its bearing is the face's own rather than the zero a hand-authored centre carried. What the programme still chooses is where along the face it stands — 78.240 m from the face's west end. IT IS NOT the position it already occupied: this building moved along the street, and the paragraph below says what moved it. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, and that it was this trade's. The dataset's 20 m working georeference uncertainty applies on top of an already invented position, and standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot. DISPLACED BY AN ATTESTED PLACEMENT, ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21, AND THE RULE IS GENERAL: where an ATTESTED placement and an INFERRED placement collide on one lot, the attested one stands and the inferred one moves or is withdrawn. First Presbyterian Church is documented at the south-west corner of Lake and Clark and reached the scene off a modern OpenStreetMap kerb, standing 1.90 m out past this block's committed Lake Street frontage line and in the platted roadway; the 3.395 m reconciliation the three Lake Street records beside it took would have set it down 0.243 m from this building, inside the 3.0 m separation gate, and moved 3.2 m the two footprints physically overlap. There is no translation along that normal that both clears the walk and leaves the pair standing apart, which is why the fork was a rule and not a metre. THE CHURCH TAKES THE GROUND AND THIS BUILDING MOVES. It is RE-SEATED RATHER THAN WITHDRAWN, which the ruling asks for first, and it is re-seated on its own evidence: its evidence is a Lake Street frontage-band assignment on the project's roadmap's rule, and it keeps the band, the street, the face and the lot it was dealt - block 34 lot 6 - moving 12.99 m west along that face and 7.40 m forward onto the street line. FORWARD IS ITS OWN CLAUSE'S ANSWER rather than a convenience: the placement policy 1835 tool seats a C1 at street line, and this building had stood 8.90 m back in the depth of its lot since it was raised, which is the clause's own outlier. The 1.50 m setback is this face's own line - what the block infill generator gives every reconstructed unit standing here, and the margin The Old Bank Building, George W. Dole's Warehouse and St. Mary's Catholic Church were reconciled to. WHAT DID NOT HAPPEN: neither footprint was narrowed to make the two fit, which the ruling refuses in terms - a dimension fitted to a neighbour is no longer a reading of anything - and the separation gate was not weakened. Nothing here is upgraded either: the placement is still `reconstructed`, its derivation is still not derivable, and standing clear of an attested building on a derived face is not standing on a recovered lot.

levels.8-10: No paper gives this lot. Papers name eight doctors in town, but no office for any of them. So we made a doctor's office on Lake Street, where people could find one. We give it no name on purpose. Linking a real doctor to a made-up building would be a false claim. It stands on the north side of block 34, 1.50 m back from the lot line, like every building on this side. It moved along the street, as told below. That a building stood here at all, and was a doctor's, is still made up. But the big things are still made up: that a building stood here at all, and that it was for this work. Its place could also be off by about 20 m. A real building pushed it aside. The owner of this project made a rule on 21 September 2026. When a proven building and a guessed one share a lot, the proven one stays. The First Presbyterian Church is proven at the corner of Lake and Clark. Set on our street line, it would have stood too close to this building, or on top of it. So the church takes the ground and this building moves. We moved it, not removed it. It keeps its street and its lot. It moved 13 m west and 7.4 m forward to the street line. Our rules put a shop like this at the street, so forward fits. It now stands 1.50 m back, like the others on this side. We did not shrink either building to make them fit, and we did not loosen the rule on spacing. Nothing here gets a better grade. It is still made up.

The band assignment above puts this building's centre at local ENU E 300 N 260, which stands 12.19 m inside Kinzie Street's platted corridor. Other work read the north bank's platted corridors into the corridor layer on 2026-09-19. Until that day the plat corridors tool returned nothing north of the main stem — one pair of street lists in the plat lots generator decided both which streets a BLOCK may be cut between and which streets a BUILDING may be reported standing in, and the North Division could not have the first, so it was denied the second. This building's own position note said its centre had been tested “against the platted street corridors of the K7 block grid so that no invented building stands in the roadway”; the K7 grid is nineteen South and West Division blocks and no north-bank street, so north of the river that test passed by covering no ground. Nothing moved and nothing was re-fitted: this building has stood on Kinzie Street's centreline since it was raised, and the first thing able to see it was the corridor. An invented placement has nothing to encroach with, so the corridor wins. 0.5 m is other work's margin, kept. The record therefore stands 16.533 m north of its band assignment, at E 300.000 N 276.533 — the LEAST this building can move and still leave its whole footprint 0.50 m clear of the platted kerb on BOTH readings of it, the corridor as drawn and the corridor centred on the street's committed control, measured through the plat corridors tool, which is the same geometry the gate refuses on. The distance is not typed anywhere: re-fit Kinzie Street again and this building moves again, instead of silently disagreeing with it.

The centre was tested against every structure footprint in the dataset, against the reserved slots of the two uninstantiated phase-2 recipes, against the platted street corridors of the K7 block grid so that no invented building stands in the roadway, and against the committed heightfield for coverage, dry ground and step tolerance; it is free ground and nothing more. The dataset's 20 m working georeference uncertainty applies on top of an already invented position.

entries.text: INVENTED METRIC, NOT MEASURED FROM GIFFORD. Total wall height is 7.8 m: the explicit first story height (m) divides it into a working 3.1 m lower storey and two 2.35 m upper storeys. These divisions supersede the earlier equal-2.6 m proposal while retaining its total height. The illustration supplies a visible count but no metric scale. Camera/height coupling remains unresolved, and a calibrated comparison may replace this working height.

levels.8-10: The wall height is our guess, not measured from Gifford's drawing. The walls are 7.8 m high in all. We split that into a ground floor of 3.1 m and two upper floors of 2.35 m. The drawing shows how many floors, but has no scale. A better reading of the drawing could change this.

entries.card: why:INVENTED OUTRIGHT, and the attribute where this record most…
entries.text: INVENTED OUTRIGHT, and the attribute where this record most needs to hold its nerve against a documented number. The two branch bridges stood 'about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice freely' (the 1883 old-settlers statement) — 1.83 m, and utterly wrong for a slough. Nothing passed under this bridge. The hydrology dossier puts the slough's thalweg 1.5 to 3.0 ft below the adjacent plain, so a deck laid at street level sits roughly half a metre over the water: 0.5 m is that reading and it is a reading of a conjectural depth, not of a measurement. Admitted in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: This height is made up. The river bridges stood about six feet above the water, so teams could pass under them on the ice. That would be wrong for a small slough. Nothing passed under this bridge. Our notes say the slough was one or two feet below the ground. So a deck at street height sits about half a meter over the water. That rests on a guessed depth, not a measure.

entries.card: why:INVENTED WITHIN A BOUND, AND IT IS THE ONLY NUMBER ON THIS M…
entries.text: INVENTED WITHIN A BOUND, AND IT IS THE ONLY NUMBER ON THIS MASS THAT IS. How far the wing runs BACK is what one sheet cannot give (the research notes on sauganash image accuracy row 11): from the plate's station the wing stands behind the main block with only its ridge showing, so the drawing carries its height and its direction and not its length. 8.0 m is the owner's own reading of the views — 'almost the same size' as the main block — taken as equal to the block's 8 m depth, which is also the span the shared apex forces on the wing, so the wing comes out square in plan. the liberties register “The Sauganash's second mass: the plate fixes its height and its span, and this fixes how far it runs back” owns the invention. The number was also chosen to leave the fenced rear yard, its Market Street gateway and its three kept trees their room: nothing about that yard is attested either, and a wing sized to fill it would be one guess crowding another.

levels.8-10: How far this wing runs back is our guess, within limits. The old drawing shows the wing behind the main block, with only its roof showing. So it gives the height and the way it runs, but not its length. The owner of this project read the pictures as showing it almost the same size as the main block. So we made it 8 m, the same as the block, which makes it square. That also leaves room for the yard and its trees behind it.

entries.text: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 4.5 in — dealt by the siding stock generator: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety other work reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. the liberties register “Every named frame building's siding stock is dealt, not found” owns the invention.

levels.8-10: No paper tells how much of each side board showed on a Chicago building. We picked one of a few common sizes, 4.5 inches. Near ones get different sizes so the town does not all look the same.

entries.card: why:INVENTED WITHIN AN ATTESTED BLOCK FACE. Andreas gives a stre…
entries.text: INVENTED WITHIN AN ATTESTED BLOCK FACE. Andreas gives a street, two cross streets and, per this project's dossier, the north side - which is a block face about 110 m long and no more. NO SOURCE PLACES THIS HOUSE ON A LOT, so the coordinate is the middle of that face and the confidence says so. METHOD, and the street names have all changed: Michigan Street on the north side is today's Hubbard Street, Cass Street is today's North Wabash Avenue, and Rush Street is unchanged - the equivalences this project's own ground control uses in the wright 1834 gcps data, where GCP G6 is 'Cass St & Illinois St... Cass is today's North Wabash Avenue'. The modern Hubbard Street / North Rush Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 448121.71, N 4637764.21 (OSM node 261149251, fetched 2026-08-11), which fixes both Rush's line and Michigan Street's; Cass/Wabash's line comes from the committed GCP G6 at E 448010.33. The mid-point of the block is E 448066.02; the north frontage line is 12.2 m north of Michigan Street's centre, half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834; the footprint is centred on the block face and its south face set on that frontage. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus about 55 m either way ALONG the block from the mid-block choice, plus an unknown setback. Facade bearing 180, due south onto Michigan Street, inferred from the street rather than from any statement. THIS IS A NORTH-SIDE BUILDING and was well outside the modelled terrain box when this note was written, standing on ground this project had not built. BLOCK 11 IS THE ONE CELL IN THE ADDITION WHOSE NUMERAL WRIGHT'S SHEET DOES NOT CARRY — that file's own reading says 'block 11's missing figure is the one place only the rule speaks' — so the block NUMBER here rests on the boustrophedon run and not on ink, while the cell's BOUNDARY rests on the Addition's measured module as usual. levels.8-10: This house is made up within a known stretch of street. A history book gives the street and two cross streets, and our notes say the north side. That is a block side about 110 m long. entries.card: why:INVENTED WITHIN AN ATTESTED NEIGHBOURHOOD. What Andreas give…
entries.text: INVENTED WITHIN AN ATTESTED NEIGHBOURHOOD. What Andreas gives is 'a log house just outside the military reservation' and nothing more precise. The reservation's western boundary on the south side WAS State Street until the town's February 1835 extension, which is documented, so 'just outside' means immediately west of State; the block between South Water and Lake is this project's dossier's reading of where that puts the school, and the dossier tags the exact lot [CONJ] itself. NO SOURCE PLACES THIS BUILDING ON A LOT, A CORNER OR A BLOCK FACE, so the coordinate is a point chosen inside a two-block-long strip and the confidence says so. METHOD: State Street survives on its plat line; the modern West Lake Street / North State Street centre (EPSG:26916 E 447902.80, N 4637282.51, OSM node 258957342) and the West Wacker Drive / North State Street centre (E 447899.81, N 4637407.66, 4 nodes averaged, spread 21.4 m), both fetched 2026-08-11, give the street's line, and the mid-point between them, E 447901.30 / N 4637345.08, is the middle of the block face. The footprint's east face is set 12.2 m west of that centreline - half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834 - and the building centred on the block face north to south. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus about 60 m either way ALONG State Street from the mid-block choice, plus the possibility that 'just outside the reservation' was read too narrowly and the house stood a lot or two back from the street. Facade bearing 90, due east onto State, a convention rather than a finding. NOTE ALSO that South Water Street's modern successor, Wacker Drive, was built on the old right of way in 1924-26 and widened northward, so the northern of the two control points is the softer one; it is used here only to fix a direction, not a frontage. Other work picture-fit proposal: the new origin is countertranslated by (+1.1875,-3.292) m in the existing footprint frame, equivalent at bearing90 to (-3.292,-1.1875) m ENU. This keeps the existing doorway centre and east-facing front-wall line exactly fixed while the declared reconstructed plan becomes narrower and deeper. These extra arithmetic digits preserve an old model anchor; they add no survey precision or new positional evidence. MOVED BACK ONTO ITS LOT 2026-11-03, on the owner's report of buildings 'placed in the middle of the walkways or alleys': its front wall stood 1.97 m out past the State Street lot line of block 16, on the plank walk's line; moved 3.47 m back so that wall stands 1.50 m inside the lot line. The translation is dE -3.47 m, dN +0.02 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447880.328 N 4637347.5525 becomes E 447876.859 N 4637347.575. NOTHING THE SOURCES SAY MOVED: the corner, side, block or cluster this record is placed by is unchanged, and so is its confidence grade; the coordinate was derived, never read, so it is re-derived against this project's own platted lot line and alley, which the structure clearance check now holds every 1835 building to. The coordinate was already a point chosen inside a two-block strip; 'just outside the military reservation' still holds, a lot's depth west of State.

levels.8-10: This spot is made up within a known area. A history book says only that it was a log house just outside the army's land. The army land's west edge was State Street until early 1835. So just outside means just west of State. Our notes put the school in the block between South Water and Lake, and call the lot a guess. So the spot is a point picked in a strip two blocks long.

entries.card: why:INVENTED WITHIN THE FACE'S OWN NUMBERS. Nothing is attested…
entries.text: INVENTED WITHIN THE FACE'S OWN NUMBERS. Nothing is attested about this building's size. 9.144 x 7.62 m is 30 x 25 ft. THE FRONTAGE is the parcel's small-shop figure, the same 30 ft Frederick Thomas's Shop wears, because 'one door' describes a single front in a row and not a corner block, and because 30 ft is what fits between the American office's east wall and the lot line with both margins kept. THE DEPTH is 25 ft rather than Thomas's 20: Holbrook advertises WHOLESALE AND RETAIL, says he intends to keep a large stock on hand and to receive additions every fifteen or twenty days through the season, and a shop taking fortnightly shipments needs a storeroom behind the counter. 25 ft is The Chicago American Office's own committed depth on this same face, so the number is the block's rather than a new invention. Both figures are borrowed; neither is evidence about this building.

levels.8-10: Its size is our guess. Nothing tells its size. We made it 30 by 25 feet. The front is 30 feet, like the shop of Frederick Thomas, since one door means a single shop front. The depth is 25 feet, a bit more than Thomas's. Holbrook sold in large amounts and got new goods every two or three weeks, so he needed a store room. The American office next door is also 25 feet deep. Both sizes are borrowed, not proof.

entries.card: why:INVENTED — the parcel's borrowed rectangle, 12.192 x 7.62 m…
entries.text: INVENTED — the parcel's borrowed rectangle, 12.192 x 7.62 m = 40 x 25 ft, taken from the Green Tree Tavern's attested frontage and room module because no source gives this building a dimension. The documented cap applies: South Water lots were 55 ft wide, so the frontage cannot have exceeded that. THE ONE FIGURE THAT MUST NOT BE USED IS THE ONE THE SOURCES DO OFFER. Andreas describes a THREE-STOREY building on this corner housing the Daily Chicago American on its third floor — in 1839, four years after the scene date, in a town whose first three-storey structure (the Saloon Building) is 1836 and is already in the exclusions record. Sizing or massing this 1835 record from the 1839 building would import the boom that had not happened yet.

levels.8-10: Its size is made up. We borrowed 40 by 25 feet from the Green Tree Tavern, since no paper gives this building's size. South Water lots were 55 feet wide, so it could not be wider than that. A history book does tell of a three story building on this corner. But that was in 1839, four years later, and the town's first three story building went up in 1836. Using it here would bring in growth that had not happened yet.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND ADDED SO THE BARN READS AS A BARN. Nothing des…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND ADDED SO THE BARN READS AS A BARN. Nothing describes a loft. The owner read this group as log houses, and a converted single-pen cabin with a stable door and no chimney is still close to the house beside it in silhouette; the hay door high in the gable is the one feature a barn has that a house of this size does not. A cabin of this period commonly had a loft under its roof already, so the conversion asks for no rebuilding — but that is a reading of the type, not of this building, and the door's place in the east gable is the archetype's choice.

levels.8-10: We added a hay loft so the barn looks like a barn. Nothing describes a loft. The owner of this project read this group as log houses. A cabin turned into a barn, with a stable door and no chimney, still looks like a house. A hay door high in the end wall is the one thing that makes it a barn. Cabins then often had a loft already. But that is about cabins in general, not this one.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND CHOSEN TO SAY WHAT THE BUILDING IS NOT. No sou…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND CHOSEN TO SAY WHAT THE BUILDING IS NOT. No source describes this roof. Until other work it was a gable at 35 degrees on the log dwelling archetype, with a chimney and a dwelling's windows, and the owner read the group as three identical log houses — which is what three records on one archetype, one pitch and one wall height draw. A single slope is the cheapest roof there is, it is the outbuilding archetype's own default for a building under 5 m deep, and it is the form a store room or shed most often carried; a gable would assert the house's form just as freely. Either is ours.

levels.8-10: This roof is made up, and chosen to show what the building is not. No paper describes it. Before, it had a two slope roof, a chimney and house windows, so the group looked like three of the same log house. A one slope roof is the cheapest there is, and common on a store room or shed. A two slope roof would be just as much a guess. Either one is ours.

entries.text: INVENTED, AND IT IS NOT THE SPAR. No source reached gives the staff a thickness, a step or a stay. This half-metre square is the ground the staff stands on - the archetype's smallest legal plan - and the mast the archetype builds inside it is 0.30 m at the butt tapering to 0.135 m at the truck, which is what a fifty-foot spar has to be to stand up. The whole profile is the archetype's; see the liberties register.

levels.8-10: This is made up, and it is not the pole itself. No paper gives the flag pole's thickness. This small square is the ground it stands on. Our rules make the pole thick at the bottom and thin at the top, as a pole of fifty feet must be to stand.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND IT IS THE ARCHETYPE'S OWN DEFAULT KEPT DELIBER…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND IT IS THE ARCHETYPE'S OWN DEFAULT KEPT DELIBERATELY. Nothing attests a storey count. The frame dwelling module argues that the story-and-a-half - a full storey with chambers in the roof lit from the gable ends over a low knee wall - 'is the characteristic form of these years', and defaults to it for that reason. Taking that default rather than inventing a fresh number is the same discipline the liberties register “The North Branch bridge stands on fifteen piers nobody recorded” records about the bridge's pier spacing: a new figure would look like a finding and would not be one. The knee wall is left at the archetype's default too.

levels.8-10: We kept our rules' usual choice on purpose. Nothing says how many floors it had. Our rules say a floor and a half, with rooms under the roof, was the common form of these years. Using that, not a new number, keeps us from making a guess look like a finding.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND IT IS THE ARCHETYPE'S VOCABULARY RATHER THAN T…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND IT IS THE ARCHETYPE'S VOCABULARY RATHER THAN THE BUILDING'S. `plan` in frame dwelling names the room arrangement behind the facade because that is what decides where a HOUSE'S door goes; a meeting house has no rooms behind its facade at all, it has one room. centre passage is chosen because it is the only value that produces a symmetrical front with a centred door, which is what a plain meeting house looked like; hall parlour, the archetype's default, would put the door two thirds of the way along the wall and make the front of a church look like the front of a farmhouse. Nothing about the door's real position is attested.

levels.8-10: This is made up, and it uses our rules' words, not the building's. Our rules pick a room plan to decide where a house's door goes. A meeting house has just one room. We chose a plan with a hall in the middle, since that puts the door in the center, as on a plain church. The usual choice would put the door off to one side, like a farmhouse. No paper says where the real door was.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND MOVED OFF THE PUBLIC SQUARE 2026-08-15 (ROADMA…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND MOVED OFF THE PUBLIC SQUARE 2026-08-15 (ROADMAP T-A16). The advertisement gives no address at all, so this is a band assignment and not a reading of any source. WHAT WAS WRONG WITH THE OLD ONE. Both buildings were placed together in 'the South Division band the recipes use for ordinary dwellings', and that band ran across the block bounded by Randolph, Clark, Washington and LaSalle - the public square, which carried the county's estray pen, its log jail and its court-house, and which this project's own ground control names as such. The old placement was tested for clearance and for buildable ground, which is every question this project knew how to ask; none of them was whether the ground was for sale. WHERE THEY WENT, AND BY WHAT RULE. Each building takes the nearest free platted lot that no committed block recipe has already spoken for - the recipes name their open lots and say why, and taking one would rewrite a parcel that has already landed. Under that rule the pair moves 83 m and 69 m, onto the Randolph Street frontage of the two blocks directly across Randolph from the square, which is the least this record can move and still stand on ground the town was selling. THE COORDINATE IS COMPUTED, NOT TYPED: the lot's own street edge and inward axis, with a 5.0 m setback, through the same lot frame every anonymous roof in the town is placed by. WHAT IS STILL INVENTED: the block, the lot, the setback, and that the two buildings stood near each other at all. One advertisement offering two buildings is not a statement that they shared a holding, and the pair is no longer on one block - the ground to keep them on one was 200 m further away and faced two different streets, which would have been a worse answer bought with a better-sounding sentence. THE SUFFIX IS A DISAMBIGUATOR AND NOT A BEARING. This record and its pair were called (east) and (west) from the single commit that minted them both, 9d208471 of 2026-08-13. THE WORDS NEVER DESCRIBED THE GROUND, NOT EVEN THEN: on that commit John Wright's Building to Let (a) stood at utm e 447555.957 and John Wright's Building to Let (b) at 447581.957, so the record called (east) was already 26 m WEST of the record called (west). The move off the public square of 2026-08-15 therefore did not reverse a true pair of words - it widened an error that was there from the first commit, to 123.198 m, and put the two on different blocks. There is no reading under which this pair has an attested east-west order: the advertisement gives no address at all, and both positions declare themselves invented band assignments in the paragraph above. A name that states a bearing is therefore a claim this project cannot make, and a reader or a later anchor pass would read it as one because that is what the words say. THE SUFFIXES ARE NOW (a) AND (b), matching the record ids: they hold the two records apart, which is the only work they have ever done, and they cannot be misread as a position. Naming each record after the block it stands on was considered and refused - the block is itself invented, so that name would carry an invention where this one carries nothing.

levels.8-10: This spot is made up. We moved it off the town square on 15 August 2026. The notice gives no address. At first we put it on the block of the town square, which held the county's jail and court house. That ground was not for sale. So we moved each building to the nearest free lot, across Randolph Street from the square. The block, the lot and the setback are still our guess, and so is that the two buildings stood near each other.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND PLACED BY A RULE RATHER THAN BY A PLATE. The p…
entries.text:
INVENTED, AND PLACED BY A RULE RATHER THAN BY A PLATE. The plate that puts sheds on this bank is image 3 of the owner's brief of 2026-08-18 (the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18), described there as: masts crowd the reach below the bridge, a light structure near the mouth, LOW WAREHOUSES ON THE BANKS. It is a PICTORIAL (a modern reconstruction) source — retrospective, drawn decades after 1835 — and this project's standing rule for one is that it may drive massing, form, materials and setting and may NEVER drive a coordinate. So the plate decides that a shed stands on this bank and nothing else about where.

WHERE IS DERIVED, from two committed things and one stated offset, and it was RE-DERIVED on 2026-08-28 when the street underneath it moved. (1) North Water Street's travelled track, the 1835 streets data, track width (m) 6.0: at local E 678.0 the drawn centreline stands at N 108.35, so its north edge is 3.00 m north of that. The front wall is set 2.00 m back from that edge — 5.00 m from the centreline, leaving the front wall 2.00 m clear of the drawn ribbon — and the building is squared to the street's own bearing at that station (1.04 degrees), so the row follows the river street rather than the grid. (2) The committed heightfield, the e1834 harbor cut data: every corner of this footprint stands on modelled ground between 1.27 m and 1.28 m above the water surface, which is 0.01 m of relief across the whole rectangle — inside the 0.35 m the infill generators allow themselves, so the walls share one walker surface without a cut or a fill.

WHY THE COORDINATE CHANGED, AND WHY THAT IS THE RULE HOLDING RATHER THAN BREAKING. Other work found North Water Street's committed line running 477.4 m of its 843.3 m inside the water mask and re-derived it from the committed north bank; nothing about this shed's rule changed, only the street the rule reads. Left where it was, this footprint stood 2.73 m from the corrected centreline and the roadway would have been drawn through it. The setback, the bearing rule, the relief clause and the plate's standing are all exactly as they were.

WHY IT IS BACK FROM THE WATER AND NOT ON IT. The traced 1834 north bank at this station is N 96.00, so the front wall stands about 17.3 m from the waterline with the river street between. That is not a compromise of the plate: it is the same relation the ATTESTED South Water row has to the south bank in image 11 of the same brief — a working frontage facing the river across the river street, with the bank itself left open. The modelled bank at this reach rises from the water to the plateau in three to four metres, and a building put on that slope would fail the relief clause above rather than stand on the bank.

WORKING UNCERTAINTY: total. Nothing states that a building stood at this station on 1835-07-01. What would replace this placement is a survey, a lot record or a contemporary view of the north bank below the draw. the liberties register “Four freight sheds on the north bank at the Dearborn crossing, every board of them invented” owns the invention.

levels.8-10: This shed is made up. An old print, drawn long after 1835, shows low warehouses on the river banks. Our rule lets a later picture decide what stands somewhere, but never the exact spot. So the print says a shed stands on this bank, and our rules set where, from the street and the bank.

It is a PICTORIAL (a modern reconstruction) source - retrospective, drawn decades after 1835 - and this project's standing rule for one is that it may drive massing, form, materials and setting and may NEVER drive a coordinate. So the plate decides that sheds stand on this bank, and that there is more than one of them, and nothing else about where.

WHERE IS DERIVED, from south bank shed dearborn e1's own committed walls and from two figures this project has already committed for a standing wagon. (1) THE EASTINGS ARE THE SHED IN FRONT OF IT. This building's west and east walls stand on the same two lines as e1's, local E 805.5000 and E 810.9864, so the pair reads as one row rather than two seatings - which is what the four north-bank sheds of other work do, and what the plate draws. (2) THE NORTHING IS THE YARD. e1's south wall stands at local N 1.5314 and its wagon door is on that wall; this building's north wall stands 5.20 m behind it at N -3.6686, and its own wagon door faces that yard. 5.20 m is 1.00 m of clearance from the wall a wagon stands at, plus the 3.20 m of ground a parked wagon needs, plus 1.00 m of clearance from the wall opposite - all three read off the town trade goods data, where the same two numbers seat the farm wagons in the Green Tree's yard. So both doors open onto one yard a wagon can stand in, and the yard's west end opens straight off the east end of South Water Street's travelled way, which is the only made approach to this ground. (3) THE BEARING is square to e1 and therefore square to the riverside plank walk e1 was squared to by other work; rotation (deg) is 0.000 rather than e1's 180.000 precisely so that `front` - the archetype's north face - is the door wall, and the two sheds face each other across the yard. (4) THE COMMITTED HEIGHTFIELD, the e1834 harbor cut data: sampled on a quarter-metre lattice, the ground under this footprint stands between 1.187 m and 1.282 m above the water surface - 0.0946 m of relief across the whole rectangle, inside the 0.30 m generate block infill max relief m allows and a shade flatter than e1's own 0.097 m.

WHY IT IS NOT ON THE BANK STRIP ITSELF, AND THIS IS THE READING'S ANSWER RATHER THAN A PREFERENCE. the south bank ground check is the south-bank ground rule, and its box is the bank strip: local N 0 to N 45 over the reach from the drawbridge to the Reservation's west line. Asked again today, with the full turn of bearings it should always have swept (see the tool), that strip takes exactly ONE more shed at the generators' own 0.30 m relief clause - and every position it admits stands on the ground e1's wagon door opens onto. The nearest square one is anchored at E 811.17 / N 0.0 at 0.0946 m of relief, which puts a second shed 1.531 m in front of e1's door: the approach e1's own record states - a cart coming east out of South Water Street's end and standing on the landward side of the shed - would be closed by it, which is the same class of fault as other work's shed on the boards and not something to build on purpose. So this record stands 5.20 m back instead - the SAME GROUND, 3.67 m further south and 0.19 m west of the station the reading names, taking six of the ten metres that station covers and four more the station does not reach, on the terrace BEHIND the bank strip, which is the ground other work asks for in as many words: the freight sheds and landings BEHIND South Water. The reading's station lattice stops at its own box floor and cannot express this exact seat, so it is not read off it and does not claim to be. It is verified against the same four predicates the reading applies, directly and on a finer lattice: the committed heightfield (dry, 0.0946 m of relief), all 33 platted corridors (the plat corridors tool reads the footprint clear; 0.717 m clear of South Water's corridor and 3.706 m of State Street's), every committed frontage walk (16.95 m clear of the riverside plank walk's boards at their nearest), every unplatted travelled way (16.51 m clear of fort road's) and every footprint the tree already places (5.20 m from e1, 14.43 m from the slough log bridge).

Its door now opens toward the street. See “One freight shed on the south bank at the Dearborn reach, on ground a filled channel gave back” and “A second freight shed on the south bank, behind the first one and not in front of its door”.

levels.8-10: This shed is made up, and a rule placed it, not a picture. An old print, drawn long after 1835, shows low sheds on the river banks. The yard is just big enough for a wagon to stand in, with room on each side. We set it back from the bank so it would not block the first shed's door. The ground here is dry and flat. entries.text: INVENTED, AND READ OFF THE BANKS THIS DECK LANDS ON RATHER THAN BORROWED FROM A DOCUMENTED CROSSING. The branch bridges stood 'about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice freely' (Statement on the first bridges over the branches of the Chicago River, agreed…) — 1.83 m, and meaningless for a backwater nothing passed under. The Slough Log Bridge's record met the same problem and answered it with 0.5 m, read off the hydrology dossier's conjectural 1.5-3.0 ft thalweg. THIS RECORD ANSWERS IT WITH THE GROUND INSTEAD, because here the ground can be measured: the committed heightfield stands at +0.63 m where the west abutment lands and +0.73 m where the east one does, over a 0.00 m water surface. 0.35 m of clearance puts the walk surface at 0.68 m (0.35 + 0.25 stringer + 0.08 plank), within 0.05 m of both banks, so the deck lies level with the street at each end and needs no approach ramp — unlike its two siblings, which needed a cut and a fill respectively. A shallow slough crossed by a low deck laid level with its banks is the least this can be and still be a crossing. The number is invented; what bounds it is the two abutment heights. Admitted in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: This height is made up, read from the banks the deck sits on. The river bridges stood about six feet above the water, so teams could pass under them. That means nothing for a small backwater no one passed under. Here we could measure the ground. Both banks stand a little above the water, so we set the deck level with them. That way no ramp is needed. The number is made up, but the banks limit it.

entries.text:
INVENTED, AND SEATED BY THE WORKS RULE BELOW RATHER THAN BY ANY SOURCE. The plant's own record says the barrelling and salting space is outside its footprint, and this is that space. WHY IT IS SOUTH OF THE PLANT AND NOT BEHIND IT: behind the plant is east, and east is Market Street. the plat corridors tool puts Market's platted corridor at local E 73.00 to E 97.00 across this whole reach, and the plant itself stands 1.30 m inside its west edge - a breach this project already carries and the corridor intrusion baseline tool already records. A works building put behind the plant would repeat that breach on purpose, and a new building standing in a platted street is not a thing to add to a town whose corridor gate exists to find them. North is worse: Randolph Street's corridor runs local N -265.00 to N -241.00 here and the plant stands 11.45 m inside it already. So the band runs SOUTH along the bank, which is the one direction with ground in it, and it is set out on two lines. THE EASTING LINE: every works building's east wall stands at local E 72.500, which is 0.50 m clear of Market's corridor edge - the same line for all three, so the band reads as one row rather than three seatings, which is other work's own idiom on the south bank. THE NORTHING: this building's north wall stands 5.20 m south of the plant's south wall at local N -271.000, the cart yard figure. MEASURED ON THIS SEAT, over a 25 x 25 lattice on the placed polygon: the ground stands 0.442 m to 0.698 m above the committed water surface - dry everywhere - with 0.256 m of relief across the whole rectangle, inside the 0.30 m clause; `intrusion` reads it clear of all 33 platted corridors; and the nearest committed footprint is the plant's own south wall at 5.20 m. WORKING UNCERTAINTY IS TOTAL and is the plant's own: Andreas gives 'on the South Branch of the river' and nothing else, so this building inherits a reach kilometres long and a coin-flip on the bank, and adds a setback nobody attested to it.

THE WORKS RULE, STATED ONCE AND APPLIED SIX TIMES. Every one of the four documented noxious trades on the branches records, in its own footprint note, that the works are outside its polygon: Newberry & Dole's Slaughter-House, South Branch says 'the pens, the yard and the barrelling and salting space that a packing operation needs are outside the footprint and outside this archetype, which builds a building rather than a works'; John Miller's Tannery says 'a tannery is its yard - bark mill, lime pits, tan vats, drying sheds, and a water supply - and none of that is in this polygon or in the model'; Archibald Clybourne's Log Slaughter-House says 'what is not modelled is arguably the bigger half'; Daniel Elston & Co.'s Soap and Candle Manufactory gives a shed 'big enough for a rendering kettle, a cooling and moulding floor and an ash leach' and nothing beside it. This building is one of the works those four sentences name, and NOTHING ATTESTS IT. It is placed by a rule and not by a plate. THE RULE: (1) a works building stands BEHIND its plant, on the side away from the water, because the plant's own bearing puts its working face on the water and the ground behind it is what is left; (2) the gap between the plant's wall and the works' wall is 5.20 m, the cart yard other work derived from the town trade goods data - 1.00 m of clearance from the wall a wagon stands at, plus the 3.20 m of ground a parked wagon needs, plus 1.00 m from the wall opposite - and the same 5.20 m separates one works building from the next, so the whole band is set out on one committed figure; (3) the works take the plant's own bearing, so the yard between them is square and the doors face it; (4) where the ground behind the plant is a platted street corridor, the works stand ALONG the bank instead, in the order the work runs, on a line that keeps them 0.50 m clear of that corridor's own edge - which is what the South Branch band does, because Market Street's corridor runs E 73.00 to E 97.00 at this reach and the plant itself stands 1.30 m inside it. THE FOUR PREDICATES each seat is held to, on a 25 x 25 lattice over the placed polygon: dry in the committed heightfield (the e1834 harbor cut data, water surface m = 0), relief inside the 0.30 m generate block infill max relief m allows, clear of all 33 platted corridors (the plat corridors tool), and clear of every footprint the committed tree already places. the research notes on branch noxious works carries the readings and the liberties register “The works the four documented noxious trades imply: six buildings on the branch frontage, and not one of them attested” owns the invention.

levels.8-10: This work building is made up, and our works rule placed it, not a paper. It is the room where barrels were filled and meat was salted, outside the plant itself. Behind the plant is Market Street, and north is Randolph Street. So it goes south along the bank, the only way with ground. All the work buildings line up in one row. Where the plant stood is already a guess, so this is too.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND SINCE 2026-10-01 SIZED FROM THE HOUSE'S GUESTS…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND SINCE 2026-10-01 SIZED FROM THE HOUSE'S GUESTS RATHER THAN FROM THE WORD 'LARGE'. The record first drew 13.0 x 7.0 m, 'about eight horses', and said the size answered the trade. It did not answer the sentence the trade is attested by: the source says the yard 'was one of the most important parts of the hostlery, for the teams were as numerous as were the guests'. the 1835 lodging model data sizes this house at 15 people on an ordinary night (its Western Hotel row, apportioned by floor area and graded `inferred`), so the attested sentence asks for about fifteen teams, and eight horses is four of them. THE ARITHMETIC, every factor of which is stated so it can be replaced: fifteen teams; a team taken as a PAIR, the ordinary draught team of a farm wagon; a pair standing in one double stall about 9 ft wide and 10 ft deep with its manger; the stalls in two ranges of eight down either side of a central passage about 8 ft wide. Sixteen double stalls hold the fifteen teams with one to spare: 8 x 9 ft = 72 ft along the yard and 10 + 8 + 10 = 28 ft deep, drawn as 22.0 x 8.5 m. None of the stall or passage figures is a reading of any source about this building or this town; they are what a pair of horses needs to stand, be fed and be led out, and the liberties register “The town's outbuildings are placed and sized by eye, on the strength of the buildings in front of them” carries them. WHAT IT DOES NOT ASSUME: that every team was horses (an ox team was as often yarded as stalled, and this is the stable for the horse teams the sentence implies), or the crowded night of 35 (the stable is sized for the ordinary night, as the beds are). The stable is now larger on the ground than the hotel's 164 m2 and smaller than its 329 m2 of floor, which is the order a wagon house's barn and house stood in. The north face, the one the wagon yard's fence meets, stays where it was; the growth is east along the yard and south away from it. WHAT WOULD REPLACE IT: an advertisement of Stow's naming his stabling, or a later description of the premises giving the stable's size — either retires this arithmetic outright.

levels.8-10: This stable's size is made up. Since October 2026 we size it from the guests, not from the word large. An old account says the yard was one of the most important parts of this inn, for the teams were as many as the guests. Our model puts about 15 guests here on a usual night. So it needs about fifteen teams of two horses. Two rows of eight double stalls hold them. Every number is ours. It is not sized for the crowded nights.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND SIZED FROM THE HOUSE'S BEDS. The lodging model…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND SIZED FROM THE HOUSE'S BEDS. The lodging model (the 1835 lodging model data) puts 11 in the Exchange Coffee House on an ordinary night (35 crowded), itself graded reconstructed. ONE STALL PER TWO ORDINARY GUESTS: 11 beds / 2 = 6 = 6 stalls. Half, because the summer of 1835's crowd came mostly by lake and many of a town house's guests arrived without a horse; the Western Hotel's 'teams as numerous as were the guests' ("Town of Chicago." Chicagology. Transcribing the Inter Ocean of 22 July 1883…) is that house's own sentence about the teamsters' road west and is not carried to a Lake Street house; one range of 6 single standing stalls 5 ft wide and 9 ft deep, a passage behind them and a mangers' run, 20 ft deep in all, plus a 6 ft bay for harness and feed at one end: 6 x 5 + 6 = 36 ft long by 20 ft deep = 10.97 x 6.1 m. The ordinary night, not the crowded one, as the beds are sized. Every factor is ours and stated so it can be replaced: an advertisement or a sale notice naming this house's stabling, a fire-loss list, or a lot-level view of the block. “Six public houses get a stable behind them, sized from their beds”.

levels.8-10: This stable's size is made up, worked out from the beds of the Exchange Coffee House. Our model puts 11 guests there on a usual night, and that is a guess too. Most guests in 1835 came by boat, without a horse, so we give one stall for every two guests. That makes 6 stalls, with room for harness and feed. Every number is ours. A paper that counts its stalls would take its place.
