entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND THE ARCHETYPE CHOICE RESTS ON IT. Andreas says…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND THE ARCHETYPE CHOICE RESTS ON IT. Andreas says 'a house'. Nothing says frame and nothing says log, and this project's dossier records the town's stock as 'overwhelmingly frame and log' without splitting it by division. Frame is adopted because the house stood in Kinzie's Addition, platted and selling in 1833, where the building going up was new building rather than the older log stock at the forks - which is an argument about a neighbourhood, not evidence about a house. Braced rather than balloon is the conservative reading for a building of unfixed date, the same argument P. F. W. Peck's Store makes. IF A SOURCE SAYS LOG, THIS RECORD MOVES TO THE log dwelling ARCHETYPE, which is a bigger change than a value: the walls, the corners and the openings would all be different. That is stated here because the archetype is not itself a graded attribute and this is the only place the choice can be argued with.

levels.8-10: This is made up, and our choice of building type rests on it. A history book says only a house. Nothing says frame or log. We use frame because the house was in Kinzie's Addition, sold from 1833, where new houses were going up. That is about the area, not proof about this house. We use the heavy frame, as for other buildings with no sure date. If a paper says log, the whole building changes.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, AND THE SAME RECTANGLE AS THE SHED IN FRONT OF IT.…
entries.text: INVENTED, AND THE SAME RECTANGLE AS THE SHED IN FRONT OF IT. 5.4864 x 9.7536 m is 18 x 32 ft, the floor of family F1 (freight or storage shed) in the 1835 building inventory data, whose band runs to 28 x 50 ft. It is the floor of the band for the reason e1 gives - it is the rectangle the south bank ground check sweeps this reach with, so a shed of this size on this reach can be checked against the reading - and it is repeated here because the two sheds stand on one pair of walls and a second size would break the row for no evidence at all. The frontage is the short side and the depth runs back from the door, which is the crosswalk's own description of F1. No source gives this building a dimension because no source gives this building.

levels.8-10: This is made up, the same size as the shed in front of it. It is 18 by 32 feet, the smallest size our rules allow a freight shed. The two sheds share their side wall lines, so a second size would break the row for no reason. The short side faces the door. No paper gives its size, since no paper names it.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, NOT DERIVED. This value comes from a typology in t…
entries.text: INVENTED, NOT DERIVED. This value comes from a typology in the reconstruction spec — what a building of this kind was ordinarily like — and NOT from evidence about this particular building, because there is no particular building: the structure itself is an invention filling a demonstrable need of the town. entries.card: why:INVENTED, and it is the archetype's default kept deliberatel…
entries.text: INVENTED, and it is the archetype's default kept deliberately. hall parlour is the commonest vernacular plan of the period and produces the plainest and least regular front the archetype builds - the door two thirds of the way along the wall, openings unevenly spaced. Nothing about this house's plan is attested. The bay count is left to the archetype to derive from the frontage rather than stated, which at 30 ft gives three openings.

levels.8-10: This room plan is made up, and we kept our rules' usual choice on purpose. It is the most common plan of the time. It gives the plainest front, with the door off to one side and the windows not evenly spaced. Nothing says what this house's plan was. With a front of 30 feet, our rules give it three openings.

entries.card: why:INVENTED, and it is the archetype's vocabulary rather than t…
entries.text: INVENTED, and it is the archetype's vocabulary rather than the building's - the same admission the two church records make. A building with a worship room below and a school room above has no hall-and-parlour behind its front wall. centre passage is chosen because it produces a symmetrical front with a centred door, which is what a plain public building looked like and what a stair to a separate upper storey implies. Nothing about the real door position, or about whether the school had its own outside stair, is attested.

levels.8-10: This room plan is made up, and it is our rules' word, not the building's. This building had a church room below and a school room above, so it had no farmhouse plan behind its front. We chose a plan with a hall in the middle. That gives an even front with the door in the center, as a plain public building had. It also fits a stair up to a second floor. No paper says where the real door was, or if the school had its own stairs outside.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. 6.0960 x 8.5344 m is 20 x 28 ft, inside family W3'…
entries.text: INVENTED. 6.0960 x 8.5344 m is 20 x 28 ft, inside family W3's band in the 1835 building inventory data (18-30 ft front, 22-40 ft deep) - W3 being the crosswalk's cooper, wagon and wheelwright shop, the family whose visible content is hoops and barrels, which is what a packing house is full of between seasons. The size answers the plant's documented CAPACITY in the same loose way the plant's own footprint does: 1,400 hogs and 300 cattle in a season is a great many barrels to fill, salt and head up, and 20 x 28 ft is a floor two men can work either side of a row of barrels on. Every number is invented and the polygon cites no sources. The frontage is the short side, on the branch; the depth runs back from the water toward Market Street.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. It is 20 by 28 feet, the size our rules give a barrel maker's shop. A packing house is full of barrels when it is not busy. The plant packed many hogs and cattle in a season, and that is a lot of barrels to fill and salt. This floor is big enough for two men to work on each side of a row of barrels. Every number is made up. The short side faces the river.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. NO SOURCE GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION. 12 x 9…
entries.text: INVENTED. NO SOURCE GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION. 12 x 9 m is about 39 x 30 ft; the whole rectangle is the log core plus the 1833 frame addition in front of it, because that is what a footprint polygon means to the log dwelling archetype. TWO WEAK ARGUMENTS SHAPED IT AND NEITHER IS EVIDENCE: it took two street numbers, 84 and 86 Lake Street, when Lake Street was numbered, which suggests a frontage of about two lots rather than one; and it held a room big enough for the Circuit Court to sit in - in the unfinished loft - at the May 1834 term. The 9 m depth is the log core plus the 4 m the frame addition needed to reach the street from 'some little distance back'. All three numbers are chosen. TO RESOLVE: the Chicago Democrat and Chicago American advertisements of the house under Haddock or Markle, which in the period habitually counted rooms; or a Cook County deed on lots 84-86.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. No paper gives it. It is about 39 by 30 feet: the old log house plus the frame part added in front in 1833. Two weak hints shaped it, and neither is proof. It later had two street numbers on Lake Street, so it may have been about two lots wide. And its loft was big enough for the court to meet in, in May 1834. Old ads for the house, which often counted rooms, or a land paper for its lots, would settle it.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION…
entries.text: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION — Andreas describes it and never measures it. 12.192 x 7.62 m is 40 x 25 ft, and BOTH FIGURES ARE BORROWED FROM THIS DATASET RATHER THAN FRESHLY INVENTED, which is the same admission P. F. W. Peck's Store, Philo Carpenter's South Water Street Store and their neighbours make in the same words: 40 ft is the frontage attested for the Green Tree Tavern and for the Western Hotel's front, and 25 ft is the depth derived from the Green Tree's attested room module. They are the only period figures for a two-storey frame commercial building this project holds. So the rectangle is a claim about the TYPE and not about this building, and the repetition across records is the honest form of that admission, not an accident. THE ONE THING THE SHAPE DOES CLAIM IS THE PROPORTION, AND THAT IS DOCUMENTED. Andreas has 'a two-story building, with eaves to the street'. The frame tavern archetype runs its ridge along the longer axis (ridge along x = width >= depth), so a footprint wider than it is deep is exactly what puts the eaves, not the gable, on Lake Street; a 25 x 40 ft rectangle would have turned the gable to the street and contradicted the one elevation fact the source states. The frontage also sits inside the committed lot: lot 7 of block 20 is 24.40 m wide, so a 12.19 m front leaves 6.1 m clear to each side line.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. A history book describes it but never measures it. It is 40 by 25 feet. We borrowed both numbers from other buildings in our records, as we did for its neighbours. They are the only sizes we have for a two floor frame store of the time. So the shape tells you about the kind of building, not this one. The one thing it does show is true: the book says the long side, with the low edge of the roof, faced the street. It also fits inside its lot.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION,…
entries.text: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION, A MATERIAL OR A FORM - Andreas says 'a house' and nothing else. 9.144 x 6.096 m is 30 x 20 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per the datum json's data units rule: an ordinary two-room house of the period, large enough that a schoolmaster could take a class in one room of it, which is the only functional constraint the evidence supplies. Everything about the shape is this record's.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. No paper gives its size, what it was built of, or its shape. A history book says only a house. It is 30 by 20 feet, a plain two room house of the time. That is big enough for a teacher to hold a class in one room, which is the one thing the record asks of it. Everything about its shape is our choice.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION,…
entries.text: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION, a plan, or a number of cells. 6.096 x 4.572 m is 20 x 15 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per the datum json's data units rule. The only constraint the evidence offers is relative and it runs in both directions: the jail was built because something more metropolitan was required than the estray pen, so it is a more substantial thing than a stock pound; and it was itself superseded within a few years, so it was small. A 20 x 15 ft log box is a two-cell lock-up and is the smallest thing that answers both. Nothing else about the shape is a finding: the plain rectangle, the proportion and the scale are all this record's.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. No paper gives its size, plan or number of cells. It is 20 by 15 feet. The jail was built because the town needed more than its pen for stray animals, so it was bigger than that. And a few years later it was replaced, so it was small. A log box with two cells fits both. Everything else about its shape is our choice.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION.…
entries.text: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION. What IS documented is a cap on one of them: Andreas states that South Water Street lots were 55 ft wide (the research notes on structures south § 5), so a store on a single lot on this street cannot have had more than 55 ft of frontage, and this rectangle's 40 ft frontage sits comfortably inside that. The two numbers are borrowed rather than freshly invented, and that is deliberate: 40 ft is the frontage attested for the Green Tree Tavern and for the Western Hotel's front, and 25 ft is the depth derived from the Green Tree's attested room module — the only period figures for a commercial building this dataset actually holds. So the shape is a claim about the TYPE and not about this building. 12.192 x 7.62 m is 40 x 25 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per the datum json's data units rule. The same rectangle is used on four records in this parcel; that repetition is the honest form of the admission, not an accident.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. No paper gives it. What we do know is a limit: lots on this street were 55 feet wide, so a store on one lot could not be wider than that. This store is 40 by 25 feet. We borrowed both numbers from other buildings in our records, the only sizes we have for a store of the time. So the shape tells you about the kind of building, not this one. We use the same size on four buildings here, and we say so on purpose.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS ENCLOSURE A DIMENSION…
entries.text: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS ENCLOSURE A DIMENSION. 9.144 x 6.096 m is 30 x 20 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per the datum json's data units rule. The reasoning behind the scale is a use rather than a measurement: a town pound had to hold several head of stray cattle or horses at once and, for the first months of its life, prisoners as well, which puts it well above a shed and well below a stock yard. Everything about the shape - the rectangle, the proportion, the size - is this record's. RE-EXPRESSED AS A PERIMETER 2026-08-18: the estray pen data walks this same rectangle as a closed fence line, from this record's own origin and these same 9.144 x 6.096 m. It re-invents nothing - it re-uses this polygon - so this note, and the liberties register “The estray pen is a fence, and the model gives it a roof” with it, is still the place the rectangle is admitted to.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. No paper gives it. It is 30 by 20 feet. A town pen had to hold several stray cows or horses at once. For a few months it also held people under arrest. So it is bigger than a shed but much smaller than a stock yard. Every part of its shape is our choice. Later we drew the same shape as a fence line too.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. No dimension of any kind is attested. 9.0 x 6.0 m…
entries.text: INVENTED. No dimension of any kind is attested. 9.0 x 6.0 m is about 30 x 20 ft — a single range of four or five stalls with room to lead a horse past them, which is the smallest building that answers the documented service and the largest that a house of this size on this bank can be argued into. It is drawn deliberately smaller than The Western Hotel's Stable, whose source at least calls it 'large', so that the two stables in this scene are not the same building twice at different addresses. Every number is invented and this polygon cites no sources.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. No paper gives any size. It is about 30 by 20 feet, a row of four or five stalls with room to lead a horse past them. That is the smallest stable that does the job, and the biggest a house this size could use. We made it smaller than the Western Hotel's stable, which a paper calls large, so the two would not look like the same building. Every number is made up.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. No source reached gives the factory building a dim…
entries.text:
INVENTED. No source reached gives the factory building a dimension. 12.192 x 6.096 m is 40 x 20 ft, and both numbers are borrowed from attested buildings in this dataset rather than freshly guessed: 20 ft is the depth of Hogan's store, the one log footprint here that is documented, and 40 ft is the frontage attested for the Green Tree Tavern. A fur company's factory building is a trade house — a store room and a counter — so a long shallow rectangle of that order is the right kind of shape for the type. THIS POLYGON IS ONE BUILDING AND THE HOMESTEAD WAS FOUR. Andreas describes the factory building, a new residence Beaubien built, a small trading post, and an earlier cabin he converted to a barn. THREE BUILDINGS STAND FOR THE FOUR, ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF other work (2026-09-28, answer b) — this house, Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Barn since 2026-08-11 and Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Trading Post since other work. Other work had also stood the residence as its own record, beaubien new residence, a third identical log house placed by eye on the fort road; other work withdrew it and FOLDS it into this record, because the research notes on jb beaubien homestead § 6a already reads Wentworth's 'traditional residence' at the corner as most likely the new residence, so two records were very probably drawing one house twice. The fold is a reading, not a finding: nothing reached says which of Andreas's two houses this is, and the scene now shows one dwelling for Col. Beaubien rather than asserting which. This polygon is still only the first of them, and it is the only one of the four whose neighbours did not have to be placed by eye; the research notes on jb beaubien homestead § 4 and the liberties register “Two of the Beaubien homestead's four attested buildings are placed and sized by eye, beside the two that already were” carry what the other three cost.

other work ONE UNRENDERED LOW-PROJECTION PROPOSAL: the accepted main core remains exactly12.192x6.096m at its existing origin. Expand only the total reconstructed depth to8.096m and use the stepped union of that core with one centered6.096x2.0m projection beyond its max-v/front wall. Native frame addition/front subtracts the stated2m from total depth, recovering the exact accepted6.096m core rather than shrinking it. Every attachment dimension/location is reconstructed picture-relative geometry, not a historic plan or survey. The earlier factory-derived size rationale is not revived as evidence. Dates and main-core world placement remain unchanged.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. No paper gives it. It is 40 by 20 feet, and we borrowed both numbers from other buildings in our records. A fur trader's building was a store room with a counter, so a long, narrow shape fits. A history book says the Beaubien home had four buildings: this one, a new house, a small trading post, and an old cabin made into a barn. The owner of this project ruled that three buildings stand for the four. We once drew the new house too, but we took it out, since it was likely this same house drawn twice. That is a reading, not a finding. Later we tried adding a small part on the front, from an old picture, but have not built it.

entries.card: why:INVENTED. The advertisement gives a trade, a corner and a st…
entries.text: INVENTED. The advertisement gives a trade, a corner and a stock list and no dimension. 9.144 x 6.096 m is 30 x 20 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per the datum json's data units rule - the same size this project gives Frederick Thomas's shop on South Water Street, kept deliberately rather than replaced with a fresh guess, on the reasoning the liberties register “The North Branch bridge stands on fifteen piers nobody recorded” states about the bridge's pier spacing: a new number would look like a finding and would not be one. WHAT THE ADVERTISEMENT DOES IMPLY, without measuring anything: the firm kept saddles, harness, bridles and trunks 'on hand', manufactured to order, and trimmed 'Coaches, Chaises and Waggons', which is a shop with a workroom behind it and enough door to get a waggon at least alongside. That argues for the larger end of a shop rather than a stall, and it is an argument, not a measurement.

levels.8-10: This size is made up. The ad gives a trade, a corner and a list of goods, but no size. It is 30 by 20 feet, the same size we give Frederick Thomas's shop. We kept that size on purpose, since a new number would look like a finding and would not be one. The ad does hint at something. The shop kept saddles, harness and trunks, made goods to order, and fitted out coaches and wagons. That means a work room at the back and a door wide enough to bring a wagon close. So it was likely on the big side for a shop. That is a reason, not a measure.

entries.card: why:IT CHANGED TRADE ONCE BEFORE THE SCENE DATE AND THE SOURCES…
entries.text:
IT CHANGED TRADE ONCE BEFORE THE SCENE DATE AND THE SOURCES SAY SO. Andreas: 'It was kept as a saloon and boarding-house by him [Alanson Sweet] and a man from Canada, named Darwin. Then the Couch brothers purchased the property and Ira Couch opened it as a hotel.' Chicago Illustrated (1866), on "Tremont House." Chicagology. Compiling city-directory entries 1846-1870, an…, calls it 'the first house making any pretensions to the character of a hotel'. Both readings are hotel-keeping in the broad sense and the change is one of style rather than of use; hotel is the value for the scene date because Couch had opened it as one by 1834. It was also a stage stop: the 1874 letter has stages driving to this corner and passengers walking two blocks when the mud beat the horses.

THE TRUSTEES SAT IN THIS HOUSE TWICE IN THE AUTUMN OF 1834. the Chicago Democrat of 1834-10-01 prints an ordinance passed 'At a Meeting of the President and Trustees of the town of Chicago, held at the [Tremon]t House, Sept. [29], 183[4]', and the Chicago Democrat of 1834-10-29 another passed at a meeting 'held at the Tre[mont House in said] town, on the 13th day of [October] A. D. 1834'. Two named sittings of the town's government in this building, four weeks apart and nine months before the scene date: a documented use, which is what is asserted. THE MEETING PLACE IS PARTLY SUPPLIED IN BOTH, and from each other — the first column keeps 'ot House' and the second 'the Tre.' — which is a second printing in the same paper and not a guess; each claim's own note carries the reasoning. WHAT IS NOT ASSERTED IS THE ORDINANCES' CONTENT: one forbids taking earth or sand off a street without the leave of the supervisor of roads, the other empowers the fire wardens to command any bystander at a fire into the line. Both are town law and neither places anything. Nothing on this record's position, form or occupants is changed.

levels.8-10: This building changed its trade once before 1835, and the papers say so. A history book says it was first a bar and boarding house, run by Alanson Sweet and a man from Canada. Then the Couch brothers bought it, and Ira Couch made it a hotel. A book of 1866 calls it the first house that tried to be a real hotel. Both are ways of keeping guests, so we call it a hotel in 1835. Stages also stopped here. The town's leaders met in this house twice in the fall of 1834, four weeks apart. A paper prints the laws they passed there. Parts of the house's name are torn in each paper, but each copy fills in the other.

The record follows the advertisement because an advertisement is the man's own word about his own business, and flags the doubt rather than resolving it.

entries.card: why:It stands inside the south wall, on the parade, and the Army…
entries.text: It stands inside the south wall, on the parade, and the Army's own beef proposals of May and June 1834 (claims the Chicago Democrat of 1834-05-28 and the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-04) call it 'the subsistance store house of Fort Dearborn'. The post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836 (the stockade's own occupants block, after Andreas), so on 1 July 1835 its service buildings were the garrison's; the people are seated on the stockade and are not repeated here.

levels.8-10: This store house stands inside the south wall of the fort, on the open drill ground. In 1834 the army asked for beef in the paper, and it names this the fort's food store house. Soldiers held the fort without a break from 1832 to the end of 1836. So in 1835 this building belonged to the soldiers. The people are shown with the fort, not here.

entries.card: why:John Gray, landlord 1838-41, correcting a drawing of the hou…
entries.text: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, correcting a drawing of the house: 'There should also be a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left.' So by the end of the 1830s the two-storey core had a low single-storey addition at each end. WHETHER THEY EXISTED ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray's testimony describes the building three to six years after the scene date — which is why this is inferred and why the additions stay out of the footprint polygon. SINCE other work the rear (east) one is BUILT, at the reconstructed grade, as form.rear ell — see that attribute for why only the rear end has ground to build on. This value stays the testimony record for BOTH ends; the street-end addition remains unbuilt.

levels.8-10: John Gray kept this house from 1838 to 1841. Looking at a drawing of it, he said there should be a low one floor part on the right, the same as on the left. So by the end of the 1830s the house had a low part at each end. We do not know if they stood in 1835, since he saw the house three to six years later. That is why this is a guess. We have built the back one, as made up, since only that end had room. The street end part is not built.

entries.card: why:KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the s…
entries.text: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (the 1834 harbor cut ground/shoreline.geojson), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS 130 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (“Seventy roofs are told who entered their ground by a survey grid nobody traced”): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

levels.8-10: This is the part of the land north of the river. We drew its edge from the survey squares and the river bank we already have. The old book spells the buyer's name more than one way, and we keep each spelling. The building stands 130 m inside the edge of the land, far more than our maps could be off. entries.text: KINZIE'S ADDITION. The north fraction of section 10 is the section north of the river, which is why the register prints 102.29 acres and not a quarter's 160. It is resolved as the section's own grid box clipped to the committed north bank of the main stem (the 1834 harbor cut ground/shoreline.geojson), so no boundary here is authored. The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE MARGIN IS 194 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (“Seventy roofs are told who entered their ground by a survey grid nobody traced”): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

The two rows the register carries for it — one plain, one with the school-section marker — are the same entry printed twice. THE REGISTER SPELLS THE PURCHASER MORE THAN ONE WAY for this same tract — Robert A Kenzie; Robert A Kinzie — and the spellings are carried rather than merged, which is the land sales crosswalk's standing rule: tract agreement is where two spellings MIGHT be one man and is never proof that they are. THE ROOF IS AN INVENTION AND THIS CANNOT OUTRANK IT. The footprint stands 83 m inside the tract's nearest boundary, which on a documented building would carry the middle row, but this building was dealt to its lot by a recipe and is not there. The tract is real and the register's words about it are read; what is graded here is the claim that THIS roof stands on it, and that claim is the recipe's. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (“Seventy roofs are told who entered their ground by a survey grid nobody traced”): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

levels.8-10: This is the part of the land north of the river. We drew its edge from the survey squares and the river bank we already have. The old book spells the buyer's name more than one way, and we keep each spelling. The building itself is made up, and our rules put it on this lot. The piece of land is real, and so are the old record's words about it. But that this building stands on it is only our rule. The state's old book of land sales says this man bought the land under this building. It does not say he still owned it on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it. A sale is not a home. The lines of the old land survey are not traced from a map. We drew them in squares a mile wide from one known corner, at State and Madison.

No figure is drawn (“No people, anywhere”). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Dickinson, Albert H. | Letter. | January 6, 1878.” (second presb 0017, printed page 154), admitted 1878-01-06 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Dickinson' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins A. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. entries.card: why:LOG CRIBS SUNK AND FILLED WITH STONE, INFERRED FROM PERIOD A…
entries.text: LOG CRIBS SUNK AND FILLED WITH STONE, INFERRED FROM PERIOD AND REGIONAL PRACTICE AND NOT STATED BY ANY SOURCE RECORD THIS PROJECT HOLDS. the research notes on terrain hydrology names the north pier 'timber crib' without a citation and gives the south pier no construction at all; the texts held here supply the works' chronology, appropriations, supervisors and lengths and never say what the piers were made of. Timber cribbing sunk and stone-filled is how Great Lakes harbour piers of the 1830s were built, it is what was available to a works run out of a frontier garrison with unlimited timber and no cement, and it is what the town's own bridge builders used for abutments in the same years. A reading, not a report. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the Chief Engineer's annual reports, or the 1833-35 contracts for the Chicago harbour appropriation.

levels.8-10: This is a guess from how such work was done, not from any paper we hold. We say the piers were log boxes sunk in the water and filled with stone. Our papers give the work's dates, money, bosses and lengths, but never what the piers were made of. Log boxes filled with stone is how lake harbours of the 1830s were built. The fort had all the wood it needed and no cement. The town's bridge builders did the same. The army engineer's yearly reports, or the work's contracts, would settle it.

entries.card: why:LOG CRIBS SUNK AND FILLED WITH STONE. NO SOURCE RECORD IN TH…
entries.text: LOG CRIBS SUNK AND FILLED WITH STONE. NO SOURCE RECORD IN THIS PROJECT STATES IT IN SO MANY WORDS. the research notes on terrain hydrology zone 24 names the structure 'North pier (timber crib)' and gives no citation for the construction; the texts this project does hold give the harbour works' chronology, appropriations, supervisors and lengths, and never say what the piers were made of. The value is an inference from period and regional practice, which is what the inferred tag is for: timber cribbing sunk and stone-filled was how every Great Lakes harbour pier of the 1830s was built, it is what was available to a works run out of a frontier garrison town with unlimited timber and no cement, and the same technique is what the town's own bridge builders used for their abutments. It is nevertheless a reading and not a report. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the Chief Engineer's annual reports, or the 1833-35 contracts and vouchers for the Chicago harbour appropriation.

levels.8-10: This is a guess from how such work was done, and no paper we hold says it. We say the piers were log boxes sunk in the water and filled with stone. Our papers give the harbour work's dates, money, bosses and lengths, but never what the piers were made of. Log boxes filled with stone is how every lake harbour pier of the 1830s was built. The fort had all the wood it needed and no cement. The town's bridge builders did the same. The army engineer's yearly reports, or the work's contracts and bills, would settle it.

entries.text: MARRIED SIXTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE AND DESCRIBED BY ANDREAS AS 'THEN LATE OF CHICAGO' AT THE TIME OF THE WEDDING - which is a statement that she had already left the town. Her school had moved out of the State Street log house in 1834. She is carried in this household under her married name because that is her status on 1 July 1835, and the household's presence field records what follows from it.

levels.8-10: She married sixteen days before our day in 1835. A history book says that by her wedding she had left the town. Her school had moved out of the log house on State Street in 1834. We list her with this family under her married name. That is who she was on 1 July 1835.

entries.card: why:MEASURED OFF THE SAME TWO RED LINES AS THE NORTH PIER, AND T…
entries.text: MEASURED OFF THE SAME TWO RED LINES AS THE NORTH PIER, AND THIS IS THE SOUTHERN OF THEM. Wright 1834 draws the harbour as two red lines with HARBOR lettered between them and a flow arrow running east down the channel between them; the southern line is this pier's inner face. Both were read at native resolution off the BPL master scan (commonwealth:js957744g) and transformed by the fitted affine recorded in the wright 1834 gcps data — the same transform the rederive datum tool checks the datum against, not a second georeference. METHOD AND RESULT. The southern line's landward end reads at resource pixel (3171, 1498), which is local E +1215.9, N +252.5. The line runs at 103.5 degrees from grid north against the northern line's 103.4, so the two are parallel to a tenth of a degree, and the perpendicular distance between them is 64.2 m against a documented entrance width of 200 ft (61.0 m). Two lines that come out parallel and four per cent from a figure neither of them supplied is the check that says the right pair was read. Picking precision about 5 resource pixels, or 3.5 m, on top of the sheet's plus or minus 20 m. The value recorded here is the footprint polygon's own origin: the landward end of the measured inner face. The crib is built SOUTH of it, away from the channel, which is why this record's polygon runs from v = -7.62 to v = 0 where the north pier's runs from 0 to +7.62 — the measured line is the channel side of both structures and they stand on opposite sides of it. Facade bearing 13.5 is the axis bearing less 90, this archetype's convention. THE DRAFTED LENGTH IS NOT USED, and on this pier the reason is at its starkest: the southern line runs about 1,165 ft on the sheet, and the south pier did not reach that length until after 1837. Wright drew the works as authorised. See form.length (m). THE POSITION WAS ALSO 900 m OUTSIDE THE MODELLED GROUND WHEN THIS NOTE WAS WRITTEN; the committed heightfield stopped at local E +320. It was extended east to E +1700 on 2026-08-11 and there is modelled ground here now — the ground contact block was regraded the same day, from outside modelled ground to approach not modelled, and that is the reason which survives: the pier stands over water with no modelled approach at either end (corrected 2026-08-22).

levels.8-10: We measured this pier off an old map of 1834. The map draws the harbour as two red lines, with the word harbor between them. The south line is this pier's inner side. We read both lines off a sharp copy of the map and turned them into our ground. The two lines come out side by side, and the gap between them is very close to the 200 feet the papers give. That tells us we read the right lines. The pier is built on the south side of the line, away from the water. We do not use the length on the map, since the pier did not reach that long until after 1837. It stands over the water with no land at either end.

entries.card: why:MOVED OFF THE AGENCY HOUSE AND ONTO HIS OWN, 2026-09-27 UNDE…
entries.text: MOVED OFF THE AGENCY HOUSE AND ONTO HIS OWN, 2026-09-27 UNDER other work, AND THE GRADE DID NOT MOVE WITH IT. The note this replaces said the link to Indian Agency House rested on one sentence of Andreas — 'In the fall of 1832, Colonel Hamilton and Colonel Owen employed John Watkins to teach a small school in the North Division, near the old Indian agency-house in which Colonel Hamilton then resided' — nearly three years before 1 July 1835, and it said in as many words that 'nothing reached follows him out of it or keeps him in it'. SOMETHING NOW FOLLOWS HIM OUT OF IT. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago vol. 2 p. 155, read as bk mose2 006, give the whole sequence: he 'lived first in the fort and, when that grew too crowded with the refugees, he moved to the Agency House; and in 1833, with Col. Owen, hired John Watkins to teach the little school in the old stable near by. At about this time he built his house on what is now Michigan street between Cass and Rush, where he lived for nineteen years.' The first two stages corroborate Andreas — the fort, then the Agency House, then the same two colonels hiring the same schoolmaster in the same year — and the third stage is the one Andreas does not have: a house of his own, built about 1833, held for nineteen years. Nineteen years from 1833 runs to about 1852 and 1835-07-01 falls inside it, so this is a SPAN enclosing the scene date rather than a fact dated outside it and carried back. THE STRUCTURE IT NAMES IS AN IDENTIFICATION AND NOT A STATEMENT. Richard J. Hamilton's house on Michigan Street is this project's record of the house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush that Andreas has Watkins teaching in 'later'; Andreas names no owner for it and Moses and Kirkland name no school in Hamilton's. The join is Hamilton himself, who hired the schoolmaster, and the reasoning, the caveat that no source gives the SIDE of Michigan Street Hamilton built on, and what would refute the whole thing are written on that record's `occupants` block rather than repeated here. NOTHING IS PROMOTED. Moses and Kirkland is a compilation of 1895; under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 it corroborates and dates and may not raise a confidence, so this stays `inferred` exactly as it was when it pointed at the Agency House. What changed is that the inference now runs forward from a span that covers the scene date instead of backward from a sentence about 1832. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR lives at AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW the Hamilton household#lives at, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start

levels.8-10: We moved this man off the old agency house and onto his own house, and how sure we are did not change. One history book says that in 1832 he lived in the old agency house. A later book tells more. He lived first in the fort, then in the agency house. In 1833 he and another colonel hired a teacher for a little school. About then he built his own house on Michigan Street, and lived there nineteen years. Those years cover 1835. Linking that house to the one in our records is our reading, not a paper's. The later book may back up a claim but not make it more sure, so this stays a good guess.

James Allen is the papers': army officer and engineer, printed at the Democrat of 25 March 1834 and of 13 August 1834 and at the American of 18 July 1835 — seventeen days after the scene date, which is what makes his household present rather than uncertain. NO SOURCE PUTS EITHER MAN IN THIS BUILDING, so the grade does not move: the Army quartered a lieutenant and a post surgeon in the subordinate officers' quarters and this dataset holds one. ELEVEN OTHER NAMES WERE RULED OUT, each for a stated clause — a militia colonel, a man on the town poll roll, a soldier's trade read once in January 1834 and never again. The whole adjudication is the research notes on fort dearborn garrison. The enlisted strength stays unwritten and unnumbered here, and Hubbard's 1827 civilian tenants belong to the years when there were no troops.

entries.card: why:NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE. THE START IS THE FIRST DAY…
entries.text: NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE. THE START IS THE FIRST DAY THE ATTESTED YEAR PERMITS, not a date anybody gives - the convention Lake House (under construction)'s own range opens on, and for the same reason: the one sighting is the morning of 26 August 1835, eight weeks AFTER the scene date, and a range opening there would put this house outside the scene it is attested in. What carries it back is that the house is described FULL - "Mrs. Kelsey had all the boarders that she could accommodate" - which is a going concern and not a week-old one, and that a painted frame house is not thrown up in eight weeks beside a boarding trade already at capacity. That is an inference and it is graded as one. THE END IS THE HONEST YEAR BOUND: nothing reached says when this house came down. IT IS NOT THE HOUSE THE DIRECTORIES PRINT, and that is the reason the range is not carried forward: Fergus' 1843 directory has "Kelsey, Patrick, boarding-house, Wolcott, bet Kinzie and Michigan" and Norris' 1844 has "Kelsey, Parnick, boarding house, Wolcott st. b Kinzie and Mich." - the same trade on a platted north-side street about 230 m WEST of the sand hills. A boarding-house keeper moving off the beach and onto a street in eight years is the ordinary reading; a range running to 1844 would assert that the sand-hill house and the Wolcott Street house are one building, which no source says. BONNELL'S WALK IS THE ONLY SOURCE THIS PROJECT HAS REACHED THAT PUTS A BUILDING ON THE SAND HILLS NORTH-EAST OF THE LAKE HOUSE, AND IT IS ONE SENTENCE LONG. J. D. Bonnell, writing to the Chicago Times on 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas (History of Chicago vol. 1, printed pages 136-137), describes the morning after he arrived: "In turning the corner of Dr. Kimball's residence, away to the north-east, among the sand-hills, close by the lake shore, stood a small yellow house, occupied by Parnick Kelsey as a boarding-house, ostensibly run by Eve, Parnick's wife, for Mr. Kelsey was a sub-contractor in removing stumps and grubs, preparatory to the grading of the street on the North Side... But as Mrs. Kelsey had all the boarders that she could accommodate, I was obliged to seek other quarters." THE DATE IS EIGHT WEEKS LATE AND THE CARRY BACK IS THE INFERENCE. The letter dates the arrival to 25 August 1835, so the walk is the morning of the 26th - eight weeks after the scene date. The same letter's "forty years ago" implies 1836 and Andreas's lead-in says Bonnell "came to Chicago in 1837"; the 1837 reading is ruled out by the letter's own content, since the Lake House was open by the autumn of 1836, and between 1835 and 1836 this project prefers the letter's explicit date, which is the ruling already committed on the record of Lake House (under construction). See the research notes on north bank east end neighbours.

levels.8-10: No paper dates either end of this house's years. We start them at the first day of the year it is seen, as we do for the Lake House. The one time anyone saw it was 26 August 1835, eight weeks after our day. Starting there would leave it out of the very scene it belongs to. We carry it back because the house was full: Mrs Kelsey had all the boarders she could take. That is a busy house, not a new one. That is a guess, and we say so. We end its years at the end of 1835, since nothing says when it came down. Later town books put the Kelseys in a boarding house on Wolcott Street, about 750 feet west. We do not say that is the same house. A man named Bonnell wrote about his walk here in a letter of 1876. It is the only paper that puts a building on the sand hills, and it is one sentence long.

entries.card: why:NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE. THE START IS THE FIRST DAY…
entries.text: NEITHER END IS DATED BY A SOURCE. THE START IS THE FIRST DAY THE ATTESTED YEAR PERMITS, not a date anybody gives - the same convention, for the same reason, that Lake House (under construction)'s own range opens on. The one sighting is the morning of 26 August 1835, eight weeks AFTER the scene date, and a range opening there would put this house outside the scene it is attested in. What carries it back is an argument about the household and not about the building: Kimberly's partnership with Pruyne is in the town from 1832-33 by this project's own committed household record, the drug store on South Water Street is a going concern in the 1835 newspapers, and nothing in Bonnell's sentence reads as a house eight weeks old. That is an inference and it is graded as one. THE END IS THE HONEST YEAR BOUND: nothing reached says when this house came down, was sold or was replaced, and the 1843 and 1844 directories that print Kimberly do not print a dwelling for him. BONNELL'S WALK IS THE ONLY SOURCE THIS PROJECT HAS REACHED THAT DESCRIBES THE GROUND EAST OF THE LAKE HOUSE BUILDING SITE, AND IT IS ONE SENTENCE LONG. J. D. Bonnell, writing to the Chicago Times on 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas (History of Chicago vol. 1, printed pages 136-137), describes the morning after he arrived: "Passing east, toward the mouth of the river, was the Lake House in course of construction, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball, who was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street. Mr. Pruyne was State Senator." THE MAN IS IDENTIFIED THREE WAYS OVER AND THE SPELLING IS BONNELL'S OR HIS TYPESETTER'S. "Dr. Kimball" is Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly: a doctor, Peter Pruyne's partner, and a druggist on South Water Street are three attributes and this project already holds all three on one household - the hh pruyne kimberly data, "The Pruyne and Kimberly partnership household", headed by Peter Pruyne, recorded trade druggist, whose own arrival note quotes Moses and Kirkland naming "Dr. E. S. Kimberly... of Vermont". Pruyne's senatorship is the fourth check and it is right: he sat for this district. No other Kimball or Kimberly in the identity master is a physician or Pruyne's partner. THE DATE IS EIGHT WEEKS LATE AND THE CARRY BACK IS THE INFERENCE. The letter dates the arrival to 25 August 1835, so the walk is the morning of the 26th - eight weeks after the scene date. The same letter's "forty years ago" implies 1836 and Andreas's lead-in says Bonnell "came to Chicago in 1837"; the 1837 reading is ruled out by the letter's own content, since the Lake House was open by the autumn of 1836, and between 1835 and 1836 this project prefers the letter's explicit date, which is the ruling already committed on the record of Lake House (under construction). See the research notes on north bank east end neighbours.

levels.8-10: No paper dates either end of this house's years. We start them at the first day of the year it is seen, as we do for the Lake House. The one time anyone saw it was 26 August 1835, eight weeks after our day. Starting there would leave it out of the very scene it belongs to. We carry it back because of the family: Dr Kimberly was in town by 1832, and his drug store was busy in the papers of 1835. Nothing about the house sounds new. That is a guess, and we say so. We end its years at the end of 1835, since nothing says when it came down. A man named Bonnell wrote about his walk here in a letter of 1876. He calls it the house of Dr Kimball, Mr Pruyne's partner in a drug store. A doctor, Pruyne's partner, and a drug store all point to Dr Kimberly, and the spelling is likely Bonnell's mistake.

entries.card: why:NEITHER END OF THIS RANGE IS ATTESTED AND THE CONFIDENCE SAY…
entries.text: NEITHER END OF THIS RANGE IS ATTESTED AND THE CONFIDENCE SAYS SO. The dossier lists the Kinzie & Hunter warehouse among the river warehouses — 'Kinzie & Hunter and Dole & Newberry each had a warehouse with its dock along the river front' — and then records the gap explicitly: 'Kinzie & Hunter: bank and date unattested in sources reached [GAP]' (the research notes on structures north section 3.10, and again in its list of highest-priority remaining gaps, item 4: 'Kinzie & Hunter warehouse — bank, date, size'). Nothing found in this slice fills it. 1834 is chosen as the opening year because it is the year the harbour cut let vessels into the river and the year river warehousing became a business worth building for, and because John H. Kinzie and Lieutenant Hunter had come to Chicago in February 1833 to lay out lots and open streets through their North Side property — so a partnership of those two names doing river trade belongs to 1833-34 and not earlier. THAT IS A GUESS WITH A REASON, WHICH IS WHAT CONJECTURAL MEANS. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim. A firm of Kinzie, Hunter & Co. is separately attested in the lumber trade a couple of years after the first cargo of pine was landed on the south bank between LaSalle and Wells (Andreas scan p. 1139), which corroborates the partnership doing river business in this decade and does not date this building.

levels.8-10: No paper dates either end of this warehouse's years, and we say so. Our notes list it among the river warehouses with docks. They also say plainly that its bank and date are not known. We start it in 1834. That is the year the harbour cut let ships into the river, so river warehouses became worth building. John Kinzie and Lieutenant Hunter came to Chicago in 1833 to lay out lots, so their business belongs to those years. That is a guess with a reason. We end it at the end of 1835. A few years later a firm with their names was in the lumber trade. That backs up the partnership, but it does not date this building.

entries.card: why:NEITHER END OF THIS RANGE IS ATTESTED. Two statements fix th…
entries.text: NEITHER END OF THIS RANGE IS ATTESTED. Two statements fix the middle of it. chicagology's Wolf Point narrative describes Robert A. Kinzie's storehouse dealing in groceries and Indian goods at Wolf Point, and the source record gives that account's describes date as 1830-1835; Andreas's list of the town's traders (scan p. 235) gives 'Indian Traders — Robert A. Kinzie, near Wentworth's tavern', in a passage enumerating who was trading where, and Andreas separately records (scan p. 249) that Robert A. Kinzie was among those licensed to sell goods at that period. So the range opens at the start of 1830 as the earliest year the descriptions can be held to, NOT as a build date — the store is generally placed at Wolf Point from the later 1820s and this record does not adopt that because no source reached here states it. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date the record needs to claim. THE SURVIVAL TO 1835-07-01 IS THE WEAK JOINT: the Indian trade at Chicago was ending in exactly these years — the 1833 Treaty of Chicago ceded the land and the removal ran through the summer of 1835 — so a store whose business was 'groceries and Indian goods' had lost half its trade by the scene date. What that did to the BUILDING is not recorded either way, and this record claims only that the building stood.

levels.8-10: No paper dates either end of this store's years. Two papers fix the middle. One says Robert Kinzie's store sold food and goods for the Native trade at Wolf Point, sometime from 1830 to 1835. A history book lists him as a trader near Wentworth's tavern, with a license to sell goods. So we start it in 1830, the earliest the papers allow. That is not when it was built. We end it at the end of 1835. The weak part is whether it lasted to July 1835. The Native trade was ending just then. The treaty of 1833 gave up the land, and the people were made to leave through the summer of 1835. So the store had lost half its trade. We do not know what that did to the building, and we only say it stood.

entries.card: why:NINE HUNDRED FEET, AND IT IS AN INTERPOLATION BETWEEN TWO YE…
entries.text: NINE HUNDRED FEET, AND IT IS AN INTERPOLATION BETWEEN TWO YEAR-END FIGURES. IT IS NOT DOCUMENTED AND NOTHING SHOULD READ IT AS THOUGH IT WERE. THE TWO ENDS OF THE ARITHMETIC. End of 1834: the north pier about 700 ft, with the entrance 200 ft wide and 3 to 7 ft deep (Wikipedia's Chicago River summary of the harbour works). End of the 1835 season: 'the north (weather) pier had been extended to 1,260 ft into the lake, to 12 ft of water' (Andreas I, scan pp. 487 and 489, per the research notes on structures south section 3). Between those two dates the pier grew 560 ft, and NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES A LENGTH FOR ANY DATE INSIDE THE 1835 SEASON. HOW 1 JULY WAS PLACED BETWEEN THEM, stated so it can be checked and disagreed with. Straight calendar interpolation puts 1 July at half the year and therefore at 980 ft. That overstates it, because pier work is not a calendar activity: crib building and sinking on Lake Michigan run in the open season, roughly April to November, so by 1 July perhaps a third of a season's work is in the water and the season-weighted figure is nearer 890 ft. the research notes on structures south section 3 reaches 'roughly 800-1,000 ft' by the same kind of reasoning. Nine hundred feet is the middle of that band and sits between the two arithmetics; it is a considered choice among defensible numbers and not a measurement. THE ERROR BAR IS THE BAND AND NOT A DECIMAL. Anything from 800 to 1,000 ft is equally consistent with the evidence, which is plus or minus about 30 m on a 274 m structure — an order of magnitude worse than the georeference this pier's position carries, and the reason the footprint is graded on it. A CONFLICT INSIDE THE PROJECT'S OWN RESEARCH, recorded rather than averaged. the research notes on terrain hydrology section 3.3 interpolates the same pier at 'roughly 1,000-1,300 ft' for summer 1835 — because it interpolates from 700 ft in 1834 to 1,850 ft in October 1837 and had not found the end-of-1835 figure. Dossier 04 found it. An interpolation that steps over a known intermediate value is superseded by one that does not, so 04's band is adopted and 01's is recorded here as the reading it replaces. A SECOND CONFLICT, at the 1834 end. Andreas has the north pier extended in spring 1834 'a like distance' to the south pier's 400-500 ft; Wikipedia has it at about 700 ft by the end of 1834. Those are consistent if the pier grew through the season from about 500 ft to about 700 ft, which is what one would expect, so both are kept and the year-end figure is the one the arithmetic starts from. WHAT WOULD REPLACE ALL OF THIS: the Chief Engineer's annual report for 1835, or the House Document series — the research notes on terrain hydrology names them as the thing to find, and a single line in either would turn this attribute documented. SETTLED 2026-09-12, other work, AND THE CONFLICT RECORDED ABOVE TURNS OUT NOT TO BE ONE. The paragraph above treats dossier 01's 'roughly 1,000-1,300 ft' as a rival reading that dossier 04's end-of-1835 figure supersedes. Do 01's own arithmetic and the rivalry disappears: from 700 ft on 31 December 1834 to 1,850 ft in October 1837 is 1,019 days and 1,150 ft, or 1.13 ft a day, and 1 July 1835 is 182 days along — 905 FT. That is five feet from the 900 recorded here, on a straight calendar interpolation with no season-weighting at all. What 01's band actually describes is a YEAR-END length: the same line reaches 1,112 ft at 31 December 1835, inside the band, and dossier 04's documented 1,260 ft for the close of that season is inside it too. So 01's figure is not wrong about the pier; it is a late-1835 figure printed under a 'summer 1835' heading, and reading it at the scene date is what made it look like a conflict. NOTHING MOVES. Three lines of reasoning — 01's endpoints interpolated to the day, 04's season-weighted band of 800-1,000 ft, and 04's documented year-end figure worked backwards — now converge on about 900 ft, where before there were two that disagreed. The band recorded above as 'the reading it replaces' is instead a THIRD agreement, and 01's own text has been corrected to date its figure rather than dropped (the research notes on terrain hydrology section 3.3 and the zone 24 row). The geometry is unchanged, so this costs no bake.

levels.8-10: Nine hundred feet is our guess, worked out between two numbers from the ends of two years. No paper gives it. At the end of 1834 the north pier was about 700 feet long. By the end of the 1835 season it was 1,260 feet. No paper gives a length for any day in between. Pier work went on only from spring to fall, so by July only about a third of a season's work was done. That gives about 890 feet. Our notes give 800 to 1,000 feet. Nine hundred is the middle. Anything in that range fits the proof just as well. Later we checked another way, using a length from 1837, and it came out at 905 feet. So three ways of reckoning now agree on about 900 feet. The army engineer's report for 1835 would settle it.

entries.card: why:NO DATE AT ALL IS ATTESTED FOR THIS BUSINESS OR ITS BUILDING…
entries.text: NO DATE AT ALL IS ATTESTED FOR THIS BUSINESS OR ITS BUILDING, AND THE RANGE IS THEREFORE THE WEAKEST KIND THIS DATASET HOLDS. What Andreas gives is a partnership and a street: Kimball was 'a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street', placed in the 1830s and no closer. The range is set to 1834-1835 because the town's commercial street barely existed before 1833 and because a range that opened in 1830 would be widened to pass rather than narrowed to what is attested — which is the failure this project's own gate warns about. The honest statement is that this record asserts the drug store was open on 1835-07-01 and cannot prove it. IF EVIDENCE DATES THE PARTNERSHIP AFTER JULY 1835 THIS RECORD BELONGS IN the exclusions record, and that is the most likely single correction to it.

levels.8-10: No paper dates this business or its building at all. So its years are our weakest kind. A history book says only that Kimball was Mr Pruyne's partner in a drug store on South Water Street, in the 1830s. We set its years at 1834 to 1835. The shop street barely existed before 1833. Opening it earlier would only stretch the years to fit. We say the store was open on 1 July 1835, but we cannot prove it. If a paper shows the two began after July 1835, this store leaves the scene. That is the most likely fix.

entries.card: why:NO DATE IS ATTESTED AND THIS RANGE IS A WINDOW, NOT A FINDIN…
entries.text: NO DATE IS ATTESTED AND THIS RANGE IS A WINDOW, NOT A FINDING. The source sentence is 'The first store building on Lake Street, a two-story frame structure, was built by Thomas Church', and it carries no year. THE PAGE INVITES A DATE IT DOES NOT GIVE: the sentences around it run 1833, then 1835, then 1837, so a reader picks up 1833 from position on the page rather than from the sentence, and this project's own source record for that page warns about exactly that. The dossier tags the date as unpinned and treats the building as circa 1833-35. The range is set to 1834-1835 as the middle of that window: Lake Street barely existed as a commercial street before 1833, and a range opened in 1833 would be widening to pass rather than narrowing to what is attested. IF THE BUILDING IS 1835 WORK IT MAY HAVE BEEN GOING UP OR NOT YET STANDING ON 1835-07-01, and this record would then be wrong to include it. That is the single most likely correction to it, and it is a correction that would move the record into the exclusions record rather than merely retag it. SOURCE CAVEAT THAT TRAVELS WITH EVERY DOCUMENTED TAG ON THIS RECORD: the claim sits in an uncredited modern editorial addendum at the foot of a chicagology map gallery, graded a historian's account by this project's own source record, which says in terms that the addendum is the weakest text in that set and must never outrank Andreas. It is cited because it is explicit and because it is the only place this building has been found, not because it is strong.

levels.8-10: No paper dates this building, so its years are a window, not a finding. The paper says only that Thomas Church built the first store on Lake Street, a two floor frame building. It gives no year. The lines around it on the page say 1833, then 1835, then 1837, so a reader is tempted to pick 1833 from where it sits. We do not. We set its years at 1834 to 1835, the middle of the window. If it was built in 1835, it may not have stood yet on 1 July, and it would have to leave the scene. That is the most likely fix. The only paper that names this building is a short modern note, our weakest kind, which never outranks the main history book.

entries.card: why:NO DATE IS GIVEN FOR THE STABLE ITSELF; the range is the hot…
entries.text: NO DATE IS GIVEN FOR THE STABLE ITSELF; the range is the hotel's, and it is the hotel's for a reason that is stated rather than assumed. chicagology describes the stable as part of the house — 'In the rear was the large stable and the yard into which the trains were driven' — inside the same passage that describes the building W. H. Stow says he put up in 1834, and a teamsters' house whose custom was 'farmers and teamsters' had no trade at all without somewhere to put their horses. So the stable is taken to be contemporary with the hotel and the range is copied from the record of Western Hotel, including its adopted 1834 date and the dispute behind it (chicagology on Stow's own word against the hotel chronology's 1835). THE SURVIVAL EVIDENCE IS BETTER FOR THE STABLE THAN FOR THE HOTEL and is deliberately not used to widen the range: the same source records that in 1849 'the boys over at the engine house, which stood on the other side of Canal street, were having some sport and came very near burning the stables of the hotel', which puts stables on this site fourteen years after the scene date. The range stops at the end of 1840 anyway, where the hotel's does, because a fifteen-year range on a building nobody dates is the kind of widening this project's own gate warns about, and because nothing in this scene needs the later years.

levels.8-10: No paper dates the stable itself. We give it the hotel's years, and we say why. A paper describes the large stable and yard at the back as part of the hotel, in the same passage as the hotel. A house for farmers and teamsters had no trade without a place for their horses. So the stable is as old as the hotel, built in 1834. A paper says the stable was still there in 1849, when boys nearly burned it. We do not use that to stretch its years. We end them at the end of 1840, as the hotel's do.

entries.card: why:NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY, and unlike the Sauganash there is no…
entries.text: NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY, and unlike the Sauganash there is no retrospective depiction in the project's hands to reason from. The witnesses describe two entrances — the front on Canal and one 'about the middle of the long side' on Lake — without mentioning a porch, veranda or gallery, which is weak negative evidence at best, since they were correcting a drawing rather than inventorying the elevation. False is the default, not a finding. The c. 1859 photograph ("Green Tree Tavern, Chicago, 1859." Photograph of the Green Tree Tavern at the…) settles this the moment anyone opens it.

levels.8-10: We do not know if it had a porch. Unlike the Sauganash, we have no later picture of it. The people who described it give two doors, one at the front and one in the middle of the long side. They say nothing of a porch. That proves very little, since they were fixing a drawing, not listing every part. No porch is what our rules do when they know nothing. It is not a finding. A photo of about 1859 would settle it the moment someone looks.

entries.card: why:NO SEAT IS CLAIMED HERE, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE POINT. Andre…
entries.text: NO SEAT IS CLAIMED HERE, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE POINT. Andreas names Billy Caldwell as the occupant of one of the small log buildings in this vicinity, and that is why this record exists. But his household card holds TWO candidate residences and refuses to choose between them: this ring of log buildings, and the frame house 'built for him by the Department for Indian Affairs on the North Side near where is now the corner of State Street and Chicago Avenue', which Andreas elsewhere calls probably the first frame building in Chicago after Robert Kinzie's store. Neither is dated to 1835. Raising this building does not settle that question — it makes one of the two candidates a thing a visitor can see — so the Caldwell household keeps lives at: null and this roof carries no occupant. THE USE IS STATED INSTEAD: a dwelling of the agency's log ring. Writing a seat here would be this project choosing, by hand, the question its own card says it cannot answer.

levels.8-10: We put no one in this building, and that is on purpose. A history book says Billy Caldwell lived in one of the small log buildings here. That is why this building exists. But his card has two possible homes and will not pick one. One is this ring of log buildings. The other is a frame house the government built for him on the North Side. Neither is dated to 1835. Drawing this building does not settle the question. So his family has no home set, and no one lives here. We only say what it was: a house in the agency's ring of log buildings.

entries.card: why:NO SOURCE COUNTS A FLUE ON THIS BUILDING, AND THE WORK IN IT…
entries.text: NO SOURCE COUNTS A FLUE ON THIS BUILDING, AND THE WORK IN IT CANNOT BE DONE WITHOUT ONE. Andreas has Pierce buying the Rev. Mr See's set of tools and setting up in business in 1833, ironing the first Chicago-to-St-Louis stage line in January 1834 and making the 'Bull' plough from the spring (scan p. 1161): forge work, all of it, and a forge under a board roof has a stack over it or the shop burns. The count is therefore reasoned from evidence about THIS building's attested trade rather than stated of it, which is what `inferred` is for, and it is one because nothing suggests two fires. The FABRIC is the archetype's and is brick on the research notes on chimneys §2's argument, not a reading of this shop. Its dimensions are the archetype's and are invented within the work: a fire bed wide enough to lay a bar across, a flue narrower than the hearth that gathers into it, and a head standing between the eighteen inches the town's by-law of 1835 required over a roof and the four feet Andreas remembered no Chicago chimney exceeding. the liberties register carries the invention.

levels.8-10: No paper counts a chimney on this building, but its work could not be done without one. A history book says Pierce bought a set of tools and set up in business in 1833. He made iron parts for the first stage line to St. Louis, and he made ploughs. That is all work at a forge, and a forge under a wooden roof needs a chimney, or the shop burns. So the count comes from what the shop did. It is one, since nothing hints at two fires. The chimney is brick, and its size comes from our rules. A town law of 1835 set how high a chimney had to stand over a roof, and we keep it inside that.

entries.text: NO SOURCE REACHED DATES THIS BUILDING AT EITHER END, and the range is a coverage statement rather than a finding. What is attested is that the house stood in the west-bank row at Wolf Point in the years chicagology's account describes; the source record gives that account's describes date as 1830-1835, so the range opens at the start of 1830 because that is the earliest year the description can be held to and NOT because anything says the house was built then. It may well be older: James Kinzie built the Wolf Point Tavern next door in 1828 (see the record of Wolf Point Tavern, where the build date is itself disputed 1823 against 1828) and he was trading at the forks through the 1820s, so a residence of the middle 1820s is entirely possible. The range closes at the end of 1835 on this project's usual rule — the last date the record needs to claim — and not on any statement about the house coming down. Extend it in either direction when evidence appears; do not widen it to make something pass.

So we start it in 1830, the earliest the paper allows. That is not when it was built. It may be older. James Kinzie built the tavern next door in 1828, and he traded here through the 1820s. We end it at the end of 1835, as we usually do. Its years can grow when proof turns up, but never just to fit.

entries.card: why:NOBODY EVER WROTE DOWN HOW WIDE THIS BRIDGE WAS. Andreas giv…
entries.text: NOBODY EVER WROTE DOWN HOW WIDE THIS BRIDGE WAS. Andreas gives its length, its draw, its pattern, its frames, its repairs and its destruction, and not its width; the 1902 text gives length and draw and nothing else; the 1883 old-settlers statement that supplies ten feet for both BRANCH bridges is explicitly about those two and not about this one. THE VALUE IS THE ARCHETYPE'S DEFAULT, KEPT DELIBERATELY RATHER THAN REPLACED WITH A FRESH GUESS — the same choice the liberties register “The North Branch bridge stands on fifteen piers nobody recorded” made about the North Branch bridge's pier spacing, and for the same reason: a new number chosen to look sensible would read as a finding and would not be one. bridge timber's default is the branch bridges' documented ten feet, which is almost certainly too narrow for the main crossing of the town's principal street, carrying teams, on a structure a shipwright framed to a premium design. It is kept because being visibly the neighbour's number is more honest than being plausibly nobody's. The chip on this row is conjectural and the whole footprint inherits it. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the town trustees' specification, the February 1834 proposals Andreas mentions, or the 1834-35 repair vouchers — the corporation paid $166.67 for repairs in September 1834 and the bridge was repaired again in 1835, and a repair account is the kind of document that states a deck width. CURRENT SOURCE-VERIFIED CORRECTION — other work, 2026-10-29. The preceding absolute statement that nobody wrote down a width is superseded. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, volume 1 (Munsell, 1895), printed page 95, actually read at archive.org, says of the 1834 Dearborn crossing: “It was 300 feet in length, by sixteen in width, and had a double draw.” Adopt sixteen feet, or 4.8768 m, as an inferred width from retrospective secondary text. This is stronger evidence than borrowing the branch bridges’ ten-foot default, but it is not a contemporary trustee specification, a surveyed width or a photographic measurement. The same sentence’s 300-foot total length describes a different extent from the independently traced 76.33 m water gap; it does not move that traced length or the source origin. Its phrase “double draw” does not settle the lifting mechanism. The existing native parameter resolver rounds this width to 4.877 m, a 0.2 mm precision difference. No dimension is fitted from the provisional drawing camera. The old ten-foot choice and reasoning remain above as history.

levels.8-10: For a long time we had no width for this bridge. A history book gives its length, its lifting part, its frames, its repairs and its end, but not its width. So we used our rules' usual width, ten feet, from the other two bridges. That was almost surely too narrow for the town's main bridge. We kept it, since a borrowed number is more honest than a made up one. Then, in October 2026, we read a later history book. It says the 1834 bridge was 300 feet long and sixteen feet wide. So the bridge is now sixteen feet wide. That book was written long after, so this is a good guess, not a fact. Its length does not change the length we traced.

entries.text: NOT A LODGE. The archetype's canvas wall tent is drawn because no committed source describes a Potawatomi, Odawa, Ojibwe or Métis lodge at Chicago in 1835, and other work adds a lodge form to the archetype only where a source describes one. The canvas is not offered as how these families lived; it is the one roof this project can draw without inventing a people's building. “One trading family's camp at Wolf Point, a declared reconstruction the owner ruled built”.

levels.8-10: This is not a lodge. We draw a canvas tent because no paper we have describes a lodge of the Potawatomi, Odawa, Ojibwe or Métis people in Chicago in 1835.
