entries.card: why:NOT THE POST OFFICE AT THE SCENE DATE, which is the fact thi…
entries.text: NOT THE POST OFFICE AT THE SCENE DATE, which is the fact this record exists to get right. It held Chicago's first post office from 31 March 1831 until about July 1834, when Andreas has the office removed to near the corner of Franklin and South Water, where it stayed through Hogan's term. What the building was doing on 1835-07-01 is NOT ATTESTED: it is recorded as a store because that is what it was before the post office arrived ('a log house occupied as a store') and alongside it for three years, and because nothing describes it changing to anything else. Brewster, Hogan & Co. advertised as forwarding and commission merchants in the early numbers of the Chicago Democrat, but no source reached puts the firm in THIS building in 1835, so the record carries no occupants block rather than guessing at one. THE STORE IS NOW ATTESTED IN HOGAN'S OWN WORDS, AND SO IS THE READING THIS ATTRIBUTE EXISTS TO GET RIGHT. Three printings of the Chicago Democrat in August and September 1834 — after Andreas has the post office removed — carry his standing card: "J. S. C. HOGAN, [O]FFERS at Wholesale and Retail, at his Store in South Water Street, one door belo[w th]e Post O[ff]ice, Dry Good[s], Grocer[i]es, [H]ardware, Cr[oc]kery and Gl[ass] W[a]re" (1834-09-03, page 3 column 6, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-09-03, dateline '[J]uly 30, 1834'; the same advertisement runs 1834-08-13 page 3 column 5 claim #c017 and 1834-08-20 page 3 column 5 claim #c007, both cut at the direction word). A fourth card, 1834-03-25 page 3 column 3 claim #c010, has him selling 300 cedar posts. So a wholesale and retail store on South Water Street is documented in the year before the scene date, which is what this attribute claims, and the value stays 'store'. THE POST OFFICE IS A FINDING AND IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN ACTED ON. Hogan places his store 'one door below the Post Office' from August 1834, which is exactly the period this record has the office already removed 'to near the corner of Franklin and South Water' — and one door is not four blocks. Both cannot be true as written. NOTHING IS MOVED ON THE STRENGTH OF IT: the register's own bound is that a placement inference never displaces a committed documented building and a conflict is a finding, not a nudge. The candidates are that Andreas's removal is later or nearer than he says, that Hogan's card is standing copy carried over from before the removal (its dateline of 30 July 1834 is within weeks of it), or that this record's reading of Andreas is too precise. Filed for the register to adjudicate against the 1835 file, which is where a scene-date fixture for Hogan already exists. THE READING IS TRANSCRIPTION-MEDIATED AND SAYS SO. Under the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 a claim read through this project's OCR-assisted transcriptions rather than off the page scan grades `attested` in this schema's vocabulary while carrying its own flag: reading = transcription mediated, with the transcription's own uncertainty brackets preserved inside the quotation rather than tidied away. Where a scan is later read, the scan is the authority and this claim upgrades under it — the standard The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday… set when a scan caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'.

levels.8-10: This building was not the post office on our day in 1835, and that is the fact this card gets right. It held Chicago's first post office from 1831 until about July 1834. Then a history book says the office moved near Franklin and South Water Streets. No paper says what this building was in 1835. We call it a store, since it was a store before the post office came, and nothing says it changed. Hogan's own ad in 1834 offers dry goods, food, hardware and dishes at his store on South Water Street. So a store is proved for the year before. But the ad puts his store one door from the post office, just when the book has the office moved four blocks away. Both cannot be true. We move nothing, and leave the question written down. We read this ad from a typed copy, not the page itself, and we say so.

entries.card: why:NOTHING DATES THIS CROSSING BECAUSE NOTHING RECORDS IT, and…
entries.text: NOTHING DATES THIS CROSSING BECAUSE NOTHING RECORDS IT, and that is the first thing to say about the record. Its sibling four hundred metres east is attested — where Water Street crossed the State Street slough 'a log bridge was needed until after 1840' ("Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology, transcribed at the research notes on terrain hydrology section 2.2) — and no comparable sentence exists for the La Salle drain. WHAT IS REASONED, and it is reasoning and not a date: the town trustees ordered South Water Street pitched and graded from the United States Reservation to Randolph Street in August 1833 (the research notes on structures south), a graded public street has to get across whatever it meets, and the drain Wright draws entering the main stem just east of La Salle Street is one of the two things it met. So the range opens with its sibling's, at the start of 1833, and closes at the end of 1835 as this project's convention rather than as a claim that the crossing went then. THE PROJECT READ THIS GROUND THE OTHER WAY UNTIL 2026-08-21: the terrain record's own note ran the drain's head to the street line and no further, on the reading that 'the street crossed on fill or a culvert nothing describes'. The owner overruled that from the street, looking west at 277 degrees: the drain should be 'a continous water drain into the river and have plank crossings for both the road and the sidewalk'. This record is the crossing that ruling requires, and it is RECONSTRUCTED throughout — see other work and the liberties register.

levels.8-10: Nothing dates this bridge, because nothing records it. Its brother bridge to the east is in a paper: a log bridge crossed the swamp at State Street until after 1840. Nothing like that exists for this drain at La Salle Street. Here is our reasoning, and it is not a date. In August 1833 the town ordered South Water Street graded. A graded street has to get across what it meets, and this drain was one of those things. So the years start with its brother's, in 1833, and end at the end of 1835. Until August 2026 we read this ground the other way, with the street crossing on fill. The owner of this project looked from the street and ruled there should be a drain into the river, with plank bridges for the road and the walk. This bridge is the one that ruling needs. It is made up all through.

entries.text: NOTHING PLACES THIS BUILDING AND THIS COORDINATE IS A CHOICE. No source reached mentions a stable at the Wolf Point Tavern at all, let alone where it stood; the building is inferred from a priced service (see function), and its position is inferred from nothing. METHOD, such as it is: the record of Wolf Point Tavern faces east onto the river at bearing 90, so the landward side of the house is west, and this coordinate puts the stable about 11 m west of the tavern's back wall and offset 3 m south of its south end — clear of the tavern, clear of Log cabins at Wolf Point 36 m to the north, and off the river frontage, which at a house whose whole trade came by water and by the Lake Street crossing is where the yard work would go. EVERY ONE OF THOSE IS AN ARGUMENT FROM THE TRADE AND NOT FROM A SOURCE. It also inherits the tavern's own placement, which the liberties register records as one of three Wolf Point buildings placed on relative descriptions rather than on a map. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: the tavern's own, roughly 40 m along the bank and 20 m across it, plus the whole of the offset recorded here, which is invention. Facade bearing 0, north, chosen so the stable's long side runs along the back of the tavern; nothing states it, and no bearing here would be better evidenced than any other.

entries.card: why:NOTHING RECORDS THIS CROSSING, and it is the third of three…
entries.text: NOTHING RECORDS THIS CROSSING, and it is the third of three on the same footing and the thinnest of them. Its eldest sibling is attested — where Water Street crossed the State Street slough 'a log bridge was needed until after 1840' ("Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology, transcribed at the research notes on terrain hydrology §2.2) — and the La Salle crossing was built on the owner's ruling that a drain reaching the river must be crossed rather than filled. This one has neither: no sentence names it and no ruling asked for it. WHAT IS REASONED, and it is reasoning and not a date: Wright 1834 draws the north-side slough running north out of the main stem ACROSS KINZIE STREET to Michigan Street, so the map that is this project's evidence for the watercourse also shows the town's own platted grid laid over it; North Water Street is the river-front street of that grid and it meets the same water two hundred metres south of where Kinzie does. A platted street that meets a stream either stops at it or gets across it, and the range therefore opens with its two siblings' at the start of 1833, when the town began building crossings at all — the North Branch log bridge is winter 1831-32, the South Branch raft bridge winter 1832-33 — and closes at the end of 1835 as this project's convention rather than as a claim that it went then. THE HONEST READING OF THE ALTERNATIVE: North Water Street may simply have stopped at the slough in 1835, with the North Division's traffic using Kinzie Street a block north. That would be a street ending at a stream, which is not what the record here says; it is what nothing says either way. This crossing is RECONSTRUCTED throughout — see other work and the liberties register.

levels.8-10: Nothing records this bridge. It is the third of three like it, and the thinnest. Its oldest brother is in a paper. The second was built on the owner of this project's ruling that a drain to the river must be crossed, not filled. This one has neither. Here is our reasoning, and it is not a date. An old map of 1834 shows a swamp on the north side running across the town's own street plan. North Water Street meets that water. A street that meets a stream either stops or gets across it. So its years start with its brothers', in 1833, and end at the end of 1835. It may be that North Water Street simply stopped at the swamp. Nothing says either way. This bridge is made up all through.

entries.card: why:No period source describes the window arrangement. A regular…
entries.text: No period source describes the window arrangement. A regular five-bay elevation with a centred entrance is the standard disposition for a building of this size and type, and both retrospective depictions show regular bays. The COUNT and SPACING are inference; that it was regularly fenestrated is safe. MEASURED 2026-09-04 (spending): the scheme this attribute has carried all along is the one the plate draws, and it is no longer typological inference. Braunhold's street face detects five openings in the upper storey and five in the ground storey, with the door the MIDDLE of the five — the darkest opening on the ground storey at ink 0.494, and nothing else on the sheet is inked like an open door onto an unlit room. The five are EQUAL: drawn gaps of 169.2, 161.1, 153.0 and 137.5 px are a 20.4 % spread that reads as an irregular rhythm and is not one, rectifying to 0.997, 1.011, 1.020 and 0.972 against the face's own vanishing point. The GRADE does not move — one sheet, a modern reconstruction, its two companions copies of it — and neither does the geometry, which already drew this. What changes is that the row now rests on a measurement: the research notes on sauganash image accuracy rows 1-4.

levels.8-10: No paper of the time describes the windows. Five openings across, with the door in the middle, is the usual plan for a building this size and kind. Both later pictures show windows spaced evenly. In September 2026 we measured one of those pictures. It shows five openings on the top floor and five below. The door is in the middle. The five are spaced evenly, once we take out the slant of the drawing. How sure we are does not change. There is only one picture, drawn long after. But this now rests on a measure.

entries.text: No source gives a storey count. One storey with a loft under the roof is the standard form for a log tavern of this date and region, and it is the conservative reading: the sources that do describe height at Wolf Point single out the Sauganash's two storeys and Miller's two-storey frame addition as remarkable, which they would not be if the Wolf Point Tavern had also been two storeys. Not attested either way. The Braunhold-style retrospective view 'Wolf Point from the south as it might have appeared in 1830' reproduced in Andreas shows this building and Miller's together and is the obvious next check — it has not been examined for this record, and it is a retrospective (a modern reconstruction) in any case. Other work L review has now inspected all eight piece of work views. Its one-storey interpretation is supported by the pictured low gable ends, but the retrospective views do not establish the exactJuly1835 state.

levels.8-10: No paper gives the number of floors. One floor with a loft under the roof is the usual form for a log inn of this time and place. It is the careful reading. The papers point out the Sauganash's two floors and Miller's two floor addition as special. They would not, if this inn had two floors as well. A later picture in the history book shows this building, and we have now looked at all eight such views. Their low gable ends back up one floor. But they cannot show exactly how it was in July 1835.

entries.text: Not stated in the notice, and inferred from date, place and vendor. The 1834-35 south-side stock this project's dossiers record is overwhelmingly frame and log with no brick dwelling of consequence before 1837, and the man advertising this house is P. Pruyne, the timber merchant whose own notice a fortnight earlier sizes the town's structural sticks (the Chicago Democrat of 1834-05-07 c012). Braced rather than balloon frame follows the Sauganash record's argument. A log house would be a log dwelling record and the archetype refuses to build one as frame, so this choice is made here rather than hidden.

levels.8-10: The notice does not say, and we reason from the date, place and seller. Our notes say the south side's buildings of 1834 and 1835 were mostly frame and log, with no brick house of note before 1837. The man selling this house is P. Pruyne, a wood seller. His own notice two weeks before lists the building timbers sold in town. We chose an older, heavier frame, as for the Sauganash. A log house would need different rules, so we make this choice here, and do not hide it.

Our notes say the shops of 1833 to 1835 were frame. We chose an older, heavier frame, as for the Sauganash. If this building was log, it needs different rules, and that is a bigger fix than new paint.

entries.card: why:Not stated. 'Pickets' in this literature means split or roug…
entries.text: Not stated. 'Pickets' in this literature means split or roughly squared timber posts set upright, and the fort was built by soldiers out of local timber. The archetype builds squared posts, which is the commonest form and the one that matches the hewn work in the town across the river. THE HEAD OF THE POST IS OURS, AND IT NOW HAS AN ATTRIBUTE OF ITS OWN - see picket head (m), which carries the number and its own reconstructed chip (the liberties register “The point on a Fort Dearborn picket is ours, and the plate that was said to draw it rules a flat top”). Every picket is sharpened over its top 0.312 m - 8.4 percent of the 3.7 m height, and CUT OUT OF that height rather than added to it, so the wall is not made taller by its own points; a visitor at the north wall reads the sawtooth, which is the whole reason the archetype does it, because a flat-topped post reads as a fence rail and a pointed one as a stockade. NOTHING REACHED DESCRIBES THE HEAD OF A FORT DEARBORN PICKET, and the plate said to draw them pointed does not. Measured on p4 0, the coloured view from across the river: the curtain's top is a RULED LINE, straight to 0.45 px rms over 138 resolved columns, while the same plate resolves individual pickets at a 10 px pitch and stands the curtain 43 px tall - so a head of this proportion would have serrated that top by 3.6 px, eight times the residual, and the draughtsman drew none. p4 1 rules the same flat cap. That refutes 'the plate draws them pointed' without settling the head either way, so the point remains a reconstruction and remains declared. the picket plate check holds the property and prints the whole reading.

levels.8-10: No paper says. In these old books, pickets means split or rough squared posts set upright. Soldiers built the fort out of local wood. Our rules build squared posts, the most common kind, and they match the work in town. The point on each post is ours. Each post is cut to a point at the top, and the point is part of its height, so the wall is not made taller. A pointed top looks like a fort wall, and a flat one looks like a fence. Nothing we have describes the top of a picket here. We measured an old coloured picture that was said to show points. It draws the top of the wall as a straight line. So the point stays made up, and we say so.

No picture shows exactly where a side door was.

This descriptive boolean remains record only; the actually consumed cupola shape and three explicit metric attributes now build it. The prior refusal to add any cupola solely because size, glazing, louvres and position were unknown is superseded: we choose one plain boarded square body with a pyramid cap at the existing ridge midpoint, without glazing, louvres or finial. Shape, position, material and every dimension are reconstructed, not measured from the plan or from an unidentified panorama building. This is the separately named barn cupola, not another version of the already-delivered blockhouse cupola.

levels.8-10: A paper names it, and we now build it. An 1830 plan of the fort writes Big Barn with Cupola, so we know the barn had a little tower on its roof. We used to draw none, since its size and look were unknown. Now we have chosen a plain square boarded tower with a pointed cap, in the middle of the roof ridge. It has no glass, slats or top piece. Its shape, place, wood and every size are made up. This is the barn's tower, not the one on the fort's lookout tower.

entries.card: why:ONE AXIS IS MEASURED AND THE OTHER IS INVENTED, AND THE LEAS…
entries.text: ONE AXIS IS MEASURED AND THE OTHER IS INVENTED, AND THE LEAST CONFIDENT WINS. The length, 76.33 m, is the distance between the two traced 1834 waterlines along the Dearborn alignment, read off shoreline.geojson at the crossing station (south bank local E +699.17, north bank local E +698.39, 76.33 m apart along the street line). That is 250.4 ft of water, and what it is worth is argued on form.overall length (m), because it is the first independent evidence this project has been able to put against a hundred-and-ninety-year-old disagreement about how long this bridge was. The width, 3.048 m, is not evidence of anything — see form.width (m) — so the polygon as a drawn shape is conjectural even though half of it was measured, on the same least-confident-wins rule the mesh uses. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT'S ERROR BAR ACTUALLY IS, and it is smaller than the georeference's headline number. The 20 m stated for anything traced from the 1834 sheets is dominated by a common-mode shift: an affine that puts the whole neighbourhood 20 m north puts both banks 20 m north and the distance between them does not move. What survives into a WIDTH is the sheet's local scale error — the fit records a 3.7 per cent difference between its two axis scales, which is real paper stretch — and the tracing tolerance of 1.78 m. Even a generous ten per cent leaves the water gap above 225 ft. NO SOURCE IS CITED ON THIS BLOCK, DELIBERATELY. The measured axis is argued in this note and cited on form.overall length (m); a conjectural block carrying a source id would claim the survey supports a shape it cannot. CURRENT WIDTH CORRECTION — other work, 2026-10-29. The former paragraph describes the historical ten-foot proxy. Width now follows the sixteen feet explicitly stated in Moses and Kirkland (1895), volume 1, printed page 95, directly read in the scan, at inferred secondary confidence. The other axis remains the independently traced 76.33 m bank-to-bank water gap on Wright’s 1834 map. Neither source attests this complete rectangle as a survey: length is traced and width comes from retrospective text. Local origin [0, 0], mapped position, rotation, traced banks and span are unchanged. Extending only local positive-v implements the stronger width evidence while preserving the existing geographic controls. No movement of the street, bank, heightfield or model origin is inferred from a picture.

levels.8-10: One side of this bridge is measured, and the other was made up, so its shape counts as a guess. Its length is the gap of water between the two banks on an old map of 1834, along Dearborn Street. That is about 250 feet. It is the first proof we have had to weigh in a very old argument about how long this bridge was. The map may be off by a lot in where it puts things. But it shifts both banks the same way, so the gap between them barely moves. Even with a big error, the gap stays over 225 feet. Its width was once a borrowed ten feet. In October 2026 we read a later history book that gives sixteen feet, so it is now sixteen feet wide. That is a good guess from a later book, not a survey.

entries.card: why:ONE OF THE SIX MEN ANDREAS COUNTS AS CHICAGO'S LAWYERS AT TH…
entries.text: ONE OF THE SIX MEN ANDREAS COUNTS AS CHICAGO'S LAWYERS AT THE END OF 1833, and one of the twelve who voted for incorporation on 5 August 1833. Andreas, scan p. 281: 'It comprised six lawyers - Russel E. Heacock, who had come in 1827; Richard J. Hamilton, 1831; and Giles Spring, John Dean Caton, Edward W. Casey and Alexander N. Fullerton, who had put out their signs in 1833.' He administered the oath of office to the first board of trustees as a notary public and acted as its clerk pro tem, and he ran the auction of the school section in October 1833 with John Bates as auctioneer. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Hamilton, R. J.” (poll 1833 013, line 34); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Hamilton, Richard J.” (tax 1833 042, line 94); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Hamilton, Richard J.” (poll 1834 049, line 218). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Hamilton' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 7 times, as “HAMILTON RICHARD J”, “HAMILTON R J”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-29: 5 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 8 in the town the register codes CHIV (L1BL8CHIV, as printed); lot 2 of block 8 in the town the register codes CHIV (L2BL8CHIV, as printed); lot 4 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL2CHIOT, as printed); the N2 of lot 7 of block 2 in the town the register codes CHIV (N2L7BL2CHIV, as printed); the S2 of lot 7 of block 3 in the town the register codes CHI (S2L7BL3CHI, as printed) and 2 parcels of the school section — lot 5 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 6 of block 25 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $17236.00 (ls0225, ls0226, ls1203, ls1204, ls1205, ls1206, ls1207). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $17160.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HAMILTON RICHARD J matches Richard Jones Hamilton: the forename names Richard Jones Hamilton of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He was one of six men a history book counts as Chicago's lawyers at the end of 1833. He was also one of the twelve who voted to make Chicago a town, on 5 August 1833. He swore in the town's first leaders. For a time he kept their notes too. In October 1833 he ran the sale of the school land. John Bates called the bids. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 3 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 7 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:ONE OF THE TWELVE WHO VOTED FOR INCORPORATION on 5 August 18…
entries.text: ONE OF THE TWELVE WHO VOTED FOR INCORPORATION on 5 August 1833 (Andreas prints the poll: 'John W. Wright'), one of the twenty-eight electors five days later, a candidate who took two votes, and one of the nine village citizens founding the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833 and one of its three first elders. Charles Butler met him on his first morning in Chicago in August 1833, at the funeral of a child. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds, and an advertisement in it is a peculiarly good witness: the advertiser was paying for it and his customers had to be able to find him. It is also NINETEEN MONTHS before the scene date, in the town's fastest-changing period, so it is strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835.

levels.8-10: He was one of the twelve who voted to make Chicago a town, on 5 August 1833. Five days later he voted again, and got two votes himself. He helped found the First Presbyterian Church in June 1833. He was one of its first three leaders. Charles Butler met him on his first morning in Chicago, at a child's funeral. He put an ad in the paper in November 1833. An ad is a good witness, since he paid for it and his buyers had to find him. But it is from nineteen months before our day, and the town changed fast. So it proves he was here in 1833. It only weakly shows he was still here in July 1835.

entries.card: why:ONE OF THE TWENTY-EIGHT ELECTORS OF 10 AUGUST 1833, listed b…
entries.text: ONE OF THE TWENTY-EIGHT ELECTORS OF 10 AUGUST 1833, listed by Andreas as 'Charles Taylor'. This project's Wolf Point Tavern record has 'Charles and Mary Taylor' keeping that house from 1831 to 1833, which would make him a tavern keeper before he was anything else and gives him a named wife; the identification is not made here because the Taylor surname is carried by at least four distinct men in this parcel's sources and merging them on a forename would be exactly the error the Isaac Harmon case was avoided for. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Taylor, Charles” (poll 1833 026, line 47); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Taylor, Charles” (poll 1834 106, line 275); Poll list of 1835 — “Taylor, Charles” (poll 1835 079, line 366). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Taylor' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Chas Taylor” (33S7-9YYJ-JM, printed page 224, line 13). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (“Sauganash Hotel: the pre-1830 position is not represented” matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Taylor, Mrs. Charle's | Letter. | Januarys, 1843. | Dismissed.” (second presb 0895, printed page 203), admitted 1843 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Taylor' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins C. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a married womans entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. THE SAME ROLL LINE IS MET BY OTHER TOWNSPEOPLE OF THIS NAME: second presb 0895 is matched under this same rule to Mrs. C. Taylor (Mrs. C. Taylor), so it is met by two townspeople of this name, and it says which of them it was about no more than it says it was about this one — the test that decided it is a surname and a given initial agreeing, which cannot tell them apart. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

levels.8-10: He was one of the twenty-eight voters of 10 August 1833. A history book lists him as Charles Taylor. Our records have a Charles and Mary Taylor keeping the Wolf Point Tavern from 1831 to 1833. That would make him an inn keeper and give him a wife. We do not join them, since at least four different men here share the name Taylor. Joining them on a first name alone is the very mistake we avoided with Isaac Harmon. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 3 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. We judged it is this same person. But 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are. A list of the members of the Second Presbyterian Church has a line with the same last name and first letter. That church list starts in 1842, so it is no proof about 1835. That same church line also fits other people of this name in the town. The test is only a last name and a first letter, so it can not tell them apart. It does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:ONE OF THE VERY FEW DOCUMENTED INTERIORS IN THIS DATASET, an…
entries.text: ONE OF THE VERY FEW DOCUMENTED INTERIORS IN THIS DATASET, and it is documented because a court sat in it. Judge J. D. Caton, quoted by Andreas under 'First Chicago Divorce': that term in May, 1834, 'when we all first met together in the UNFINISHED LOFT of the old Mansion House, just north of where the Tremont now stands'. So on 1835-07-01 the building had a roof space, it was reached and used, and thirteen months earlier it was unfinished. The archetype builds a loft as a gable-end opening and nothing else, which is honest: a loft leaves no other external trace and inventing a dormer would be adding evidence. The interior itself is not modelled anywhere in this project - the liberties register “Four documented interiors, and no interior is modelled”.

levels.8-10: This is one of the very few insides of a building our papers describe, and only because a court met in it. Judge Caton says that in May 1834 they all first met in the unfinished loft of the old Mansion House. So in 1835 the building had a roof space that was used, and a year before it was not finished. Our rules draw a loft as just an opening in the end wall. That is honest, since a loft leaves no other sign on the outside. Adding a roof window would be making up proof. We do not build the inside of any building.

entries.card: why:ONE SOURCE, ONE YEAR, AND THE LONGEST UNSUPPORTED RUN IN THI…
entries.text: ONE SOURCE, ONE YEAR, AND THE LONGEST UNSUPPORTED RUN IN THIS DATASET. Wau-Bun, describing 1831: 'Near him [Wentworth's tavern] were two or three log cabins occupied by Robinson, the Pottowattamie chief, and some of his wife's connexions.' That is the whole of the evidence, and it is a single sentence in a book written twenty-five years after the year it describes. Nothing reached follows these cabins to 1832 or to any year after. The range is closed at the end of 1835 on the ordinary continuity argument — a standing building stands until something says otherwise — and that argument is under more strain here than anywhere else in the dataset, because THE FOUR YEARS THIS RANGE CROSSES ARE THE YEARS OF THE REMOVAL. The 1833 Treaty of Chicago ceded the land; through 1835 the Potawatomi were assembled around the town awaiting removal west; Billy Caldwell, who Wau-Bun says resided at Wolf Point occasionally, led his people west in 1835; and Alexander Robinson held a reserve of his own on the Des Plaines from the 1829 treaty and lived out his life there. A house left by the people who built it is a house that comes down or is taken over, and no source records either happening to these. WHAT THIS RECORD CLAIMS IS THAT THE BUILDINGS STOOD, NOT THAT ANYONE WAS IN THEM. If evidence turns up that they were gone by July 1835 this record leaves the scene for the exclusions record, and that is a likelier outcome for this record than for any other in the parcel.

levels.8-10: This rests on one paper, about one year. It must stretch further than any other here. A book about 1831 says there were two or three log cabins near Wentworth's tavern. Robinson, the Potawatomi chief, lived there with some of his wife's family. That one line is all the proof. The book was written twenty five years later. Nothing follows these cabins past 1831. We keep them standing to the end of 1835, since a building stands until something says it does not. But these four years are the years the Native people were made to leave. The treaty of 1833 gave up the land. In 1835 Billy Caldwell led his people west. Robinson lived on his own land on the Des Plaines. A house its builders leave comes down or is taken over, and no paper says which. We only say the cabins stood, not that anyone was in them. If they turn out to be gone by July 1835, they leave the scene.

entries.card: why:ONE TENT A HOUSEHOLD, for the 11 households the 1835 transie…
entries.text: ONE TENT A HOUSEHOLD, for the 11 households the 1835 transient persons data deals to 'a tent at the landing place' and then to this shore: the American says SOME built tents at the landing, so four stand there and the rest of the class is drawn here, off the working wharf frontage. One family to one tent is the reading that invents no sharing. “The open sky the store houses spared, and the emigrants' tents moved off the wharves to the shore”.

levels.8-10: One tent for each family. Our list deals eleven families to a tent at the landing, then to this shore. A paper of 1835 says some built tents at the landing. So four stand there, and the rest are drawn here, off the busy wharves. One family to one tent is the reading that makes up no sharing.

entries.card: why:ONE TENT A HOUSEHOLD, for the 4 households the 1835 transien…
entries.text: ONE TENT A HOUSEHOLD, for the 4 households the 1835 transient persons data deals to 'a tent at the landing place' AND to this ground. The American says SOME built tents, and then 'Westward Ho!': a handful, pitched by people pressing on west, so the count here is kept to four and the rest of the class is dealt to the shore south of the fort (“The open sky the store houses spared, and the emigrants' tents moved off the wharves to the shore”). How many people a tent held is not stated, and one family to one tent is the reading that invents no sharing. “The emigrants' tents at the landing: the ground documented, the tents invented, the count the paper's "some"”.

levels.8-10: One tent for each family. Our list deals four families to a tent at the landing, and to this ground. A paper of 1835 says some built tents, then cries Westward Ho! That means a handful, put up by people going on west. So we keep the count here to four, and the rest are dealt to the shore south of the fort. No paper says how many people a tent held. One family to one tent is the reading that makes up no sharing.

entries.card: why:ONE WITNESS, AND THE RECORD SAYS SO EVERYWHERE. The plan let…
entries.text:
ONE WITNESS, AND THE RECORD SAYS SO EVERYWHERE. The plan letters 'Shop' against a drawn building south-east of the stockade and that is the entire evidence for this building's existence, its position and its size. Hubbard, who names the barn, the well, the wash-houses, the Factor House, the road and Mrs Jouett's grave on the same two pages, does not mention a shop; his silence is not a denial, and it is not treated as one, but it is why nothing here reaches the two-witness standing the barn and the wash house have.

READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN, BY THE SAME RULE AS THE ELEVEN RECORDS ALREADY TAKEN FROM IT. Internet Archive leaf n242 of historyofchicago01andr (Andreas vol. 1, p. 113), rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise so the sheet's own true-north arrow stands vertical, is 2715 x 2003 px. On that image the stockade's ink runs from x 1356 to x 1535 and from y 553 to y 730, so the enclosure's centre is pixel (1445, 644); the committed palisade record hangs that centre on local E +1152, N +221, which is UTM 448224.70 E, 4637616.80 N. Pixels convert at 1.10 ft/px (0.33528 m/px), the scale the research notes on fort dearborn section 3 derives from the commandant's quarters. THE ANCHOR AND THE SCALE ARE CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED, and the check is the garrison garden — the one thing on this plate that is both drawn and already committed. Its committed centre lands at pixel (1209, 1008) under this transform; the drawn diamond's centre measures (1207, 1002). Seven pixels, 2.3 m. A second check runs the other way: the committed blockhouse centre predicts pixel (1385, 698) and the drawn blockhouse square measures (1375, 710), 16 px or 5.4 m. WHAT THE TRANSFORM CANNOT DO is beat its own inputs. The enclosure measures 180 px across at this scale, which is 60 m against the committed palisade's 53 m — a 13 % spread, inside the +/-20 % the scale carries, and the reason is visible on the plate: 180 px is the OUTER edge of an engraved line four to six pixels thick. So carry +/-20 % on this offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself, exactly as every plate-derived record here does.

THE PIXEL. The drawn building is a tilted block whose corners measure (1629, 912), (1645, 932), (1624, 957) and (1608, 938), centre (1626.5, 934.8) — 181.5 px east and 290.8 px south of the fort centre, which is 60.9 m east and 97.5 m south of it.

levels.8-10: One witness only, and the card says so. An 1830 plan of the fort writes Shop beside a building south east of the fort. That is all the proof for this building, its spot and its size. Gurdon Hubbard names many buildings on the same pages, but not a shop. His silence does not mean there was none, but it is why this is less sure than the barn. We read its spot off the old plan, the same way as eleven other buildings. We checked our reading against the fort's garden, which is on the plan and already placed. They land within about eight feet of each other. Our reading is likely right to within a fifth of its distance from the fort.

entries.card: why:OUTSIDE ACCESS COMPLETED AS A BOUNDED RECONSTRUCTION. Hubbar…
entries.text: OUTSIDE ACCESS COMPLETED AS A BOUNDED RECONSTRUCTION. Hubbard, printed p.36 (leaf74, text2353-2358), says the upper piazza was reached by stairs on the outside. This supplies the occurrence in1818, carried conditionally to1July1835 under the existing gallery continuity interpretation; it gives no side, run, width, material or rail. We choose one straight timber flight continuing from the right (south) end of the existing upper walk, entirely outside the wall: 1.0m clear width, 3.6m run to its existing2.4m floor,14risers of171mm,70mm treads, two stringers and0.95m handrails. The gallery end rail opens only at this access; the wall and its openings remain unchanged. Exact geometry and side are liberties, not historical measurements. This explicitly supersedes gallery.note’s prior refusal to model any stair merely because its location was unknown. It does not identify either unnamed stair/galleried range in the1893 retrospective with these quarters.

levels.8-10: We built the outside stairs as a guess. Gurdon Hubbard says the upper porch was reached by stairs on the outside. That was in 1818, and we carry it to 1835. He does not give the side, size, wood or rail. We chose one straight wooden stair at the south end of the upper porch, all outside the wall. Its exact shape and side are made up, not measured. We once drew no stair, since its place was unknown. That choice is set aside now.

entries.card: why:OWNER RULING — other work, 2026-11-03. The owner, on the clo…
entries.text: OWNER RULING — other work, 2026-11-03. The owner, on the closed draw rising to a ridge at mid-river: “when the bridge was down did it really have a peak in the center like this, it seems very odd to me that would be the case”. Withdrawn and laid level. The rise rests on one composition only: Braunhold’s plate in Andreas 1884 p. 631 and the Baker-Co engraving (credited to the Chicago Tribune, 15 February 1880, original unverified), which share their schooner, lighthouse and viewpoint and so are one composition drawn twice, not two witnesses — both made more than forty years after the bridge was chopped up in 1839 by artists who never saw it. No text gives a rise: Andreas has a draw ‘hoisted’ by ‘gallows’ frames, Moses and Kirkland 1895 p. 95 ‘a double draw’, and neither says the leaves stood above the approaches when down. Against it is the bridge’s use: it carried the town’s main street and its teams, and 1.2 m over a 9.14 m leaf is a 1-in-7.6 grade each way with the leaves’ joint at its crest. A hinged leaf lowered onto its bearing lies at the bearing’s height, and the drawings’ rise reads as the engraver’s or as leaves caught part-way up. So the closed draw is laid level with the approaches. This departs from the pictures on purpose and both match records carry it as an `owner ruling` difference. The earlier reading is kept below as history. SUPERSEDED: The retrospective Andreas 1884 p. 631 plate shows a central rise in the closed draw and boarded parapet. This supports qualitative form, not a surveyed profile, a geographic coordinate or an attested operating mechanism. The exact rise and folded timber joints are separately reconstructed. The same native pure profile drives the mesh and nominal walk surface.

levels.8-10: The owner of this project ruled this in November 2026. Looking at the lowered bridge rising to a peak in the middle, he asked if it really had a peak like this, since it seemed very odd. So we laid it flat. The peak came from one old picture, drawn twice, more than forty years after the bridge was gone, by artists who never saw it. No paper of the time says it rose when it was down. The bridge carried the town's main street and its teams, and a peak like that would be a steep hill each way. A lowered part lies flat on its rest. The peak in the pictures was likely the artist's, or the bridge caught partway up. So we lay it level with the road on each side. This differs from the pictures on purpose.

entries.card: why:Occupied by the commanding officer of the post; on 1835-07-0…
entries.text: Occupied by the commanding officer of the post; on 1835-07-01 that is Maj. John Greene, 5th Infantry (see Fort Dearborn — the stockade's occupants block). In 1827, with the post ungarrisoned, Dr. Alexander Wolcott the Indian Agent was living in it - which is Hubbard's reason for mentioning it at all.

levels.8-10: The fort's commander lived here. On 1 July 1835 that was Major John Greene, of the 5th foot soldiers. In 1827, when no soldiers held the fort, Dr Alexander Wolcott, the agent to the Native people, lived in it. That is why Gurdon Hubbard mentions it at all.

The back wall stands about ten feet inside Market Street, and the front faces the river it would load from, like the Newberry and Dole packing house on the same bank. levels.8-10: This spot is off the town plan. The strip between Market Street and the water has no lot lines. The back wall stands about ten feet inside Market Street, and the front faces the river the boards would come off. Our rule for lumber landings chose it. A lumber yard stacked what a ship brought in. No South Water lot is free, and this is the one bank left, where the ground first allows a roof. No paper puts a building here.

entries.card: why:One of the nine village citizens among the twenty-six foundi…
entries.text: One of the nine village citizens among the twenty-six founding members of the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833, and a signatory of the 1832 militia agreement submitting to Gholson Kercheval as captain 'until all apprehension of danger from the Indians may have subsided'.

levels.8-10: He helped start the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833. Twenty six people started it, and he was one of nine from the town. In 1832 he also signed a paper with the town's armed men. They agreed to follow Gholson Kercheval as their captain. They would do so until they no longer feared the Native people.

entries.card: why:One stack is visible above the roof in Cameron's retrospecti…
entries.text: One stack is visible above the roof in Cameron's retrospective picture of the post office in 1833. This supports an inferred visible count, not a scene-date attestation or a finding about hidden stacks. chimney ridge at states its provisional position; ridge stack w (m) states a reconstructed section while ridge stack head (m) chooses a reconstructed 0.75 m head and the construction retains the archetype's treatment, recorded in the liberties register “a first form reading of the first post office” and “Every chimney stands where the archetype puts it”.

levels.8-10: An old picture by Cameron shows one chimney above the roof of the post office in 1833. That backs up a count of one that you can see. It does not prove 1835, or rule out chimneys you cannot see. Where it stands, its size and its top are made up.

entries.card: why:Other work FRONT APERTURE INCREMENT, AND THE COUNT IS THE ON…
entries.text: Other work FRONT APERTURE INCREMENT, AND THE COUNT IS THE ONLY THING THE PICTURE GIVES. The keyed panorama 'Fort Dearborn and Chicago in 1831', read here at full resolution on its Agency-House subject (the chicago fort dearborn 1831 1 image, sha256 624d8f1f52a75bf30653e8cbf37a388478b0ddf5a02f1fadf727cf2144b84c3f), draws the front gable with THREE dark marks: TWO upright ones standing on the ground line, and ONE small one high on the face at the head of the wall. The archetype's compound path states one opening per room, so that front could not be expressed at all and every data-only attempt at it was refused by the archetype's own validation; this attribute is the opt-in that lets one room state its own set, and it OVERRIDES the centre door that room's front opening would otherwise put here, so the old opening does not survive among the new marks. WHAT IS READ AND WHAT IS INVENTED. Read from the picture: that there are two lower marks and one upper one; that the lower pair stand on the ground; and roughly where the three fall along the face, the lower pair in its left and middle leaving the right-hand stretch blank, the upper mark a little left of the apex. Invented: every dimension, every band, the depth and section of the recesses, and which of the two lower marks is the way in. The marks are a few pixels across a thirty-pixel gable in a retrospective engraving whose proportions are not this model's, so no fraction of them is carried across as a measurement: the coordinates here are set out from this record's own 5 m central wall and the rake of its own roof, inside the bounds the archetype validates. The face is drawn slightly oblique, which compresses its right-hand side, so even the arrangement is read with that caution. THE ENTRY ROLE IS A DESIGN INFERENCE AND NOT A READING. The picture does not say which mark was a door, or that either was. The right-hand one carries `kind: door` because it stands where this record's previous single centre door stood, so the town's entrance, apron and doorway clearance keep the ground they already held; the other is `kind: aperture`, which claims a hole and nothing else. No glazing, closure, interior, attic room, white paint or historic function is claimed by any of the three, and the white of the engraving's paper is not evidence of paint. Other work FINAL FORM SUPERSESSION: the three marks, their heights, widths, relative positions and recess depth are retained as the central room is rebased with the narrower wings. The final compound, roofs and stack have a canonical illustrative view in the kinzie 1831 data; its match record carries actual picture acceptance. The drawing remains retrospective 1831 context, not a measured survey or proof of an unchanged July 1835 condition. See “three marks on the Agency House's gable, and all of them set out by us” and “final compact Agency-House form”.

levels.8-10: An old picture gives us only the count of openings on the front. A view of the fort and Chicago in 1831 draws the front end of the agency house with three dark marks. Two stand on the ground, and one small one is high up near the top of the wall. Our rules used to allow just one opening a room, so they could not draw this. Now one room can have its own set, and the old center door is gone. What we read from the picture is the count and roughly where the marks fall. Every size is made up. The picture does not say which mark was a door. We made the right one the door, since the old door stood there. The other is just a hole. We claim no glass, paint or use for any of them.

entries.card: why:Other work L trial gives the separate slender roof projectio…

entries.card: why:Other work MOVED THIS BUILDING 82.7 m, AND THE INVENTION THA…
entries.text: Other work MOVED THIS BUILDING 82.7 m, AND THE INVENTION THAT REMAINS IS SMALLER THAN THE ONE IT REPLACES. The record until now stood at local E 461.6 N -619.6, which the note below called Monroe Street and which is not Monroe Street: it is the middle of the unnamed north-south corridor of the School Section grid at local E 458.8 - La Salle Street in the modern grid, and a corridor the 1835 streets data does not draw south of local N -400 - in the row between Madison and Monroe, 39.0 m north of Monroe Street's own north kerb. The northing was never measured; the old note says so, and says how it was got: "estimated from the plat module - the block pitch implied by the reconstruction recipes' Randolph-to-Washington bands, carried two blocks further south". That carry was made before other work read Wright's 1834 sheet, and the sheet puts Monroe's centreline at local N -670.774 inside a 24.384 m corridor (the 1835 streets data § monroe, the school section blocks 1834 data § grid.ew lines j=1), 51.2 m south of where the carry landed. TWO SOURCES AGREE ON THE BLOCK AND NEITHER WAS CONSULTED FOR THE OLD POSITION. The federal register sells Russel E Heacock lot 7 of block 117 on 22 October 1833 for $80 (the entries data § ls0237), and block 117 is the block bounded north by Monroe and south by Adams - the one pair of streets Andreas's anecdote names, and the only block in Section 16 bounded by both. Andreas has him build on what he supposed was his lot and find he was on Monroe and not Adams; the register has him own ground whose two street faces are Monroe and Adams. The position therefore moves onto the Monroe corridor at block 117's north line, where the two witnesses put it, and the building's 9.144 m depth sits wholly inside the 24.384 m corridor. WHAT IS STILL INVENTED: the easting along the block face, and only that. No source places the house east-west, and lot 7's own ground cannot supply it - this project has never read a School Section lot line, and the four-lots-to-a-face reading it does hold is one block of the Original Town and is graded conjectural where it stands (the plat lots generator). The footprint is therefore centred on block 117's own 98.3 m face, which is a neutral choice and not a derivation. Covered by the liberties register “Eighty households nobody named, and the thirty-eight buildings they justify”, the same entry that covered the old easting.

levels.8-10: We moved this building about 270 feet, and the part that is made up is now smaller. It used to stand in the middle of a street that was not drawn there, and its spot came from carrying a block size two blocks south. That was before we read the old map of 1834. Two papers now agree on the block. The land office sold Russel Heacock lot 7 of block 117 in 1833. Block 117 lies between Monroe Street and Adams Street. A history book says he built on what he thought was his lot, then found he was on Monroe, not Adams. So the house now stands on Monroe Street at the block's north edge, where both papers put it. It sits inside the street. The only part still made up is how far east or west along the block it stands. We put it in the middle of the block's face, which is a plain choice, not a finding.

entries.card: why:Other work PICTURED BOXED GABLE CORNICE, WITH RECONSTRUCTED…
entries.text: Other work PICTURED BOXED GABLE CORNICE, WITH RECONSTRUCTED SECTIONS. The Andreas/Braunhold plate draws a boxed band following both rakes of the hotel's visible main gable and a short horizontal return turning the corner at each eaves end; the archetype has never built either, so that gable has been standing with a bare rake the picture does not draw. THE OCCURRENCE AND THE FORM ARE READ OFF THE PICTURE; THE THREE SECTIONS ARE NOT. The plate is a retrospective 1884 engraving whose only scale datum is a standing man, and a direct reading of the drawn return against the gable's own eaves-to-eaves width and against the 0.85 m attic sash gives roughly 0.7-0.9 m with several tenths of a metre of line-weight and perspective uncertainty either way; the 0.55 m taken here sits at the conservative end of that range and is a working choice, not a measurement. The 0.18 m section and 0.18 m projection are the same kind of choice, bounded by the plate showing a band plainly deeper than a clapboard course and plainly shallower than the entrance cornice already built. Drawn in the existing wall finish, hanging below the rake line, so the roof planes, ridge, eave, pitch, footprint, placement, openings, shutters, stacks, cross wing and the separate Carpenter shop are all unchanged. Occurrence on the opposite, unseen end is not claimed and nothing is built there. the liberties register “the Sauganash's boxed gable cornice, drawn without a dimension” owns the invention. This does not settle the provisional camera, the roof silhouette or any other open difference on the original picture comparison.

The picture is a print of 1884, and its only guide to size is a man standing by. So we chose small, careful sizes. The rest of the building does not change. entries.card: why:Other work adds exact birth data and independent biography:…
entries.text: Other work adds exact birth data and independent biography: born April 7, 1803 at Troy, New York; Union College graduate; medical training in New York; married Marie Theresa Ellis May 16, 1829; moved to Chicago in 1832. He was clerk of the August 5, 1833 incorporation meeting and one of the first town trustees. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kimberly, Edmund S.” (tax 1833 057, line 109); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Kimberly, Dr. E. S.” (poll 1834 063, line 232). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kimberly' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Ed. Kimberley” (33S7-9YYJ-99F, printed page 234, line 3). This project has ruled the head a CANDIDATE and no more: the name agrees and is unique on both sides, but nothing independent of the name was found. A candidate is not an identity — nothing is asserted from it, no household of 1840 is carried back, and the ruling is recorded so that a reader can see it was made rather than missed. Under the rule that decided it (L6b reached through a card merge caps at candidate), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “KIMBERLEY EDMUND S”, “KIMBERLY EDMUND S”, “KIMBERLY E S”, 1833-10-25 to 1836-09-05: 1 federal land entry — E2SE sec 32 T39N R14E and 2 lots in the platted town — lot 5 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHI (L5BL1CHI, as printed); lot 9 of block 48 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L9BL48CHIOTV, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — lot 6 of block 119 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 80.00 acres stated in all, for $5042.00 (ls0263, ls0479, ls1281, ls1282). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $4300.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: KIMBERLEY EDMUND S matches Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly: the forename names Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. The surname reaches him through a ruled card merge and not off his card: the town held kimberley ed until the card merge rulings data folded it onto this person, and the register's spelling is the one that card carried. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: Other work adds his birth and life story. He was born on 7 April 1803 at Troy, New York. He went to Union College and learned medicine in New York. He married Marie Theresa Ellis in May 1829 and moved to Chicago in 1832. He kept the notes at the meeting of 5 August 1833 that made Chicago a town, and was one of its first leaders. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. The name was hard to read on the old sheet, so we call it only a maybe. Nothing is built on a maybe. And 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 4 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

The existing log builder's 0.30 m blind recess replaces the generic closed board-and-batten leaf as a reconstructed shadow proxy. It supplies no real interior, passable opening, person, swung leaf or historical hinge position. Existing doorway station and size, wall/roof/stack, footprint, placement, dates and former-use/current-use qualifications remain unchanged. Petford and the dependent Trowbridge 1902 depiction also retain a dark annex doorway, but do not independently attest an open door on 1 July 1835; no July fitting/state or grade is promoted. The source-camera/group fit and all other visible differences remain open.

levels.8-10: An old picture of 1884 draws a dark doorway in this log side building, with a person standing in it. So we drew the doorway as a dark space set back into the wall, not a closed door. It gives no real room inside. Two later pictures also show a dark doorway, but they do not prove the door stood open on 1 July 1835. Nothing else changes.

entries.card: why:Other work bounded four-lower-front-sash correction. Direct…
entries.text: Other work bounded four-lower-front-sash correction. Direct comparison with the held Andreas/Braunhold1884 engraving shows tall narrow lower facade sash, with heads near the high entrance case, rather than the stock squat 0.85-by-1.35m rectangles. Keep their four existing bay stations, every upper and rear opening and all wall/roof/placement fields. The selected 0.70m width, 1.85m height and 0.90m sill put their heads at2.75m, below the unchanged storey division; open blue leaves follow these same four envelopes. These are reconstructed visual proportions, bounded by the separately reconstructed entrance and the retained provisional own-hotel camera, not historic measurements or an independent 1835 survey. The engraving and camera have unresolved perspective/date limits; no whole-hotel or compound match is claimed by this change.

levels.8-10: An old print of 1884 shows tall, narrow windows on the lower front, with tops near the high front door. We had drawn short, wide ones. So we made the four lower windows tall and narrow, in the same places. Their sizes are our choice, shaped to look right, not measured. The print's viewpoint and date are not settled, and we claim no full match.

entries.card: why:Other work bounded ridge-end stack placement trial. Andreas/…
entries.text:
Other work bounded ridge-end stack placement trial. Andreas/Braunhold's public-domain 1884 retrospective plate draws the two ridge stacks near the gable ends; the current comparison has them farther inward at the generic frontage fractions 0.22/0.78. Select the existing gable ends kit instead. Its 0.60 m end inset, 0.90 m square shafts and ridge + 0.55 m tops are reconstructed generator choices, not dimensions measured from the engraving. The source supports relative disposition only; it supplies no coordinate, July 1835 fitting date, historical camera or independent metric calibration. Count 2, brick finish, shaft section/top, main roof/cornice/wing, openings, position and the separate Carpenter shop remain selected as before. The retained diagnostic-camera projection suggests improved horizontal placement but leaves vertical/roof and broader compound differences unresolved; no rendered acceptance or full image match is claimed by this data trial. the liberties register “The Sauganash stacks move toward the ridge ends”.

CURRENT WIDTH-ONLY TRIAL: the 0.90 m shaft figure above describes the earlier placement-only increment. The explicit ridge end chimney section (m) trial now supersedes that horizontal section with a reconstructed 0.60 m square shaft, leaving the two ridge-end stations, ridge + 0.55 m tops, plain heads and brick finish unchanged. This is a relative-profile trial, not an attested dimension or a new picture-match acceptance.

levels.8-10: This is a trial. An old print of 1884 draws the hotel's two chimneys near the ends of the roof ridge. We had them further in. So we moved them out toward the ends. Their exact place, size and tops are our choice, not measured from the print. The print shows only where they sit compared to each other. Later we made them thinner too, as another trial. We claim no full match.

entries.card: why:Other work bounded shared-ridge trial. The existing source r…
entries.text: Other work bounded shared-ridge trial. The existing source reading interprets the main and rear roofs as perpendicular ridges meeting at one height; the old model gave them equal heights but stopped the rear crest 3.75 m short of the main crest. Select the explicit join, using the existing main depth and roof overhang to locate the rendezvous, without changing the existing site, footprint, wall height, pitch or the unmeasured outer wing depth. This is a trial of the producer-intended shared-join contract, not proof that the engraving determines this exact historic roof intersection. It supplies no historical junction measurement, dimension, camera or July-1835 alteration date. Actual native picture and visitor comparison must still accept the trial. “Sauganash roof join and stack section”.

levels.8-10: This is a trial. We read the main roof and the back roof as two ridges meeting at the same height. Our old model stopped the back ridge short of the main one. Now the two ridges meet. Nothing else changes. This does not prove the old print shows exactly how the roofs met. It still has to be checked against the picture.

levels.8-10: We gave the roof a thin edge that sticks out a little, since it was missing. The sizes are our choice, not measured. Nothing else changes. The roof edge still has to be checked against the picture.

entries.card: why:Other work continuation reconstructs a local sapling/sign po…
entries.text: Other work continuation reconstructs a local sapling/sign pose from the governing sheet: pole base around[350,915]sourcepx, head[303,610], rising cross-arm toward[363,598], tilted hanging board around[322..378,611..652]. Same provisional square-pixel camera and5m building gauge; no historical metre or geographic coordinate follows from these picks. Place the base in the actual empty L courtyard, keep it and the shaft clear of the walls, lean screen-left, enlarge/tilt the board and add a slim supporting brace. All local coordinates, pole height/taper, arm reach/section, board dimensions/drop and iron pieces are chosen proxies; original wolf silhouette and neutral colours remain reconstructed. Base screen-height residual is deliberately retained instead of moving the pole tens of metres toward the camera to overfit the common-grade drawing. Existing sign occurrence/mount evidence and all world position uncertainty remain.

levels.8-10: We drew the tall sign pole from the old sheet. We read where the pole stands, where its top is, and where the arm and hanging board are, from points on the picture. No real size or spot comes from those points. We put the pole in the empty yard inside the L, clear of the walls, leaning a little. We made the board bigger and tilted, and added a thin brace. Every size is our choice. The wolf shape and colors are made up.

entries.card: why:Other work final bounded reconstruction: the text-attested c…
entries.text: Other work final bounded reconstruction: the text-attested centre, two symmetrical wings and two rear tails occupy a 9 by 4.5 m envelope. The 5 m centre is retained; each former 4 m wing is narrowed to 2 m and its front recessed 1 m behind the central front. The central room is 3.5 m deep, and each 1.5 m wide rear tail runs 1 m back. These are choices within Wau-Bun's compact five-part composition and the small keyed panorama's dominant front gable and subordinate visible side gable, not measured historic dimensions or a survey. Room-coordinate rebasing keeps the polygon at local zero; position and rotation are unchanged. The central openings retain their earlier relative offsets, count, heights and depths. The generator builds the exact union, including re-entrant corners. The unseen wing, tails and continuation to July 1835 remain reconstructed. Supersedes the former 13 by 9 m trial; see “final compact Agency-House form”.

levels.8-10: This is our last shape for this house, and it is made up. A book says it had a center, two wings and two back parts. We fit them inside a space about 30 by 15 feet. The wings are narrower now and set back from the center's front. These are our choices, inside what the book and one small old picture allow. They are not measured. Its spot and turn do not change. This takes the place of our bigger earlier try.

entries.card: why:Other work final composition: five connected rooms exactly p…
entries.text: Other work final composition: five connected rooms exactly partition the reconstructed footprint. Parallel front-to-back gables replace the former transverse wing roofs: the 5 m centre has a dominant ridge, while each 2 by 2 m wing makes a subordinate gable recessed 1 m behind the front. Overlapping eaves meet at the room junctions; no valley flashing or hidden interior is claimed. The panorama bounds the hierarchy and visible side gable; Wau-Bun supplies two wings and two tails. Exact dimensions, depths, roof axes and unseen rear junctions remain reconstructed. The central and tail eaves retain 2.6 m; wing eaves are reconstructed at 2.0 m and all pitches retain 35 degrees.

levels.8-10: This is our last shape for this house. Five joined rooms fill its made up outline. Each part has a roof that runs front to back. The center roof is the biggest, and the two wing roofs are smaller and set back. An old picture limits which roof is biggest, and a book gives two wings and two back parts. All sizes and roof joins are made up. The wings' walls are lower, and all the roofs keep the same slope.

entries.card: why:Other work final pictured stack-head reconstruction. Andreas…
entries.text: Other work final pictured stack-head reconstruction. Andreas/Braunhold draws two slender brick shafts with projecting masonry heads; the earlier plain 0.60 m square stacks omitted that visible shape. Retain those shafts and the two ridge-end stations, and select a complete top 0.75 m above the ridge, with a 0.12 m deep cap projecting 0.06 m on each side. The exposed shaft therefore ends at ridge +0.63 m, beneath a 0.72 m square head. These are bounded working dimensions at the reconstructed grade, not metres measured from the retrospective engraving. The source supports the relative slender, capped silhouette; its line weight and diagnostic camera cannot establish exact brick courses, historic dimensions, a fitting date or a July 1835 alteration. “Sauganash pictured masonry heads” records the choice. Actual rebuilt comparison remains required before picture acceptance.

levels.8-10: An old print of 1884 draws two thin brick chimneys with wider tops. Our old plain chimneys left that out. So we gave each a wider cap at the top, a little above the roof. The sizes are our choice. The print shows the thin, capped shape, but not its exact size, bricks or date. It still has to be checked against the picture.

levels.8-10: This is a trial of how the front door looks. An old print of 1884 shows a wide, high door frame, with a window above and narrow windows beside it. entries.text: Other work next single-surface proposal follows the owner-approved attributed journal drawing in continuing horizontal logs into the visible +Y gable. Keep the current roof slopes, overhang outline, ridge, mass, openings, camera and blind doorway unchanged. levels.8-10: An old drawing, which the owner of this project approved, shows the log rows running up into the roof end you can see. So we carry the logs up there too. The size of the logs and their color are made up. Only that roof end changes. We claim nothing about the far end, who lived here or who drew it.
