Its woman occupies a dark/open-looking doorway; the actual proposed model still has a closed planked leaf. Omit that leaf and use the existing blind 300 mm exterior recess with cut skin, casing, reveals and threshold. The depth and exact construction are reconstructed proxies, not an inferred room, passage, door swing or 1835 occupant. Preserve all opening sizes/stations, gable-axis choice, physical footprint/placement/dates and the unknown former-school 1835 use. The school/annex identification and original publication/date remain unresolved; no accepted camera or grade promotion follows.

levels.8-10: An old picture, which the owner of this project approved, shows a woman standing in a dark, open looking doorway. Our model had a closed door. So we took the door off and drew a dark space set back into the wall. Its depth is our choice. It does not claim a room behind it, which way a door swung, or who lived here in 1835. Who drew the picture, and when, is still not settled.

entries.card: why:Other work partial-clapboarding reconstruction: McKee's acco…
entries.text: Other work partial-clapboarding reconstruction: McKee's account printed by Andreas says the agency house was 'afterward clapboarded part way up'. The 1.30 m band is half the current inferred 2.6 m model wall, not a historical measurement. The exterior lower-wall fields use the existing neutral board finish and lap rhythm; upper logs and existing notched ends remain exposed, joined internal walls are not boarded, and all current apertures stay clear. Exact extent, corner treatment and the presence of this finish on 1 July 1835 are reconstructed choices; the account supplies no completion date. The 1.30 m band is retained in the final compound reconstruction; historical date uncertainty remains. Native and picture acceptance are recorded in the canonical reference view.

levels.8-10: An old account in a history book says the agency house was later covered with boards part way up. So we cover the lower half of the outside walls with boards. The logs above still show. The half way line is our choice, not a measure. The account gives no date. So we do not know if the boards were there on 1 July 1835.

entries.card: why:Other work picture-bounded roof tone: select the optional de…
entries.text: Other work picture-bounded roof tone: select the optional deep brown stock, exactly one quarter of the existing darkened linear RGB with unchanged alpha and roughness. The actual first darkened-preset native mobile comparison remained visibly pale; the inspected NYPL Wolf's Point in 1833 lithograph bounds a darker warm field. Rufus Blanchard published it and Chas. Shober & Co. lithographed it in Chicago in 1867. This explicit reconstructed colour is not a roof-condition, brown-pigment, weather-blackening, age or calibrated-reflectance attestation. The retrospective 1833 depiction does not prove unchanged appearance on 1 July 1835. Existing covering/normal-ORM relief, geometry, coordinates, other finishes and source rights remain unchanged. All eight source pictures and actual current master comparisons still govern original acceptance.

levels.8-10: We darkened the roof color to a deep brown. Our first darker try still looked pale on a phone. An old print of Wolf Point, made in 1867, shows a darker, warm roof. This color is our choice. It does not prove the roof's state, paint or age. The print shows 1833, so it does not prove how the roof looked in July 1835.

entries.text: Other work retains the earlier reconstructed 5.05 m head, now on one central ridge stack. The retained 2.6 m eave, 5 m central span and 35-degree pitch put the central ridge about 4.526 m over grade, leaving about 0.524 m of head. The section 18 by-law clearance cited for other work bounds this choice; it does not prove July 1835 compliance or a historical height. Placement and square section are separate reconstructed choices in compound ridge stacks.

levels.8-10: We keep the chimney top at about the same height, now on one middle chimney. That leaves it standing about one and a half feet above the roof's peak. A town law about chimney heights limits this choice. It does not prove the chimney followed the law in 1835.

entries.card: why:Other work retires the old rear ell as a July-1835 depiction…
entries.text:
Other work retires the old rear ell as a July-1835 depiction choice. Its original position was a reconstruction made under the obsolete Canal placement, using the pictured lower wing and Gray's later testimony without a dated rear plan. The governing drawings do not resolve or show that projecting right/rear form. Gray explicitly recalls a right addition 'the same as on the left' during his 1838–41 tenancy, and the historical note promised a second wing if the Lake-and-West-Water placement won; that later bilateral testimony and the promise remain counterevidence, not proof that either addition was absent in 1835 or that both were the same pictured building. The revised model builds the pictured left connector/range, keeps the competing shoulder readings, and leaves an unverified 1835 rear/bilateral stage unmodeled rather than presenting the old placement proxy as another established wing. No historic absence, alteration date, tenant identity or room count is asserted.

HISTORICAL PRE-RETIREMENT NOTE:
THE LOW ADDITION, BUILT AT THE REAR AND DECLARED. John Gray, landlord 1838-41, attests 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left'; the 1838 Braunhold engraving (owner brief 2026 08 18 README, image 6) draws 'a lower gabled wing at the left with a wide (carriage) door', and plate '11' (prefire views kevin 2026 08/the p6 0 image) draws the low gabled wing with the ship masts behind it. WHETHER A WING STOOD ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray describes the house three to six years after the scene date — so this is a reconstruction under the owner's 2026-08-18 standing ruling, sized by the views and claimed at the liberties register “The Green Tree's fabric from the plates: bays, end stacks, and the rear ell”. WHY THE REAR END AND ONLY THE REAR: Gray names additions at BOTH ends, but this record's committed placement puts the west face ON Canal Street's east frontage with zero offset, so the street end has no ground to build on — only the east (rear, yard) end does. That asymmetry is itself evidence worth recording: a west wing fits the ground only under the 'Lake and West Water' placement reading the position note carries as this record's largest residual uncertainty. If that reading ever wins, the second wing goes up with the move. The wing the views draw beside masts is consistent with either.

levels.8-10: We took away the old back wing. We had placed it when the house stood on an old spot, using a picture and a later witness, with no dated plan. The drawings we now follow do not show it. John Gray kept the house from 1838 to 1841. He remembered a side part on the right, the same as on the left. That is a reason to doubt, but it does not prove what stood in 1835. So we build the left part the pictures show, and leave the unproved right and back parts unbuilt. We claim no date for them, and do not say they were missing.

The retrospective Andreas/Braunhold plate draws relatively slender shafts; ordinary Lake Street review confirms the current wide squat bodies are visible at human eye height. The selected 0.60 m square section is a bounded working reconstruction, not metres read from the plate or a source-calibrated camera. Count two, ridge-end stations, brick finish, the ridge + 0.55 m tops and plain heads remain unchanged. No height or cap lip is added, and no source date, metric or whole-Hotel match is asserted before actual native comparison. “Sauganash roof join and stack section”.

levels.8-10: This is a trial. An old print of 1884 draws the hotel's chimneys as thin. Walking Lake Street at eye height, ours looked too wide and squat. So we made them thinner. The size is our choice, not read from the print. Their count, spots, brick and tops do not change. We claim no full match.

entries.text: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT. This building does not stand centred on a lot at a typology setback: it stands ON the north face of block 16, the block's South Water Street frontage, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in the thompson lots data — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its east wall is fixed by the east end of the run's own frontage, 1.5 m clear of the side lot line at that end. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at South Water Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

levels.8-10: This building stands on the north side of block 16, along South Water Street. We took the line of the block from the town plan. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from the lot line. That is as close as our plan lets it come, not a measure. It shares a wall with the next building, so it stays in line and does not shift. But the big things are still made up: that a building stood here at all, and that it was for this work. Its place could also be off by about 20 m.

Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its west wall is fixed by the west end of the run's own frontage, 1.5 m clear of the side lot line at that end. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at Washington Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

levels.8-10: This building stands on the south side of block 42, along Washington Street. We took the line of the block from the town plan. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from the lot line. That is as close as our plan lets it come, not a measure. It shares a wall with the next building, so it stays in line and does not shift. But the big things are still made up: that a building stood here at all, and that it was for this work. Its place could also be off by about 20 m.

entries.card: why:PICTURE-BOUNDED FRONTAGE, other work. The undated Moss engra…
entries.text: PICTURE-BOUNDED FRONTAGE, other work. The undated Moss engraving published by Andreas in 1884 p.291 shows five long-wall sash and an end door. The transfer of that opening topology to the original 1835 footprint is reconstructed: the engraving may show a later enlarged or relocated state and cannot date this arrangement to 1835. The original 25 by 35 ft footprint, location, dates, height, roof and existing stack are retained. Chosen centres are snapped to the existing stud module; their fractions are not surveyed measurements. The former centre-passage house front is superseded, and no interior plan is asserted. The chapel mode leaves the pictured near gable blank; its unseen opposite end is also reconstructed blank. No interior partition arrangement is asserted.

levels.8-10: An old print by Moss, in a history book of 1884, shows five windows on the long wall and a door at the end. So we use that plan for this building in 1835. That is a guess: the print may show it later, after it was made bigger or moved. Its size, spot, dates, height, roof and chimney stay the same. The window spots are our choice. We no longer use the old front with a door in the middle. We claim no plan inside. Both end walls are left plain.

entries.card: why:PICTURE-LED SOUTH EAVES OPENING PATTERN FOR THE 1835 MODEL,…
entries.text: PICTURE-LED SOUTH EAVES OPENING PATTERN FOR THE 1835 MODEL, not a finding that this inn never had a side door. The held Andreas/Braunhold reproduction shows seven sash on the south long elevation on each floor, with a sash at the middle ground-floor station. The independently held original Trowbridge plate in Gale 1902, facing p.35 / scan n55, captioned 'The Green Tree Tavern in 1835', shows the same seven-bay window rhythm and no middle ground-floor door; its frontmost lower sash is partly obscured by the hanging board and people, while the middle station is visible. Setting this existing attribute to null selects the archetype's normal sash at all seven existing south-wall stations instead of substituting a door at the fourth station. The earlier John Gray testimony is retained here verbatim: 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side', with the hall and stairway behind it ("Green Tree Tavern." Chicagology. Transcribing the Inter Ocean of 1 July 1883…, transcribing the Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883; Gray kept the inn in 1838-41). That later recollection may describe a changed or schematic form, but it does not date the door to 1 July 1835, and the drawings do not prove its historical absence on that date. The choice follows the two pictured opening patterns as inferred form; exact July-1835 appearance remains uncertain. The original undated Andreas plate is not dated by the local reproduction's 1838 caption, and Trowbridge is retrospective, not an independent contemporary 1835 survey. Existing south-wall seven-bay count, even spacing, stock sash dimensions and height bands, north-wall rhythm, primary front entrance, footprint, geographic placement and all other form values stay unchanged. No c.1859 check required photograph or Gray-derived new geometry supplies this correction; the two public-domain picture records supply the visible sash pattern.

levels.8-10: This side of the inn follows the pictures. It does not say the inn never had a side door. Two old pictures show seven windows on the south side, on each floor, with a window, not a door, in the middle. One is labelled The Green Tree Tavern in 1835. So we draw seven windows there. John Gray kept the inn from 1838 to 1841. He later said there was a door in the middle of the long side on Lake Street. He may describe a later form. His memory does not date the door to 1835, and the pictures do not prove it was missing then. How it looked in July 1835 is still not sure.

entries.card: why:PICTURED, AND ONLY PICTURED. Panel 5 of the Kurz & Allison s…
entries.text: PICTURED, AND ONLY PICTURED. Panel 5 of the Kurz & Allison sheet, captioned 'Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835', draws this blockhouse with a small square body at the centre of its four-sided cap, under a little four-sided cap of its own; the two Wau-Bun reproductions of the 1831 view draw the same body. Two independent-looking depictions of this fort's blockhouse agree on the feature, which is what carries INFERRED rather than attested: the sheet is an 1893 retrospective, it is a modern reconstruction, it dates several of its own subjects wrongly, and its caption is not proof that this feature stood on 1 July 1835. EVERY DIMENSION IS RECONSTRUCTED and none of it is in this record: the side, the height, the cap's pitch, the plain boarded sides and the absence of louvres are the archetype's working reconstruction at the proportions the panel shows, and the liberties register owns them. The louvres and the ambiguous secondary projection of the 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print are NOT built: that print depicts about 1836-1849.

levels.8-10: Only a picture shows this. A sheet of 1893, labelled Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835, draws a small square box on top of the lookout tower's roof, with its own little cap. Two copies of an 1831 view show the same box. Two pictures that seem to agree make this a good guess, not a fact. The sheet was drawn long after, and it gets some of its own dates wrong. Every size is made up. We do not build the slats shown in a print of 1856, since that print shows the years 1836 to 1849.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-09. NO SURVIVING INTERSECTION LOCATES THIS BU…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-09. NO SURVIVING INTERSECTION LOCATES THIS BUILDING, so the method used for the Sauganash — half an 80 ft platted street off a documented corner — does not apply. The coordinate is derived from the datum origin at the forks confluence and from bank geometry instead, and it is the weakest placement in this parcel. What is attested: the tavern stood on the WEST BANK at the forks, north of the Lake Street crossing (chicagology, which puts it 'on the ground north of Lake Street Bridge'); James Kinzie's residence was next south of it and Father Walker's log meeting house north of it, so it sits in the middle of a three-building river-front row; and Wau-Bun's 1831 sequence reads 'Facing down the river from the west was, first a small tavern kept by Mr. Wentworth', which is why the facade is put on the river. Method: Lake Street's centreline northing at the west bank is 4637286.5, interpolated along Lake between the two OpenStreetMap control points (Lake and Canal, Lake and Market); its north kerb is 12.2 m beyond that at 4637298.7, half an 80 ft platted street. The footprint's south face is set 40 m north of that kerb, which places the building clearly north of the crossing while leaving room to the south for the Kinzie residence and about 50 m to the north for the meeting house, in the documented order. Across the bank, the footprint's east face is set back between about 11 m at its north end and 19 m at its south end from the MODERN west-bank line read from OpenStreetMap water polygons, the setback varying because the modern bank runs north-west across the building. WORKING UNCERTAINTY IS ABOUT 40 m ALONG THE BANK AND ABOUT 20 m ACROSS IT — the along-bank figure is this record's own, since nothing fixes how far north of the bridge the tavern stood; the across-bank figure is the georeference's, compounded by the modern bank not being the 1835 bank (this reach was wharfed and rebuilt, and the direction of that change is not established here). Facade bearing 90, due east onto the water; the bank runs north-west here, so anything from about 75 to 105 is equally defensible. Other work physical-L trial retains this numericUTM origin and90degree bearing. The old40m south-face placement and approximate11/19m modern-bank setbacks describe the former12x7m placeholder, not a newly verified contact after the plan change. The new7.2m localX span moves the former south extent4.8m north and the10.1m localY span moves the max-east frontage3.1m east; bbox centre changes(+1.55E,+2.4N)m. These are consequences of reconstructed geometry, not new surveyed coordinates; existing40m along-bank/20m across-bank uncertainties remain. Normal scene/contact/terrain/route compilation and actual app review are still required. Other work CENTRE-PRESERVING REBASE supersedes the retained-origin L trial in the preceding paragraph. The former12x7m placeholder bbox centre is kept at its old world position while replacing its outline with7.2x10.1m L. At the retained90degree bearing this changes only the model-origin coordinates by(-1.55E,-2.40N)m; it does not move that coarse old world centre or derive a historical coordinate from picture pixels. Exact new origin and plan are reconstructed, so this position attribute is explicitly reconstructed; west-bank/relative-order textual sources and40m along/20m across uncertainty remain. Numeric anchor becomesE446993.85,N4637348.30. Compared with the original rectangle, south extent is now2.4m north, max-east frontage1.55m east and max-north extent2.4m south. Checks against the committed the committed 1834 harbor-cut river outline river (not the modern bank cited earlier) keep body/apron dry at about3.69/2.18m; these are model-clearance diagnostics, not historical bank setbacks or surveyed precision. No source has established an exact1835 location, and terrain/contact/application checks still follow normally.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026. No street corner that still exists locates this inn, so the method we used for the Sauganash does not work here. We placed it from the river banks instead, and it is the weakest spot here. What papers say: the inn stood on the west bank where the rivers meet, north of the Lake Street bridge. James Kinzie's house was just south of it, and Father Walker's log church north. A book of 1831 says it faced down the river from the west, so its front faces the water. We set it about 130 feet north of Lake Street, leaving room for the Kinzie house. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet along the bank and 65 feet across it. Later we changed its shape to an L, which moved its edges a little. The spot itself did not change.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-09. The corner is documented and agreed by bo…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-09. The corner is documented and agreed by both sources — chicagology gives 'southeast corner of Randolph and Canal streets' and the hotel chronology gives 'the S.E. corner of Canal and Randolph streets' — but the COORDINATE is derived, so the tag follows the weaker half. MOVED 4.44 m ON 2026-08-10, and the move is the correction the control file owed. Method, the same as the Sauganash's: the modern intersection centre is read from OpenStreetMap and the footprint offset half an 80 ft platted street east and south of it, so that the building's west face sits on the Canal frontage and its north face on the Randolph frontage of a south-east corner lot; the offset south is taken from the footprint's north face, which is 18.29 m above its origin. WHAT CHANGED IS THE INTERSECTION CENTRE, not the method and not the corner. The 2026-08-09 reading (E 446919.6, N 4637148.5) was taken without recording which nodes it averaged, and re-deriving the junction on 2026-08-10 showed why that mattered: Randolph and Canal is a single crossing of the two street centrelines at E 446917.46, N 4637144.61, and the older number is reproduced only by averaging the roadway crossing together with three BIKEWAY crossings, which sit a few metres off the centrelines they follow. The road-only reading is adopted (the street control data § node rule), so the origin is now 446917.46 + 12.192 east and 4637144.61 - 12.192 - 18.29 north. The building moves 2.14 m west and 3.89 m south. That is an order of magnitude inside the georeference's own ±20 m and changes nothing about the corner, the lot or the frontages; what it changes is that the coordinate can now be re-fetched from the source it cites, which it could not be before. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's, not an additional guess. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Randolph. WHICH STREET THE 40 FT FRONT FACED IS NOT ATTESTED: chicagology says only 'The front was about forty feet and the wing sixty feet. It was in an L.' Randolph is adopted because it was the through street from the west and this was the house 'for all the farmers town from the west', for farmers and teamsters. If the front was on Canal instead, the same L is rotated to bearing 270 and the wing runs east rather than south — an alternative that costs nothing to test once the lot geometry is read off Wright 1834.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026. Two papers agree on the corner: the south east corner of Randolph and Canal Streets. But our spot on that corner is worked out, so we count it as a good guess. We read the crossing from a modern map, then moved in half the width of a street each way. The next day we found our first reading had mixed in bike paths. So we moved it about fifteen feet, which is tiny next to the map's own error. Its front faces north, onto Randolph. No paper says which street the front faced. A paper says the front was about forty feet, with a wing of sixty feet, in an L. We chose Randolph, since farmers and teamsters came along it from the west. If the front faced Canal, the L would just turn.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-10, AND THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED WHERE THE CO…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-10, AND THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED WHERE THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half — the same rule the Green Tree's placement uses. Andreas locates the bridge 'near the southeast corner of Kinzie and Canal streets, in the vicinity of the present bridge of the Chicago & Northwestern Railroad Company'; the war-dance account of 18 August 1835 corroborates the line by having a procession cross the North Branch bridge and then turn south along West Water Street in front of the Green Tree and Wolf Point taverns. Method: the modern Kinzie and Canal intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap (three shared nodes, mean 41.889068 N, -87.640156 W = EPSG:26916 E 446891.7, N 4637657.8, local N +262.0), and Kinzie Street is one of the streets that survives on its 1835 alignment. The DECK CENTRELINE is set on that northing and its ends are set where the traced 1834 waterline crosses it — not where the modern banks are, because the modern channel is a dredged and walled successor and using it would put the abutments on nineteenth-century engineering. The value recorded here is the footprint polygon's own origin, which is the deck's south-west corner (west end, upstream side), per the project's notes on glb contract. Facade bearing 0: this archetype's convention is that a deck at rotation 0 runs east-west with its upstream side north, and the Kinzie alignment runs east-west. WHAT THE CORNER DOES NOT SAY: modern Canal Street at this northing lies 63 m WEST of the traced 1834 west bank, so 'the south-east corner of Kinzie and Canal' is where the approach began and not where the bridge did. That gap is a fact about the two streets, not an error bar. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus the trace's own; along the street the position is better constrained than across it, because the crossing has to meet both banks.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026. The corner is in a paper, but our spot is worked out, so we count it as a good guess. A history book puts the bridge near the south east corner of Kinzie and Canal Streets. An account of a war dance on 18 August 1835 backs this up. In it, people cross this bridge and then turn south along West Water Street. We read the Kinzie and Canal crossing from a modern map. Kinzie Street still runs where it did in 1835. We set the bridge on that line. Its ends meet the banks as traced on the 1834 map, not today's banks, which were dug out and walled later. Today's Canal Street lies about 200 feet west of the old bank. So the corner is where the road to the bridge began, not the bridge itself.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-10. THE SOURCES AGREE ON A JUNCTION AND NEITH…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-10. THE SOURCES AGREE ON A JUNCTION AND NEITHER GIVES A CORNER. Andreas, twice: 'near the present corner of Lake and South Water streets' and 'a small log building near the corner of Lake and South Water streets'. Currey: 'about where South Water street intersects Lake street, near the east end of the bridge'. Both say NEAR and ABOUT, and neither names a side of either street, so this coordinate is a placement inside a named junction rather than a corner lot read off a plat — which is the opposite of the Sauganash's and the Green Tree's positions, where the corner is documented and only the metres are derived. WHERE THAT JUNCTION IS: Lake Street and South Water Street run parallel through the town and meet only at their west ends, where the main stem turns south into the south branch and the block between them narrows to a wedge against Market Street. Currey's 'east end of the bridge' is the Lake Street raft bridge over the south branch and puts the same site at the same place. Method: the modern Lake Street / Market Street intersection centre (Market is today's N Wacker Drive) was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447161.9, N 4637285.4 — the same node this project used for the Sauganash — giving Lake Street's north kerb 12.2 m north of it and Market Street's east kerb 12.2 m east of it, half an 80 ft platted street in each direction. The footprint's south face is set on that Lake Street frontage and its west end about 5 m east of the Market kerb, one narrow lot in from the corner rather than hard against it, because both sources say near and about. NOTE A DISAGREEMENT THE OFFSET RESTS ON: this project's placement offsets use the 80 ft street width annotated on Hathaway 1834, and the Currey page states the Thompson 1830 plat laid out streets 'uniformly 66 feet wide'. The difference is 2.1 m in each offset, an order of magnitude inside the georeference's own error, so it does not move this building — but it is the first time the two figures have been seen to disagree in this dataset and it is recorded here and in the research notes on hogan store § 5 rather than being quietly averaged. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for 'near', which is the larger of the two here — the wedge block this building sits in is roughly 40 m of frontage before the ground runs out at the water. Facade bearing 180, due south onto Lake Street, and it is INFERRED FROM THE STREET RATHER THAN FROM ANY STATEMENT: nothing says which way this building faced, and a store fronting South Water and the river instead would rotate it 180 degrees and put its back to Lake. The choice also decides which of the building's two documented dimensions runs along the street — the 45 ft is set along Lake, because a store's long elevation is its frontage — and that assignment is inference, not evidence, even though both numbers are. AND THE PAPERS DO SAY SOMETHING ABOUT IT. Hogan advertised on his own account in the Chicago Democrat from March 1834, and from 13 August 1834 to the issue of 1 July 1835 itself — eight printings — his standing notice gives his address as “at hi[s store] in South Water Street, one [door … of] the Post Office”. That is the man's own street for his own store, and it is South Water and not Lake. It does not move this coordinate and it is not read as a corner: the sources behind the position give a junction, this record sits in the wedge where Lake and South Water converge, and a building near that convergence can honestly be described as being in either street. What it does do is take the ground out from under the FACING. The bearing of 180 was inferred from the street because nothing said which way the building faced, and the only statement this project now holds about which street Hogan's store addressed gives the other one. The rotation is left where it is, because turning it would decide on one printing's preposition a question the sources still do not answer, and because the 45 ft dimension is assigned along whichever face is the frontage — but the inference is no longer unopposed, and the card says so. See research note for the harder reading of the same eight printings.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026. The papers agree on a crossing, but neither gives a corner. A history book says near the corner of Lake and South Water Streets. Another book says about where South Water meets Lake, near the east end of the bridge. Both say near and about, and neither names a side of the street. So we put it inside that crossing, not on a known corner lot. Lake and South Water meet only at their west ends, by the river. We set it on Lake Street, one small lot in from the corner. Our street width and one book's width differ a little, but too little to move the building. Its front faces south onto Lake Street. That is our reading from the street, not from any paper.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11 AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING, NOT AGAINST THE…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11 AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING, NOT AGAINST THE GROUND. What is attested is proximity and a foot of a street: Andreas, 'his shop being situated near the Agency House, at the foot of State Street'; the 1825 tax list gloss, 'David McKee lived on the North Side, near the agency-house of Dr. Wolcott'; the Scott family notice, 'lived on the north side of the river near the foot of what is now North State Street'; and Wau-Bun's ring — 'Around the Agency House were grouped a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government... blacksmith, striker, and laborers.' Method: this record's coordinate is set 32 m west of this project's Indian Agency House placement, on the same riverbank strip, its south face 16 m north of the drawn 1834 bank. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE INVENTED. 'Near' is unquantified and no source says which side of the agency house the smithy stood on; west was chosen because it keeps the shop inside the ring the sources describe and off the State Street frontage, and it could as easily have been north or east. Working uncertainty about 40 m — the georeference's 20 m plus the unquantified 'near'. A COMPETING PLACEMENT IS ON THE RECORD AND IS NOT ADOPTED: one of Andreas's recollections of the 1820s puts 'the blacksmith shop of David McKee and Joseph Porthick (Porthier)' next to a double log house 'nearly opposite the fort' occupied jointly by John Kinzie and Alexander Wolcott, which is the Kinzie house cluster some 400 m further east. Three statements name the agency house or the foot of State Street against that one, so the outlier is treated as a conflation of the two north-bank clusters. Facade bearing 180, due south, follows the agency house it is grouped with; nothing states it. There is no modelled terrain under this building — it stands about 450 m east of the terrain box.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, next to another building, not on the ground. The papers say only that the blacksmith shop was near the agency house, at the foot of State Street. Three papers say this. A book of 1831 says log houses of the government's workers, a blacksmith among them, stood around the agency house. So we set it about 100 feet west of the agency house, on the same strip by the river. That direction and distance are made up. Near gives no number, and it could as easily be north or east. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet. One other memory puts the shop much further east, by the Kinzie house. Three papers point the other way, so we treat that one as a mix up. Its front faces south, like the agency house.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11 AGAINST THE HOTEL, WHICH IS THE ONLY THING…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11 AGAINST THE HOTEL, WHICH IS THE ONLY THING THE SOURCE PLACES IT AGAINST. What is attested is a RELATION and not a location: 'In the rear was the large stable and the yard into which the trains were driven. There were entrances to the yard from both streets.' The hotel's own facade bearing in this dataset is 0, due north onto Randolph, so 'the rear' is south, and this coordinate shares the hotel's easting exactly (UTM E 446931.8) and stands 28.7 m south of the hotel's origin — which is to say the stable's north face is about 20 m behind the hotel's south wall. (Until the origin stood 27.2 m south; the stable was deepened from 7.0 to 8.5 m away from the yard, so the origin, which is the south-west corner, moved 1.5 m south and the north face did not move.) THE 20 M IS DERIVED FROM THE YARD, NOT PICKED: the yard is what the two buildings enclose, and the attested thing that happened in it is that wagon trains were driven in off two streets and turned. Twenty metres is about the least depth in which a two-horse team and its wagon can be driven in, unhitched and turned; less and the source's sentence stops being true of the drawing. It is still a number nobody wrote down. WHAT THIS INHERITS: the hotel's coordinate is itself derived from a modern OpenStreetMap reading of the Randolph and Canal intersection with a working uncertainty of about 20 m, and its facade bearing is an argued reading rather than an attested one — chicagology does not say which street the 40 ft front faced. If the hotel is turned to face Canal, this stable turns with it and stands east of the block instead of south of it, at the same distance. WORKING UNCERTAINTY about 20 m from the georeference, plus the hotel's own bearing question, plus the invented yard depth. Facade bearing 0: the stable faces north across the yard at the back of the hotel, which is where the teams stood; nothing states it.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, behind the hotel, since that is the only thing the paper places it against. A paper says that at the back were the large stable and the yard, where the wagon trains were driven in. The yard had a way in from both streets. The hotel faces north, so the back is south. So the stable stands right behind the hotel, about 65 feet back. We chose that gap because it is about the least room in which a team and wagon could be driven in, unhitched and turned. No one wrote down that number. If the hotel really faced Canal Street, the stable turns with it. Its front faces north across the yard.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11 AT THE MIDPOINT OF A BAND, BECAUSE THE TWO…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11 AT THE MIDPOINT OF A BAND, BECAUSE THE TWO ACCOUNTS PULL OPPOSITE WAYS AND THE MIDPOINT IS THE ONLY STATION THAT PREFERS NEITHER. the research notes on structures north section 5 gives the crossing as 'South Branch, between Lake and Randolph' and 'just north of the present Randolph street bridge'; the war-dance account has the procession come south along West Water Street from the North Branch bridge to 'the log raft bridge across the south branch near Lake Street', and then reach the Sauganash at Lake and Market. One source pulls the crossing to Randolph and the other to Lake. METHOD, the same one the North Branch record used. The modern Lake and Randolph centrelines were read from OpenStreetMap — Lake from Canal Street (OSM control already committed in the wright 1834 gcps data G5, the best-fitting point in that set at 1.8 m residual) to Dearborn Street (node 27477597), Randolph from LaSalle Street (G3) to Dearborn Street (node 28290271) — and both survive on their 1830s alignment. They lie 137.69 m apart; the crossing line is drawn parallel to them through the midpoint of that separation, at local N -177.2, and its ends are set where the traced 1834 waterlines cross it, not where the modern channel is. The value recorded here is the footprint polygon's own origin, which is the deck's south-west corner: the traced west waterline point on the crossing line, taken as the corner rather than the centre, an offset of 1.52 m that is two per cent of the georeference's own uncertainty. Facade bearing 0.292: the archetype's convention is that a deck at rotation 0 runs due east, and the Lake and Randolph line runs at 90.292 degrees from grid north. WHAT THE CONVENTION'S OTHER HALF DOES NOT SAY HERE: it also has the upstream side facing north, which is true of the North Branch and false of this crossing, because the South Branch flows north into the forks. Nothing in the mesh turns on it — this archetype's section is symmetric across the deck — but the record should not be read as claiming the upstream side is the north one. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus the trace's own, plus the 69 m of river along which the crossing could have stood. THE PARENTHETICAL ‘now Canal Street’ IS WITHDRAWN FROM THE LOCATION SENTENCE, 2026-09-12, AND WHAT IT WAS IS RECORDED HERE BECAUSE A READER WILL MEET IT AGAIN IN THE SOURCE. Until this date the sentence read ‘… its west landing on West Water Street (now Canal Street) below Wolf Point’, and the parenthesis was never this project’s identification. It is carried verbatim out of "Chicago's Last Great War Dance." Chicagology, transcribing the Chicago Tribune…, whose account moves the procession of 18 August 1835 ‘south along West Water street (now Canal street), in front of the “Green Tree Tavern” and “Wolf’s Point Tavern” to the log raft bridge across the south branch’ — the same sentence this record cites for the crossing and its load. THAT SOURCE’S OWN RECORD ALREADY RULES ON THIS CLASS OF WORDS, which is what makes the carry an error rather than a disagreement: the page is one attribution line, ‘Chicago Tribune, August 14, 1910’, over John Dean Caton’s written account printed after his death, and "Chicago's Last Great War Dance." Chicagology, transcribing the Chicago Tribune… says the Tribune ‘glosses him in 1910’s voice’, naming the parallel gloss ‘the “North Branch bridge” (which stood where the railroad bridge stands now)’ as ‘the newspaper locating the crossing for its readers, not the witness, and no placement here uses it’. A 1910 editor’s street-name equation is the newspaper’s voice on the same terms, and it had been let into the one sentence that tells a reader WHY this bridge stands where it does. AND THE COMMITTED GEOMETRY REFUSES THE EQUATION INDEPENDENTLY OF WHO SAID IT. Other work seated west water in the 1835 streets data off the committed 1834 west bank, and `canal` is fitted to modern Canal Street’s own surviving intersections (records the OSM nodes). AT THIS BRIDGE’S OWN NORTHING, local north −178, the two centrelines stand 152.09 m apart, and 131.00 to 159.44 m apart over the whole reach they share — recomputed from committed files by the west division streets check § 4, which the project's gate runs. The plat’s own module is 458 ft = 139.60 m, so the separation is a module and not a rounding, and the Thompson plat draws West Water and Canal as two of the West Division’s five north-south streets. Two streets a module apart cannot be one street under two names, so the landing is on the eastern of them and the gloss is withdrawn rather than restated. NOTHING ABOUT THE BRIDGE’S POSITION MOVES: what is withdrawn is a modern name for the street, not the street, and the coordinate above is still the midpoint of the band argued for at the head of this note. the research notes on west division streets § 1 holds the seating and the measurement; the research notes on south branch raft bridge § 3a holds this withdrawal.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, in the middle of a stretch, since two accounts pull opposite ways. Our notes put the bridge between Lake and Randolph Streets, just north of Randolph. The war dance account has people reach the log raft bridge near Lake Street. One pulls it to Randolph and the other to Lake. So we drew the bridge halfway between the two streets, which takes neither side. Its ends meet the banks as traced on the 1834 map, not today's channel. Our spot may be off by about 65 feet, and the bridge could have stood anywhere along about 225 feet of river. We also took out a note in brackets that called West Water Street now Canal Street. That was never our own reading.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11 FROM A REAL LOCATING SENTENCE, WHICH THE D…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11 FROM A REAL LOCATING SENTENCE, WHICH THE DOSSIER SAID DID NOT EXIST. the research notes on structures north section 3.12 records the brickyard's site as unattested and tags it [GAP]; a full-text search of Andreas vol. 1 closes that gap outright — 'on the North Side, not far from the river bank, between Dearborn and Clark streets' (scan p. 1161). That is a block of north-bank frontage about 120 m wide, which is a better fix than most buildings in this dataset have. METHOD: Clark Street's line at this latitude is taken from this project's own records on the same grid — the Chicago Democrat office at South Water and Clark sits at local E +551 to +564 — and Dearborn's from Madore Beaubien's house and Bates's auction room at South Water and Dearborn, local E +678 to +687, which puts the two streets about 120 m apart with the yard between them. The shed is set at local E +620 to +634, in the middle of that span, and at local N +109 to +114, about 17 m back from the traced north bank of the main stem, which is the reading of 'not far from the river bank' this record adopts. WHAT IS INFERRED RATHER THAN DOCUMENTED: the position WITHIN the two-street span and the exact setback from the water, both free within the sentence, and the fact that a yard is an area while this coordinate is a point — the working ground reached further in every direction than the shed this record draws. Working uncertainty about 60 m along the bank and 30 m across it, on top of the georeference's 20 m. Facade bearing 0, the open side of the drying shed facing north away from the river and into the yard, which is a working arrangement this record invents; see the form attributes.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, from a real sentence our notes said did not exist. Our notes called the brickyard's spot unknown. But a search of the history book found it: on the North Side, not far from the river bank, between Dearborn and Clark Streets. That is a stretch of about 400 feet along the bank, which is better than most buildings here have. We set the shed in the middle of it, about 55 feet back from the bank. Its exact spot in that stretch, and how far from the water, are our choice. Our spot may be off by about 200 feet along the bank. The shed's open side faces north into the yard, which is our own choice.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11 ON THE SOUTH-WEST CORNER; MOVED TO THE NOR…
entries.text:
PLACED 2026-08-11 ON THE SOUTH-WEST CORNER; MOVED TO THE NORTH-EAST 2026-09-06 UNDER other work, AFTER THE TWO PASSAGES THE OLD ARGUMENT WEIGHED AGAINST EACH OTHER WERE READ DIRECTLY OFF THE SCAN RATHER THAN AT SECOND HAND. The move is about 47 m north-east. Confidence stays `inferred` and the working uncertainty is unchanged: a better-argued corner is still a retrospective corner.

WHAT THE OLD ARGUMENT SAID, AND WHY IT DOES NOT SURVIVE THE READING. It adopted the south-west on the ground that Andreas scan p. 185 is a statement ABOUT the homestead while scan p. 339 uses the corner as a waypoint in a boundary walk through Block 5, and that a statement about the thing outranks a statement that passes it. The rule is right. The reading of p. 339 was wrong. P. 339 IS NOT A BOUNDARY WALK AND IT IS NOT ANDREAS: it is John Wentworth's address of 21 May 1881, reprinted, and the sentence is an instruction for finding this house. Verbatim off the scan (archive.org historyofchicago01andr, scan p. 339): 'If you wish to find the traditional residence of General Jean Baptiste Beaubien, after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house, go east upon South Water Street until you come to the northeast corner of South Water Street and Michigan Avenue, and you will find it.' Applied honestly, the old rule now points at the north-east: p. 339 is the passage that is about the building.

ONE WITNESS, NOT TWO. That sentence is word for word the sentence "Fort Dearborn History." Chicagology reprints and Wentworth, John. "Fort Dearborn: An Address delivered at the unveiling of the… holds as a document, so Andreas p. 339 and Wentworth are ONE witness reaching this project twice — Andreas 1884 carrying Wentworth 1881. This does not weaken the reading; it identifies it, and it is written here so that no later run counts the north-east twice.

THE SOUTH-WEST SENTENCE CITES THE TRANSACTION THAT CONTRADICTS IT. Andreas scan p. 185, read directly: 'The homestead of Colonel Beaubien was where now is the southwest corner of South Water Street and Michigan Avenue. This was bid in at the land sale in June, 1839, by James H. Collins, for $1,049.' The sale it names is the one Wentworth narrates on p. 339 — same buyer, same price — and Wentworth says which land it was: 'the land upon the east side of Michigan Avenue, in Block 5, between South Water Street and the lots reserved, where the Marine Hospital afterward was, except the corner lot, known as Lot 11... Mr. Collins bid $1,049 for the next five lots, 10, 9, 8, 7, and 6, where Beaubien's house, out-buildings, and garden were.' East side of Michigan Avenue, north of South Water Street, south of the reserved lots: that is the north-east quadrant, and it is the only quadrant of the four the sale can have been in. So p. 185's second clause places the ground its first clause mis-sites, and the south-west now rests on a single word inside a sentence that argues against it.

WHAT IS STILL NOT KNOWN, AND WHY THE CORNER IS TAKEN AS THE INSTRUCTION GIVES IT. Wentworth's own lot list puts the house, out-buildings and garden on lots 6 to 10 — the five lots NORTH of corner lot 11, which Beaubien kept — so the buildings stood some distance north of the corner itself and 'go until you come to the north-east corner and you will find it' is the finder's approximation, not a survey. No plat of the Fort Dearborn Addition carrying a lot dimension for Block 5 has been read by this project, so that distance is not quantified and is not invented here. The committed point is therefore a floor: the true position is at the corner or NORTH of it, never south or west of it.

THE CAVEAT THAT STILL MATTERS MORE THAN THE CORNER, UNCHANGED. NEITHER STREET EXISTED HERE IN 1835. The reservation was unplatted, no street crossed it, and South Water Street was ordered pitched only 'from the United States Reservation to Randolph Street'. Wentworth is speaking in 1881 and Andreas writing in 1884, both locating an old building by the streets of their own day, and the Fort Dearborn Addition whose Block 5 they cite was not platted until 1839. 'The corner of South Water and Michigan' is a retrospective locator and not an address this building ever had; any future evidence should be read as fixing it relative to the FORT, not to a grid that arrived later.

METHOD, THE MIRROR OF THE OLD ONE SO THE TWO ARE COMPARABLE. The modern East Upper Wacker Drive / North Michigan Avenue intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 448187.6, N 4637558.4 (four nodes averaged, spread 18.3 m, fetched 2026-08-11). The south-west placement put the origin 12.2 m west and 12.2 m south of that centre less the building's own width and depth; this one puts it 12.2 m EAST and 12.2 m NORTH of the same centre, so the footprint sits in the north-east quadrant with the same clearance from the retrospective kerb lines. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference, plus an unquantified allowance for the retrospective locator itself, plus the unmeasured northward offset above. The 45 m the two corners disagreed by is no longer an uncertainty on this record; it is a decided question, and the decision is written above rather than averaged away.

GROUND. The point stands on traced ground in the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield at +3.48 m above the summer-1835 water surface, against +2.51 m where it stood before — it has moved up the sand ridge east of the fort rather than off it, and the south bank of the main stem at this easting lies about 70 m further north again. Facade bearing 0 is unchanged, north toward the river, and it still has NO attested basis whatever: the streets it would face did not exist, and the bearing is a placeholder inherited from the retrospective grid.

WHAT other work MEASURED, 2026-09-11, AND IT DOES NOT MOVE THIS POINT. The question other work left open was a bearing: two passages put the factory building 'just south of the fort' and this record was said to stand north of it. BOTH HALVES OF THAT SENTENCE WERE WRONG ABOUT THE COMMITTED GEOMETRY. Resolved by the project's notes on glb contract md's own transform, this footprint's centroid is local ENU (1133.2, 177.8) and the palisade's southernmost corner is N 191.1, so the record already stands 10 m SOUTH of the fort's nearest corner and 43 m south of its centre — 'north of the fort' was the modern intersection's NAME, read off a street grid that did not exist here in 1835, and never the georeference. And the 1830 Harrison plan, the plate this project's fort is placed from, LETTERS 'U.S. Factor's House' against three solid blocks whose ink-weighted centre is local (1145.6, 38.7) — 140 m SOUTH of this point, and 152 m south of the stockade. the harrison 1830 us factors house data is the reading, with the same transform, the grave and the Out Buildings reproduced as checks, and the per-block figures. SO THE POSITION STANDS AND THE IDENTITY DOES NOT: what this record is placed by is the 1839 sale — Block 5, east of Michigan Avenue, between South Water Street and the reserved lots — and that ground is not the ground the plate letters, 140 m away inside the reservation. Moving this point onto the Factor's House would assert the identity the same measurement refuses.

levels.8-10: We first placed it on the south west corner, and in September 2026 we moved it about 150 feet to the north east corner. We moved it after reading two passages in the old scan ourselves. How sure we are does not change. The old reasoning said one passage was about the house, and the other just passed it on a walk. But the second one is really John Wentworth's speech of 1881, telling how to find this house. It says to go east on South Water Street to the north east corner of Michigan Avenue, and you will find it. So it is the passage about the house. The south west passage names a land sale of 1839. Wentworth tells which land that sale was, and it was on the east side of Michigan Avenue. So the north east wins.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11, AND IT IS A POSITION DERIVED FROM A NEIGH…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND IT IS A POSITION DERIVED FROM A NEIGHBOUR RATHER THAN FROM ANYTHING SURVEYED. What the source gives is an ORDER along the west bank and no distances: chicagology's Wolf Point narrative puts James Kinzie's residence south of Wentworth's tavern and Father Walker's log meeting house north of it, which is the same three-building sequence this project's Wolf Point Tavern record already carries in its own symbolic location. So this coordinate is anchored to that record: the tavern's south face sits at local N -57.1 and the north kerb of Lake Street at local N -97.1, leaving a 40 m stretch of west-bank frontage between the tavern and the crossing, and this house is set inside it with its south face at local N -87.8 — about 9 m clear of the street line and about 30 m south of the tavern, with room left between for Robert A. Kinzie's Store, which Andreas puts 'near Wentworth's tavern' (scan p. 235). ACROSS THE BANK: the east face is set about 13 m back from the modern west-bank line read from OpenStreetMap water polygons at the house's north face, widening to about 26 m at its south face because the bank swings east here as it runs down to the Lake Street crossing. That is the same setback band the tavern's record uses (11 to 19 m) and it is chosen for consistency with the row, not measured. UNCERTAINTY IS THE TAVERN'S PLUS THIS RECORD'S OWN: about 40 m along the bank (the liberties register “Wolf Point: three buildings placed from bank geometry, not from a corner” — nothing fixes how far north of the bridge the tavern stood, and everything hung off it inherits that) and about 20 m across it from the georeference, compounded by the modern bank not being the 1835 bank on a reach that was wharfed and rebuilt. Facade bearing 90, due east onto the water, following the row: Wau-Bun's 1831 sequence reads 'Facing down the river from the west was, first a small tavern kept by Mr. Wentworth', and the tavern, the Robinson cabins and the meeting house are all given that bearing in this dataset. Anything from about 75 to 105 is equally defensible.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, from a neighbour, not from any survey. A paper gives only an order along the west bank: James Kinzie's house was south of Wentworth's tavern, and Father Walker's church north of it. So we set this house south of the tavern, in the stretch between the tavern and Lake Street. It stands about 30 feet from the street and about 100 feet from the tavern. That leaves room between for Robert Kinzie's store, which a history book puts near the tavern. It stands back from the bank about as far as the tavern does. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet along the bank. Its front faces east onto the water, like the row.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11, AND IT IS A POSITION RELATIVE TO ANOTHER…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND IT IS A POSITION RELATIVE TO ANOTHER RECORD RATHER THAN TO ANY SURVIVING FEATURE. Andreas gives the direction — 'run a tannery just north of Miller's tavern' — and DRLOIH gives only proximity, 'near his brother's tavern'. Method: this project's own Miller House placement (local E +14, N +61, its north face on N +61) is taken as the anchor and this building is set 11.5 m north of that face on the same easting, so its south wall faces the tavern across a yard. THIS INHERITS EVERY UNCERTAINTY THE MILLER HOUSE CARRIES AND ADDS ONE. That record's own note says no surviving intersection locates it, that its coordinate comes from the datum origin and modern bank geometry, and that the along-bank axis is the softer one; on top of that, the 11.5 m separation recorded here is invented outright — 'just north' fixes a direction and no distance. Working uncertainty about 40 m, which is the Miller house's ~20 m plus the separation. WHY NORTH AND NOT INTO THE WATER: the point of land here is narrow, and the modelled 1834 waterline puts the North Branch about 40 m west of this building and the main stem about 15 m south of the tavern, so 'just north' is also the only direction with ground in it. A tannery is a nuisance trade — bark, lime and hides — and putting it behind the tavern rather than between the tavern and the water is consistent with that, but no source says so and it is not offered as evidence. Facade bearing 180, due south onto the tavern yard, inferred from nothing better than the building it is described against; nothing states which way it faced.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, from another building, not from anything that still stands. A history book says the tannery ran just north of Miller's tavern. Another paper says only near his brother's tavern. So we set it about 40 feet north of the Miller house, with a yard between. That gap is made up, since just north gives a direction but no distance. It also takes on every doubt of the Miller house's own spot. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet. The point of land here is narrow, with water close on two sides. So north is also the only way with ground. Its front faces south onto the tavern yard. Nothing says which way it faced.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11, AND THE STREET IS BETTER EVIDENCE HERE TH…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND THE STREET IS BETTER EVIDENCE HERE THAN IT IS ANYWHERE ELSE IN THIS DATASET, because this crossing is named for the street it is on. Andreas has Norton cutting his lumber 'on the land adjoining Michigan Avenue' and the bridge in line with Dearborn; the research notes on structures south section 12 puts the south abutment at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street. METHOD, the same one the North Branch and South Branch records use. The modern Dearborn Street centreline was read from OpenStreetMap at its Randolph Street crossing (node 28290271) and its Kinzie Street crossing (node 4336042974) — two points 528 m apart, straddling the river, on a street that survives on its 1830s alignment; the line through them runs at 359.419 degrees from grid north. Its ends are set where the traced 1834 waterlines cross it: the south bank of the main stem at local E +699.17, N +20.72 and the north bank at local E +698.39, N +97.05, read off the shoreline data, which carries the main stem east of the forks box. The value recorded here is the footprint polygon's own origin, which for this crossing is the deck's SOUTH end on its EAST side. Facade bearing 269.419: this archetype's convention is that a deck at rotation 0 runs due east with its upstream side facing north, so a deck running north up the Dearborn line has its upstream (west) elevation facing 269.419 degrees. THE STRUCTURE STANDS ON MODELLED GROUND, AND DID NOT WHEN THIS NOTE WAS WRITTEN. The 2026-08-11 text said, correctly at the time, that the committed heightfield was a 640 m box centred on the forks stopping at local E +320 while this bridge stands at E +699, so the terrain ended 380 m west of the south abutment. The box has since been extended east to E +1700 (the terrain spec data, grid), and other work graded approach fills at both ends (approaches dearborn south and dearborn north), so the deck is reachable on foot from either bank. Corrected 2026-08-21; the superseded reading is recorded here rather than deleted, because a reader of an older render deserves to know why the crossing hung in the air. Working uncertainty about 20 m from the georeference, plus the trace's own; across the river the position is better constrained than along it, because the crossing has to meet both banks. CURRENT WIDTH CORRECTION — other work. Widening the deck to sixteen feet changes only its footprint’s positive-v extent. This mapped origin, bearing, independently traced 76.33 m water gap and riverbank controls stay unchanged. The placement and its uncertainty remain independently stated; no new geographic derivation is claimed.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, and here the street is better proof than anywhere else, since the bridge is named for its street. A history book has the bridge in line with Dearborn Street. Our notes put the south end at the foot of Dearborn on South Water Street. We read Dearborn Street from a modern map, at two points on either side of the river. It still runs where it did in the 1830s. The bridge's ends meet the banks as traced on the 1834 map. When we first wrote this, our ground stopped far west of the bridge, so it hung in the air. Later we grew the ground east and added ramps at both ends. Now you can walk onto it from either bank. Making the deck sixteen feet wide did not move it.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11, AND UNIQUELY IN THIS PARCEL IT IS PLACED…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11, AND UNIQUELY IN THIS PARCEL IT IS PLACED AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING RATHER THAN AGAINST A STREET. The sources give a relation, not an address: a log building on Lake Street near the river, 'immediately adjacent to the Sauganash's public bar' (the research notes on structures north section 1), and since 2026-09-04 also "The History of Chicagoan Mark Beaubien, the Hospitality Guru began in 1830."…'s 'his original log cabin, adjacent to his Sauganash Tavern'. So this position is derived from the sauganash hotel json's data own placement and inherits every uncertainty in it. MOVED 2.08 M WEST ON 2026-09-04, and only because the wall it is set against moved: the Sauganash's frame 1831 footprint stopped being a 12 x 8 m placeholder and became a measured 9.92 x 8 m block, so its east face came in from E 447186.1 to E 447184.02 and this shop came with it. Nothing here is a new claim about where the shop stood; it is the same claim re-derived from a corrected wall. THE SAUGANASH'S PLACEMENT, RESTATED SO THIS RECORD CAN BE RE-DERIVED: the Sauganash stands at the south-east corner of Lake and Market, its frame 1831 footprint origin at EPSG:26916 E 447174.1, N 4637265.2, 9.92 m wide and 8 m deep with a facade bearing of 0, so its north face is on the Lake Street frontage at N 4637273.2 and its east face at E 447184.02. THIS SHOP IS SET HARD AGAINST THAT EAST FACE, its own west wall on E 447184.02 and its north face on the same Lake Street frontage, which is what 'immediately adjacent' means and is why the two footprints touch. WHICH SIDE THE BAR WAS ON IS NOT ATTESTED and the east side is chosen by elimination: the Sauganash's west face stands on the Market Street frontage, so there is no room for a building there at all. THAT ELIMINATION NOW CARRIES A SECOND BUILDING TOO. Until 2026-09-04 this note read that the retrospective depictions put the surviving 1829 log wing on the hotel's LEFT FRONT, 'which is the Market side', and the hotel's own record drew a log wing there. Both were wrong in the same way: the views are drawn from a station, not from a compass, and a log annex on the Market side would stand in Market Street exactly as a shop would. The annex at the left of every view IS THIS BUILDING — "The History of Chicagoan Mark Beaubien, the Hospitality Guru began in 1830."… captions the engraving 'The log cabin on the left was Chicago's first drugstore' — so the hotel's log wing attribute is retired and the hotel's second, TALL wing takes the same east end, standing back off the rear beside this cabin. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, the georeference's residual (the datum data, 17.5 m RMS), carried in from the Sauganash rather than added to; the 2.08 m correction above is inside it many times over and changes nothing about what this record knows. Facade bearing 0, north onto Lake Street, and the 20 ft dimension is set along the street with the 16 ft as the depth — the same convention Hogan's Store's record argues for and, like it, an inference rather than evidence. Turning the shop through 90 degrees would make it a 16 ft frontage 20 ft deep, and nothing decides.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026. Unlike any other here, it is placed against another building, not a street. The papers say it was a log building on Lake Street, right next to the Sauganash's bar. A later paper calls it his first log cabin, next to his tavern. So this spot comes from the hotel's own spot. In September 2026 we moved it about seven feet west. That was only because the hotel's wall moved when we measured the hotel. The shop stands hard against the hotel's east side, so the two touch. entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11, RE-DERIVED ONTO THE COMMITTED STREETS 202…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11, RE-DERIVED ONTO THE COMMITTED STREETS 2026-09-06, AND PUT ON THE NORTH BANK'S OWN FRONTAGE RULE 2026-09-11. THE STREET IS DOCUMENTED, THE CROSS-STREET IS A PROXIMITY, AND NO SOURCE GIVES A CORNER OR A SIDE. Both sources say the same thing in the same words — 'on North Water Street, near Kinzie' — which is one statement twice, since DRLOIH follows Andreas here as it does elsewhere. THE 2026-08-11 READING OF KINZIE STREET, AND WHY IT DOES NOT STAND. That placement read the Wright 1834 sheet at this project's fitted affine and wrote that the Kinzie Street alignment runs due east at local N +276. The committed `kinzie` record in the 1835 streets data runs at N +252.8 at this easting — 23.2 m south of the prose — and THE COMMITTED LINE WINS, on three counts. Other work made its geometry `attested` on the owner's ruling, because James Thompson's 1830 plat DRAWS the street. Its west end is anchored to real ground control: kinzie canal, Kinzie × Canal, five committed OSM node ids and a GCP, at local E −183.4, N +264.9, which is the record's own second vertex to within the 3.8 m correction that control already has queued against it; its east end is traced from OpenStreetMap contributors. Street centerline intersection nodes for downtown…. And other work derived North Water Street's east end INDEPENDENTLY of all that — as the crossing of the committed bank's offset curve with the committed kinzie line — and landed at local E +973.6, N +252.9, which is 0.1 m from the kinzie record. The argument is written out in full at the research notes on kinzie alignment; the reading was wrong about the NORTHING and right about everything else. THE ACROSS-STREET OFFSET IS THE NORTH BANK'S RULE AND NOT THE PLATTED MODULE. The street face stands 5.00 m from North Water Street's committed centreline: the street record's own track width (m) 6.0 gives a kerb 3.00 m out, and the front wall is set 2.00 m back from that kerb. That is not a figure invented for this house — it is the rule the four Dearborn sheds on this same bank are already placed by, stated four times over in their own notes and now argued once, in the place placement rules are stated, at the research notes on street module § 11. the north bank frontage check --gate re-derives it on every commit. Facade bearing 131.4 is the street's own bearing there, 41.4, turned to face it: south-east, across the roadway to the river. TWO 2026-09-06 DERIVATIONS PUT THIS HOUSE 36.79 M APART AND BOTH WERE GREEN; THIS RECORD SAYS WHICH IS TAKEN AND WHY THE OTHER IS NOT. PR #974, which landed, offset 12.192 m — half the 80 ft platted module — from the same centreline. IT IS NOT TAKEN, because the north bank has no platted module in this dataset: the street control data applies the 80 ft figure to Lake, Market, Canal, Randolph and Kinzie, its `measured` block records eleven corridors read off the two 1834 sheets and NOT ONE of them is north of the river, and the plat corridors tool gives north water no corridor ring at all because generate plat lots ew streets/ns streets name no north-bank street. Half a module this street is not known to carry is a number borrowed from the other side of the river, and it left this house standing 12.20 m back where every other building on the bank stands between 0.06 and 5.05 m. PR #975, which was closed, offset 7.00 m and moved the along-street station to 28.9 m short of the convergence. IT IS NOT TAKEN EITHER, on two measurements: its figure does not reproduce — it was argued from a neighbour band of '2.15 to 7.31 m' that re-measures on the committed records as 0.06 to 5.05 m, and its own `derivation.reason` says 3.00 m where its note says 7.00 — and its station put this facade 6.24 m from the committed `kinzie` centreline, which is 5.95 m INSIDE the platted corridor of an `attested`, module-bearing street. The placement committed here keeps #974's along-street station and takes neither of the two offsets: it is 7.87 m from where #974 left it and 32.66 m clear of Kinzie Street's centreline. THE ALONG-STREET STATION IS NOT A FREE CHOICE, AND IT IS #974'S, UNCHANGED IN SUBSTANCE. The house sits short of the convergence because the ground nearer to it is taken: Council House stands across the frontage from about 30 to 61 m short of the crossing, and this house is set one platted alley — 18 ft, 5.486 m, the other figure on the same Thompson annotation as the 80 ft street — west of that footprint. Moving the facade forward onto the frontage line opened that gap to 7.86 m, because the Council House stands further back than this house now does, so the station was slid 3.17 m north-east along the street's own bearing to close it again: the committed gap is 5.486 m and the anchor is 56.2 m from the derived convergence at E +973.6, N +252.9. Council House is `conjectural` and admits ±110 m along the bank inside a 215 m attested band, so it is the record with room to move and this one is the record with a frontage to keep; if it is ever re-sited, this house has the first claim on the ground it vacates. The correction was the large one and it stands: the 2026-08-11 placement stood 38.2 m north of the committed kinzie line, past the convergence and in the block NORTH of Kinzie, on no frontage at all. levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, and moved it twice since. The street is in the papers, the cross street is only near, and no paper gives a corner or a side. entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE ADJACENCY IS ATTESTED AND THE SIDE IS NOT. Andreas's trader list (scan p. 235) reads 'Indian Traders — Robert A. Kinzie, near Wentworth's tavern', which is a real locating statement and better than the dossier expected — the research notes on structures north section 2.4 records the exact corner as unattested. 'Near' does not say which side, and BOTH SIDES OF THE TAVERN ARE ALREADY SPOKEN FOR IN THIS DATASET: the gap immediately north of the tavern carries Log cabins at Wolf Point, placed there from Wau-Bun's 'Near him were two or three log cabins occupied by Robinson', and the ground south of the tavern carries James Kinzie's Residence from chicagology's 'south of Wentworth's tavern'. So the store is set in the south gap, between the tavern and James Kinzie's residence, which keeps every attested adjacency intact — Robert Kinzie near the tavern, James Kinzie south of it, Robinson's cabins near it to the north, Walker's meeting house beyond them — and inserts nothing into a stated sequence. That is a choice among defensible arrangements, not a derivation, and it is the reason this position is inferred rather than documented. METHOD: the south face sits at local N -69.8, about 5.7 m south of the tavern's south face and about 10 m north of James Kinzie's Residence; the east face is set about 12 m back from the modern west-bank line read from OpenStreetMap water polygons at the north face, widening to about 19 m at the south face as the bank swings east, which is the same setback band the tavern's own record uses. UNCERTAINTY: about 40 m along the bank, inherited whole from the tavern (the liberties register “Wolf Point: three buildings placed from bank geometry, not from a corner” — nothing fixes how far north of the Lake Street crossing the tavern stood), and about 20 m across it from the georeference, compounded by the modern bank not being the 1835 bank. Facade bearing 90, due east onto the water, following the row and Wau-Bun's 'Facing down the river from the west'; a storehouse trading goods off canoes has a positive reason to face the landing, but the bearing is the row's convention and not a finding.

levels.8-10: The papers say it was near the tavern, but not which side. A history book lists Robert Kinzie as a trader near Wentworth's tavern. That is a real clue, better than our notes expected. Both sides of the tavern are already taken. North of it stand Robinson's log cabins, and south of it James Kinzie's house. So we set the store in the gap south of the tavern, before James Kinzie's house. That keeps everyone the papers name in their places, and adds nothing to a known order. It is a choice among fair ways to arrange them, not a finding. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet along the bank, taken whole from the tavern, and about 65 feet across it. Its front faces east, onto the water, like the row. A store that traded goods off canoes had a good reason to face the landing. But the way it faces is the row's habit, not a finding.

entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE BLOCK FACE IS DOCUMENTED AND THE POINT ALONG IT IS NOT. Andreas gives 'west side of Dearborn Street between Lake and South Water' — a side of a street and a pair of cross streets, which fixes one axis tightly and leaves the other free over the whole 126 m of the block. METHOD: Dearborn Street is unchanged; its modern centreline easting was taken as the mean of the two intersection centres read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 — West Upper Wacker Drive / North Dearborn E 447771.8, N 4637409.0 and West Lake Street / North Dearborn E 447772.7, N 4637283.0 (fetched 2026-08-11) — giving E 447772.2, and the west kerb 12.2 m west of that at E 447760.0. The footprint's east face is set on that kerb and the building centred on the block face at N 4637346. THE UNCERTAINTY IS NOT ISOTROPIC AND THAT IS THE POINT: across the street it is about 20 m, the georeference's residual (the datum data, 17.5 m RMS); ALONG the street it is about 55 m, half the block, because nothing says where on the face the room stood. A COLLISION RECORDED RATHER THAN NUDGED: Madore Beaubien's Log House is documented on Lot 1 at the south-west corner of South Water and Dearborn, which is the north end of this same block face. The two records do not overlap only because this one is centred for want of a statement. If the auction room stood at the north end of the face it stood on Madore Beaubien's lot, and one of the two records is then wrong about something. Facade bearing 90, due east onto Dearborn: the street the source names is the one it fronts, which is the only bearing argument this record has. MOVED BACK ONTO ITS LOT 2026-11-03, on the owner's report of buildings 'placed in the middle of the walkways or alleys': its front wall stood 0.98 m out past the Dearborn Street lot line of block 17, on the plank walk's line; moved 2.48 m back so that wall stands 1.50 m inside the lot line; and it stood 4.70 m inside the 18 ft platted alley of block 17; moved 5.00 m away from the alley, square to it, so its alley wall stands 0.3 m clear of the alley line. The translation is dE -2.42 m, dN +5.02 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447752.4 N 4637352.1 becomes E 447749.985 N 4637357.116. NOTHING THE SOURCES SAY MOVED: the corner, side, block or cluster this record is placed by is unchanged, and so is its confidence grade; the coordinate was derived, never read, so it is re-derived against this project's own platted lot line and alley, which the structure clearance check now holds every 1835 building to. The point along the block face was never a source's (it was the middle of the face, which is where the platted alley comes out), so moving it north along Dearborn changes no claim. SLID NORTH 2026-11-15, ALONG THE FACE AND NOT ACROSS IT. Gifford's view of the first Tremont House draws seven stores running north from the hotel up this face, five before the block alley and two after it; the room's place along the face was never documented, so it now stands after them, its north end 26.5 m south of the block's South Water corner.
