entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE SOURCE SAYS 'NEAR', NOT 'AT', AND THIS RECORD DOES NOT UPGRADE IT. Verbatim: 'In a few weeks the building was erected NEAR the corner of Franklin and South Water streets' (baptisthistoryhomepage). Andreas elsewhere calls it 'a small house of worship belonging to the First Baptist Church Society, on South Water Street, near Franklin'. This project's own dossier renders both as 'corner of Franklin and South Water' at the research notes on structures south lines 130 and 220, which is a hardening the sources do not support: the page does not say 'at' and does not say which of the four corners. THE POSITION IS THEREFORE INFERRED, NOT DOCUMENTED, and two of the four quadrants are argued away rather than guessed away. The NORTH side of South Water is excluded because it was the river bank - wharves, landings and lumber piles the whole length of the street (the research notes on structures south section 12) - and a subscription meeting house was not built on the dock line. Of the two south quadrants, EAST of Franklin is adopted because this project's own block-by-block reading puts the Temple Building in the Franklin-to-Wells block with the post office and Brewster, Hogan & Co., and because Andreas's phrase is 'on South Water Street, near Franklin' rather than 'at Franklin', which reads as a position along the street measured from the corner. If it stood west of Franklin instead, the building belongs about 25 to 60 m west of this coordinate. METHOD: the modern West Wacker Drive / North Franklin Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447281.16, N 4637407.21 (2 nodes averaged, spread 15.3 m, fetched 2026-08-11), and the footprint origin set 12.2 m east of it and 12.2 m south of it less the building's own depth, so the north face sits on the South Water frontage and the west face on the Franklin frontage of a south-east corner lot. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference, plus the quadrant risk above, plus the standing caveat that MODERN WACKER DRIVE IS NOT EXACTLY THE 1835 SOUTH WATER LINE - Wacker was built on South Water's right of way in 1924-26 and widened northward over the old dock line, which the P. F. W. Peck's Store record sets out at length. Facade bearing 0, due north onto South Water, inferred from the street; nothing says which way the building faced. RECONCILED WITH THE COMMITTED PLAT 2026-08-24, AND THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE — ONLY THE LINE IT WAS DERIVED AGAINST. The method above set this footprint's north face on the South Water frontage, and it found that frontage by taking the MODERN West Wacker Drive centreline out of OpenStreetMap and stepping 12.2 m south of it. That is not this project's own South Water Street: the committed centreline in the 1835 streets data, offset by half the committed 80 ft corridor, is what the plat lots generator builds every platted block edge from, and it is the line every derived layer in this scene reads. Measured against it, this record's north wall stood 5.40 m OUT PAST the block 20 frontage line, in the platted roadway — far enough into it that the frontage works generator refused the plank sidewalk along this stretch of South Water in writing and named this building in the refusal. THE REPAIR IS THIS RECORD'S OWN METHOD RUN AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S OWN LINE: the footprint is translated 6.90 m along the face's inward normal — dE +0.063 m, dN -6.899 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447293.36 N 4637387.39 becomes E 447293.423 N 4637380.491 — which leaves its north wall 1.50 m back from the committed frontage line, the same margin the block infill generator gives every reconstructed unit standing on this face. NOTHING ALONG THE STREET MOVED: the along-face position, the block, the corner and the side are untouched, and so is the confidence grade — re-deriving a coordinate from better geometry is not new evidence. WHAT IS STILL WRONG AND IS LEFT WRITTEN DOWN: the facade bearing stays 0 while this face runs at 359.478 (i.e. -0.522), so the front wall is 1.50 m back at its worst corner and up to 1.58 m at the other. That skew is smaller than the walk's own daylight and it is not corrected here, because rotating a documented record is a second claim and this one is a repair. A THIRD PRINTING OF THE SAME LOCATOR, AND IT DOES NOT NARROW IT. Moses and Kirkland, vol. 2, printed page 79, put the First Baptist church 'on South Water street near Franklin' - the same street, the same cross street and the same 'near' as Andreas. It names no side, no corner and no lot, so the confidence stays inferred and the quadrant argument above is unchanged.

levels.8-10: The paper says near, not at, and we do not make it stronger. One paper says the building went up in a few weeks near the corner of Franklin and South Water Streets. A history book says it was a small church of the First Baptist group, on South Water Street, near Franklin. Our own notes had turned both into at the corner, which the papers do not support. So its spot is a good guess, not a fact. Two of the four corners we rule out with reasons. The north side of the street was the river bank, with wharves and lumber piles, and a church was not built on the docks. Of the two south corners, we chose east of Franklin. The book's words, on South Water Street near Franklin, read like a spot along the street, measured from the corner. If it stood west of Franklin, it belongs about 80 to 200 feet west. Our spot may be off by about 65 feet more. Its front faces north onto South Water Street, from the street. Our first spot for this building was measured from a modern street, not from our own street of 1835. Against our own street, its front wall stood 5.40 m out in the road, so the plank walk could not pass it. So we moved it back. What we claim about it did not change, only the line we measured from. We moved this building 6.90 m so its north wall stands 1.50 m back from the street line. Our other made-up buildings on this street stand the same way. Nothing moved along the street. Fixing a point with better lines is not new proof, so how sure we are stays the same. One small thing is still off. The front is turned a tiny bit from the line of the street, so one corner sits a little farther back. We leave it, since turning a real building would be a new claim. A third book gives the same words, and they do not narrow it. A later history book puts the First Baptist church on South Water Street near Franklin. It is the same street, the same cross street and the same near. It names no side, corner or lot, so how sure we are does not change.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-11. THE STREET AND THE CROSS-STREET ARE DOCUM…
entries.text: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE STREET AND THE CROSS-STREET ARE DOCUMENTED, THE SIDE OF LAKE STREET IS AN INFERENCE FROM TWO STATEMENTS THAT AGREE, AND THE POSITION ALONG THE BLOCK IS THIS RECORD'S CHOICE. What is attested: Andreas p. 635, 'it stood on Lake near Dearborn and almost opposite the old Tremont House'; Andreas in his inventory of the town in the fall of 1833, 'the Mansion House, where are now numbers 84 and 86 Lake Street'; and Judge J. D. Caton, quoted by Andreas, recalling the May 1834 court term 'in the unfinished loft of the old Mansion House, JUST NORTH OF WHERE THE TREMONT NOW STANDS'. The Tremont standing when Caton spoke was the post-1850 brick house, which "Tremont House." Chicagology. Compiling city-directory entries 1846-1870, an…'s header places at the SOUTH-EAST corner of Lake and Dearborn; 'just north of' that is the NORTH-EAST corner of the crossing, i.e. the north side of Lake immediately east of Dearborn. That agrees with 'almost opposite the old Tremont House', since the first Tremont stood on the north-west corner and the two houses face each other across Dearborn Street rather than across Lake - 'almost opposite' is doing loose work in that sentence and is read here as the diagonal. METHOD: the modern West Lake Street / North Dearborn Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 447772.72, N 4637283.04 (OSM node 27477597, fetched 2026-08-11), the building's south face set on the Lake frontage 12.2 m north of it and its west face on the Dearborn frontage 12.2 m east of it, 12.2 m being half of an 80 ft street as annotated on Hathaway 1834. The stored coordinate is the polygon origin AFTER the 180 degree facade bearing, which under the renderer's convention (the walkthrough's walker code) puts it at the building's north-east corner. THE SOUTH FACE IS SET ON THE STREET LINE ON PURPOSE AND IT IS ATTESTED: the 1833 frame addition 'came out to a line with the street', which is a rare thing to be told about a Chicago building and is the one dimension-like statement this record has. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (the datum data, 17.5 m RMS), PLUS AT LEAST A LOT'S WIDTH ALONG LAKE STREET: 'near Dearborn' is not 'at the corner', so the house may have stood one or two lots further east - South Water lots were 55 ft and Lake's were probably similar, so read the along-street position as good to about plus or minus 20 m on top of the georeference. Facade bearing 180, due south onto Lake Street, which follows from the attested street line and not from any statement about the front. THE GROUND UNDER IT IS NOW MODELLED: the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield was extended east and its box now runs local E -320..+1700 and N -400..+400 (the heightfield data), so this footprint sits on real terrain and the validator measures its contact rather than clamping at a box edge. It lands within the walker's 0.35 m step-up rule, so the phase carries no ground contact declaration. That is new as of this parcel: the liberties register “Two thirds of the town stands on ground that has not been built” - two thirds of the town standing on ground that had not been built - is already in that document's Resolved section, and this record is written on the far side of that resolution: no Lake Street building in this parcel needed a ground contact declaration. APPENDED 2026-08-29, other work — A LOT AND BLOCK NUMBER FOR THIS HOUSE, WHICH THIS RECORD CANNOT YET USE, AND ONE READING THAT IT CAN. G. Spring's For-Sale notice ran in the Chicago Democrat six times between 1834-06-18 and 1834-11-19: 'LOT No. 7, in block No. 16, ONE LOT EAST OF HADDOCK'S TAVERN, on Lake street, in the town of Chicago. There is on said lot a large Dwelling-House and fine well' (1834-06-18 c006; also 1834-09-03 c005, 1834-10-15 c006, 1834-11-19 c010). Haddock's Tavern is this house - see the occupants note for the succession and the research note for the spelling. THE BLOCK NUMBER WAS UNUSABLE HERE WHEN THIS PARAGRAPH WAS WRITTEN, and it is usable now — see the note at the end of this field. Nothing committed carried the Thompson plat's block NUMBERING: the thompson lots data keyed its nineteen blocks on their bounding streets and no record in the sources data numbered one, so the most precise placement statement the whole newspaper corpus makes about any building in this town resolved to nothing on the committed plat. WHAT IS USABLE IS THE NEIGHBOUR: the lot immediately EAST of the tavern carried a large DWELLING-HOUSE and a well, so it was not a shop. J. K. Botsford advertised in the same paper both 'next door to Graves' Tavern' and at the 'Corner of Dearborn and Lake-sts.', and other work found the corpus supports reading those as ONE frontage; if they are one, Botsford stood on this house's WEST side - the Dearborn corner - and this house stood on the SECOND lot from Dearborn rather than on the corner lot. THAT AGREES WITH THIS RECORD AND DOES NOT MOVE IT. 'Near Dearborn' is not 'at the corner' - the along-street allowance stated above already says the house may stand one or two lots further east - and one lot is about 24 m, inside the plus-or-minus this note already carries. The stored coordinate is UNCHANGED: shifting a building inside its own declared uncertainty on the strength of an inference buys precision the evidence has not paid for. The argument is written out in the research notes on botsford graves. APPENDED 2026-08-29, other work — BLOCK 16 IS NOW ON THE COMMITTED PLAT, AND IT PUTS THIS HOUSE ONE LOT EAST OF WHERE IT STANDS. WITHOUT MOVING IT. The owner's crop of Wright's 1834 sheet carries two adjacent block numbers, 19 west of 18, in the row fronting South Water Street; counting east at one block per step reaches 16 on the Dearborn-State block, whose Lake Street frontage is its south row, and the lot scheme the same crop shows runs 5 6 7 8 west to east along a south row. So Spring's lot 7 is the third lot east of Dearborn and Haddock's Tavern, one lot west of it, is the SECOND — which is where other work had already put this house from Botsford, and which is exactly the reading recorded in the paragraph above. THE COUNT IS INFERRED AND SO IS THE PLACEMENT IT AGREES WITH; three statements agreeing is not a survey. The measurable consequence: this record's west face stands on the Dearborn frontage at local E +712.2, on lot 5, and lot 6 begins 24.2 m east of it at E +736.4. That gap is ONE LOT, and it is inside the along-street allowance this note already declares. THE STORED COORDINATE IS STILL UNCHANGED, for the reason given above and one more: moving a committed building on the strength of an inference authored in the same commit is precision the evidence has not paid for. What has changed is that the discrepancy is now a number. the thompson block numbering data and the research notes on thompson block numbering. MOVED 2026-10-04, other work — ONE PLATTED LOT EAST, ONTO PLAT LOT 6 (block 16#03), THE LOT THREE READINGS NOW AGREE ON. The two paragraphs above twice left the coordinate where it was, each time for the same stated reason: precision the evidence had not paid for. That reason no longer holds, for three things that were not true when they were written. (1) THE PHRASE DOES NOT HAVE TO BE A MEASUREMENT. Whether Spring's 'one lot east of Haddock's Tavern' is a surveyor's count or a seller's 'next door', it names the lot ADJACENT to lot 7 on the west, and on a row numbered 5 6 7 8 west to east that is lot 6 under both readings; lot 5, where the house stood, is not next door to lot 7 in either. The only reading that keeps it on lot 5 is a house spanning lots 5 and 6, and nothing says it did. (2) THE TOWN ALREADY ACTED ON THE NOTICE ONE LOT OVER: other work re-dealt lot 7's roof to an H1 house on the strength of the same advertisement's 'large Dwelling-House', so the town has been answering the notice's lot 7 while standing the tavern it is measured from two lots west of it, with an invented plank shanty on the lot between them that the notice says was the tavern's. (3) THE BOTSFORD READING PUTS A STORE ON THE CORNER AND THE TAVERN NEXT DOOR TO IT, which is the same lot by an independent route. Three statements agreeing is still not a survey, which is why the confidence stays inferred and the block and lot count it rests on (the thompson block numbering data) is still an inference from Wright's 1834 crop. AN 1834 NOTICE MAY PLACE THIS HOUSE IN 1835 BECAUSE IT IS NOT ASSERTING AN 1835 FACT: the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 refuses an earlier source as evidence that a thing EXISTED at the scene date, and this house's existence across 1833-1850 rests on Andreas, not on the notice. The notice dates where the house stood in 1834, and the phase itself is the claim that nothing about the house changed between its 1833 frame addition and its 1850 removal; a log tavern with a frame front was not moved along Lake Street in the meantime by anything any source records. METHOD: the house keeps exactly the seat it had on lot 5 — its south face where it was relative to the Lake Street line, its west face 1.8 m inside the lot's west line — translated by the committed plat's own lot-to-lot vector along the Lake face, (+25.92, -0.22) m local, read from the thompson lots data (lot 5's south-west corner 710.44,-103.26 to lot 6's 736.36,-103.48). No other coordinate is authored. WHAT IT COSTS 'ALMOST OPPOSITE THE OLD TREMONT HOUSE': the first Tremont stood on the north-west corner, so the two houses now face each other across Dearborn Street and one lot of Lake frontage rather than across the crossing alone, which 'almost' already allowed. Its stable moved with it, and the anonymous D2 shanty that stood where it now stands took the Dearborn corner it left (the liberties register “The plank shanty on Lake Street takes the Dearborn corner the Mansion House left”). The working uncertainty along the street is now the lot's own width, not a lot's width ON TOP of it.

levels.8-10: A paper names the street and the cross street. Which side of Lake Street it stood on is a guess from two papers that agree. Where along the block it stood is our choice. A history book says it stood on Lake near Dearborn, almost opposite the old Tremont House. Judge Caton remembered holding court in its unfinished loft in May 1834, just north of where the Tremont then stood. That later Tremont was on the south east corner, so just north of it is the north side of Lake, east of Dearborn. A paper also says the frame front of 1833 came out to the street line. That is rare to be told, so its front sits right on the street. In 1834 an ad by G. Spring offered lot 7 in block 16, one lot east of Haddock's tavern, with a large house and a fine well on it. Haddock's tavern is this house. Another ad puts a store at the Dearborn corner, next door to this house. Counting lots on the old map, three readings now agree: this house stood on lot 6, the second lot from Dearborn. For a while we did not move it, since that would buy more exactness than the proof had paid for. In October 2026 we moved it one lot east, onto lot 6, keeping the same spot within the lot. Its stable moved with it. A small shed took the corner it left. The 1834 ad only dates where the house stood in 1834. A history book says the house stood from 1833 to 1850, and nothing says it moved.

entries.card: why:PLACED 2026-08-29, AND THE PLACEMENT IS THE WEAKEST HALF OF…
entries.text:
PLACED 2026-08-29, AND THE PLACEMENT IS THE WEAKEST HALF OF THIS RECORD — say so first. Andreas gives the address in six words: 'a frame building on the north side of Lake Street, near Wells' (Andreas I, scan pp. 913, 971; carried into this project's own dossier at the research notes on structures south § 6). 'Near Wells' is a neighbourhood, not a corner, and this record does not upgrade it into one. WHAT THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED FROM. The north side of Lake Street between Franklin and Wells is the SOUTH row of the committed platted block block 20, whose lot grid is the thompson lots data — the same committed geometry the block infill generator stands every reconstructed roof on this face on, and the same geometry the plat lots generator builds the block edge from. Lot 7 of that grid is the south-row lot at the WELLS end of the block: its east line is the Wells corridor edge, so it is the lot on the north side of Lake Street nearest Wells, and it is unoccupied — the block's committed deal (the 1835 platted block parcels data) places its Lake-face roofs on lots 3 and 5 and leaves this one empty. The footprint is CENTRED on that lot's Lake frontage, its front wall set back 1.50 m from the committed frontage line — the same margin the generator gives every unit standing on a block face — which puts the front wall at local ENU (305.492, -98.470) and the polygon origin at (311.651, -90.900), i.e. UTM 16N E 447384.351 N 4637304.900. THE CORNER IS REFUSED, IN WRITING. The obvious temptation is to push the building east to the Wells corner and call it the corner of Lake and Wells: it would read better in the scene and it would give the two American offices below a smarter address. Andreas says 'near Wells' and this project's rule is that a placement inference never sharpens a source. Centring on the Wells-end lot is the least specific placement that still satisfies the words; the residual is the lot, about 24 m of frontage, and it is smaller than the georeference's own working uncertainty. THE SIDE OF WELLS IS AN OPEN QUESTION AND IS NOT HIDDEN. 'Near Wells' is satisfied by the Lake frontage on EITHER side of Wells Street — the block west of it (this one) or block 19 east of it — and nothing reached decides between them. The west block is chosen because its Wells-end lot on Lake is free while the east block's Lake face already carries three dealt roofs, so standing here displaces nothing; that is a reason about this dataset, not evidence about 1835, and it is recorded at the liberties register rather than argued away. A source that names the side, or a lot number, moves this building one block east at no cost to anything else on the record. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 30 M: the georeference's own residual (the datum data: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834) plus the half-lot the 'near Wells' reading leaves free along the frontage. FACADE BEARING 180.47 DEGREES, which is the outward normal of this lot's own committed Lake frontage line and not a claim about the building: a hotel with 'eaves to the street' fronts the street it is addressed from, and Lake Street lies south of it.

MOVED 2026-10-23, 8.0 M WEST, BECAUSE THE LOT WAS NOT FREE. The paragraph above calls the Wells-end lot on this Lake face unoccupied, reading the block's dealt roofs; it was not, because the Exchange Coffee House — 'a new house on the northwest corner of Wells and Lake streets', placed a fortnight before this record — already stood on its Wells corner. The two hotels' footprints overlapped by about 50 square metres, 6.5 m deep, and in the scene one frame building stood half inside the other. The Exchange keeps the corner, which is what its source names; this house moves west along the same Lake frontage until its east wall stands 1.4 m clear of the Exchange's west wall. That is still the north side of Lake Street and still the lot at the Wells end, so 'near Wells' is read exactly as loosely as before; it is no longer CENTRED on that lot's frontage, and the residual that centring was chosen to state is unchanged. Bearing, set-back and footprint are as they were.

levels.8-10: We placed it in August 2026, and its spot is the weakest part of this card, so we say that first. A history book gives the address in a few words: a frame building on the north side of Lake Street, near Wells. Near Wells is an area, not a corner, and we do not make it one. We set it on the empty lot at the Wells end of the block, on the north side of Lake Street, set back from the street line like its neighbours. We refuse to push it to the corner. That would look better and give the paper's offices a smarter address, but our rule is that a guess never makes a paper sharper than it is. Near Wells also fits the block on the other side of Wells. We chose this side only because its lot was free, which is about our records, not about 1835. A paper naming the side or lot would move it a block east. Our spot may be off by about 100 feet.

entries.card: why:PLACED AGAINST ONE BUILDING AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND, AND…
entries.text: PLACED AGAINST ONE BUILDING AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND, AND THE BUILDING IT IS PLACED AGAINST IS ITSELF RECONSTRUCTED. The evidence is the word "east": "the Lake House in course of construction, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball". No source gives this house a street, a corner, a lot or a distance. METHOD: the west face is set 12.0 m east of Lake House (under construction)'s committed east face, and the north face on the same line as the Lake House's own north face, so the two front the same frontage with a yard between them. THE 12.0 m AND THE SHARED FRONT LINE ARE BOTH INVENTED. This position therefore inherits every uncertainty the Lake House's carries and adds one of its own: the Lake House's own note records that which side of Rush Street its block is on is not documented at all and that if the east side is wrong the building belongs about 110 m west, and that this project's georeference of that corner carries about 20 m of working uncertainty. If the Lake House moves, this house moves with it, which is the honest consequence of a placement whose whole content is "east of". WORKING UNCERTAINTY about 110 m, governed by the side of Rush Street and not by the survey. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Michigan Street, follows the Lake House, which is the one building on this frontage a source orients; nothing states this one's. The ground here is the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield at about +1.51 m above the summer-1835 water surface - traced ground - so the record declares no ground contact of its own. ONE DISAGREEMENT THIS POSITION DOES NOT RESOLVE, and it is not this record's to resolve: the committed michigan north centreline runs at local N 390.0 here, which puts this frontage 21.6 m back from the street corridor's south edge rather than on it. The Lake House stands at the same setback for the same reason - its frontage was fitted to the modern Hubbard/Rush corner and not to the committed street - and moving either building onto the committed line is a question about michigan north's geometry, filed rather than answered here.

levels.8-10: We placed it next to one building, not on the ground, and that building is itself made up. The only proof is the word east. A man named Bonnell wrote that the Lake House was being built, and east of it was the house of Dr Kimball. No paper gives this house a street, corner, lot or distance. So we set it about 40 feet east of the Lake House, with its front in line with the Lake House front, and a yard between them. That gap and that line are both made up. It takes on every doubt of the Lake House's spot, and adds its own. No paper says which side of Rush Street the Lake House's block was on. If that is wrong, both belong about 360 feet west. If the Lake House moves, this house moves with it. Its front faces north, like the Lake House. It also stands back from our Michigan Street line, as the Lake House does, a question we write down and leave open.

entries.card: why:PLACED AGAINST THE AGENCY HOUSE AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND.…
entries.text: PLACED AGAINST THE AGENCY HOUSE AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND. Two sentences describe this group and neither describes a building. Wau-Bun, of 1831: "Around the Agency House were grouped a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government... blacksmith, striker, and laborers." Andreas, of the settlement about 1830: "In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell, an Indian chief, who was also interpreter for the agency." Between them the group is attested four ways over — that it existed, that it stood round the Agency House at the foot of State Street, that it was of logs, and who lived in it — and NOT ONCE is a single building given a shape, a size or a place of its own. METHOD: 22 m west of this project's Indian Agency House placement and 23 m east of its Government Blacksmith Shop placement, on the same bank strip, south face about 22 m north of the 1834 drawn bank. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE INVENTED. The one thing that is reasoned is the ORDER: the agency's interpreter is put nearest the agency house of the three buildings this parcel raises, which is reasoning about an office and not a reading of a sheet. The building is kept west of local E +814.8, the west edge of the Wolcott Street corridor this project derives, so it claims no roadway. Working uncertainty about 40 m. The ground here is the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield at about +1.34 m, so the house stands on traced ground and declares no ground contact. Facade bearing 180 follows the group; nothing states it.

levels.8-10: We placed it next to the agency house, not on the ground. Two lines tell of this group, and neither tells of one building. A book of 1831 says log houses stood around the agency house. The men who worked for the government lived in them, a blacksmith among them. A history book says small log houses near it were home to the blacksmith, Mr McKee. Billy Caldwell, a Native chief, lived there too. He spoke for the agency in Native tongues. So we know the group was there, around the agency house, made of logs, and who lived in it. But no one gives one house a shape, size or spot. We set this one between the agency house and the blacksmith shop, on the same strip by the river. The direction and distance are made up. The one thing we reason is the order. Caldwell worked for the agency, so his house goes nearest it. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet. Its front faces south, like the group.

entries.card: why:PLACED AGAINST THE GROUP AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND. Two sen…
entries.text:
PLACED AGAINST THE GROUP AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND. Two sentences describe this group and neither describes a building. Wau-Bun, of 1831: "Around the Agency House were grouped a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government... blacksmith, striker, and laborers." Andreas, of the settlement about 1830: "In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell, an Indian chief, who was also interpreter for the agency." Between them the group is attested four ways over — that it existed, that it stood round the Agency House at the foot of State Street, that it was of logs, and who lived in it — and NOT ONCE is a single building given a shape, a size or a place of its own. METHOD: 21 m west of this record's David McKee's log house and 42 m west of Government Blacksmith Shop, on the same bank strip, south face about 15 m north of the 1834 drawn bank. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE INVENTED and so is the order: the striker is put at the far end of the row because he is the junior of the two men at the anvil, which is reasoning about a wage and not about a house. 'Around the Agency House' is the whole of the locational evidence and this point is 87 m from it — inside a vicinity, and further out than the other two, which is stated here rather than hidden. Working uncertainty about 40 m. The ground is the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield at about +1.28 m, so the house stands on traced ground and declares no ground contact. Facade bearing 180 follows the group; nothing states it.

MOVED 2026-10-23, ABOUT 31 M EAST, BECAUSE A SHED HAD BEEN BUILT THROUGH IT. The low warehouses this project stands on the north bank from the owner's 1830s riverbank plate were seated by their own rule, a set-back off North Water Street, and the second of them east of the Dearborn bridge line landed on this house: the two overlapped by about 12 square metres, 2.9 m deep, and the log walls showed through the shed's. This house is the softer of the two to move: the shed's place is a stated rule and this one's distance west of McKee's house is, as said above, invented. It now stands in the open ground between McKee's house and the agency blacksmith shop — the smithy the striker worked at — 4.9 m east of McKee's and 4.9 m west of the shop, its south face in line with the shop's. That gives up the 'far end of the row' ordering, which was reasoning about a wage and not evidence about a house; it keeps every part of the group's attested description (log, round the Agency House, in its vicinity), and brings it about 31 m nearer the Agency House than it was.

levels.8-10: We placed it with the group, not on the ground. Two lines tell of this group, and neither tells of one building. A book of 1831 says log houses stood around the agency house. The men who worked for the government lived in them, a blacksmith among them. A history book says small log houses near it were home to the blacksmith, Mr McKee. Billy Caldwell, a Native chief, lived there too. He spoke for the agency in Native tongues. So we know the group was there, around the agency house, made of logs, and who lived in it. But no one gives one house a shape, size or spot. We first set this helper's house at the far end of the row. He was the junior man at the forge. In October 2026 we moved it about 100 feet east. A shed had been built right through it. The shed's spot comes from a rule, but this house's spot was made up. So the house moved. It now stands in the open ground between McKee's house and the blacksmith shop he worked at. That gives up the end of the row, but keeps all the papers say. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet. Its front faces south, like the group.

entries.card: why:PLACED AGAINST THE TOWER AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND, and the…
entries.text: PLACED AGAINST THE TOWER AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND, and the direction and the distance are invented. No source of any kind puts these quarters anywhere: 'with quarters' is a term of the appointment and not a description of a site. METHOD: the coordinate is an offset of 23.7 m due west of this project's own committed position for Chicago Lighthouse (1832 tower) — itself read off Wright's 1834 sheet in 2026-09-12 and carrying about 22 m of its own uncertainty. WEST was taken for two reasons that are reasoning rather than reading: it keeps the house on the landward side of the tower, away from the water at the inside of the bend, and it is the only quadrant that clears both the garrison's big barn (Fort Dearborn — the Big Barn with Cupola, 32 m away on this line; 14 m if the house were set south-west) and the fort's own ground east of the light. The working uncertainty is therefore the tower's 22 m plus the whole of the unstated offset — call it 40 m, the same figure the agency log houses' notes carry for the same kind of placement. The ground here is the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield at +2.45 m above the summer-1835 water surface, 0.03 m below the tower's own sample, so the house stands on traced ground and declares no ground contact. Facade bearing 90 — the door east, toward the light it served — is invented; nothing states it.

levels.8-10: We placed it next to the light tower, not on the ground, and the direction and distance are made up. No paper puts these rooms anywhere. With quarters is part of the keeper's job, not a place. We set the house about 80 feet due west of the tower. We chose west to keep it on the land side, away from the water, and clear of the fort's big barn and the fort's own ground. The tower's own spot may be off by about 70 feet. With the made up gap, this one may be off by about 130 feet. It stands on traced ground. Its door faces east, toward the light it served, which is made up.

entries.card: why:PLACED AGAINST TWO OTHER BUILDINGS AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUN…
entries.text: PLACED AGAINST TWO OTHER BUILDINGS AND NOT AGAINST THE GROUND. Two sentences describe this group and neither describes a building. Wau-Bun, of 1831: "Around the Agency House were grouped a collection of log buildings, the residences of the different persons in the employ of Government... blacksmith, striker, and laborers." Andreas, of the settlement about 1830: "In its vicinity were small log buildings occupied by the blacksmith, Mr. McKee, and Billy Caldwell, an Indian chief, who was also interpreter for the agency." Between them the group is attested four ways over — that it existed, that it stood round the Agency House at the foot of State Street, that it was of logs, and who lived in it — and NOT ONCE is a single building given a shape, a size or a place of its own. METHOD: this coordinate sits on the same riverbank strip as Indian Agency House and Government Blacksmith Shop, 66 m west of the first and 21 m west of the second, its south face about 20 m north of the 1834 drawn bank. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE INVENTED, exactly as the shop's own note admits of itself: 'near' is unquantified, no source says which side of the agency house anything stood on, and west was taken because it keeps the house inside the ring the sources describe, off the State Street frontage, and clear of the Wolcott Street corridor this project derives. A SMITH'S HOUSE BY HIS FORGE is the only part of the arrangement that is reasoned rather than chosen, and it is reasoning about a trade, not a reading. Working uncertainty about 40 m — the georeference's 20 m plus the unquantified 'near'. The ground here is the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield at about +1.30 m above the summer-1835 water surface, so the house stands on traced ground and declares no ground contact. Facade bearing 180, due south onto the river, follows the two records it is grouped with; nothing states it.

levels.8-10: We placed it next to two other buildings, not on the ground. Two lines tell of this group, and neither tells of one building. A book of 1831 says log houses stood around the agency house. The men who worked for the government lived in them, a blacksmith among them. A history book says small log houses near it were home to the blacksmith, Mr McKee. Billy Caldwell, a Native chief, lived there too. He spoke for the agency in Native tongues. So we know the group was there, around the agency house, made of logs, and who lived in it. But no one gives one house a shape, size or spot. We set this house on the same strip by the river, just west of the blacksmith shop. The direction and distance are made up. Near gives no number. No paper says which side anything stood on. A smith's house by his forge is the one part we reason, from his trade. Our spot may be off by about 130 feet. Its front faces south, onto the river, like the others.

entries.card: why:PLACED BY EYE INSIDE A GROUP, WHICH IS THE HONEST DESCRIPTIO…
entries.text:
PLACED BY EYE INSIDE A GROUP, WHICH IS THE HONEST DESCRIPTION OF IT, and it is the same method and the same admission Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Barn carries. NOTHING LOCATES THIS BUILDING. Andreas records it in a list of what the homestead held and gives it no bearing, no distance and no neighbour.

MOVED 2026-10-03 UNDER other work, AND THE OLD PLACE WAS A FAULT, NOT A READING. Other work put this record 17.9 m east of the house on the yard line, and that easting is the centreline of fort road (the 1835 streets data), which runs north to the fort's south gate at about E 1146–1148: the building stood IN the road, 0.0 m from its centreline, and nothing asked. The owner ruled on the piece of work (answer b) that the group is the house plus two small outbuildings sited behind — west of — the frontage on that road. METHOD NOW: west of Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Homestead, this record's east wall 4.0 m clear of the house's west wall and its front 4.2 m north of the house's frontage line (local origin 1117.0, 179.0). The frontage line itself was tried first and refused by the ground, not by taste: the house stands on a low rise that falls away west, and a 6.1 m store on that line would stand 0.39 m into the slope at its uphill corner, past the walker's 0.35 m step; 4.2 m north the same store lands within 0.27 m. THE DIRECTION AND THE DISTANCE ARE BOTH STILL INVENTED. West rather than south because the barn already holds the yard line behind the house, and because west is the one side of the house with open ground: the fort road is east, the stockade north, and the garrison garden's nearest corner is about 40 m south-west. the structure corridors check --gate now refuses any footprint standing in a street corridor, so the old place could not be drawn again.

THE CAVEAT THAT TRAVELS WITH THE PARENT, UNCHANGED: neither South Water Street nor Michigan Avenue existed on the reservation in 1835 — it was unplatted and no street crossed it — so the corner both books locate this group by is a grid that arrived with the 1839 plat. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference, plus the parent's own unmeasured northward offset (lots 6-10 lie north of corner lot 11, so the group's true position is at the corner or north of it), plus an unquantified allowance for placing an undescribed building beside a building located by a retrospective address. Facade bearing 0, north toward the river, inherited from the parent record and attested nowhere.

levels.8-10: We placed it by eye inside a group, which is the honest way to say it. Nothing places this building. A history book lists it among what the Beaubien home held, with no direction, distance or neighbour. In October 2026 we moved it, since the old spot was a mistake. It had stood right in the middle of the fort road. The owner of this project ruled that the group is the house plus two small sheds, set behind it, west of the road. So it now stands west of the house, a little to the north. We tried the house's own front line first, but the ground slopes there, and the shed would sink into it. The direction and distance are still made up. Our checks now stop any building standing in a street. In 1835 neither South Water Street nor Michigan Avenue crossed this army land. The corner the books use came with the plan of 1839. Its front faces north, toward the river, like the house.

entries.card: why:PLACED FROM THE ONLY PLAN OF THIS FORT ANYONE HAS FOUND. F.…
entries.text: PLACED FROM THE ONLY PLAN OF THIS FORT ANYONE HAS FOUND. F. Harrison Jr.'s 1830 survey of the mouth of the Chicago River, drawn for the harbour works and reproduced by Andreas at vol. 1 p. 113, draws Fort Dearborn IN PLAN: a quadrangular picket enclosure with a work at three of its four angles, four ranges set against the walls, two small buildings flanking a break in the south wall, and a larger block outside the south-west angle. Positions in this record were read off that plate in pixels, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel of the archive.org page image, rotated to the sheet's own true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221 - the Wright 1834 reading that the project's roadmap S5a records as cross-checked to 35 m against the modern successor landmark. THE SCALE IS THE WEAK LINK AND IT IS STATED RATHER THAN BURIED: the sheet carries no scale bar, so 1.10 ft/px comes from setting the north range equal to the commandant's quarters at 'about 25x50 ft' in the key to the 1855 photograph, and it is checked by the gap between the west and east ranges coming out 71 ft against that key's 80 ft parade width. Carry +/-20 percent on every dimension derived this way, on top of the +/-20 m the datum already carries. THE ARRANGEMENT IS BETTER EVIDENCE THAN THE SCALE, and it is corroborated: Gurdon S. Hubbard, describing the inside of this fort in 1827 (Andreas I, p. 264), names the same buildings on the same sides in the same relation to the same two gates. An 1830 engineer's plan and an 1827 eyewitness agreeing building by building is what licenses inferred here rather than conjectural. See the research notes on fort dearborn sections 3 and 4. THE ROTATION IS READ OFF THE SAME PLATE and is the least expected number in this record: the fort's walls are drawn about 8 degrees clockwise of true north, measured as the mean of all four walls against the sheet's own north arrow, which sits within 0.2 degrees of vertical once the leaf is rotated. Eight degrees is inside what a woodcut re-engraving can invent, so it is inferred and not documented - but the fort sat on a river bank inside a bend and had no grid to align to, and a square post whose walls all lean the same way by the same amount is more likely to be a fort that was not square with the meridian than an engraver who tilted four lines consistently.

levels.8-10: We placed it from the only plan of this fort anyone has found. An 1830 survey of the mouth of the river, drawn for the harbour works, draws Fort Dearborn from above. It shows a fence of posts, with a work at three corners, four rows of buildings along the walls, two small buildings beside a gap in the south wall, and a bigger block outside the south west corner. We read every spot off that plan and set it from the fort's center. The plan has no scale bar, and that is its weak point. We worked out a scale from the known size of the commander's house, and checked it against the drill ground's width. Every size read this way may be off by a fifth. The layout is better proof than the scale. Gurdon Hubbard, inside this fort in 1827, names the same buildings on the same sides by the same two gates. A plan and a witness agreeing makes this a good guess. The walls are drawn turned about 8 degrees from north. The fort sat on a river bend with no street grid to line up with, so we keep the turn.

entries.card: why:PLACED ON A BEARING AND TWO LANDMARKS, WITH NO DISTANCE IN T…
entries.text: PLACED ON A BEARING AND TWO LANDMARKS, WITH NO DISTANCE IN THE SOURCE AT ALL. Bonnell gives three things and they are all qualitative: "away to the north-east" of Dr. Kimberly's corner, "among the sand-hills", and "close by the lake shore". METHOD: the bearing from Dr. Kimberly's residence's north-east corner to this footprint's centre is N 58 deg E, which is the north-east quadrant; the east face sits 61.9 m west of the committed shore 1835 harbor cut lake shore, which is the "close by"; and the west face is 19.6 m east of the platted `sand` street corridor, on the ground that street was named for. EVERY NUMBER IS INVENTED - the 238.5 m of "away to", the 61.9 m of "close by" and the 19.6 m east of Sand Street are this project's and not Bonnell's. THE SAND HILLS ARE THE ONE PART OF THIS THAT IS CORROBORATED BY A COMMITTED READING RATHER THAN CHOSEN. The the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield stands at +2.59 m above the summer-1835 water surface under this footprint, against +1.51 m under Dr. Kimberly's house on the Michigan Street frontage and +1.51 m at the Lake House site - a rise of 1.08 m: the ground Bonnell calls sand hills is about a metre higher than the bank strip he walked out from, measured off a heightfield derived years before this sentence was read. That does not fix the house's place, but it does say the described ground is where this project already put it. Traced ground, so the record declares no ground contact of its own. Facade bearing 180, due south toward the town and the river mouth: THIS IS INVENTED AND THERE IS NO STREET HERE TO ORIENT IT. Sand Street was platted, unopened and unworn on the scene date, so this house did not front a street at all, and a house on open sand faced whichever way its builder chose. WORKING UNCERTAINTY at least 150 m: the bearing is a quadrant, "away to" is not a distance, and "close by the lake shore" is a strip about 80 m wide between Sand Street and the water.

levels.8-10: We placed it from a direction and two landmarks, with no distance in the paper at all. Bonnell gives three things, none of them numbers: away to the north east of Dr Kimberly's corner, among the sand hills, and close by the lake shore. So we set it north east of Dr Kimberly's house, about 200 feet back from the lake, and just east of the planned Sand Street. Every number is made up. The sand hills are the one part a measure backs up. Our ground here stands about three and a half feet higher than the bank strip Bonnell walked out from. We made that ground years before we read his line. So the ground he calls sand hills is where we already had it. Its front faces south, toward the town, which is made up. Sand Street was planned but not yet opened, so the house did not face a street. Our spot may be off by at least 500 feet.

entries.card: why:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, AND THE POLYGON IS O…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, AND THE POLYGON IS ONE CABIN WHERE THE DOSSIER SAYS THERE WERE TWO. 7 x 5.5 m is about 23 x 18 ft, an ordinary single-pen log cabin of the type and period, and every number in it is invented; the polygon cites no sources. The second cabin is carried on the record as cabin count with a geometry declaration rather than drawn, because this archetype builds one building per record and a second polygon would have to invent a spacing and an orientation on top of the size — see that attribute's note and the liberty it owes. To resolve: any description of the Clybourne place, in Andreas at page-image level around scan pp. 215-225 or in the Clybourne family material the same volume carries.

levels.8-10: This is a stand in, with no size in any paper, and it is one cabin where our notes say there were two. It is about 23 by 18 feet, a plain one room log cabin of the time. Every number is made up. We list the second cabin on the card, but we do not draw it. Our rules build one building for each record, and a second one would need a made up gap and turn on top of a made up size. A description of the Clybourne place in the history book would settle it.

entries.card: why:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, and as with Archibal…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED, and as with Archibald Clybourne's Log Slaughter-House the size answers a documented CAPACITY rather than being chosen freely. Andreas records 300 head of cattle and 1,400 hogs packed here during 1834 (scan p. 1151), a throughput a little larger than the Clybourne plant's for the same season, so this footprint is drawn a little larger: 12 x 10 m, about 39 x 33 ft, with the 12 m along the bank and the 10 m as the depth. Every number is invented and the polygon cites no sources; the capacity constrains the order of magnitude and nothing finer. The pens, the yard and the barrelling and salting space that a packing operation needs are outside the footprint and outside this archetype, which builds a building rather than a works.

levels.8-10: This is a stand in, with no size in any paper. Like the Clybourne slaughter house, its size comes from how much it did. A history book says 300 cattle and 1,400 hogs were packed here in 1834, a little more than the Clybourne plant. So we drew it a little bigger: about 39 by 33 feet, with the long side along the river. Every number is made up. How much it did only limits its rough size. The pens, the yard and the room to fill and salt barrels are not drawn, since our rules build a building, not a whole works.

entries.card: why:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 6.5 x 5 m is about 2…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION IS ATTESTED. 6.5 x 5 m is about 21 x 16 ft, an ordinary single-pen log cabin of the type and period. Every number is invented. AND THE POLYGON IS ONE CABIN WHERE THE SOURCE COUNTS TWO OR THREE: see form.cabin count, which records the number and declares that the model does not build it.

levels.8-10: This is a stand in, with no size in any paper. It is about 21 by 16 feet, a plain one room log cabin of the time. Every number is made up. And it is one cabin where the paper counts two or three. The card records the number, and says the model does not build them.

entries.card: why:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION OF THIS CROSSING IS ATTESTED. The…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSION OF THIS CROSSING IS ATTESTED. The polygon is the DECK: its u extent is the span, 8 m, and its v extent the width, 3 m. THE SPAN IS SIZED OFF THE STREAM, NOT OFF THE BRIDGE: the research notes on terrain hydrology md's hydrology inventory gives the slough a width of 15 to 40 ft (zone 14) and tags the width and depth conjectural while calling the route documented, so 8 m of deck is a crossing of the narrow end of that range with a little bank at each side. THAT GUESS CAN BE CHECKED NOW, AND IT HOLDS. The stream was carved into this terrain epoch long after this polygon was drawn (then): under the deck the cut is 6.0 m across the top and holds 3.30 m of standing water, so the 8 m span lands about a metre outside the carve and 2.35 m clear of the water at each end. THE SPAN WAS NOT RESIZED TO FIT — it was measured against a stream it predates, and a figure that turns out to be workable is still a figure nobody recorded. Every number here is invented and the polygon cites no sources. THIS IS NOT A RIVER BRIDGE AND MUST NOT BE SIZED LIKE ONE: the two branch bridges in this dataset span 72 m and 56 m and carried the documented ten-foot width and six-foot clearance of the town's main crossings; this is a street culvert in all but name, and the record deliberately does not borrow their measurements — see the width and clearance notes.

levels.8-10: This is a stand in. No size of this bridge is in any paper. It is about 26 feet long and ten feet wide. We sized it from the stream, not from a bridge. Our notes give the swamp a width of 15 to 40 feet, and call that a guess. So the deck crosses the narrow end, with a bit of bank at each side. We can check that guess now, and it holds. The stream was carved into our ground long after we drew the bridge, and the bridge clears it at both ends. We did not change the bridge to fit. A number that turns out to work is still a number no one wrote down. Every number is made up. This is not a river bridge, and we do not size it like one. It is really a street drain.

entries.card: why:PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSIONS ARE ATTESTED FOR THIS BUILDING I…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NO DIMENSIONS ARE ATTESTED FOR THIS BUILDING IN ANY SOURCE REACHED. No period map shows building footprints (see Hathaway, Joshua. Chicago with the School Section, Wabansia, and Kinzie's… and the wright 1834 data), and the textual sources describe the tavern's materials, its sign, its rates and its landlords without ever measuring it. This 12 x 7 m rectangle is a plausible envelope for a log-and-frame tavern that lodged travellers at 12 1/2 cents a night and briefly housed Gen. Winfield Scott's Black Hawk War headquarters, and it carries no evidence whatsoever. The 12 m runs north-south along the river frontage and the 7 m is the depth. Sources are deliberately omitted from this attribute because none supports it. To resolve: Andreas vol. 1, 'Wharfs, Piers and Early Hotels' pp. 626-631, at page-image level. Other work L trial supersedes the former12x7 placeholder with a physical concaveL union. The NYPL sheet supports two outward gable ends meeting at an inside corner; exact5m spans,7.2x10.1m extents and absolute scale remain reconstructed. This is a5m gauge shape/camera hypothesis, not a traced survey. Geographic record origin/bearing remain, while bbox centre moves(-2.4,+1.55)m in local plan and actual occupied ground changes. Other work centre-preserving rebase supersedes the retained-origin trial above: physicalL dimensions stay, but origin is rebased so old world bbox centre remains; exact origin/shape remain reconstructed. See the current position note for coordinates, grade and clearances.

levels.8-10: This was a stand in, with no size for this building in any paper. No old map shows buildings' outlines. The papers describe the inn's wood, its sign, its prices and its keepers, but never measure it. It once let rooms for twelve and a half cents a night, and was briefly General Winfield Scott's headquarters in the Black Hawk War. We first drew a plain box about 40 by 23 feet, backed by no proof. Later we changed it to an L shape, from an old sheet in the New York library. That sheet shows two end walls meeting at an inside corner. The exact sizes are still made up. We kept the center of the building where it was.

entries.card: why:PLACEHOLDER — NOTHING ABOUT THIS BUILDING'S SIZE, SHAPE OR P…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER — NOTHING ABOUT THIS BUILDING'S SIZE, SHAPE OR PLAN IS ATTESTED, and unlike Newberry & Dole's Forwarding and Commission Warehouse there is not even a reported 'square' to hang a proportion on. 12 x 10 m is about 39 x 33 ft, a river warehouse of ordinary size for the town and the decade, drawn with its long side to the water. Every number is invented and the polygon cites no sources. To resolve: the dossier's own item 4 in its list of highest-priority gaps — 'Kinzie & Hunter warehouse: bank, date, size'.

levels.8-10: This is a stand in. Nothing about this building's size, shape or plan is in any paper. Unlike the Newberry and Dole warehouse, there is not even a word like square to go on. It is about 39 by 33 feet, a usual size for a river warehouse of the town and time, with the long side to the water. Every number is made up. Our notes list it among the most wanted gaps: which bank, what date, what size.

entries.card: why:PLACEHOLDER, AND A PARTIAL ONE: THIS IS THE DRYING SHED, NOT…
entries.text: PLACEHOLDER, AND A PARTIAL ONE: THIS IS THE DRYING SHED, NOT THE YARD. No source gives this yard a dimension, a plan or a building. 14 x 5 m is about 46 x 16 ft — a long shallow open-sided shed of the kind green brick is stacked under to dry out of the rain, which is the one structure a brickyard cannot work without and the only part of a yard this dataset has an archetype for. Every number is invented and the polygon cites no sources. THE YARD ITSELF IS THE THING BEING MODELLED AND IT IS NOT DRAWN: the clamp or kiln where the brick was burned, the hacks and racks, the clay pit, the pug mill and the spoil are carried on the record as yard works with a geometry declaration and stand nowhere in the mesh. A visitor will see one open shed where the sources describe an industry. To resolve the shed: nothing found describes it. To resolve the yard: it needs a works or parcel archetype, which this project does not have — the same limitation the liberties register “Western Hotel: the stable and wagon yard are attested and not modelled” records against the Western Hotel's wagon yard.

levels.8-10: This is a stand in, and only part of one: it is the drying shed, not the brickyard. No paper gives the yard a size, plan or building. It is about 46 by 16 feet, a long, low open shed where fresh bricks were stacked to dry out of the rain. A brickyard cannot work without one, and it is the only part of a yard our rules can draw. Every number is made up. The yard itself is not drawn: the kiln, the racks, the clay pit and the mixing mill. So a visitor sees one open shed, where the papers describe a whole trade. Drawing the yard would need rules for a whole works, which we do not have.

entries.card: why:PLANTED BY THE FLORA LAYER, NOT THIS FENCE MESH (correction)…
entries.text: PLANTED BY THE FLORA LAYER, NOT THIS FENCE MESH (correction). Juliette Kinzie1831: Beyond the parade-ground, which extended south of the pickets, were the company gardens, well filled with currant-bushes and young fruit-trees. The prior note saying no planting was built is stale: the fruit plantings 1835 generator generates the fort company garden 1835 data, and the flora data enrolls its young fruit trees and currant bushes for the actual1835 app. This structure generates the worm fence only, so this descriptive attribute is record only rather than a second set of vegetation in its GLB. Occurrence is the text’s; species choices, counts, rows and offsets remain the planting record’s reconstructed liberties (“The fort's company-garden fruit trees and currants, and Dr. Harmon's young orchard by the lake”). The analytical picture renderer omits flora unless explicitly enrolled; its empty review ground is not missing app planting. The separate pre1812 garden description is not used as evidence for this second-fort garden.

levels.8-10: The garden's plants are drawn by our plants layer, not by this fence. Juliette Kinzie wrote in 1831 that beyond the drill ground, south of the fort, were the company gardens, full of currant bushes and young fruit trees. An older note said no plants were built here, but that is out of date. Our plants layer now grows the fort's young fruit trees and currant bushes. This fence builds only the zigzag rail fence. That the garden was there is from the book. Which plants, how many and in what rows are our choices. We do not use a description of the garden from before 1812 as proof for this later fort.

entries.card: why:PRESIDENT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES FOR THE YEAR BEFORE THE S…
entries.text: PRESIDENT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES FOR THE YEAR BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. He was elected a trustee at the second town election of 11 August 1834 and chosen president, and the 1834 roster is: 'J. H. Kinzie, President; Isaac Harmon, Clerk and Collector; J. S. C. Hogan, Treasurer.' Whether he was still president on 1 July 1835 depends on the date of the third election, which Andreas places only 'in July, 1835' - see the research note. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kinzie, John” (tax 1833 062, line 114); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Kinzie, John H.” (poll 1834 067, line 236). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kinzie' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). HALF BROTHER, NOT BROTHER, AND THE SOURCE IS AN EDITOR'S NOTE OF 1881. Hurlbut's bracketed note under the American Fur Company's 1821 consignment entry reads “[The late James Kinzie, formerly of Chicago, and half brother of the late John H. Kinzie.]” — the same father and different mothers, which is the form this dataset keeps, because flattening it to ‘brother’ is the move that lets the three Chicago Kinzies collapse into one another. The two men are John Harris Kinzie in the John H. Kinzie household and James Kinzie in the James Kinzie household, and this project models them as separate households. Read as bk afc 015 and cited to Henry H. Hurlbut, Chicago Antiquities: Comprising original items and relations…. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it is an 1881 recollection about 1821, the ladder abstains on it (rung G5), and it moves no grade, no arrival, no placement and no household membership — both men are attested here on other evidence and stay so. THE LINK ITSELF IS THIS RECORD'S `kin` ROW, NOT THIS PROSE. Other work found that the residents schema had no field for a kinship BETWEEN two households; other work then gave the layer one while this reading was in flight, and both records now carry the reciprocal half brother row, graded inferred against this same source. What stands here is the READING that row rests on — the note as printed, the page it stands on and what an 1881 editorial note is worth — so the card cites its own evidence rather than asserting a link with nothing beside it. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “John H. Kinzie” (33S7-9YYJ-W6, printed page 232, line 25). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (“Sauganash Hotel: the pre-1830 position is not represented” matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

The papers print 'Baldwin, Eimer' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (the liberties register “Three quarters of this town's people are a name on a post-office list and nothing else”), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (the letter list residents generator). No figure is drawn (“No people, anywhere”). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Cone, Miss Josephine | Profession. | June 2, 1886.” (second presb 0124, printed page 160), admitted 1886-06-02 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Cone' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a married womans entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “John A. Nelson” as sheriff of cook county, 1864 (f1839 r0104, printed page 39). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Stallord, Arnold' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 6 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (the liberties register “Three quarters of this town's people are a name on a post-office list and nothing else”), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (the letter list residents generator). No figure is drawn (“No people, anywhere”).

The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Thacker, Mrs. Anna Rommeiss | Letter. | March 21, 1888.” (second presb 0337, printed page 172), admitted 1888-03-21 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Thacker' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins A. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a married womans entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'samuel stout' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 2 July 1834, column 32, reprinted over 3 consecutive issues — dated 1834-07-02 to 1834-07-16. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (the liberties register “Three quarters of this town's people are a name on a post-office list and nothing else”), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (the letter list residents generator). No figure is drawn (“No people, anywhere”).

WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. poll 1833 names this person at Chicago by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (“No people, anywhere”). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Ballard, C. A.” (poll 1833 002, line 23). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Ballard' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data).

entries.card: why:PROMOTED 2026-08-10 WITH ITS RE-BAKE, AND THE REASON IS BETT…
entries.text: PROMOTED 2026-08-10 WITH ITS RE-BAKE, AND THE REASON IS BETTER THAN THE NUMBER. Andreas prints at the foot of pp. 631-632 a statement signed by J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble: 'These were both wagon bridges, and were about six feet above the water, so that teams passed under them on the ice freely.' The clearance is not a builder's convenience — it is the winter road under the deck, stated by four men who used the crossing. The VALUE does not move; only the confidence does, and a confidence float is a mesh input (see the mesh inputs generator), so this promotion could not land without the geometry beside it, which is why it waited one slice. What it changes in the view is real rather than cosmetic: clearance is one of the attributes that says what this structure WAS, so the deck and the stringers come out of the half-dithered state the inferred tag put them in. WHAT THE TAG SAID BEFORE, kept because the reasoning was right at the time: the project's crossings dossier, the research notes on structures north section 5, gives both branch bridges as 'about 10 ft wide, clearing the water by about 6 ft' and tags the pair as documented. The width is documented and now has its source; the clearance does not. Searching the transcriptions that carry the rest of this bridge's evidence returns the width, the log abutments, the stringers and the 1832 date, and nothing anywhere about a height above the water. The number is kept because it is the dossier's and because it is plausible for a stringer bridge crossing shallow water with cribbed abutments, but it is recorded as INFERRED until the page behind it is found. THE DEMOTION WAS CORRECT AND SO WAS THE DOSSIER: the figure was right, the tag was ahead of any page this project could point at, and the honest state in between was the weaker one.

levels.8-10: We made this more sure in August 2026, and the reason is better than the number. A history book prints a note signed by four men: J. D. Caton, John Bates, Charles Cleaver and John Noble. It says both were wagon bridges, about six feet above the water, so that teams could pass under them on the ice. The height was the winter road under the bridge, told by four men who used it. The number did not change, only how sure we are. That changes how the bridge looks: it no longer shows as half faded. Before, our notes gave the bridges as about ten feet wide and six feet above the water. We found a paper for the width but not the height, so we kept the height as a guess until now. The guess was right, and so was holding off.

entries.card: why:Peck arrived at Chicago in July 1831 with a stock of goods i…
entries.text: Peck arrived at Chicago in July 1831 with a stock of goods in the schooner Telegraph and was among the town's first licensed merchants. He is attested keeping this store and living in it across 1833-35. No source reached names a clerk, a partner or a lodger at the scene date; the Porter lodging is May 1833 and is not carried forward as an 1835 occupancy. PECK'S OWN ADVERTISEMENTS ARE NOW READ, AND THEY ARE A CONTEMPORARY WITNESS WHERE THIS RECORD HAD ONLY A RECOLLECTION WRITTEN FIFTY YEARS LATER. He heads seven printings of the Chicago Democrat between 1833-12-03 and 1834-12-10 with his own name and his own corner: "P. F. PECK, CORNER OF LA SALLE AND SOUTH WATER-STREETS, [has] now on hand, many of the staple ar[t]icles requisite to the exigenci[e]s of use and consumption … His stock comprises, Dry Goods, Hardware, [Groceries, Crockery,] BOOTS & SHOES, HATS" (1833-12-03, page 3 column 4, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1833-12-03, dateline 'Chicago, De[c.] 3, 1833'), and again as "P. F. [W.] PECK, CORNER OF LASALLE AND SOUTH-WATER STS. [H]AS just received from New-York, a full stock of fresh GOODS" (1834-07-02, page 4 column 4, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-07-02). The initials run both ways across the file — 'P. F. PECK' and 'P. F. W. PECK' head the same standing card — and the gazetteer holds them as one man. WHAT THIS CHANGES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The trade and the corner were already attested here from Andreas and the grades do not move; what is new is that they are now attested TWICE, once by a contemporary who signed the line, and that the goods are itemised rather than summarised. Still nothing names a clerk, a partner or a lodger at the scene date, and none is supplied. THE READING IS TRANSCRIPTION-MEDIATED AND SAYS SO. Under the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 a claim read through this project's OCR-assisted transcriptions rather than off the page scan grades `attested` in this schema's vocabulary while carrying its own flag: reading = transcription mediated, with the transcription's own uncertainty brackets preserved inside the quotation rather than tidied away. Where a scan is later read, the scan is the authority and this claim upgrades under it — the standard The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday… set when a scan caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'.

levels.8-10: Peck came to Chicago in July 1831 on the ship Telegraph, with a stock of goods. He was one of the town's first merchants with a license. Papers show him keeping this store and living in it from 1833 to 1835. No paper names a clerk, partner or boarder on our day. One man boarded with him in May 1833, but we do not carry that to 1835. We have now read Peck's own ads, and they are a witness from the time. Before, this card had only a memory written fifty years later. His ad runs seven times in the Chicago Democrat in 1833 and 1834, with his own name and corner. It says P. F. Peck, corner of La Salle and South Water Streets, has many goods on hand: dry goods, hardware, food, dishes, boots, shoes and hats. In July 1834 it says he has just got a full stock of fresh goods from New York. Some ads say P. Peck and some P. W. Peck. They are the same man. Here is what this changes and what it does not. His trade and corner were already in the history book, and how sure we are does not change. What is new is that they are now in two papers, one written by the man himself, and his goods are listed. Still nothing names a clerk, partner or boarder on our day, and we add none. We read this from a typed copy made with the help of a machine, not from the page itself, and we say so. The owner of this project ruled that such a reading still counts as found in the paper, with a flag on it. The copy's own doubtful letters are kept as they are. If someone reads the page itself later, the page wins.
