entries.card: why:Purpose-built for confinement, and it is the building that e…
entries.text: Purpose-built for confinement, and it is the building that ended the practice recorded on the Estray pen record - prisoners held in the stock pound for want of anywhere else. Cook County was organised in 1831 and the county's business was conducted in rented rooms; this is the first purpose-built county structure of any kind and it precedes the court-house on the same block by about two years.

levels.8-10: It was built to hold prisoners. Before it, prisoners were kept in the pen for stray animals, since there was nowhere else. This jail ended that. Cook County began in 1831. At first it did its work in rented rooms. This was the first building the county put up. It came about two years before the court house on the same block.

entries.card: why:RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT: 5.80 m WEST, the…
entries.text:
RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT: 5.80 m WEST, the northing and bearing unchanged. The owner, in the 1835 scene: "green tree tavern in 1835 is sunken, it needs to be on the ground". It was: the renderer beds a building on the lowest ground under it, and the seat below was measured on the footprint polygon alone, while the rear ell (form.rear ell, built since off the east gable) runs 4.5 m further down the bank, its far corner 1.54 m from the traced waterline. Bedded to the ell's foot, the inn stood 0.58 m under its own front door; bedded to its bounding box, as the renderer then did, 0.88 m. The rule is the rule with the whole building in it: walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, this is the first seat at which every wall foot the mesh puts on the ground, ell included, meets the modelled ground within 0.10 m, the relief 95% of the 1835 town's structures stand on. Here it is 0.099 m, and the ell's far corner stands 4.59 m from the bank. The move is inside the 20 m working uncertainty below and argues nothing new about the corner: the source still puts the inn at Lake and West Water, and the bank still decides how close to it the inn can come. The paragraphs below are the seat as it was measured, kept as the reading this one corrects.

MOVED 2026-09-24 ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21: from the north-east corner of Lake and Canal to the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, 116.40 m east, measured between the old east face and the new one. The northing did not change at all. THE MOVE IS ARGUED FROM THE SOURCE AND NOT FROM A PICTURE'S FRAMING. DRLOIH's article on this tavern gives the corner as 'Lake and West Water Streets'; West Water was the street that ran along the west bank while Canal lay a full plat module further west, and the owner ruled that statement preferred over the same article's gloss 'now Canal Street'. The ship masts that read beside and beyond the inn rather than above its own roofline from the green tree stand are the SYMPTOM that sent somebody to look at the placement; they are not a reason to move a building.

WHAT THE OLD PLACEMENT WAS, because a committed building that moves without its previous reading surviving is a town quietly rewriting itself. PLACED 2026-08-09 at EPSG:26916 E 446937.4, N 4637299.6, facade bearing 270: the west face on Canal Street's east frontage and the south face on Lake's north frontage, each half an 80 ft platted street from the modern Lake-and-Canal intersection centre read from OpenStreetMap (E 446913.0, N 4637287.4). That reading rested on chicagology's 'Northeast Corner of Lake and Canal Streets' and on DRLOIH's own body text, 'the N.E. corner of what is now Lake and Canal Streets' — both name Canal in modern terms and one says 'what is now', which is why Canal was adopted at the time. The residual was recorded then and is the thing the ruling settled: modern Canal at Lake stands about 146 m back from the modern west-bank line, so the two readings are a full plat module apart. The check that would settle it from paper is still the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834, which nobody has read.

HOW THE NEW COORDINATE IS ARRIVED AT — two constraints, one of them recomputed by the validator. (1) NORTH OF LAKE, unchanged: the south face stands 12.192 m north of the Lake-and-Canal control's northing, half the 80 ft platted module, which is the platted corner derivation below and keeps the building out of Lake's platted corridor. (2) THE RIVER END: the footprint's north-east corner stands 3.01 m from the 1834 traced west bank of the South Branch (the river data) — 5.71 m measured due east at that corner's own northing — and the standoff is the MODELLED GROUND'S OWN LIMIT rather than a chosen setback. The bank falls away toward the water, and a 12.19 m sill plate cannot sit level across that fall: seated hard on the bank the footprint's perimeter stands 0.88 m off the terrain beneath it, which is a building arriving nowhere and would owe a liberty. Walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, the first seat whose whole perimeter comes within the walker's 0.35 m step-up of the modelled ground is this one, at 0.294 m, with the footprint dry at all 425 samples of a 24-by-16 grid over it. So the tavern comes forward to the bank as far as the committed ground carries it, which is what 'forward to the bank' can mean here. Facade bearing is UNCHANGED at 270, due west onto West Water: F. H. Taylor's 'The fornt was on Canal street and this side was on Lake' is a claim about the street the front faced, and on the ruling's reading that street is West Water; the long elevation still runs east-west along Lake, and John Gray's second entrance is still 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side'. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's and the traced bank's and not an additional guess.

WHAT THE MOVE DISPLACED, AND ON WHOSE RULE. The committed west water centreline ran through this footprint. Other work carried the bank offset 37.12 m past the Wolf Point turn under a stated rule — carry it until the riverward corridor reaches a committed footprint that stands ACROSS the roadway rather than beside it, and cut the line there — and the Green Tree is now the first such footprint, its nearest corner 3.01 m from the bank and its furthest 15.90 m, so it stands across the roadway exactly as James Kinzie's house does. So the line is cut at local [-20.32, -98.49]: 22.53 m shorter, ending 2.30 m south of Lake's own north platted kerb. The owner's ruling anticipated a collision and named other work to settle it — the loser re-seated on its own evidence before it is withdrawn — and this line's own evidence is the rule above. The cost is written where the street is, in the 1835 streets data: Fergus 1839's 'W. Water st north of West Lake st' again attests a street this reconstruction gives no modelled length north of Lake. Nothing already placed was displaced; the nearest committed footprint is James Kinzie's house, whose nearest corner stands 9.14 m north-west of this one.

AND THE PLATE'S COMPOSITION NOW READS, which is what other work asked for and what the old placement could not give. Plate "11" of the 2026-08-11 prefire views hangs ship masts over this tavern's roofline; from the old stand the nearest water on that bearing was 157 m out and a 14.5 m mast on a 1.1 m deck needed to be inside 83 m, so the masts read beside and beyond the inn instead. The schooner moored in the reach below the forks (the era boats data, boat schooner wolf point 2, whose own note already called this reach 'the one open water on the Green Tree Tavern's own eastward sight line') now lies 29.16 m beyond the ridge. The ridge stands 7.98 m above the building's base — 5.0 m of wall and a 38 degree gable over a 7.62 m width — which is 8.96 m on the committed heightfield, and the masthead is 15.6 m above the water. A viewer has to stand at least 0.93 of the ridge-to-mast distance back from the ridge before the masthead clears it, so the green tree stand moved with the building, to Lake Street's own south platted frontage 34.85 m from the ridge on the schooner's bearing (local [-44.11, -121.52], yaw 33.3). The masthead reads 1.44 m above the roofline there, and between 1.36 m and 1.52 m for an eye anywhere from 1.6 m to 1.8 m. From the old standoff — 12.2 m off the front wall — it still does not clear, and that is geometry rather than a placement question: an 8 m ridge seen from 12 m subtends more than a 15.6 m masthead seen from 41 m, wherever the building stands.

levels.8-10: We moved it in October 2026, about 20 feet west, after the owner of this project's report. He said the Green Tree Tavern in 1835 looked sunken, and needed to be on the ground. It was. Our builder set the inn on the lowest ground under it, and its back wing ran down the river bank. So the inn stood about two to three feet under its own front door. We walked it west a little at a time until every wall met the ground closely. It still stands well back from the water. This small move is inside how far off our spot may be anyway. In September 2026 we had already moved it about 380 feet east, on the owner's ruling. A paper puts it at Lake and West Water Streets. West Water ran along the river bank, while Canal Street lay a whole block west. The owner ruled that this paper's corner wins over its note that says now Canal Street. Its north side did not move.

entries.card: why:RE-SEATED BY other work (2026-09-26), AND THE STREET IT CARR…
entries.text: RE-SEATED BY other work (2026-09-26), AND THE STREET IT CARRIES CHANGED WITH IT — which is a real loss against the source and is written here rather than smoothed over. WHAT THE SOURCE SAYS, unchanged: the slough 'entered the river at the end of State Street', and 'where Water Street crossed it a LOG BRIDGE was needed until after 1840'. One sentence fixes the mouth and the other fixes the crossing by naming a street. WHAT THE OWNER RULED, 2026-09-26, flying the reach against Wright 1834 and Hathaway 1834: there is ONE slough here, its mouth is the notch Wright draws just EAST of State (E +848.6, 's pixel), the built mouth west of State was the invention, and 'keep the inland state slough, move the bridge'. THE TWO CANNOT BOTH BE HELD, and the geometry is what decides it: the drain's inland course runs west of State, the mouth is east of it, so the reach crosses STATE STREET at local E +826.9 N -8.4 — while South Water Street's committed path ENDS at local E +805 N +4 because the street stops at the United States Reservation (the 1833 order, and the Reservation's west line is State), 27 m west of and 12 m north of nothing the drain now touches. So the drain meets no part of Water Street anywhere. This record keeps what the source supports — that the town bridged this drain where its graded street met it, in log, and that the crossing stood past 1840 — and records that the STREET NAME in that sentence is not what this reconstruction can carry. `confidence` stays `inferred` and does not rise. Recorded in the liberties register. THE DECK, MEASURED FROM THE COMMITTED LINES: State Street's centreline is E +824.4 N -400 to E +827.1 N +20 (the 1835 streets data, attested from the Thompson plat), which puts it at E +826.92 where the drain crosses; the drain's centreline is state slough mouth in the terrain spec data. The deck is laid at rotation 90, which in this dataset is a COMPASS BEARING measured clockwise from north (the walkthrough's walker code, and the validate py's tool ground-contact outline), so the footprint's u axis - the span - runs SOUTH and its v axis - the width - runs EAST. Its 8 m span therefore runs NORTH-SOUTH along the street and its 3 m width east-west across it, where at the old seat the span ran east-west - and it occupies local E +825.42..+828.42, N -12.36..-4.36, centred on the street's own centreline and on the crossing. THE SPAN IS NOT RESIZED: the cut's half-width is unchanged at 3 m, the drain crosses the street 18 degrees off square, so the water the deck has to cross measured ALONG the street is a little wider than at the old seat and the 8 m span still lands on dry committed ground at both ends. the slough crossing check prints the numbers on every commit. WHAT IS INVENTED: the twenty-odd metres between the mouth and the crossing (a street meets a drain upstream of its mouth, not in it), and the bearing, which is now the street's rather than a guess — that much the move BUYS, because the old seat's note admitted inventing a bearing on the assumption the slough ran north under an east-west street, and here the deck is square to a committed street line. WORKING UNCERTAINTY about 20 m along the street and 10 m across it, on top of the georeference's 20 m. THE COST, STATED: the terrace along State Street stands level at 5.09 ft for 45 m either side of the crossing, so the deck's walk surface at 2.723 ft sits 0.72 m BELOW grade at both ends and both approaches are cuts 8.7 m long at 1 in 12 — deeper than the 0.35-0.49 m the old seat needed, which is the ridge-toe cost other work declined and the owner accepted. See approaches slough west and slough east in the terrain spec data, whose ids are stale and whose geometry is not.

levels.8-10: We moved this bridge in September 2026, and the street it carries changed with it. That is a real loss against the paper, and we say so. A paper says the swamp met the river at the end of State Street. It says a log bridge was needed where Water Street crossed it until after 1840. In September 2026 the owner of this project looked at the old maps of 1834 and ruled there is one swamp here, meeting the river just east of State. So the drain now crosses State Street, not Water Street, which stops before it. We keep what the paper backs: the town bridged this drain in log where its street met it, and the bridge lasted past 1840. We cannot keep the street's name. How sure we are does not change. The bridge now sits square across State Street. The ground there is higher than the bridge, so the road dips down to it at both ends. The owner accepted that.

entries.card: why:READ OFF GIFFORD'S DRAWING of the first Tremont House and it…
entries.text: READ OFF GIFFORD'S DRAWING of the first Tremont House and its street (N. Roswell Gifford. View of the first Tremont House and the storefront row on…): a dark three-storey block standing up behind the low stores at the Clark end of the row, its flat-looking top and two stacks above them: read as the corner building across Clark. Graded reconstructed, not inferred: the value is the drawing's, but which building of 1835 the drawn front was is ours (the roof is an invented count-unit), the drawing is retrospective, and taking it as the street on 1 July 1835 is the owner's reading of 2026-11-15 (the liberties register “The Lake and Dearborn street faces round the first Tremont House, built to Gifford's drawing as a view of 1835”). The drawn value stands over the family's typology band where the two differ.

levels.8-10: We read this off a drawing by Roswell Gifford of the first Tremont House and its street. Which building of 1835 it shows is our choice, and the drawing was made years later. The owner of this project chose to read it as the street in 1835. Where the drawing and our usual rules differ, the drawing wins.

entries.card: why:READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN, which draws it as a large d…
entries.text: READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN, which draws it as a large diamond labelled 'Garden for the Garrison' with the Big Barn with Cupola on the river bank beyond its north-west corner and, beyond its south-east one, the grave of MRS Charles Jouett — the plate letters it 'Grave of Mrs Chas Jouett', Gurdon Hubbard independently calls it 'the grave of his wife' in 'a picket-fence inclosure' by the west side of the road, and Charles Jouett himself died at Trigg County, Kentucky on 28 May 1834 (the death notices data, fdn0347) and is not buried here. This record said 'Charles Jouett's grave' from the day it was written until other work read the label; the geometry described here is unchanged and only the name is corrected. Its four corners were read in pixels and converted at the same 1.10 ft/px scale as the fort itself; the plot is set square to nothing on the sheet, so the 53-degree rotation is the diamond's own and is measured rather than assumed. Carry +/-20 percent on the size and +/-25 m on the position.

levels.8-10: We read this off an 1830 plan of the fort. It draws a big diamond labelled Garden for the Garrison. The fort's big barn sits on the river bank past one corner. Past the other is the grave of Mrs Charles Jouett. The plan writes Grave of Mrs Chas Jouett. Gurdon Hubbard also calls it the grave of his wife, inside a picket fence by the road. Charles Jouett himself died in Kentucky in 1834, and is not buried here. This card used to say Charles Jouett's grave, until we read the label. Only the name is fixed. We read the four corners off the plan at the same scale as the fort. The garden is set at its own angle on the plan, so we measured its turn. Its size may be off by a fifth, and its spot by about 80 feet.

The 1830 plan draws exactly two small buildings flanking the break in the south wall, which is that sentence in ink. WHICH OF THE TWO IS WHICH IS NOT STATED by either source, and the assignment here is not a coin flip: Hubbard's next clause puts the magazine 'about half way between the west end of the guard and block-houses', and the block-house is at the south-west angle. That sentence only describes a real gap if the guard-house is the WESTERN of the two, so this record takes the west building and Fort Dearborn — store house takes the east. If the assignment is wrong the two buildings swap and nothing else in the complex moves.

Position in pixels on the plate Andreas reproduces at vol. 1 p. 113, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel (the scale derivation is on Fort Dearborn — the stockade and in the research notes on fort dearborn section 3), rotated to the sheet's true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221. Carry +/-20 percent on the offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself. The facade bearing is the fort's 8-degree rotation plus the side of the parade this building faces, because every range in this fort fronts the parade. Hubbard, 1827: 'a number of voyageurs with their families were living in the soldiers' quarters, on the east side of the inclosure'. Andreas: 'the soldiers' barracks on the east side'. The 1830 plan draws its longest range against the east wall, south of the sutler's, which is where Hubbard's sentence puts the barracks in relation to it.

levels.8-10: We read this spot off an 1830 plan of the fort, printed in a history book. We measured it on the drawing and set it from the fort's center. It may be off by a fifth of its distance from the fort, and the fort itself by about 65 feet. Gurdon Hubbard's memory of the fort in 1827 agrees with where the plan draws it.

entries.card: why:READ OFF WRIGHT'S SHEET, 2026-09-12, AND UNTIL THAT DAY THIS…
entries.text: READ OFF WRIGHT'S SHEET, 2026-09-12, AND UNTIL THAT DAY THIS COORDINATE WAS AN INVENTION. Wright's 1834 map draws a ring with L. House lettered round it, west of the fort on the south bank at the inside of the bend, and it is the first independent witness this placement has ever had. The ring's centre was picked twice, at 15x and again at 20x in a differently-framed crop so the eye was not anchored, at resource pixel (2941, 1604) on the BPL master scan (commonwealth:js957744g); transformed through the one fitted affine this project keeps — the wright 1834 gcps data, the same transform the two piers were measured on and the rederive datum tool checks the datum against — that is local E +1055.6, N +172.5. The reading, its crops, its uncertainty budget and what it agrees and disagrees with are committed at the wright 1834 lighthouse glyph data, and the wright lighthouse check recomputes this coordinate from that pixel on every gate: the two files are one statement and cannot drift apart silently. WHAT IT OVERTURNS. The point stood at local E +1105.2, N +229.2 — 47.5 m west-north-west of the fort's centre — and the note that stood here said in as many words that the adjacency was documented and the offset was ours. Wright's glyph is 75.3 m south-west of it. The reading's own uncertainty is 22.4 m combined (1.4 m picking, 10 m for the drawn ring's half-width, 20 m for the affine here — the whole-sheet RMS is 17.5 m and the two nearest controls residual at 12.6 and 23.0 m), so the disagreement is 3.4 sigma and is a disagreement rather than noise. A witness beats a bearing we picked, so the record moves, and the invented point is kept in the trace file rather than deleted. THE QUADRANT MOVES WITH IT: 108 m west-SOUTH-west of the fort centre where we had 48 m west-NORTH-west. 'North-west of the fort' was never a source's phrase; it was ours. WHAT STILL AGREES AND WHAT NOW DOES NOT. Andreas — 'Fort Dearborn and the light-house are placed at the angle thus formed' — agrees, and better than before: the ring sits at the inside of that bend. Wentworth, disposing of the reservation in 1839, says the land 'upon which the old light-house was located' was lots near the Rush Street bridge, north of the river, and that DISAGREES. A sheet surveyed a year before the scene is preferred to a recollection written five years after it about which lots a disposal covered, but nothing here shows Wentworth wrong and the tension is recorded rather than resolved. THE GROUND. +2.48 m and inside the modelled field: the flat of the peninsula, about 50 m south of the bank edge and 50 m east of the river's western bend. The August 2026 failure — a lighthouse standing in the channel because nothing modelled the ground under it — does not recur here. Rotation is zero and still means nothing: a round tower has no facade. WHAT WOULD REPLACE THIS: a second contemporary sheet, or Wentworth's lots plotted. SUPERSEDED NOTE, kept because a reading that overturns something should show what it overturned — ADJACENCY IS DOCUMENTED AND THE OFFSET IS INVENTED. Andreas puts the two together at the bend: 'Fort Dearborn and the light-house are placed at the angle thus formed'. Wentworth, disposing of the reservation in 1839, says the land left over 'upon which the old light-house was located' was lots near the Rush Street bridge, which is at the river north of the fort, and Fergus's 1850 note has River Street running between the block-house and the light-keeper's. All of that says close, and north or west, and near the water. This point is about 65 m north-west of the fort's centre on the river bank; the distance and the bearing are ours, and the uncertainty is nearer 60 m than the 20 m the rest of the complex carries. Rotation is zero and means nothing: a round tower has no facade. MOVED 2026-08-11, AND THE REASON IS THE GROUND RATHER THAN THE SOURCES. This point was first set about 65 m north-west of the fort centre while the terrain stopped 832 m short of here and nothing could check it. S2e parcel (b) landed the heightfield the same day, and that first point turned out to be below the top of the river bank - in the water. The tower is now at local E +1108, N +232, about 48 m west-north-west of the fort centre on the bank top, which satisfies every source statement as well as the first point did and satisfies the modelled ground too. The offset is still invention; it is now invention constrained by a surface.

levels.8-10: We read this off Wright's map in September 2026. Until then this spot was made up. Wright's map of 1834 draws a ring with L. House written round it, west of the fort, on the south bank at the inside of the bend. It is the first witness this spot has ever had. We picked the ring's center twice, at two different close ups, so our eye would not be led. We turned that point into our ground the same way we did the two piers. Our checks work it out again every time. It moved the light house about 250 feet south west of where we had it. Our old spot was a guess we picked, and a witness beats a guess. The history book agrees, placing the fort and light house at the bend. Wentworth, writing of a land sale in 1839, puts the old light house's land north of the river, which does not agree. A map made a year before our day wins over that memory, but nothing proves Wentworth wrong. It stands on flat dry ground, as it should. A round tower has no front.

entries.card: why:RECONSTRUCTED AT NONE, AND THAT IS A CHOICE ABOUT WHAT TO DE…
entries.text: RECONSTRUCTED AT NONE, AND THAT IS A CHOICE ABOUT WHAT TO DEPICT, NOT A FINDING ABOUT HEATING. This record used to count one stack — 'a blockhouse manned in a Chicago winter is heated' — and the archetype stands a single stack at the exact centre of the plan, which is where this fort's own pictures put a cupola instead. Panel 5 of the Kurz & Allison sheet and the two Wau-Bun reproductions of the 1831 view all draw the small square cupola on this roof and none of them draws a stack beside it, so the invented stack was both unattested and in the way of a pictured feature, and the pictured feature wins. WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM: that the blockhouse was unheated, that it had no flue, or that nothing ever stood on this roof besides the cupola. Pictorial sources are a modern reconstruction and their silence is not testimony; the 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print (filed, misleadingly, as the chicago fort dearborn river mouth 1830 image) depicts about 1836-1849 and does show a small ambiguous projection beside a louvred cap, and that later detail is left unresolved rather than backdated onto 1 July 1835. The count is recorded at 0 because nothing reached counts one, and a stack has not been quietly moved somewhere else to keep it.

levels.8-10: We draw no chimney here. That is a choice about what to show, not a finding about heat. This card used to count one chimney, since a lookout tower with soldiers in a Chicago winter is heated. Our rules put that chimney right in the middle of the roof. But the fort's own pictures put a small square box on top there instead. A sheet of 1893 and two copies of a view of 1831 all draw that box, and none draws a chimney beside it. So the made up chimney was not in any paper, and it was in the way of something pictured. The picture wins. We do not claim the tower had no heat, no flue, or nothing else on its roof. Pictures leaving something out are not proof. A print of 1856 shows a small unclear thing on the roof, but it shows the years 1836 to 1849, so we do not carry it back to 1835.

entries.card: why:RECONSTRUCTED STILL, BUT NO LONGER 'NOT ATTESTED ANYWHERE'.…
entries.text: RECONSTRUCTED STILL, BUT NO LONGER 'NOT ATTESTED ANYWHERE'. That phrase was stale. Hubbard, describing the fort as he first saw it in October 1818, says 'The officers' quarters were outside of the pickets, fronting east on the parade, and was a two-story building of hewn logs' (Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard…, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358). That is earlier evidence for two storeys than anything this note used to rest on. IT DOES NOT PROMOTE THE GRADE, for two reasons the same book supplies. First, Hubbard contradicts himself on where the building stood: page 36 puts the officers' quarters OUTSIDE the pickets, while his 1827 walk round the fort puts 'The old officers' quarters, built of logs, on the west, and within the pickets' (Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard…, leaf 205, printed p. 167, committed text lines 7612-7613), which is where the 1830 plan draws this range; the source record lists the contradiction as something it does not supply. Second, nothing says the two-storey building of 1818 is the same range that stood in July 1835 rather than an earlier one — the post stood ungarrisoned from October 1823 to October 1828 and again from May 1831 to June 1832 (Hubbard's own table, printed p. 35), and no building inside it is dated. So the 1818 sentence is carried forward only CONDITIONALLY, on the reading that p. 36's 'outside' is a slip and the range never changed. The count's older argument still stands beside it: this range and the commandant's quarters are the two buildings the 1855 photograph shows as 'the principal buildings of the Fort', and a single-storey log range would not read as one of two principal buildings beside a two-storey brick one. That photograph is a diagnostic only, twenty years after the scene date, and no camera has been solved on it as a matched view of July 1835.

levels.8-10: This is still made up, but no longer missing from every paper. Gurdon Hubbard saw the fort in October 1818. He wrote that the officers' rooms were outside the posts, facing east on the drill ground, a two floor building of shaped logs. That is older proof for two floors than we had. It does not make us more sure, for two reasons from the same book. First, he says two things about where it stood. Here he says outside the posts, but on his walk of 1827 he puts the old officers' rooms inside the posts on the west, where the 1830 plan draws them. Second, nothing says the building of 1818 is the same one that stood in 1835. The fort stood empty for some years, and no building inside is dated. So we carry the 1818 line only if outside was a slip. An 1855 photo also shows this and the commander's house as the fort's main buildings. A one floor log row would not look like one of two main buildings. But that photo is twenty years late, and only a hint.

No person is made up, no paper puts this business here, and no home is claimed. Our town list for July 1835 sets how many we need. This is our own choice of who goes where, not a found address.

entries.card: why:RECONSTRUCTED, AND IT IS THE FIRST LANDING THIS PROJECT HAS…
entries.text: RECONSTRUCTED, AND IT IS THE FIRST LANDING THIS PROJECT HAS PUT ON THE WEST BANK. NO SOURCE STATES A DOCK, WHARF OR LANDING ANYWHERE AT WOLF POINT — that absence is why this value is reconstructed and not inferred, one grade below the two river warehouses whose dock the dossier states (the research notes on structures north §3.10) and level with the five South Water merchant landings the owner's ruling of 2026-08-18 authorised (the liberties register “Five South Water landings, stated by no source and asked for by name”). What bounds the invention: (1) THE TRADE, AND HERE IT IS THIS RECORD'S OWN — chicagology's Wolf Point narrative gives a storehouse 'dealing in groceries and Indian goods' and Andreas's trader list (scan p. 235) gives 'Indian Traders — Robert A. Kinzie, near Wentworth's tavern'. Groceries and trade goods at the forks in the early 1830s came in and went out on the water; this record's own position note already reasons from it in as many words — 'a storehouse trading goods off canoes has a positive reason to face the landing' — and the facade was set due east onto the river on that reading before any wharf layer existed. A store that faces the water to work cargo is the trade this layer's rule asks for. (2) THE REACH — the west bank at the forks, the one shore of the three this layer had never considered: the North Division shore already carries Kinzie & Hunter's attested dock and the South Division shore carries four stated landings, while the west bank had no candidate at all, not because it was measured and refused but because other work's rule named South Water merchants and stopped there. (3) THE WATER IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED — the traced 1834 bank runs 11.2 m off this building's river wall, and a standard-form deck at that foot stands in about 1.06 m of water for the whole 13.0 m of its face on the committed heightfield, with its heel about 0.5 m clear on dry bank. The boat layer independently floats a schooner in this same reach abreast this store and a skiff off the bank below it (the era boats data), so the reach is one this project's own bed already carries a hull in. The landing itself is the wharf layer's standard form, every dimension of it invented within the bounds “Two river docks, stated in one clause and invented in every dimension” states; geometry 'simplified' is the exact claim — a standard-form deck stands for a statement this record cannot make from evidence. WHAT THE SAME RULE REFUSES ON THIS BANK, and it is four of the five buildings in the row: Wentworth's tavern, James Kinzie's residence, the Robinson and Caldwell cabins and Father Walker's log meeting house state no dock and get none — lodging, dwelling and worship take nothing off a canoe, which is the Temple Building's exclusion carried across the river. WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM: that the trade was still running on 1835-07-01. The 1833 Treaty of Chicago ceded the land and the removal ran through the summer of 1835, so the 'Indian goods' half of this business was ending as the scene opens; the record models a standing store and a standing landing and makes no claim about what crossed either. What would replace the invention: the Chicago Democrat's advertising columns, the 1833-1836 harbour reports, or either retrospective Wolf Point view examined at plate level for works along the west bank.

levels.8-10: This landing is made up, and it is the first we have put on the west bank. No paper says there was a dock anywhere at Wolf Point. That is why it is made up, not a guess. Its trade is the reason. A paper says this store sold food and goods for the Native trade, and a history book lists Robert Kinzie as a trader near Wentworth's tavern. Goods like that came and went by water. We had already turned the store to face the river for that reason. We measured the water too: the landing stands in about three and a half feet of water, with its back on dry bank. Our boats layer already floats a ship and a small boat here. Every size of the landing is made up. The same rule gives no landing to the tavern, the houses, the cabins or the church on this bank, since they took nothing off a canoe. We do not claim the trade was still running in July 1835. The treaty of 1833 gave up the land, and the people were made to leave that summer.

entries.card: why:RECONSTRUCTED, UNDER THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-08-18 — 'you…
entries.text: RECONSTRUCTED, UNDER THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-08-18 — 'you can add more docks!', given with the general instruction to be liberal with reconstructed items and label them as such (the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18). NO SOURCE STATES A DOCK, WHARF OR LANDING AT THIS FRONTAGE — that absence is exactly why this value is reconstructed and not inferred, one grade below the two river warehouses whose dock is stated in the dossier. What bounds the invention: (1) THE TRADE — a forwarding and commission house, advertising as such in 1834 — the business of taking other men's goods off the schooners and getting them inland. A forwarding house without a landing would work its entire trade over someone else's bank. (2) THE REACH — this building stands on the South Water river frontage between the forks and the Dearborn drawbridge, the working bank the 2026-08-18 brief shows crowded with masts (image 3) and the reach every schooner cargo landed on; a street of merchants whose whole stock came in by water did not work it over two landings. (3) THE PRACTICE — wharfing-out along the south bank is the practice other work's research note records as the thing that would move this layer off reconstruction, and the docks it drew are this landing's pattern. The landing itself is the wharf layer's standard form (the river landings data, the river wharves generator), every dimension invented within the bounds “Two river docks, stated in one clause and invented in every dimension” states; geometry 'simplified' is the exact claim — a standard-form landing stands for a statement this record cannot make from evidence. Claimed at the liberties register “Five South Water landings, stated by no source and asked for by name”. The Temple Building on the same frontage gets NO landing from the same rule: worship and a school take nothing off a schooner.

levels.8-10: This landing is made up, as the owner of this project asked: add more docks, and say they are made up. No paper says there was a dock here. But this business got its goods off the boats, and it stands on the busy river bank where the ships unloaded. So we give it a plain landing of the usual kind. Every size of it is made up.

entries.card: why:RECONSTRUCTED: THE ADVERTISEMENT SAYS 'IN WABANSIA' AND NOTH…
entries.text: RECONSTRUCTED: THE ADVERTISEMENT SAYS 'IN WABANSIA' AND NOTHING ELSE - no block, no lot, no street, no distance (the wabansia seating data § the Occupancy Before of 1835-07-01 records it as ONE household, unplaced). So the survey is attested and everything inside it is this record's choice, bounded as follows. THE BLOCK: the Wabansia C T7 block, Wright's 1834 block 59 (the wabansia block numbering data), the south-east block of the survey's dry ground, on Kinzie Street beside the North Branch. It is chosen because it is the block nearest the town and the Kinzie Street road into it - the ground a physician practising in Chicago would most plausibly take - and because the boustrophedon numbering begins there; neither is evidence that the house stood on it. THE LOT: the block's eastern lot (lot index 1, order 2), the one nearer the river. THE COORDINATE IS COMPUTED, NOT TYPED: the committed lot polygon's Kinzie Street edge and inward axis (the block infill generator lot frame and place, with the block's Hubbard Street edge standing where an alley would, because Wabansia's sheet rules no alley), a 6.0 m setback from the Kinzie line and 6.0 m west of the lot's centre line, facade to Kinzie Street. The setback and the offset are a period typology and not a measurement. Covered by the liberties register “The doctor's house in Wabansia: an attested house, barn and garden on ground the advertisement names only as Wabansia”.

levels.8-10: This spot is made up. The ad says in Wabansia and nothing else: no block, lot, street or distance. So the area is in the paper, and everything inside it is our choice. We chose the south east block, on Kinzie Street by the North Branch. It is the block nearest the town and the road into it, the ground a doctor working in Chicago would most likely take. That is not proof the house stood there. We chose the lot nearer the river. Our builder works out the spot from the lot's lines, set back from Kinzie Street, with the front to the street. The setback is the usual one of the time, not a measure.

entries.card: why:RECOVERED CONFIRMED RESIDENT. The v4 census/resident researc…
entries.text: RECOVERED CONFIRMED RESIDENT. The v4 census/resident research classifies William H. Adams as A — CONFIRMED 1835 VOTER with High confidence and identifies the 1840 household head as William Hanford Adams. This record restores that direct 1835 evidence to the canonical resident layer while leaving residence, occupation and family structure unasserted where the evidence does not support them. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Adams, William H., 451 Wabash avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Adams, W. H.” (poll 1833 001, line 22); Poll list of 1835 — “Adams, William H.” (poll 1835 001, line 286). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Adams' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Adams, William H. | 1837, Sept. | Westport, Conn. | 64 | Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Adams, W. W. | Profession. | July 3, 1846. | Dismissed.” (second presb 0399, printed page 176), admitted 1846-07-03 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Adams' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins W. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

levels.8-10: We bring back a man who was proved to live here. Our research lists William H. Adams as a voter in 1835. We are very sure of it. It also finds the head of a family in 1840 named William Hanford Adams. This card puts that 1835 proof back on him. We still claim nothing about his home, his work or his family. The proof does not reach that far. In 1882 a club in Chicago held a party for people who lived here before 1840, and this man was there. So he lived here some time before 1840. It gives no year he came. It does not change how sure we are. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. In 1879 a club in Chicago held a party for people who came before 1840. Its list has this man and the year he said he came. He gave that year forty or more years later, so it is his memory, not proof. A list of the members of the Second Presbyterian Church has a line with the same last name and first letter. That church list starts in 1842, so it is no proof about 1835.

entries.text: REVISED 2026-08-09 after examining the images directly. No period source attests a gallery or porch either way, but the two surviving retrospective depictions both show the building WITHOUT one: the F. Braunhold engraving in Andreas (1884) and panel 14 of the Kurz and Allison sheet (1893) each show a plain two-story clapboard block with a modest entrance and no veranda. Caveat on independence — the Kurz and Allison panel closely follows the Andreas composition and is probably derived from it, so these are not two witnesses so much as one witness and a copy. 'No gallery' is therefore better attested than 'gallery' without being documented. See the research notes on sauganash hotel.

levels.8-10: We changed this in August 2026, after looking at the pictures ourselves. No paper of the time says if it had a porch. But the two later pictures both show it without one. One is a print in a history book of 1884, and the other is a sheet of 1893. Each shows a plain two floor board building with a small front door and no porch. But the 1893 picture closely follows the 1884 one, and is likely copied from it. So they are one witness and a copy, not two. No porch is better backed than a porch, but it is still not a fact.

levels.8-10: We chose to show it open, with no roof, on 1 July 1835, and that is made up. A notice of 10 June shows the work had begun before our day. It does not date a roof or how high the walls were. The inside was still unfinished in June 1836, and it opened that fall, but neither proves it had no roof in July 1835. So we leave all the roofs off and show an open building site. A later print shows it finished with a roof and a small tower, but that is from 1836 to 1849, so it cannot tell us how it stood in July 1835.

entries.card: why:SAWN AND FRAMED CARPENTRY, NOT THE ROUND LOGS OF THE BRANCH…
entries.text: SAWN AND FRAMED CARPENTRY, NOT THE ROUND LOGS OF THE BRANCH BRIDGES, and the archetype has only two words for it. Norton was a ship-carpenter who 'commenced cutting the lumber for a drawbridge' over the winter of 1833-34 and began building in March: that is a stocked and framed structure, built by a tradesman to a design that won a premium, and it is a different thing from the four heavy logs the settlers describe under the branch bridges. bridge timber offers 'log' and 'timber crib' and rejects anything else with the message that a framed bridge is not this archetype; 'timber crib' is the nearer of the two and it is what the substructure of a low timber causeway across a navigable river in this decade would in fact have been. THE HONEST STATEMENT IS THAT THIS RECORD IS AT THE EDGE OF ITS ARCHETYPE. bridge timber builds a fixed log stringer crossing; this was a framed timber causeway with a hoisted draw. What it can carry faithfully is the fixed part, and the rest of this form block says which parts of the real bridge are not here at all.

levels.8-10: This bridge was sawn and framed wood, not the round logs of the river bridges, but our rules have only two words for it. Norton was a ship builder. Over the winter of 1833 he began cutting the wood for a bridge that could open, and he started building in March. That is a framed bridge, built by a tradesman to a plan that won a prize. It is not like the four heavy logs the settlers describe under the other bridges. Our bridge rules offer log or a log box filled with stone, and nothing else. The log box is the closer one. It is likely what held up a low timber bridge across a river in these years. The honest truth is that this bridge is at the edge of what our rules can build. We draw the fixed part faithfully. The rest of its card says which parts of the real bridge are missing.

entries.card: why:SEATED AT THE BARRACKS, AND other work RE-EXAMINED THAT AGAI…
entries.text: SEATED AT THE BARRACKS, AND other work RE-EXAMINED THAT AGAINST THE PLAN THE CARD ASKS FOR. The 1835 General Regulations quarter washerwomen inside the same allowance as the men (art. 31), so the barracks is where the Regulations themselves put them and the seating is not a shortcut. The plan this project holds is the 1830 Harrison survey, and it was read again for this: it letters the barn, the wash house, the shop, the well and a pair of blocks it calls `Out Buildings`, and it letters NO married quarters. The pair is the only candidate and it is refused — 24 x 19 ft and 13 x 10 ft, unlabelled, and already built as Fort Dearborn — out building (a) and `_b` on a record that declines to name a use; moving eight households onto them would be naming one. A hut outside the palisade, which is where married soldiers often were, is still a structure nobody drew. WHAT CHANGED IS THE ARITHMETIC THAT ARGUED AGAINST IT: the quartering check used to report the barracks 26 quarters short and offer the storey count as an open reading, and the record asserts two storeys, so on what stands the allowance is met with room over. The seating is still reconstructed and still replaceable by a plan that assigns quarters; it is no longer the weakest line on this card. Reconstructed on the rule no married quarters are drawn so the barracks carries them; no source places this household.

levels.8-10: We put this family in the soldiers' barracks, and we looked at that again against the fort plan, as the card asks. The army's rules of 1835 house the women who washed for the soldiers in the same space as the men. So the barracks is where the rules themselves put them. The plan we hold is the 1830 survey of the fort. We read it again for this. It labels the barn, the wash house, the shop, the well and two blocks called out buildings, and no rooms for married soldiers. Those two blocks are the only choice, and we say no to them. They are not labelled, and naming a use for them would be making it up. Married soldiers often lived in huts outside the fort, but no one drew any. Our count of room in the barracks once came up short. With two floors, it now fits with room to spare. This is still made up, and a plan that shows the real rooms would replace it. No paper places this family.

entries.card: why:SEATED BY THE LOT-ADDRESS POLICY (the project's notes on lot…
entries.text: SEATED BY THE LOT-ADDRESS POLICY (the project's notes on lot address; liberty “The one lot-and-block address in the corpus is seated on a roof nothing says is that house”). The Lake Street notice prints a LOT AND A BLOCK — LOT No. 7, in block No. 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street, in the town of Chicago — which is the plat's own language and the strongest placement statement in the corpus; 6 printings, 1834-06-18 to 1834-11-19, 4 of them cited here as legible, claims the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-18, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-09-03, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-10-15, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-11-19. THE ADDRESS IS WHAT THIS ROOF GAINS AND THE ONLY THING IT GAINS: its existence, its position, its footprint and every form value are the 665-roof programme's and are unchanged, its `function` still reads as the anonymous family the recipe dealt it, and no coordinate moved to seat this. THE NOTICE SAYS OF THIS LOT: a large dwelling-house; a fine well. The notice says 'There is on said lot a large Dwelling-House'. Four of the six printings carry the words unbroken. WHAT IS DRAWN AT THIS ADDRESS IS STILL NOT THIS HOUSE, and it now answers the word: the roof standing on the lot is the 665-roof programme's own count-unit, and other work re-dealt it out of the D3 one-room cottage band into H1, 'Larger one-and-a-half-story house', at 8.03 x 9.96 m and one and a half storeys. H1 is the lowest rung the family crosswalk itself calls larger and calls a house, which is the whole of what this notice's adjective supports; the south district's remainder paid for the slot and the displaced D3 went back into it, so no total moved. Until 2026-09-04 the fabric was a 5.36 x 6.38 m one-room cottage and this note said the mismatch was stated rather than repaired. The ADDRESS is still what this record gains: existence, position, footprint and every form value stay conjectural and the grade does not move. the project's notes on lot address § 'When the notice describes the building' is the rule and “A documented address re-deals the family under it: the one lot-and-block notice says LARGE, and the town's first H1 answers the word” is the ruling. NOT DRAWN, and other work has now settled why. The notice's second structure is a well and it is documented as plainly as the house; what was missing was a rule to place it by, and the reason recorded here used to be an absence — 'the town has no well' — which described the model rather than the town. THE READING IS the research notes on wells AND ITS ANSWER IS NOT A WELL. Chicago in July 1835 took its drinking water from the lake by cart: the Board of Trustees paid $95.50 on 10 November 1834 for the digging of ONE public well, in Kinzie's Addition, and after that the town was served by two-wheeled carts carrying a hogshead, filled by pail at the foot of Randolph Street and run off at a customer's door through a short leathern hose at five to ten cents the barrel (town findings andreas v1, #c013); the Chicago Hydraulic Company was not chartered until 18 January 1836 and its works were not finished until 1842 (#c014). No ordinance of this town requires, sites or pays for a well — the fire ordinances of 1833, September and October 1834 and the code of 5 August 1835 legislate wardens, bystanders and a bucket line and never the water in the buckets. So there is no density to deal a well class from, and inventing one would misdescribe the town more badly than leaving it with none. THE WELL STAYS DOCUMENTED AND ABSENT, on that argument rather than on an absence. It is one of only three wells this project can name in a town of 3,265 people, and the fact that G. Spring advertised it in all six printings, beside the size of his house, is the argument that a well was a thing worth mentioning rather than a thing every lot had. The notice ends 'For terms enquire of G. SPRING' and says NOTHING ELSE about him. He is the man to apply to, which is not a statement that he owned the lot, and is certainly not a statement that he lived in the house — the same G. Spring is the attorney whose office the papers put second door west of the corner of Franklin and South Water. So this house is not named for him, and the register's business g spring is not moved here. Other work is the same trap read from the other side: a building offered FOR SALE must not mint a placement on its vendor. THE ADDRESS IS READ; WHERE THE ADDRESS LANDS IS THE BOTTOM grade, and the chain is short enough to state in one breath. The words 'lot 7, block 16' are a direct reading of four printings. The block number is `inferred` — three blocks counted east of the one numeral the Wright sheet shows (the thompson block numbering data). The lot number is `conjectural` twice over: four lots to a block face is a reading of one block, the lot lines it numbers are the plat module's and are drawn from no sheet, and the counter-clockwise scheme itself was read off block 18. A chain is as strong as its weakest link, so which committed roof stands at this address is graded at the bottom grade — the same grade the roof already carried, and it does not rise because a documented address was put on it.

levels.8-10: We put this address on a building by our rule for lot addresses. A notice on Lake Street prints a lot and block: lot 7, in block 16, one lot east of Haddock's tavern. That is the plan's own words, and the strongest address in all our papers. It ran six times in 1834. The notice says the lot had a large house and a fine well. The address is the only thing this building gains. Its spot, size and shape are our own, and unchanged. In September 2026 we made the house on it bigger, a larger house of a floor and a half, to fit the word large. We do not draw the well. In 1835 Chicago got its water from the lake, by cart. The town paid for one public well in 1834, and no law asks for wells. So we have no rule for where wells went, and making one up would be worse than leaving it out. This is one of only three wells we can name in a town of 3,265 people. The notice ends: for terms ask G. Spring. That does not say he owned the lot or lived in the house, so we do not name it for him. Which building stands at this address is our weakest kind of guess, since the lot count rests on readings of one block.

entries.card: why:SEATED BY THE PLACEMENT POLICY'S PLATTED DEAL (the 1835 plat…
entries.text: SEATED BY THE PLACEMENT POLICY'S PLATTED DEAL (the 1835 platted seats data, dealt by and carried onto this roof by; liberties “The plat's 338 lots are enumerated from records this project already held, and then 183 of the town's households are dealt onto them by a policy and not by a source” and “Seventy-seven roofs across six districts now NAME the household the placement policy dealt them, and the rest do not because a ruling refuses them one”). NO SOURCE PLACES THIS HOUSEHOLD HERE, OR ANYWHERE. Its own record gives a name and no address — no street, no lot and not even a division — so both halves of its band were dealt rather than read, and the lot under this roof is the policy's labourer dwellings clause answered on the committed plat: block 16#04, fronting south water, a standing roof of family D1 the clause admits. THE SOURCES BELOW CARRY THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE. THE SOURCES BELOW CARRY THE NAME AND NOTHING ELSE. The roof's own existence, position and footprint remain conjectural and are unchanged by the seating — it is still a count-unit of the 665-roof programme, adopted rather than raised, so nothing was drawn off the reconstruction plan. entries.text: SEATED BY THE STREET-FACE ADOPTION POLICY (the project's notes on street face adoption, the owner's ruling of 2026-08-29 for, extended 2026-08-30 for; liberty “Nineteen documented businesses are seated on reconstructed roofs, and no source puts them there”). The newspaper register places this business on Canal Street AND NOTHING NARROWER — 5 printings, 1834-06-25 to 1834-12-17, claims the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-25, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-07-02, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-09-10, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-11-19, the Chicago Democrat of 1834-12-17 — so it takes the STREET FACE and not a lot. THE ROOF'S PLATTED LOT FACES Canal Street, which is the plat's own answer to which street it fronts. WHICH roof on that face it is given is an allocation by the adopt street faces tool and not a reading of any source, and nothing here says this business stood nearer the corner than any other on the same face. THE ROOF'S OWN EXISTENCE, POSITION AND FOOTPRINT REMAIN CONJECTURAL and are unchanged by the adoption: the business is documented, the building under it is not, and this attribute is graded `reconstructed` because the invented part is the whole of the placement.

levels.8-10: A Chicago paper puts this business on Canal Street, and nothing more exact. So it gets a spot on that street, not a lot. Which house on the street it gets is our choice, not from any paper.

entries.card: why:SEATED BY other work IN THE HOUSE BONNELL GIVES HIM. J. D. B…
entries.text: SEATED BY other work IN THE HOUSE BONNELL GIVES HIM. J. D. Bonnell's letter of 1876, quoted by Andreas (vol. 1, printed pages 136-137): "east of which [the Lake House] was the residence of Dr. Kimball, who was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street." A doctor, Pruyne's partner, and a druggist on South Water Street identify this man three ways over; the record of Dr. Kimberly's residence raised the building on that sentence and named him its occupant, and refused to write the household link while he shared a record with Pruyne, because seating the partnership there would have carried Pruyne across the river on a sentence about Kimberly. With the two men on two records the link is written from this side, which is the direction the evidence runs in. GRADED AT THE INFERENCE, NOT THE SENTENCE: the walk is the morning of 26 August 1835, eight weeks after the scene date, and the carry back to 1 July is the inference. A LATER DIRECTORY AGREES AND IS NOT LEANED ON: Fergus's 1839 directory prints 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S., res. N. Water st next Lake House' (f1839 e0850) - the same spot four years on, which corroborates the house and dates nothing in 1835. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR lives at AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW the Kimberly household#lives at, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start

levels.8-10: We put him in the house Bonnell gives him. A history book quotes Bonnell's letter of 1876: east of the Lake House was the house of Dr Kimball, partner of Mr Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street. A doctor, Pruyne's partner, and a druggist on South Water Street all point to this man. We held off while he shared a card with Pruyne, since that would carry Pruyne across the river on a line about Kimberly. Now the two men have two cards, so we link him here. It is a good guess, not a fact, since the walk was eight weeks after our day. A town book of 1839 puts him at the same spot, next to the Lake House. That backs up the house, but does not date it in 1835. We copied this from his family's home, and changed nothing.
