entries.card: why:SETTLED AT 1 ON other work, 2026-09-11, AND THE SOURCE THAT…
entries.text:
SETTLED AT 1 ON other work, 2026-09-11, AND THE SOURCE THAT SAYS TWO IS ABOUT A DIFFERENT BUILDING. bk hub 063 (Hubbard, 1911, describing the place as he found it in 1818) calls the Factor House 'a two-story, squared-log structure, inclosed by a neat split-picket fence'. Other work left this value at 1 provisionally, because the identity was open and a storey is a bake; other work closed the identity by measuring it rather than arguing it. The 1830 Harrison plan letters 'U.S. Factor's House' against three blocks at local ENU (1145.6, 38.7); this record's footprint centroid is (1133.2, 177.8), 140 m north, against about 20 m of working uncertainty here and 25 m on the plate. HUBBARD'S TWO STOREYS THEREFORE DESCRIBE A BUILDING 140 m FROM THIS ONE, and carrying them here would double the massing of the oldest building in the dataset on a description of somewhere else. The reading stays named on this value rather than buried, because it is the reason the number was ever in doubt. So: 1, inferred from the type and the date, as before — and now for a measurement rather than for caution. the harrison 1830 us factors house data.

other work ONE EXTERNAL MAIN-MASS PROTOTYPE, NOT ADOPTED: The keyed main block reads markedly taller than the one-storey proxy after the accepted diagnostic gable-right/longwall-left role test. Two storeys is the bounded visual interpretation used for this trial, not a measured floor count or printed description. This is based on the conditional Beaubien image identification, NOT Hubbard's two-storey Factor House140m away. Other work's separation of that building remains valid. Native upper opening bands follow this two-storey parameter and remain reconstructed defaults, not newly attested bay/window counts.

other work DATED SUPERSESSION,2026-10-30: the prior one-storey default is superseded by the actual native/root-reviewed conditional graphic two-level working mass. Hubbard/Harrison belong to the separately modeled Factor House and do not source this number; the present two-level inference comes only from this keyed drawing. Numerical dimensions remain reconstructed, and July1835 survival remains uncertain.

levels.8-10: We set this at one floor in September 2026. The paper that says two floors is about a different building. Gurdon Hubbard tells of the fort in 1818. He calls the Factor House a two floor house of squared logs, with a neat fence. The 1830 plan writes U.S. Factor's House at one spot. We measured it. It is about 460 feet south of this house. So Hubbard's two floors are about a house far from this one. If we used them here, the oldest house we have would double in size, from words about some other place. Then, in October 2026, we tried two floors after all. One old drawing seems to show this house taller. That comes only from the drawing, if we know who it shows. It does not come from Hubbard. The sizes are made up. We are not sure it stood like this in July 1835.

entries.card: why:SIXTEEN SUPPORTS IN THE RIVER, AND NOT ONE OF THEM IS ATTEST…
entries.text: SIXTEEN SUPPORTS IN THE RIVER, AND NOT ONE OF THEM IS ATTESTED. Nothing anybody wrote describes the middle of this bridge. Something had to hold up 76 m of crossing, so intermediate supports are not the invention; their number, their spacing and their form are. THE VALUE IS THE ARCHETYPE'S FALLBACK MADE VISIBLE. bridge timber divides a span whose middle nobody described by a 4.5 m default spacing, which over 76.33 m gives seventeen bays and sixteen supports. That fallback exists because of the liberties register “The North Branch bridge stands on fifteen piers nobody recorded”, where the same arithmetic put fifteen cribs under the North Branch bridge and the number went unnoticed for a slice because it was hidden in the generator instead of stated on the record. Writing it here as a conjectural count is the repair “The North Branch bridge stands on fifteen piers nobody recorded” earned: the same invention, in the open, with a chip on it. Sixteen bents at 4.5 m under a low timber causeway is not an unreasonable trestle for 1834 — which is exactly what makes it dangerous, because a plausible invention is the kind a visitor believes. TWELVE OF THE SIXTEEN ARE ACTUALLY BUILT: four of the evenly spaced stations fall inside the sixty-foot draw and are dropped, because an opening for the passage of craft with a pier in it is not an opening. So the number on this chip is the count the arithmetic produced and not the count in the mesh, and the difference is documented evidence removing an invented support rather than a discrepancy. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the February 1834 proposals, the trustees' specification, or the repair accounts of September 1834 and 1835.

levels.8-10: Sixteen posts stand in the river, and not one of them is in any paper. Nothing anyone wrote describes the middle of this bridge. Something had to hold up about 250 feet of bridge, so posts in the middle are not the made up part. Their number, spacing and shape are. The number is what our rules do when no one tells us. Then they space posts about 15 feet apart. Over this bridge that gives sixteen posts. Our rules once put fifteen log boxes under the North Branch bridge the same way. No one saw it, since the number was hidden. Writing it here, marked as a guess, is the fix. Sixteen posts under a low wood bridge is not unlikely for 1834. That is just what makes it risky. A likely guess is the kind a visitor believes. Only twelve of the sixteen are built. Four would fall inside the sixty foot opening for boats, so they are dropped. An opening for boats with a post in it is not an opening. So the number here is what the sum gave, not what is drawn. The difference is a known fact taking away a made up post. Papers from the time, like plans, reports, surveys or bills for the work, would settle it.

entries.card: why:SIXTY FEET, AND IT IS THE ONE DIMENSION EVERY TELLING AGREES…
entries.text: SIXTY FEET, AND IT IS THE ONE DIMENSION EVERY TELLING AGREES ON. Andreas: 'the opening for the passage of craft about sixty feet.' The 1902 text that halves the bridge's length keeps the same draw: 'with a draw of sixty feet at one end.' Two accounts that disagree by fifty per cent on the length agree exactly on the opening, which is what a number looks like when it descends from a specification rather than from an estimate by eye. Andreas elsewhere (scan p. 301, per the research notes on structures south section 4) records that a premium of twenty-five dollars had been offered for the best plan, 'the draw to be forty feet' — so the built opening was half again what the town asked for. That is a fact about the design competition, not a third figure for the draw. WHAT THE OPENING DOES IN THE MESH: it clears the intermediate supports out of itself and it stations the two gallows frames at its ends. A sixty-foot passage for craft with a pier standing in it is not a passage, so four of the sixteen evenly spaced supports of form.pier count are dropped, twelve are built, and the deck crosses the opening in one clear run. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO IS OPEN. The draw is built CLOSED, and that is the choice that avoids picking a side in the one thing the sources do not settle — see form.draw lifting gear.

levels.8-10: Sixty feet, and it is the one size every telling agrees on. A history book says the opening for boats was about sixty feet. A text of 1902 makes the bridge half as long. But it keeps the same opening: sixty feet at one end. Two tellings differ by half on length, yet agree on the opening. That is how a number looks when it comes from a plan, not a guess by eye. The book also says the town offered a prize of $25 for the best plan, with an opening of forty feet. So the built opening was half again what the town asked for. In our model, the opening keeps posts out. It sets the two tall frames at its ends. But it does not open. We build it closed. That way we do not have to choose how it was lifted. The papers do not say.

entries.card: why:STATED 2026-08-10, AND IT WAS THE ARCHETYPE'S UNTIL THEN. 'O…
entries.text:
STATED 2026-08-10, AND IT WAS THE ARCHETYPE'S UNTIL THEN. 'On these stringers puncheons or split logs were laid for a floor' — the 1883 old-settlers statement. bridge timber has built a puncheon deck since it was written, so the mesh does not change on this attribute alone; what changes is that the floor is now the record's claim rather than a default nobody could see or check. That distinction is the whole of the liberties register “Wolf Point Tavern: the frame half and the painted wolf sign are recorded and unbuilt”'s lesson: a value the generator does not read is a value that can be silently wrong, and a value stated in prose and not in a field is a value the walkthrough cannot show. The archetype's other reading is 'plank', sawn stock, which nothing in this dataset carries.

AND THE DECK IS SPECIFIED IN THE TOWN'S OWN BILL OF MATERIALS. the Chicago Democrat of 1834-02-04, the Board of Trustees' call for proposals of 4 February 1834 for repairing both town bridges, asks for 'sufficient plank for the floors of both bridges of oak plank 2 inches in thickness — the flooring to be secured at the plank by oak pins 1 1-2 inches in diameter and 2 feet in length'. Two-inch oak plank, pinned down with oak trenails an inch and a half through and two feet long: a decking detail from the body that owned the bridge, agreeing in kind with the value above. The same fabric is described from the other side by the ordinance of 7 November 1833 (The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday…), which fines anyone removing 'any plank or any piece of timber' from either bridge. IT IS A REPAIR SPECIFICATION AND NOT A MEASUREMENT OF THE BRIDGE AS BUILT, it is seventeen months before the scene date, and it does not separate the two bridges — so nothing here is changed and no confidence moves.

levels.8-10: We wrote this down in August 2026. Before, it was only our rules' choice. An 1883 account of the old settlers says that on the long beams, split logs were laid for a floor. Our bridge rules already build a split log floor, so the bridge does not change. What changes is that the floor is now this card's claim, not a hidden choice no one could check. A value our builder does not read can be wrong without anyone seeing. The town's own list of materials also describes the floor. In February 1834 the town's leaders asked for bids to repair both bridges. They asked for oak planks two inches thick, held down with oak pins two feet long. A law of November 1833 fines anyone who takes a plank or piece of wood off either bridge. But that is a repair plan, not a measure of the bridge as built. It is from before our day and does not tell the two bridges apart. So nothing changes, and we are no more sure.

entries.card: why:STATED AND NOT BUILT — the largest omission in this record a…
entries.text: STATED AND NOT BUILT — the largest omission in this record and the reason it should not be read as a building. No source describes this yard's plant; what is inferred is only that a brickyard which supplied the town's first brick building had the ordinary apparatus of the trade in the 1830s: a clay pit, a pug mill or tempering pit, hacks and racks for drying, and a CLAMP — brick stacked into its own kiln and burned in place with the fuel built into the stack — rather than a permanent kiln, which is what a two-season frontier yard would have used. None of it reaches the mesh: the outbuilding archetype builds a building, so this record shows one drying shed standing on empty ground where the sources describe a works. Owed an admission in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: The papers name this yard, but we do not build it. That is the biggest gap here, so do not read it as a building. No paper describes the yard's works. We only guess that a brickyard that made bricks for the town's first brick building had the usual tools of the trade. It would have a clay pit, a mill to mix the clay, racks to dry the bricks, and a stack of bricks burned in place as its own kiln. None of it is drawn. Our rules build one building, so you see one drying shed on empty ground, where the papers describe a whole works. We owe a note about this in our list of liberties.

entries.card: why:STATED AND NOT BUILT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE BUILD…
entries.text: STATED AND NOT BUILT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE BUILDING. Andreas records that Pierce bought the Rev. Mr See's old set of tools and set up in business, that he ironed the first Chicago-to-St-Louis stage line in January 1834 and that he began making the 'Bull' plough in the spring — none of which is possible without a forge, a bellows and a stack to take the smoke. The outbuilding archetype has no chimney parameter and no interior, so the mesh shows a shed with a doorway and NO SMOKE, which is the one feature of a smithy anybody in the street would have noticed. Nothing about the forge's size, position or the stack's material is attested in any case. Owed an admission in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: The papers say there was a forge here, but we do not build it. And the forge is the whole point of the building. A history book says Pierce bought an old set of tools and set up shop. In January 1834 he made iron parts for the first stage line to St. Louis. That spring he began making ploughs. None of that can be done without a forge, a bellows and a chimney for the smoke. Our shed rules have no chimney and no inside. So you see a shed with a door and no smoke. That is the one thing anyone in the street would notice about a blacksmith. No paper gives the forge's size or spot anyway. We owe a note about this in our list of liberties.

entries.card: why:STATED AND NOT BUILT. What the advertisement documents is th…
entries.text: STATED AND NOT BUILT. What the advertisement documents is the PROCESS, not the plant: Elston & Co. paid cash for tallow and for house ashes, which are the two inputs of soap making — tallow rendered, ashes leached for lye, the two boiled together — and candles are the same tallow moulded or dipped. So a kettle, a leach and a moulding floor are inferred from the raw materials the firm advertised for, which is a good inference and still an inference. None of it reaches the mesh: the outbuilding archetype builds a shed, and this record shows an empty one. The chimney or flue that a rendering fire needs is not modelled either — outbuilding has no chimney parameter — so the works have no smoke, which is the one thing a neighbour would have noticed about them. Owed an admission in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: The papers point to the works here, but we do not build them. The ad tells the process, not the tools. Elston and Company paid cash for fat and for wood ashes. Those are what soap is made from: the fat melted down, the ashes soaked for lye, and the two boiled together. Candles are made from the same fat. So a big pot, a tub for the ashes and a floor for shaping candles are a good guess from what the business bought. It is still a guess. None of it is drawn, so you see an empty shed. There is no chimney for the fire either, so the works give off no smoke, the one thing a neighbour would notice. We owe a note about this in our list of liberties.

entries.card: why:SURNAME ONLY, NO FORENAME, NO SEX RECORDED. Andreas prints '…
entries.text: SURNAME ONLY, NO FORENAME, NO SEX RECORDED. Andreas prints 'Oscar Pratt and Bcckford, printers' with the first letters damaged in the scan. The sex field is omitted rather than assumed: a compositor in 1833 was overwhelmingly likely to be a man, but 'overwhelmingly likely' is not what documented means and this record has no other information about the person at all.

levels.8-10: We have a last name only. There is no first name, and no sex is given. A history book prints Oscar Pratt and Bcckford, printers. The first letters are damaged in the scan. We leave out the sex. We do not guess. A printer's helper in 1833 was very likely a man. But very likely is not proof. We know nothing else about this person at all.

entries.card: why:Seven opening stations are drawn on the visible long elevati…
entries.text: Seven opening stations are drawn on the visible long elevation in the public-domain Andreas/Braunhold plate, held locally as the chicago green tree inn 1838 image; the seven upper sash centres are approximately x 822, 928, 1041, 1146, 1243, 1347 and 1443 in its 1600-pixel-wide reproduction. This is a modern reconstruction retrospective form evidence, not a dimension, coordinate or demonstrated 1835 elevation. The existing west-facing gable and Lake Street south-side reading assign that pictured long wall to local x min; no position or footprint changes. The opposite x max face is not overridden and retains its six-bay reconstruction. Seven bays fit the existing 12.19 m length at about 1.74 m per bay, keeping the archetype's existing 0.85 m sash and 1.35 m height. Their equal spacing, vertical bands and hidden treatment remain reconstructed. The earlier form replaced the middle lower sash with Gray's textually described south-side entrance. The current other work picture-priority choice uses the existing side entrance:null option to retain that seventh sash. Gray's later entrance recollection remains explicit counterevidence: no alteration date or absence of that door on 1 July 1835 is established. Other gable, wing and attic-light differences are classified in the individual picture match records.

levels.8-10: An old print of 1884 draws seven windows along the long side you can see. We read their centers off the picture. That is a later picture, not a size, a spot or proof of how it looked in 1835. We put that long side where the picture shows it. Nothing moves. The far side keeps its six made up openings. Seven fit along the wall, using our usual window size. Their even spacing is made up. Our earlier form put John Gray's side door in the middle, from his memory. We now follow the picture and keep a window there. Gray's later memory still goes against this. Nothing proves when a door was added, or that it was missing on 1 July 1835.

levels.8-10: This stored the fort's big guns. It is named once, in a description of the fort written about the year 1850. We put it in 1835 because buildings stand until we learn otherwise.

entries.card: why:TEN FEET, from Charles Cleaver, of both branch bridges. This…

This is the only dimension of any structure in this dataset that a source actually states, and it is worth saying why it is trusted at a witness remembering: Cleaver was recalling a bridge he had used and had driven a team across, and a width is the kind of number a user of a narrow bridge remembers. Recorded as 3.048 m exactly, being the conversion and not a rounding.

levels.8-10: Ten feet wide, from Charles Cleaver, for both river bridges. It is the only size of any building here that a paper truly states. We trust a memory here for a reason. Cleaver had used the bridge. He had driven a team across it. A width is the kind of number you remember, if you used a narrow bridge.

entries.card: why:THAT A WOLF WAS PAINTED ON THE BOARD IS ATTESTED; HOW IT WAS…
entries.text: THAT A WOLF WAS PAINTED ON THE BOARD IS ATTESTED; HOW IT WAS DRAWN IS LOST, AND THE OUTLINE IN THE MESH IS THE PROJECT'S OWN. “Lieutenant Allen made one for him out of a piece of a box. He painted a picture of a wolf on it” — "Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology. THE DECISION THIS REVERSES, and it was this project's for eleven months of its own history: the liberties register “Wolf Point Tavern: the wolf on the sign is not drawn” held that the board must stay blank, because painting a wolf from imagination would be the most conspicuous fabrication in the scene. That reasoning was right about the risk and wrong about where the risk lay. A blank board is not neutral. A source says a picture of a wolf was on this board, so an empty one asserts the opposite of the evidence, in the one place a visitor is guaranteed to look. The three-grade vocabulary exists for exactly this case (the project's rules § RECONSTRUCTED IS A grade): the honest move is to build at the lowest grade that carries it and say what bounded the invention, not to leave the object wrong and undocumented. The owner's standing ruling of 2026-08-18 is the same instruction in his own words. WHAT IS BOUNDED AND BY WHAT: a flat dark silhouette of a standing canine in profile, ears up and brush low, painted on both faces of the board — the plainest reading of “a picture of a wolf” that a sign painter with lampblack in oil could lay on box stock. It carries no attitude, no snarl, no ground line and no lettering, because each of those would be a further claim on top of this one; the engraving of the tavern shows a device on the board and is not held here at a resolution that could be copied even if a plate (a modern reconstruction) were allowed to drive one. Graded at the bottom grade and admitted in the liberties register “The Wolf Tavern's sign: the pole it flies from, and the wolf painted on it”, which is where the outline itself is claimed.

levels.8-10: A paper says a wolf was painted on the board. How it was drawn is lost, and the shape we draw is our own. A paper says Lieutenant Allen made the tavern a sign from a piece of a box, and painted a picture of a wolf on it. For eleven months we kept the board blank. We feared that painting a wolf from imagination would be the most noticeable thing we made up. That fear was right about the risk, but wrong about where it lay. A blank board is not neutral. A paper says a wolf was on it, so an empty board says the opposite, in the one place every visitor looks. The honest move is to build it as made up and say what limited it. The owner of this project had asked for the same. So we draw a plain dark shape of a standing wolf, seen from the side, ears up and tail low, on both sides of the board. It has no snarl, no ground and no words, since each would be another claim. The old print of the tavern is too small to copy.

entries.card: why:THAT IT WAS BUILT OF SAWN LUMBER IS DOCUMENTED BY IMPLICATIO…
entries.text: THAT IT WAS BUILT OF SAWN LUMBER IS DOCUMENTED BY IMPLICATION AND THE REST IS THE ARCHETYPE'S. Andreas: 'Being unable to find suitable lumber in Chicago, he was obliged to haul his material from Plainfield, forty miles' — a man does not haul boards forty miles by ox team to build a log pen, so the shop was a board building and not log, which is a genuine finding and the reason this record uses outbuilding rather than log dwelling. WHICH WAY THE BOARDS WENT IS NOT ATTESTED: light frame is the archetype's term for boards laid horizontally on a stick frame and `plank` for boards nailed on vertically, and nothing chooses between them here. The horizontal reading is taken because it is the more finished of the two and this was a shop on the town's main street rather than a field shelter. That last step is a preference.

levels.8-10: A paper shows it was built of sawn boards, and the rest is our rules' choice. A history book says he could not find good wood in Chicago, so he had to haul it from Plainfield, forty miles away. No one hauls boards forty miles by ox team to build a log pen. So the shop was a board building, not log. That is a real finding. Which way the boards ran is not in any paper. We chose boards laid flat on a frame, since that is the more finished look, and this was a shop on the town's main street. That last step is just a choice.

entries.card: why:THE 1834 OCCUPANT IS ATTESTED AND THE 1835 ONE IS NOT. The n…
entries.text: THE 1834 OCCUPANT IS ATTESTED AND THE 1835 ONE IS NOT. The name is cut at the right edge of the column and stays bracketed. Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly stands in this dataset at the record of Dr. Kimberly's residence, in Kinzie's Addition, on Bonnell's evidence; a doctor leaving a let house in Wabansia in 1834 and a Dr Kimberly living in Kinzie's Addition in 1835 would agree, but no source says they are the same man and no merge is declared (the same restraint the wabansia seating data takes). No household is seated under this roof.

levels.8-10: A paper names who lived here in 1834, but not in 1835. The name is cut off at the edge of the column. So we keep it in brackets. Dr Edmund Kimberly is in our records at his house in Kinzie's Addition. That comes from Bonnell's letter. A doctor left a rented house in Wabansia in 1834. A Dr Kimberly lived in Kinzie's Addition in 1835. That would fit. But no paper says they are the same man, so we do not join them. No family is put in this house.

entries.card: why:THE 1835 GROUNDBREAKING IS NOT ANDREAS. The separately admit…
entries.text: THE 1835 GROUNDBREAKING IS NOT ANDREAS. The separately admitted June 10 Chicago Democrat notice establishes an active project before the scene; modern compilations are not the only evidence for this site. "Lake House." Chicagology. Transcribing a passage of A. T. Andreas, History of… prints an Andreas passage and then two uncredited editorial paragraphs with no typographic break. ANDREAS says: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House, located on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter. This hotel, which was built of brick, was three stories and a basement in height, was elegantly furnished throughout, and cost its owners nearly $100,000.... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836.' He gives NO groundbreaking. THE UNCREDITED PARAGRAPH says: 'ground was broken in 1835, and opened in the fall of 1836'. The same paragraph drops Andreas's basement and gives $90,000 against his nearly $100,000, so it is demonstrably not a faithful restatement of the text it sits under, and 'ground broken in 1835' must not be cited as Andreas. the exclusions json's data Lake House hotel (completed) entry sources the 1835 groundbreaking to "A Chronology of Early Chicago Area Hotels." Digital Research Library of…, which is a second unfootnoted compilation saying the same thing; two compilations agreeing is not two witnesses. SO: from 1835-01-01, the first day the attested year permits and not a date anybody gives. TO 1836-12-31, a bound at the end of the year the hotel opened - Andreas's 'autumn of 1836' ends this construction state and no source dates the day. WHAT NARROWS THE MIDDLE, and it is the best anchor this record has: J. D. Bonnell, in a letter to the Chicago Times dated 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas, describes arriving in Chicago and walking the town the next morning - 'Passing east, toward the mouth of the river, was THE LAKE HOUSE IN COURSE OF CONSTRUCTION, east of which was the residence of Dr. Kimball.' Bonnell dates his arrival in the same letter to 'August 25, 1835'. That is eight weeks after the scene date and it is an eyewitness saying the building was visibly going up and not finished. HIS DATE IS NOT CLEAN AND THE CONFLICT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the letter opens 'My first entry into the city of Chicago was forty years ago, August 25, 1835' - forty years before 1876 is 1836 - and Andreas's own lead-in says Bonnell 'came to Chicago in 1837'. The 1837 reading is ruled out by the letter's own content, since the Lake House was open by the autumn of 1836; between 1835 and 1836 the letter's explicit date is preferred. Harriet Martineau, quoted by Andreas from June 1836, still calls it 'a new hotel then building', which is consistent with either. CURRENT EVIDENCE CORRECTION: the earlier ONLY THING wording is superseded by the separate Chicago Democrat notice of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, already cited under function. Its transcription-mediated reading supports an active named project before the scene but no precise groundbreaking day, roof or construction stage. The existing January 1 bound remains inferred, not an observed start date.

levels.8-10: The ground breaking in 1835 is not from the history book. A notice in the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 shows the work was going on before our day. A web page prints a passage from the history book. Then it adds two notes by someone else, with no break between. The history book says the Lake House was a grand brick hotel. It had three floors and a cellar, and cost nearly $100,000. It opened in the fall of 1836. The book gives no ground breaking. The other note says ground was broken in 1835. It also leaves out the cellar and gives a new cost. So it is not the book's words, and must not be cited as the book. The building's years start on 1 January 1835, the first day the year allows. They end at the end of 1836, when it opened. The best clue in between is Bonnell. He came to Chicago on 25 August 1835. The next morning he saw the Lake House being built. That is eight weeks after our day. His date is not clean. His letter also says forty years ago, which would be 1836. We keep the date he wrote.

entries.text: THE 1835 POLL LIST AND A SECOND INDEPENDENT SOURCE. Read from census 1840, directory 1843, directory 1844, newspaper 1833 1835, poll 1834, poll 1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1a), applied to every identity at once by the consolidate resident evidence tool and spent onto this card by the civic residents generator; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. THE SPRING OF 1833, FROM THE COMPILER'S LIST OF THAT SEASON'S ARRIVALS. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (1895), printed page 90 (claim bk mose1 005; the moses kirkland history of chicago v1 data): "Among the new arrivals in the spring of 1833 are the names of John Dean Caton, John K. Botsford, Silas B. Cobb, Charles Cleaver, Walter Kimball, H. W. Knickerbocker, Ezekiel Morrison, Asahel Pierce, Hibbard Porter, Stephen Rexford, Henry Whitehead, Eli B. Williams, Dr. John T. Temple, Rev. Jeremiah Porter and Rev. Allan B. Freeman." Season precision, carried at 1833-03-01, the first day this project reads a season at (the Pearsons household, the brickyard household, the Kimball household, minted off this same list). THE LIST SAYS "AMONG", SO IT IS A ROLL OF EXAMPLES AND NOT A REGISTER: it can date the men it names and it can never be read to exclude anybody it leaves out. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois (1895) is a compiler sixty years after the fact, crediting Andreas and Hurlbut on the pages read here; every claim taken off it is transcription mediated and none is scan verified, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` however plainly it is printed (the rule set for the settlers table, kept here). The catalogue of those present is: Rev. Allen B. Freeman and Hannah C., his wife, S. T. Jackson, Martin D. Harmon, Peter Moore, Nathaniel Carpenter, John K. Sargent, Peter Warden, Willard Jones, Ebenezer and Betsey Crane, Susanna Rice, Samantha Harmon and Lucinda Jackson." THE CATALOGUE NAMES 'Willard Jones' and the crosswalk joined it to this card on the forename alone, which is the whole join and is enough: this project holds six Joneses and 'Willard' reaches exactly one. A PRESENCE IS NOT AN ARRIVAL, AND IT BOUNDS ONE: a person standing in the settlement on 19 October 1833 had reached it by that day, so the bound is carried at 1833-10-19 with not later than precision — the same kind of statement the register made, moved earlier by a reading that saw the person sooner. THE CATALOGUE IS A ROLL AND NOT A CENSUS: the compiler says twenty-five Baptists were in the settlement and names the fourteen who were PRESENT that day, so the list is a floor. It can date the people it names and it can never be read to exclude anybody it leaves out. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. entries.card: why:THE ADDRESS IS DOCUMENTED IN A STREET NAME NOBODY ELSE USES,…
entries.text: THE ADDRESS IS DOCUMENTED IN A STREET NAME NOBODY ELSE USES, AND THE CROSS-REFERENCE IS WHAT PLACES IT. 'Main-street' appears nowhere in the street control data, the Thompson plat module or either 1834 sheet. Graves' Tavern is Dexter Graves's log tavern, which this dataset models as Mansion House at what became 84-86 Lake Street, on the NORTH side of Lake near Dearborn. 'Nearly opposite' therefore puts the smithy on the SOUTH side of Lake Street facing north across it, and 'Main-street' in November 1833 is very probably Lake Street under a colloquial name. The northing is the Lake Street south frontage band this dataset's reconstruction recipes already use; the easting is set opposite Mansion House. WHAT IS INVENTED: the exact lot, the setback and the facade bearing. AND THE ADVERTISEMENT DOES NOT KEEP THIS ANCHOR. Seven printings to 11 June 1834 read 'nearly opposite Graves' Tavern'; from 10 September 1834 the same standing copy, word for word otherwise and under the same 26 November 1833 dateline, reads 'opposite the Tremont House' - four printings, the last on 10 December 1834. The Democrat carries no printing of it between those two dates, so the change is bracketed by 1834-06-11 and 1834-09-10 and no closer. The first Tremont House stands at the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn in this dataset, about 36 m west of Mansion House and on the same north side of the street, so the later reading would put this shop the same distance west along the same south frontage. NOTHING PRINTED SAYS WHICH CHANGED - the shop may have moved, or the house across from it may have changed hands and name, or a compositor may have been handed fresh copy for a reason nobody printed; all three read exactly like this. THE POSITION HERE IS THE EARLIER READING'S AND HAS NOT BEEN MOVED, because moving it would decide that question on no evidence. The scene date is 1835-07-01, ten months after the later reading first ran, and the dated history of both anchors is carried in the register 1835 data under business matthias mason co.

levels.8-10: The ad gives a street name no one else uses. A second clue is what puts the shop on the map. No street list or map from the time has a Main Street. The ad says the smithy is nearly across from Graves' Tavern. That tavern was a log inn on the north side of Lake Street, near Dearborn. So the smithy sat on the south side of Lake Street, facing north. Main Street in November 1833 was most likely a common name for Lake Street. We guessed the exact lot, how far back it sat, and which way its front faced. The ad also changes. Seven printings, up to June 11, 1834, say nearly across from Graves' Tavern. From September 10, 1834, the same ad says across from the Tremont House. It ran that way four times, the last in December 1834. The paper has no printing between those two dates. So the change came some time in that summer, and we cannot say when. The first Tremont House stood at a corner of Lake and Dearborn. It was west of the tavern, on the same north side.

entries.card: why:THE ADDRESS IS THE PAPER'S OWN AND IT IS SHORT: 'on South-Wa…
entries.text:
THE ADDRESS IS THE PAPER'S OWN AND IT IS SHORT: 'on South-Water st. one door from Dearborn street' (Chicago Democrat, 1835-06-10) and '[… South] Water [st]reet, one door from De[arborn]' (Chicago American, 1835-06-13). That is a street, a cross street and a count of doors.

WHAT 'ONE DOOR FROM DEARBORN' IS READ AS, AND WHO DECIDED IT. The owner ruled on 2026-08-30 that a count of doors off a named corner is AN ORDINAL OFF THE CORNER — a position along the face, narrower than the street — and not a reach of the street and nothing narrower. the project's notes on corner ordinal is that policy and the register compiler reads the phrase under it, so this record's placement is the register's own reading and not this file's. A door is a premises, not a plat lot: it means the shop next along the row from the premises on the corner. The premises on the corner of this face is already committed — The Chicago American Office stands with its west wall on the Dearborn frontage, 'immediately east of Dearborn Street' — so one door from Dearborn is the next front east of it, and that is where this record stands.

AN ORDINAL IS STILL NOT A LOT, and this record claims none. See lot claim on this record and the project's notes on corner ordinal § the one limit: 'one door from the corner' fixes a position in a sequence along a face and names no platted lot, so this building is transparent to the plat's lot entitlements. It stands where it stands; it entitles nobody to anything and exhausts nothing.

WHICH SIDE OF DEARBORN, AND WHY EAST. The phrase does not say, and this is the one real fork. East is taken for two reasons that are not arbitrary. First, west of Dearborn the first premises on South Water is Madore Beaubien's Log House, a documented dwelling and not a store, and the second is off the block face entirely. Second, and this is the argument worth having: the town's own press carries three addresses on this one face — the American's office at the corner, Holbrook one door from Dearborn, and (through Andreas, quoting an 1835 advertisement) Frederick Thomas two doors from the American office — and read eastward they describe a continuous row of three fronts with no contradiction and no gap. Read westward they describe nothing that closes. A reading that makes three independent statements consistent is preferred to one that makes none of them so, and that is a reading, not a source. THE STREET ITSELF IS CORROBORATED: the American's transcription cuts the street word and it was read as South Water by argument, and the Democrat's printing of the same card sets 'South- Water' plainly — so the street is now two witnesses and only the SIDE is inferred.

THE ARITHMETIC, STATED SO IT CAN BE CORRECTED, AND THE METRES ARE OURS. The count of doors is the paper's; how far one door is from the corner is this project's reconstruction and is declared as such at “John Holbrook's store: the count of doors is the paper's, the metres between them are ours”. THE DOOR-GAP RULE, which produced the one number this placement turns on: a neighbouring front is set 3.048 m (10 ft) clear of the wall it neighbours — a gap, because 'one door from' describes a neighbouring front and not a party wall, and 10 ft is the smallest gap that reads as two buildings rather than one at walking distance. Applied here: The Chicago American Office's footprint origin is at local ENU E 711.06 and it is 12.192 m (40 ft) wide, so its east wall stands at E 723.25; this record's west wall is 3.048 m east of it at E 726.30, and its 9.144 m (30 ft) front therefore runs E 726.30 to E 735.44. That leaves 1.53 m clear of the block 16 lot line at E 736.97 — just inside the 1.5 m margin the block infill generator gives every roof on this face — and 9.14 m clear of Frederick Thomas's Shop's west wall at E 744.58. NORTH-SOUTH, IT IS SEATED ON THE COMMITTED FRONTAGE AND NOT ON A MODERN STREET. The block's own north edge in the thompson lots data runs from local (711.05, -5.54) to (814.72, -8.47); at this record's eastern corner, E 735.44, that line is at N -6.23. The north wall is set 1.50 m back from it, at N -7.73, which is the same setback the reconciled South Water records carry after other work and the same margin the anonymous units on this face stand at. The footprint origin is therefore local (726.30, -15.35), i.e. UTM E 447799.000 N 4637380.451.

WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M, dominated by the georeference (the datum data, 17.5 m RMS), plus whatever is carried in from The Chicago American Office's own 'near the draw-bridge' inference, plus the side-of-Dearborn fork above, plus the door-gap rule, which is a convention and not a measurement. The grade is INFERRED rather than reconstructed because the street, the cross street and the ordinal are all stated in two contemporary printed sources and the reasoning above is about how to read them, not about what to invent; it is not attested, because no source gives a lot.

WHAT IS STILL WRONG AND IS LEFT WRITTEN DOWN: the facade bearing is 0 while this frontage runs at about -1.62 degrees, so the north wall is 1.50 m back at its east corner and about 1.76 m at its west. That skew is the whole face's, it is smaller than the walk's own daylight, and it is not corrected here for the reason Frederick Thomas's Shop gives — rotating a record is a second claim.

levels.8-10: The paper gives a short address. It says the shop was on South Water Street, one door from Dearborn Street. Two papers printed it in June 1835. That gives a street, a cross street and a count of doors. The owner of this project made a rule in August 2026. A count of doors from a corner means a spot along the row, counted from that corner. It is more than just the street, but it is not a lot. A door means the next shop along the row. The corner shop on this side is already placed. It is the Chicago American office, right east of Dearborn Street. So one door from Dearborn is the next front east of it, and that is where this shop stands. A count of doors still does not name a lot. This shop claims no lot. It stands where it stands and gives no one a right to any land.

entries.card: why:THE ADVERTISEMENT ATTESTS THE HOUSE STANDING ON 16 JULY 1834…
entries.text: THE ADVERTISEMENT ATTESTS THE HOUSE STANDING ON 16 JULY 1834, ELEVEN AND A HALF MONTHS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE; THAT IT STILL STOOD ON 1 JULY 1835 IS INFERRED. Chicago Democrat, issue of 16 July 1834, p. 3 col. 2 (claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-07-16 in the chicago democrat 1834 07 16 data): 'To Rent, or Lease. [A] CONVENIENT Dwelling House, in W[a]bansia, now occupied by Doctor Kimberl[y]. It has four rooms, with a kitchen, barn, an[d] garden attached to it. For terms, apply at t[he] office of Col. Hamilton.' A house offered to rent or lease is a house its owner meant to keep, and nothing in the corpus records its removal, so it is carried to the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs, not as an attested end. The from date is the advertisement's own date and not a build date: no source says when it was raised.

levels.8-10: An ad shows the house was standing on July 16, 1834. That is almost a year before our scene. That it still stood on July 1, 1835 is our guess. The ad was in the Chicago Democrat. It offered a handy house in Wabansia to rent or lease. Doctor Kimberly lived in it then. It had four rooms, a kitchen, a barn and a garden. A house offered for rent is one the owner meant to keep. Nothing we have says it was taken down. So we keep it standing to the end of 1835, the last date we need. That end date is not proven. The start date is the date of the ad, not the date it was built. No paper says when it went up.

entries.card: why:THE ASSUMPTION THE NOTICE DOES NOT MAKE, STATED RATHER THAN…
entries.text: THE ASSUMPTION THE NOTICE DOES NOT MAKE, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT SILENT — required by this record's piece of work and by the claim's own reading note, which says in terms that WHICH of the two dimensions runs along Lake is not printed. Two things argue the 30 ft face is the front. FIRST, THE PLAN: 16 ft is a single-pile depth — one room deep, the ordinary small-house section of the period — while a 16 ft front on a 30 ft depth is a double-pile plan, which is not what $250 bought in Chicago in 1834. The claim's own note reaches the same reading: 'the 30-foot dimension is almost certainly the frontage-or-depth of a single-pile plan'. SECOND, THE FORM: this project's frame dwelling archetype builds an EAVES-FRONT house, ridge parallel to the facade, because that is the 1835 form here — the gable-front house is a Greek Revival habit that arrives with the Clarke House in 1836 — so the long dimension is the front by the same argument that shapes every other dwelling in the town. WHAT IS STILL A GUESS, AND IT IS A DIFFERENT ONE: that the front faces LAKE rather than LASALLE. Lake Street was the town's principal street and the notice names the house by a corner on it, but the printing does not say, and on the north-east quarter either street could carry the door. The fork is recorded here rather than resolved silently; turning the house to face LaSalle is a rotation of this record and nothing else.

levels.8-10: The notice does not say which side of the house faced Lake Street. So we say what we chose, and why. Two things point to the 30 foot side as the front. First, the plan. A 16 foot depth makes a house one room deep. That was the usual small house of the time. A 16 foot front with a 30 foot depth makes a house two rooms deep. That is more than $250 bought in Chicago in 1834. Second, the shape. Our rules build a house with its roof ridge running along the front. That was the way houses were built here in 1835. The house with its pointed end to the street came with the Clarke House in 1836. What is still a guess is a different thing. We guessed the front faces Lake Street, not LaSalle. Lake Street was the main street, and the notice names the house by a corner on it. But the paper does not say. Either street could have had the door. We say so here, and turning the house to face LaSalle would be an easy change.

entries.card: why:THE BANK WAS CONFLICTED IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOSSIERS UNTIL…
entries.text: THE BANK WAS CONFLICTED IN THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOSSIERS UNTIL other work READ THE FIRM'S NEIGHBOURS IN THE CHICAGO DEMOCRAT, AND THE RULING IS THE LAST PARAGRAPH OF THIS NOTE; what follows it is kept as the argument stood before. READING A, THE SOUTH BANK, ADOPTED HERE: the research notes on structures north section 3.10 reports 'a square frame building on South Water Street, "Newberry and Dole's Forwarding and Commission House", in views of c. 1835 — i.e., the south bank at that date', tagged [DOC]; that dossier names no source record for the views, which is why this record cannot cite them and why the reading is carried as inference rather than attestation. READING B, THE NORTH BANK: Andreas, 'It was made by Newberry & Dole, whose warehouse was on the North Side, immediately east of where Rush-street bridge now stands' (scan p. 1139), and the research notes on structures south turns that into an explicit instruction — 'Do not put it on South Water Street.' WHY THE SOUTH BANK IS ADOPTED, STATED AS REASONING AND NOT AS PROOF: Andreas's sentence is not about 1835. Read in place it describes the warehouse from which a named grain shipment was made — the paragraph runs 'The history of the next shipment, in 1839, of three thousand six hundred and seventy-eight bushels, on board the brig "Osceola"... It was made by Newberry & Dole, whose warehouse was on the North Side' — so the building it locates is the firm's warehouse in 1839, four years after the scene date, in a decade when the firm plainly moved and grew. The c. 1835 view evidence is contemporaneous with the scene and the Andreas sentence is not, so the south bank is the better reading FOR THIS DATE while remaining the weaker citation. A READER SHOULD KNOW THE MODELLING CONSEQUENCE TOO, AND THAT IT IS NOT A REASON: the Rush Street site lies about 1 km east of the datum origin, which in August 2026 was some 700 m beyond the modelled terrain box, so reading B would THEN have put the building outside modelled ground. That consequence has lapsed: the heightfield was extended east on 2026-08-11 to local E -320..+1700 and there is traced ground at the Rush Street site now (corrected 2026-08-22). That did not decide the choice and is recorded so nobody has to wonder whether it did. THE BLOCK IS UNATTESTED UNDER EITHER READING. South Water Street ran the length of the south bank and nothing says where on it this house stood, so the coordinate is a point chosen on a street, and it is conjectural, not inferred. IT WAS FIRST CHOSEN AT local E +200 to +211, north face about 8 m back from the traced bank, and that put the whole body in the roadway: it stood across the head of Franklin Street and inside South Water Street's platted corridor, 9.8 m into Franklin's and 12.1 m into South Water's by the corridor intrusion check. OWNER RULING, 2026-10-04, verbatim: "i feel like the forwarding and commission warehouse should be moved in so it is inside the south water and franklin corner... still facing out to the river like it is but should come back south and west so it sits at that northwest inside corner of franklin and south water... this way it is not in the road". So the house now stands in the inside corner of the block west of Franklin and south of South Water (plat block 21, which this dataset does not lot), its east wall about 1.2 m clear of Franklin's drawn corridor and its river wall about 1.2 m clear of South Water's, origin local E +184.0, N -31.3. That is still free choice within a documented street — the same street, the same frontage, a few metres back — and the move is claimed at the liberties register “Newberry & Dole's warehouse stands back in the Franklin corner, across the street from its dock” alongside “Two river warehouses stand on banks that are disputed or unattested, and neither has its dock”. Facade bearing 345, square to South Water Street where it bends here and so facing across the street to the river and its dock — a forwarding house faces its wharf — which is an argument from the trade, not a source. The dock is re-derived from this wall by the river wharves generator and lands on the traced bank across the street; a South Water house with its landing across the roadway is how the street's own stores stood. READING C ARRIVED ON 2026-09-28 AND IT IS THE FIRST WITNESS ON THIS QUESTION WHO WAS STANDING IN 1835. J. D. Bonnell's walk of the morning of 26 August 1835, written to the Chicago Times on 15 March 1876 and quoted by Andreas (vol. 1, printed pages 136-137), goes east along the north bank past the Lake House building site and the residence of Dr. Kimball and then says: "Opposite Dr. Kimball's was Hunter & Hinsdale's warehouse. Adjoining on the west was Newberry & Dole's warehouse, and on one part of the latter building was the hat store of McCormick & Moon, of Detroit... In the back part of the store was Jesse Butler's tailor shop." That is THIS FIRM'S WAREHOUSE, on the NORTH bank, at the east end by the Lake House block - which is where Andreas's 1839 sentence puts it too, "immediately east of where Rush-street bridge now stands". THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE REASONING ABOVE IS PLAIN AND IT IS NOT DISCHARGED HERE. The whole argument for adopting reading A is that reading B's citation "is not about 1835" and the c. 1835 views are contemporaneous. Bonnell is about 1835: eight weeks after the scene date, not four years, and by the same date preference this project already applies to his letter on Lake House (under construction). So the north bank now has a contemporaneous witness and the south bank has an untraceable [DOC] tag naming no source record, and the balance of the two readings has moved against the position this record stands on. NOTHING IS MOVED IN THIS COMMIT, AND THE REASON IS SCOPE AND NOT DOUBT. Moving a committed warehouse across the river moves its dock, the wharf and river-works layers that read it, its signboard, the yard goods on its frontage and the block it is counted on, and it wants the c. 1835 views identified rather than merely doubted - that is its own parcel and it is filed as one. What changes here is the record's honesty about where it stands: this position is now the WEAKER of two readings by date as well as by citation, and a reader should not have to find that out by reading a third dossier. TWO BUSINESSES BONNELL PUTS INSIDE THIS BUILDING are also unrecorded by this project and are filed with the move: the hat store of McCormick & Moon of Detroit, and Jesse Butler's tailor shop in the back part of it. See the research notes on north bank east end neighbours section 4. THE BANK IS RULED ON 2026-10-05, AND THE WITNESS IS THE TOWN'S OWN PAPER ON THE SCENE DATE. Reading C was weighed as 'a contemporaneous witness against an untraceable dossier tag', and that framing was wrong about the south bank: the reading it needed was already in this project's own newspaper corpus (the extracted data), unlinked to this record. Newberry & Dole's premises are the most-cited anchor in the Chicago Democrat's advertising columns, and the neighbours who hang off them put them on the SOUTH side in plain words and at every date the corpus holds. Peter Cohen, 'at his store next door below Messrs. Newberry and Dole's store house, on south water street' (copy dated 3 November 1834; the Chicago Democrat of 1834-11-12, 1834 12 03), still standing in the paper on the scene date itself, 1 July 1835 ('[…]low Messrs. Newberry and Dole's', the Chicago Democrat of 1835-07-01), and on 11 June 1835 at 'his old stand' (1835 06 17). W. H. Brown 'on Dearborn street, one door from Newberry & Dole's store' (1834 05 28). W. H. Taylor's boot, shoe and leather store 'on Dearborn street, a few rods north of Messrs. Newberry & Dole's Store' (1835 05 20, six weeks before the scene date). South Water Street and Dearborn Street were both south-bank streets in 1835, so a store house on one with neighbours on the other is a south-bank building, and four advertisers who did not mention one another agree on it. That is a contemporaneous source record, The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1 (November 26, 1833) through Vol. II, No. 18…, and it is now cited on this position: the south bank no longer rests on the dossier's untraced 'views of c. 1835'. BONNELL IS NOT OVERRULED AND IS NOT WRONG: he is eight weeks LATER than the scene date, and the paper is ON it. A forwarding house this size could hold two houses — the firm's own card is 'STORAGE, Forwarding & Commission' — and the north-bank warehouse he walked past on 26 August 1835 beside Hunter & Hinsdale's, with McCormick & Moon's hat store in one part of it, may be a second house newly built or newly taken that summer; nothing reached dates it before the scene, so it is not added to the July scene here and the question of whether it stood on 1 July is filed (see the research notes on north bank east end neighbours section 4). WHAT THE READING DOES NOT SETTLE, AND IT IS STATED SO NOBODY RELIES ON IT: 'opposite to Fort Dearborn', which the paper sets over this firm's card on 14 May 1834 (1834 05 14) and over John H. Kinzie's the week before, is a direction and not a bank, and is not used either way. AND THE PAPER POINTS AT A DIFFERENT CORNER FROM THE ONE THIS RECORD STANDS ON: both Dearborn-street neighbours put the store house at the Dearborn end of South Water Street, four blocks and about half a kilometre east of the Franklin corner the owner's ruling set it in (this record's origin to George W. Dole's Warehouse's is 528 m east), and Andreas's Lake-and-Dearborn warehouse (George W. Dole's Warehouse) stands one block south of that end. Nothing is moved here, because this piece of work's question was the bank and the block was the owner's free choice on 2026-10-04; that the evidence now names a street end is filed as other work. The bank is now inferred on a source; the block is still ours. THE BLOCK IS RULED ON 2026-10-05: THE FRANKLIN CORNER STANDS, BECAUSE THE DEARBORN NEIGHBOURS ARE PLACING A DIFFERENT BUILDING. Read together, the paper's Dearborn advertisers put the firm's STORE on Dearborn Street with a neighbour on each side of it on that same street: Tuttle & Brown 'on Dearborn street, one door south of Messrs. Newberry & Dole's store' (copy of 27 May 1834; the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-04, and J. B. Brown's setting 1834 07 02), and Wm. H. Taylor 'on Dearborn street, a few rods north of' it (1835 05 20). D. Graves's bakery is 'on South Water-street, a few doors north of' the same store (1834 03 25, 1834 07 09). A store with Dearborn-street lots both north and south of it is not on a South Water corner, where the lot to the north is the roadway and then the river; it stands on the Dearborn face somewhere south of South Water, and Andreas's Lake-and-Dearborn house (George W. Dole's Warehouse, 'close to the present site of the Tremont House') is the committed building that fits all four. That record now carries the firm's store, inferred, and its signboard says so. THE STORE HOUSE IS A SECOND PREMISES, AND ONLY ONE NEIGHBOUR PLACES IT: Peter Cohen 'next door below Messrs. Newberry and Dole's store house, on south water street' (1834 12 03, standing to the scene-date issue). Cohen gives the street and no cross street, so he does not move this house off the corner the owner set on 2026-10-04, and nothing else in the corpus does. The three readings the piece of work put were weighed so: (a) store house and store one building, refused, because Cohen's neighbour is on South Water and Taylor's is a few rods north on Dearborn, and no single lot touches both; (b) a second house on South Water at Dearborn, refused, because the only Dearborn evidence is about the store and both South Water corners at Dearborn are already held by the records Andreas places there (Madore Beaubien's Log House on Lot 1, The Chicago American Office 'near the draw-bridge'); (c) kept, with this paragraph as the reason. The corner is still ours, and the next thing that would move it is a printing that gives the store house a cross street.

levels.8-10: Our own notes did not agree about which bank of the river this firm was on. Then later work read the firm's neighbours in the Chicago Democrat. The answer is at the end of this note. The rest shows how the case stood before. The first view puts it on the south bank. One of our notes says a square wood building on South Water Street was Newberry and Dole's store, in views from about 1835. That note does not name the views, so we cannot point to them. That is why we call this a guess and not proof. The second view puts it on the north bank. A history book says their warehouse was on the North Side, east of where the Rush Street bridge later stood. Another of our notes says not to put it on South Water Street. We chose the south bank. That is our thinking, not proof. The history book's line is not about 1835. It tells about a load of grain sent in 1839.

entries.card: why:THE BEST-DOCUMENTED ARRIVAL IN THE WHOLE PARCEL, and the onl…
entries.text: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED ARRIVAL IN THE WHOLE PARCEL, and the only one that gives a month, a party size, an origin AND a reason in a single sentence. Andreas, scan p. 281: 'Dr. John T. Temple, who had arrived early in July, 1833, with his family, consisting of a wife and four children. He was a pious and earnest Baptist Christian, and came to Chicago from Washington, D. C., armed with a contract to carry the mails from Chicago to Fort Howard, Green Bay.' He then headed the subscription for the Temple Building with $100. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Temple, John T.” (poll 1833 027, line 48); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Temple, John” (tax 1833 102, line 154); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Temple, John T.” (poll 1834 107, line 276). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Temple' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 10 times, as “TEMPLE JOHN T”, “TEMPLE J T”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-21: 2 lots in the platted town — lot 4 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL20CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL20CHIOT, as printed) and 8 parcels of the school section — BL103 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL110 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL111 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL112 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL17 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL76 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL77 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL99 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 30.31 acres stated in all, for $21107.00 (ls0353, ls0354, ls0355, ls0356, ls0357, ls0358, ls0359, ls0360, ls1505, ls1506). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $20000.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: TEMPLE JOHN T matches Dr John Taylor Temple: the forename names Dr John Taylor Temple of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: This is the best known arrival in the whole set. It is the only one that gives a month, the size of the family, where they came from and why, all in one line. A history book says Dr. John T. Temple came early in July 1833. He brought his wife and four children. He was a strong Baptist. He came from Washington, D.C., with a deal to carry the mail from Chicago to Fort Howard at Green Bay. Later he gave the most money, $100, toward the Temple Building. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 3 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 10 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:THE BEST-EVIDENCED FOOTPRINT IN THE DATASET, AND STILL NOT D…
entries.text: THE BEST-EVIDENCED FOOTPRINT IN THE DATASET, AND STILL NOT DOCUMENTED - read why. Both dimensions are attested: the church is a plain frame building 'about 40 x 25 ft' costing $600 (the research notes on structures south section 6, from Andreas I scan p. 623). 12.192 x 7.62 m is 40 x 25 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated here per the datum json's data units rule. WHAT IS INFERRED IS EVERYTHING ELSE ABOUT THE SHAPE. First, that the plan was a plain rectangle: no source describes a vestibule, a projecting entry, a chancel or a session room, and a plain box is the type for a frontier meeting house of $600, but nothing states it. Second, WHICH DIMENSION IS THE FRONTAGE. The 40 ft is put on Lake Street here for the reason given in the position note - the attested 'south 25 ft' strip runs east-west - and the frame dwelling archetype independently forces the same answer, because it refuses a range deeper than 1.5x its frontage. That agreement is convenient rather than evidential and should not be read as two witnesses. A source that gave the lot's depth, or a plat showing Block 34's lot lines, would settle both halves.

levels.8-10: This is the best known floor plan in the whole set, and it is still not proven. Here is why. We know both sizes. The church was a plain wood building about 40 by 25 feet. It cost $600. That comes from a history book. All the rest of the shape is our guess. First, we guess it was a plain box. No paper tells of a porch, an entry, or any extra room. A plain box is what a $600 meeting house in a new town would be. But nothing says so. Second, we guess which side faced the street. We put the 40 foot side on Lake Street. The strip of land it stood on ran east and west. Our house rules also give the same answer, since they will not build a house much deeper than it is wide. That match is handy, but it is not two pieces of proof. A paper with the lot's depth, or a map with the lot lines, would settle both guesses.

entries.card: why:THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED AND IS NOT RESOLVED HERE. Two rea…
entries.text: THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED AND IS NOT RESOLVED HERE. Two readings: 1828, James Kinzie, west bank at Wolf Point ("The Beginning of Wolf Point in Chicago, Illinois, including the history of the…, and the same date in general circulation); and 1823, James Kinzie with David Hall ("A Chronology of Early Chicago Area Hotels." Digital Research Library of…' chronology, which gives the tavern as 'opened in 1823'). 1828 is adopted because it is the reading of the narrative account that also carries the operator succession and the wolf sign, and because the 1823 date sits oddly with the licensing record — Archibald Caldwell's liquor licence is 8 December 1829 and the first Peoria County tavern licence in the settlement went to Clybourn and Miller. The two sources are the SAME PUBLICATION disagreeing with itself, which is a reason to distrust both dates rather than to prefer one confidently, so this range is inferred, not documented. A five-year error in the start does not affect the 1835 scene: the building stood under either reading. The end of the range is set at the end of 1836, the last year of William Walters's attested tenancy — NOT a demolition date. No source reached gives the building's fate, so the phase is closed where the evidence stops rather than run on speculatively.

levels.8-10: People do not agree on when this was built, and we do not settle it here. One date is 1828. It says James Kinzie built it on the west bank at Wolf Point. The other date is 1823. It says James Kinzie built it with David Hall. We use 1828. That account also tells who ran the tavern after him and about its wolf sign. The 1823 date also fits badly with the town's licence records. The first tavern licence here went to Clybourn and Miller. Both dates come from the same place, which does not agree with itself. That is a reason to doubt both. So we call the dates a guess, not proof. Being five years off does not change our 1835 scene. The tavern stood either way. We end it in 1836, the last year William Walters is known to have run it. That is not the year it was torn down. No paper says what became of it, so we stop where the proof stops.

entries.card: why:THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED BY A YEAR AND THE DISPUTE DOES NO…
entries.text:
THE BUILD DATE IS DISPUTED BY A YEAR AND THE DISPUTE DOES NOT REACH THE SCENE. Andreas: 'In the summer of 1832 Samuel Miller... built the first bridge over the North Branch.' Charles Cleaver, recalled in 1893, gives the winter of 1831-32. Summer 1832 is adopted, on the ground that Cleaver did not reach Chicago until October 1833 — so his date is hearsay reported sixty years later, while Andreas's is a compiler's date from the 1880s working over the town's own records. Either way the bridge stood well before 1835-07-01 and this record models one phase. THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE ONLY ONE THIS PROJECT HAS THAT IS ACTUALLY ATTESTED: the Kinzie Street chronology closes bridge #1 in 1839, superseded by a pontoon swing. That is a table's summary rather than Andreas's prose, so the range carries the same inferred tag as its opening. What the range does NOT claim is that the structure was unchanged across it — see the form notes: a bridge described as useless for teams in 1833 carried a large procession in August 1835, and nothing reached records what happened in between.

THE TOWN'S OWN ORDINANCES CARRY A BRIDGE ON THIS BRANCH FROM ITS FIRST FORTNIGHT TO THE MONTH AFTER THE SCENE DATE. Five readings of the Chicago Democrat, written on THIS block because what they document is that the crossing existed and was maintained, continuously, and not where it stood. (1) The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday…, the village ordinances of 7 November 1833: a fine on 'every person who shall remove from either of the bridges in said town, any plank or any piece of timber belonging thereto'. 'Either' is a two-term word, so the incorporated town had exactly TWO bridges in its first fortnight, and what it forbids men to carry off describes them — plank on timber. (2) the Chicago Democrat of 1833-12-10 records that on 4 December 1833 the Board appointed G. W. Dole, Medore B. Beaubien, Edmund S. Kimberly and John Miller a committee 'to make a contract with some person, for repairing the Bridges on the North and South branches of the Chicago River in said town' — bridges on BOTH branches, inside the town limits, in want of repair eighteen months before the scene date. (3) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-01-07 prints the same ordinance from a different forme, 'building the Bridges on the North and South [branches]'. (4) the Chicago Democrat of 1834-05-14, 14 May 1834: five dollars forfeit from 'any person who shall ride or drive over any bridge within the limits of said town, faster than a walk' — a decked crossing carrying ridden and driven traffic, legislated for by the corporation and attested by its clerk. (5) the Chicago Democrat of 1835-08-19, seven weeks after the scene date: 'No person shall ride or drive on the side walk of the bridges in said town, but shall walk', at five dollars, five times the penalty for riding along an ordinary sidewalk — so the town's bridges had a footway a horse was kept off. WHAT THEY DO NOT SUPPLY IS WHICH BRIDGE. Every one of the five says 'the bridges' or 'any bridge'; none names this crossing apart from the other. They are read onto both bridge records on the identification those records already make from other evidence, and this note adds no position, no span and no date to either.

levels.8-10: People do not agree on when the bridge was built. They are a year apart, and it does not change our scene. A history book says Samuel Miller built the first bridge over the North Branch in the summer of 1832. Charles Cleaver, writing in 1893, says the winter of 1831. We use summer 1832. Cleaver did not come to Chicago until October 1833. So his date was something he heard, told sixty years later. Either way, the bridge stood long before July 1835. The end date is the only one we have that is shown. A list of the Kinzie Street bridges says the first one ended in 1839, when a floating bridge took its place. That is a short list, not a full account, so we still call it a guess. We do not claim the bridge stayed the same the whole time. In 1833 it was called no good for wagons. In August 1835 a big parade crossed it. Nothing says what happened in between. The town's own laws name a bridge on this branch from the town's first two weeks to the month after our scene. Five of them, in the Chicago Democrat, show the bridge was there and kept up. They do not show where it stood.

entries.card: why:THE BUILD YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE D…
entries.text: THE BUILD YEAR IS DOCUMENTED AND THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS NOT, which is why this range is tagged inferred rather than documented. Andreas: 'a two roomed log house which was the first building on lot No. 1', built 1831; Madore Beaubien was licensed as a merchant in 1831 and was a town trustee in 1833. No month is given, so the range opens at the start of the year. NO SOURCE REACHED FOLLOWS THE BUILDING PAST ITS ERECTION. It stands in this scene on the ordinary continuity argument — a standing building stands until something says otherwise, and the exclusions record is where documented removals go — and the counter-argument belongs here rather than in a footnote: the south-west corner of South Water and Dearborn was prime frontage on the town's business street in the 1835 boom, the drawbridge landed at the foot of Dearborn a year before the scene date, and a four-year-old log house on that corner is exactly the building a boom replaces first. The same weakness, argued the same way, carries Hogan's Store. If evidence turns up that this building came down before July 1835 it belongs in the exclusions record and this record leaves the scene.

levels.8-10: We know the year it was built, but not that it still stood in our scene. So we call its dates a guess. A history book says it was a two room log house, the first building on lot 1, built in 1831. Madore Beaubien had a store licence in 1831 and was on the town board in 1833. No month is given, so we start at the start of the year. No paper we found tells of the house after it was built. We keep it standing because a building stands until something says it is gone. But there is a case against it. The corner of South Water and Dearborn was the best spot on the town's business street in 1835. The new bridge came down at the foot of Dearborn a year before. A four year old log house on that corner is just the kind of building a busy town tears down first. Hogan's Store has the same weak spot. If proof turns up that it came down before July 1835, we will take it out of the scene.

entries.card: why:THE BUILDING FRONTS ON A GABLE END, AND ITS EVEN BAYS RUN AL…
entries.text: THE BUILDING FRONTS ON A GABLE END, AND ITS EVEN BAYS RUN ALONG THE EAVES ELEVATIONS. Two halves, separately grounded. That the front is a gable end is a join of attested facts already in this record: the front on Canal (F. H. Taylor), the long side on Lake, and the gable ends facing east and west (John Gray's attic window note, and the roof type note's own reading). The bay ARRANGEMENT — even 6-over-6 sash in regular bays along the long elevation, doors and attic lights on the gable faces — is read off plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set, committed at the source files for prefire views kevin 2026 08: a retrospective (a modern reconstruction) view, which may drive fenestration rhythm as inferred and may never drive a coordinate. The plate is not yet held as a source record (owns that), so the citation is a committed path. The pictured south eaves elevation's bay count is now stated separately by eaves bays on other work; the opposite elevation keeps the archetype's footprint arithmetic as a reconstruction under the liberties register “The Green Tree's fabric from the plates: bays, end stacks, and the rear ell”. No dimension or geographic placement is taken from the plate.

levels.8-10: The front of this building is a pointed end wall. Its even rows of windows run along the long sides. Each half has its own proof. The front faced Canal Street. The long side was on Lake Street. The pointed ends faced east and west. All of that is already on this card. The window pattern comes from a picture in the owner of this project's set from August 2026. It shows even rows of windows, six panes over six, along the long side. It shows doors and attic windows on the end walls. That picture was made long after, so it may guide the windows but never where the building stands. The picture is not yet in our list of sources, so we point to the file instead. The south side's window count is set by other work. The far side keeps our usual rules, and we list it as a guess. No size or place is taken from the picture.

entries.card: why:THE BUILDING IS ATTESTED AND ITS DATES ARE NOT, SO BOTH BOUN…
entries.text: THE BUILDING IS ATTESTED AND ITS DATES ARE NOT, SO BOTH BOUNDS ARE HOUSEKEEPING BOUNDS AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. Andreas, scan p. 185, lists what the Beaubien homestead held; the research notes on jb beaubien homestead § 1 reads it as the American Fur Company factory building, a new residence, a small trading post and a cabin converted to a barn. The list gives no year to any of the three that are not the factory building. THE OPENING BOUND IS THE SAME FLOOR THE PARENT RECORD USES AND FOR THE SAME REASON: Andreas has Beaubien in the Dean house at the lake shore from 1817 'for several years' and at the factory building from 1822 (scan pp. 191, 205), and Wentworth finds the residence at this corner 'after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house', so 1822-01-01 is the earliest date the sources leave open and not a construction date. THE CLOSING BOUND IS THE END OF THE SCENE YEAR, not a demolition date: what carries the survival is Wentworth's own account of the sale of June 1839, where James H. Collins bids $1,049 for lots 10, 9, 8, 7 and 6 'where Beaubien's house, out-buildings, and garden were' — four years after 1835-07-01, and evidence that the group was still standing, not that this building was one of the things named. THE 13-YEAR SPAN WILL RAISE THIS PROJECT'S WIDE-RANGE WARNING and is left standing rather than trimmed to silence it, exactly as both siblings do: the warning is correct that nothing documents the middle years.

levels.8-10: We know this building was there, but not its dates. So both dates are just for keeping records, and we say so. A history book lists what stood at the Beaubien home. Our notes read it as the old fur company store, a new house, a small trading post, and a cabin turned into a barn. The list gives no year for any but the store. The start date is the same as for the main house, for the same reason. Beaubien lived in the Dean house by the lake from 1817. He moved to the store building in 1822. So 1822 is the earliest date the papers leave open. It is not the year it was built. The end date is the end of 1835, not a date it was torn down. What keeps it standing is the sale of June 1839.
