James H. Collins paid $1,049 for lots 6 to 10, where Beaubien's house, barns and garden were. That is four years after our scene. It shows the group still stood. It does not show this building was one of them.

entries.card: why:THE BUILDING IS ATTESTED AND ITS SIZE IS PRINTED. Chicago De…
entries.text: THE BUILDING IS ATTESTED AND ITS SIZE IS PRINTED. Chicago Democrat, 21 May 1834, page 3 column 6, claim c001: '[W]E offer for sale the House on [the corner] of Lasalle and Lake streets. [It] is 16 by 30 feet, and possession can [be had on] the first day of next month.' The copy is dated Ap'l. 22 and is signed P. PRUYNE. The same notice is still running on 18 June 1834 (the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-18 c014), where the interleaved second half gives the price, $250, and the word 'dwelling'. THE RANGE OPENS on the copy date, 22 April 1834, because that is the first day a source puts the house in existence — it was standing and untenanted then, and still advertised a month later. THE CLOSE IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY ARGUMENT and it is untested: nothing reached mentions the house again, and 1835-12-31 is the last date this record needs rather than a date anything attests. What is genuinely unknown is the sale: whether it sold on the first of June 1834, to whom, and who lived in it fourteen months later on the scene date.

levels.8-10: We know this house stood, and the paper gives its size. The Chicago Democrat of May 21, 1834 has an ad. It offers the house on the corner of LaSalle and Lake Streets. It is 16 by 30 feet, and a buyer could move in on the first of the next month. The ad is dated April 22 and signed by P. Pruyne. The same ad still ran on June 18, 1834. There, the rest of the ad gives the price, $250, and calls it a home. We start the house on April 22, 1834. That is the first day a paper shows it. It was standing and empty then. We keep it to the end of 1835, since nothing says it was torn down. Nothing we found names the house again, so this is not proven. What we do not know is the sale. Did it sell in June 1834? Who bought it? Who lived there in July 1835?

entries.card: why:THE CONVERSION IS DATED BY THE MOVE THAT CAUSED IT AND NOT B…
entries.text: THE CONVERSION IS DATED BY THE MOVE THAT CAUSED IT AND NOT BY ITSELF. Andreas, scan p. 183: 'In 1817, Mr. Beaubien purchased this house, which was a low, gloomy building of five rooms, for $1,000... After this purchase he lived in the Dean house for several years, his son Alexander being born there. He used the old cabin after this for a barn.' So the building is older than 1817 as a dwelling and becomes a barn 'after' Beaubien moved out of it into the Dean house in 1817; no month is given and the range opens at the start of that year, exactly as its parent record the record of Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Homestead does. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS BETTER ATTESTED THAN FOR MOST OUTBUILDINGS IN THIS DATASET, and the evidence is on the far side of the scene: Andreas, scan p. 339, describing the 1839 public sale of the Fort Dearborn reservation lots, has James H. Collins bidding '$1,049 for the next five lots, 10, 9, 8, 7, and 6, where Beaubien's house, OUT-BUILDINGS, and garden were'. That is a documented statement that Beaubien still had out-buildings standing on his homestead ground four years after 1835-07-01. It does not say the barn was one of them, and it is not used to extend this range; the range closes at the end of the scene year, as a housekeeping bound and not a demolition date, on the same reasoning the homestead record gives. THE 19-YEAR SPAN WILL RAISE THIS PROJECT'S WIDE-RANGE WARNING and is left standing rather than trimmed to silence it: the building is genuinely old, the warning is correct that nothing documents its middle years, and the parent record carries the identical span for the identical reason.

levels.8-10: We date the change to a barn by the move that caused it. A history book says Beaubien bought this house in 1817 for $1,000. It was a low, dark house of five rooms. After that he lived in the Dean house for some years, and his son Alexander was born there. He used the old cabin as a barn. So the cabin was a house before 1817. It became a barn after Beaubien moved out that year. No month is given, so we start at the start of 1817, as the main house does. We have better proof that it still stood than for most sheds. The proof comes from after our scene. At the 1839 land sale, James H. Collins paid $1,049 for lots 6 to 10, where Beaubien's house, barns and garden were. That shows Beaubien still had barns there four years after July 1835. It does not say this barn was one of them. So we do not use it to stretch the dates. We end it at the end of 1835, just for keeping records.

entries.card: why:THE COORDINATE IS A POINT CHOSEN INSIDE AN ATTESTED BAND, WH…
entries.text: THE COORDINATE IS A POINT CHOSEN INSIDE AN ATTESTED BAND, WHICH IS NOT A DERIVATION, so it is tagged conjectural and cites no sources — the rule this project applied to the Walker meeting house. THE BAND IS REAL AND IT IS WIDE. The Tribune: the dancers 'assembled at the "Council House" on the north side of the river, east of the present State street and west of the "Lake House," a hotel which was at the northeast corner of Rush and Water streets'. State Street is local E +827 in this project's frame; Rush Street, from the modern OpenStreetMap intersection used as ground control for the 1834 sheets, is local E +1045. So the source bounds the building inside a 215 m stretch of the north bank and says nothing else about where in it. This record places it near the middle of that stretch, on the bank a little north of the drawn 1834 waterline, and the along-bank position is good to no better than ±110 m — five times the georeference's own uncertainty and the largest positional error in this dataset. The sidecar's flat uncertainty (m) of 20 badly understates it; that is admitted in the liberties register. Facade bearing 180, due south to the river, is the bank's orientation and nothing more; no source says which way the building faced. There is no modelled terrain under it — it stands about 620 m east of the terrain box.

levels.8-10: We picked a spot inside a known stretch. That is not the same as working it out, so we call it a guess with no source. We did the same for the Walker meeting house. The stretch is real, and it is wide. The Tribune says the dancers met at the Council House on the north side of the river. It was east of State Street and west of the Lake House hotel, at Rush and Water Streets. In our map those two streets are about 700 feet apart. So the paper puts the building somewhere in that stretch of the north bank, and says no more. We put it near the middle, on the bank, a little north of the 1834 water line. It could be off by about 360 feet along the bank. That is the biggest guess about where anything stands in our town. Our record says it could be off by 66 feet, and that is far too small. We say so in our list of guesses. We faced it south, toward the river, only because that is the way the bank runs. No paper says which way it faced.

entries.card: why:THE COUNT IS KINZIE'S AND THE POINT IS OURS. Kinzie, of 1831…
entries.text:
THE COUNT IS KINZIE'S AND THE POINT IS OURS. Kinzie, of 1831: 'The bank of the river which stretches to the west... was then occupied by the root-houses of the garrison.' ROOT-HOUSES, PLURAL, IS THE ONLY THING ANY SOURCE SAYS ABOUT HOW MANY, and until this record it was the one clause in her sentence the model did not carry: one mound stood for a plural, and Fort Dearborn — root house's own position note said so in as many words. Two is the smallest number that reads her sentence rather than half of it, and it is the number built. NOTHING SUPPORTS A THIRD and none is raised: the plural states a floor and no source, plan or return gives a count, a spacing or a size, so a row of five would be an invention this one is not.

THE POSITION IS A SECOND POINT ON THE SAME BANK TOP, 9.0 m due west of the first, on the stretch Kinzie names and outside the pickets. It is chosen and not derived, exactly as the first one is. WHAT WAS CHECKED, because the first mound had to be moved once for getting this wrong: the committed 1834-harbour-cut heightfield was sampled over this footprint and the ground runs 3.59-3.61 m across it, a fall of 0.02 m, against the 0.85 m fall that displaced the first point in August 2026. The bank's face begins about 6 m further west again (3.42 m at E +1100, 3.21 m at E +1096), so this is the last full footprint the bank top carries before it drops, and a third mound west of it would straddle the fall. EAST is where the fort is: the palisade's west face stands about 13 m east of the first mound, so the pair occupies the whole of the open bank top between the stockade and the drop, which is what 'occupied by the root-houses' describes.

Local E +1108.7, N +235.4. Carry the same uncertainty the first mound carries: the bank is evidence and the point on it is not.

levels.8-10: The number comes from Kinzie, and the spot is ours. Writing of 1831, she says the river bank to the west held the fort's root houses. Root houses, more than one, is all any paper says about how many there were. Until now we built only one mound, so we used only half of her line. Two is the smallest number that fits her words, and two is what we build. Nothing supports a third, so we do not build one. Her words only say more than one. No paper or map gives a count, a space between them or a size. A row of five would be made up. We placed the second mound on the same bank top, about 30 feet west of the first, on the stretch she names and outside the fort's fence. We picked the spot; we did not work it out. We checked the ground, because the first mound had to be moved once for getting this wrong. The ground here is flat, with a drop of less than an inch. The bank starts to fall about 20 feet further west. So this is the last full spot on the bank top. A third mound west of it would sit on the slope. The fort is to the east.

entries.card: why:THE COUNTRY CAME TO THE SALE BY ROAD. A buyer from the settl…
entries.text: THE COUNTRY CAME TO THE SALE BY ROAD. A buyer from the settlements west of the town drove in, and the owner has asked that wagons not be rationed (the project's rules, 2026-08-18); the number is invented. “Two camps on conjectural ground: the land-sale crowd on the reservation shore and a wagon party at the west approach”.

levels.8-10: People from the country came to the sale by road. A buyer from the farms west of town drove in. The owner of this project asked that we not hold back on wagons. The number of wagons is made up. We list two camps as guesses: the land sale crowd on the shore, and a wagon party at the west road into town.

entries.card: why:THE CROSSING IS ATTESTED AND THE QUARTER IS NOT. The notice…
entries.text: THE CROSSING IS ATTESTED AND THE QUARTER IS NOT. The notice gives 'the corner of Lasalle and Lake streets' and no side, exactly as Andreas gives no side for The Old Bank Building at the same crossing, so the corner is a one-in-four choice and the whole position is graded at that choice rather than at the crossing. THE QUARTER WAS CHOSEN ON GROUND, NOT ON EVIDENCE, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS RECONSTRUCTED. Each of the four quarters is the corner lot of a committed platted block: south-east is block 34 lot 0, which already carries The Old Bank Building and a two-room frame cottage; south-west is block 33 lot 6, carrying a dwelling and two anonymous roofs; north-west is block 19 lot 7, carrying a one-room frame cottage. The north-east quarter — block 18 lot 1, plat lot 5 of that block — is the only one of the four carrying no committed roof at all, and it is the single free lot the 665-roof programme records for its block. Standing the house there displaces nothing and re-deals no parcel; standing it on any other quarter would have moved a record that is already placed, on no better evidence than this one has. THAT IS A PRODUCTION REASON AND NOT A READING, so it buys no confidence: if a source ever names the side, this record moves and the move costs nothing. THE COORDINATE IS COMPUTED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT, NOT TYPED. Lot 1 of block 18 is bounded on the south by the Lake Street frontage line from local ENU (464.05, -101.26) to (488.81, -101.46) and on the west by the LaSalle frontage line running north from that same south-west corner. The house's own south-west corner is set 1.50 m inward from each — lot margin m, the margin the plat occupancy tool keeps off every lot line and the same setback The Old Bank Building carries across the street — and the facade bearing 0.463 deg clockwise from grid north is the Lake frontage line's own bearing, so the front wall stands parallel to the street rather than to the UTM grid. Measured on the placed polygon: 1.500 m clear of the Lake line, 1.503 m clear of the LaSalle line, and the front range runs 9.144 m east along a 24.76 m frontage, leaving the rest of the lot open. WORKING UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the plat's own georeference, plus about 40 m for the choice of quarter — the four candidates are that far apart.

levels.8-10: We know the crossing, but not which corner. The notice says the corner of LaSalle and Lake Streets, but not which side. So the corner is one of four, and we judge the whole spot at that guess. We chose the corner by what was free, not by proof. That is why we call it a guess. Three of the four corners already have buildings on them. The north east corner is the only one with nothing on it. It is the one free lot in that block. Putting the house there moves nothing else. Putting it on any other corner would have moved a building already placed, on proof no better than this. That is a reason about building the model, not about the past. So it does not make us more sure. If a paper ever names the side, this house moves, and that is easy. Its spot comes from the town map, not typed in by hand.

entries.card: why:THE DATE IS THE RISK IN THIS RECORD AND IT IS NOT RESOLVED.…
entries.text: THE DATE IS THE RISK IN THIS RECORD AND IT IS NOT RESOLVED. Two sources put the house in 1835 and neither gives a month: Andreas, 'The Steamboat Hotel, on North Water Street, near Kinzie, was kept in 1835 by John Davis, and from 1836 to 1839 by William McCorrister, as the American Hotel'; DRLOIH, 'The Steamboat Hotel... opened in 1835 on North Water Street, near Kinzie Street, and was operated by John Davis.' The range therefore opens on 1 January 1835 because that is the earliest day the attested year permits, NOT because anything says the house was open then. THE SCENE DATE IS SIX MONTHS INTO THAT WINDOW AND THE BUILDING COULD BE ON EITHER SIDE OF IT. What narrows it, a little: John Davis advertised the Steamboat Hotel in the Chicago American, whose first issue Andreas dates 8 June 1835 — so the house was trading under Davis inside the paper's 1835 run, which begins three weeks before the scene date; and DRLOIH has J. Dorsey and J. Force announcing on 9 November 1835 that they had taken over the management, which closes Davis's tenure at that end. Both anchors sit after 1 July and neither reaches back before it. THIS PROJECT EXCLUDES THE TOWN'S FIRST FIRE ENGINE ON EXACTLY THIS GROUND — right year, wrong month — and the difference here is that no source dates the opening at all, so the balance of evidence is that a house 'kept in 1835 by John Davis' and advertising in a paper that began in June was more likely than not in business by 1 July. Tagged inferred, argued rather than assumed, and if a dated advertisement or a licence puts the opening after 1 July this record leaves the scene for the exclusions record. NOTE ALSO that neither source says the BUILDING was new in 1835: 'opened in 1835' is a statement about a business. The fabric may be older, in which case the risk above disappears and only the record's silence about it remains.

levels.8-10: The date is the weak spot here, and we have not settled it. Two sources put the hotel in 1835, and neither gives a month. A history book says John Davis ran the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street, near Kinzie, in 1835. From 1836 to 1839 William McCorrister ran it as the American Hotel. Another source says it opened in 1835 and Davis ran it. So we start it on January 1, 1835. That is the earliest day that year allows. Nothing says it was open then. Our scene is six months into that year, and the hotel could have opened before or after it. A little helps. Davis put an ad for the hotel in the Chicago American. That paper's first issue was June 8, 1835, three weeks before our scene. In November 1835, two new men said they had taken over the hotel. That ends Davis's time. Both of these dates come after July 1. We left the town's first fire engine out for this reason: right year, wrong month. Here, no paper dates the opening at all. A hotel run by Davis in 1835, with ads in a paper that began in June, was more likely than not open by July 1. So we call it a guess, and we argue for it.

entries.card: why:THE DECK OUTLINE, AND BOTH OF ITS DIMENSIONS COME FROM SOMET…
entries.text: THE DECK OUTLINE, AND BOTH OF ITS DIMENSIONS COME FROM SOMETHING. The width, 3.048 m, is the ten feet the 1883 old-settlers statement and Cleaver's 1893 recollection both give for both branch bridges, recorded in its original unit. The length, 55.96 m, is MEASURED rather than chosen: it is the distance between the two traced 1834 waterlines along the crossing line described in the position note, read off the river data at the midpoint station (west bank local E +6.86, east bank local E +62.82), which is the same Wright 1834 segmentation the ground and the river are built from. THE CROSS-CHECK IS THE INTERESTING PART: the same file's drafted mean width for the South Branch reach is 57.3 m, and the measured crossing comes out 55.96 m — an agreement to 1.3 m, exactly the agreement the North Branch bridge's 71.83 m makes against its own reach's 72.9 m. Two crossings measured the same way, each landing within a metre and a half of its reach's independent mean. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT CANNOT DO IS CHOOSE THE STATION, and that is the honest error bar rather than the georeference. This reach narrows fast: the same method gives 74.38 m at the Lake Street line and 46.79 m at Randolph, so a crossing anywhere in the band the sources allow is between about 47 and 74 m and the recorded 55.96 m is the middle of the band and not the middle of that range. AND AS ON THE NORTH BRANCH, THE SPAN OVERSTATES THE CLEAR SPAN BY AN UNRECORDED AMOUNT: the 1883 statement puts the abutments 'in the shallow water near the banks', inside the drawn line, and nobody said how far inside. Landing the deck on the traced waterline is chosen because that line is the evidence — the terrain surface crosses Z=0 along it by construction — and an inset would be a second invention on top of the first.

levels.8-10: Both sizes of this bridge floor come from something. The width is ten feet. An 1883 account of the old settlers and a man's memories from 1893 both give that width for both river branch bridges. The length is about 184 feet. We measured it, and did not just pick it. It is the distance between the two banks on the 1834 map, along the line where the bridge crosses. That is the same map our ground and river are built from. Here is a good check. The same map gives this part of the river a width of about 188 feet on average. Our crossing comes out within about four feet of that. The North Branch bridge matches its own stretch of river just as closely. But the measuring cannot choose where along the river the bridge crossed. That is the real doubt. The river narrows fast here. At Lake Street it is about 244 feet wide, and at Randolph about 154 feet. So the bridge could be anywhere from about 154 to 244 feet long. Like the North Branch bridge, our length is also a bit too long. The 1883 account says the ends sat in the shallow water near the banks.

entries.card: why:THE DECK OUTLINE, AND THE ONLY FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THA…
entries.text: THE DECK OUTLINE, AND THE ONLY FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS NOT A PLACEHOLDER — both of its dimensions come from something. The width, 3.048 m, is Cleaver's 'These bridges were ten feet wide', recorded here in its original unit. The length, 71.83 m, is MEASURED rather than chosen: it is the distance between the two traced 1834 waterlines along the Kinzie alignment, read off the river data at the crossing station (west bank local E -117.52, east bank local E -45.69), which is the same Wright 1834 segmentation the ground and the river are built from. It agrees with the reach's drafted mean width of 72.9 m to about a metre. THE SPAN IS THEREFORE AN OVERSTATEMENT OF THE CLEAR SPAN, deliberately and by an unrecorded amount: Cleaver puts the abutments 'in the shallow water near the banks', which is inside the drawn line, and nobody recorded how far inside. Landing the deck exactly on the traced waterline was chosen because that line is the one thing here that is evidence — the terrain surface crosses Z=0 along it by construction — and an inset would have added a second invention on top of the first. Carried uncertainty: the georeference's plus or minus 20 m, which is larger than the difference being argued about.

levels.8-10: This is the bridge floor, and the only floor plan in our town that is not a stand-in. Both its sizes come from something. The width is ten feet, from Cleaver's words: these bridges were ten feet wide. The length is about 236 feet. We measured it, and did not just pick it. It is the distance between the two banks on the 1834 map, along Kinzie Street. That is the same map our ground and river are built from. It matches the river's average width there to about three feet. So the bridge is a little longer than the open span really was, on purpose. Cleaver says the ends sat in the shallow water near the banks, inside the drawn line. Nobody wrote down how far inside. We put the ends right on the drawn banks, because that line is the one real piece of proof here. Moving them in would add a second guess on top of the first. The map itself could be off by about 66 feet, which is more than this small gap.

entries.card: why:THE DECK, AND NOT ONE OF ITS NUMBERS IS A RECORD'S. Its u ex…
entries.text: THE DECK, AND NOT ONE OF ITS NUMBERS IS A RECORD'S. Its u extent is the span, 12 m, and its v extent the width, 4.27 m. THE SPAN IS SIZED OFF THE STREAM, exactly as the Slough Log Bridge's 8 m is: on the committed heightfield the water along the deck's own centre line runs 5.55 m, 0.17 m deep, and 6.3 m under its south edge and 5.2 m under its north, 0.38 m deep at each — leaving 3.10 m and 3.35 m of dry seat at the two abutments. Twelve metres over five and a half of water is the same proportion its sibling holds — 8 m over 3.30, seat 2.35 — applied to a wider drain. THE WIDTH IS THE ONE FIGURE THAT EXCEEDS ITS SIBLING AND IT IS THE OWNER'S ASK, said plainly: Cleaver's ten feet (3.05 m) is documented for the BRANCH bridges and this project treats a street culvert as no wider, so the sibling takes 3.0 m. The owner asked for plank crossings 'for both the road and the sidewalk', and 4.27 m — fourteen feet — is the narrowest deck that carries a wagon way of eight feet with a six-foot plank footway beside it, which is the walk width this project lays everywhere else. The extra 1.22 m is the footway and nothing else. Recorded in the liberties register.

levels.8-10: This is the bridge floor, and none of its numbers come from a record. It is about 39 feet long and 14 feet wide. We sized the length to the stream, just as we did for the Slough Log Bridge. On our ground, the water under the middle of the bridge is about 18 feet wide and a few inches deep. That leaves about ten feet of dry ground for each end to sit on. The width is the one size bigger than its sister bridge. That was the owner of this project's ask, and we say so. Cleaver's ten feet is shown for the river branch bridges. We treat a street drain bridge as no wider, so its sister is about ten feet wide. But the owner asked for plank crossings for both the road and the sidewalk. Fourteen feet is the least that fits an eight foot road for wagons, with a six foot plank walk beside it. That is the walk width we use everywhere else. The extra four feet is the walk, and nothing else. We list it as a guess.

entries.card: why:THE DISTINCTION THIS RECORD EXISTS TO MAKE. What is document…
entries.text: THE DISTINCTION THIS RECORD EXISTS TO MAKE. What is documented is a use that had ENDED by the scene date: Eliza Chappel's infant school occupied this house in 1833-34 and moved into the First Presbyterian Church during 1834 - reported in this project's dossier from PBS and Encyclopedia of Chicago summaries which have no source record in the sources data, so it is stated here as reported rather than cited. On 1835-07-01 the building is inferred to stand and nothing says what was happening inside it. A dwelling is the likeliest use in a town where housing was scarce and rents were high, but that is a guess and the value says so instead of making it. THE SCHOOL IS NOT SHOWN TWICE: the schooling that moved into the church is carried on the First Presbyterian Church record's function note, not here.

levels.8-10: This card is here to make one point clear. What we know of is a use that had ended by our scene. Eliza Chappel ran a school for small children in this house in 1833 and 1834. In 1834 it moved into the First Presbyterian Church. Our notes got this from short summaries that are not in our list of sources. So we say it was reported, and do not cite it. On July 1, 1835, we think the building still stood. Nothing says what went on inside. A home is the most likely use, since houses were scarce and rents were high. But that is a guess, and we say so instead of picking one. The school is not shown twice. The school that moved into the church is told on the church's card, not here.

entries.card: why:THE DRAW BEARS ON THE CRIBS. The retrospective Andreas 1884…
entries.text: THE DRAW BEARS ON THE CRIBS. The retrospective Andreas 1884 p. 631 plate shows a crib beneath each frame/draw-end assembly. Align the nearest existing surviving approach support on each side with the existing text-derived draw end. The current stations move inward 2.081 m, from 26.94/49.39 m to 29.021/47.309 m along the unchanged 76.33 m local span; these numbers are model arithmetic, not dimensions measured from the engraving or a geographic placement. The 12 surviving support stations remain reconstructed. The two selected frame-bearing crib platforms and the general approach bents are separately declared reconstructions. The approaches retain their previous height; the separately declared closed-draw profile raises only the centre. This finite correction does not settle the central rise, gallows proportions/mechanism, approach trestle or provisional camera, and original other work remains open/differs. CURRENT PLATFORM CORRECTION: the two selected bearing foundations are open vertical-pile/boarded-cap reconstructions, replacing the rejected solid-crib visual trial. CURRENT PROFILE — other work: the closed draw is now level (form.draw profile); the bearing positions are unchanged.

levels.8-10: The bridge's middle part rests on wood boxes in the water. A picture made long after, in an 1884 history book, shows a box under each end of the lifting part. We line up the nearest support on each side with the end of the lifting part. That moves them in by about seven feet. The whole bridge stays the same length. These numbers are our own sums, not sizes measured from the picture or from a map. The other supports are still our guesses. The two boxes the lifting part rests on are guesses too, and so are the rest of the supports. The ends keep their height. Only the middle is raised. This fix does not settle the hump in the middle, the frame that lifts the bridge, or how it worked. Now the two boxes are built as open posts with boards on top. That took the place of a solid box we tried and did not like. Later work made the middle part lie level when it is closed. The supports did not move.

entries.card: why:THE END OF THIS CROSSING'S LIFE IS BETTER ATTESTED THAN ITS…
entries.text: THE END OF THIS CROSSING'S LIFE IS BETTER ATTESTED THAN ITS BEGINNING, WHICH IS UNUSUAL AND WORTH SAYING. The source, transcribed at the research notes on terrain hydrology section 2.2, describes the slough draining the Public Square pond and the Wells Street marsh, passing over the site of the Tremont House and entering the river at the end of State Street, and adds that WHERE WATER STREET CROSSED IT A LOG BRIDGE WAS NEEDED UNTIL AFTER 1840. So the crossing stood well past the scene date and the only question is when it went in. Nothing dates that. The range opens at the start of 1833 because that is the year South Water Street was ordered pitched and graded from the United States Reservation to Randolph Street (the research notes on structures south, from the town trustees' order of August 1833) — a street being made passable across a stream is a street acquiring a bridge — and because 1833 is when the town began building crossings at all: the North Branch log bridge is winter 1831-32 and the South Branch raft bridge winter 1832-33. THAT IS REASONING, NOT A DATE. The bridge may be older and may be younger by a year; it was certainly standing on 1835-07-01, which is the only claim the scene needs. The range closes at the end of 1835 as this project's convention, NOT because the crossing went then — the source explicitly runs it past 1840.

levels.8-10: We know more about the end of this crossing than its start. That does not happen often, so we say so. Our notes copy an old account of the stream. It drained the pond in the Public Square and the Wells Street marsh. It ran past where the Tremont House stood and met the river at the end of State Street. Where Water Street crossed it, a log bridge was needed until after 1840. So the crossing stood long after our scene. The only question is when it was built. Nothing dates that. We start it at the start of 1833. That year the town ordered South Water Street made level, from the fort's land to Randolph Street. A street made fit to use across a stream gets a bridge. And 1833 is when the town began to build crossings at all. The North Branch log bridge was built in the winter of 1831. The South Branch raft bridge came the next winter. That is our thinking, not a date. The bridge may be a year older or younger. It surely stood on July 1, 1835, and that is all our scene needs. We end it at the end of 1835 only as our habit. The account says it lasted past 1840.

entries.card: why:THE END OF THIS RANGE IS THE WEAKEST CLAIM IN THIS RECORD AN…
entries.text: THE END OF THIS RANGE IS THE WEAKEST CLAIM IN THIS RECORD AND IT IS WEAKER THAN HOGAN'S, WHICH IS SAYING SOMETHING. What is attested: Philo Carpenter reached Chicago on 18 July 1832 and opened the town's first drug store in a log building 16 x 20 ft on Lake Street near the river. The range opens on the day he arrived because no source gives the shop a build date and he cannot have opened it earlier. THE PROBLEM IS WHAT HE DID NEXT. In the summer of 1833 Carpenter bought a lot on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells and 'erected a small store' — Philo Carpenter's South Water Street Store in this dataset — and no source reached says what became of the log shop when he moved his trade into it. So this building is placed in a scene set two years after its proprietor built himself a better one, on nothing but the ordinary continuity argument that a standing building stands until something says otherwise. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS SPECIFIC AND STRONG. Lake Street beside the Sauganash was the most valuable frontage at the forks; a 16 x 20 ft log shop is the smallest building in this dataset; and its one attested occupant demonstrably left it. A CONTEMPORARY DOCUMENT NARROWS NOTHING HERE. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries Carpenter's own advertisement, dated 22 November 1833, offering drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs and also dry groceries, glass and nails — proof that he was trading at Chicago sixteen months after arriving and nineteen months before the scene date, but it gives no address, so it cannot say WHICH of his two buildings he was trading from, and it must not be read as evidence that the log shop survived. GRADE: this record's existence at the scene date is the single most likely thing in this parcel to be wrong. If evidence turns up that the log shop came down or was moved before July 1835 it belongs in the exclusions record and this record leaves the scene.

levels.8-10: The end date is the weakest claim on this card. It is weaker than the one for Hogan's store, and that is saying something. Here is what we know. Philo Carpenter came to Chicago on July 18, 1832. He opened the town's first drug store in a log building on Lake Street near the river. It was 16 by 20 feet. We start it on the day he came, since no paper says when it was built and he could not have opened it sooner. The trouble is what he did next. In the summer of 1833, Carpenter bought a lot on South Water Street and built a small store. That store has its own card. No paper says what became of the log shop when he moved. So we put it in a scene two years after its owner built a better one. All we have is that a building stands until something says it is gone. The case against it is strong. Lake Street by the Sauganash was the best land in that part of town. This log shop is the smallest building in our town. And its one known user left it. A paper from the time does not help. The Chicago Democrat of November 1833 has Carpenter's own ad. He sold drugs, oils, paints and dyes, and also food, glass and nails. That shows he was in business in Chicago. It does not say where.

entries.card: why:THE FAMILY IS NAMED, AND THE BUILDING STANDS IN THE WRONG PL…
entries.text: THE FAMILY IS NAMED, AND THE BUILDING STANDS IN THE WRONG PLACE, so the seat is refused on purpose. Andreas puts Jonas Clybourne 'several miles up the North Branch, where now are the North Chicago rolling-mills', and has him and his son Archibald as the early butchers who furnished the garrison. This record says of itself that it stands at the northern edge of the modelled ground, beside the family's slaughter-house, and not at that attested reach, which lies far outside the terrain. the Clybourne household is NOT LINKED to it for that reason: pointing a household at a building the dataset says is displaced would turn a known error into a residence claim. Archibald also had a larger house of his own from 1829, and who was living in the cabins eleven years after they went up is not recorded. So the roof states its use, a farmstead at the head of a butchering business, and the refusal, and seats nobody.

levels.8-10: We know the family, but the building stands in the wrong place. So on purpose, we do not put them in it. A history book says Jonas Clybourne lived several miles up the North Branch, where the steel mills later stood. He and his son Archibald were early butchers. They sold meat to the fort. This card says the building stands at the north edge of our map, next to the family's slaughter house. That is not the real spot, which is far off our map. So we do not link the Clybourne family to it. We know this spot is wrong. If we put a family in it, we would turn that error into a claim about their home. Archibald also had a bigger house of his own from 1829. No one knows who lived in the cabins eleven years after they were built. So the roof says what it was. It was a farm, the home base of a butcher's business. And it says no one lives there.

entries.card: why:THE FIRM IS DOCUMENTED AND THE PARTNER WAS MIS-ATTRIBUTED; o…
entries.text: THE FIRM IS DOCUMENTED AND THE PARTNER WAS MIS-ATTRIBUTED; other work IS THE RULING (2026-09-12). This field read 'Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole' at `attested` on Andreas's packing-house chapter (scan p. 1151). Andreas is wrong on the Newberry, and the firm's own paid advertisement is what says so. IN EVERY SETTING OF THE NEWBERRY & DOLE CARD THAT NAMES OLIVER NEWBERRY HE STANDS IN ITS REFERENCE LIST, UNDER DETROIT — 'Oliver Newberry, [Det]roit' (Chicago Democrat, 1 April 1834, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-04-01) and 'OLIVER NKWBERRY, Detroit.' (1 July 1835, the Chicago Democrat of 1835-07-01) — one correspondent per port, beside Coenties Slip in New York, Barker & Holt of Buffalo, Calvin Britain at the mouth of the St Joseph and James B. Campbell at Ottawa. Both claims' own entity blocks give his role as a reference named in the advertisement, and neither gives him a trade. A house does not print its own resident partner as the man to write to in another city. THE SETTING OF 5 AUGUST 1835 (the Chicago Democrat of 1835-08-05) HOLDS BOTH MEN AT ONCE, which is what makes this a decision and not a preference: its partner entity reads 'NEWRERRY' at the trade of forwarding and commission merchant, while 'Oliver Newb[err]y, Detro[it]' still stands in the same card's reference list. THE TWO LIMBS ARE GRADED SEPARATELY, and the weaker one sets the confidence of the whole attribute. That Oliver Newberry was NOT the Chicago partner rests on the firm's own contemporary card against a compiler writing in 1884. WHICH Newberry he was is INFERRED: Fergus's directory of 1839 prints 'Newberry, Walter L., att'y and real est., office Newberry & Dole' — the firm's office as his office; the Chicago American of 8 June 1835 prints 'W. L. NEWBERRY' over the great sale of town lots and sets 'NEWBERRY & DOLE' over the same date in the adjacent column of the same issue; and no other Newberry forename is printed for Chicago anywhere in this corpus. The firm style is unbroken from 26 November 1833 to 5 August 1835 and no printing records a change of partner, so the ruling reaches across this record's whole range rather than only the scene date. THE ONE RIVAL LEFT UNRESOLVED IS NOT A PRINTING: the land register's WALTER S / W S, read at the land sales data § The two Newberrys the register writes. The ruling itself is declared at the identity data § proprietor distinctions, which is where the corpus put the question. The value records who had it erected and worked it, not who was on the premises on any given day. `aka` KEEPS ANDREAS'S OWN PHRASE, 'Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole's slaughter-house', because it is what the literature calls this building and a reader arriving with that phrase must still find the record; it is kept as the received name it is and not as an attribution this dataset makes.

levels.8-10: We knew the firm, but we had the wrong partner. Later work set this right in September 2026. This card used to name Oliver Newberry and George W. Dole as the partners, from a history book. The book is wrong about Newberry. The firm's own paid ad shows it. Every time the ad names Oliver Newberry, he is in its list of people to write to, under Detroit. That is true in April 1834 and in July 1835. The list has one person for each port, such as New York, Buffalo, St. Joseph and Ottawa. A firm does not print its own partner here as the man to write to in another city. The ad of August 5, 1835 has both men at once. It names a Newberry as a partner in the trade. And it still lists Oliver Newberry of Detroit as a man to write to. So we had to decide. We judge the two parts on their own, and the weaker part sets how sure we are. That Oliver Newberry was not the Chicago partner rests on the firm's own ad from the time.

entries.card: why:THE FIRM THAT OPENED THIS SHOP WAS DISSOLVED FOUR AND A HALF…
entries.text:
THE FIRM THAT OPENED THIS SHOP WAS DISSOLVED FOUR AND A HALF MONTHS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, AND THE PAPER THAT PRINTS THE DISSOLUTION PRINTS WHO CARRIED ON. The Chicago American runs the notice in its first two issues — the Chicago American of 1835-06-08 and the Chicago American of 1835-06-13, the second legible where the first is not: 'NOTICE. [Th]e co-partnership heretofore [existing under] the firm of Go[ss] & Cob[b] [is] this day [dis]solved by m[ut]ual consent. OL[IVE]R GOS[S]. S. B. [C]O[BB]. Chicago, Feb. 18, 183[5].' Beside it, in the same issue, Cobb's own card: 'S[. ]B[. ]COB[B] [w]il[l] [c]o[nt]in[ue] the [above business] at his shop' (the Chicago American of 1835-06-13). A dissolution dated 18 February and still running in June is ordinary; what is not ordinary is having both halves of it — the end of the partnership and the survivor's continuation — set on the same page.

SO ON 1 JULY 1835 THIS IS COBB'S SHOP AND NOT THE FIRM'S, and the record says so on the attribute rather than in a footnote. The firm name is kept in `aka` and in the range's own note, because it is what opened the building and what the Democrat's 1833 advertisement attests; deleting it would lose the better-attested of the two facts to record the later one.

WHAT IS STILL NOT SETTLED. The initials are completed to 'S. B. Cobb' by the firm name and by his own signed card, and the corpus mints him as a person on that card and not on the dissolution notice. Whether he is the Silas B. Cobb whom DRLOIH names as the carpenter who built the Green Tree Tavern on the opposite corner of this same crossing in 1833 is STILL NOT ESTABLISHED HERE — no source reached connects the saddler to the carpenter in terms, and the American does not either. Oliver Goss's forename, which this record could not read before, is printed in the 1835-06-13 setting of the notice.

levels.8-10: The firm that opened this shop broke up four and a half months before our scene. The paper that printed the break also printed who kept the shop going. The Chicago American ran the notice in its first two issues, in June 1835. It says the firm of Goss and Cobb has ended, by choice of both men, Oliver Goss and S. B. Cobb, on February 18, 1835. Beside it is Cobb's own notice. He says he will keep on the same work at his shop. A notice dated in February and still running in June is common. What is rare is having both halves on the same page: the end of the firm and the man who kept on. So on July 1, 1835, this is Cobb's shop, not the firm's. We say so on the card itself. We keep the firm's name too, because it opened the building, and an 1833 ad shows it. Dropping it would lose the better known of the two facts. Some things are still not settled. We fill out his name as S. B. Cobb from the firm's name and his own signed notice. We do not yet know if he is the same as Silas B. Cobb.

entries.card: why:THE FIRST BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS NOT A P…
entries.text: THE FIRST BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS NOT A PLACEHOLDER. Andreas gives the size twice, in two independently written passages: 'The building was twenty by forty-five feet in size, was partitioned off so as to serve as a post-office on one side, and as the store of Brewster, Hogan & Co., on the other', and, in the postmaster chronology, 'the store only occupied an area of forty-five by twenty feet'. 45 x 20 ft is 13.716 x 6.096 m, recorded here converted with the original figures stated, per the datum json's data units rule. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THE SIZE AND NOT THE PLAN: 'twenty by forty-five feet' is a rectangle in any reading, and this polygon is that rectangle, but nothing attests a door, a partition line on the ground, or that the building was exactly rectangular rather than a rectangle with something small attached. WHICH AXIS RUNS ALONG THE STREET IS NOT IN THE SOURCE either; it is decided by the facade bearing and argued in the position note, where it belongs, because rotating the building is what changes it. The 20 ft depth is worth reading twice: this is a 6 m deep building 13.7 m long, partitioned into a post office and a store, which is why Andreas offers it as evidence of 'the limited accommodations that were ample for the post-office of those days'.

levels.8-10: This is the first floor plan in our town that is not a stand-in. A history book gives the size twice, in two different places. It says the building was 20 by 45 feet. It was split inside, with the post office on one side and the store of Brewster, Hogan and Company on the other. Later the book says again that the store took up only 45 by 20 feet. What we know is the size, not the plan. Twenty by 45 feet is a long box in any reading, and our shape is that box. But nothing tells us where the door or the inside wall was. Nothing says it was a plain box, with nothing small built on. The book also does not say which side ran along the street. That is set by which way the front faces, and we explain it with the building's place. The depth is worth a second look. This building was only 20 feet deep and 45 feet long, and it held a post office and a store. That is why the book uses it to show how small a post office was enough in those days.

entries.card: why:THE FIRST MOUND'S INVENTED FIGURE, REPEATED RATHER THAN RE-I…
entries.text: THE FIRST MOUND'S INVENTED FIGURE, REPEATED RATHER THAN RE-INVENTED. No source gives either cellar a size. 5.0 x 3.6 m is the figure Fort Dearborn — root house chose for a cellar big enough to hold a garrison's roots through a winter, and this record takes it unchanged on purpose: a second, different number would be a second invention and would imply a distinction between the two that nothing states.

levels.8-10: We use the first mound's made up size again, and do not make up a new one. No paper gives either cellar a size. The first root house uses about 16 by 12 feet. We chose that as big enough to hold the fort's roots through a winter. This one takes the same size on purpose. A second, different number would be a second guess. It would also hint that the two were not alike, and nothing says that.

entries.card: why:THE FORENAME IS A GUESS AT AN INITIAL AND THE RECORD SAYS SO…
entries.text: THE FORENAME IS A GUESS AT AN INITIAL AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The advertisement gives 'Goss' with no initial. Andreas's table of first purchasers of canal lots carries an 'O. Goss, Washington Co. Vermont' buying on 3 September 1832, which is the only Goss in the volume near this date and place, and this record adopts that initial while grading the person derived because the identification is a reading and not a statement. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later.

levels.8-10: The first name is a guess from one letter, and we say so. The ad gives only the name Goss, with no first letter. A history book lists the first buyers of canal lots. It has an O. Goss of Washington County, Vermont, who bought land on September 3, 1832. He is the only Goss in the book near this time and place. So we use that letter, but we mark him as worked out, since it is our reading and not a plain fact. The Chicago Democrat of November 26, 1833 is the only Chicago paper from the time that we have. A man who paid for an ad wanted to be found. So the ad is strong proof that he was here, at that address, in November 1833. It is weak proof that he was still here on July 1, 1835. That was nineteen months later, after about 2,400 more people had come.

entries.card: why:THE FRAMES ARE AN A, NOT TWO BARE POSTS. Built from 2026-08-…
entries.text: THE FRAMES ARE AN A, NOT TWO BARE POSTS. Built from 2026-08-11 to 2026-08-21 as a plain portal — two uprights under a lapped head — because no text describes the bracing and the generator refused to invent it. Both engravings in the 2026-08-18 owner brief (README images 2 and 3) draw raking timber in the frames; the brief's own words are 'twin timber A-frames/gallows posts above the deck'. A pictorial (a modern reconstruction) view may drive form as `inferred`, and the thing being inferred here is weak enough to carry it: that a frame tall enough to hold a sixty-foot draw suspended for forty-eight hours was braced is nearly carpentry rather than evidence, and the plate is what says it was braced VISIBLY, above the deck, where it reads. WHAT IS BUILT AND WHAT IS INVENTED IN IT: two knee braces per frame rising from the posts to the underside of the head, and one shore per post raking down the span away from the opening to the bearing line. The members' sections, angles, count and footing are the archetype's own — a plate shows a braced frame and not a schedule of scantlings — and are recorded in the liberties register “The Dearborn drawbridge, built to its engravings: the frames' bracing, the hoist chains, a two-leaf draw and a railed deck”. The frames' HEIGHT is untouched and remains the most visible unknown on this record; see form.gallows height (m).

levels.8-10: The bridge's frames are shaped like an A, not two bare posts. From August 11 to 21, 2026, we built them as two plain posts with a beam across the top. No book told how they were braced, so our builder would not make it up. Then the owner of this project sent two old pictures. Both show slanting beams in the frames. The owner's own words were twin wood A frames above the floor. A picture made long after may guide the shape, and we mark it as worked out. Here that is a small step. A frame tall enough to hold up a sixty foot bridge for two days must have been braced. That is just how builders work. The picture shows the bracing could be seen above the floor. Here is what we built, and what we made up. Each frame has two short slanting braces from the posts up to the top beam. Each post also has a long prop slanting down, away from the opening. The sizes, angles, count and footings of these beams are our own rules. We list them as guesses. The frames' height did not change. It is still the biggest unknown on this card.

entries.card: why:THE GROUND IS A CONJECTURE AND SO IS THE USE. Open, level, u…
entries.text: THE GROUND IS A CONJECTURE AND SO IS THE USE. Open, level, unplatted, unsold, and the nearest large ground to the landing that carried no lot line in July 1835 — 22.57 ha of United States Reservation and 9.53 ha of sand bar, by the no-build file's own measurement, with no street across either. No committed source says anybody camped there. It is offered because a crowd turned out of the public houses walks to the nearest open ground, and that sentence is an argument about crowds and not a reading of Chicago. Since other work (the owner's report of 2026-10-02) it is also where the transient model deals the tent households beyond the first four: the American says SOME built tents at the landing, and a row of canvas along the town's working wharf frontage for the season is more than that sentence carries. The candidacy stays conjectural; being dealt to does not make it evidence. Built at the reconstructed grade on the owner's ask and labelled so; “Two camps on conjectural ground: the land-sale crowd on the reservation shore and a wagon party at the west approach”.

levels.8-10: This camp is a guess, and so is its spot. This shore was the nearest open ground to the landing that nobody owned in 1835. No paper says anyone camped there. But a crowd with no room at the inns would walk to the nearest open ground. A paper of 1835 says some people put up tents at the landing. It is built as made up, and labelled so.

entries.text: THE GROUND IS A CONJECTURE AND SO IS THE USE. The overland road came in from the west and the wagons that carried immigrant families came with it; the ground beyond the westernmost platted corridor is where a wagon party stops without entering the town. No committed source names a camp here. The candidacy rests on the direction of the traffic and nothing else. Built at the reconstructed grade on the owner's ask and labelled so; “Two camps on conjectural ground: the land-sale crowd on the reservation shore and a wagon party at the west approach”.

levels.8-10: This camp is a guess, and so is its spot. The road came into town from the west, and families came along it in wagons. The American puts tents 'upon the spot they were landed from the boats', and the 1835 camp grounds data resolves that to the bank the landings stand their decks on, taken landward of the deck line. This camp stands on the stretch of that bank where the dry strip is widest: its south edge 1.3 m clear of South Water's DRAWN roadway (the line the scene's road stands on), every corner at least 0.22 m above the water plane on the committed heightfield, and clear of: wharf decks 19.8 m, river walks 84.2 m, beached boats 28.4 m, footprints 27.2 m. On the street's CONTROL line (the project's rules rule 10) the platted street ran to the water and this ground is roadway; a camp of people nobody had a room for is the ordinary reading of a crowd on the riverfront, and it is drawn there. That lap is REFUSED IN WRITING (the corridor intrusion baseline tool): the whole dry strip lies inside the control corridor, so the only escape runs north across the camp's own front and off the bank into the river, and a camp moved anywhere else would no longer stand on the ground the American names. The point recorded is the camp's north-east corner, the footprint's origin at rotation 180. Placed by the place landing camps 1835 tool; “The emigrants' tents at the landing: the ground documented, the tents invented, the count the paper's "some"”.

levels.8-10: The ground is known, and the spot is ours. The Chicago American says people put up tents on the spot where they came off the boats. Our camp list reads that as the river bank where the landings are, on the land side. This camp stands where the dry strip of bank is widest. Its south edge is about four feet from the drawn road of South Water Street. Every corner stands above the water. It is also well clear of the docks, the river walks, the boats pulled up on shore and the buildings. On the town map, the street ran all the way to the water. So this ground was really part of the street. But a camp of people with no room to stay is just what a crowd on the riverside would be, and we draw it there. We say in writing that it sits in the street. The whole dry strip lies in the street. The only way out would be across the camp's own front and off the bank into the river.
