entries.card: why:THE HANDOVER FALLS IN THE SCENE YEAR AND NO SOURCE GIVES A M…
entries.text: THE HANDOVER FALLS IN THE SCENE YEAR AND NO SOURCE GIVES A MONTH, so on 1835-07-01 the keeper is one of two men and this record declines to choose. Andreas, p. 635: Graves 'sold it to a Mr. Haddock, his son-in-law, who kept it UNTIL 1835 when it passed into the hands of Abram A. Markle, who, for two years thereafter accommodated and entertained many of Chicago's early residents'. A transfer somewhere inside 1835 is, on a flat prior, about as likely to be after 1 July as before it. A SECOND, LOOSER COMPLICATION: Andreas elsewhere quotes a stage-line advertisement of 6 August 1836 in which seats are taken at 'Markle's Exchange Coffee House' - so Markle is attached to two different houses in overlapping years, and either he ran both or one of the two datings is loose. Recorded rather than resolved. APPENDED 2026-08-29, other work — THE PAPER BRACKETS THE HANDOVER ANDREAS DOES NOT DATE. It is the GRAVES-to-HADDOCK one, not the Haddock-to-Markle one this field turns on, so nothing below changes the answer for 1835-07-01; it is recorded here because this is the field that carries the succession. Andreas gives only 'about this time'. The Chicago Democrat gives: the Board of Trustees adopting ordinances 'at the house of Dexter Graves' on 1833-12-04 and on 1834-03-05; an employment notice of 1834-04-01 (c017) reading 'enquire of MR. GRAVES, AT HIS TAVERN'; the ordinances of 1834-06-06 adopted 'at the house of E. Haddock' (1834-06-18 c002, reset as 'E. H. Haddock' on 1834-07-02 c017); and a Fourth of July meeting called at 'H. HADDOCK'S MANSIO[N HOUSE]' on 1834-06-25 (c002). SO THE HOUSE IS GRAVES'S ON 1 APRIL 1834 AND HADDOCK'S BY 25 JUNE 1834, and probably before 6 June. Dexter Graves commences the Baking Business on South Water Street over a copy date of 1834-03-25 (1834-03-25 c003), which is the same spring. THE WEAK LINK, STATED: the trustees' venue is not by itself a tenancy - the same board met at Starr Foot's house, the Presbyterian church, the Tremont House and 'the Exchange' later in 1834, so it tracks convenience. The bracket rests on Graves's own advertisement and on the house being named as Haddock's; the venue agrees with it rather than proving it. WHO KEPT IT ON THE SCENE DATE IS STILL OPEN and this record still declines to choose.

levels.8-10: The tavern changed hands in our scene year, and no paper gives the month. So on July 1, 1835, the keeper is one of two men, and we do not choose. A history book says Graves sold it to Mr. Haddock, his son-in-law. Haddock kept it until 1835, when it passed to Abram A. Markle. Markle then hosted many of Chicago's early people for two years. A sale some time in 1835 is just as likely after July 1 as before. There is a second, looser problem. The same book quotes a stage coach ad from August 1836. It says seats could be booked at Markle's Exchange Coffee House. So Markle is tied to two houses in the same years. Either he ran both, or one of the dates is loose. We write it down and do not settle it. Later work in August 2026 found what the papers say about the earlier sale, from Graves to Haddock. That does not change the answer for July 1835. In December 1833 and March 1834, the town board met at the house of Dexter Graves. In April 1834 a job ad said to ask Mr. Graves at his tavern. In June 1834 the board met at the house of E. Haddock.

entries.card: why:THE HANDOVER FALLS INSIDE THE SCENE YEAR AND NO SOURCE GIVES…
entries.text: THE HANDOVER FALLS INSIDE THE SCENE YEAR AND NO SOURCE GIVES A MONTH. On a flat prior a transfer somewhere in 1835 is about as likely to be after 1 July as before it, so this household names Haddock, records Markle in this note, and declines to choose - exactly as the record of Mansion House does. He was Dexter Graves's son-in-law, which is the only family relation in this parcel that reaches across two households. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — A DATE OF DEATH, AND NOTHING ABOUT 1835. John Wentworth's roll of old settlers who had died since 1 January 1881, kept for the Calumet Club and printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 April 1882, carries “Edward H. Haddock, May 30, 1881.”. That corroborates a Chicago residence before 1840 and fixes the END of this life, which this record did not carry; it is not an arrival and it places nobody in the town on 1 July 1835. Under the ratified ladder a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: other work consolidates the identity and other work regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (the crosswalk data). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Haddock, E. H.” (tax 1833 041, line 93); Poll list of 1835 — “Haddock, E. H.” (poll 1835 028, line 315). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Haddock' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Edw. II. Haddock,” (f1839 v0142, printed page 42, ward 1, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Haddock' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins E. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “E. H. Haddock”. 3 lot rows, $534 in all: block 9 lot 30 at $232 (f1839 lot0171, printed page 48); block 10 lot 12 at $151 (f1839 lot0185, printed page 49); block 10 lot 13 at $151 (f1839 lot0186, printed page 49). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 of those rows prints the bidder as a ditto mark under the name above rather than the name itself; 3 carry the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Haddock' folds to the same string as the bidder's, and the given name of both begins E. (the fergus 1839 lots crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a lot sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 6 times, as “HADDOCK E H”, “HADDOCK EDWARD H”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-28: 1 federal land entry — E2NE sec 27 T38N R14E and 1 lot in the platted town — lot 8 of block 3 in the town the register codes CHI (L8BL3CHI, as printed) and 4 parcels of the school section — BL134 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 1 of block 94 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 7 of block 120 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 8 of block 94 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 80.00 acres stated in all, for $1575.00 (ls0169, ls0170, ls0171, ls1199, ls0172, ls0669). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $1025.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HADDOCK E H matches Edward H. Haddock: the forename names Edward H. Haddock of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees as an initial only. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: The tavern changed hands in our scene year, and no paper gives the month. A sale some time in 1835 is just as likely after July 1 as before. So this family names Haddock, tells of Markle in this note, and does not choose. The Mansion House card does the same. Haddock was Dexter Graves's son-in-law. That is the only family tie in this group that reaches across two homes. In 1882 a list was printed of old settlers who had died. It gives the day this person died. That backs up that they lived in Chicago before 1840. It says nothing about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. In June 1839 this person bid for land at a sale of lots by the old fort. A Chicago book of 1839 prints it. That shows they were in Chicago then. It is not proof about 1835. In 1835 that land was still the army's ground, not town lots. So the lot places nobody in the town of 1835. It does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 6 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:THE HEIGHT IS DOCUMENTED AND THE POSITION IS ENTIRELY OURS,…
entries.text: THE HEIGHT IS DOCUMENTED AND THE POSITION IS ENTIRELY OURS, and two positions that look like evidence were both refused. Andreas says only 'a flagstaff AT THE FORT'; no source reached says where in it. (1) The 1808 Whistler draught puts the FIRST fort's staff 'in the center of' the parade - that fort is excluded whole in the exclusions record, which closes 'none of it may be borrowed for the second fort's records', and it is NOT the warrant for this point. (2) p4 0, the retrospective ways plate, draws a staff which other work measured at 0.495 of the drawn wall run - over the GATE, wedged between the two roofed lanterned works other work read as first-fort signature. Staff and towers are one composition on that sheet, so raising the staff on it would raise the two blockhouses with it, and the image-accuracy pass refused exactly that. What is left is a free choice constrained by the model rather than by a source: the parade is the only open ground inside the stockade that a fifty-foot spar can stand on without standing on a range or a roof, and the centre of a rectangle is the only point on it that does not require a SECOND invention to say why it is there rather than a metre away. That this lands where Whistler's first-fort staff stood is a coincidence of two rectangles and MUST NOT be read as corroboration - if the first fort's placement were admissible here the record would say so and cite it. Set to the parade record's own centre, so the staff moves when the parade does. Rotation is the fort's 8 degrees and means nothing to a round spar; it is carried so the footprint square lies with the rest of the complex.

levels.8-10: The height is known, but the spot is all ours. We turned down two spots that look like proof. A history book says only that there was a flag pole at the fort. No paper says where in the fort. First, an 1808 drawing puts the first fort's pole in the middle of the parade ground. But the first fort is left out of our town, and none of it may be used for the second fort. So that drawing is not why the pole is here. Second, an old picture made long after draws a pole over the gate. It sits between two roofed towers that later work read as signs of the first fort. The pole and towers go together in that picture. Using the pole would mean using the two towers too, and our picture check turned that down. What is left is a free choice. The parade ground is the only open ground inside the fence where a fifty foot pole can stand. Its middle is the only spot that needs no second guess to explain it. That it lands where the first fort's pole stood is just because both grounds are boxes. It must not be read as proof. The pole is set to the middle of the parade ground, so it moves when the parade ground does.

entries.card: why:THE HEWN-VERSUS-ROUND DISTINCTION the project's roadmap ASKS…
entries.text: THE HEWN-VERSUS-ROUND DISTINCTION the project's roadmap ASKS FOR, ATTESTED. Andreas says HEWN logs, which is the more finished construction and the commoner one at the forks; the log dwelling archetype builds hewn logs, so the record and the mesh agree without any further parameter. When K4 adds a round-log variant, this record is the reference for the other side of the distinction.

levels.8-10: Our plan asks us to show the difference between squared logs and round logs. Here we have proof. A history book says squared logs. That is the more finished way to build, and the more common one here. Our log house rules build squared logs. So the card and the model agree with no more work. When we add round logs later, this card will be the example for the other side.

entries.card: why:THE HOUSEHOLD THAT TURNED UP THE PARCEL'S SHARPEST DATE PROB…
entries.text: THE HOUSEHOLD THAT TURNED UP THE PARCEL'S SHARPEST DATE PROBLEM. Andreas: 'In the spring of 1835, Mr. Porter was chosen by the Presbytery of Ottawa its first delegate to the General Assembly which met that spring in Pittsburgh. After the adjournment of the Assembly, Mr. Porter was married, at Rochester, N. Y., to Miss Eliza Chappel, then late of Chicago, and with his wife visited his parents who were living in Massachusetts.' The marriage is dated elsewhere in the same volume to 15 June 1835 - SIXTEEN DAYS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, at Rochester, New York. Andreas also says he stayed 'until Mr. Porter left Chicago, in September, 1835'. So he is the town's Presbyterian minister on 1 July 1835 and may well have been eight hundred miles away that morning.

levels.8-10: This family gave us the worst date problem in the group. A history book tells of spring 1835. Mr. Porter was picked to go to a big church meeting. It met in Pittsburgh. After it, he wed Miss Eliza Chappel in Rochester, New York. She had lived in Chicago not long before. Then the two went to see his mom and dad in Massachusetts. The same book gives the date of the wedding. It was June 15, 1835. That is sixteen days before our scene, and far off in New York. The book also says Mr. Porter left Chicago in September 1835. So he is still the town's Presbyterian minister on July 1, 1835. But that day he may well have been far away, eight hundred miles off.

entries.card: why:THE IDENTIFICATION IS THE FINDING AND IT IS AN INFERENCE, NO…
entries.text: THE IDENTIFICATION IS THE FINDING AND IT IS AN INFERENCE, NOT A STATEMENT. Two compilations put a house on this one block face and neither knows the other is describing it. Andreas has John Watkins employed by Cols. Hamilton and Owen in 1833 and teaching 'later in a house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush' — a house with no owner named. Moses and Kirkland, at vol. 2 p. 155 — the reading bk mose2 006 — give the owner and not the school: Hamilton 'lived first in the fort and, when that grew too crowded with the refugees, he moved to the Agency House; and in 1833, with Col. Owen, hired John Watkins to teach the little school in the old stable near by. At about this time he built his house on what is now Michigan street between Cass and Rush, where he lived for nineteen years.' THE JOIN IS HAMILTON HIMSELF: the same two employers, the same teacher, the same year and the same first schoolroom by the Agency House appear in both, and then the same 110 m of street frontage appears in one as a house Watkins taught in and in the other as the house Hamilton built and kept. A house on that face whose owner one page names and whose schoolroom the other page names is most economically one house. WHAT WOULD REFUTE IT, and it is a live possibility rather than a formality: Moses and Kirkland give no SIDE of Michigan Street, and this record stands on the north side on Andreas's authority alone (see position.note). If Hamilton's house was on the south side — the river row of Kinzie's Addition, blocks 3 to 7 — then these are two houses and this one has no owner again. A source naming the side, or naming the owner of the house Watkins taught in, settles it either way. NOTHING IS PROMOTED BY IT. Moses and Kirkland is a compilation of 1895 and under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 it corroborates and dates and may not raise a confidence, so this block is `inferred` and not `attested`; the parallel ruling in the spend rulings data is the prose placement is identified with a structure the town already holds. NO HOUSEHOLD ID IS WRITTEN IN THIS PROSE, deliberately: the dooryard pickets generator admits a lot for a garden on an id appearing here, and an inferred identification is not a measurement of anybody's garden. The household is the Hamilton household, whose lives at names this record and carries the same reasoning.

levels.8-10: Matching these two accounts is the finding, and it is our reading, not a plain fact. Two books put a house on this one stretch of street. Neither knows the other is telling of it. One book says Cols. Hamilton and Owen hired John Watkins to teach in 1833. It says he later taught in a house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush. It names no owner. The other book names the owner but not the school. It says Hamilton first lived in the fort, then moved to the Agency House. In 1833, with Col. Owen, he hired John Watkins to teach the little school in the old stable near by. At about that time he built his house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush. He lived there for nineteen years. The link is Hamilton himself. Both books have the same two men who hired the teacher, the same teacher, the same year and the same first school room. Then the same short stretch of street shows up in each. One calls it a house Watkins taught in. The other calls it the house Hamilton built and kept. The simplest answer is that it was one house. Here is what could prove us wrong, and it is a real chance. The second book does not say which side of the street. We put it on the north side, from the first book alone.

entries.card: why:THE INITIALS ARE RESOLVED BY A SENTENCE IN ANOTHER CHAPTER,…
entries.text: THE INITIALS ARE RESOLVED BY A SENTENCE IN ANOTHER CHAPTER, which is the find that makes this household possible. Andreas's life of Dr Elijah Dewey Harmon lists his five surviving children: 'Charles Loomis Harmon, Isaac Dewey Harmon, Harriet Harmon, Lucretia Harmon, and Welthyan Loomis Harmon.' C. and I. are therefore the doctor's two eldest sons, and the firm in the town's first newspaper is a family partnership. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Harmon, C. L.” (poll 1834 051, line 220). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Harmon' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Chas. L. Harmon” (f1839 v0709, printed page 40, ward 1). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Harmon' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins C. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 6 times, as “HARMON CHARLES L”, “HARMON CHAS L”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-30: 1 federal land entry — NW sec 04 T39N R13E and 4 lots in the platted town — lot 10 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L10BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 7 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L7BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 8 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L8BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 9 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L9BL20CHIV, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — BL137 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 80.45 acres stated in all, for $5540.55 (ls0227, ls1210, ls1211, ls1212, ls1213, ls0751). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $5310.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HARMON CHARLES L matches Charles Loomis Harmon: the forename names Charles Loomis Harmon of the 6 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: A line in another part of the book tells us what the letters C. and I. stand for. That find is what lets us build this family. The book tells the life of Dr. Harmon. It names his five living children. Two were Charles and Isaac. The rest were Harriet, Lucretia and Welthyan. So C. are the doctor's two oldest sons. The shop in the town's first paper was run by one family. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 6 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:THE JUNCTION IS DOCUMENTED AND THE CORNER IS NOT, which is t…
entries.text:
THE JUNCTION IS DOCUMENTED AND THE CORNER IS NOT, which is the same shape of gap the Chicago Democrat's own imprint leaves at South Water and Clark. Andreas gives 'a blacksmith shop, on Lake Street, corner of Canal' (scan p. 1161) and no more. ONE CORNER IS ALREADY SPOKEN FOR: the Green Tree Tavern, built the same year, stands on the NORTH-EAST corner of Lake and Canal in this dataset, with its front on Canal and its long side on Lake, so three corners remain. THE SOUTH-EAST IS TAKEN, and the reason is a preference rather than evidence: it is the town side of Canal and the first corner a traveller coming out of Chicago along Lake Street reaches, which is where a smith who lives off passing horses and wagons wants to be, and it keeps the shop off the Green Tree's ground and out of its yard. The north-west and south-west corners are equally available and would move the building 25 to 50 m. METHOD: the modern Canal Street and Lake Street intersection is one of this project's ground control points, EPSG:26916 E 446913.0, N 4637287.4 (the wright 1834 gcps data), and the platted streets are 80 ft wide, so the kerb lines sit 12.2 m from the centreline: Canal's east kerb at local E -147.5, Lake's south kerb at local N -121.5. The shop is set 2.5 m inside both, which is a corner lot with the building close up to the street on two sides, as the Green Tree opposite is modelled. WORKING UNCERTAINTY about 20 m from the georeference, plus the corner choice, which is a discrete 25-to-50 m error rather than a radius. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Lake Street, the through road.

MOVED 2026-10-23, 8.2 M EAST AND 3.0 M NORTH, BECAUSE IT WAS STANDING INSIDE ANOTHER BUILDING. The owner sent a screenshot from above this crossing: two roofs grown into one another and the Lake Street rail fence running into them. The saddlery of Goss & Cobb, whose own advertisement puts it 'on the conner of Lake and Canal-streets', had taken the same south-east corner for the same reasons a fortnight before this shop was placed, and the two footprints overlapped by about 18 square metres — 2.7 m deep. Neither source places a building finer than the junction, so neither has the better claim to the corner itself; the saddlery keeps it because it was there first, and this shop stands NEXT DOOR on Lake Street, on the same corner lot, its front wall 0.3 m behind the saddlery's — the Lake Street corridor's own edge, which runs a little south going east — and its west wall 1.5 m clear of the saddlery's east wall. Every reason given above for the south-east corner still holds, and 'on Lake Street, corner of Canal' is read no more sharply than before: it is the corner lot, which is the residual the corner choice always carried. The 2.5 m set-back from the Lake Street kerb is given up for the street's own line, so the two shop fronts read as one street face rather than one standing behind the other.

levels.8-10: We know which streets met here, but not which corner. The Chicago Democrat's address on South Water and Clark leaves the same kind of gap. A history book says only that there was a blacksmith shop on Lake Street, at the corner of Canal. One corner is already taken. The Green Tree Tavern, built the same year, stands on the north east corner, so three corners are left. We chose the south east corner. That is our liking, not proof. It is the town side of Canal Street. It is the first corner a traveller leaving town on Lake Street comes to. A smith who lives off passing horses and wagons wants to be there. It also keeps the shop off the Green Tree's land. The other two corners would do just as well. They would move the shop about 80 to 160 feet. The streets were 80 feet wide, so each curb is 40 feet from the middle of the street. We set the shop about eight feet in from both curbs. That puts it close to the street on two sides, like the Green Tree across the way. Our map could be off by about 66 feet, and the corner choice could move it more.

entries.card: why:THE KIMBALL READING, STATED AS A READING AND NOT AS A FACT.…
entries.text: THE KIMBALL READING, STATED AS A READING AND NOT AS A FACT. The first issue of 26 November 1833 carries an advertisement beginning 'Just Opened and for sale AT the New Store on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' — dry goods, crockery and glass ware, hardware, cutlery, caps, cotton batting, yarn, sheeting, blankets — which the transcription supplied with the scan attributes to W. Kimball. Three things line up and none of them is proof. The paper's own imprint places it 'in THE building on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets', definite and singular. Andreas says the building Calhoun took his office in was UNFINISHED in November 1833, and a store advertising itself as 'Just Opened' at 'the New Store' on that corner in that month is what an unfinished building looks like a few weeks later. And the two notices sit in the same four pages. THE ALTERNATIVE IS THAT THE JUNCTION HELD TWO OR MORE BUILDINGS and the store was in another of them, which is perfectly possible on a four-cornered crossing — see Harmon & Loomis's Store, recorded at the south-east corner of this same junction. NO SEPARATE STRUCTURE RECORD WAS CREATED FOR KIMBALL'S STORE, deliberately: building one would assert a second building at a junction where the only contemporary document says 'the building', and would put an invented footprint on top of this one. Note also that the attribution of the advertisement to W. Kimball rests on the supplied transcription rather than on the scan, and that transcription is demonstrably imperfect elsewhere in the same issue (it reads 'C. & L. HARMON' where the scan reads 'C. & I. HARMON'). See the research notes on chicago democrat office. THE DEMOCRAT'S CLAUSE IS NOW DATED 1833-1834, AND THAT IS A READING OF THE PAPER'S OWN COLOPHON RATHER THAN A CHANGE OF MIND ABOUT THIS BUILDING. The imprint gives this corner on 1833-11-26, 1834-01-07, 1834-08-27, 1834-09-17 and 1834-12-03. Then the Chicago Democrat of 1835-05-20 c007 reads the colophon of that issue 'over Messrs. Jones & King['s] Hard[ware store]' in South Water street, and the Chicago Democrat of 1835-08-05 c026 prints the same. Between those two readings stands the Chicago Democrat of 1834-10-08 c005, which offers 'the store now occupied by W. Kimball, and as the office of the Democrat' FOR SALE with possession in November — a landlord clearing the building. So the press left this corner between 1834-12-03 and 1835-05-20, seven weeks at the latest before the scene date, and an occupants line that put it here on 1835-07-01 was asserting a tenancy the paper itself had already printed its way out of. The range is written 1833-1834 because that is the stretch the corpus witnesses; the departure is bracketed, not dated. WHAT IS NOT DECIDED BY IT. W. KIMBALL'S CLAUSE IS LEFT UNDATED, deliberately: the same 1834-10-08 notice is the only word on his tenancy either, it offers the store rather than reporting it sold, and nothing reached says whether he stayed, so dating him out on the strength of a for-sale advertisement would be inventing a second departure to keep the first one company. AND THE BUILDING DOES NOT MOVE. It is documented at this corner by the 26 November 1833 imprint and is the only fixed thing here; a building does not move when its tenant does, no coordinate is touched, and nothing is re-baked. AND THE NAME, THE BOARD AND THE FUNCTION ARE NOW DECIDED, each the way its own kind of object deserves. THE NAME STAYS: this record is still 'The Chicago Democrat Office' and still `aka` "John Calhoun's printing office", because a name is this project's label for a structure — the thing a reader searches on and the one fact that makes this building findable at all — and throwing it away to tidy a tenancy would lose more than it corrected. THE BOARD GOES: the town business signboards data no longer paints CHICAGO DEMOCRAT / Printing Office / South Water & Clark Streets on this front, because a board is a visible assertion standing in the scene and a walker reads it in the present tense. NOTHING REPLACES IT, and that is the honest end of it: the only name the corpus offers for what traded here afterwards is W. Kimball's, out of a notice that OFFERS his store for sale, and lettering it on the wall would assert at the scene date the very tenancy the source declines to report. THE FUNCTION NARROWS to `store`, which is the same reasoning applied to the field that drives the layers — see the function block. The general rule is the project's provenance guide § A label may outlive a tenancy; a sign may not, and the sign rule's own clause 8 in the business signboards generator. What that repaint cost is recorded in the PR: removing one board re-deals the mountings of every board alphabetically after it.

levels.8-10: We read this ad as Kimball's, and that is our reading, not a fact. The first issue of the paper, on November 26, 1833, has an ad. It begins: just opened, for sale at the new store on the corner of South Water and Clark Streets. It sells cloth, dishes, glass, tools, knives, caps, yarn, sheets and blankets. The copy that came with the scan says W. Kimball placed it. Three things line up, and none of them is proof. The paper's own address puts it in the building on that corner, as if there was just one. A history book says the building where the paper's office was had not been finished in November 1833. A store just opened at the new store on that corner that month is what an unfinished building looks like a few weeks later. And the two notices are in the same four pages. The other answer is that more than one building stood at these corners, and the store was in another. That could well be, with four corners. Harmon and Loomis's Store stands at the south east corner. We did not make a card for Kimball's store, on purpose. It would claim a second building where the only paper says the building. It would also put a made up floor plan on top of this one. The link to W. Kimball comes from the copy, not from the scan itself.

entries.text: THE LAST OCCUPANT ANY SOURCE NAMES IS THIRTEEN YEARS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Hubbard has the house occupied by Jouett, the United States factor. Hurlbut has the American Fur Company buy 'the Factory House' from the United States in 1822, and Jean Baptiste Beaubien move his family into it. By 1 July 1835 this project seats Beaubien's household at his homestead (Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Homestead, inferred). His pre-emption entry over this ground on 28 May 1835 is a transaction in the land register, not a sighting of anybody living here, and the land owner block says so. Nothing this project holds places a household in this house on the scene date, and writing one in would be a claim no witness makes. So the roof states its use, a private house that used to be the government's trading house, and the gap. The 1835 pre-emption case papers over the reservation are the likeliest place an occupant would be named.

levels.8-10: The last person any paper names in this house was here thirteen years before our scene. One book says Jouett lived in it. He ran the trading post for the government. Another book says a fur company bought the house in 1822. Then Jean Baptiste Beaubien moved his family into it. By July 1, 1835, we put Beaubien's family at his own home. On May 28, 1835, he put in a claim for this land. That is a deal on paper. It does not show that anyone lived here. Nothing we have puts a family in this house on our scene date. Writing one in would be a claim no one made. So the roof says what it was. It was a home that used to be the government's trading post. And it says what we do not know. The 1835 land claim papers are the best place to look for the name of someone who lived here.

entries.card: why:THE MAN THE SAUGANASH HOTEL IS NAMED AFTER, which is how thi…
entries.text: THE MAN THE SAUGANASH HOTEL IS NAMED AFTER, which is how this dataset first met him: 'It was suggested to Mark that he should name his house after some great man. He could think of no greater personage than Billy Caldwell and so his tavern became celebrated as the "Sauganash."' Andreas: son of a Colonel Caldwell, an Irish officer in the British army at Detroit, and a Potawatomi mother; born about 1780; educated at the Jesuit schools of Detroit and fluent in French and English besides several Indian languages; secretary to Tecumseh from about 1807 until Tecumseh's death and present at the Thames on 5 October 1813; a captain in the British Indian Department as late as 1816. By the treaty of Prairie du Chien of 1829 he was granted two and a half sections on the Chicago River, about six miles up the North Branch, and by the treaties of 1832 and 1833 annuities aggregating $1,000; he sold the land early. When John Watkins started his school in 1832 Caldwell offered to pay the tuition and buy books and clothes for any Indian children who would attend.

levels.8-10: The Sauganash Hotel is named after this man. That is how we first met him. Someone told Mark to name his house after some great man. He could think of no one greater than Billy Caldwell, so his tavern became known as the Sauganash. A history book says he was the son of Colonel Caldwell, an Irish officer in the British army at Detroit, and a Potawatomi mother. He was born about 1780. He went to church schools in Detroit. He spoke French and English, and several Native tongues. He worked for Tecumseh, writing for him, from about 1807 until Tecumseh died. He was at the Battle of the Thames on October 5, 1813. He was still a captain for the British as late as 1816. An 1829 treaty gave him land on the Chicago River, about six miles up the North Branch. Treaties in 1832 and 1833 gave him yearly payments of $1,000 in all. He sold the land early. When John Watkins started his school in 1832, Caldwell offered to pay for any Native children who would go. He would buy their books and clothes too.

entries.card: why:THE MAN WHO BUILT THE ONLY BRIDGE TEAMS COULD CROSS. Andreas…
entries.text: THE MAN WHO BUILT THE ONLY BRIDGE TEAMS COULD CROSS. Andreas: the log bridge across the South Branch between Randolph and Lake 'was, prior to 1834, the only bridge across the river or its branches over which teams could pass', and its total cost was $486.20, 'of which sum the Pottawatomie Indians contributed $200'. That last clause is a documented fact about who paid for the town's first serious piece of infrastructure and it is recorded here because it belongs to the population question as much as to the bridge. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “TAYLOR ANSON H”, 1835-06-08: 1 federal land entry — SW sec 30 T40N R14E, 160.00 acres stated in all, for $200.00 (ls0552). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: TAYLOR ANSON H matches Anson H. Taylor: the forename names Anson H. Taylor of the 7 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Taylor, Miss Anna M. | Letter, | January 29, 1890.” (second presb 0334, printed page 172), admitted 1890-01-29 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Taylor' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins A. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE SAME ROLL LINE IS MET BY OTHER TOWNSPEOPLE OF THIS NAME: second presb 0334 is matched under this same rule to Augustine Deodat Taylor, so it is met by two townspeople of this name, and it says which of them it was about no more than it says it was about this one — the test that decided it is a surname and a given initial agreeing, which cannot tell them apart. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

levels.8-10: This man built the only bridge wagons could cross. A history book says the log bridge over the South Branch, between Randolph and Lake, was the only one wagons could use before 1834. It cost $486.20 in all. Of that, the Potawatomi people gave $200. That is a known fact about who paid for the town's first big public work. We put it here because it tells about the people of the town as much as the bridge. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land once. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. A list of the members of the Second Presbyterian Church has a line with the same last name and first letter. That church list starts in 1842, so it is no proof about 1835.

entries.card: why:THE MAN WHO MADE THE TOWN'S FIRST BRICKS, which matters to t…
entries.text: THE MAN WHO MADE THE TOWN'S FIRST BRICKS, which matters to this dataset out of all proportion to his household: almost every building in the 1835 scene is timber, and the brick court-house going up on the square in the autumn of 1835 is the first thing this ground produced brick for. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. A YEAR off it is documented; a MONTH is not, and neither is anything about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Blodgett, Tyler K.” (poll 1834 015, line 184). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Blodgett' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Tyler K. Blodgett,” (f1839 v0115, printed page 42, ward 1, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Blodgett' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins T. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: This man made the town's first bricks. That matters to us far more than the size of his family. Almost every building in our 1835 scene is wood. The brick court house going up on the square in the fall of 1835 is the first thing here made of brick. A history book has a list, not complete, of the people in town in the fall of 1833. It gives a name, a trade and most often the year they came. It was put together fifty years later. So the year he came is known. The month is not, and nothing tells about 1835. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are.
