entries.card: why:THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL INFERENCE IN THIS RECORD, AND THE PAG…
entries.text: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL INFERENCE IN THIS RECORD, AND THE PAGE DOES NOT USE THE WORD. What is documented is that 'Augustine D. Taylor was the architect and builder', that the lumber came by scow from St Joseph, Michigan at $12 per thousand, and that the frame was raised in August 1833. Taylor is the man to whom the invention of balloon framing is credited, and this building is the one most often named as the first balloon frame - the research notes on structures south section 6 calls it 'an early balloon frame' and the frame storefront and frame dwelling archetype modules both cite it as the reason balloon framing is a first-class parameter in this project. Balloon frame is adopted on that identification. It is an identification, not a quotation, and if it is wrong the wall gets a heavier corner post and a wider stud module. The choice moves geometry here rather than sitting in the sidecar: studs at 16 in on centre set the rhythm the openings are laid out on, and a balloon frame shows no girt line.

levels.8-10: This is the guess that matters most on this card, and the page does not say the word. Here is what we know. Augustine D. Taylor drew it and built it. The wood came by boat from St. Joseph, Michigan, at $12 for each thousand feet. The frame was raised in August 1833. Taylor is the man often said to have come up with the balloon frame, a light frame of thin boards. This building is the one most often named as the first balloon frame. Our notes call it an early balloon frame. Our store and house rules both point to it as the reason we build balloon frames at all. So we build it as a balloon frame. That is a match we made, not a quote. If it is wrong, the wall gets a heavier corner post and wider spacing between its boards. This choice changes the shape we build. The boards stand sixteen inches apart, and the windows line up with them. A balloon frame shows no beam across the wall at the floor line.

entries.card: why:THE OCCUPANT IS ATTESTED AND, SINCE other work, SO IS THE HO…
entries.text: THE OCCUPANT IS ATTESTED AND, SINCE other work, SO IS THE HOUSEHOLD THAT CARRIES HIM. Bonnell names the man and gives him this building, which is as direct as this corpus gets. Until other work the household record that held him was the Pruyne household, a PARTNERSHIP household headed by Peter Pruyne and banded to the south division on the evidence of the store, and seating that household here would have moved Pruyne across the river on a sentence about Kimberly - so this roof named its occupant and claimed no household. Other work split the partnership: Kimberly heads the Kimberly household, whose lives at names this roof, and Pruyne stays on the Pruyne household with the store. AND THE PARTNER IS NAMED IN THIS NOTE AND NOT IN THE VALUE, WHICH IS NOT squeamishness: the register compiler matches a firm onto a committed roof on its partners' surnames read out of the `occupants` line, so writing Peter Pruyne into the occupants of Kimberly's HOUSE moved P. Pruyne & Co.'s premises off Pruyne & Kimball's Drug Store and onto this roof - the drug store on South Water Street relocated to a dwelling on the north bank by a sentence about somebody else. The occupants line says who occupied the building; the partnership is a fact about the man and is recorded here and in the research note.

levels.8-10: We know who lived here, and now we know the family too, thanks to later work. A book names the man and puts him in this building. That is as plain as our sources get. Before, he was part of the Pruyne family record. That record was a business group led by Peter Pruyne and placed south of the river because of the store. Putting that group here would have moved Pruyne across the river on a line about Kimberly. So this roof named the man and no family. Later work split the group. Kimberly now leads his own family, and it lives here. Pruyne stays with his store. We name the partner here in this note, and not in the list of who lived here. That is for a reason. Our tools match a firm to a roof by the last names in that list. Writing Peter Pruyne in that list moved his drug store on South Water Street onto this house on the north bank. That happened just because of a line about someone else. The list says who lived in the building. The business tie is a fact about the man, and we write it here.

entries.card: why:THE OCCUPANTS ARE ATTESTED AND NO HOUSEHOLD LINK IS WRITTEN,…
entries.text: THE OCCUPANTS ARE ATTESTED AND NO HOUSEHOLD LINK IS WRITTEN, BECAUSE NO TOWN CARD HOLDS THIS MAN. The identity layer holds him ONCE since other work (2026-10-05): the identity master data carries id kelsey parnick, joined under D1 by the reading merge crosswalk data from Fergus 1843 ("Kelsey, Patrick, boarding-house, Wolcott", f1843 e1462) and Norris 1844 ("Kelsey, Parnick, boarding house, Wolcott st.", n1844 e1003). What ties the two printings is the house and not the name: the same two Hough boarders are under him in both books ("bds Pat. Kelsey" in 1843, "res P. Kelsey's" in 1844). BONNELL DOES NOT SPELL HIM BOTH WAYS. This note used to say his sentence did, and it does not: the page image of Andreas vol. 1, printed page 137, reads "occupied by Parnick Kelsey" and "Eve, Parnick's wife" - Parnick both times. So the four printings that name him in full split two and two (Bonnell and Norris print Parnick, Fergus 1839 and 1843 print Patrick), and which was his own spelling is not ruled; the value above carries both. The identity is a directory man of 1843-44 graded not 1835 resident by the ladder, so it reaches no card and no household, and seating him here would be the resident layer's ruling and not a structure record's. Eve Kelsey is in no directory and in no identity of this corpus: Bonnell is the only source that names her, and naming her here is the whole of what this record can do for her. See the research notes on north bank east end neighbours section 5.

levels.8-10: We know who lived here, but we link no family. That is because no card in our town holds this man. Since October 2026 our list of people holds him once. He shows up in two city lists. In 1843 he is Patrick Kelsey, with a boarding house on Wolcott Street. In 1844 he is Parnick Kelsey, with a boarding house on Wolcott Street. What ties the two is the house, not the name. The same two Hough boarders live with him in both books. This note used to say the book that puts him here spells his name both ways. It does not. The page says Parnick Kelsey lived here, with Eve, Parnick's wife. Parnick both times. So four printings name him in full, and they split two and two. Two say Parnick and two say Patrick. We have not ruled which was his own, so we keep both. The lists show him in 1843 and 1844, and our rules do not count that as living here in 1835. So he gets no card and no family. Placing him here is for our people work to rule, not for a building card. Eve Kelsey is in no list at all. Only this one book names her. Naming her here is all this card can do for her.

entries.card: why:THE OLD LAYOUT, WRITTEN DOWN, NOT A NEW READING. These are e…
entries.text: THE OLD LAYOUT, WRITTEN DOWN, NOT A NEW READING. These are exactly the rectangles the archetype's procedural default already built on this range — five bays to the parade front with the ground-floor centre bay given to a door, four to the back, each storey's sills at 0.30 and heads at 0.72 of its 2.4 m — declared explicitly so that the upper piazza's supports can be set clear of them. Nothing moves: every opening stands where it stood before, and the left and right gable ends keep no openings, as before. No picture or text gives this building's openings; Hubbard's room list (kitchen, dining and store rooms below, one large room above) is not a fenestration, and every rectangle remains reconstructed.

levels.8-10: This is the old plan of windows and doors, now written down. It is not a new reading. These are the same openings our rules already built on this building. The front, on the parade ground, has five openings on each floor, with a door in the middle on the ground floor. The back has four. They sit at the same heights as before. We wrote them down so the posts of the upper porch could be set clear of them. Nothing moves. Every opening stands where it was, and the end walls still have none. No picture or book shows this building's openings. A list of its rooms tells us there was a kitchen, a dining room and store rooms below, and one big room above. That does not tell us where the windows were. Every opening is still our guess.

entries.card: why:THE ONE DATED FACT IS A USE, NOT A BUILDING DATE. Andreas re…
entries.text: THE ONE DATED FACT IS A USE, NOT A BUILDING DATE. Andreas records that in 1834 Gurdon S. Hubbard packed 'in the old bank building, corner of Lake and La Salle streets' — the season in which he packed some five thousand hogs. The building is therefore standing in 1834 and is older than that by an unknown margin; the range opens at the start of 1834 because that is the first year a source puts it in existence, not because it was built then. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY ARGUMENT and it is untested: nothing reached mentions the building again. Hubbard's own packing moved on — his Kinzie Street packing house is 1837-38 and his South Water Street house is 1840, both already in the exclusions record — so the building's 1835 USE is unknown even if the building stood. A NOTE ON THE NAME, WHICH IS AN ANACHRONISM AND IS KEPT ONLY BECAUSE IT IS THE ONLY NAME THERE IS: Chicago had no bank in 1834. The Illinois State Bank branch opened in December 1835, five months after the scene date. So 'the old bank building' is Andreas in 1884 naming a building by something it became, and on 1835-07-01 nobody in Chicago called it that. The id is retained because renaming a record is worse than annotating one; the name field and this note carry the caution.

levels.8-10: The one dated fact is a use, not the year it was built. A history book says that in 1834 Gurdon S. Hubbard packed meat in the old bank building, at the corner of Lake and LaSalle Streets. That season he packed about five thousand hogs. So the building stood in 1834. It was older than that, but we do not know by how much. We start it in 1834 because that is the first year a paper shows it. It was not built then. We keep it standing to our scene, since a building stands until something says it is gone. That is not tested. Nothing we found names the building again. Hubbard's packing moved on. His later packing houses came in 1837 and 1840, and they are left out of our town. So even if the building stood in 1835, we do not know its use. A note on the name. It is wrong for the time, and we keep it only because there is no other. Chicago had no bank in 1834. The state bank's branch opened in December 1835, five months after our scene. So the old bank building is the book in 1884 naming it for what it later became. On July 1, 1835, no one in Chicago called it that. We keep the name because renaming a card is worse than adding a note.

entries.card: why:THE ONE DESCRIBED THING ABOUT THIS BUILDING, and it is expli…
entries.text: THE ONE DESCRIBED THING ABOUT THIS BUILDING, and it is explicit: 'a two-story frame structure'. It is the reason the record exists at all — a two-storey store was worth remarking on when Lake Street was still mostly cabins and mud, and the sentence is offered precisely as a first-of-its-kind. SOURCE CAVEAT THAT TRAVELS WITH EVERY DOCUMENTED TAG ON THIS RECORD: the claim sits in an uncredited modern editorial addendum at the foot of a chicagology map gallery, graded a historian's account by this project's own source record, which says in terms that the addendum is the weakest text in that set and must never outrank Andreas. It is cited because it is explicit and because it is the only place this building has been found, not because it is strong.

levels.8-10: This is the one thing anyone tells about this building, and it is plain. It was a two storey wood building. That is the reason the card exists at all. A two storey store was worth talking about when Lake Street was still mostly cabins and mud. The line says it was the first of its kind. A warning goes with every claim on this card. The line comes from a short note, by no one named, at the foot of a modern page of old maps. Our own source list calls that note the weakest text in the set. It says it must never count for more than the history book. We use it because it is plain and it is the only place we found this building. Not because it is strong.

entries.card: why:THE ONE DOCUMENTED DIMENSION. Andreas: 'Another tower, forty…
entries.text: THE ONE DOCUMENTED DIMENSION. Andreas: 'Another tower, forty feet high, was begun and completed by Mr. Jackson in 1832.' 40 ft is 12.192 m, recorded converted with the original figure stated, per the datum json's data units rule. GUARD: the fifty feet in the same paragraph is the height the FIRST tower had reached when it fell. PICTURE-BOUNDED PROTOTYPE: the literal 12.19 m is retained, but the historical 40 ft datum is not identified as shaft, gallery, crown or finial. The reconstructed top is 12.84968 m and does not establish that datum.

levels.8-10: This is the one size we know. A history book says Mr. Jackson began and finished another tower, forty feet high, in 1832. We keep the forty feet. Be careful: the fifty feet in the same part of the book is how tall the first tower got before it fell. We built it from a picture. We keep the forty feet. But we do not know if the forty feet is to the top of the main part, the walkway, the crown or the very tip. Our top is a little higher, about 42 feet. That does not tell us which part the forty feet was.

entries.card: why:THE ONE PART OF THIS RECORD THAT IS MEASURED RATHER THAN REA…
entries.text: THE ONE PART OF THIS RECORD THAT IS MEASURED RATHER THAN REASONED. Wright 1834 draws the harbour as TWO RED LINES with HARBOR lettered between them and a flow arrow running east down the channel; the northern of the two is this pier's inner face. Both lines were read at native resolution off the BPL master scan (commonwealth:js957744g) and transformed by the same fitted affine that the wright 1834 gcps data records and the rederive datum tool checks the datum against — not a second georeference. METHOD AND RESULT. The northern line's landward end reads at resource pixel (3211, 1417), which is local E +1243.5, N +311.9; its drafted seaward end at pixel (3705, 1540). The line runs at 103.4 degrees from grid north, and the southern line — the south pier's inner face — runs at 103.5. THE CHECK THAT SAYS THE RIGHT TWO LINES WERE READ: the perpendicular distance between them is 64.2 m, against a documented entrance width of 200 ft, which is 61.0 m. Four per cent, from a direction that shares nothing with the text that supplies the 200 ft. Picking precision is about 5 resource pixels, or 3.5 m, on top of the sheet's own plus or minus 20 m. WHAT THE SAME READING DOES NOT SUPPLY IS A LENGTH, and the reason is on form.length (m): both drafted lines run about 1,165 ft, which is longer than this pier was at the end of 1834 and longer than the south pier ever was before 1837, so Wright drew the harbour as authorised rather than as built. Bearing and root survive that; extent does not. The value recorded here is the footprint polygon's own origin: the landward end of the measured inner face. The crib is built NORTH of it, away from the channel, because the line that was read is the channel side of the structure — see the footprint. Facade bearing 13.36 is the axis bearing less 90, this archetype's convention. THE POSITION WAS ALSO 900 m OUTSIDE THE MODELLED GROUND WHEN THIS NOTE WAS WRITTEN: the committed heightfield stopped at local E +320 and this pier starts at E +1243. It was extended east to E +1700 on 2026-08-11 and there is modelled ground here now — the ground contact block was regraded the same day, from outside modelled ground to approach not modelled, and that is the reason which survives: the pier stands over water with no modelled approach at either end (corrected 2026-08-22).

levels.8-10: This is the one part of this card that we measured, and did not just reason out. An 1834 map by Wright draws the harbour as two red lines, with the word HARBOR between them and an arrow pointing east down the channel. The north line is the inside face of this pier. We read both lines from a sharp scan of the map. We turned them into our map with the same math we use for that map. The north line runs a little south of east. So does the south line, which is the inside face of the south pier. Here is the check that we read the right two lines. The space between them is about 211 feet. A paper says the harbour mouth was 200 feet wide. We are off by about four in a hundred, and the two answers come from things that share nothing. Our reading could be off by about eleven feet, on top of the map's own 66 feet. The same reading does not give a length. Both drawn lines run about 1,165 feet. That is longer than this pier was at the end of 1834, and longer than the south pier ever was before 1837. So Wright drew the harbour as it was planned, not as it was built. The way the pier ran and where it started still hold. The length does not.

entries.card: why:THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS STRUCTURE'S FABRIC THAT IS DOCUMENT…
entries.text: THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS STRUCTURE'S FABRIC THAT IS DOCUMENTED, and it is documented in the source's own words: 'This hotel, WHICH WAS BUILT OF BRICK, was three stories and a basement in height' (Andreas, transcribed on "Lake House." Chicagology. Transcribing a passage of A. T. Andreas, History of…, and confirmed in the printed volume). The uncredited paragraph on the same page repeats 'built of brick'. It is also locally plausible rather than merely asserted: Tyler K. Blodgett established Chicago's first brickyard on the North Side in the spring of 1833 (the research notes on structures north section 3.12; the record of Blodgett's Brickyard). NOTE WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED BY IT: that any brick had been laid by 1835-07-01. Andreas describes the FINISHED hotel of 1836. The material is carried into the scene-date shell as an inference about continuity of intention, which is a small step and still a step.

levels.8-10: This is the one thing about what this building was made of that we know, and the source says it in its own words. A history book says this hotel was built of brick. It was three storeys high, with a basement. Another short note on the same page also says built of brick. It also makes sense here. Tyler K. Blodgett opened Chicago's first brickyard on the North Side in spring 1833. That yard has its own card. Here is what this does not show. It does not show that any brick had been laid by July 1, 1835. The book tells of the finished hotel of 1836. We use brick in our scene because we guess the plan was the same all along. That is a small step, but still a step.

entries.card: why:THE ONE VOTE AGAINST THE TOWN. He cast the single 'against i…
entries.text: THE ONE VOTE AGAINST THE TOWN. He cast the single 'against incorporation' ballot on 5 August 1833 - Andreas prints the poll - 'he living at that time beyond the extreme southern border of the proposed town, although having his business and professional interests at the settlement. He moved into the town the following year.' Andreas calls it 'exceptional fidelity to conviction and independence of opinion'. He received one hundred dollars at the Indian treaty of 26 September 1833 and was among the original subscribers to the Chicago Democrat in November 1833. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 13 times, as “HEACOCK RUSSEL E”, “HEACOCK RUSSELL E”, 1833-10-22 to 1835-06-26: 3 federal land entries — E2NW sec 32 T39N R14E; E2SE sec 34 T39N R13E; W2NE sec 32 T39N R14E and 8 parcels of the school section — BL129 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL20 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL30 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL61 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL9 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 2 of block 23 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 7 of block 117 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 7 of block 25 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 417.29 acres stated in all, for $1145.00 (ls0230, ls0231, ls0232, ls0233, ls0234, ls0235, ls0236, ls0237, ls0475, ls0476, ls0477, ls0478, ls0869). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS COOK, UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. The register states this purchaser's residence as COOK, so the sale is contemporary evidence that a man of this name lived in Cook County on the date of sale. It is not evidence that he lived in the town. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: HEACOCK RUSSEL E matches Russel E. Heacock: the forename names Russel E. Heacock of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: This is the one vote against the town. On August 5, 1833, he cast the only vote against making Chicago a town. A history book prints the vote. It says he lived just past the south edge of the planned town then, though his work was in the town. He moved into the town the next year. The book praises him for standing by what he thought. He got one hundred dollars at the treaty with the Native people on September 26, 1833. He was one of the first to sign up for the Chicago Democrat paper in November 1833. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 13 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there.

entries.card: why:THE ONLY BUILDING IN THIS FORT WHOSE SIZE A SOURCE STATES. T…
entries.text: THE ONLY BUILDING IN THIS FORT WHOSE SIZE A SOURCE STATES. The key to Alexander Hesler's 1855 photograph, printed in Wentworth's 1881 address: 'the Commandant's Quarters, A (brick, about 25x50 ft.)'. 25 x 50 ft is 7.62 x 15.24 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per the datum json's data units rule. IT IS ALSO THE CALIBRATION FOR EVERY OTHER DIMENSION IN THIS COMPLEX, which is worth stating plainly because it makes one number load-bearing far beyond its own building: the 1830 plan draws this range 48 pixels long, and setting 48 px = 50 ft is where the 1.10 ft/px scale comes from. The check that the calibration is not circular is the plate's own aspect - the drawn range is 1.9 times as long as it is deep against the key's stated 2.0 - and the parade width falling out at 71 ft against the same key's 80. THE DATE IS THE WEAKNESS: 'about 25x50' is a caption to a photograph taken twenty years after the scene date, and it is graded documented because it is a stated measurement of this building, not because 1855 is close to 1835.

levels.8-10: This is the only building in the fort whose size a source gives. A photo was taken by Alexander Hesler in 1855. Its key, printed in 1881, says the Commandant's Quarters, A, were brick and about 25 by 50 feet. This size also sets every other size in the fort. That makes one number count for far more than its own building. The 1830 plan draws this building 48 dots long. Setting 48 dots to 50 feet gives the scale for the whole plan. We checked that this is not going in a circle. The drawn building is 1.9 times as long as it is deep. The key says 2.0. The parade ground comes out 71 feet wide, and the same key says 80. The weak spot is the date. The size is a caption on a photo taken twenty years after our scene. We call it known because it is a measured size of this building, not because 1855 is close to 1835.

entries.card: why:THE ONLY MAN IN THIS PARCEL WHOSE ADDRESS IS SELF-REPORTED I…
entries.text: THE ONLY MAN IN THIS PARCEL WHOSE ADDRESS IS SELF-REPORTED IN PRINT IN THE TOWN'S OWN WEEK. The Democrat was designated the official newspaper of the town in November 1833. Note precisely what the imprint settles: the JUNCTION, not the corner - 'on the corner of' leaves which of the four unsaid, and the pencilled 'S. W.' in the margin of the scan is a later reader's gloss that this project quarantines. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of 1835 — “Calhoun, J.” (poll 1835 012, line 297). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Calhoun' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “John Calhoun,” (f1839 v0009, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Calhoun' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “John Calhoun”. 1 lot row, $319 in all: block 14 lot 5 at $319 (f1839 lot0244, printed page 49). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 carries the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Calhoun' folds to the same string as the bidder's, and the given name of both begins J. (the fergus 1839 lots crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a lot sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “John Calhoun” (33SQ-GYYJ-93Y, printed page 209, line 16). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (“Sauganash Hotel: the pre-1830 position is not represented” matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He is the only man in this group whose address he printed himself, in the town's own week. The Democrat was named the town's official paper in November 1833. Note just what the paper's address settles. It settles which streets met, not which corner. On the corner of does not say which of the four. Someone later wrote S. W. in pencil in the edge of the scan. That is a later reader's note, and we do not use it. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. In June 1839 this person bid for land at a sale of lots by the old fort. A Chicago book of 1839 prints it. That shows they were in Chicago then. It is not proof about 1835. In 1835 that land was still the army's ground, not town lots. So the lot places nobody in the town of 1835. It does not change how sure we are. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. We judged it is this same person. But 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:THE ONLY PERSON IN THIS PARCEL WHO IS ALSO ONE OF ITS SOURCE…
entries.text: THE ONLY PERSON IN THIS PARCEL WHO IS ALSO ONE OF ITS SOURCES. Wau-Bun's descriptions of the forks in 1831 - Wentworth's tavern, the log cabins occupied by Robinson, the small square log building meant for a school, the white Sauganash with bright blue shutters - are the evidence behind four structure records in the structures data. That a household member of the 1835 town is also the eye behind a quarter of the west-bank model is worth stating plainly, and it cuts both ways: Wau-Bun is a memoir of 1856 describing 1831 and this project grades it accordingly.

levels.8-10: She is the only person in this group who is also one of its sources. Her book tells of the river forks in 1831. It tells of Wentworth's tavern, the log cabins where Robinson lived, the small square log building meant for a school, and the white Sauganash with bright blue shutters. Those are the proof behind four buildings in our town. A woman in a family of the 1835 town is also the eye behind a quarter of our west bank. That is worth saying plainly, and it cuts both ways. Her book was written in 1856 about 1831, and we judge it that way.

entries.card: why:THE ONLY TEACHER IN THIS PARCEL DOCUMENTED AT WORK IN THE SC…
entries.text: THE ONLY TEACHER IN THIS PARCEL DOCUMENTED AT WORK IN THE SCENE YEAR ITSELF, and the only person in it who contradicts Andreas in his own book. Of the purpose-built schoolhouse Andreas says 'it is stated in Mr. Wells's report that these gentlemen afterwards built a house on the north bank of the river, just east of Clark Street, in which Mr. Watkins continued his school, and that it was the first house built for a school in Chicago. But this does not recur to Mr. Watkins's recollection.' Watkins wrote to the Calumet Club from Joliet in later life and Andreas quotes him directly on his first quarter: thirty scholars subscribed for but only twelve attending, 'only four of them were white: the others were quarter, half, and three-quarters Indians', and after the first quarter he moved the school into a double log house on the West Side owned by the Rev. Jesse Walker, who lived in one end while Watkins taught in the other and preached in the schoolroom on Sundays. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. It is the densest population passage this project holds and it is a retrospective, so a YEAR off it is documented and a MONTH is not. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Watkins, John” (poll 1833 028, line 49). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Watkins' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data).

levels.8-10: He is the only teacher in this group known to be at work in our scene year. He is also the only one who disagrees with the history book in the book itself. Of the first school house, the book says a report claims these men later built a house on the north bank, just east of Clark Street. It says Mr. Watkins kept his school there, and it was the first house built for a school in Chicago. But Mr. Watkins did not remember this. Later in life, Watkins wrote a letter from Joliet, and the book quotes him on his first months. Thirty pupils were signed up, but only twelve came. Only four were white. The others were part Native. After the first months he moved the school into a double log house on the West Side. It was owned by the Rev. Jesse Walker. Walker lived in one end while Watkins taught in the other, and Walker preached in the school room on Sundays. The book also has a list, not complete, of people in town in the fall of 1833. It was put together fifty years later. So the year he came is known, but not the month. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person once. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:THE OPENING DATE IS THE DATE OF THE DOCUMENT THAT REQUIRES T…
entries.text: THE OPENING DATE IS THE DATE OF THE DOCUMENT THAT REQUIRES THE BUILDING, NOT A BUILD DATE, and the distinction is the whole of this record. On 13 April 1831 the Cook County Court of County Commissioners sat at Chicago and, in one session, granted the county's first two tavern licenses — to Elijah Wentworth for $7 and to Samuel Miller for $5 — and then ordered the rates 'allowed to tavern keepers', which include 'For each horse fed 25' and 'Keeping horse one night 50' (Andreas, scan p. 249). Wentworth kept the Wolf Point Tavern from early 1830 to 1831-32 ("The Beginning of Wolf Point in Chicago, Illinois, including the history of the…). From that date onward this house is a licensed tavern in a county whose price list assumes it keeps horses overnight, which is the earliest date at which the building this record models has to have existed. The tavern itself is attested from 1828 and the stable may be as old; nothing says so, so the range does not claim it. THE CLOSING DATE is copied from the record of Wolf Point Tavern, whose own phase ends at the end of 1836 as a housekeeping bound rather than a demolition date. Nothing reached follows the stable at either end.

levels.8-10: The start date is the date of the paper that needs this building, not the date it was built. That is the whole point of this card. On April 13, 1831, the county board met at Chicago. In one meeting it gave the county's first two tavern licences. One went to Elijah Wentworth for $7, and one to Samuel Miller for $5. Then it set the prices tavern keepers could charge. They include 25 cents to feed a horse and 50 cents to keep a horse one night. Wentworth ran the Wolf Point Tavern from early 1830 to 1831. From that date on, this house is a licensed tavern, in a county whose price list expects it to keep horses overnight. That is the earliest date this stable must have stood. The tavern is known from 1828, and the stable may be as old. Nothing says so, so we do not claim it. The end date is copied from the Wolf Point Tavern, which ends at the end of 1836. That is just for keeping records, not the year it was torn down. Nothing we found tells of the stable at either end.

entries.card: why:THE PETFORD VIEW'S TONE, AND ONLY ITS: the 1831 watercolour…
entries.text: THE PETFORD VIEW'S TONE, AND ONLY ITS: the 1831 watercolour (image 8 of the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18) gives the shingle roof a dark green/moss colour — weathered shingles gone green, or the painter's reading of them — and the engravings, being monochrome, can neither agree nor disagree. A single a modern reconstruction watercolour may drive a material tone as inferred; the exact colour value is the archetype's, claimed at the liberties register “The Sauganash's fabric from the three views: wing door and hood, frontispiece, brick and moss, and the louvre pitch”. The brief's binaries are not yet committed, so the citation is the README until other work lands identifications.

levels.8-10: This is the colour from the Petford picture, and only from it. That 1831 painting gives the wood shingle roof a dark green, mossy colour. It may be old shingles gone green, or just how the painter saw them. The other pictures are black and white, so they cannot agree or disagree. One painting made long after may guide a colour, and we mark it as worked out. The exact shade is our rules' choice, and we list it as a guess. The owner of this project's picture files are not yet saved in the project. So for now we point to the note that lists them.

entries.card: why:THE PLATE GIVES THE COORDINATE AND HUBBARD CORROBORATES THE…
entries.text:
THE PLATE GIVES THE COORDINATE AND HUBBARD CORROBORATES THE GROUND. Read off the 1830 Harrison plan by the transform other work stated and other work reused, unchanged and not re-derived here: Internet Archive leaf n242 of historyofchicago01andr (Andreas, History of Chicago, vol. 1, p. 113), rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise so the sheet's own true-north arrow stands vertical, 2715 x 2003 px, anchor pixel (1445, 644) on the committed palisade centre at local E +1152.0, N +221.0, at 0.33528 m/px. The full reading, its per-block pixels and its four checks are the harrison 1830 us factors house data; this note does not repeat them.

THE PIXEL. The plate letters `U.S. Factor's House` in three lines against THREE solid blocks, and this record is block A — the one the label touches, and the largest. Its ink centres at pixel (1445.6, 1194.5), which is 0.2 m east and 184.6 m south of the enclosure centre: local ENU (1152.2, 36.4), UTM 448224.90 E, 4637432.20 N. CARRY +/-20 % on size and +/-25 m on position, exactly as every plate-derived record here does — the sheet has no scale bar and its own source record says it is used for arrangement and proportion rather than absolute size.

WHY BLOCK A AND NOT THE GROUP CENTRE. The label stands beside A and could as easily name all three (the trace says so and does not pretend otherwise), but A is what this record builds, so A's own ink is what it stands on. The group centre is 6.7 m away — well inside the +/-25 m this plate carries — so nothing turns on the choice except honesty about which pixels were measured.

WHERE IT STANDS RELATIVE TO THE FORT AND THE ROAD. 152 m south of the palisade's southernmost corner and 182 m south of its centre: outside the pickets, inside the fence line bk hub 060 runs from river to river, about 48 m south of the Gate the same plate letters in that fence, and east of the road band whose north-west edge is the committed garrison garden's south-east face. That is where Hubbard independently puts it — 'Just east of the road, and adjoining the fence running east to the river' — and Hubbard never saw this plate.

THE BEARING IS THE DRAWN ONE; WHICH LONG WALL IS THE FRONT IS NOT. The block's long axis runs at 40 degrees anticlockwise from east, which is a bearing of 50 degrees, and that is measured. rotation (deg) 320 faces the facade north-west, onto the road the house stood 'just east of'; the opposite choice, 140, gives the identical footprint and moves only the openings. It is INVENTED and it is covered at “The Factor House's fabric is read and its roof is invented, and the fence it is attested to have had is not drawn”.

IT IS NOT Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Homestead. That record stands at local (1133.2, 177.8), 139.7 m north of this one, and carried this building's identity as an alias until other work measured the separation. The alias came off there; this is the ground the plate actually letters.

levels.8-10: The old plan gives the spot, and Hubbard backs up the ground. We read it off the 1830 Harrison plan, printed in a history book. We used the same steps as the other cards from this plan, and did not work them out again. The plan's full reading and its checks are kept in their own file. The plan writes U.S. Factor's House over three lines, beside three solid blocks. This card is block A. It is the one the words touch, and the biggest. That puts it right below the middle of the fort, about 600 feet south. The plan could be off by a fifth on size and about 80 feet on spot, like every card from it. The sheet has no scale bar. Its own record says to use it for layout and how things compare, not true size. The words sit beside A, but they could just as well name all three. We say so. We build A, so we stand it on A's own ink. The middle of the group is only about 20 feet away. That is well inside how far off the plan could be.

entries.text:
THE PLATE GIVES THE COORDINATE AND HUBBARD GIVES THE CLASS, and they are consistent about the side of the fort without being identical about the ground. The plan letters 'Wash house' against a drawn building east and a little south of the stockade. Hubbard, of the same fort: 'On the east side of the fort the river was from four to five hundred feet from the pickets, and a part of this distance was a low, sandy beach, where rude wash-houses had been constructed, in which the men and women of the garrison conducted their laundry operations' (Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard…, leaf 76, printed p. 38, committed text lines 2419-2428).

TWO DISAGREEMENTS ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED. Hubbard says wash-houseS, plural, and the plan draws and names ONE. This record builds the one that is drawn, because the plan is the only witness that can carry a coordinate and a plural cannot be placed — how many, and how far apart, are two more inventions. And Hubbard puts them on the low sandy beach, while the plan draws this one on the open ground short of the beach hatching, about 46 m east of the pickets against his 400 to 500 ft from pickets to river. The plan wins the position, under this project's standing rule that a drawn plan beats a remembered description for WHERE; Hubbard is not overruled about the beach, he is simply describing a strip this building stands at the landward edge of.

READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN, BY THE SAME RULE AS THE ELEVEN RECORDS ALREADY TAKEN FROM IT. Internet Archive leaf n242 of historyofchicago01andr (Andreas vol. 1, p. 113), rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise so the sheet's own true-north arrow stands vertical, is 2715 x 2003 px. On that image the stockade's ink runs from x 1356 to x 1535 and from y 553 to y 730, so the enclosure's centre is pixel (1445, 644); the committed palisade record hangs that centre on local E +1152, N +221, which is UTM 448224.70 E, 4637616.80 N. Pixels convert at 1.10 ft/px (0.33528 m/px), the scale the research notes on fort dearborn section 3 derives from the commandant's quarters. THE ANCHOR AND THE SCALE ARE CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED, and the check is the garrison garden — the one thing on this plate that is both drawn and already committed. Its committed centre lands at pixel (1209, 1008) under this transform; the drawn diamond's centre measures (1207, 1002). Seven pixels, 2.3 m. A second check runs the other way: the committed blockhouse centre predicts pixel (1385, 698) and the drawn blockhouse square measures (1375, 710), 16 px or 5.4 m. WHAT THE TRANSFORM CANNOT DO is beat its own inputs. The enclosure measures 180 px across at this scale, which is 60 m against the committed palisade's 53 m — a 13 % spread, inside the +/-20 % the scale carries, and the reason is visible on the plate: 180 px is the OUTER edge of an engraved line four to six pixels thick. So carry +/-20 % on this offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself, exactly as every plate-derived record here does.

THE PIXEL. The drawn building is an upright block spanning x 1660-1687 and y 795-832, centre (1673.0, 813.0) — 228 px east and 169 px south of the fort centre, which is 76.4 m east and 56.7 m south of it.

levels.8-10: The old plan gives the spot, and Hubbard gives the kind of building. They agree about which side of the fort, but not about the exact ground. The plan writes Wash house beside a building east and a little south of the fort. Hubbard says that on the east side of the fort, the river was four to five hundred feet from the fence. Part of that was a low, sandy beach. Rough wash houses had been built there, where the men and women of the fort did their washing. We write down two ways they do not agree, and do not smooth them over. Hubbard says wash houses, more than one. The plan draws and names one. We build the one that is drawn. The plan is the only witness that can give a spot. Building more would mean making up how many there were and how far apart. Hubbard also puts them on the low sandy beach. The plan draws this one on open ground short of the beach, about 150 feet east of the fence. Our rule is that a drawn plan beats a memory for where things were. So the plan wins on the spot. Hubbard is not wrong about the beach. He is telling of a strip that this building stands at the land side of.

entries.text:
THE PLATE GIVES THE COORDINATE AND NOTHING ELSE DOES. The plan letters `Out Buildings` — plural — against a PAIR of solid blocks on the fort's south ground, and this record is the larger of the two.

READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN, BY THE SAME TRANSFORM AS THE FOURTEEN RECORDS ALREADY TAKEN FROM IT. Internet Archive leaf n242 of historyofchicago01andr (Andreas vol. 1, p. 113), rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise so the sheet's own true-north arrow stands vertical, is 2715 x 2003 px. On that image the stockade's ink runs from x 1356 to x 1535 and from y 553 to y 730, so the enclosure's centre is pixel (1445, 644); the committed palisade record hangs that centre on local E +1152, N +221, which is UTM 448224.70 E, 4637616.80 N. Pixels convert at 1.10 ft/px (0.33528 m/px), the scale the research notes on fort dearborn section 3 derives from the commandant's quarters. THE ANCHOR AND THE SCALE ARE CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED: the garrison garden's committed centre lands at pixel (1209, 1008) under this transform against a drawn diamond measuring (1207, 1002), and the committed blockhouse predicts (1385, 698) against a drawn square at (1375, 710). CARRY +/-20 % on this offset and +/-20 m on the fort itself, exactly as every plate-derived record here does.

HOW THE TWO BLOCKS WERE SEPARATED FROM THE FENCE, because they touch it. Ink is every pixel below luminance 110 in the window x 1495-1565, y 1100-1160; that mask is eroded by a 3 x 3 window, which deletes the 2-3 px fence line and leaves the two solid blocks whole; the survivors are grouped into connected components and each component's centre, orientation and extents are its own second moments, with the two eroded pixels added back on each dimension. The method is stated because it is the only thing that makes this reading reproducible: the fence crosses both blocks and an eye-read bounding box would have carried it.

THE PIXEL. The larger block is 224 px of eroded ink centred on (1517.3, 1134.4), with principal extents 21.8 x 17.4 px and its long axis at -25.6 degrees in image coordinates, which is a bearing of 64 degrees. That centre is 72.3 px east and 490.4 px south of the fort centre, which is 24.2 m east and 164.4 m south of it.

WHERE IT STANDS RELATIVE TO ITS PAIR AND TO THE FENCE. The smaller block stands 14.2 px north-east of this one — 7.0 m centre to centre — and the outer enclosure's fence line runs BETWEEN the two and touches this block's north corner. WHICH OF THE PAIR STOOD INSIDE THE FENCE AND WHICH OUTSIDE IS NOT CLAIMED: the drawn line is two to three pixels wide, which is a metre on the ground at this scale, and both blocks touch it. Reading a side off that would be reading the engraver's pen.

levels.8-10: The old plan gives the spot, and nothing else does. The plan writes Out Buildings, more than one, beside a pair of solid blocks on the fort's south ground. This card is the bigger of the two. We read it off the 1830 Harrison plan in a history book. We used the same steps as the fourteen other cards from this plan. We turned the page so the plan's own north arrow points up. We set the middle of the fort's fence on the plan to the fence's place in our town. The scale comes from the size of the Commandant's Quarters. We checked the steps, and did not just trust them. The fort garden and a blockhouse each land within a few feet of where the plan draws them. The plan could be off by a fifth, and the fort itself by about 66 feet, like every card from it. The two blocks touch the fence on the plan. So we used a picture tool to strip out the thin fence line and leave the two blocks.

entries.card: why:THE POST COMES FROM A TEXT, THE CROSS-ARM FROM A PICTURE, AN…
entries.text: THE POST COMES FROM A TEXT, THE CROSS-ARM FROM A PICTURE, AND NEITHER IS STRONG ENOUGH TO CARRY MORE THAN `inferred`. “The fort blacksmith made hinges, and the wolf sign was hung on a sapling” ("Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology). A sapling is a slender standing trunk; it is not a wall bracket, and until 2026-08-21 this building carried the archetype's bracket — a board on a short arm beside the door — which is the arrangement a tavern sign usually has and which nothing here ever said. THE OTHER HALF OF THE VALUE IS A PICTURE. The owner's brief of 2026-08-18 supplies an engraving of this tavern (the source files for owner brief of 2026-08-18, image 4) drawing a very tall pole beside the log building with a cross-arm at its head and the board flying from the arm; the owner read it as “almost like a flag”, which is what a board on a yard looks like. That is a PICTORIAL (a modern reconstruction) view — retrospective, drawn decades after 1835 — and the standing rule for one is that it may drive form as `inferred` and may never drive a coordinate. sapling pole names the pole AND the cross-arm it carries, so by least-confident-wins the whole value is graded at the picture's grade even though the post itself sits on a text. WHAT THE VALUE DRIVES AND WHAT IT DOES NOT: the mesh gets a set pole standing clear of the facade, a cross-arm lashed at its head, two iron hinge straps and the board flying from them. Its height, its taper, the arm's reach, where along the front it stands and the board's proportions are the archetype's own numbers within bounds it states, and are recorded in the liberties register “The Wolf Tavern's sign: the pole it flies from, and the wolf painted on it” rather than claimed here. WHERE THE TEXT SITS, WHICH IS THE HONEST LIMIT ON IT: the sapling sentence is in a NOTE at the foot of the chicagology page, not in the 1857 Chicago Magazine body that earned that source its a witness remembering. The note names no author and cites nothing. It is the only description anybody wrote of how this board was hung, and it is a compiler's summary of the standard retellings — better than nothing and not as good as the page it sits on.

levels.8-10: The post comes from a book, and the cross arm from a picture. Neither is strong enough to make us more than fairly sure. A page about Wolf Point says the fort's blacksmith made hinges, and the wolf sign was hung on a sapling. A sapling is a thin young tree trunk, still standing. It is not a bracket on a wall. Until August 21, 2026, this building had our rules' bracket, a board on a short arm by the door. That is how a tavern sign is most often hung, but nothing here ever said so. The other half comes from a picture. In August 2026 the owner of this project sent a print of this tavern. It draws a very tall pole beside the log building, with a cross arm at its top and the board hanging from the arm. The owner said it looked almost like a flag, and that is what a board on an arm looks like. That print was drawn long after 1835. Our rule is that such a picture may guide the shape, marked as worked out, but never the spot. The card names both the pole and its cross arm. So the whole thing is judged at the picture's level, even though the post itself comes from a book. Here is what we build. A pole stands clear of the front wall. A cross arm is tied at its top. Two iron hinge straps hold the board, which hangs from them. Its height, its taper and how far the arm reaches are our own choices.

entries.card: why:THE POST TRADER, DRAWN. A man stands here because a building…
entries.text: THE POST TRADER, DRAWN. A man stands here because a building of this function stood at a held post; his name is invented and his household is not claimed at all.

levels.8-10: This is the post trader, drawn. A man stands here because a building like this stood at a fort with a trading post. His name is made up, and we do not claim any family for him.

entries.card: why:THE PROPRIETORS ARE ANDREAS'S AND THE TENANTS ARE THE PAPER'…
entries.text: THE PROPRIETORS ARE ANDREAS'S AND THE TENANTS ARE THE PAPER'S, and the two halves are attested independently. Andreas p. 635 names Lathrop Johnson and George Stevens as the men who opened the house in 1835 and conducted it until the fall of 1839, so both are proprietors at the scene date. THE TWO PROFESSIONAL TENANTS ARE DOCUMENTED IN THEIR OWN ADVERTISEMENTS, seventeen days before the scene date. First: 'DR. J. [B.] BARNARD, a[t] t[h]e New Yor[k] Ho[u]se, La[k]e [s]t[r]eet' — the Chicago American, 13 June 1835, page 3 column 3, claim the Chicago American of 1835-06-13, a card tendering his professional services to the inhabitants of Chicago. Second: 'His office at the New York House, where he will remain until after the Land [S]ale' — J. C. Bradley, dentist, the same paper, 13 June 1835, page 3 column 2, claim the Chicago American of 1835-06-13, repeated 1835-06-20 column 1, under the dateline 'Chicago, June 14, 1835'. BRADLEY IS A TRAVELLING PRACTITIONER AND HIS OWN COPY SAYS SO: he will remain until after the Land Sale. He is carried as an occupant on 1835-07-01 because the Land Sale ran into the summer and his notice was still running on 20 June, not because a dentist is claimed to have lived here. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. Nothing reached says how many rooms the house had, who else lodged in it, whether Johnson or Stevens slept under its roof, or where in the building either office was. No figure is drawn for any of them — the standing constraint in the project's rules holds and v1 ships no human figures. THE READING IS TRANSCRIPTION-MEDIATED AND SAYS SO. Under the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 a claim read through this project's OCR-assisted transcriptions rather than off the page scan grades `attested` in this schema's vocabulary while carrying its own flag: reading = transcription mediated, with the transcription's own uncertainty brackets preserved inside the quotation rather than tidied away. These two cards are among the most heavily damaged in the American's file — the transcription of Barnard's heading reads 'ar tie New Yous Horse, Lane atneet' — so the brackets are doing real work here and the page images would settle both. Where a scan is later read, the scan is the authority and this claim upgrades under it.

levels.8-10: The owners come from a history book, and the renters come from the paper. Each half has its own proof. The book names Lathrop Johnson and George Stevens as the men who opened the house in 1835 and ran it until the fall of 1839. So both are owners on our scene date. The two men who rented rooms for their work are shown by their own ads, seventeen days before our scene. First, Dr. J. B. Barnard, at the New York House on Lake Street. The Chicago American ran his ad on June 13, 1835. In it he offers his care to the people of Chicago. Second, J. C. Bradley, a tooth doctor. His ad in the same paper says his office is at the New York House, where he will stay until after the land sale. It ran on June 13 and again on June 20, 1835. Bradley was a tooth doctor who moved from town to town, and his own ad says so. He will stay until after the land sale. We count him as here on July 1, 1835, because the land sale ran into the summer and his ad was still running on June 20. We do not claim he lived here. Here is what we do not claim. Nothing we found says how many rooms the house had. It does not say who else stayed there, if Johnson or Stevens slept there, or where in the building either office was. We draw no person for any of them. Our standing rule held then, and this first version showed no people. We read this from a typed copy made with the help of a machine, not from the page itself, and we say so. The owner of this project ruled that such a reading still counts as found in the paper, with a flag on it. The copy's own doubtful letters are kept as they are. These ads are badly damaged, so the page itself would settle them. If someone reads the page itself later, the page wins. No figure is drawn.

entries.card: why:THE QUARTERS ARE THE DOCUMENTED PART OF THE APPOINTMENT. And…
entries.text: THE QUARTERS ARE THE DOCUMENTED PART OF THE APPOINTMENT. Andreas gives the first keeper of this light $350 a year AND QUARTERS; a keepership paid partly in housing is evidence that housing stood at the station, and a light kept nightly was kept by somebody who slept beside it. What the phrase does NOT give is a building: it does not say a separate house, it does not say where, and it does not say what of. So the USE is inferred from the terms of a federal appointment, and every drawn attribute of the thing that carries the use is invented under “The keeper's quarters at the Chicago light: a house raised out of one word in a salary”. Read at the research notes on chicago lighthouse § 4 and the 1835 institutional lodging data.

levels.8-10: The rooms to live in are the known part of the job. A history book says the first keeper of this light got $350 a year and rooms. A job paid partly in a place to live shows there was housing at the light. A light lit every night was kept by someone who slept beside it. What the words do not give is a building. They do not say a house of its own, or where, or what it was made of. So we work out the use from the terms of the job. Every part we draw is made up, and we list it as a guess. We call it a house raised from one word in a pay deal.

entries.card: why:THE RANGE IS BORROWED FROM ANOTHER BUILDING BECAUSE THE ONLY…
entries.text: THE RANGE IS BORROWED FROM ANOTHER BUILDING BECAUSE THE ONLY DATE THIS ONE HAS IS ANOTHER BUILDING'S. Andreas records that Frederick Thomas advertised from 'two doors from the American office'; an address expressed relative to the Chicago American can only have been used after the American existed, and the American was established on 8 June 1835. So the range opens there, and that is a floor on the ADVERTISEMENT, not on the building, which is necessarily older and undated. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR. This is the thinnest documented range in the parcel: what it really records is that a man was trading at a describable spot on South Water Street in the summer of 1835.

levels.8-10: We borrow the dates from another building. The only date this one has belongs to another building. A history book says Frederick Thomas put out ads from two doors from the American office. An address that points to the paper's office could only be used once the paper was there. The paper began on June 8, 1835. So we start there. That is the earliest date for the ad, not the building. The building must be older, and we do not know by how much. We end it at the end of 1835, as usual. These are the thinnest known dates in the group. What they really show is this. In the summer of 1835, a man ran a business at a spot on South Water Street, and people could find it.

entries.card: why:THE RANGE IS THE REASON THIS BUILDING EXISTS AS A RECORD RAT…
entries.text: THE RANGE IS THE REASON THIS BUILDING EXISTS AS A RECORD RATHER THAN AS AN EXCLUSION, so it is stated in full. Andreas p. 635: 'The New York House was built in 1834 and opened to the public the following year by Lathrop Johnson and George Stevens, who conducted it until the fall of 1839.' The BUILD YEAR and the CLOSING SEASON are both his; neither end carries a month, which is why the range is graded inferred rather than attested and why it is bounded to the calendar years rather than to invented dates inside them. THE OPENING MONTH WAS THE OPEN QUESTION AND THE AMERICAN CLOSES IT. Andreas says only 'the following year', which leaves 1835 open at both ends and would leave the scene date of 1835-07-01 an argument rather than a reading. Two advertisements in the Chicago American of 13 June 1835 give a professional address AT this house: Dr. J. B. Barnard, 'at the New York House, Lake street' (page 3 column 3, claim the Chicago American of 1835-06-13), and J. C. Bradley, the travelling dentist, 'His office at the New York House, where he will remain until after the Land [S]ale' (page 3 column 2, claim the Chicago American of 1835-06-13, repeated 1835-06-20#c001, dateline 'Chicago, June 14, 1835'). A house letting office rooms to two professional men and advertised as a landmark address was OPEN AND TRADING seventeen days before the scene date. That is contemporary evidence where Andreas is a recollection published in 1884, and it is the specific thing the exclusions json's data falsified entry asked for. THE DISSENT IS RECORDED AND NOT RESOLVED BY PREFERENCE. drloihjournal's chronology of early Chicago hotels dates the New York House 1836, and that date is what put this building on this project's EXCLUDE list in the first place. It is departed from because Andreas states a build year plainly and a contemporary newspaper puts offices in the house eleven months before drloihjournal's date; a secondary chronology that disagrees with a named primary printing and with the earlier standard history is the reading this project drops. See the research notes on new york house § 2. THE END OF THE RANGE IS NOT A DEMOLITION DATE. Andreas's 'fall of 1839' is when Johnson and Stevens stopped conducting the house, not when the building came down, and nothing reached follows it further. 1839-12-31 is a housekeeping bound on the tenancy, and the scene date sits four years inside it either way.

levels.8-10: These dates are the reason this building is in our town and not left out, so we tell them in full. A history book says the New York House was built in 1834. It opened the next year, run by Lathrop Johnson and George Stevens until the fall of 1839. The year it was built and the season it closed both come from that book. Neither gives a month. That is why we call the dates worked out, not proven, and we use whole years and not made up dates. The month it opened was the open question, and the Chicago American answers it. The book says only the next year. That leaves our scene date of July 1, 1835 a guess. Two ads in the Chicago American of June 13, 1835 give an office at this house. One is Dr. J. B. Barnard, at the New York House on Lake Street. The other is J. C. Bradley, the tooth doctor, whose office was there until after the land sale. A house that rented offices to two men and was used as a known address was open seventeen days before our scene. That is proof from the time. The book is a memory printed in 1884.

entries.card: why:THE RANGE IS WIDE BECAUSE THE BUILDING IS OLD, NOT BECAUSE T…
entries.text:
THE RANGE IS WIDE BECAUSE THE BUILDING IS OLD, NOT BECAUSE THE RESEARCH IS THIN, and the project's own gate warns about ranges this long so the reason is stated here. No month is given for the opening year, so the range opens at the start of it. THE SURVIVAL TO THE SCENE DATE IS BETTER ATTESTED THAN ON MOST RECORDS IN THIS DATASET: Beaubien was living on the reservation in 1835 and filed a pre-emption claim for the whole 75.69-acre fort reservation dated 28 May 1835 and recorded 26 June 1835 at $94.61 — five weeks old on the scene date — and the Chicago Historical Society's later plaque still placed the homestead on the block that became the Public Library. What is NOT attested is the date the building came down, so 1835-12-31 is a housekeeping bound at the end of the scene year and not a demolition date. The claim was voided by the Supreme Court in Wilcox v. Jackson in 1839, which is four years after this scene and outside it.

THE OPENING BOUND MOVED FROM 1817-01-01 TO 1822-01-01 ON other work, 2026-09-11, AND THE PHASE ID MOVED WITH IT FROM factory 1817 TO log 1822. Both halves of the old id were wrong, and they were wrong for two different reasons found on two different pieces of work.

THE YEAR, found by other work (2026-09-06). The 1817 fused two buildings. Andreas scan p. 183: an army contractor named Dean built a house in 1815 'on the lake shore, at the mouth of the Chicago River, near where is now the foot of Randolph Street', and 'In 1817, Mr. Beaubien purchased this house, which was a low, gloomy building of five rooms, for $1,000... After this purchase he lived in the Dean house for several years'. THAT 1817 BELONGS TO A THIRD BUILDING this project models nothing of, not to anything on this record. The year the same sources give for Beaubien leaving it is 1822: Andreas scan p. 205, 'In 1822, after the abandonment of the United States Factory at Chicago, by Government, the factory building was bought by the American Fur Company, and soon after sold to John B. Beaubien, who made it his dwelling house'; Andreas scan p. 191, the same building 'whose residence it remained until 1839'; and Hurlbut's Hubbard, claim bk afc 009, 'In 1822... the American Fur Company bought from the U.S. the Factory House... to which Beaubien removed his family'. Andreas and Hubbard AGREE on 1822 and on the chain, and the disagreement this record used to report between them was the conflation talking.

THE WORD 'factory', withdrawn by other work (2026-09-11) BY MEASUREMENT. The 1830 Harrison plan letters 'U.S. Factor's House' against three blocks whose ink-weighted centre is local ENU (1145.6, 38.7); this record's footprint centroid is (1133.2, 177.8), 140 m north, against about 20 m of working uncertainty here and 25 m on the plate. So this record is NOT the factory building, and an id reading factory 1822 would re-assert on this line the identity that measurement refused. The id therefore takes this record's CONSTRUCTION and its opening year, which is what log 1820, log 1823 and log 1831 carry elsewhere in this dataset and which claims nothing about which building of the homestead group this is.

SO WHAT IS THE 1822 DOING HERE, IF THE PASSAGES THAT CARRY IT ARE ABOUT A BUILDING 140 M AWAY? It is a FLOOR, and it is the same kind of bound 1817-01-01 was meant to be. What places this record is the 1839 sale — Block 5, east of Michigan Avenue, between South Water Street and the reserved lots — and Wentworth finds Beaubien's residence there 'after he moved from what was before known as the John-Dean house'. Beaubien was in the Dean house at the lake shore from 1817 'for several years' and moved in 1822. He is therefore not at this corner before 1822 on any reading reached: either the residence the retrospectives follow from 1822 to 1839 IS this building, and 1822 opens it, or the homestead group held more than one building across that span and this is a different one of them, which can only be LATER. THE RESIDUAL IS STATED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED: nothing reached names the year this particular building went up, so 1822-01-01 is the earliest date the sources leave open and not a construction date. CONFIDENCE STAYS `inferred`. Two retrospectives agreeing is still a retrospective, and moving a bound onto better reasoning is not grounds to regrade it.

The 'erected by Capt. Bradley' attribution this note used to carry could not be relocated on any of the four Andreas pages read under other work; the source record warns that the archive.org index is lossy, so that is 'not found', not 'not present'. It came off the change note on other work with the rest of the factory identity.

other work DATED LIMIT,2026-10-30: residency and pre-emption evidence in1835 do not independently prove that THIS pictured1831 corner dwelling or its exact pictured form survived unchanged to1July1835. The existing inferred date range is retained as a scene assumption;1822 remains an earliest allowed bound, not a known construction date.

levels.8-10: The dates span many years because the building is old, not because we did little research. Our own checks warn about long spans like this, so we give the reason here. No month is given for the year it went up, so we start at the start of that year. We have better proof it still stood in our scene than for most buildings in our town. Beaubien was living on the fort's land in 1835. He put in a claim for the whole fort land, about 76 acres, on May 28, 1835. It was recorded on June 26, 1835, at $94.61. That was just five weeks before our scene. A later plaque still put the home on the block that became the Public Library. We do not know when the building came down. So we end it at the end of 1835 just for keeping records, not because it was torn down then. The high court threw out his claim in 1839. That is four years after our scene, and outside it. In September 2026, later work moved the start from 1817 to 1822. The old 1817 date mixed up two buildings. A man named Dean built a house in 1815 on the lake shore, at the mouth of the river. Beaubien bought that house in 1817. This is a different building.

entries.card: why:THE RELATIVE POSITION IS DOCUMENTED AND THE ABSOLUTE ONE IS…
entries.text: THE RELATIVE POSITION IS DOCUMENTED AND THE ABSOLUTE ONE IS DERIVED FROM IT. 'The first building in the rear of this store' puts the boarding house immediately behind Peck's store, which this dataset places at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle. This record sits directly south of P. F. W. Peck's Store's footprint, on the same lot line, facing north onto the same yard. WHAT IS NOT DOCUMENTED: the distance behind the store, the orientation, and whether 'in the rear' means the same lot or the next one. The 20 m working georeference uncertainty of the whole dataset applies on top.

levels.8-10: Where it stood next to the store is known. Its spot on the map is worked out from that. A book says it was the first building behind this store. That puts the boarding house right behind Peck's store. We place the store at the south west corner of South Water and LaSalle Streets. This card sits right south of Peck's store, on the same lot line, facing north onto the same yard. Here is what is not known. We do not know how far behind the store it was, which way it faced, or if behind means the same lot or the next one. Our whole map could also be off by about 66 feet.

entries.card: why:THE ROLLERS ARE THE FINDING. A documented instance of a Chic…
entries.text: THE ROLLERS ARE THE FINDING. A documented instance of a Chicago house being moved bodily one block in 1835 is evidence about construction, weight and the town's attitude to its own buildings, and it belongs to the project's roadmap as much as to K1. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD: any date for the removal, which would settle which street the house stood on at the scene date; The terrain epoch reaching south of Madison, which this record asked for, arrived on 2026-09-13: other work carried the heightfield to Twenty-Second Street and the house now stands on modelled ground.

levels.8-10: The rollers are the finding. We have proof of a Chicago house moved whole, one block, on rollers, in 1835. That tells us how houses were built, how heavy they were, and how the town felt about its own buildings. It belongs in our plans as much as in this card. Here is what would make us more sure. Any date for the move would settle which street the house stood on in our scene. This card asked for our ground to reach south of Madison Street. That came on September 13, 2026, when later work stretched the ground to 22nd Street. The house now stands on ground we built.

entries.card: why:THE ROOF IS AN INVENTION AND THIS CANNOT OUTRANK IT. The foo…
entries.text: THE ROOF IS AN INVENTION AND THIS CANNOT OUTRANK IT. The footprint stands 0 m inside the tract's nearest boundary, which on a documented building would carry the middle row, but this building was dealt to its lot by a recipe and is not there. The tract is real and the register's words about it are read; what is graded here is the claim that THIS roof stands on it, and that claim is the recipe's. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (“Seventy roofs are told who entered their ground by a survey grid nobody traced”): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

levels.8-10: The building itself is made up, and our rules put it on this lot. The piece of land is real, and so are the old record's words about it. But that this building stands on it is only our rule. The state's old book of land sales says this man bought the land under this building. It does not say he still owned it on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it. A sale is not a home. The lines of the old land survey are not traced from a map. We drew them in squares a mile wide from one known corner, at State and Madison.

entries.card: why:THE SALE, NOT THE CAMP. The Public Domain register enters 23…
entries.text: THE SALE, NOT THE CAMP. The Public Domain register enters 232 purchases at Chicago on 26-27 June 1835; the range opens a fortnight before the sale, when the crowd it drew was arriving, and closes a month after it, by when the buyers had gone to see their land. No source dates any tent here, or says there was one. What the range says is that on 1 July 1835, four days after the sale, canvas stood here. Other work.

levels.8-10: This is about the sale, not the camp. The land office book lists 232 land buys at Chicago on June 26 and 27, 1835. We start two weeks before the sale, when the crowd it drew was coming in. We end a month after it, when the buyers had gone to see their land. No paper dates any tent here, or even says there was one. These dates just say that on July 1, 1835, four days after the sale, tents stood here.
