entries.card: why:THE SECOND BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS EVIDEN…
entries.text: THE SECOND BUILDING FOOTPRINT IN THIS DATASET THAT IS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN A PLACEHOLDER, after Hogan's store. Andreas gives the size: a 16 x 20 ft log building. 16 x 20 ft is 4.877 x 6.096 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per the datum json's data units rule. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THE SIZE AND NOT THE PLAN: '16 x 20' is a rectangle in any reading and this polygon is that rectangle, but nothing attests a door, a counter, or that the building was exactly rectangular rather than a rectangle with a shed on the back. WHICH AXIS RUNS ALONG THE STREET IS NOT IN THE SOURCE either; it is decided by the facade bearing and argued in the position note, where it belongs. This is the smallest building in the dataset — 30 square metres, a single pen — and that is worth reading twice: Chicago's first drug store was a room.

levels.8-10: This is the second floor plan in our town that is real proof and not a stand-in. Hogan's store was the first. A history book gives the size: a log building 16 by 20 feet. What we know is the size, not the plan. Sixteen by 20 feet is a box in any reading, and our shape is that box. But nothing tells where the door or the counter was. Nothing says it was a plain box, with no shed on the back. The book also does not say which side ran along the street. That is set by which way the front faces, and we explain it with the building's place. This is the smallest building in our town, just one room. That is worth a second look. Chicago's first drug store was a single room.

entries.card: why:THE SECOND TOWER, AND THE ONLY ONE STANDING ON THE SCENE DAT…
entries.text: THE SECOND TOWER, AND THE ONLY ONE STANDING ON THE SCENE DATE. Andreas: 'Another tower, forty feet high, was begun and completed by Mr. Jackson in 1832.' No month is given by any source reached, so the range opens at the last day of 1832 rather than at an invented date inside it - which is deliberately conservative and still leaves the tower two and a half years old on 1835-07-01. The end of the range is an upper bound rather than a terminus: the Government put a new light at the end of the North Pier and the old one was eventually given away with its ground by an act of 1 August 1854, with Mark Beaubien the last keeper. THE FIRST TOWER IS NOT THIS ONE and is excluded in the exclusions record: it fell on 30 October 1831, unfinished, and everything usually quoted about its fabric - three-foot walls, fifty feet of height - is about the tower that collapsed.

levels.8-10: This is the second tower, and the only one standing on our scene date. A history book says Mr. Jackson began and finished another tower, forty feet high, in 1832. No source gives a month. So we start it on the last day of 1832, and do not make up a date inside the year. That is careful on purpose, and it still makes the tower two and a half years old on July 1, 1835. The end date is the latest it could be, not when it fell. The government later put a new light at the end of the North Pier. The old one was given away with its land by a law of August 1, 1854. Mark Beaubien was its last keeper. The first tower is not this one, and it is left out of our town. It fell on October 30, 1831, before it was done. What people most often say about its walls, three feet thick and fifty feet high, is about the tower that fell.

entries.card: why:THE SECOND TWO-STOREY MASS, AND THE PLATE PROVES IT BY ARITH…
entries.text: THE SECOND TWO-STOREY MASS, AND THE PLATE PROVES IT BY ARITHMETIC. The owner reported it missing on 2026-09-03 from the dev preview: 'i think there is a structure missing but you have it on the front and they have it on the rear in pictures, and it looks like the full height of the main building and similar design as the main building appears to be almost the same size, it connects from the back and side in the images.' other work measured the near apex at (648, 350) with one line running out of it at image slope -0.318 and one at +0.095, and called the right-hand one a ridge on the strength of the asymmetry alone. Other work finished the sum. Project each line onto the vertical through the vanishing point of the plane it lies in — the plate gives both horizontal vanishing points and its own focal length, recovered from their orthogonality — and BOTH come out horizontal in the world: 1.35 deg and 0.11 deg, where a 38 deg rake in the same plane would have been DRAWN at image slope -1.99 against the -0.318 measured. So they are two RIDGES meeting at one apex, not a ridge and a rake, and the mass the owner reported is on the sheet as a measurement rather than as an impression. the sauganash apex lines tool is that arithmetic and the project's gate gates on it. THE SHARED APEX IS ALSO WHAT SIZES THE WING: two gable ridges of one wall height and one pitch meet at a point only when they span the same width, so the wing's span is this block's own depth and the archetype refuses to build it at any other. GRADE. One sheet — Braunhold's. The Petford watercolour and the Trowbridge drawing are the same composition from the same station, so they copy it rather than corroborate it (the research notes on sauganash image accuracy section 1), and a retrospective (a modern reconstruction) that passes its own perspective test may be read for PROPORTION and never for a coordinate. CITED ON BRAUNHOLD ALONE. The Petford and Trowbridge views were dropped from this row on 2026-09-04 for the reason the reading itself gives: they are the same composition from the same station, so listing them would dress a copy as a corroboration. The earlier separate rights concern is now superseded by verified 1902 publication, but the dependence argument still applies: a later copy is not independent corroboration.

levels.8-10: This is the second two storey part of the building, and the old picture proves it with sums. The owner of this project saw it was missing on September 3, 2026, in the test version. The owner said a part was missing. We had it on the front, but the pictures had it on the back. It looked as tall as the main building and about the same size and style, joined at the back and side. Later work measured two roof lines meeting at one high point in the picture. At first it called one of them a roof ridge just because the two lines did not match. Then more work finished the sums. Working from how the picture was drawn, both lines turn out to be flat in real life. A sloped roof edge would have been drawn much steeper. So they are two roof ridges meeting at one point, not a ridge and a slope. The part the owner saw is now a measured fact, not just a feeling. Our checks test that sum. The shared high point also sets the size of the wing. Two roofs of the same height and slope meet at one point only when they are the same width. So the wing is as wide as the main block is deep.

entries.text: THE SHAPE CARRIES EVIDENCE AND THE SIZE DOES NOT, which is the same distinction Miller House's footprint note draws and it should not be blurred. What is reported is a SQUARE frame building (the research notes on structures north section 3.10, from views of c. 1835), so the polygon is square on purpose rather than by chance; the 11 m, about 36 ft on a side, is invented outright. The polygon cites no sources because the dossier's description of the views names none. To resolve: identify and read the c. 1835 view the dossier is describing — the candidates are the Blanchard & Shober 1867 'Wolf's Point in 1833' chromolithograph, the Chicago History Museum's early South Water Street drawings, and the Edgar S. Cameron painting of South Water Street; every one of them is retrospective, so even a positive identification gives a proportion rather than a measurement.

The shape names no sources, because our notes on the views name none. Here is how to settle it. Find and read the view from about 1835 that our notes tell of. It might be an 1867 colour print of Wolf Point in 1833, early drawings of South Water Street at the Chicago History Museum, or a painting of South Water Street by Edgar S. Cameron. Every one of them was made long after. So even if we find the right one, it would give us the shape, not the size.

entries.card: why:THE SINGLE MOST VIVID DOCUMENTED FACT ABOUT THIS BUILDING. A…
entries.text: THE SINGLE MOST VIVID DOCUMENTED FACT ABOUT THIS BUILDING. Andreas has an 'unfinished loft' over the two storeys, used as lodging: the Rev. Jeremiah Porter, arriving in May 1833 to found what became the First Presbyterian church, slept in it. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED IS THAT THE LOFT WAS THERE AND THAT IT WAS UNFINISHED IN MAY 1833. Whether it was still unfinished twenty-six months later on the scene date is NOT attested, and this record does not claim it — framing exposed is deliberately not stated, because the archetype would then leave the loading gable open and show a visitor a building site two years after the one moment anybody described. The archetype builds a loft as one gable opening and nothing else, which is the honest external trace of a loft.

levels.8-10: This is the most lively fact anyone tells about this building. A history book says there was an unfinished loft above the two floors, used as a place to sleep. The Rev. Jeremiah Porter came in May 1833 to start what became the First Presbyterian Church, and he slept in it. What is known is that the loft was there, and that it was not finished in May 1833. We do not know if it was still unfinished twenty-six months later, on our scene date. We do not claim it. We chose not to show the frame open. Our rules would then leave the end wall open and show a building site, two years after the one time anyone told of it. Our rules build a loft as one opening in the end wall and nothing else. That is the honest sign of a loft from outside.

The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Murray, Mrs. Cornelia A. | Letter. | November 29, 1886. | Dismissed.” (second presb 0759, printed page 196), admitted 1886-11-29 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Murray' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins C. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” THE LINE IS A MARRIED WOMAN'S ENTRY, and the crosswalk's own Mrs rule governs what it can have met: “a line flagged a married womans entry that meets a MAN in the 1835 layer has met his name, not him: it corroborates that the name was a Chicago name in the 1840s and it does not put that man on this roll.” The match is filed rather than suppressed, because a suppressed match is invisible and a flagged one can be argued with. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

entries.card: why:THE START IS A DEDICATION DATE AND IT IS THE FIRMEST DATE ON…
entries.text: THE START IS A DEDICATION DATE AND IT IS THE FIRMEST DATE ON ANY OF THE THREE WORSHIP BUILDINGS IN THIS PARCEL: the church was dedicated 4 January 1834, which is eighteen months before the scene date, and the Temple Building record carries the same date from the other side - the shared denominational use of that building ended when 'the Presbyterian church was dedicated January 4. 1834' (baptisthistoryhomepage). The building was therefore complete and in use on 1835-07-01. THE END IS SOFTER. This project's own dossier (the research notes on structures south, section 6) says the congregation 'Remained here until 1837-38' and no source reached fixes a month, so 1837-12-31 is the late end of that window rather than a date anybody recorded. The range is tagged inferred because its second half is a reading of a range, not a reading of a record. NOTHING IN THE RANGE IS AT RISK FOR THIS SCENE: any reading of the end that has been proposed is at least eighteen months after 1835-07-01.

levels.8-10: The start date is the day the church was opened for worship. It is the firmest date on any of the three church buildings in this group. The church was opened on January 4, 1834. That is eighteen months before our scene. The Temple Building card has the same date from the other side. Its shared church use ended when the Presbyterian church was opened on January 4, 1834. So this building was done and in use on July 1, 1835. The end is softer. Our own notes say the church stayed here until 1837 or 1838. No source gives a month. So the end of 1837 is the late end of that span, not a date anyone wrote down. We call the dates worked out, because the end is a reading of a span, not of a record. Nothing in the dates is at risk for our scene. Every end date anyone has given is at least eighteen months after July 1, 1835.

entries.card: why:THE START IS AN OCCUPANCY DATE WITH A MONTH BUT NO DAY. The…
entries.text: THE START IS AN OCCUPANCY DATE WITH A MONTH BUT NO DAY. The frame was raised in August 1833 - Deacon John Wright 'had, in August, assisted in raising the frame of the building' - and the church 'was not completed sufficiently for occupancy and dedication until in October' ("St. Mary's Church." Chicagology. Transcribing A. T. Andreas, History of…). 1833-10-01 is the first day of the attested month, a bound rather than a date. THE END MOVED FROM 1836-12-31 TO 1837-06-01 ON 2026-09-06, AND IT IS THE SAME KIND OF BOUND AS THE START. The building was later removed to Michigan Avenue and Madison Street, enlarged, and given the low open belfry that is the tower trap on this record. THREE READINGS OF THAT REMOVAL EXIST AND THE END NOW RESTS ON THE THIRD. (1) REFUSED: "St. Mary's Church." Chicagology. Transcribing A. T. Andreas, History of…'s uncredited building summary dates the removal to 1836. It is refused because a source outside that page contradicts it - Joseph J. Thompson has Father Timothy O'Meara finding 'the little church that Father St. Cyr had built standing near the southwest corner of what is now State and Lake Streets' when he came, and dates his coming to 'the early or middle part of June, 1837' (Joseph J. Thompson, "The Illinois Part of the Diocese of Vincennes", Illinois…, printed pp. 258 and 256; claims bk ichr4 001 and bk ichr4 004). A building standing in June 1837 was not removed in 1836. (2) TRUE BUT NOT A BOUND: the same page's Andreas transcription attributes the removal to Father O'Meara, who succeeded St. Cyr, and St. Cyr did not leave until 1837. That puts the removal after St. Cyr's departure and gives it no date at all; it agrees with (3) and can bound nothing by itself. (3) ADOPTED: the church stood at Lake and State when O'Meara arrived, early or middle June 1837. 1837-06-01 IS THE FIRST DAY OF THAT WINDOW, NOT THE LAST, AND IT IS NOT THE REMOVAL - it is the earliest day on which the building is attested still standing, so it keeps the phase as short as the evidence allows, exactly as 1833-10-01 does at the other end. Until 2026-09-06 the same instinct produced 1836-12-31, and it was applied to a page that contradicted itself rather than to the evidence; a third source now agrees with the later of that page's two readings and dates it, so 'take the earlier because the sources disagree' no longer describes what is held. WHY THE AUCTION CANNOT SUPPLY A CEILING - ASKED, AND ANSWERED RATHER THAN LEFT OPEN. The removal was forced by the sale of the ground: the congregation stood 'upon ground controlled by the Canal Commissioners', meant to buy the lot at the canal lots' public auction, and lost it to a private party when the commissioners' valuation was announced at $10, 000 (bk ichr4 001, bk ichr4 002). THAT AUCTION IS NOT DATED IN ANY SOURCE THIS PROJECT HOLDS. Thompson dates neither the sale nor the valuation. The only held record of a canal lot sale after this church was built is Norris's 1844 historical sketch, which reports 'another sale of Canal lots' in 1836 at YEAR precision, with no month and no day (J. W. Norris, General Directory and Business Advertiser of the City of Chicago…, claim n1844 tf 030). That sale falls BEFORE the June 1837 sighting, so if the church's lot went at it the sale bounds nothing; and if the lot went at a later sale, this project holds no record of that sale at all. The removal therefore has a floor - mid-June 1837 - and no ceiling, and no phase end is picked off it, because a date picked that way would be a guess wearing a citation. THE GRADE DOES NOT MOVE, AND IT IS `inferred` ON BOTH BOUNDS. Thompson 1921 is a retrospective (a historian's account) and "St. Mary's Church." Chicagology. Transcribing A. T. Andreas, History of… is another; a second retrospective agreeing with the later of the first one's two readings is CORROBORATION, NOT DOCUMENTATION, and nothing here rests on a record made at the time. EITHER READING PUTS THE CHURCH AT LAKE AND STATE ON THE SCENE DATE, and moving the end bound changes nothing about 1835-07-01 - it lengthens the attested standing from fourteen months past the scene date to twenty-three. NO GEOMETRY MOVES WITH IT: position, footprint, bearing and form are untouched by this change. DO NOT DATE THIS BUILDING FROM THE PAGE'S HEADER, which gives 'Life Span: 1835-1843' and contradicts the page's own body text. Other work SOURCE REASSESSMENT, 2026-10-23: Garraghan 1921 p.106 and footnote 26 now give a retrospective upper window for the removal: government purchaseJune 21, 1839, and a narrative already describing the church as moved when St Palais came inDecember 1839. These are not a relocation day. The conservativeJune 1837 end bound is retained; neither endpoint nor 1835 geometry changes. The tower addition is NOT securely tied to the removal: Andreas p.290 says only some time afterwards, and Thompson's later sequential retelling cites that same undated passage. See Gilbert J. Garraghan, The Catholic Church in Chicago, 1673–1871 (Chicago… and the research notes on st marys other the project's notes on work chronology.

levels.8-10: The start date is when the church was first used, with a month but no day. The frame was raised in August 1833. A deacon, John Wright, helped raise it that month. The church was not ready to use and open for worship until October. So we start it on October 1, 1833. That is the first day of that month, not the exact date. In September 2026 the end moved from the end of 1836 to June 1, 1837. It is the same kind of date as the start. The building was later moved to Michigan Avenue and Madison Street. It was made bigger and given a low, open bell tower. There are three readings of that move, and the end now rests on the third. The first, which we turn down, says the move was in 1836. Another source says it was wrong. Joseph J. Thompson says that when Father Timothy O'Meara came, he found the little church still standing near the corner of State and Lake Streets. He says the priest came in early or mid June 1837. A building still standing in June 1837 was not moved in 1836.

entries.card: why:THE START IS DATED BY AN ARRIVAL, WHICH IS BETTER THAN A YEA…
entries.text: THE START IS DATED BY AN ARRIVAL, WHICH IS BETTER THAN A YEAR. Dr John T. Temple reached Chicago 'about the 4th of July, 1833', started a subscription for a building and headed it with $100; 'in a few weeks the building was erected'; and then, exactly: 'When Rev. Allen B. Freeman, with his wife, arrived on the 16th of August, he found the church building ready for use' (baptisthistoryhomepage, transcribing Andreas I pp. 315-325 with print page markers). So the structure is standing and usable on 1833-08-16, which is the date taken here - a date somebody recorded about somebody else's journey, which is why it is firm. THE END IS A HOUSEKEEPING BOUND, NOT A DEMOLITION DATE. No source reached says how long the building stood or what became of it. 1835-12-31 is the ordinary continuity cut at the scene year that this dataset uses where a fate is unattested, the same convention P. F. W. Peck's Store, Madore Beaubien's Log House and Hogan's Store carry. The range is tagged inferred because of that second half. WHAT IS NOT IN DOUBT is the scene date: the building was in shared denominational use until the Presbyterian church was dedicated on 4 January 1834, and Sproat's school occupied the upper storey from December 1833.

levels.8-10: The start is dated by someone coming to town, which is better than just a year. Dr. John T. Temple reached Chicago about July 4, 1833. He started a fund for a building and gave $100 first. In a few weeks the building was put up. Then, to the day: when the Rev. Allen B. Freeman and his wife came on August 16, he found the church building ready for use. So the building stood and could be used on August 16, 1833. We use that date. It is a date someone wrote down about someone else's trip, and that is why it is firm. The end is just for keeping records, not the date it was torn down. No source we found says how long it stood or what became of it. We end it at the end of 1835, as we do when no one tells what became of a building. Peck's store, Madore Beaubien's log house and Hogan's store do the same. We call the dates worked out because of that end. What is not in doubt is our scene date. Several churches shared the building until the Presbyterian church was opened on January 4, 1834. Sproat's school used the upper floor from December 1833.

entries.card: why:THE START IS THE COMPLETION OF A BUILDING SOMEBODY ELSE BEGA…
entries.text: THE START IS THE COMPLETION OF A BUILDING SOMEBODY ELSE BEGAN. Andreas's chronology enters "'Cobweb Castle,' completed by Dr. Wolcott" against 1820, the year Wolcott was appointed agent, and his narrative says Wolcott 'finished and resided in a building commenced during Judge Jouett's incumbency' — Jouett was agent 1816-18. So the fabric is older than 1820 by up to four years and this range does not claim the earlier part. THE FORM THIS RECORD MODELS IS LATER STILL: the centre, two wings and two tails are Wau-Bun's description of 1831, and Wau-Bun says in as many words that the wings and tails were ADDITIONS made when 'there was found no more room for additions at the sides'. A record that split those additions into phases would have to invent their dates; instead the phase runs from 1820 and carries the 1831 form throughout, which overstates the building's size in the 1820s. THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE HONEST MINIMUM AND IT IS THE WEAKEST THING HERE. No source reached gives this building a fate. It is on this project's own watch list in the exclusions record for that reason: standing and in civilian occupation in the autumn of 1832, when Andreas has Colonel Hamilton residing in 'the old Indian agency-house', and nothing after. The agency itself wound down through the 1833 treaty and the 1835 removal, and an agency house whose agency has gone is exactly the kind of building that comes down without anyone writing it down. Presence on 1835-07-01 is an inference from continuity, not a finding. If evidence turns up that it was gone, this record leaves the scene and moves to the exclusions record.

levels.8-10: The start is when someone finished a building that another man began. A history book's list of dates says Cobweb Castle was finished by Dr. Wolcott in 1820. That was the year Wolcott became the agent. The book's story says Wolcott finished and lived in a building begun while Judge Jouett was agent, from 1816 to 1818. So the building is older than 1820 by up to four years, and we do not claim that earlier part. The shape we build is later still. The middle, two wings and two back parts come from a book that tells of 1831. That book says plainly that the wings and back parts were added on when there was no more room at the sides. To split those parts into their own dates, we would have to make the dates up. So we start in 1820 and keep the 1831 shape the whole time. That makes the building too big in the 1820s. The end is the least we can honestly say, and it is the weakest thing here. No source says what became of it. That is why we keep watch on it in our list of left out buildings. It stood, and people lived in it, in the fall of 1832, when Colonel Hamilton lived in the old Indian agency house. After that, nothing. The agency itself wound down after the 1833 treaty and the 1835 move west. An agency house with no agency is just the kind of building that comes down with no one writing it down. That it stood on July 1, 1835 is only a guess.

entries.card: why:THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THIS BUILDING IN E…
entries.text: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THIS BUILDING IN EXISTENCE, NOT ITS BUILD DATE, and the record does not claim otherwise: on 31 March 1831 Jonathan N. Bailey was appointed postmaster and 'opened the post-office in a log house occupied as a store by John Stephen Coates' Hogan' (Andreas). The building was therefore already standing and already a store on that date, and nothing reached says when it went up — Hogan came to Chicago 'as early as 1830'. THE END OF THE RANGE IS THE HONEST MINIMUM AND IT IS THE WEAKEST THING IN THIS RECORD. What is attested is that the building stood and held the post office from March 1831 until about July 1834, when Andreas has the office removed to Franklin and South Water; that is eleven months before the scene date, and NO SOURCE REACHED FOLLOWS THE BUILDING PAST IT. The range is closed at the end of 1835 on the ordinary continuity argument — a standing building stands until something says otherwise, and this project's the exclusions record is where documented removals go — but the counter-argument is real and belongs here rather than in a footnote: Lake and South Water was the corner most exposed to the 1835 boom, log buildings on prime frontage were exactly what got replaced first, and the post office's own move out of it in July 1834 is unexplained. Tagged inferred, not documented, for that reason. If evidence turns up that this building came down before July 1835 it belongs in the exclusions data and this record leaves the scene.

levels.8-10: The start is the first date a source shows this building, not the date it was built. On March 31, 1831, Jonathan N. Bailey was made postmaster. A history book says he opened the post office in a log house that John Stephen Coates Hogan used as a store. So the building already stood, and was already a store, on that date. Nothing says when it went up. Hogan came to Chicago as early as 1830. The end is the least we can honestly say, and it is the weakest thing on this card. Here is what we know. The building stood and held the post office from March 1831 until about July 1834. Then the book says the office moved to Franklin and South Water. That is eleven months before our scene. No source we found tells of the building after that. We end it at the end of 1835, since a building stands until something says it is gone. But the case against it is real, and it belongs here. Lake and South Water was the corner most open to the 1835 boom. Log buildings on the best land were the first to be replaced. And no one says why the post office moved out in July 1834. So we call it a guess, not proven. If proof turns up that it came down before July 1835, we will take it out of the scene.

entries.card: why:THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THIS BUILDING IN E…
entries.text: THE START IS THE FIRST DATE A SOURCE PUTS THIS BUILDING IN EXISTENCE, NOT ITS BUILD DATE. Andreas has the Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging in the store's unfinished loft in May 1833, so the building stood and was already a store then; this project's own dossier dates the store '1832-33' (the research notes on structures south § 5) and no source reached fixes a month or a year for its erection. Peck himself arrived in July 1831 with goods in the schooner Telegraph and was a licensed merchant, so a store of his could be a year older than this range says. THE END IS THE ORDINARY CONTINUITY CUT AT THE SCENE YEAR AND IT IS STRONGER HERE THAN ON MOST RECORDS IN THIS DATASET: Andreas has Peck still advertising dry goods, hardware and groceries in 1834-35 and still LIVING at the store, and this project's own the exclusions record says so in the entry that keeps his 1837 brick house out of the scene. What is not attested is when the building came down; 1835-12-31 is a housekeeping bound, not a demolition date.

levels.8-10: The start is the first date a source shows this building, not the date it was built. A history book says the Rev. Jeremiah Porter slept in the store's unfinished loft in May 1833. So the building stood and was already a store then. Our notes date the store to 1832 or 1833, and no source gives a month or year it was built. Peck himself came in July 1831, bringing goods on the ship Telegraph, and he had a licence to sell. So a store of his could be a year older than our date. The end is the usual cut at the end of our scene year, and it is stronger here than for most buildings. The book says Peck still put out ads for cloth, tools and food in 1834 and 1835, and still lived at the store. Our list of left out buildings says so too, where it keeps his 1837 brick house out of the scene. We do not know when the building came down. The end of 1835 is just for keeping records, not the date it was torn down.

entries.card: why:THE SURVIVAL THIS RECORD ASKED FOR IS NOW READ, AND THE RANG…
entries.text:
THE SURVIVAL THIS RECORD ASKED FOR IS NOW READ, AND THE RANGE MOVES OFF `reconstructed` FOR IT. The note this replaces closed with the sentence "TO RESOLVE: further issues of the Chicago Democrat or the Chicago American. One line of an 1834 or 1835 advertisement would settle the survival and might settle the corner." The Chicago American carries three such lines, and they settle the first half of that and not the second.

WHAT IS PRINTED. The Democrat of 26 November 1833 opens the range over the firm's own name: 'they have opened a shop in this village, on the conner of Lake and Canal-streets' (the 'conner' is the page's). The American then sets the same trading card three times in the weeks either side of the scene date — 1835-06-08 p3 c5 (the Chicago American of 1835-06-08), 1835-06-13 p3 c6 (the Chicago American of 1835-06-13) and 1835-07-11 p2 c1 (the Chicago American of 1835-07-11) — reading, in the second and clearest of them, '[S]A[D]DLE, HARNESS & TRUNK M[anufa]c[tor]y. S[. ]B[. ]COB[B] [w]il[l] [c]o[nt]in[ue] the [above business] at his shop, corner [o]f [… ][st]re[et]s'. The last of the three is dated ten days AFTER 1 July 1835.

WHY `inferred` AND NOT `attested`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF WHAT IS BEING CLAIMED. That the saddlery trade was carried on at a corner of Lake Street in the first week of July 1835 is printed. That it was carried on in THIS BUILDING is reasoned: the same trade, one of the same two partners, the words 'will continue the above business AT HIS SHOP', and Lake Street named in all four printings. The American never resolves the cross street — 'Lake anc Amor. streets', then no street names at all, then 'corner of Lake and THE Balle' — so the corner is still the Democrat's and the identification of the two shops is an argument rather than a statement. Other work holds that cross street open on the page images.

THE `to` DATE IS UNCHANGED AND IS STILL HOUSEKEEPING: 1835-12-31 is the end of the scene year, not a closure. Nothing dates an end. What has changed is that the nineteen-month gap the old note carried forward on nothing is now bridged by four printed dates, the last of them past the scene date.

levels.8-10: This card asked to find out if the shop still stood, and now we have read it. So the dates are no longer just our guess. The old note ended by saying more issues of the papers would settle it. One line of an 1834 or 1835 ad would show if the shop still stood, and might show which corner. The Chicago American has three such lines. They settle the first question but not the second. Here is what was printed. The Democrat of November 26, 1833 starts it, in the firm's own name. It says they have opened a shop in this village, on the corner of Lake and Canal Streets. The American then ran the same notice three times, in the weeks on either side of our scene. They are dated June 8, June 13 and July 11, 1835. The clearest says S. B. Cobb will keep on the same saddle, harness and trunk making business at his shop, at a corner. The last one is dated ten days after July 1, 1835. Here is why we say worked out and not proven. That the saddle trade went on at a corner of Lake Street in early July 1835 is printed. That it went on in this building is our reasoning. It is the same trade and one of the same two men, and he says he will keep on the business at his shop.

entries.card: why:THE THINNEST DOCUMENTED PERSON IN THE PARCEL AND THE RECORD…
entries.text: THE THINNEST DOCUMENTED PERSON IN THE PARCEL AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The whole of the evidence is one sentence in an uncredited editorial addendum at the foot of a chicagology page, which this project already grades as the weakest text in its own source set. A Thomas Church appears in Andreas's city rosters as an alderman in 1845, ten years past the scene date, which corroborates a man of that name in Chicago and dates nothing here.

levels.8-10: This is the person we know least about in the group, and the card says so. All the proof is one line in a short note, by no one named, at the foot of a web page. We already call that the weakest text in our set of sources. A history book's lists name a Thomas Church on the city council in 1845, ten years after our scene. That backs up that a man of that name lived in Chicago. It dates nothing here.

entries.card: why:THE THREE STREETS ARE DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS; WHICH SID…
entries.text: THE THREE STREETS ARE DOCUMENTED TWICE IN ANDREAS; WHICH SIDE OF RUSH STREET IS NOT DOCUMENTED AT ALL, AND THAT IS WHY THIS POSITION IS CONJECTURAL RATHER THAN INFERRED. Andreas in the hotel chapter: 'located on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting on the latter'. Andreas in his account of the First Unitarian Society, whose first Chicago service was held in the unfinished building in June 1836: 'The services were held in the Lake House, WHICH STOOD AT THE CORNER OF RUSH AND MICHIGAN STREETS.' Two chapters, one corner, and no side. A block between Kinzie and Michigan has two faces on Rush, about 110 m apart, and nothing reached says which one this is; the east side is adopted because the backers' own ground - Kinzie's Addition - and the north-bank commercial group Bonnell describes east of Rush lie that way, which is an argument about a neighbourhood and not evidence about a building. IF IT IS WRONG THE BUILDING BELONGS ABOUT 110 M WEST. A SECOND AND LARGER TRAP IS IN THE STREET NAME ITSELF. 'Michigan Street' on the north side in 1835 is the east-west street one block north of Kinzie - today's East Hubbard Street - and it is NOT Michigan Avenue, which did not cross the river until 1920. "Lake House." Chicagology. Transcribing a passage of A. T. Andreas, History of…'s uncredited paragraph glosses the site as 'near where the Wrigley Building stands today', and the Wrigley Building stands on Michigan AVENUE at the river, about 150 m south-east of the block Andreas's three streets describe and on the wrong side of Kinzie. the research notes on structures north section 3.8 carries the same gloss and additionally renders the third street as 'Michigan (Water)', equating it with North Water Street, which no source reached supports. This record follows Andreas's street names and records the gloss as the error it appears to be. METHOD: the modern East Hubbard Street / North Rush Street intersection centre was read from OpenStreetMap at EPSG:26916 E 448121.71, N 4637764.21 (OSM node 261149251, fetched 2026-08-11); the building's north face is set on the Michigan Street frontage 12.2 m south of it and its west face on the Rush frontage 12.2 m east of it, 12.2 m being half of an 80 ft street as annotated on Hathaway 1834. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Michigan Street, which is the one orientation Andreas does state - 'fronting on the latter'. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (the datum data, 17.5 m RMS), plus the block width if the side of Rush is wrong, plus whatever a building site's outline means when the building is not finished. NO SOURCES ARE CITED ON THIS ATTRIBUTE, deliberately: the streets are quoted in this note and are Andreas's, but the COORDINATE turns on a side of Rush Street that no source states, and a citation on a conjectural position would be decorative. THE GROUND UNDER IT IS MODELLED - the the 1834 harbor cut ground heightfield now runs local E -320..+1700 and N -400..+400, and this footprint at E +1061.2..+1085.2, N +341.2..+356.2 lands on it within the walker's 0.35 m step-up rule, so the phase carries no ground contact declaration. WHAT IS STILL NOT MODELLED is the excavation: a construction site is a hole in the ground before it is anything else, and this project has no way to cut a cellar into the terrain, so the shell sits ON the surface rather than in it.

levels.8-10: A history book names the three streets twice. It never says which side of Rush Street. That is why we call this spot a guess, not even worked out. The hotel chapter says it was on the corners of Kinzie, Rush and Michigan Streets, facing Michigan. Another chapter tells of the first Unitarian church service in Chicago. It was held in June 1836, in the building, which was not yet done. The book says it met in the Lake House, at the corner of Rush and Michigan. Two chapters, one corner, and no side. A block between Kinzie and Michigan has two faces on Rush, about 360 feet apart. Nothing says which one. We chose the east side. The land of the men who paid for it lay that way. So did a group of stores on the north bank, east of Rush. That is a reason about the area. It is not proof about the building. If we are wrong, the building belongs about 360 feet west. A second, bigger trap is the street name itself. Michigan Street on the north side in 1835 was the street one block north of Kinzie. Today it is East Hubbard Street. It is not Michigan Avenue. That road did not cross the river until 1920. One web page says the hotel was near where the Wrigley Building stands today. But the Wrigley Building is on Michigan Avenue at the river, about 490 feet south east of this block.

entries.card: why:THE THREE TENANTS ARE NAMED AND THEIR TENANCIES ARE OVER, wh…
entries.text: THE THREE TENANTS ARE NAMED AND THEIR TENANCIES ARE OVER, which is the whole point of this field and is why it is written with end dates rather than carried forward. Mark Beaubien owned the cabin and let it: Carpenter from the late summer of 1832 and 'soon' out, John S. Wright next, then Eliza Chappel's school from September 1833 until it moved into the First Presbyterian Church in 1834. NO SOURCE REACHED NAMES ANYONE IN THIS BUILDING IN 1835. The school's mistress is a person this dataset already holds: the hh chappel eliza mir data, where she appears under her married name — "Eliza Emily Chappell, the First Chicago Teacher Paid by Public Funds in 1833."… dates the marriage to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter to 15 June 1835, sixteen days before the scene date, and by then she had left both this room and, shortly, the town. THE SITE OF HER FIRST SCHOOL IS AN OPEN CONFLICT AND IS NOT RESOLVED HERE. "The History of Chicagoan Mark Beaubien, the Hospitality Guru began in 1830."… puts it in this cabin at Lake and Market. Andreas puts a log school-house west of State Street between South Water and Lake, which this dataset holds separately as the record of Eliza Chappel's infant school. "Eliza Emily Chappell, the First Chicago Teacher Paid by Public Funds in 1833."…'s own opening line says 'roughly at Lake and Clark', which is where the school MOVED in 1834. Three sitings from three readings of two unfootnoted pages and one compiled secondary, and nothing reached decides between them — so both records stand, both say so, and neither is promoted. What is NOT in doubt on any of the three is that the school had left wherever it started by 1834.

levels.8-10: The three renters are named, and their time here was over. That is the whole point of this part. So we give them end dates, and do not carry them on. Mark Beaubien owned the cabin and rented it out. Carpenter rented it from late summer 1832 and soon left. John S. Wright came next. Then Eliza Chappel's school was here from September 1833. In 1834 it moved into the First Presbyterian Church. No source we found names anyone in this building in 1835. The school's teacher is already in our town, under her married name. A source dates her wedding to the Rev. Jeremiah Porter to June 15, 1835, sixteen days before our scene. By then she had left this room, and soon after, the town. Where her first school was is an open question, and we do not settle it here. One page puts it in this cabin at Lake and Market. A history book puts a log school house west of State Street, between South Water and Lake. That one has its own card. Another page says near Lake and Clark. That is where the school moved in 1834. That makes three spots, and nothing we found decides between them.

entries.card: why:THE TOWN'S FIRST SURVEYOR AND ASSESSOR, WHICH IS AS CLOSE AS…
entries.text: THE TOWN'S FIRST SURVEYOR AND ASSESSOR, WHICH IS AS CLOSE AS THE 1833 TOWN COMES TO A CENSUS-TAKER. An assessor's roll for 1834 or 1835 would settle a great deal of what this programme has had to infer, and none is in the sources data. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. A YEAR off it is documented; a MONTH is not, and neither is anything about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Snow, George W.” (tax 1833 096, line 148); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Snow, George W.” (poll 1834 102, line 271). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Snow' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “George W. Snow,” (f1839 v0139, printed page 42, ward 1, voting for John H. Kinzie). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Snow' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins G. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 3 times, as “SNOW GEORGE W”, 1833-10-24 to 1836-06-29: 1 lot in the platted town — lot 1 of block 7 in the town the register codes CHI (L1BL7CHI, as printed) and 2 parcels of the school section — BL46 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL55 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 5.51 acres stated in all, for $1979.00 (ls0334, ls0335, ls1460). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $1730.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: SNOW GEORGE W matches George W. Snow: the forename names George W. Snow of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

levels.8-10: He was the town's first surveyor and the man who set its taxes. That is as close as the 1833 town comes to someone who counted its people. A tax list for 1834 or 1835 would settle much of what we have had to guess. We do not have one. A history book has a list, not complete, of people in town in the fall of 1833. It gives a name, a trade and most often the year they came. It was put together fifty years later. So the year he came is known. The month is not, and nothing tells about 1835. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 2 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 3 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. Some of what they bought was town lots. A lot is still only a sale, and it places nobody. It backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are.

entries.card: why:THE TRADE CANNOT BE GRADED BETTER, AND THE REASON IS THAT IT…
entries.text: THE TRADE CANNOT BE GRADED BETTER, AND THE REASON IS THAT IT IS NOT A READING. Other work stood hitching posts at the street edge's trading frontages and had to refuse this one by the grade on this field; other work asked which of two things that refusal was — a finding, or a field left under-graded. For the OTHER frontage it named the answer was under-graded: Frederick Thomas's Shop read 'shop'/reconstructed until the Chicago American of 4 July 1835 was read for other work and printed the man's own card, and 'drug store'/attested lit a board and a post at a stroke. THIS RECORD CANNOT MOVE THE SAME WAY, and the difference is not how hard anybody has looked. Frederick Thomas is a named man trading at a describable spot: his building is a guess and his BUSINESS is a fact, so a newspaper could settle his trade and did. Here the arrow runs the other way — the trade is the PREMISE and the building is the conclusion drawn from it. Eight physicians are documented in the 1833 town, four of them as households in this dataset, and no doctor's office was; the inferred-household programme raised a roof so that the trade the town demonstrably had would stand somewhere. 'a physicians office' is the name of that argument. Upgrading this field would cite this project's own reconstruction as evidence for this project's own reconstruction, which is the one move the confidence model exists to prevent. WHAT THE TWO CITED SOURCES ACTUALLY CARRY, since between them they are what makes this field look under-graded at a glance: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time attests the eight doctors — the PREMISE — and says nothing whatever about an office; Chicago · July 1835: Building Inventory and Architectural Reconstruction… authorises the reconstruction, which is a licence to build and not a reading of anything. Neither is a source about premises at this place, and no source is. 'reconstructed' is the grade this field has to wear, and no page image, directory or advertisement can change that, because there is nothing here for one to be about. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT is not evidence for this record but the end of it: a documented physician's office recovered from a source would SUBSTITUTE for this roof rather than upgrade it, which is what this record's own change note already says the parcel does. SO THE REFUSAL IN BOTH DERIVED LAYERS IS CORRECT, AND IT IS A FINDING RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. the town business signboards data refuses a board here on its ANONYMITY clause — this record's name begins 'Reconstructed', and now that a board carries a name there is not even one to paint — and the town street edge data refuses a hitching post on THIS GRADE. Both refuse, both say why, and they arrive by different clauses on purpose: the frontage works generator states at edge hitch along that it deliberately does not copy the anonymity exclusion, because a post carries no lettering. THAT IS WORTH KNOWING ON THIS FIELD, because it is what the field is holding up: in the frontage layer this grade is the ONLY clause standing between an unoccupied invented building and street furniture at its door. The occupant was retired to anonymous stock on 2026-09-02 — the roof stands and nobody is in it — so an upgrade here would not light up a card, it would stand a post for a stranger at a door no one keeps. Whether that second clause should exist is the owner's question about what furniture means and is filed as other work; it does not change the answer here, which is that there is nothing to upgrade. EIGHT DOCUMENTED DOCTORS AND NOT ONE OFFICE. A physician's office and apothecary's back room on the Lake Street frontage, where a doctor is found by people who need one. It is left unnamed on purpose: four of the eight are documented households in this dataset and attaching any of them to an invented building would turn a hypothesis into a false attribution.

levels.8-10: We cannot mark this trade any surer, because it is not a reading of a source. Later work put hitching posts at the shops along the street edge. It had to leave this one out, because of how sure we are of this part. Then more work asked why. Was that a real finding, or a part we had marked too low? For one other shop, the answer was that we had marked it too low. Frederick Thomas's shop said just shop and was our guess. Then we read the Chicago American of July 4, 1835, which printed his own ad. It said drug store, and that gave it a sign board and a post at once. This card cannot change the same way, and not because no one looked hard enough. Frederick Thomas was a named man in business at a spot people could find. His building is a guess, but his business is a fact. So a paper could settle his trade, and it did. Here it runs the other way. The trade is where we start, and the building is what we guessed from it. Eight doctors are known in the 1833 town, and four are families in our town. No doctor's office is known. So we raised a roof so that a trade the town surely had would stand somewhere. A doctor's office is the name of that reasoning. Marking it surer would use our own guess as proof of our own guess. That is the one step our rules for how sure we are exist to stop.

entries.card: why:THE TRADE IS DOCUMENTED FROM NOVEMBER 1833 AND THE BUILDING…
entries.text: THE TRADE IS DOCUMENTED FROM NOVEMBER 1833 AND THE BUILDING IS NOT DATED AT ALL. The range opens in November 1833 because that is the first contemporary evidence this project holds that the firm was doing this business in this town: the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries 'NEWBERRY & DOLE, Forwarding & Commission MERCHANTS' as a paid advertisement, and Andreas's summary of the paper's early advertising columns lists the same firm in the same trade (scan p. 755). An advertisement proves a trade was carried on and does not prove a building, which the source record for the Democrat states in as many words. The second fixed point is better for a warehouse: on 12 July 1834 the schooner Illinois, the first vessel through the new cut, was cheered at 'Newberry & Dole's wharf' (Andreas scan p. 503, via the research notes on structures south), and a wharf of one's own with a name on it implies premises behind it. So a warehouse existed by the summer of 1834, twelve months before the scene date. THE 1838-39 NORTH-BANK GRAIN WAREHOUSE IS A DIFFERENT BUILDING AND IS DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE THIS RANGE — see the position note and the exclusions json's data treatment of later structures. The range closes at the end of 1835 as the last date this record needs to claim.

levels.8-10: The trade is known from November 1833, but the building has no date at all. We start in November 1833. That is the first proof from the time that the firm did this business in this town. The Chicago Democrat of November 26, 1833 has a paid ad for Newberry and Dole. They shipped goods and sold them for others. A history book sums up the paper's first ads. It lists the same firm in the same trade. An ad shows a trade went on, but not a building. Our own record for the paper says so plainly. The second date is better for a warehouse. On July 12, 1834, the ship Illinois was the first through the new cut to the lake. People cheered it at Newberry and Dole's dock. A dock with your own name on it means there was a building behind it. So a warehouse stood by the summer of 1834, a year before our scene. The firm's grain warehouse on the north bank came in 1838. It is a different building, so we leave it out of these dates. We end it at the end of 1835, the last date this card needs.

entries.card: why:THE TRADE THIS RECORD ASKED FOR, AND THE PAPER IT NAMED AS T…
entries.text: THE TRADE THIS RECORD ASKED FOR, AND THE PAPER IT NAMED AS THE THING THAT WOULD SETTLE IT. Until 2026-08-29 this attribute read 'shop', reconstructed, over the admission that "the Chicago Democrat and Chicago American files for 1835 would settle it in one line, because the advertisement Andreas is quoting from is in one of them". The American is now read and the line is his own: "FREDERIC[K] THOMA[S], D[r]ug[gi]st and Apothec[ary], W[at]er Street. [R]ESPECTFULLY inform[s] the [citizens of] Chicago and vicinity that [fresh sup]plies in Dr[u]gs, Perfumery, Oils, Paint[s and Dye] Stuffs have been received by the scho[oner …]" — The Chicago American, 1835-07-04, page 4 column 5, claim the Chicago American of 1835-07-04, over the dateline 'Chicago, June [2]d, 18[35]', which is four weeks BEFORE the scene date. TWO EARLIER PRINTINGS CARRY THE SAME ADVERTISEMENT and are what make the identification checkable rather than asserted: 1835-06-08 page 3 column 6 (claim #c016) sets it without a legible name — "a general assortment of articles in the ab[ove line, together with] Chemicals, Perfumery [and] Dye Stuffs; and hopes, with his experience [of] more than twelve years in the business" — and 1835-06-13 page 4 column 6 (claim #c018) sets it again with the name: "[F]REDERICK THOMAS, la[te of N]ew York, [has] taken a store a[t the] Drawbridge". The three share their wording sentence for sentence. SO THE TRADE IS 'drug store' AND NOT 'shop': a druggist and apothecary keeping drugs, paints, chemicals, perfumery and dye stuffs, restocking by lake schooner, over a counter open to the street — which is what qualifies this frontage under the business signboards py's generator public trades rule, where 'shop' at the reconstructed grade was refused in writing. WHAT DID NOT MOVE. The building, its footprint, its storey count and its position are untouched and stay exactly as conjectural as they were: a documented trade is evidence about the BUSINESS and not about the premises, and this record's own research note is the place that distinction is argued. THE READING IS TRANSCRIPTION-MEDIATED AND SAYS SO. Under the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 a claim read through this project's OCR-assisted transcriptions rather than off the page scan grades `attested` in this schema's vocabulary while carrying its own flag: reading = transcription mediated, with the transcription's own uncertainty brackets preserved inside the quotation rather than tidied away. Where a scan is later read, the scan is the authority and this claim upgrades under it — the standard The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday… set when a scan caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'.

levels.8-10: This is the trade this card asked for, from the paper it said would settle it. Until August 29, 2026, this part said shop, and it was our guess. It also said the 1835 papers would settle it in one line, since the ad the history book quotes is in one of them. Now we have read the Chicago American, and the line is his own. It says Frederick Thomas, druggist, Water Street. He tells the people of Chicago and nearby that fresh drugs, perfume, oils, paints and dyes have come in by ship. It ran on July 4, 1835, and is dated June 2, 1835, four weeks before our scene. Two earlier printings of the same ad let us check that it is him, and not just say so. The one of June 8 has no name we can read. It tells of drugs, perfume and dyes, and of more than twelve years in the business. The one of June 13 has the name. It says Frederick Thomas, lately of New York, has taken a store at the drawbridge. All three use the same words, line for line. So the trade is drug store, not shop. Here is what did not change. The building, its floor plan, how many floors it has and where it stands are just as much a guess as before. A known trade is proof about the business, not the building. This card's own research note is where we argue that point. We read this from a typed copy made with the help of a machine, not from the page itself, and we say so. The owner of this project ruled that such a reading still counts as found in the paper, with a flag on it. The copy's own doubtful letters are kept as they are. If someone reads the page itself later, the page wins.

entries.card: why:THE TWO-MASS PLAN, AND THE 12 x 8 m PLACEHOLDER IS RETIRED (…
entries.text: THE TWO-MASS PLAN, AND THE 12 x 8 m PLACEHOLDER IS RETIRED (spending 's reading). THE FRONTAGE IS DERIVED AND THE DEPTH IS NOT, and the block is graded at the weaker of the two. FRONTAGE 9.92 m: Braunhold's engraving draws five bays on the street face and rectified against that face's own vanishing point the five are EQUAL to 2.4 % (the sauganash plate check, bay rhythm rectified gaps 0.997 / 1.011 / 1.020 / 0.972). The bay measures 1.984 m at the plate's stated scale datum — a standing adult at 1.70 m, hat included, the two men on the walk reading 147 and 143 px — so five bays are 9.92 m. THE DATUM'S BIAS IS SMALL AND BOUNDED, which is what makes this a measurement rather than a floor: the men stand a pace forward of the wall, and the plate's own focal length puts them 43.0 m from the station (f 3664.7 px on a 145 px figure of 1.70 m), so a pace is 2.7 %. The frontage is therefore 9.9-10.2 m and 12 m IS REFUTED rather than merely unsupported. The value taken is the measured 9.92 and is not fudged up into the correction. What does still move it is the 1.70 m datum itself: at 1.60 m the frontage reads 9.3 m and at 1.80 m 10.5 m. DEPTH 8.0 m IS UNCHANGED AND IS STILL A RECONSTRUCTION. One plate gives no depth (the research notes on sauganash image accuracy row 11), so nothing has measured it; it is held at the placeholder's own figure deliberately, because the placement above offsets this origin by the footprint's own 8 m depth to stand the north face on the Lake Street frontage, and moving a number with no evidence behind it would move the building. THE SECOND MASS IS NOT IN THIS POLYGON, on the precedent Green Tree Tavern's rear ell set: an attached wing is the archetype's, sized by this phase's own form attributes (cross wing, cross wing depth (m), cross wing end), and the polygon is the main block's plan. The one lead this note used to carry is still open: Andreas vol. 1 p. 106 ('Eagle Exchange'), not yet read at page-image level, and the individual building rectangle on Hathaway 1834. NOTE ON WHAT THIS TAG MEANS: conjectural here is about SIZE, not about existence or character. That the building was a two-storey white frame block is documented (Wau-Bun); how big it was is measured off one retrospective sheet and no better. The renderer therefore does NOT dither the massing on account of this tag — see the frame tavern generator — and the dimensional uncertainty is carried in the sidecar instead.

levels.8-10: The plan has two parts, and the old stand-in size of about 39 by 26 feet is gone. The width along the front is worked out, but the depth is not. We judge the block by the weaker of the two. The front is about 33 feet wide. Braunhold's print draws five windows across the street side. We measured them, allowing for how the picture was drawn, and the five are the same to within a few parts in a hundred. To get a size, we used the two men on the walk. We took a grown man with his hat to be about 5 feet 7 inches tall. That makes each window space about six and a half feet, so five make about 33 feet. The men stand a step in front of the wall, but that changes the answer only a little. So the front is about 33 feet, and 39 feet is shown to be wrong. We use the measured size and do not push it up. What could still move it is the man's height. A shorter man gives about 31 feet, and a taller one about 34. The depth of about 26 feet is the same as before, and it is still a guess. One picture gives no depth, so nothing has measured it. We keep the old stand-in size on purpose, since the building's place is set using that depth.

entries.card: why:THE TWO-SHOP PROBLEM, INHERITED FROM THE STRUCTURES LAYER. T…
entries.text: THE TWO-SHOP PROBLEM, INHERITED FROM THE STRUCTURES LAYER. This dataset holds both Beaubien's log cabin, beside the Sauganash on Lake Street near the river and Philo Carpenter's South Water Street Store, and Andreas says he removed FROM the first TO the second. The South Water store is the later of the two and is where the sources leave him, so it is the link; the log shop's own record already argues that its survival to the scene date is doubtful. Inferred, because 'subsequently' is not a date. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR works at AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW the Carpenter household#works at, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start

levels.8-10: Two shops make a problem, and it comes from our building cards. We have both Beaubien's log cabin, beside the Sauganash on Lake Street near the river, and Philo Carpenter's South Water Street store. A history book says he moved from the first to the second. The South Water store is the later one, and it is where the sources leave him. So we link him to it. The log shop's own card already says it may not have lasted to our scene. We call it worked out, because the book's word later is not a date. This part is copied from his family's card, with nothing changed. That card names the place as of July 1, 1835, and dates neither end of the tie. So we leave this one undated, and do not use the scene date as a start.

entries.card: why:THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract “A qua…
entries.text: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract “A quarter of the modelled land was federal ground or a sand bar, and nothing refused a house on either” already derives for the 1835 no build ground data — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and the project's gate already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date “A quarter of the modelled land was federal ground or a sand bar, and nothing refused a house on either” quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons “A quarter of the modelled land was federal ground or a sand bar, and nothing refused a house on either” states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS 102 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (“Seventy roofs are told who entered their ground by a survey grid nobody traced”): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

levels.8-10: This was land the United States kept for the fort. We use the same edge for it that we use elsewhere in the town. The old book of land sales is a second proof of the date in May 1835 when Beaubien claimed it. That claim was argued over. We give the entry the old book has, and nothing about how it ended. The building stands 102 m inside the edge of the land, far more than our maps could be off. The state's old book of land sales says this man bought the land under this building. It does not say he still owned it on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it. A sale is not a home. The lines of the old land survey are not traced from a map. We drew them in squares a mile wide from one known corner, at State and Madison.

entries.card: why:THIS COORDINATE IS NOT WHERE THE BUILDING STOOD AND THE RECO…
entries.text: THIS COORDINATE IS NOT WHERE THE BUILDING STOOD AND THE RECORD SAYS SO IN AS MANY WORDS. The site is attested twice over and both statements agree: Andreas scan p. 1149, 'The first slaughter-house was built on the south bank of the North Branch of the Chicago River, south of the Bloomingdale Road and opposite the North Chicago Rolling Mills'; and scan p. 1151, 'his log slaughter-house on the east side of the North Branch'. The two banks named are the same bank — the North Branch runs north-west out of the forks, so its east side and its south bank are one and the same face along that reach. Andreas scan p. 215 puts the family in the same country: 'Jonas Clybourne and John K. Clark lived several miles up the North Branch, where now are the North Chicago rolling-mills.' Bloomingdale Road is modern Bloomingdale Avenue, 1800 north on the Chicago grid; carried through the modern street grid that puts the site somewhere around 3 km north-north-west of this project's datum origin at the forks, in the neighbourhood of modern Cortland and the river. That figure is an estimate off the grid, not a survey, and it is stated so a later parcel can go and place the building properly. THE MODELLED TERRAIN BOX IS 640 m SQUARE, local E and N -320 to +320 (the heightfield data: 257 x 257 samples at 2.5 m from origin -320, -320), so the real site is roughly 2.8 km beyond its northern edge. Under the project owner's instruction of 2026-08-11 the building is placed at the edge of modelled ground rather than dropped, because a building nobody can see is a building nobody can correct. It is set on the correct BANK — the east side of the North Branch, about 14 m back from the traced bank line — at the northern limit of the modelled field, local N +294 to +306. Treat the coordinate as a placeholder with an error of kilometres, not metres, and the BANK and the setback as the only parts of it that carry evidence. Facade bearing 270, due west onto the branch: a slaughter-house works to the water, for the offal and for the boats, which is an argument from the trade and not a statement in any source. WHAT WOULD RESOLVE IT: extending the terrain epoch north up the North Branch, at which point this record moves to its attested reach and the position can be re-tagged.

levels.8-10: This is not where the building stood, and the card says so plainly. Where it stood is known twice, and both agree. A history book says the first slaughter house was built on the south bank of the North Branch. It was south of the Bloomingdale Road. It was across from the steel mills. Later it says his log slaughter house was on the east side of the North Branch. Those are the same bank. The North Branch runs north west from the forks. So along there, its east side is its south bank. The book also says Jonas Clybourne lived far up the North Branch, near the same mills. Bloomingdale Road is today's Bloomingdale Avenue. On today's map, that is about two miles north of the middle of our map, near Cortland Street. That is a guess from the street grid. It is not a survey. We give it so later work can place the building right. Our ground covers a square about 2,100 feet on each side. So the real spot is about one and three quarter miles past its north edge. The owner of this project said in August 2026 to put such buildings at the edge of our ground. Do not drop them.

entries.card: why:THIS COORDINATE IS NOT WHERE THE CABINS STOOD. What is attes…
entries.text: THIS COORDINATE IS NOT WHERE THE CABINS STOOD. What is attested is a REACH and not a point: Andreas puts Jonas Clybourne 'several miles up the North Branch, where now are the North Chicago rolling-mills' (scan p. 215), and the same family's slaughter-house on that bank 'south of the Bloomingdale Road and opposite the North Chicago Rolling Mills' (scan p. 1149). Carried through the modern grid — Bloomingdale Road is 1800 north — that is roughly 3 km north-north-west of this project's datum origin, an estimate off the street grid rather than a survey. The modelled terrain box is 640 m square, local E and N -320 to +320, so the real ground is some 2.8 km beyond its northern edge. Under the project owner's instruction of 2026-08-11 the cabins are placed at the edge of modelled ground rather than dropped. They are set on the correct BANK — the east side of the North Branch — about 36 m back from the traced bank line and about 60 m south of this dataset's Archibald Clybourne's Log Slaughter-House, which is displaced to the same edge for the same reason and which the sources put in the same family's ground. THE 60 m BETWEEN THEM IS INVENTED ENTIRELY: no source gives the distance from the cabins to the slaughter-house, and the two are placed within sight of each other because they belonged to one household, which is an argument about how a farm works and not a statement anybody made. Treat the coordinate as a placeholder with an error of kilometres. Facade bearing 270, due west onto the branch, which is the bearing this dataset gives every North Branch structure and is a convention, not a finding.

levels.8-10: This is not where the cabins stood. What is known is a stretch of river, not a spot. A history book puts Jonas Clybourne several miles up the North Branch, where the steel mills later stood. It puts the family's slaughter house on that bank, south of the Bloomingdale Road and across from the mills. Using today's streets, that is about two miles north north west of the middle of our map. That is a guess from the street grid, not a survey. Our ground covers a square about 2,100 feet on each side. So the real spot is about one and three quarter miles past its north edge. The owner of this project said in August 2026 to put such buildings at the edge of our ground and not drop them. They are on the right bank, the east side of the North Branch. They sit about 120 feet back from the bank, and about 200 feet south of the Clybourne slaughter house, which is moved to the same edge for the same reason. The 200 feet between them is all made up. No source gives it. We put them within sight of each other because one family owned both. That is a reason about how a farm works, not something anyone said. The spot could be off by miles.
