entries.text: THIS IS A BUILT-BY LINK AND NOT A WORKPLACE, and the grade says so. Andreas credits the log bridge across the South Branch between Randolph and Lake to Anson H. Taylor and his brother in 1832; the record of South Branch Bridge is this project's record of a crossing at that reach. Whether the raft bridge of 1835 is the same fabric as the log bridge of 1832 is a structures question this record does not settle. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR works at AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW the Anson Taylor household#works at, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start

levels.8-10: This link says who built it, not where they worked, and the grade says so. A history book says Anson H. Taylor and his brother built the log bridge over the South Branch, between Randolph and Lake, in 1832. Our South Branch Bridge card is the crossing there. We do not settle here if the raft bridge of 1835 is the same one as the log bridge of 1832. That is a question for the building card. This part is copied from his family's card, with nothing changed. That card names the place as of July 1, 1835, and dates neither end of the tie. So we leave this one undated, and do not use the scene date as a start.

entries.card: why:THIS PHASE BEGINS AT A CHANGE OF FABRIC, NOT AT A BUILD DATE…
entries.text: THIS PHASE BEGINS AT A CHANGE OF FABRIC, NOT AT A BUILD DATE. Andreas, printed p. 635: 'The Mansion House was built in 1831 by Dexter Graves; it stood on Lake near Dearborn and almost opposite the old Tremont House. As originally built, the Mansion House was situated some little distance back from the street, but TWO YEARS LATER Mr. Graves erected a FRAME ADDITION IN THE FRONT, which came out to a line with the street.' 1831 plus two years is 1833, and 1833-01-01 is the first day that year permits rather than a date anybody gives - the YEAR of the change is attested, the month is not, so the from date is a bound inside a documented year. The 1831 log tavern standing set back from Lake Street is the previous state and is NOT modelled as a separate phase: see the change note for why. THE END IS THE LAST ATTESTED EVENT IN THE BUILDING'S LIFE, not a demolition and not a guess - Andreas, on the succession of proprietors: 'In 1848 Jacob R. Bates took it. Two years later the greater part of the house was removed to the northwest corner of Lake Street and Michigan Avenue, and was fitted up as a hotel under the name of the Dearborn House.' BOTH ENDS ARE THEREFORE ATTESTED EVENTS IN THE BUILDING'S OWN LIFE - a dated change of fabric and a dated removal - which is why the range is tagged documented despite its width, the same reading the record of Green Tree Tavern takes for a forty-seven-year span. A SEVENTEEN-YEAR PHASE IS STILL TOO LONG TO BE ONE FORM-STATE, and that is a known limitation rather than a claim that nothing changed: the house demonstrably grew once already, and nothing dates any alteration between the 1833 frame addition and the 1850 removal. Split it the moment anything does.

levels.8-10: This stage starts when the building changed, not when it was built. A history book says Dexter Graves built the Mansion House in 1831. It stood on Lake Street near Dearborn, almost across from the old Tremont House. At first it sat some way back from the street. Two years later, Graves built a wood addition on the front, out to the street line. 1831 and two years makes 1833. We start on January 1, 1833, the first day that year allows. The year of the change is known, but not the month. The 1831 log tavern, set back from Lake Street, came before. We do not build it as its own stage. The end is the last known event in the building's life. It is not a guess, and it is not when it was torn down. The book says Jacob R. Bates took it in 1848. Two years later most of the house was moved to the corner of Lake Street and Michigan Avenue, and made into a hotel called the Dearborn House. So both ends are known events in the building's own life, a dated change and a dated move. That is why we call the dates known, even though they span many years. The Green Tree Tavern card does the same for 47 years. But seventeen years is still too long for one shape, and we know that.

entries.card: why:THIS VALUE IS THE LOG CORE'S, AND UNTIL 2026-08-10 IT CARRIE…
entries.text: THIS VALUE IS THE LOG CORE'S, AND UNTIL 2026-08-10 IT CARRIED THE FRAME RANGE'S. It read 'value 2, documented', with a note saying in as many words that the two storeys described the river-fronting range rather than the whole building — but log dwelling reads `stories` as the storey count of the log core, the range having its own frame addition stories, so the documented claim was being spent on the cabin and the range then took the archetype's default. The result was the composition inverted: a two-storey log cabin standing behind a shorter frame block, which is the opposite of every description of this building. The two-storey claim now sits on frame addition stories, where the archetype reads it and where the source's sentence actually points. ONE STOREY FOR THE CABIN IS INFERENCE, not attestation: no source gives the log part a height, and the reading rests on the 1833 view from the south bank — 'a two-story building and adjoining log cabin' — which only reads as a contrast if the cabin stood lower, together with the single-pen log house being the near-universal form at the forks. Recorded rather than assumed, because the number the archetype builds from should be the number a reader can argue with.

levels.8-10: This number is for the log part, and until August 10, 2026, it held the frame part's number. It used to say two storeys, known. A note said plainly that the two storeys were the frame part facing the river, not the whole building. But our rules read this number as the height of the log part. The frame part has its own number. So the known two storeys went to the cabin, and the frame part took our usual height. The result was upside down: a two storey log cabin behind a shorter frame block. That is the opposite of every account of this building. Now the two storeys sit on the frame part, where our rules read it and where the source's words point. One storey for the cabin is our guess, not proof. No source gives the log part a height. Our reading rests on an 1833 view from the south bank. It tells of a two storey building and a log cabin next to it. That only makes sense if the cabin was lower. And a one room log house was by far the most common kind here. We write it down so a reader can argue with the number we build from.

entries.card: why:THREE DOCUMENTED FORMER USES AND NO CURRENT ONE, AND THE REC…
entries.text: THREE DOCUMENTED FORMER USES AND NO CURRENT ONE, AND THE RECORD MUST NOT INVENT A FOURTH. Corrected 2026-09-04 on the owner's explicit instruction; before that this field read 'drug store' and the record was titled Philo Carpenter's Log Drug Store, which named a trade that had left the building three years before the scene date. THE CHAIN, in order, from "The History of Chicagoan Mark Beaubien, the Hospitality Guru began in 1830."…: 'In the late summer of 1832, he rented his original log cabin, adjacent to his Sauganash Tavern, to the newly arrived Philo Carpenter for use as - Chicago's 1st - drugstore. An ardent enemy of alcohol, Carpenter soon moved out. Mark next rented the space to John S. Wright, and in 1833, the cabin became a school under Eliza Chappel's direction.' "Eliza Emily Chappell, the First Chicago Teacher Paid by Public Funds in 1833."… dates and ends the school independently: it opened in September 1833 in 'a small log house formerly used as a store', and 'in 1834, the school was moved into the First Presbyterian Church'. Andreas corroborates the first link from a different direction, giving Carpenter's drug store a size and a street — 16 x 20 ft of log on Lake Street near the river. SO ON 1 JULY 1835 IT IS NEITHER A DRUG STORE NOR A SCHOOL. Carpenter's own advertisement in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 proves the trade was still his that month but carries no address, and he had built his South Water Street store the previous summer, so it cannot put the trade in this room. A dwelling is the likeliest use in a town where housing was scarce, and that is a guess, so the value says 'unattested' instead of making it — the same construction the record of Eliza Chappel's infant school and the record of Richard J. Hamilton's house on Michigan Street already use. THE TAG FOLLOWS THE WEAKEST HALF: the uses are documented, their ENDING before the scene date is documented, and what is inferred is that the building stood empty or in some unrecorded use rather than gone.

levels.8-10: This building had three known past uses and no known use now. We must not make up a fourth. The owner of this project told us to fix it on September 4, 2026. Before that, this part said drug store, and the card was called Philo Carpenter's Log Drug Store. That named a trade that had left the building three years before our scene. Here is the chain, in order. A web page says that in late summer 1832, Mark Beaubien rented his first log cabin, next to his Sauganash Tavern, to Philo Carpenter, who had just come. It was Chicago's first drug store. Carpenter was strongly against drink, and he soon moved out. Then Mark rented it to John S. Wright. In 1833 the cabin became a school, run by Eliza Chappel. Another page dates the school on its own. It opened in September 1833 in a small log house once used as a store. In 1834 the school moved into the First Presbyterian Church. A history book backs up the first step in another way. It gives Carpenter's drug store a size and a street: a log room 16 by 20 feet on Lake Street near the river. So on July 1, 1835, it is not a drug store or a school. Carpenter's own ad of November 1833 shows the trade was still his that month. But it gives no address, and he had built his South Water Street store the summer before.

entries.card: why:THREE UPPER FRONT SASH, other work categorical omission corr…
entries.text: THREE UPPER FRONT SASH, other work categorical omission correction. Direct review of the actual native9dd Trowbridge pair shows the model has two upper main-gable sash where the verified public-domain 1902 illustration clearly draws three. The earlier two-versus-three tolerance classification is withdrawn: this is a missing opening and remains OPEN until the genuine corrected native is rendered and reviewed. Andreas and Kurz show two fully legible upper sash plus a narrow/partly obscured left-edge detail at the shoulder junction; that earlier reading did not safely establish a historic two-window row. Adopt the clearly pictured three-station Trowbridge row as an evidence-bounded reconstruction for the early inn, without inventing an alteration date or declaring three independent contemporary witnesses. The chosen local-u fractions.20/.50/.78 match the existing ground stations, with the existing.85x1.35m sash and upper sill/head band retained. Those fractions, exact stock dimensions, trim, even vertical alignment and July1835 continuity are RECONSTRUCTED, not measured from the drawing. Only the main +y upper row changes: ground door/sash, rear and eaves rows, attic lights, completed left group, footprint, geographic placement and source rights/grades stay unchanged. No held c1859 photograph or site1859 engraving supplies geometry.

levels.8-10: There are three upper windows on the front, not two. Later work fixed this. A close look at the Trowbridge drawing shows our model has two upper windows on the main end wall. The 1902 drawing, free for anyone to use, clearly draws three. We used to say two or three was close enough. We take that back. A window is missing, and this stays open until the fixed model is drawn and checked. The other two pictures show two clear upper windows and something hard to see at the left edge. That did not prove a row of two. So we use the row of three from the Trowbridge drawing, as a guess bound by the proof. We do not make up a date for a change, and we do not claim three pictures from the time agree. The three windows line up with the ones on the ground floor. They keep the same window size and heights as before. Those spots, the sizes, the trim and that it stayed this way to July 1835 are our guesses, not measured from the drawing. Only the upper row on the main front changes. Nothing else changes. No 1859 photo or print gives us any shapes here.

entries.card: why:THREE WITNESSES ACROSS EIGHTEEN YEARS, AND NOT ONE OF THEM D…
entries.text:
THREE WITNESSES ACROSS EIGHTEEN YEARS, AND NOT ONE OF THEM DATES THE BUILDING. The range opens 1 January 1818 because that is the year Gurdon Hubbard reached Chicago and the year his inventory of the place describes (bk hub 063, leaf 76, printed p. 38); the house he found was older — he has Jouett in it as United States factor 'from 1804 to about the year 1810' and John Dean succeeding him 'at the second construction of the fort' — so 1818 IS A FLOOR ON THE RECORD AND NOT A CONSTRUCTION DATE, and no source this project holds gives one. What stands between that floor and the scene is two further sightings: Hurlbut has the American Fur Company buy 'the Factory House, located just south of Fort Dearborn' from the United States in 1822 and Jean Baptiste Beaubien move his family into it (bk afc 009), and the Harrison plan of 24 February 1830 letters `U.S. Factor's House` against the three blocks this record's position is read from.

IT CLOSES 29 DECEMBER 1836, the evacuation, and that is the same floor every Fort Dearborn record here carries rather than a demolition: nothing attests when the reservation's buildings came down.

WHAT CARRIES THE SCENE DATE OF 1 JULY 1835 is the middle of that range and not either end. A building three independent texts have standing in 1818, 1822 and 1830 is standing five years after the last of them unless something says it stopped, and nothing does. THAT ARGUMENT IS STRONGER HERE THAN AT THE OUT BUILDINGS NEXT DOOR, which rest on the plate alone; it is still an argument from silence about the last five years, and the grade says so. A fourth fact bears on the same five years without being read as occupancy: the Illinois land-sale register has John Baptist Baubian entering this ground on 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene — a pre-emption entry over the reservation, which is a transaction and not a sighting of a house.

levels.8-10: Three witnesses over eighteen years, and none of them dates the building. We start on January 1, 1818. That is the year Gurdon Hubbard came to Chicago, and the year his list of the place tells of. The house he found was older. He says Jouett lived in it as the government trader from 1804 to about 1810, and John Dean came after him when the fort was rebuilt. So 1818 is the earliest record, not the year it was built. No source we have gives that. Two more sightings stand between 1818 and our scene. One book says the fur company bought the trading house, just south of Fort Dearborn, from the government in 1822. Jean Baptiste Beaubien moved his family into it. And the Harrison plan of February 24, 1830 writes U.S. Factor's House beside the three blocks we place it from. It ends on December 29, 1836, when the troops left. Every Fort Dearborn card uses that same end. It is not when it was torn down. Nothing says when the fort's buildings came down. What keeps it in our scene is the middle of that span. A building three books show standing in 1818, 1822 and 1830 is still standing five years later, unless something says it stopped. Nothing does. That is a stronger case than for the out buildings next door, which rest on the plan alone.

entries.card: why:THREE, AND THREE IS A FIGURE THIS PROJECT STATES, NOT A COUN…
entries.text: THREE, AND THREE IS A FIGURE THIS PROJECT STATES, NOT A COUNT. Other work found no roll, census, annuity schedule or estimate that counts the Native and Métis people at Chicago on 1 July 1835 and refused to invent one (the 1835 native and metis data § the counted but unnamed); the owner then ruled one small camp built, bounded by a stated figure. Three tents is the fewest that reads as a camp and not as one household. It sizes no population and no count moves with it. “One trading family's camp at Wolf Point, a declared reconstruction the owner ruled built”.

levels.8-10: Three is a number we chose, not a count. Later work found no list, count or guess of the Native and mixed people at Chicago on July 1, 1835. It would not make one up. Then the owner of this project ruled that we build one small camp, with a number we state. Three tents is the fewest that looks like a camp and not one family. It does not set the size of any group, and no count changes with it. We list it as a guess that the owner ruled we build.

entries.card: why:TOWN TREASURER TWICE AND TRUSTEE TWICE - the most continuous…
entries.text: TOWN TREASURER TWICE AND TRUSTEE TWICE - the most continuously documented office-holder in the dataset. Elected trustee 10 August 1833 with 26 of 28 votes (tied top of the poll with Owen), appointed town treasurer at the board's first business meeting on 4 September 1833, and elected trustee AND treasurer again at the third town election of July 1835 (Andreas, scan pp. 273, 369). He is therefore in office on the scene date on the face of the record. Also a provision packer: this dataset holds two slaughtering and packing buildings under his name. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Dole, George W.” (poll 1833 010, line 31); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Dole, George W.” (tax 1833 025, line 77); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Dole, George W.” (poll 1834 034, line 203). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — other work applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Dole' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (the voter crosswalk data). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “George W. Dole” as treasurer (f1839 r0005, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Dole' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins G. (the fergus 1839 election crosswalk 1835 data and the fergus 1839 register crosswalk 1835 data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “DOLE GEORGE W”, 1833-10-22 to 1833-10-24: 4 parcels of the school section — BL73 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL75 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 3 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 6 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 9.07 acres stated in all, for $500.50 (ls0147, ls0148, ls0149, ls0150). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: DOLE GEORGE W matches George Washington Dole: the forename names George Washington Dole of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (the resident crosswalk data). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Geo. W. Dole” (33SQ-GYYJ-RJ, printed page 233, line 12). This project has ruled the head a MATCH for this person: the full name agrees, it is unique on both sides, and a discriminator independent of the name — directory persistence — separately places the same person in Chicago after the 1840 book was taken. Under the rule that decided it (“Sauganash Hotel: the pre-1830 position is not represented” matched), by the crosswalk's own ladder (the resident crosswalk data). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. Other work applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Dole, George W. | Letter. | June I, 1842. | Dismissed.” (second presb 0551, printed page 184), admitted 1842-06-01 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Dole' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins G. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with other work, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

levels.8-10: He was town treasurer twice and on the town board twice. He held office longer than anyone else we have on record. He was elected to the board on August 10, 1833, with 26 of 28 votes, tied for the most with Owen. He was made town treasurer at the board's first working meeting on September 4, 1833. He was elected to the board and as treasurer again at the town vote of July 1835. So the record shows he was in office on our scene date. He also packed meat. We have two slaughter and packing buildings under his name. The town's own lists of voters and taxes, from 1833 to 1835, name this person 3 times. Each one says a man of that name was on that list that year, and no more. We read them in a copy others made, not the first papers. They back up the name, but they do not change how sure we are. A Chicago book of names from 1839 has this person in its later lists. That shows they were in Chicago in 1837 or later. It is not proof about 1835, and it does not change how sure we are. The state's old book of land sales shows this person bought land 4 times. A sale is not a home. It does not show that they lived here. This land was set aside for schools and sold in town lots in 1833. It is closer to this town than a farm would be. But it is still only a sale. It names a buyer, not someone who lived there. The count of 1840 in Chicago lists the head of a house with this name. We judged it is this same person. But 1840 is five years after this town, so it says nothing sure about 1835. Our rules say a name from 1839 or 1840 alone does not make someone a person of 1835. A family from 1840 is not read back to 1835 either. This backs up the name, but it does not change how sure we are. A list of the members of the Second Presbyterian Church has a line with the same last name and first letter. That church list starts in 1842, so it is no proof about 1835.

entries.card: why:TWENTY-FIVE FEET, AND NOBODY MEASURED IT — the same inventio…
entries.text: TWENTY-FIVE FEET, AND NOBODY MEASURED IT — the same invention the north pier carries, from the same archetype constant, so that both structures inherit one guess a reader can find in one place rather than two that could drift apart. Not one source reached states how wide either Chicago pier was in the 1830s, and the master survey cannot supply it: Wright 1834 is drawn at about 1:7,200, where a 25-ft crib is 0.13 mm on the paper and about a fifth of the width of the pen that drew the pier line. The red bands on that sheet are line weight; measuring one would be measuring the draughtsman's nib. The only argument behind the number is that a gravity crib standing in open lake and carrying a working deck cannot be narrow, which supports 'not narrow' and not twenty-five feet. Graded conjectural, and the footprint it draws is graded with it. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: J. D. Graham's 1857 and 1858 hydrographic surveys of the Chicago bar, named in the research notes on terrain hydrology, or any specification or voucher for the crib work.

levels.8-10: It is about 25 feet wide, and nobody measured it. No source we found says how wide either Chicago pier was in the 1830s. The 1834 map cannot tell us either. It is drawn so small that a 25 foot pier would be thinner than the pen line that drew it. The red bands on that map are just the width of the pen. Measuring one would be measuring the pen's tip, not the pier. The only reason behind the number is that a heavy wood pier standing in the open lake, with a deck to work on, cannot be narrow. That shows it was not narrow. It does not show it was 25 feet. Both piers use the same number, from one place in our rules, so a reader can find the guess once. We call it a guess, and the shape it draws too. Papers from the time, like plans, reports, surveys or bills for the work, would settle it.

entries.card: why:TWENTY-FIVE FEET, AND NOBODY MEASURED IT. Not one source rea…
entries.text: TWENTY-FIVE FEET, AND NOBODY MEASURED IT. Not one source reached states how wide either Chicago pier was in the 1830s. THE MASTER SURVEY CANNOT SUPPLY IT EITHER, and that is worth stating precisely because the same sheet supplies this record's bearing and root. Wright 1834 is drawn at about 1:7,200. At that scale a 25-ft crib is 0.13 mm on the paper, about a fifth of the width of the pen that drew the pier line; the red bands on the sheet are line weight and nothing else, so the drafted pier carries a direction and a position and no thickness at all. Measuring the drawn band would be measuring the draughtsman's nib. THE VALUE IS THE ARCHETYPE'S CONSTANT, kept in one place so that both piers in this dataset inherit the same invention and a reader can find it once. The only argument behind it is that a gravity crib standing in up to twelve feet of water and carrying a working deck cannot be narrow, which is an argument for 'not narrow' and not an argument for twenty-five feet. Graded conjectural, and the footprint it draws is graded with it. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the Chief Engineer's reports, a harbour survey of the 1840s or 1850s showing the piers in plan at a usable scale — J. D. Graham's 1857 and 1858 hydrographic surveys of the bar are named in the research notes on terrain hydrology and are the best candidate — or any specification for the crib work.

levels.8-10: It is about 25 feet wide, and nobody measured it. No source we found says how wide either Chicago pier was in the 1830s. The 1834 map cannot tell us either. It is drawn so small that a 25 foot pier would be thinner than the pen line that drew it. The red bands on that map are just the width of the pen. Measuring one would be measuring the pen's tip, not the pier. The only reason behind the number is that a heavy wood pier standing in the open lake, with a deck to work on, cannot be narrow. That shows it was not narrow. It does not show it was 25 feet. Both piers use the same number, from one place in our rules, so a reader can find the guess once. We call it a guess, and the shape it draws too. Papers from the time, like plans, reports, surveys or bills for the work, would settle it.

entries.card: why:TWO CABINS ARE STATED AND ONE IS BUILT. the research notes o…
entries.text: TWO CABINS ARE STATED AND ONE IS BUILT. the research notes on structures north section 3.6 says the family built two log cabins on the north branch and tags it [DOC] without naming a source; Andreas's full-text index does not return the phrasing, which is not proof it is absent. The count is therefore carried as inference rather than attestation. The mesh shows a single cabin, so this value does not drive geometry and says so: a second polygon would need an invented spacing, an invented orientation and an invented relationship to the first, which is three inventions to express one number that is itself second-hand. The honest arrangement is one cabin standing for the pair with the shortfall declared. This is the same treatment Log cabins at Wolf Point gives Wau-Bun's 'two or three log cabins'.

levels.8-10: Two cabins are told of, and we build one. Our notes say the family built two log cabins on the North Branch. They mark it as known, but name no source. A search of the history book does not find those words, though that does not prove they are not there. So we count the two as worked out, not proven. The model shows one cabin, so this number does not change the shape, and we say so. A second cabin would need a made up space between them, a made up facing and a made up link to the first. That is three guesses to show one number that is itself second hand. The honest way is one cabin standing for the pair, with the gap said out loud. The Log cabins at Wolf Point card does the same for a book's two or three log cabins.

entries.card: why:TWO LEAVES, AND THIS IS THE PROJECT CHOOSING, WHICH IT SAID…
entries.text: TWO LEAVES, AND THIS IS THE PROJECT CHOOSING, WHICH IT SAID FOR TEN DAYS IT WOULD NOT DO. form.draw lifting gear enumerates three arrangements that fit every word of Andreas: one leaf, two leaves, or the whole opening lifted bodily. The two engravings in the 2026-08-18 owner brief (README images 2 and 3) draw a chain to each side of the draw from each frame, which is what a two-leaf draw looks like and is not what the other two look like. A pictorial (a modern reconstruction) view is not strong enough to make that `inferred` about an 1834 mechanism — see the contamination argument on draw lifting gear — so the count is graded `reconstructed`: invented within bounds, the bounds being the plate. WHAT IT PUTS IN THE MESH, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY MODEST. Not a raised leaf and not a hinge: a bearing timber across the deck at each end of the opening, an edge beam down each side of each leaf, and the two leaves' ends butted at the centre of the draw with a finger of daylight between them. The deck boards run through underneath, so the crossing is exactly as walkable as it was and the timber stands 55 mm proud — a threshold, not a step. A visitor sees where the bridge opened; a visitor is not told it is open. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the February 1834 proposals Andreas mentions, the trustees' specification, the twenty-five-dollar premium drawing, or the 1834-35 repair vouchers. Recorded in the liberties register “The Dearborn drawbridge, built to its engravings: the frames' bracing, the hoist chains, a two-leaf draw and a railed deck”.

levels.8-10: Two halves, and this is us choosing. For ten days we said we would not. Our notes list three ways the bridge could open that fit every word of the history book: one half lifting, two halves lifting, or the whole middle lifted up. The owner of this project sent two old pictures in August 2026. Both draw a chain from each frame to each side of the opening part. That is what a two half bridge looks like, and not the other two. A picture made long after is not strong enough to mark how an 1834 bridge worked as worked out. So we mark the count as a guess, made within limits set by the pictures. What we build for it is kept small on purpose. It is not a raised half and not a hinge. It is a beam across the floor at each end of the opening, a side beam down each half, and the two halves meeting in the middle with a thin crack of daylight between them. The floor boards run on under them, so the bridge is just as easy to walk as before. The beam stands about two inches up, like a door sill, not a step. A visitor sees where the bridge opened. A visitor is not told it is open. Papers from the time, like plans, reports, surveys or bills for the work, would settle it.

entries.card: why:TWO SMALL SIDE POSTERNS, NOT AN ADDITIONAL PAIR OF LARGE GAT…
entries.text: TWO SMALL SIDE POSTERNS, NOT AN ADDITIONAL PAIR OF LARGE GATES. Actual Wau-Bun ch.XVII paragraph independently reread10November2026 at the existing source URL: Large gates opened to the north and south, and there were small posterns here and there for the accommodation of the inmates. The conjunction distinguishes small additional openings; the plural does not give a count, side, metric size, exact place or carpentry. Two is the minimum plural and our bounded choice. Each is1.5m wide, the supported narrow wicket kit: one at east-wall localv41.0m (offset+14.5), in the gap between barracks and sutler, and one at west-wall localv11.5m (offset-15), between blockhouse and officers’ range. Both use one inward-swinging paling leaf at existing wall height, safely shut initially. The south/north main gates, their3.6m spans and positions stay unchanged. These seats, width, leaf construction, same-height head and swing are reconstructed liberties rather than mapped postern marks. They avoid occupied building footprints and do not borrow the first fort’s separately attested west wicket.

levels.8-10: These are two small side doors, not another pair of big gates. On November 10, 2026, we read again the line from the book. It says big gates opened to the north and south, and there were small doors here and there for the people inside. The words tell us these were small, extra openings. More than one is said, but not how many, which side, how big, where, or how they were built. Two is the fewest that makes more than one, and that is our choice. Each is about five feet wide. One is in the east wall, in the gap between the soldiers' rooms and the trader's store. One is in the west wall, between the blockhouse and the officers' rooms. Each has one gate of fence boards, as tall as the wall, that opens inward and starts shut. The big north and south gates stay the same. Where these doors stand, how wide, how they are built and how they swing are our guesses, not marks on a plan. They keep clear of buildings. We do not borrow the first fort's known west door.

entries.card: why:TWO SOURCES ON ONE PAGE GIVE TWO DIFFERENT PARADE GROUNDS AN…
entries.text: TWO SOURCES ON ONE PAGE GIVE TWO DIFFERENT PARADE GROUNDS AND THIS PROJECT DOES NOT AVERAGE THEM. The key to the 1855 photograph: 'C is the parade-ground (80x250 ft.)'. Robert Fergus, of the same fort in 1850: 'about 80 feet wide, and extended from the river bank south, the full length of the enclosure - say 400 feet'. Eighty by two hundred and eighty by four hundred are not the same rectangle, and the research notes on structures south records only the first, as documented. IT IS GRADED INFERRED HERE. What this polygon actually is: 21.8 x 33.2 m, about 71 x 109 ft, the court the 1830 plan leaves between the ranges. The WIDTH agrees with both later sources to about 11 percent, which is the check that the derived scale is reading the plate. The LENGTH agrees with neither, and the likeliest reading of that is that both later figures describe the compound AFTER the stockade came down, when the 'enclosure' was a board fence running from the river bank south - which is exactly what Fergus says his 400 ft is measured between. A third witness supports the split: Juliette Kinzie, inside the stockaded fort in 1831, says the parade-ground 'extended south of the pickets', so there was drill ground outside the south gate as well as court inside. That outside ground is NOT modelled - nothing gives its extent. Other work source transcription correction: direct actual1881printedp93 was visually reread10November2026; its1855key says80x250ft, not the previously transcribed80x200ft. The later extent remains a different state and the existing1830-plan court is unchanged.

levels.8-10: Two sources on one page give two different parade grounds, and we do not split the difference. The key to the 1855 photo says the parade ground was 80 by 250 feet. Robert Fergus, of the same fort in 1850, says it was about 80 feet wide, and ran from the river bank south the full length of the fort, about 400 feet. Those are not the same box. Our notes record only the first, as known. Here we call it worked out. Our shape is about 71 by 109 feet, the yard the 1830 plan leaves between the buildings. The width agrees with both later sources to about one part in ten. That is the check that our scale reads the plan right. The length agrees with neither. Most likely both later sizes tell of the fort after the old wall came down. Then the edge was a board fence running from the river bank south. That is just what Fergus says his 400 feet was measured between. A third witness backs this up. Juliette Kinzie, inside the fort in 1831, says the parade ground ran south of the fence. So there was drill ground outside the south gate as well as the yard inside. We do not build that outside ground, since nothing gives its size. On November 10, 2026, later work read the 1881 page again and found it says 80 by 250 feet, not 80 by 200 as we had copied it.

entries.card: why:TWO STEPS, BOTH STATED. Wau-Bun puts a striker's residence i…
entries.text: TWO STEPS, BOTH STATED. Wau-Bun puts a striker's residence in this ring; Andreas and the 1830-31 agency staffing name Joseph Porthier as the striker — 'and Joseph Porthier as striker' — and his own household card already carries works at: Government Blacksmith Shop at attested, 'the same shop as McKee'. So the office is attested in the ring and the man is attested in the office, and the seat is the join of the two. His card carried lives at: null with the note 'Not attested in anything this project holds', which was true of his NAME and not of his OFFICE; that is the gap this record closes. Inferred, not attested: no source puts this man in any building.

levels.8-10: Two steps, and we state both. A book puts the home of a smith's helper in this ring. A history book and the 1830 agency staff list name Joseph Porthier as the helper. His own card already says he worked at the Government blacksmith shop, the same shop as McKee, and that is known. So the job is known to be in the ring, and the man is known to have the job. We seat him here by joining the two. His card used to give him no home, with a note that nothing we have shows one. That was true of his name, but not of his job. This card fills that gap. We call it worked out, not proven, because no source puts this man in any building.

entries.card: why:TWO TALL TIMBER FRAMES, ONE AT EITHER END OF THE DRAW, AND T…
entries.text: TWO TALL TIMBER FRAMES, ONE AT EITHER END OF THE DRAW, AND THEY ARE THE SILHOUETTE THIS BRIDGE IS REMEMBERED BY. Andreas: 'It was of the "gallows pattern," and for five years, the frames, one at either end, stood like instruments of death to frighten the timid stranger at night.' And, of the occasion the machinery jammed: 'for forty-eight hours the gallows frames held the draw suspended in mid-air.' The count and the arrangement are as well attested as anything on this record, and 'either end' is either end of the DRAW rather than of the bridge — the same sentence pairs the frames with the draw hanging between them. THEY ARE BUILT, as of 2026-08-11, and the archetype grew a draw to do it: two heavy posts straddling the deck under a lapped cross-head, at the two ends of the sixty-foot opening. What is documented is how many and where. Everything about their SIZE is conjectural and the whole frame carries that confidence — see form.gallows height (m) — so the feature a visitor sees first is also the one the confidence view dithers hardest, which is the correct way round.

levels.8-10: Two tall wood frames, one at each end of the lifting part. They are the shape this bridge is remembered by. A history book says it was of the gallows kind. For five years the frames, one at each end, stood like tools of death and scared the timid stranger at night. When the lifting part jammed, the frames held it up in mid air for forty-eight hours. How many there were and how they stood are as well known as anything on this card. Each end means each end of the lifting part, not of the whole bridge. The same line has the frames with the lifting part hanging between them. We have built them since August 11, 2026, and our rules grew a lifting part to do it. Each is two heavy posts on either side of the floor, with a beam across the top, at the two ends of the sixty foot opening. What is known is how many and where. Everything about their size is a guess, and the whole frame is marked that way. So the thing a visitor sees first is also the one our sureness view marks weakest. That is the right way round.

entries.card: why:TWO WITNESSES PUT THIS BARN IN THE SAME PLACE, TWICE, AND TH…
entries.text:
TWO WITNESSES PUT THIS BARN IN THE SAME PLACE, TWICE, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS INFERRED RATHER THAN CONJECTURAL. The plate names it — Big Barn with Cupola, lettered beside a drawn building west-south-west of the fort — and Gurdon Hubbard, describing the same ground from memory of the late 1820s, writes: 'West, and a little south, of the fort was the military barn, adjoining which, on the east, was the fort garden, of about four acres' (Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard…, leaf 75, printed p. 37, committed text lines 2392-2399). THE SECOND CLAUSE IS THE CHECK, and it is a strong one: the fort garden is already committed, independently, as Fort Dearborn — the garrison garden. Its polygon's nearest corner stands 36.4 m from the position this record derives, and the garden lies east and a little south of the barn — which is Hubbard's sentence, in coordinates neither he nor this record's derivation had sight of. Nothing was moved to make that come out.

READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN, BY THE SAME RULE AS THE ELEVEN RECORDS ALREADY TAKEN FROM IT. Internet Archive leaf n242 of historyofchicago01andr (Andreas vol. 1, p. 113), rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise so the sheet's own true-north arrow stands vertical, is 2715 x 2003 px. On that image the stockade's ink runs from x 1356 to x 1535 and from y 553 to y 730, so the enclosure's centre is pixel (1445, 644); the committed palisade record hangs that centre on local E +1152, N +221, which is UTM 448224.70 E, 4637616.80 N. Pixels convert at 1.10 ft/px (0.33528 m/px), the scale the research notes on fort dearborn section 3 derives from the commandant's quarters. THE ANCHOR AND THE SCALE ARE CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED, and the check is the garrison garden — the one thing on this plate that is both drawn and already committed. Its committed centre lands at pixel (1209, 1008) under this transform; the drawn diamond's centre measures (1207, 1002). Seven pixels, 2.3 m. A second check runs the other way: the committed blockhouse centre predicts pixel (1385, 698) and the drawn blockhouse square measures (1375, 710), 16 px or 5.4 m. WHAT THE TRANSFORM CANNOT DO is beat its own inputs. The enclosure measures 180 px across at this scale, which is 60 m against the committed palisade's 53 m — a 13 % spread, inside the +/-20 % the scale carries, and the reason is visible on the plate: 180 px is the OUTER edge of an engraved line four to six pixels thick. So carry +/-20 % on this offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself, exactly as every plate-derived record here does.

THE PIXEL. The drawn barn is a hatched parallelogram whose four corners measure (1118, 872), (1140, 892), (1110, 925) and (1088, 905), centre (1114.0, 898.5) — 331 px west and 254.5 px south of the fort centre, which is 111.0 m west and 85.3 m south of it.

IT IS NOT BEAUBIEN'S BARN, and the question is worth answering because the two stand 50 m apart, which is inside the error either carries. the record of Col. Jean Baptiste Beaubien's Barn is the old cabin Jean Baptiste Beaubien had lived in before 1817 and afterwards used as a barn, placed by eye inside his own group on Block 5; this is the garrison's barn, drawn on a military plan inside the fort's fenced ground and called 'the military barn' by a man who walked through it. Different owner, different evidence, different enclosure. They are not distinguishable by distance and they do not need to be.

levels.8-10: Two witnesses put this barn in the same place, twice. That is why we call it worked out, not just a guess. The 1830 plan names it, Big Barn with Cupola, beside a building west and a bit south of the fort. Gurdon Hubbard tells of the same ground from his memory of the late 1820s. He says west and a little south of the fort was the army barn. Next to it, on the east, was the fort garden, of about four acres. The second part of his line is the check, and a strong one. We had already placed the fort garden on its own. Its nearest corner is about 120 feet from where we place this barn. The garden lies east and a little south of the barn. That is just what Hubbard says, in places that neither he nor our reading of the plan could see. Nothing was moved to make that come out. We read the barn off the 1830 Harrison plan in a history book, in the same way as the eleven other cards from this plan.

entries.card: why:TWO, AND IT REPLACES FIFTEEN. The 1883 old-settlers statemen…
entries.text: TWO, AND IT REPLACES FIFTEEN. The 1883 old-settlers statement at Andreas pp. 631-632 says both branch bridges 'were built on abutments and two "bents"', with 'stringers of heavy logs stretched from the abutments to the bents, and between the bents' — a three-span crossing, stated twice over in one sentence. The attribute this replaces was pier spacing (m), and the change is a different PARAMETER rather than a different number: a spacing is a builder's convenience that no witness would remember, a count is what a user of a bridge does remember, and dividing a span by the archetype's 4.5 m default is what put fifteen supports in a river that had two. bridge timber now takes pier count and falls back to a spacing only where nobody described the middle. WHAT IS STILL THE ARCHETYPE'S IS WHERE THEY STAND: the letter puts the bents 'in deeper water' between abutments 'in the shallow water near the banks' and gives no station for either, so the two are built at the third points of the span because that is what a builder would do, not because anybody wrote it down. The confidence chip on this row grades HOW MANY and nothing else — the liberties register “The two bents are where a builder would put them, not where anybody saw them” is the only place the positions are admitted. THE ORIGINAL NOTE ON THE ATTRIBUTE THIS SUPERSEDES, which is the reasoning the invention was made under: NOT ATTESTED IN ANY FORM. Nothing reached says how many supports this bridge had, how far apart they stood, or whether it had any at all between its abutments. It must have had some — 71.83 m is far beyond any log stringer — but the number is the archetype's default, retained deliberately rather than replaced by a fresh guess, and it sets the bay count at 16 and therefore puts 15 cribs in the river. That was the most conspicuous invention in this structure and it was answerable all along, in a footnote under a paragraph this project had been quoting for weeks.

levels.8-10: Two, and it takes the place of fifteen. An 1883 account by the old settlers says both river branch bridges were built on two end supports and two middle supports. It says heavy logs ran from the ends to the middle supports, and between the middle supports. That makes three spans, said twice in one line. What this replaces was a spacing between supports. This change is a different kind of number, not just a new number. A spacing is a builder's choice that no one would remember. A count is what someone who used a bridge does remember. Our rules split the span by a set spacing of about fifteen feet. That put fifteen supports in a river that had two. Now our bridge rules take a count, and use a spacing only where no one told of the middle. Where they stand is still our rules' choice. The account puts the middle supports in deeper water, and the end ones in the shallow water near the banks. It gives no spot for either. So we build the two at the thirds of the span, because that is what a builder would do, not because anyone wrote it down. The sureness mark on this row is for how many and nothing else. Our list of guesses says the spots were picked, not seen. The old note said nothing showed how many supports this bridge had or how far apart they stood.

entries.card: why:The First Baptist Church was organised on 19 October 1833 wi…
entries.text: The First Baptist Church was organised on 19 October 1833 with nineteen members and Rev. Allen B. Freeman; Andreas calls this structure 'a small house of worship belonging to the First Baptist Church Society' by December 1833. Sproat's school is Andreas's. THE SHARED USE BY METHODISTS AND PRESBYTERIANS ENDED IN JANUARY 1834 and is not carried forward to the scene date: by 1835 the Presbyterians had their own building at Lake and Clark, which is a separate record here, and the Methodist meeting house is a north- or west-bank building (see Walker Meeting House and the exclusions record). A SECOND COMPILER PUTS THE SCHOOL IN THIS SAME BUILDING, BY THE SAME STREET AND CROSS STREET. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 2 (1895), printed page 79, the reading bk mose2 003: Sproat 'established an English and classical school for boys, occupying for that purpose the First Baptist church, a small frame building located on South Water street near Franklin', with 'Miss Sarah L. Warren (afterwards Mrs. Abel E. Carpenter)' his assistant from the spring of 1834. That is the Andreas building and the Andreas school under the Andreas street, so it corroborates this record rather than adding a second meeting house: the town has ONE First Baptist building near Franklin on South Water, and it is this one. The volume spells him Granville; Andreas and this record keep Grenville.

It has its own card. The Methodists met on the north or west bank. A second book puts the school in this same building, on the same streets. It says Sproat started a school for boys in the First Baptist church. That was a small wood building on South Water Street near Franklin. Miss Sarah L. Warren helped him from spring 1834. She later wed Abel E. Carpenter. That is the same building, school and street as the first book. So it backs up this card. It does not add a second church. The town had one First Baptist church near Franklin, and it is this one. That book spells his name Granville. The first book and this card keep Grenville.

entries.card: why:The building's purpose is documented and its completion date…
entries.text:
The building's purpose is documented and its completion date is documented, and between them they make the scene-date function a construction site rather than a hotel. Andreas: 'Chicago did, however, have a really grand hotel as early as 1835; this was the Lake House... The hotel was completed and thrown open to the public in the autumn of 1836, Jacob Russel, of Middleton, Conn., assuming control of its management.' The men behind it are documented too and are worth carrying because they are the town's commercial leadership rather than innkeepers: Gurdon S. Hubbard, General David S. Hunter, John H. Kinzie, Dr W. B. Egan and Major James B. Campbell - 'the men whose enterprise led them into building a house which for those days was far in advance of the needs of the town'.

AND THE SCENE-YEAR PRESS DATES THE SITE, WHICH ANDREAS DOES NOT. 'There is [a] new house building in Kinzie's addition [to be] named we understand, the "Lake Hous[e]."' — the Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1835-06-10, the same paragraph that reports the Sauganash freshly refitted. Both halves are load-bearing. IT IS A BUILDING SITE three weeks before the scene date, north of the main branch, which is what makes hotel under construction an attested function at 1835-07-01 rather than a back-projection from the 1836 opening. AND ITS NAME IS STILL SECOND-HAND — 'we understand' — so on the scene date the town has an unfinished building that people are calling the Lake House and not a hotel with a sign. The same paragraph contains an editorial proposal for a house 'about double the size of that latter' near the centre of Lake Street on this side of the river. The comparison expresses a desired relative hotel size; it supplies no measured dimensions or July construction stage and does not establish the Lake House's rank among existing buildings. The proposal is not an existing-house observation and does not prove that the suggested site was vacant.

Fergus's 1876 recollection of the 1839 hotel is included here only for later establishment identity and the conflicting Rush/North Water address, not as evidence of the July 1835 construction stage, position or dimensions. Its Hotels entry was directly checked at the printed page; the existing contemporary project notice remains the evidence for work before the scene date.

levels.8-10: We know what the building was for and when it was finished. Together they make it a building site in our scene, not a hotel. A history book says Chicago had a really grand hotel as early as 1835, the Lake House. It was done and opened in the fall of 1836. Jacob Russel ran it. The men behind it are known too. They were not inn keepers. They were the men who led the town's trade. They were Hubbard, Hunter, Kinzie, Egan and Campbell. The book says they built a house far ahead of what the town needed then. A paper from our scene year dates the site, which the book does not. The Chicago Democrat of June 10, 1835 says a new house is going up in Kinzie's Addition. It says it will be named, we understand, the Lake House. The same news tells of the Sauganash, just fixed up. Both halves matter. It is a building site three weeks before our scene, north of the river. So a hotel being built is a known use on July 1, 1835. It is not just a guess back from the 1836 opening. entries.card: why:The garrison's provision store. Destroyed with the barracks…
entries.text:
The garrison's provision store. Destroyed with the barracks in the September 1827 lightning fire and standing again on the 1830 plan; see Fort Dearborn — soldiers' barracks for what that does and does not establish.

THE ARMY'S OWN CONTRACT NOTICES NAME THIS BUILDING AND SAY WHAT WENT IN AT ITS DOOR. Two printings of the Fort Dearborn beef proposals — Chicago Democrat 28 May 1834, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-05-28, and 4 June 1834, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1834-06-04 — require the contractor's fresh beef to be delivered in quarters 'at the store house of Fort Dearborn', which the second printing calls 'the subsistance store house of Fort Dearborn', 'in such quarters and at such times as the Assistant Commissary of Subsistence may require', not more than three times a week nor less than once, 'amounting probably to 400 pounds per week'. So this range was the post's PROVISION store: the receiving door for the garrison's meat, worked by the commissary, reached by a contractor's cart two or three mornings a week. The weekly poundage is the notice's own estimate of what the garrison ate and is recorded as an estimate. WHAT IS NOT TAKEN FROM IT: the notices do not say which range, which face or which door, so no position, footprint or opening is changed here — the fort's buildings stand where the 1830 survey and Andreas put them. Nor is the thirteen-month gap to the scene date closed: the fresh-beef contract advertised over the same fort in the scene month names no building at all.

levels.8-10: This was the fort's food store. It burned with the soldiers' rooms when lightning struck in September 1827, and it stands again on the 1830 plan. See the soldiers' rooms card for what that does and does not show. The army's own ads for meat name this building and say what came in its door. Two printings of the Fort Dearborn beef ads, in May and June 1834, ask the seller to bring fresh beef, in quarters, to the store house of Fort Dearborn. The second calls it the food store house. The beef was to come when the officer in charge of food asked, not more than three times a week and not less than once. It was likely about 400 pounds a week. So this building was the fort's food store. It was the door where the meat came in, run by the food officer, with a seller's cart coming two or three mornings a week. The weekly weight is the ad's own guess at what the fort ate, and we keep it as a guess. Here is what we do not take from it. The ads do not say which building, side or door. So we change no spot, shape or opening. And the thirteen months to our scene are still a gap. The beef ad for the same fort in our scene month names no building.

entries.card: why:The partnership is documented; that it was trading on 1835-0…
entries.text: The partnership is documented; that it was trading on 1835-07-01 specifically is the inference, since Andreas dates it only to the 1830s. A NAME COLLISION WORTH KEEPING SEPARATE: a W. Kimball is named in the transcription of the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 as advertising dry goods, crockery, hardware, cutlery, caps and cloth from a new store at the corner of South Water and Clark. Dry goods and drugs are different trades and there is no evidence the two Kimballs are one man; that advertisement is discussed on The Chicago Democrat Office and is deliberately not attached here. THE INFERENCE THIS NOTE RESTED ON IS NOW A READING: P. PRUYNE & CO. IS TRADING SEVEN DAYS AFTER THE SCENE DATE. The firm advertises continuously across the corpus from 1833-12-03 to 1835-07-08 — "Wholesale and Retail. STORE BETWEEN CLARK AND DEARBORN-STREETS. P. PRUYNE & CO. WOULD respectfully inform their friends and [the] public that they have just receive[d] a large addition to their former Stock, whic[h] [m]akes it one of the most extensi[v]e in Chicago, consisting of Groceries, Hardware, Crockery, Glassware, A LARGE ASSORTMENT OF DRUGS & MEDICINES, BOOTS AND SHOES, IRON AND STEEL, WINDOW GLASS" (The Chicago Democrat, 1833-12-03, page 3 column 4, claim the Chicago Democrat of 1833-12-03, dateline 'Chicago, Dec. 3, 1833'), the same standing card reprinted through 1834, and the run reaching 1835-07-08. So 'trading on 1835-07-01 specifically' is no longer the inference it was: it is bracketed by printings either side of the date. WHAT THE PAPERS DO NOT SETTLE, AND IT IS THE INTERESTING HALF. The firm advertising is P. PRUYNE & CO. and never 'Pruyne & Kimball' — no printing reached names Kimball as the partner — so the PARTNERSHIP stays Andreas's and this record's `name` stays his word. And the address the firm gives is a BLOCK FACE and not a frontage: "between Clark and Dearborn streets" names the two cross streets and not the street it fronts, and Clark and Dearborn are one block apart on South Water, Lake, Water and Randolph alike. This record's South Water Street placement is Andreas's and is CONSISTENT with the advertisement without being confirmed by it; supplying South Water here from this line would be an invention the evidence does not carry, and the extraction refuses it for the same reason. THE W. KIMBALL COLLISION ABOVE IS UNAFFECTED and stays separate. THE READING IS TRANSCRIPTION-MEDIATED AND SAYS SO. Under the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 a claim read through this project's OCR-assisted transcriptions rather than off the page scan grades `attested` in this schema's vocabulary while carrying its own flag: reading = transcription mediated, with the transcription's own uncertainty brackets preserved inside the quotation rather than tidied away. Where a scan is later read, the scan is the authority and this claim upgrades under it — the standard The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday… set when a scan caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'.

levels.8-10: The business is known. That it was open on July 1, 1835 is our guess. The history book dates it only to the 1830s. Two men share a name, and we keep them apart. The Chicago Democrat of November 26, 1833 names a W. Kimball. He sold cloth, dishes, tools, knives and caps. His new store was at the corner of South Water and Clark. Cloth and drugs are different trades. Nothing shows the two Kimballs are one man. That ad is told on the card for the paper's office. We do not tie it here, on purpose. This note used to guess. Now we can read it in the paper. It names P. Pruyne and Company. The store was open seven days after our scene. The firm put out ads all through our papers, from December 3, 1833 to July 8, 1835. It sold both in bulk and by the piece. The store was between Clark and Dearborn Streets. The ad says P. Pruyne and Company have just got a large new stock. It makes their store one of the biggest in Chicago. They sell food, tools, dishes, glass, a large choice of drugs and medicines, boots and shoes, iron and steel, and window glass. It ran in the Chicago Democrat on December 3, 1833. The same ad was printed again all through 1834, and ran to July 8, 1835. So we no longer just guess that it was open on July 1, 1835. Printings on both sides of that date show it. Here is what the papers do not settle, and it is the more interesting half. The ads always say P. Pruyne and Company, never Pruyne and Kimball. No printing names Kimball as the partner. So the partners still come from the history book, and this card keeps its name. The address the firm gives is a block, not a street front. Between Clark and Dearborn names the two cross streets, but not the street the store faced. Clark and Dearborn are one block apart on South Water, Lake, Water and Randolph alike. We put it on South Water Street because the history book does. The ad fits with that, but does not prove it. Taking South Water from this line would be making it up, and our tools will not do it. The two Kimballs stay apart, as above. We read this from a typed copy made with the help of a machine, not from the page itself, and we say so. The owner of this project ruled that such a reading still counts as found in the paper, with a flag on it. The copy's own doubtful letters are kept as they are. If someone reads the page itself later, the page wins.

entries.card: why:The source says 'frame' and no more. Both systems were avail…
entries.text: The source says 'frame' and no more. Both systems were available at Chicago in the summer of 1833 and the alternative is live enough to state: the building went up 'in a few weeks', and speed of erection is precisely what balloon framing was for - Augustine D. Taylor was raising St Mary's frame in the same weeks, a few blocks east. Braced frame is adopted as the conservative reading for a building whose framer is unnamed, the same argument P. F. W. Peck's Store and the Presbyterian church record make. In this archetype the choice is not cosmetic: a braced frame shows a girt line at the upper floor, which on a two-storey building is the single most legible exterior difference between the two systems.

levels.8-10: The source says frame and no more. Two ways to build a frame were in use at Chicago in the summer of 1833, and the other one is a real chance. The building went up in a few weeks. Speed is just what the balloon frame was for. Augustine D. Taylor was raising St. Mary's frame in those same weeks, a few blocks east. We use the older, heavier braced frame as the safe reading, since no one names who built it. Peck's store and the Presbyterian church use the same reasoning. This choice shows. A braced frame has a beam across the wall at the upper floor. On a two storey building, that is the clearest outside difference between the two ways.

entries.card: why:The sources say 'plain frame' and no more, and the word does…
entries.text: The sources say 'plain frame' and no more, and the word does not distinguish the two systems available in Chicago in 1833. Balloon framing was being introduced here in exactly these months - Augustine D. Taylor raised St Mary's frame in August 1833 - so a balloon frame is entirely possible and this record does not exclude it. Braced frame is adopted as the conservative reading for the earlier of two live options, the same argument P. F. W. Peck's Store and Sauganash Hotel make. The choice is not cosmetic in this archetype: a braced frame gets a heavier corner post, a girt line at the upper floor (absent here, at one storey) and studs at 24 in rather than 16 in, which sets the rhythm the openings are laid out on.

levels.8-10: The sources say plain frame and no more. That word does not tell us which of the two ways to build a frame was used in Chicago in 1833. The balloon frame was coming in here in just those months. Augustine D. Taylor raised St. Mary's frame in August 1833. So a balloon frame could well be, and we do not rule it out. We use the older, heavier braced frame as the safe reading. Peck's store and the Sauganash Hotel use the same reasoning. This choice shows in our model. A braced frame has a heavier corner post, and a beam across the wall at the upper floor, which this one storey building does not have. Its upright boards stand two feet apart, not sixteen inches. That sets where the windows go.

entries.card: why:Two independent statements twenty-eight years apart. Hubbard…
entries.text: Two independent statements twenty-eight years apart. Hubbard, 1827: 'the brick building, just within the north stockade'. The 1855 key: '(brick, about 25x50 ft.)'. THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS BUILDING: the research notes on structures south section 11 says there was 'no brick building of consequence yet on the south side' in 1835 and excepts the fort - correctly, and this is the building it means.

levels.8-10: Two statements, made twenty-eight years apart, each on its own. Hubbard, in 1827, tells of the brick building just inside the north fence. The 1855 key says brick, about 25 by 50 feet. This matters past this building. Our notes say there was no brick building that counted on the south side in 1835, except at the fort. That is right, and this is the building it means.

entries.card: why:Two independent statements. Kinzie: 'Large gates opened to t…
entries.text: Two independent statements. Kinzie: 'Large gates opened to the north and south.' Andreas: 'It had two gates, one on the north and the other on the south side.' The 1830 plan draws a break in each of those two walls and in neither of the others, and Hubbard's 1827 account places buildings by reference to both - 'the store-house and guard-house were on either side of the southern gate; the sutler's store was east of the north gate'. Three sources, one arrangement. two smaller side posterns are now a bounded reconstruction of Kinzie’s distinct additional clause, not two more large gates. Her actual paragraph reads: Large gates opened to the north and south, and there were small posterns here and there for the accommodation of the inmates. The two main gates retain their attested sides and existing3.6m width; the additional east/west sides and count of two are reconstructed, with separate gate overrides.

levels.8-10: Two statements, each on its own. Kinzie says large gates opened to the north and south. A history book says it had two gates, one on the north and one on the south side. The 1830 plan draws a gap in each of those two walls and in neither of the others. Hubbard's 1827 account places buildings by both gates. He says the store house and guard house were on each side of the south gate, and the trader's store was east of the north gate. Three sources, one plan. Two small side doors are now our guess from a separate line of Kinzie's, not two more big gates. Her words are: big gates opened to the north and south, and there were small doors here and there for the people inside. The two main gates keep their known sides and their width of about twelve feet. The east and west sides of the small doors, and the count of two, are our guesses.

entries.card: why:Two levels because Hubbard puts the piazza 'on a line with t…

Graded reconstructed, not inferred, because the identification of Hubbard's building with this range is unresolved (see gallery and stories). The upper floor sits at the existing 2.4 m storey line of the unchanged 4.8 m wall; the helper's other dimensions are reconstructed.

levels.8-10: There are two levels because Hubbard puts the porch in line with the floor of the second storey. So the walk is the upper one, and the ground under it is open. We call it a guess, not worked out, because we have not settled if Hubbard's building is this one. The upper floor sits at the same height as before, about eight feet up a wall of about sixteen feet. The porch's other sizes are our guesses.

entries.card: why:Two sash left of a rightmost front-gable entrance agree in t…
entries.text: Two sash left of a rightmost front-gable entrance agree in the actually viewed Andreas 1884 p634/n1301 plate, Trowbridge/Gale 1902 plate facing p35/n55, and Kurz & Allison 1893 panel11. This is retrospective form agreement, not independent contemporaneous proof of 1 July 1835; Kurz may derive from Andreas and Trowbridge may rely on later material. The ascending LOCAL-u fractions are door.20, sash.50, sash.78: exterior +y viewers see higher u toward screen left, so this yields two screen-left sash and a screen-right entrance. Exact centre fractions.20/.50/.78 across the existing 7.62 m wall, equal existing.85x1.35 m sash and 1.20x2.10 m door stock, sill bands, sections and hidden joinery are RECONSTRUCTED, not measured or attested by those pictures. Only the +y front ground floor opts in. The current two upper sash versus Trowbridge's three, attic light, text-attested south-side door, disputed additions, roof, geographic placement and all existing source/camera uncertainties stay unresolved. The held-rights/unverified 1859 source is excluded as a geometry witness. Original other work remains open/differs; this is not a solved camera or picture match. The same pure resolved front ground stations dataclass property (whose actual values are covered by the existing native mesh recipe) is consumed by the mesh and the native entrance/apron/clearance reader after resolving exactly the sidecar-selected source phase; no renderer facade API or bearing is changed. AMENDMENT 2026-11-10: the earlier statement calling two upper sash versus Trowbridge three unresolved is superseded by form.front upper layout. The omission is being physically corrected as three upper stations, not closed by a camera/tolerance label; genuine follow-up native and three source rerenders remain required.

levels.8-10: Three pictures agree on two windows to the left of a door at the right of the front end wall. We looked at each one: a print in an 1884 history book, a 1902 drawing, and an 1893 panel. They were all made long after, so this is not proof from July 1, 1835. One may copy another, and one may use later things. We set the door and the two windows in the spots that give two windows on the left and the door on the right, as you look at the front. The exact spots, the window and door sizes, the sills and the hidden joints are our guesses, not measured from the pictures. Only the ground floor of the front changes. Other questions stay open. Should there be two upper windows or the three in one drawing? What about the attic window, a door on the south side that a book tells of, and later additions? Those stay as they were. An 1859 picture we cannot check is not used for any shape. This is not a solved picture match.

entries.card: why:Two sources put Couch here across the scene date and neither…
entries.text: Two sources put Couch here across the scene date and neither leaves a gap. "Tremont House." Chicagology. Compiling city-directory entries 1846-1870, an…'s 1874 letter: 'In 1833 there was built... the Tremont House, and the following year Ira Couch became its proprietor' - i.e. 1834. Andreas: 'Ira Couch opened it as a hotel. He ran it until 1836, when his brother James took control.' So 1835-07-01 falls squarely inside Ira Couch's tenure. TWO CLAIMS IN CIRCULATION ARE NOT ADOPTED BECAUSE NOTHING THIS PROJECT HOLDS SUPPORTS THEM: the research notes on structures south line 155 names Starr Foot as first proprietor and has the house 'sold to Mallory & Able 1835'. Neither name attaches to this building anywhere in Andreas vol. 1 - Starr Foot appears once, in an unrelated list, and no Mallory but a Hiram Mallory in another context - and neither is on the chicagology page. They are left out rather than repeated.

levels.8-10: Two sources put Couch here across our scene date, and neither leaves a gap. An 1874 letter says the Tremont House was built in 1833, and the next year Ira Couch became its owner. That is 1834. A history book says Ira Couch opened it as a hotel and ran it until 1836, when his brother James took over. So July 1, 1835 falls well inside Ira Couch's time. Two other claims go around, and we do not use them, because nothing we have backs them. Our notes name Starr Foot as the first owner, and say the house was sold to Mallory and Able in 1835. Neither name ties to this building anywhere in the history book. So we leave them out and do not repeat them.
