entries.card: why:Unattested. Roughly a ten-inch face, which is what a split o…
entries.text: Unattested. Roughly a ten-inch face, which is what a split oak or cedar picket of that height needs to stand without racking. IT MOVES WITH picket spacing (m) OR NOT AT ALL, because what a wall reads as is the ratio between the two and neither means anything alone - other work asked whether the pair should be coarsened to the proportion p4 0 draws, and the reasoning that kept them is written out on picket spacing (m) rather than twice. In short: at the plate's own scale this face is 2.78 px wide and the gap beside it 0.70 px, under the 2 px the plate's finest stroke work can hold, so the plate could not have drawn this wall whatever the fort was made of. the liberties register “Fort Dearborn's stockade: the plan is evidence and the wall is not”.

levels.8-10: No source gives this. It is about a ten inch face, which a split oak or cedar post of that height needs to stand without leaning. It moves with the space between the posts, or not at all. What a wall looks like comes from the two together, and neither means anything alone. Later work asked if both should be made coarser, to match an old picture. The reason we kept them is written once, on the spacing. In short, the picture is too small to show posts this size. It could not have drawn this wall, whatever the fort was made of. We list it as a guess: the plan is proof, and the wall is not.

entries.card: why:Unattested. Set so the posts stand shoulder to shoulder with…
entries.text: Unattested. Set so the posts stand shoulder to shoulder with the narrow gap a hand-set picket line actually leaves, rather than touching perfectly, which reads as a fence panel. THE ONLY PICTURE ANYONE HAS OF THIS FORT DISAGREES, AND other work IS WHY IT DOES NOT MOVE THIS NUMBER. p4 0 resolves separate posts at a 10 px rhythm on a curtain 42.9 px tall - 0.23 of the wall's height per post, which on a 3.7 m wall is an 0.86 m post nobody ever split, and nearly three times coarser than the 0.081 this record builds. That disagreement was measured rather than argued about (the picket plate check). At the plate's own scale of 11.6 px per metre, THIS wall's rhythm would be 2.78 px of post and 0.70 px of GAP - and the narrowest gap that plate holds anywhere on the same curtain is 2 px, 2.9 times wider. The draughtsman drew the finest picket line his medium could carry. His pitch is a reading of the lithograph and not of the fort, so it is not evidence about 1816 and cannot be adopted. THE OTHER HALF IS ABOUT THE MODEL AND IS WHY THE FINE RHYTHM IS KEPT: the picket reading check finds the wall resolving as separate posts at every stand a visitor can reach - a 34 px rhythm at the north gate on a desktop, 16 px on a phone, and 4 px against an expected 4.49 px from p4 0's own stand across the river. It falls under the pixel grid at exactly one place, a phone at that river stand, where a 1.62 px pitch beats into a 4 px moire; that is the same bind the draughtsman was in and other work owns it. A drawing has one viewing distance and a walkable reconstruction has all of them, so the two cannot be held to one rhythm. This number answers to the near one, which is the only one a visitor can choose. the liberties register “Fort Dearborn's stockade: the plan is evidence and the wall is not”.

levels.8-10: No source gives this. We set the posts to stand side by side, with the thin gap a fence set by hand really leaves. If they touched just right, it would look like a fence panel. The only picture anyone has of this fort does not agree. Later work is why that does not change this number. The picture shows posts so wide that each would be almost three feet across. No one ever split a post that big. That is nearly three times wider than we build. We measured this, and did not just argue about it. At the picture's own size, our posts would be less than three dots wide, with a gap of less than one dot. The thinnest gap the picture shows anywhere on that wall is two dots. So the artist drew the finest fence line he could. His spacing is a reading of the print, not of the fort, so it is not proof about 1816 and we cannot use it. The other half is about our model, and it is why we keep the fine spacing. Our check finds the wall shows as separate posts from every place a visitor can stand. There is one spot where the posts blur together: on a phone, from across the river. The artist had that same problem.

entries.card: why:Verbatim from the page, read from the scan on 2026-08-11: '[…
entries.text: Verbatim from the page, read from the scan on 2026-08-11: '[Saddle & H]arness Making. GOSS & COBB, respectfully inform the inhabitants of Chicago and the neighboring settlements, that they have opened a shop in this village, on the conner of Lake and Canal-streets, where they have on hand and will manufacture to order, Ladies' and Gentlemens SADDLES, Brass, Silver and Common Mounted HARNESS, Bridles; Martingales, &c. &c. Hard leather and common TRUNKS. Coaches, Chaises and Waggons Trimmed in [best] style. Repairing immediately attended to when brought to their shop. N.B. By strict attention to business, they hope for a share of patronage.' Andreas's summary of the same advertising columns carries 'Goss & Cobb, saddle and harness making' and adds nothing. THE ENGRAVING OF A SADDLE ABOVE THE ADVERTISEMENT IS A PRINTER'S STOCK CUT and no fact about this shop or its goods may be read out of it - the same rule The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1. Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, Tuesday… sets for the building cut over 'Two Buildings to Let'. THE AMERICAN WIDENS THE TRADE BY ONE WORD AND CORRECTS ITSELF DOING IT. Its three 1835 printings of Cobb's card head the same shop 'SADDLE, HARNESS & TRUNK MANUFACTORY' — trunks were already in the 1833 list of goods ('Hard leather and common TRUNKS') and are now in the heading. The first of the three, 1835-06-08 p3 c5, sets that heading as 'LB, HA & TRUNK M' and was read in this corpus as a HAT manufactory before 1835-06-13 p3 c6 set it legibly over the same name; the misreading is left standing in that issue's extraction file rather than quietly swapped. The function VALUE does not move — a saddlery and harness shop that also made trunks in 1833 is the same trade in 1835 — and the grade does not move either; what the American adds is a second, independent witness three weeks either side of the scene date.

levels.8-10: This comes from the page, read from the scan on August 11, 2026. In the ad, Goss and Cobb tell the people of Chicago and the farms near by that they have a new shop. It is at the corner of Lake and Canal Streets. They have saddles for ladies and men, and will make them to order. They make harness with brass, silver or plain fittings, and bridles and straps. They have hard leather and plain trunks. They trim coaches and wagons in the best style. They fix things right away. By hard work they hope you will buy from them. A history book's summary of the same ads lists Goss and Cobb, saddle and harness making, and adds nothing. The picture of a saddle above the ad is one the printer used for any saddle maker. We may not read any fact about this shop from it. The Chicago American adds one word to the trade, and fixes its own mistake doing it. Its three 1835 printings of Cobb's notice head the same shop saddle, harness and trunk works. Trunks were already in the 1833 list of goods, and now they are in the heading. The first of the three, on June 8, prints the heading so badly that we read it as a hat works. The June 13 printing set it clearly.

entries.card: why:WAS printing office and store UNTIL other work, AND THE HALF…
entries.text: WAS printing office and store UNTIL other work, AND THE HALF THAT WENT IS THE PRINTING OFFICE. A `function` in this dataset is a SCENE-DATE attribute — it says what the building was for on 1835-07-01 — and every layer that furnishes the town off it reads it in the present tense: the business signboards generator deals a board from it, the yard goods generator stands the trade's goods in the yard from it, the frontage works generator reads it at the street edge, and the register prints it on the card. Other work established that the press was gone before the scene date: the Democrat's colophon gives this corner on 1833-11-26, 1834-01-07, 1834-08-27, 1834-09-17 and 1834-12-03, and then prints the office 'over Messrs. Jones & King['s] Hard[ware store]' in South Water street on 1835-05-20 (the Chicago Democrat of 1835-05-20 c007) and again on 1835-08-05 (c026). A function that still read printing office and store on 1835-07-01 was asserting a trade the paper itself had printed its way out of, and every layer above inherited the assertion. WHAT IS LEFT IS THE STORE HALF, AND IT IS LEFT RATHER THAN ADDED. The store is the same reading the occupants block has always argued — 'Just Opened and for sale AT the New Store on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets' in the paper's own first issue, and 'the store now occupied by W. Kimball' in the 1834-10-08 notice — and nothing reached says the store went. The earlier note's argument for the store half is unchanged and stands: Andreas says Calhoun secured an office IN a building, not that he took a building, so the building held a counter as well as a press, and it is the press that the corpus follows out of the door. NOTHING IS UPGRADED BY THE NARROWING. The confidence stays `inferred`, on the same evidence and the same reasoning it rested on before; a value that covers less of the building than it did is not a better-evidenced value. Nor is a KEEPER named by it: who kept this counter on 1835-07-01 is still open, with one candidate in it on a notice that OFFERS his store rather than reporting it kept — see occupants, and see the board this record does not carry. AND THE BUILDING IS NOT RENAMED. `name` and `aka` keep the Democrat, because a name is this project's label for a structure and not an assertion about who was inside it on a day. The rule, and the reason a name may outlive a tenancy where a signboard may not, is written once in the project's provenance guide § A label may outlive a tenancy; a sign may not.

levels.8-10: This used to be a printing office and store, until later work. The half that went is the printing office. In our town, a building's use says what it was for on July 1, 1835. Every part that fills the town reads it as true on that day. The sign boards, the goods in the yard, the street front and the card all come from it. Later work showed the press was gone before our scene. The paper's own address gives this corner from November 1833 to December 1834. Then, in May 1835, it puts the office over Jones and King's hardware store on South Water Street. It says so again in August 1835. A use that still said printing office on July 1, 1835 claimed a trade the paper itself had printed its way out of. Every part above took on that error. What is left is the store half. We keep it, and do not add it. The store comes from the same reading as before. The paper's own first issue tells of a new store just opened at the corner of South Water and Clark. An October 1834 notice names the store W. Kimball was in. Nothing we found says the store went.

entries.card: why:WHAT IS DATED IS A SCHOOL, NOT A BUILDING, AND THE DIFFERENC…
entries.text: WHAT IS DATED IS A SCHOOL, NOT A BUILDING, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE POINT OF THIS RECORD. Andreas has Eliza Chappel's infant school in 1833-34 in 'a log house just outside the military reservation... divided into school-room and lodging quarters' (the research notes on structures south section 9, from Andreas I scan p. 431). During 1834 the school MOVED INTO THE FIRST PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH at Lake and Clark. Nothing reached says what became of the log house. 1833-01-01 is the first day of the year the school is attested in it and is a bound; the house itself is older than the school by an unknown amount. 1835-12-31 IS AN INFERENCE ABOUT PERSISTENCE, NOT AN ATTESTATION: a sound log house eighteen months old is not pulled down when its tenant leaves, and the town in 1835 was short of buildings and growing, so the structure very probably still stood. That is the reasoning, and it is the whole of it. IF THE HOUSE WAS DEMOLISHED, MOVED OR BURNT BETWEEN 1834 AND THE SCENE DATE, THIS RECORD IS WRONG AND NOTHING IN THE SOURCES WOULD SHOW IT.

levels.8-10: What is dated is a school, not a building, and that difference is the point of this card. A history book says Eliza Chappel's school for small children was in a log house just outside the fort's land, in 1833 and 1834. It was split into a school room and a place to live. During 1834 the school moved into the First Presbyterian Church at Lake and Clark. Nothing we found says what became of the log house. We start it on January 1, 1833, the first day of the year the school is known there. The house itself is older than the school, by we do not know how much. The end of 1835 is a guess that it lasted, not proof. A sound log house a year and a half old is not torn down when its renter leaves. The town in 1835 was short of buildings and growing. So the house most likely still stood. That is the reasoning, and that is all of it. If the house was torn down, moved or burnt between 1834 and our scene, this card is wrong, and nothing in the sources would show it.

entries.card: why:WHAT IS DATED IS A TEACHER'S MOVE AND — SINCE other work — A…
entries.text: WHAT IS DATED IS A TEACHER'S MOVE AND — SINCE other work — AN OWNER'S NINETEEN YEARS. Andreas has John Watkins employed by Cols. Hamilton and Owen in the spring of 1833 to teach near the old Indian agency-house, and 'later in a house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush' (the research notes on structures south section 9 and the research notes on structures north, from Andreas I scan p. 305). The house therefore stood in 1833; how much earlier it was built is unattested, and 1833-01-01 is the first day of the attested year and is a bound. THE END OF THE RANGE WAS THIS RECORD'S WEAKEST FIELD AND IT NO LONGER STANDS ALONE. It used to read as an inference about persistence with nothing behind it — a house two years old in a town whose population was doubling was not pulled down — and the note said plainly that if the building had gone by the scene date nothing in the sources would show it. Moses and Kirkland, vol. 2 p. 155, give a SPAN and not a date: Hamilton built his house on this street between these two cross streets and 'lived for nineteen years' in it. Nineteen years from about 1833 runs to about 1852, and 1835-07-01 falls inside it. THAT IS CORROBORATION AND NOT A PROMOTION.
